citations.cite: the federal personal-representative standard, tied to state health-care-decision authority
citations.quote: As specified in this paragraph, a covered entity must, except as provided in paragraphs (g)(3) and (g)(5) of this section, treat a personal representative as the individual for purposes of this subchapter. (2) If under applicable law a person has authority to act on behalf of an individual who is an adult or an emancipated minor in making decisions related to health care, a covered entity must treat such person as a personal representative under this subchapter, with respect to protected health information relevant to such personal representation.

clauses.title: How This Directive Can Be Revoked
clauses.body: While having capacity, {{patientName}} may revoke the designation of {{agentName}} as agent only by a signed writing or by personally informing the supervising health care provider — not by any other method. Any other part of this directive can be revoked at any time and in any manner that communicates an intent to revoke, without needing a signed writing.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual, non-uniform revocation mechanics — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 4695) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4695(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the stricter method for revoking an agent designation
citations.quote: A patient having capacity may revoke the designation of an agent only by a signed writing or by personally informing the supervising health care provider.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4695(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the looser method for revoking everything else
citations.quote: A patient having capacity may revoke all or part of an advance health care directive, other than the designation of an agent, at any time and in any manner that communicates an intent to revoke.

clauses.title: What a Later Divorce Does to an Agent Designation
clauses.body: If {{agentName}} is {{patientName}}'s spouse and, after this directive is executed, {{patientName}}'s marriage to {{agentName}} is dissolved or annulled, the designation of {{agentName}} as agent is automatically revoked by that dissolution or annulment alone. If {{patientName}} later remarries {{agentName}}, the revoked designation is automatically revived.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a real, automatic default specific to this state's Health Care Decisions Law — not an assumption that it mirrors this state's separate rule for wills, and not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 4697) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4697(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: automatic revocation of a spouse-agent designation on divorce
citations.quote: If after executing a power of attorney for health care the principal’s marriage to the agent is dissolved or annulled, the principal’s designation of the former spouse as an agent to make health care decisions for the principal is revoked.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4697(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: automatic revival on remarriage
citations.quote: If the agent’s authority is revoked solely by subdivision (a), it is revived by the principal’s remarriage to the agent.

clauses.title: A Health Care Provider's Duty to Comply or Transfer
clauses.body: Except for two statutory exceptions described below, a health care provider or health care institution treating {{patientName}} must comply with {{patientName}}'s individual health care instructions and with any health care decision made by {{agentName}} or another person then authorized to decide for {{patientName}}, to the same extent as if {{patientName}} had made the decision personally. A health care provider may decline for reasons of conscience, or because the instruction or decision requires medically ineffective health care or health care contrary to generally accepted health care standards; a health care institution may decline based on a conscience-based policy that was timely communicated to {{patientName}} or {{agentName}}. In any of these cases, the provider or institution must promptly say so, make all reasonable efforts to transfer {{patientName}} to a provider or institution willing to comply, and continue care — including pain relief and other palliative care — until the transfer happens or appears impossible.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual compliance duty and its real exceptions — reasons of conscience, and a separate exception for care that's medically ineffective or contrary to generally accepted health care standards — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4733 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the compliance duty
citations.quote: Except as provided in Sections 4734 and 4735, a health care provider or health care institution providing care to a patient shall do the following: (a) Comply with an individual health care instruction of the patient and with a reasonable interpretation of that instruction made by a person then authorized to make health care decisions for the patient. (b) Comply with a health care decision for the patient made by a person then authorized to make health care decisions for the patient to the same extent as if the decision had been made by the patient while having capacity.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4736 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the notify-and-transfer duty when a provider declines
citations.quote: A health care provider or health care institution that declines to comply with an individual health care instruction or health care decision shall do all of the following: (a) Promptly so inform the patient, if possible, and any person then authorized to make health care decisions for the patient. (b) Unless the patient or person then authorized to make health care decisions for the patient refuses assistance, immediately make all reasonable efforts to assist in the transfer of the patient to another health care provider or institution that is willing to comply with the instruction or decision. (c) Provide continuing care to the patient until a transfer can be accomplished or until it appears that a transfer cannot be accomplished. In all cases, appropriate pain relief and other palliative care shall be continued.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4734 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the reasons-of-conscience exception
citations.quote: (a) A health care provider may decline to comply with an individual health care instruction or health care decision for reasons of conscience. (b) A health care institution may decline to comply with an individual health care instruction or health care decision if the instruction or decision is contrary to a policy of the institution that is expressly based on reasons of conscience and if the policy was timely communicated to the patient or to a person then authorized to make health care decisions for the patient.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4735 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the medically-ineffective/contrary-to-standards exception
citations.quote: A health care provider or health care institution may decline to comply with an individual health care instruction or health care decision that requires medically ineffective health care or health care contrary to generally accepted health care standards applicable to the health care provider or institution.

clauses.title: Good-Faith Immunity for Providers and Agents
clauses.body: A health care provider or health care institution that acts in good faith, consistent with generally accepted health care standards, is not subject to civil or criminal liability or professional discipline for complying with a health care decision it believes in good faith was made by someone with authority to make it. {{agentName}}, acting as agent, is likewise not subject to civil or criminal liability or professional discipline for health care decisions made in good faith.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual immunity and its real limit — the protection runs only to good-faith conduct, and the same statute separately imposes civil damages, and in some circumstances criminal homicide liability, on a provider, agent, or anyone else who acts in bad faith, such as by intentionally falsifying, concealing, or fraudulently inducing a directive — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4740 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: provider/institution good-faith immunity
citations.quote: A health care provider or health care institution acting in good faith and in accordance with generally accepted health care standards applicable to the health care provider or institution is not subject to civil or criminal liability or to discipline for unprofessional conduct for any actions in compliance with this division, including, but not limited to, any of the following conduct: (a) Complying with a health care decision of a person that the health care provider or health care institution believes in good faith has the authority to make a health care decision for a patient, including a decision to withhold or withdraw health care.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4741 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: agent/surrogate good-faith immunity
citations.quote: A person acting as agent or surrogate under this part is not subject to civil or criminal liability or to discipline for unprofessional conduct for health care decisions made in good faith.

clauses.title: California's Optional Statutory Form
clauses.body: California Probate Code provides an optional statutory form for an advance health care directive. Using that state-provided form is not required — any writing that satisfies the execution requirements described above is legally sufficient, and an individual may complete or modify all or any part of the statutory form.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a state-provided model form actually exists and is optional — not a recommendation about which format to use, and not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 4700); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4700 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the optional statutory form
citations.quote: The form provided in Section 4701 may, but need not, be used to create an advance health care directive. The other sections of this division govern the effect of the form or any other writing used to create an advance health care directive. An individual may complete or modify all or any part of the form in Section 4701.

clauses.title: Declaration and Appointment of Agent
clauses.body: I, {{patientName}}, being an adult of sound mind, make this Advance Health Care Directive to make known my wishes regarding my own health care and to designate an agent to make health care decisions for me as described in this document. I revoke any prior advance health care directive or power of attorney for health care I have made. I designate {{agentName}} as my agent to make health care decisions for me. If {{agentName}} is unable, unwilling, or not reasonably available to act, I designate {{alternateAgentName}} as my alternate agent.

clauses.title: Specific Wishes for End-of-Life Care
clauses.body: Regarding treatment intended to prolong my life: ☐ {{lifeProlongingWishes}}. Regarding relief from pain or discomfort: ☐ {{painReliefWishes}}. Additional instructions regarding my physical or mental health care: ☐ {{additionalHealthCareWishes}}.

clauses.title: Signatures
clauses.body:
Signature of {{patientName}}: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________

This directive is signed either before a notary public or in the presence of two qualified witnesses, whose acknowledgment or signatures and declarations appear on an attached page.

clauses.title: How a Trust Is Created
clauses.body: California law recognizes several distinct methods of creating a trust: a declaration by the owner of property that the owner holds the property as trustee; a transfer of property by the owner, during the owner's lifetime, to another person as trustee; a transfer of property by will or other instrument taking effect at the owner's death; the exercise of a power of appointment in favor of a trustee; or an enforceable promise to create a trust. This trust is created by {{settlorName}}'s lifetime transfer of property to {{trusteeName}} as trustee.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual methods California recognizes for creating a trust — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. A declaration or transfer that satisfies one of these methods still has to satisfy the separate requirements for a valid trust — settlor intent, a legal purpose, and (except for a charitable trust) an ascertainable beneficiary — addressed elsewhere in this document. This is a single statutory section (§ 15200); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15200 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the statutory methods of creating a trust
citations.quote: Subject to other provisions of this chapter, a trust may be created by any of the following methods: (a) A declaration by the owner of property that the owner holds the property as trustee. (b) A transfer of property by the owner during the owner's lifetime to another person as trustee. (c) A transfer of property by the owner, by will or by other instrument taking effect upon the death of the owner, to another person as trustee. (d) An exercise of a power of appointment to another person as trustee. (e) An enforceable promise to create a trust.

clauses.title: Requirements for a Valid Trust
clauses.body: Beyond using one of the statutory methods of creation, a trust is valid only if {{settlorName}} properly manifests an intention to create a trust, the trust is created for a purpose that is not illegal or against public policy, and — unless the trust is a valid charitable trust — there is a beneficiary who is ascertainable with reasonable certainty, or sufficiently described that it can be determined whether a given person meets the description, or whose selection is left to the trustee's or another person's discretion under a stated standard.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual requirements for a valid trust — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. These three requirements — intent, lawful purpose, and an ascertainable beneficiary — are independent of the funding requirements addressed elsewhere in this document; a trust can satisfy all three and still fail to hold property that was never actually transferred into it.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15201 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the settlor's-intent requirement
citations.quote: A trust is created only if the settlor properly manifests an intention to create a trust.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15203 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the lawful-purpose requirement
citations.quote: A trust may be created for any purpose that is not illegal or against public policy.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15205 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the ascertainable-beneficiary requirement and charitable-trust exception
citations.quote: (a) A trust, other than a charitable trust, is created only if there is a beneficiary. (b) The requirement of subdivision (a) is satisfied if the trust instrument provides for either of the following: (1) A beneficiary or class of beneficiaries that is ascertainable with reasonable certainty or that is sufficiently described so it can be determined that some person meets the description or is within the class. (2) A grant of a power to the trustee or some other person to select the beneficiaries based on a standard or in the discretion of the trustee or other person.

clauses.title: Personal Property vs. Real Property — Different Formality Requirements
clauses.body: A trust of personal property carries no special formality requirement beyond what the law otherwise requires for the underlying transaction — an oral trust of personal property is legally possible, though its existence and terms can be established only by clear and convincing evidence, and the settlor's oral declaration alone is not enough. A trust relating to real property is held to a stricter standard: it isn't valid unless evidenced by a written instrument signed by the trustee (or the trustee's authorized agent), a written instrument conveying the property signed by the settlor (or the settlor's authorized agent), or by operation of law.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a real, easy-to-miss distinction — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This distinction matters beyond formality: a trust holds only the property actually transferred into it in a legally effective way, and real property that was never conveyed to the trustee by a qualifying written instrument remains outside the trust regardless of what the trust instrument says about it — meaning it stays subject to probate at the settlor's death rather than passing under the trust.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15206 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the written-instrument requirement for a trust of real property
citations.quote: A trust in relation to real property is not valid unless evidenced by one of the following methods: (a) By a written instrument signed by the trustee, or by the trustee's agent if authorized in writing to do so. (b) By a written instrument conveying the trust property signed by the settlor, or by the settlor's agent if authorized in writing to do so. (c) By operation of law.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15207(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: an oral trust of personal property is legally possible
citations.quote: (a) The existence and terms of an oral trust of personal property may be established only by clear and convincing evidence. (b) The oral declaration of the settlor, standing alone, is not sufficient evidence of the creation of a trust of personal property.

clauses.title: Revocability — the Default Rule and How to Revoke
clauses.body: Unless {{trustName}} is expressly made irrevocable by its own terms, it is revocable by {{settlorName}} — revocability, not irrevocability, is the default under California law for a trust the settlor creates while domiciled in California, executed in California, or that states California law governs. {{settlorName}} can revoke the trust, in whole or in part, by following any revocation method the trust instrument itself provides, or — if the trust instrument doesn't make its own method the exclusive one — by a signed writing, other than a will, delivered to {{trusteeName}} during {{settlorName}}'s lifetime.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual default rule and revocation methods — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. Where more than one person contributed property to the same trust, or where someone other than the settlor holds a power of revocation, additional statutory provisions address revocation of just that person's contributed share; those situations aren't addressed here.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15400 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: revocability is the statutory default
citations.quote: Unless a trust is expressly made irrevocable by the trust instrument, the trust is revocable by the settlor. This section applies only where the settlor is domiciled in this state when the trust is created, where the trust instrument is executed in this state, or where the trust instrument provides that the law of this state governs the trust.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15401(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the statutory methods of revocation
citations.quote: (a) A trust that is revocable by the settlor or any other person may be revoked in whole or in part by any of the following methods: (1) By compliance with any method of revocation provided in the trust instrument. (2) By a writing, other than a will, signed by the settlor or any other person holding the power of revocation and delivered to the trustee during the lifetime of the settlor or the person holding the power of revocation. If the trust instrument explicitly makes the method of revocation provided in the trust instrument the exclusive method of revocation, the trust may not be revoked pursuant to this paragraph.

clauses.title: Trustee's Duty of Loyalty and Duty to Keep Trust Property Separate
clauses.body: {{trusteeName}}, acting as trustee, has a duty to administer the trust solely in the interest of the beneficiaries, and a separate duty to keep trust property separate from {{trusteeName}}'s own property and to see that trust property is identified as property of the trust.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of two genuine, specific fiduciary duties among several a trustee owes — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust, and not a complete list of a trustee's duties. A trustee who also administers a second trust may sell or exchange property between the two trusts without violating the duty of loyalty if the exchange is fair to both trusts' beneficiaries and both sets of beneficiaries are notified of the material facts — a narrow statutory exception to the general rule stated above.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16002(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the trustee's duty of loyalty
citations.quote: (a) The trustee has a duty to administer the trust solely in the interest of the beneficiaries.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16009 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the trustee's duty to keep trust property separate
citations.quote: The trustee has a duty to do the following: (a) To keep the trust property separate from other property not subject to the trust. (b) To see that the trust property is designated as property of the trust.

clauses.title: Whose Interests the Trustee Serves While the Trust Is Revocable
clauses.body: For as long as the trust remains revocable and {{settlorName}} (or whoever else holds the power to revoke) is competent, the rights the law otherwise gives to trust beneficiaries belong instead to the person holding the power to revoke, and the trustee's duties run to that person — not to the beneficiaries named in the trust. Where a beneficiary's consent would otherwise be required or permitted for some action, it's the person holding the power to revoke, not the beneficiary, who has the power to give or withhold that consent, during that same period.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuinely counter-intuitive default — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. If, while the trust is still revocable, no one holding the power to revoke remains competent, the statute shifts the trustee's accounting and disclosure duties to the beneficiaries who would receive income or principal if the settlor had died at that point — the rule addressed in this clause is specifically about the period when someone with the power to revoke is still competent.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15800(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: trustee's duties run to the person holding the power to revoke
citations.quote: (a) Except to the extent that the trust instrument otherwise provides or where the joint action of the settlor and all beneficiaries is required, during the time that a trust is revocable and at least one person holding the power to revoke the trust, in whole or in part, is competent, the following shall apply: (1) The person holding the power to revoke, and not the beneficiary, has the rights afforded beneficiaries under this division. (2) The duties of the trustee are owed to the person holding the power to revoke.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15801(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: consent rights belong to the person holding the power to revoke
citations.quote: (a) In any case where the consent of a beneficiary may be given or is required to be given before an action may be taken, during the time that a trust is revocable and the person holding the power to revoke the trust is competent, the person holding the power to revoke, and not the beneficiary, has the power to consent or withhold consent.

clauses.title: Filling a Vacancy in the Office of Trustee
clauses.body: If {{trustName}} has no trustee — including because {{trusteeName}} has died or become incapacitated — the vacancy is filled first by whatever practical method or named successor the trust instrument itself provides. Only if the trust instrument doesn't fill the vacancy that way does the law step in: a trust company that agrees to accept the trust may fill the vacancy with the agreement of all adult beneficiaries currently entitled to income or principal, or a court may appoint a trustee on petition of an interested person or a person named as trustee in the trust instrument.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the statutory fallback for filling a vacant trusteeship — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This is the mechanism a revocable living trust relies on to keep the trust administered without a court-supervised conservatorship if the settlor becomes incapacitated or dies — but it works automatically only if the trust instrument's own successor-trustee provision is functional; where it fails or is silent, the statutory fallback above requires either beneficiary agreement or a court petition, neither of which is automatic. This is a single statutory section (§ 15660); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15660(b)-(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: filling a vacancy in the office of trustee
citations.quote: (b) If the trust instrument provides a practical method of appointing a trustee or names the person to fill the vacancy, the vacancy shall be filled as provided in the trust instrument. (c) If the vacancy in the office of trustee is not filled as provided in subdivision (b), the vacancy may be filled by a trust company that has agreed to accept the trust on agreement of all adult beneficiaries who are receiving or are entitled to receive income under the trust or to receive a distribution of principal if the trust were terminated at the time the agreement is made. If a beneficiary has a conservator, the conservator may agree to the successor trustee on behalf of the conservatee without obtaining court approval. Without limiting the power of the beneficiary to agree to the successor trustee, if the beneficiary has designated an attorney in fact who has the power under the power of attorney to agree to the successor trustee, the attorney in fact may agree to the successor trustee. (d) If the vacancy in the office of trustee is not filled as provided in subdivision (b) or (c), on petition of any interested person or any person named as trustee in the trust instrument, the court may, in its discretion, appoint a trustee to fill the vacancy.

clauses.title: Consideration Is Not Required
clauses.body: Unlike a contract, a trust does not require consideration to be valid — {{settlorName}} can create a trust as a gift, with nothing given in exchange. A promise to create a trust in the future is treated differently: that promise is enforceable only if it independently satisfies the requirements for an enforceable contract, consideration included.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a real, easy-to-miss statutory rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This is a single statutory section (§ 15208); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15208 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: consideration is not required to create a trust
citations.quote: Consideration is not required to create a trust, but a promise to create a trust in the future is enforceable only if the requirements for an enforceable contract are satisfied.

clauses.title: Trustee's Duty to Account — and Its Limits While the Trust Is Revocable
clauses.body: {{trusteeName}}, acting as trustee, has a duty to account at least annually, at the trust's termination, and upon any change of trustee, to each beneficiary currently entitled — or authorized in the trustee's discretion — to receive income or principal. That duty doesn't run to beneficiaries generally while the trust is revocable and someone holding the power to revoke remains competent — during that period, as stated elsewhere in this document, the accounting duty runs to the person holding the power to revoke instead.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the accounting duty and how the statute itself reconciles it with the revocable-trust settlor's-interest rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. Additional statutory exceptions to the accounting duty exist beyond the revocable-trust exception addressed here, including a trust instrument's waiver of accounting (subject to its own limits) and a beneficiary's individual written waiver.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16062(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the trustee's duty to account
citations.quote: (a) Except as otherwise provided in this section and in Section 16064, the trustee shall account at least annually, at the termination of the trust, and upon a change of trustee, to each beneficiary to whom income or principal is required or authorized in the trustee's discretion to be currently distributed.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16069(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the accounting duty doesn't run to beneficiaries while the trust is revocable
citations.quote: (a) The trustee is not required to account to the beneficiary, provide the terms of the trust to a beneficiary, or provide requested information to the beneficiary pursuant to Section 16061, in any of the following circumstances: (1) In the case of a beneficiary of a revocable trust, as provided in subdivision (a) of Section 15800, for the period when the trust may be revoked.

clauses.title: Relationship to a Pour-Over Will
clauses.body: California law allows a will to devise property to the trustee of a trust that the testator established, or is establishing, elsewhere — a trust identified in the will, with its terms set out in a written instrument other than the will itself, executed before, at the same time as, or within 60 days after the will. Property devised this way isn't treated as held under a separate trust created by the will; it simply becomes part of the trust it's given to, administered under that trust's own terms, and the devise isn't invalidated merely because the trust is amendable or revocable.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual statutory basis for a pour-over provision — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust or will. This is the mechanism connecting a companion will to a living trust: property the settlor never transferred into the trust during life, but that the will directs to the trust at death, still has to pass through probate to get there — a pour-over provision routes probate property into the trust rather than avoiding probate for that property. If the trust is revoked or terminated before the testator's death, the devise lapses unless the will itself says otherwise. This is a single statutory section (§ 6300); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6300(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a will may devise property to a trustee (the pour-over statute)
citations.quote: (a) A devise, the validity of which is determinable by the law of this state, may be made by a will to the trustee of a trust established or to be established by the testator, by the testator and some other person, or by some other person (including a funded or unfunded life insurance trust, although the settlor has reserved any or all rights of ownership of the insurance contracts) if the trust is identified in the testator's will and its terms are set forth in a written instrument (other than a will) executed before, concurrently with, or within 60 days after the execution of the testator's will or in the valid last will of a person who has predeceased the testator (regardless of the existence, size, or character of the trust property). The devise is not invalid because the trust is amendable or revocable, or both, or because the trust was amended after the execution of the will or after the death of the testator. (b) Unless the testator's will provides otherwise, the property so devised (1) is not deemed to be held under a testamentary trust of the testator but becomes a part of the trust to which it is given and (2) shall be administered and disposed of in accordance with the provisions of the instrument or will setting forth the terms of the trust, including any amendments thereto made before or after the death of the testator (regardless of whether made before or after the execution of the testator's will).

clauses.title: Declaration
clauses.body: I, {{settlorName}}, of {{settlorCounty}} County, California, as settlor, declare that I am creating the {{trustName}}, and that I am transferring the property described in the attached schedule to {{trusteeName}}, as initial trustee, to hold, administer, and distribute according to the terms of this trust. Upon the death, resignation, or incapacity of {{trusteeName}}, {{successorTrusteeName}} shall serve as successor trustee.

clauses.title: Distribution on Death
clauses.body: Upon my death, the trustee then serving shall distribute the trust property remaining after payment of my debts, expenses, and applicable taxes as follows: ☐ _________________________, with the remainder distributed to {{beneficiaryName}}.

clauses.title: Signature and Notarization
clauses.body:
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, {{settlorName}}, as settlor, and {{trusteeName}}, as trustee, have signed this trust instrument on the date written below.

_________________________ Date: _________________________
{{settlorName}}, Settlor

_________________________ Date: _________________________
{{trusteeName}}, Trustee

A notary public or other officer completing a notarial certificate for this instrument verifies only the identity of the individual who signed the document, not the truthfulness, accuracy, or validity of that document.

clauses.title: Authorization Required to Use or Disclose Protected Health Information
clauses.body: Under the HIPAA Privacy Rule, a covered entity (a health care provider, health plan, or health care clearinghouse) may not use or disclose {{patientName}}'s protected health information without a valid authorization, except as otherwise permitted or required by the Privacy Rule. This document is {{patientName}}'s written authorization for {{authorizedRecipientName}} to receive the protected health information described below, consistent with the terms stated here.
clauses.gap: This is a single regulatory subsection (45 C.F.R. § 164.508); no additional independent source was found for this. This is a federal regulation that applies nationwide — unlike the state-law documents elsewhere in this project's Estate Planning category, this authorization's legal basis does not vary by state.

citations.cite: authorization required: general rule
citations.quote: Except as otherwise permitted or required by this subchapter, a covered entity may not use or disclose protected health information without an authorization that is valid under this section. When a covered entity obtains or receives a valid authorization for its use or disclosure of protected health information, such use or disclosure must be consistent with such authorization.

clauses.title: Required Core Elements of a Valid Authorization
clauses.body: A valid authorization under the Privacy Rule must contain: a specific and meaningful description of the information to be used or disclosed; the identity of the person(s) authorized to make the disclosure; the identity of {{authorizedRecipientName}} as the person to whom disclosure may be made; a description of the purpose of the disclosure; an expiration date or expiration event ({{expirationDate}}); and the signature of {{patientName}} and the date signed.
clauses.gap: This is a single regulatory subsection (45 C.F.R. § 164.508); no additional independent source was found for this. This is a federal regulation that applies nationwide — unlike the state-law documents elsewhere in this project's Estate Planning category, this authorization's legal basis does not vary by state.

citations.cite: core elements
citations.quote: A valid authorization under this section must contain at least the following elements: (i) A description of the information to be used or disclosed that identifies the information in a specific and meaningful fashion. (ii) The name or other specific identification of the person(s), or class of persons, authorized to make the requested use or disclosure. (iii) The name or other specific identification of the person(s), or class of persons, to whom the covered entity may make the requested use or disclosure. (iv) A description of each purpose of the requested use or disclosure. The statement "at the request of the individual" is a sufficient description of the purpose when an individual initiates the authorization and does not, or elects not to, provide a statement of the purpose. (v) An expiration date or an expiration event that relates to the individual or the purpose of the use or disclosure. (vi) Signature of the individual and date. If the authorization is signed by a personal representative of the individual, a description of such representative's authority to act for the individual must also be provided.

clauses.title: Required Notice Statements Within an Authorization
clauses.body: In addition to the core elements above, the Privacy Rule requires that an authorization state: that {{patientName}} has the right to revoke this authorization in writing, subject to stated exceptions; whether treatment, payment, enrollment, or eligibility for benefits may be conditioned on signing this authorization; and that information disclosed under this authorization may be subject to redisclosure by {{authorizedRecipientName}} and, once redisclosed, may no longer be protected by the Privacy Rule.
clauses.gap: This is a single regulatory subsection (45 C.F.R. § 164.508); no additional independent source was found for this. This is a federal regulation that applies nationwide — unlike the state-law documents elsewhere in this project's Estate Planning category, this authorization's legal basis does not vary by state.

citations.cite: required statements
citations.quote: In addition to the core elements, the authorization must contain statements adequate to place the individual on notice of all of the following: (i) The individual's right to revoke the authorization in writing... (ii) The ability or inability to condition treatment, payment, enrollment or eligibility for benefits on the authorization... (iii) The potential for information disclosed pursuant to the authorization to be subject to redisclosure by the recipient and no longer be protected by this subpart.

clauses.title: Right to Revoke an Authorization
clauses.body: {{patientName}} may revoke this authorization in writing at any time, except to the extent a covered entity has already taken action in reliance on it, or, if this authorization was obtained as a condition of obtaining insurance coverage, to the extent other law gives the insurer a right to contest a claim under the policy.
clauses.gap: This is a single regulatory subsection (45 C.F.R. § 164.508); no additional independent source was found for this. This is a federal regulation that applies nationwide — unlike the state-law documents elsewhere in this project's Estate Planning category, this authorization's legal basis does not vary by state.

citations.cite: revocation of authorizations
citations.quote: An individual may revoke an authorization provided under this section at any time, provided that the revocation is in writing, except to the extent that: (i) The covered entity has taken action in reliance thereon; or (ii) If the authorization was obtained as a condition of obtaining insurance coverage, other law provides the insurer with the right to contest a claim under the policy or the policy itself.

clauses.title: What Makes an Authorization Invalid
clauses.body: Under the Privacy Rule, a signed authorization is not valid if: its stated expiration date has passed or its expiration event is known to a covered entity to have occurred; it was not filled out completely as to a required element; a covered entity knows it has been revoked; it violates the compound-authorization rules, or the separate rule against conditioning treatment, payment, enrollment, or benefits eligibility on signing the authorization, where either applies; or a covered entity knows material information in it to be false.
clauses.gap: This is a single regulatory subsection (45 C.F.R. § 164.508); no additional independent source was found for this. This is a federal regulation that applies nationwide — unlike the state-law documents elsewhere in this project's Estate Planning category, this authorization's legal basis does not vary by state.

citations.cite: defective authorizations
citations.quote: An authorization is not valid, if the document submitted has any of the following defects: (i) The expiration date has passed or the expiration event is known by the covered entity to have occurred; (ii) The authorization has not been filled out completely, with respect to an element described by paragraph (c) of this section, if applicable; (iii) The authorization is known by the covered entity to have been revoked; (iv) The authorization violates paragraph (b)(3) or (4) of this section, if applicable; (v) Any material information in the authorization is known by the covered entity to be false.

clauses.title: How This Authorization Differs From Treatment-Related Disclosures
clauses.body: Separately from this authorization, the Privacy Rule permits a covered entity to use or disclose protected health information for its own treatment, payment, and health care operations without an authorization, and permits a covered entity to obtain a patient's optional consent for that separate purpose. This authorization is a different instrument: it is the specific mechanism the Privacy Rule requires before protected health information can be used or disclosed for purposes outside that treatment-payment-operations category, or in the manner and to the recipient {{patientName}} specifies here.
clauses.gap: This is a federal regulation that applies nationwide — unlike the state-law documents elsewhere in this project's Estate Planning category, this authorization's legal basis does not vary by state.

citations.cite: authorization required: general rule
citations.quote: Except as otherwise permitted or required by this subchapter, a covered entity may not use or disclose protected health information without an authorization that is valid under this section.

citations.cite: uses and disclosures to carry out treatment, payment, or health care operations
citations.quote: Except with respect to uses or disclosures that require an authorization under § 164.508(a)(2) through (4) or that are prohibited under § 164.502(a)(5)(i), a covered entity may use or disclose protected health information for treatment, payment, or health care operations as set forth in paragraph (c) of this section, provided that such use or disclosure is consistent with other applicable requirements of this subpart... A covered entity may obtain consent of the individual to use or disclose protected health information to carry out treatment, payment, or health care operations. (2) Consent, under paragraph (b) of this section, shall not be effective to permit a use or disclosure of protected health information when an authorization, under § 164.508, is required or when another condition must be met for such use or disclosure to be permissible under this subpart.

clauses.title: A Note on California's Separate Medical-Privacy Statute
clauses.body: Independent of HIPAA, California's Confidentiality of Medical Information Act separately restricts a California health care provider's disclosure of medical information about {{patientName}} without first obtaining an authorization, subject to statutory exceptions. This state statute exists alongside, and is not part of, the federal HIPAA authorization requirements described above.
clauses.gap: This is a single state-law citation (Cal. Civ. Code § 56.10(a)); no additional independent source was found for this. Unlike the federal HIPAA baseline elsewhere in this clause set, this specific point of California law does not apply nationwide — it supplements, rather than substitutes for, the federal Privacy Rule requirements above.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 56.10(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Confidentiality of Medical Information Act — disclosure by providers
citations.quote: A provider of health care, health care service plan, or contractor shall not disclose medical information regarding a patient of the provider of health care or an enrollee or subscriber of a health care service plan without first obtaining an authorization, except as provided in subdivision (b) or (c).

clauses.title: Authorization to Disclose Protected Health Information
clauses.body: I, {{patientName}}, authorize the use and disclosure of my protected health information as described in this document to {{authorizedRecipientName}}. This authorization is separate from, and does not depend on, any health care agent designation or health care decision-making authority I may have granted elsewhere. This authorization remains in effect until {{expirationDate}}, unless I revoke it in writing before that date.

clauses.title: Signature
clauses.body:
Signature of {{patientName}}: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________

If signed by a personal representative on behalf of {{patientName}}, printed name of representative and description of the representative's authority to act: ☐ _________________________

clauses.title: What a Codicil Is Under California Law
clauses.body: California's Probate Code treats a codicil not as a separate category of legal instrument with its own rules, but as a type of will. The Probate Code's general definitions provide that the term "will" includes a codicil, and that these definitions govern the construction of the Probate Code's provisions unless context requires otherwise. As a result, any Probate Code statute that refers to a "will" — including execution formalities, revocation rules, and revival rules — presumptively applies to a codicil, such as this one executed by {{testatorName}} of {{testatorCounty}}, in the same way it applies to the original will.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how "codicil" is defined and treated in relation to "will" — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific codicil. The definition itself (Probate Code § 88) is a single sentence with no further codicil-specific elaboration; this clause does not overstate its brevity into something more detailed than the statute provides.

citations.case: Cal. Probate Code § 88 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: definition of 'will'
citations.quote: “Will” includes codicil and any testamentary instrument which merely appoints an executor or revokes or revises another will.

citations.case: Cal. Probate Code § 20 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: definitions govern construction of the code
citations.quote: Unless the provision or context otherwise requires, the definitions in this part govern the construction of this code.

clauses.title: A Codicil Must Independently Satisfy Will-Execution Formalities
clauses.body: Because "will" is statutorily defined to include "codicil," a codicil to {{testatorName}}'s will dated {{originalWillDate}} is not exempt from the formalities that apply to wills generally. Probate Code § 6110 requires that a will be in writing and satisfy the section's signature and witnessing requirements. A codicil that fails to independently meet these formalities does not receive any special exemption from them merely because it amends, rather than replaces, an already-valid will.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the execution requirements applicable to a codicil — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific codicil. The full detail of California's signature and witnessing requirements (including the two-witness rule and the harmless-error exception) is addressed at length in this project's companion Last Will and Testament document and is not re-derived here; this clause states only that a codicil is not exempt from those requirements, not what all of their details are.

citations.case: Cal. Probate Code § 6110(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: execution of wills
citations.quote: Except as provided in this part, a will shall be in writing and satisfy the requirements of this section.

citations.case: Cal. Probate Code § 88 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: definition of 'will'
citations.quote: “Will” includes codicil and any testamentary instrument which merely appoints an executor or revokes or revises another will.

clauses.title: Revoking a Codicil Does Not Automatically Revive What It Changed
clauses.body: If a codicil that revoked or changed part of {{testatorName}}'s will dated {{originalWillDate}} is itself later revoked, the terms of the original will that the codicil had changed are not automatically restored. California's revival statute provides that when a later testamentary instrument that would have revoked part of an earlier one is itself thereafter revoked, the earlier instrument's revoked terms are revived only if it is evident from the circumstances of the later instrument's revocation, or from the testator's contemporaneous or subsequent declarations, that the testator intended the earlier terms to take effect as originally executed.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's revival rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific codicil. Probate Code § 6120, which defines revocation generally, does not itself use the word "codicil" and does not separately address the scenario of two physically distinct paper instruments (an original will and a separate codicil document) — it is Probate Code § 88's definitional inclusion of "codicil" within "will" that extends §§ 6120 and 6123 to codicils at all. Neither § 6120 nor § 6123 expressly states, in so many words, whether physically revoking the original will instrument automatically revokes a separate codicil to it, or the reverse; that specific multi-document question is not resolved by the statutory text found.

citations.case: Cal. Probate Code § 6123(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: revival
citations.quote: If a second will which, had it remained effective at death, would have revoked the first will in whole or in part, is thereafter revoked by acts under Section 6120 or 6121, the first will is revoked in whole or in part unless it is evident from the circumstances of the revocation of the second will or from the testator’s contemporary or subsequent declarations that the testator intended the first will to take effect as executed.

citations.case: Cal. Probate Code § 6120(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: revocation by subsequent will
citations.quote: A will or any part thereof is revoked by any of the following: (a) A subsequent will which revokes the prior will or part expressly or by inconsistency.

clauses.title: A Later Codicil Inconsistent With an Earlier Instrument
clauses.body: California's Probate Code does not contain a statute written specifically for the scenario of a later codicil that conflicts with an earlier codicil or with the original will. Two general principles govern instead. First, a subsequent testamentary instrument revokes a prior one, in whole or in part, "expressly or by inconsistency" — a rule that, because "will" includes "codicil," applies to a later codicil in relation to an earlier one or to the original will. Second, general rules of construction direct that all parts of an instrument be construed in relation to each other so as, if possible, to form a consistent whole, with any ambiguity resolved by reference to other parts of the instrument.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California addresses conflicting testamentary provisions — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific codicil. Beyond the general "expressly or by inconsistency" revocation rule and the general construction principles cited here, no codicil-specific inconsistency statute was found in the Probate Code's Division 6 or Division 11.

citations.case: Cal. Probate Code § 6120(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: revocation by inconsistency
citations.quote: A will or any part thereof is revoked by any of the following: (a) A subsequent will which revokes the prior will or part expressly or by inconsistency.

citations.case: Cal. Probate Code § 21121 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: construing an instrument as a consistent whole
citations.quote: All parts of an instrument are to be construed in relation to each other and so as, if possible, to form a consistent whole. If the meaning of any part of an instrument is ambiguous or doubtful, it may be explained by any reference to or recital of that part in another part of the instrument.

clauses.title: A Lost Codicil Is Presumed Revoked, Separately From the Will
clauses.body: California law presumes that a will last in the testator's possession, which cannot be found after the testator's death, was destroyed by the testator with intent to revoke it. Because "will" includes "codicil," this presumption applies separately to a codicil that was last in {{testatorName}}'s possession and cannot be located after death, independent of whether the original will dated {{originalWillDate}} is itself found.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's lost-instrument presumption — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific codicil. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 6124); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Probate Code § 6124 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: presumption of revocation
citations.quote: If the testator’s will was last in the testator’s possession, the testator was competent until death, and neither the will nor a duplicate original of the will can be found after the testator’s death, it is presumed that the testator destroyed the will with intent to revoke it. This presumption is a presumption affecting the burden of producing evidence.

clauses.title: Declaration Identifying the Original Will and the Amendment
clauses.body: I, {{testatorName}}, of {{testatorCounty}}, declare this instrument to be a codicil to my Last Will and Testament dated {{originalWillDate}} (the "Will"). I identify below the specific provision(s) of the Will that this codicil adds, deletes, or amends: ☐ _________________________. Except as specifically changed by this codicil, I confirm and republish the Will, and all of its provisions not specifically amended by this codicil, in all other respects.

clauses.title: Signature and Witness Block
clauses.body:
Signed by {{testatorName}} as a codicil to the Will dated {{originalWillDate}}, on {{codicilDate}}, at {{testatorCounty}}, California.

We, the undersigned, being at least two in number, each declare under penalty of perjury that {{testatorName}}, in our presence and in the presence of each other, signed this codicil, or acknowledged the signature or the codicil already made, and declared to us that it is {{testatorName}}'s codicil; that we understood this instrument to be {{testatorName}}'s codicil; and that we, and each of us, in {{testatorName}}'s presence and at {{testatorName}}'s request, and in the presence of each other, sign our names below as witnesses.

Signature of {{testatorName}}: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________
Witness 1 — Signature: ☐ _________________________ Printed name: ☐ _________________________
Witness 2 — Signature: ☐ _________________________ Printed name: ☐ _________________________

clauses.title: Nomination by Written Document Outside a Will
clauses.body: {{parentName}} nominates {{nominatedGuardianName}}, and if that person is unable or unwilling to serve, {{alternateGuardianName}}, as guardian of the person of {{minorChildName}}, by this written document. California Probate Code § 1500 permits a parent to nominate a guardian of a minor child's person or estate, or both. California Probate Code § 1502(a) permits that nomination to be made "in a writing signed either before or after the petition for the appointment of the guardian is filed" — meaning a signed nomination document can exist and take legal significance independent of a will and independent of an already-pending court case — and the same subsection directs a court to give the nomination "due weight," by cross-reference to Family Code § 3043.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how a parent's guardian nomination may be documented outside a will — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific guardianship nomination. Section 1500 itself is subject to Section 1502's conditions (e.g., when the other parent has not consented), and neither section makes a nomination self-executing; a court guardianship proceeding is still required to give it legal effect.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1500 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1500
citations.quote: Subject to Section 1502, a parent may nominate a guardian of the person or estate, or both, of a minor child in either of the following cases: (a) Where the other parent nominates, or consents in writing to the nomination of, the same guardian for the same child. (b) Where, at the time the petition for appointment of the guardian is filed, either (1) the other parent is dead or lacks legal capacity to consent to the nomination or (2) the consent of the other parent would not be required for an adoption of the child.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1502(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1502(a)
citations.quote: A nomination of a guardian under this article may be made in the petition for the appointment of the guardian or at the hearing on the petition or in a writing signed either before or after the petition for the appointment of the guardian is filed. The court shall give due weight to the nomination of a guardian of the person pursuant to Section 3043 of the Family Code.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3043 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the court's duty to give a guardian nomination due weight
citations.quote: In determining the person or persons to whom custody should be granted under paragraph (2) or (3) of subdivision (a) of Section 3040, the court shall consider and give due weight to the nomination of a guardian of the person of the child by a parent under Article 1 (commencing with Section 1500) of Chapter 1 of Part 2 of Division 4 of the Probate Code.

clauses.title: Timing and Conditions of a Nomination's Effect
clauses.body: A nomination made under this document may be drafted to take effect immediately, or only upon the occurrence of a stated condition, such as {{parentName}}'s absence, travel, incapacity, or death. California Probate Code § 1502(b) allows a nomination in writing to specify the condition or conditions under which it becomes effective. Absent a contrary statement in the writing, § 1502(c) provides that a nomination remains effective notwithstanding the nominating parent's later absence, incapacity, or death.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how a written guardian nomination's timing and conditions can be structured — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific guardianship nomination. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 1502); no additional independent source was found for this. A nomination's stated effective date or condition does not itself create a guardianship; a court proceeding is still the mechanism by which a guardian is actually appointed. Separately, Prob. Code § 1502(a) itself directs a court to give a parent's nomination "due weight" by cross-reference to Family Code § 3043 — a related fact addressed in this document's companion clause on standalone written nominations, not repeated here.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1502(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1502(b)
citations.quote: The nomination of a guardian under this article is effective when made except that a writing nominating a guardian under this article may provide that the nomination becomes effective only upon the occurrence of such condition or conditions as are specified in the writing, including, but not limited to, conditions as to the subsequent absence, legal incapacity, or death of the person making the nomination.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1502(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1502(c)
citations.quote: Unless the writing making the nomination expressly otherwise provides, a nomination made under this article remains effective notwithstanding the subsequent absence, legal incapacity, or death of the person making the nomination.

clauses.title: The Minor Child's Own Role in a Guardianship Nomination
clauses.body: Under California law, a minor who is 12 years of age or older may personally file a petition for the appointment of a guardian. In a proceeding to appoint a guardian of the person, the court is directed by Probate Code § 1514(b)(1) to the Family Code chapters governing custody of a minor, which include Family Code § 3042: where a child is of sufficient age and capacity to form an intelligent preference, the court must consider and give due weight to that preference, and a child 14 or older who wishes to address the court about the matter must be permitted to do so absent a contrary best-interest finding.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a minor's own statutory role in who is nominated or appointed as their guardian — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific guardianship nomination. Family Code § 3042 is written for custody and visitation orders generally and is incorporated into guardian-of-the-person appointments only by Probate Code § 1514(b)(1)'s cross-reference to that Family Code chapter; it does not independently mention "guardian" nominations by name. A related, more directly on-point provision — Family Code § 3043, one section over — does require a court to give a parent's guardian nomination "due weight"; that provision is addressed in this document's companion clause on standalone written nominations.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1510(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1510(a)
citations.quote: A relative or other person on behalf of the minor, or the minor if 12 years of age or older, may file a petition for the appointment of a guardian of the minor.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1514(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: In appointing a guardian of the person, the court is governed by Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 3020) and Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 3040) of Part 2 of Division 8 of the Family Code, relating to custody of a minor.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3042(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: If a child is of sufficient age and capacity to reason so as to form an intelligent preference as to custody or visitation, the court shall consider, and give due weight to, the wishes of the child in making an order granting or modifying custody or visitation.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3042(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: If the child is 14 years of age or older and wishes to address the court regarding custody or visitation, the child shall be permitted to do so, unless the court determines that doing so is not in the child’s best interest, in which case, the court shall state its reasons for that finding on the record.

clauses.title: The Caregiver's Authorization Affidavit — What It Allows Without Court Action
clauses.body: California Family Code §§ 6550–6552 create a Caregiver's Authorization Affidavit that operates without any court proceeding. A caregiver 18 or older who completes items 1–4 of the statutory affidavit form and signs it is authorized to enroll {{minorChildName}} in school and consent to school-related medical care. A caregiver who is a "relative" — defined by statute as an adult related to the child by blood, adoption, or affinity within the fifth degree of kinship, including stepparents, stepsiblings, and "great," "great-great," or "grand" relatives, or their spouses — who additionally completes items 5–8 and signs has the same rights to authorize medical and dental care given to guardians under Probate Code § 2353, which may include mental health treatment subject to the limits of Probate Code § 2356.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a no-court caregiver-authorization mechanism distinct from a court-appointed guardianship — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific guardianship nomination. The affidavit's authority to consent to medical/dental care beyond school-related care is available only to a caregiver who is a statutory "relative"; a non-relative caregiver's authority under this affidavit is limited to school enrollment and school-related medical care.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6550(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: A caregiver’s authorization affidavit that meets the requirements of this part authorizes a caregiver 18 years of age or older who completes items 1 to 4, inclusive, of the affidavit provided in Section 6552 and signs the affidavit to enroll a minor in school and consent to school-related medical care on behalf of the minor. A caregiver who is a relative and who completes items 1 to 8, inclusive, of the affidavit provided in Section 6552 and signs the affidavit shall have the same rights to authorize medical care and dental care for the minor that are given to guardians under Section 2353 of the Probate Code. The medical care authorized by this caregiver who is a relative may include mental health treatment subject to the limitations of Section 2356 of the Probate Code.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6552 (statutory affidavit form text, California Legislative Information)
citations.quote: When signed by a relative, this affidavit shall confer the same rights to authorize medical care and dental care for the minor that are given to guardians under Section 2353 of the Probate Code. The medical care authorized by a relative caregiver may include mental health treatment subject to the limitations of Section 2356 of the Probate Code.

clauses.title: The Caregiver's Authorization Affidavit — What It Does Not Do
clauses.body: The Caregiver's Authorization Affidavit does not create a legal guardianship and does not affect the legal rights of {{minorChildName}}'s parents or legal guardian over the child's care, custody, and control. A caregiver's decision to consent to or refuse medical or dental care for the minor is superseded by any contravening decision of a parent or other person with legal custody, unless that decision would jeopardize the minor's life, health, or safety.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the stated limits of a no-court caregiver authorization — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific guardianship nomination. These are the limits stated in the cited text; the affidavit's interaction with a parent's or guardian's decision in a specific factual situation is not addressed further by these sections.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6552 (statutory affidavit form text, California Legislative Information)
citations.cite: Fam. C. § 6552 Notice 1
citations.quote: This declaration does not affect the rights of the minor’s parents or legal guardian regarding the care, custody, and control of the minor, and does not mean that the caregiver has legal custody of the minor.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6550(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The decision of a caregiver to consent to or to refuse medical or dental care for a minor shall be superseded by any contravening decision of the parent or other person having legal custody of the minor, provided the decision of the parent or other person having legal custody of the minor does not jeopardize the life, health, or safety of the minor.

clauses.title: When a Caregiver's Authorization Affidavit Stops Being Valid
clauses.body: The Caregiver's Authorization Affidavit does not carry a fixed expiration date; instead, California Family Code § 6550(f) ties its validity to the minor's living arrangement. If {{minorChildName}} stops living with the caregiver who signed the affidavit, that caregiver is required to notify any school, health care provider, or health care service plan that received the affidavit, and the affidavit becomes invalid once that notice is received.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a stated termination mechanism for a no-court caregiver authorization — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific guardianship nomination. The statute ties invalidity to actual notice being received by the school or provider, not automatically to the date the child stops living with the caregiver.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6550(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: If the minor stops living with the caregiver, the caregiver shall notify any school, health care provider, or health care service plan that has been given the affidavit. The affidavit is invalid after the school, health care provider, or health care service plan receives notice that the minor is no longer living with the caregiver.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6552 (statutory affidavit form text, California Legislative Information)
citations.cite: Fam. C. § 6552, To Caregivers ¶3
citations.quote: If the minor stops living with you, the affidavit is no longer valid. You are required to notify any school, health care provider, or health care service plan to which you have given this affidavit that the minor is no longer living with you and that, as a result, the affidavit is no longer valid.

clauses.title: Formal Court Guardianship, in Contrast to the Affidavit
clauses.body: Unlike the Caregiver's Authorization Affidavit, a legal guardianship of a minor's person or estate is established only through a court proceeding. A petition requesting appointment of a guardian must specify the proposed guardian's name and address, the proposed ward's name and date of birth, and must state that the appointment is necessary or convenient. At the hearing on that petition, the court — not the petition alone — decides whether to appoint a guardian of the person, the estate, or both.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a formal guardianship (unlike the affidavit mechanism) requires an actual court petition and hearing — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific guardianship nomination, and not a description of the full court guardianship process, which involves additional notice, investigation, and ongoing court-oversight requirements not covered here.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1510(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1510(b)
citations.quote: The petition shall request that a guardian of the person or estate of the minor, or both, be appointed, shall specify the name and address of the proposed guardian and the name and date of birth of the proposed ward, and shall state that the appointment is necessary or convenient.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1514(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1514(a)
citations.quote: Upon hearing of the petition, if it appears necessary or convenient, the court may appoint a guardian of the person or estate of the proposed ward or both.

clauses.title: The Affidavit's Effect on School Enrollment Residency
clauses.body: A separately codified Education Code provision reinforces the affidavit's practical, no-court effect for school purposes: a pupil who lives in the home of a caregiving adult satisfies school-district residency requirements once that caregiving adult executes the Family Code § 6550 affidavit, and no guardianship or custody order is required for that determination, unless the school district determines from actual facts that the minor does not live with the caregiver.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a caregiver's affidavit — not a guardianship — can independently satisfy a school residency requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific guardianship nomination. The school district retains authority to determine from actual facts that the minor is not living with the caregiver, which can override this residency effect.

citations.case: Cal. Educ. Code § 48204(a)(5) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: A pupil who lives in the home of a caregiving adult that is located within the boundaries of that school district. Execution of an affidavit under penalty of perjury pursuant to Part 1.5 (commencing with Section 6550) of Division 11 of the Family Code by the caregiving adult is a sufficient basis for a determination that the pupil lives in the home of the caregiver, unless the school district determines from actual facts that the pupil is not living in the home of the caregiver.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6552 (statutory affidavit form text, California Legislative Information)
citations.cite: Fam. C. § 6552, To School Officials ¶1
citations.quote: Section 48204 of the Education Code provides that this affidavit constitutes a sufficient basis for a determination of residency of the minor, without the requirement of a guardianship or other custody order, unless the school district determines from actual facts that the minor is not living with the caregiver.

clauses.title: Nomination Declaration
clauses.body: I, {{parentName}}, being the parent of {{minorChildName}}, a minor child, hereby nominate {{nominatedGuardianName}} to serve as guardian of the person of {{minorChildName}}. If {{nominatedGuardianName}} is unable, unwilling, or unavailable to serve, I nominate {{alternateGuardianName}} as guardian in their place. This nomination is made by written document as permitted under California law and is separate from any nomination made in a will.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment Block
clauses.body:
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{parentName}}: ☐ _________________________

[Notary acknowledgment or witness signature lines, as applicable, attached.]

clauses.title: What a Premarital Agreement Is, and When It Takes Effect
clauses.body: California statute defines a "premarital agreement" as an agreement between prospective spouses made in contemplation of marriage and to be effective upon marriage. This document is intended by {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} to be such an agreement. Under the same statutory scheme, a premarital agreement becomes effective upon marriage — it has no effect if the parties do not marry.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how a premarital agreement is defined and triggered — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific premarital agreement. Family law, including whether and how prospective spouses may contract before marriage, varies by state; a document intended for use in another state is evidence of nothing beyond what that state's own law provides.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 1610(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the statutory definition of a premarital agreement
citations.quote: “Premarital agreement” means an agreement between prospective spouses made in contemplation of marriage and to be effective upon marriage.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 1613 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: when a premarital agreement becomes effective
citations.quote: A premarital agreement becomes effective upon marriage.

clauses.title: Execution Requirements
clauses.body: Under this statute, a premarital agreement must be in writing and signed by both prospective spouses. This document is intended to be signed by {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} before the marriage occurring on or planned for {{marriageDate}}.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the minimum written-and-signed formality some states impose on premarital agreements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific premarital agreement, and not a claim that no other formality (such as notarization, witnesses, or particular disclosure procedures) is ever required by a court applying a different rule or a different provision of the same body of law. This is a single statutory section (§ 1611); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 1611 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the written-and-signed execution requirement
citations.quote: A premarital agreement shall be in writing and signed by both parties.
