clauses.title: No Consideration Required
clauses.body: Under this statute, a premarital agreement — and any later written amendment or revocation of one signed after marriage — is enforceable without consideration, meaning without either party having to show they received something of value in exchange for signing.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that at least one state does not require consideration to enforce a premarital agreement or a post-marital amendment of one — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific premarital agreement, and not a claim that every state dispenses with consideration the same way.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 1611 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: no consideration required for the original agreement
citations.quote: It is enforceable without consideration.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 1614 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: no consideration required for a post-marital amendment or revocation
citations.quote: The amended agreement or the revocation is enforceable without consideration.

clauses.title: What a Premarital Agreement Can Address
clauses.body: Under this statute, prospective spouses may contract with respect to: (1) the rights and obligations of each party in property either or both of them acquire, wherever located; (2) the right to buy, sell, use, transfer, exchange, abandon, lease, consume, expend, assign, encumber, mortgage, dispose of, or otherwise manage and control property; (3) the disposition of property on separation, marital dissolution, death, or another specified event; (4) the making of a will, trust, or other arrangement to carry out the agreement; (5) ownership and disposition of life insurance death benefits; (6) the choice of law governing the agreement's construction; and (7) any other matter, including personal rights and obligations, not in violation of public policy or a criminal statute. Two further, separately-sourced statutory limits on this list — concerning child support and spousal support — are addressed elsewhere in this document.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one state's list of permitted subject matter for a premarital agreement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific premarital agreement, and not a claim that another state's list is identical. This is a single statutory section (§ 1612); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 1612(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the statutory list of permitted subject matter
citations.quote: Parties to a premarital agreement may contract with respect to all of the following: (1) The rights and obligations of each of the parties in any of the property of either or both of them whenever and wherever acquired or located. (2) The right to buy, sell, use, transfer, exchange, abandon, lease, consume, expend, assign, create a security interest in, mortgage, encumber, dispose of, or otherwise manage and control property. (3) The disposition of property upon separation, marital dissolution, death, or the occurrence or nonoccurrence of any other event. (4) The making of a will, trust, or other arrangement to carry out the provisions of the agreement. (5) The ownership rights in and disposition of the death benefit from a life insurance policy. (6) The choice of law governing the construction of the agreement. (7) Any other matter, including their personal rights and obligations, not in violation of public policy or a statute imposing a criminal penalty.

clauses.title: Child Support Cannot Be Limited by This Agreement
clauses.body: Under this statute, the right of a child to support may not be adversely affected by a premarital agreement between {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}, regardless of what property or support terms the agreement otherwise contains.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that at least one state places child support outside what a premarital agreement can alter — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific premarital agreement. Child support is typically treated by courts as belonging to the child rather than the parents, and statutory protection of it from private agreement is common, but its exact scope and mechanics vary by state. This is a single statutory section (§ 1612); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 1612(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: child support is not adversely affected by the agreement
citations.quote: The right of a child to support may not be adversely affected by a premarital agreement.

clauses.title: Spousal Support Waivers — the Independent-Counsel and Unconscionability Conditions
clauses.body: Under this statute, a provision in a premarital agreement addressing spousal support — including a waiver of it — is not enforceable if the party against whom it is being enforced was not represented by independent counsel at the time the agreement containing the provision was signed, or if the provision is unconscionable at the time enforcement is sought. The same statute states that an otherwise-unenforceable spousal support provision does not become enforceable merely because the party against whom enforcement is sought had independent counsel — independent representation is a condition for enforceability, not a guarantee of it.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one state's specific double condition on spousal-support provisions in a premarital agreement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific premarital agreement. Some states do not permit prospective spouses to limit spousal support at all; others impose different conditions. This is a single statutory section (§ 1612); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 1612(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the independent-counsel and unconscionability conditions on spousal-support provisions
citations.quote: Any provision in a premarital agreement regarding spousal support, including, but not limited to, a waiver of it, is not enforceable if the party against whom enforcement of the spousal support provision is sought was not represented by independent counsel at the time the agreement containing the provision was signed, or if the provision regarding spousal support is unconscionable at the time of enforcement. An otherwise unenforceable provision in a premarital agreement regarding spousal support may not become enforceable solely because the party against whom enforcement is sought was represented by independent counsel.

clauses.title: When a Premarital Agreement Is Not Enforceable
clauses.body: Under this statute, a premarital agreement is not enforceable if the party against whom enforcement is sought proves either that the party did not execute the agreement voluntarily, or that the agreement was unconscionable when executed and, before execution, the party was not provided a fair, reasonable, and full disclosure of the other party's property or financial obligations; did not voluntarily and expressly waive, in writing, the right to disclosure beyond what was provided; and did not have, and could not reasonably have had, adequate knowledge of the other party's property or financial obligations. The same statute directs that whether an agreement is unconscionable is decided by the court as a matter of law, not a question of fact for a jury.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one state's two-part test for unenforceability — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific premarital agreement. Standards for involuntariness, unconscionability, and required financial disclosure between prospective spouses vary by state. This is a single statutory section (§ 1615); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 1615(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the two-part unenforceability test
citations.quote: A premarital agreement is not enforceable if the party against whom enforcement is sought proves either of the following: (1) That party did not execute the agreement voluntarily. (2) The agreement was unconscionable when it was executed and, before execution of the agreement, all of the following applied to that party: (A) That party was not provided a fair, reasonable, and full disclosure of the property or financial obligations of the other party. (B) That party did not voluntarily and expressly waive, in writing, any right to disclosure of the property or financial obligations of the other party beyond the disclosure provided. (C) That party did not have, or reasonably could not have had, an adequate knowledge of the property or financial obligations of the other party. (b) An issue of unconscionability of a premarital agreement shall be decided by the court as a matter of law.

clauses.title: The Voluntariness Presumption — Independent Counsel and the Seven-Day Rule
clauses.body: Under this statute, for purposes of the voluntariness test, a premarital agreement is deemed not executed voluntarily unless a court finds, in writing or on the record, that the party against whom enforcement is sought was represented by independent legal counsel at the time of signing, or, after being advised to seek independent counsel, expressly waived that representation in a separate writing — with the advisement to seek counsel required at least seven calendar days before the final agreement was signed. For an agreement executed between January 1, 2002 and January 1, 2020, the statute further requires that the party against whom enforcement is sought had not less than seven calendar days between first being presented with the final agreement and advised to seek independent counsel, and the time the agreement was signed. For an agreement executed on or after January 1, 2020, the statute instead requires not less than seven calendar days between first being presented with the final agreement and the time it was signed, regardless of whether that party was represented by counsel. Neither seven-day requirement applies to nonsubstantive amendments that do not change the agreement's terms. If the party against whom enforcement is sought was unrepresented by counsel, the statute additionally requires that the party was fully informed, in writing memorialized before signing, of the agreement's terms and basic effect and of the rights and obligations being given up, in a language the party was proficient in, and that the unrepresented party executed, on or before signing, a document declaring receipt of that information and identifying who provided it. The statute also requires a finding that the agreement and related writings were not executed under duress, fraud, or undue influence, that the parties had capacity to enter into the agreement, and permits the court to weigh any other relevant factors.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one state's specific voluntariness presumption, its seven-calendar-day mechanic, and its independent-counsel and unrepresented-party conditions — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific premarital agreement, and not a claim that seven days (or any waiting period, counsel requirement, or disclosure procedure) is required in any other state. This is a single statutory section (§ 1615); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 1615(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the voluntariness presumption and its conditions
citations.quote: For the purposes of subdivision (a), it shall be deemed that a premarital agreement was not executed voluntarily unless the court finds in writing or on the record all of the following: (1) The party against whom enforcement is sought was represented by independent legal counsel at the time of signing the agreement or, after being advised to seek independent legal counsel, expressly waived, in a separate writing, representation by independent legal counsel. The advisement to seek independent legal counsel shall be made at least seven calendar days before the final agreement is signed. (2) One of the following: (A) For an agreement executed between January 1, 2002, and January 1, 2020, the party against whom enforcement is sought had not less than seven calendar days between the time that party was first presented with the final agreement and advised to seek independent legal counsel and the time the agreement was signed. This requirement does not apply to nonsubstantive amendments that do not change the terms of the agreement. (B) For an agreement executed on or after January 1, 2020, the party against whom enforcement is sought had not less than seven calendar days between the time that party was first presented with the final agreement and the time the agreement was signed, regardless of whether the party is represented by legal counsel. This requirement does not apply to nonsubstantive amendments that do not change the terms of the agreement. (3) The party against whom enforcement is sought, if unrepresented by legal counsel, was fully informed of the terms and basic effect of the agreement as well as the rights and obligations the party was giving up by signing the agreement, and was proficient in the language in which the explanation of the party's rights was conducted and in which the agreement was written. The explanation of the rights and obligations relinquished shall be memorialized in writing and delivered to the party prior to signing the agreement. The unrepresented party shall, on or before the signing of the premarital agreement, execute a document declaring that the party received the information required by this paragraph and indicating who provided that information. (4) The agreement and the writings executed pursuant to paragraphs (1) and (3) were not executed under duress, fraud, or undue influence, and the parties did not lack capacity to enter into the agreement. (5) Any other factors the court deems relevant.

clauses.title: Amendment and Revocation After Marriage
clauses.body: Under this statute, after marriage a premarital agreement between {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} may be amended or revoked only by a written agreement signed by both parties.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that at least one state requires a signed writing from both spouses to amend or revoke a premarital agreement after marriage — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific premarital agreement or amendment. This is a single statutory section (§ 1614); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 1614 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the written-agreement requirement for amendment or revocation
citations.quote: After marriage, a premarital agreement may be amended or revoked only by a written agreement signed by the parties.

clauses.title: Statute of Limitations — Tolled During Marriage, Subject to Laches
clauses.body: Under this statute, any statute of limitations that would otherwise apply to a claim for relief under a premarital agreement is tolled — paused — during the marriage of the parties to the agreement. The same statute preserves equitable defenses limiting the time for enforcement, including laches and estoppel, as available to either party.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one state's tolling rule for claims arising under a premarital agreement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific premarital agreement, and not a claim that every state tolls limitations periods during marriage the same way. This is a single statutory section (§ 1617); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 1617 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: tolling during marriage, and preserved equitable defenses
citations.quote: Any statute of limitations applicable to an action asserting a claim for relief under a premarital agreement is tolled during the marriage of the parties to the agreement. However, equitable defenses limiting the time for enforcement, including laches and estoppel, are available to either party.

clauses.title: If the Marriage Is Later Determined Void
clauses.body: Under this statute, if a marriage is later determined to be void, an agreement that would otherwise have been a premarital agreement between {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} is enforceable only to the extent necessary to avoid an inequitable result.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how at least one state treats a premarital agreement when the underlying marriage is later found void — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific premarital agreement or a specific marriage's validity. This is a single statutory section (§ 1616); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 1616 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: enforceability limited to avoiding an inequitable result if the marriage is void
citations.quote: If a marriage is determined to be void, an agreement that would otherwise have been a premarital agreement is enforceable only to the extent necessary to avoid an inequitable result.

clauses.title: Declaration of Parties and Intent to Marry
clauses.body: This Premarital Agreement is entered into by {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} ("the parties"), who state that they intend to marry each other and that this Agreement is made in contemplation of that marriage. The parties anticipate marrying on or about {{marriageDate}}. This Agreement sets out the parties' understanding regarding property and support matters as described in the sections that follow.

clauses.title: Financial Disclosure and Property Schedule Reference
clauses.body: Each party has attached to this Agreement, as Schedule A ({{party1Name}}) and Schedule B ({{party2Name}}), a listing of that party's property, assets, and financial obligations as of the date below. The parties acknowledge that these schedules are incorporated into this Agreement by reference. ☐ Schedule A and Schedule B attached.

clauses.title: Signatures and Acknowledgment
clauses.body:
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, the parties have signed this Agreement on the date(s) indicated below.

{{party1Name}}: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________

{{party2Name}}: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________

Notary acknowledgment block, if used, follows on a separate page.

clauses.title: Equal Division of Community Estate (Default Rule)
clauses.body: Except upon the written agreement of {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}, or their oral stipulation in open court, or as otherwise provided by statute, a court presiding over a dissolution of marriage or legal separation is required to divide the community estate of the parties equally. This agreement, if it allocates community property other than by an equal in-kind division, is an exercise of that written-agreement exception.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how community-property jurisdictions default to equal division of marital estates — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marital settlement agreement. Community property is itself a minority framework among U.S. states; many states divide marital property under an "equitable distribution" standard instead, which does not start from a 50/50 baseline. This is a single statutory section (§ 2550); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2550 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the equal-division default rule and its written-agreement exception
citations.quote: Except upon the written agreement of the parties, or on oral stipulation of the parties in open court, or as otherwise provided in this division, in a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or for legal separation of the parties, the court shall, either in its judgment of dissolution of the marriage, in its judgment of legal separation of the parties, or at a later time if it expressly reserves jurisdiction to make such a property division, divide the community estate of the parties equally.

clauses.title: Community Property vs. Separate Property
clauses.body: Property acquired by a married person during the marriage while domiciled in this state is generally community property, except as otherwise provided by statute. Separate property includes all property owned by a spouse before marriage, all property acquired after marriage by gift, bequest, devise, or descent, and the rents, issues, and profits of such property. This agreement's characterization of specific assets and debts as community or separate property of {{party1Name}} or {{party2Name}} draws on this statutory framework.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one community-property jurisdiction distinguishes community from separate property — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marital settlement agreement. Characterization rules, presumptions, and their exceptions (commingling, transmutation, tracing) vary significantly by state and are fact-specific; this clause states the general statutory categories only.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 760 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the community property default
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided by statute, all property, real or personal, wherever situated, acquired by a married person during the marriage while domiciled in this state is community property.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 770(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the separate property definition
citations.quote: Separate property of a married person includes all of the following: (1) All property owned by the person before marriage. (2) All property acquired by the person after marriage by gift, bequest, devise, or descent. (3) The rents, issues, and profits of the property described in this section.

clauses.title: Date of Separation and Post-Separation Earnings
clauses.body: "Date of separation" means the date a complete and final break in the marital relationship has occurred, as evidenced by both (1) a spouse expressing to the other spouse the intent to end the marriage, and (2) conduct of that spouse consistent with that intent; a court considers all relevant evidence in making this determination. The parties identify {{separationDate}} as the date of separation for purposes of this agreement. The earnings and accumulations of a spouse (and of minor children living with or in that spouse's custody) after the date of separation are that spouse's separate property.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction defines "date of separation" and its consequence for post-separation earnings — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marital settlement agreement. This is a specific, litigated statutory test (the Legislature enacted it in 2015 to abrogate the California Supreme Court's contrary holding in In re Marriage of Davis), and comparable concepts in other states carry different names, tests, and effective dates entirely.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 70(a)-(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the statutory test for date of separation
citations.quote: “Date of separation” means the date that a complete and final break in the marital relationship has occurred, as evidenced by both of the following: (1) The spouse has expressed to the other spouse the intent to end the marriage. (2) The conduct of the spouse is consistent with the intent to end the marriage. (b) In determining the date of separation, the court shall take into consideration all relevant evidence. (c) It is the intent of the Legislature in enacting this section to abrogate the decisions in In re Marriage of Davis (2015) 61 Cal.4th 846 and In re Marriage of Norviel (2002) 102 Cal.App.4th 1152.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 771(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: post-separation earnings are separate property
citations.quote: The earnings and accumulations of a spouse and the minor children living with, or in the custody of, the spouse, after the date of separation of the spouses, are the separate property of the spouse.

clauses.title: Factors a Court Considers in Ordering Spousal Support
clauses.body: In ordering spousal support, a court is directed to consider all of the following circumstances: the marketable skills of the supported party and the job market for those skills; the extent to which the supported party's earning capacity was impaired by periods of unemployment incurred during the marriage to permit devotion of time to domestic duties; the extent to which the supported party contributed to the supporting party's education, training, career position, or license; the supporting party's ability to pay, considering earning capacity, income, assets, and standard of living; the needs of each party based on the marital standard of living; the obligations and assets, including separate property, of each party; the duration of the marriage; the supported party's ability to work without unduly interfering with the interests of dependent children in that party's custody; the age and health of the parties; documented evidence of domestic violence between the parties; tax consequences to each party; the balance of hardships to each party; the goal that the supported party become self-supporting within a reasonable period of time (generally one-half the length of the marriage, except for a marriage of long duration); and any other factors the court determines are just and equitable.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the kind of factor list a court applies to spousal support — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marital settlement agreement, and not advice about how these factors apply to any specific marriage. Both the existence of a factor-based standard and the "one-half the length of the marriage" self-support benchmark are jurisdiction-specific; many states use different frameworks (formulaic guidelines, different factor lists, or no comparable benchmark at all) for spousal or "alimony" support. This is a single statutory section (§ 4320); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 4320(a)-(l) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the statutory factor list for spousal support
citations.quote: In ordering spousal support under this part, the court shall consider all of the following circumstances: (a) The extent to which the earning capacity of each party is sufficient to maintain the standard of living established during the marriage... (l) The goal that the supported party shall be self-supporting within a reasonable period of time. Except in the case of a marriage of long duration as described in Section 4336, a "reasonable period of time" for purposes of this section generally shall be one-half the length of the marriage.

clauses.title: The "Long Duration" Marriage Presumption (10-Year Rule)
clauses.body: Except on written agreement of the parties to the contrary or a court order terminating spousal support, a court retains jurisdiction indefinitely over spousal support in a dissolution or legal separation proceeding where the marriage is of long duration. For this purpose, a rebuttable presumption applies that a marriage of 10 years or more, measured from the date of marriage to the date of separation, is a marriage of long duration; a court may also determine that a marriage of less than 10 years is of long duration, and may consider periods of separation during the marriage in making that determination. The parties identify {{marriageDate}} as the date of marriage and {{separationDate}} as the date of separation for purposes of this agreement.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific "10-year marriage" jurisdiction-retention rule for spousal support — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marital settlement agreement. The presumption is expressly rebuttable, not automatic, and the 10-year threshold, the indefinite-jurisdiction consequence, and the ability to contract around it by written agreement are all particular to this jurisdiction's statute. This is a single statutory section (§ 4336); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 4336(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the long-duration-marriage presumption and indefinite jurisdiction
citations.quote: (a) Except on written agreement of the parties to the contrary or a court order terminating spousal support, the court retains jurisdiction indefinitely in a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or for legal separation of the parties where the marriage is of long duration. (b) For the purpose of retaining jurisdiction, there is a presumption affecting the burden of producing evidence that a marriage of 10 years or more, from the date of marriage to the date of separation, is a marriage of long duration. However, the court may consider periods of separation during the marriage in determining whether the marriage is in fact of long duration. Nothing in this subdivision precludes a court from determining that a marriage of less than 10 years is a marriage of long duration.

clauses.title: Custody and Visitation Stipulations Remain Subject to Best-Interest Review
clauses.body: A statutory presumption favors joint custody as being in a child's best interest where the parents have agreed to joint custody, or so agree in open court at a custody hearing — but that presumption operates subject to the court's best-interest analysis. Where parents stipulate in writing or on the record regarding custody or visitation, the statute does not eliminate the requirement that the contents of the stipulation be in the best interest of the child and be specific as to the time, day, place, and manner of transfer of the child. Any custody or visitation terms in this agreement concerning children of {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} are subject to that same court review and are not self-executing by agreement alone.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that parental custody agreements remain subject to a court's independent best-interest review rather than being enforceable purely by private contract — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marital settlement agreement. Best-interest standards, the weight given to parental agreement, and joint-custody presumptions all vary by state; this document does not address the fuller custody-factor scheme, which is covered separately.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3080 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the joint-custody agreement presumption
citations.quote: There is a presumption, affecting the burden of proof, that joint custody is in the best interest of a minor child, subject to Section 3011, where the parents have agreed to joint custody or so agree in open court at a hearing for the purpose of determining the custody of the minor child.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3011(a)(5)(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a custody stipulation still must be in the child's best interest
citations.quote: Nothing in this paragraph eliminates the requirement that the contents of the stipulation be in the best interest of the child and be specific as to time, day, place, and manner of transfer of the child if the parties do stipulate in writing or on the record regarding custody or visitation.

clauses.title: Private Agreement vs. Enforceable Court Judgment
clauses.body: A written settlement between parties to pending litigation may, upon motion, be entered by the court as a judgment on the terms of that settlement, where the parties have stipulated to the settlement in a signed writing or orally before the court. Family law property-division judgments are themselves entered as part of "its judgment of dissolution of the marriage" or "its judgment of legal separation," rather than arising automatically from a private agreement standing alone. This agreement between {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} states the parties' negotiated terms; whether and how it is presented to a court for entry as a judgment is a separate procedural step from the agreement's execution.
clauses.gap: This is a mix of a Family Code provision and a general Code of Civil Procedure statute governing settlements, not one clean, dedicated statutory section stating that marital settlement agreements specifically must be "incorporated" to be enforceable as judgments. That specific proposition is established primarily through California case law and court procedure (the mechanics of presenting a stipulated judgment for entry), not a single codified rule — this clause states only what these two statutes actually say, and does not claim more. This is one state's statutory and procedural framework, used as real evidence that a private settlement and a court judgment are legally distinct things — not a claim about which state's law or procedure governs a specific marital settlement agreement; procedures for converting a signed agreement into an enforceable judgment vary by state and by court.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2550 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: property-division judgments are entered as part of the dissolution/separation judgment
citations.quote: the court shall, either in its judgment of dissolution of the marriage, in its judgment of legal separation of the parties, or at a later time if it expressly reserves jurisdiction to make such a property division, divide the community estate of the parties equally

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 664.6(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the general mechanism for entering a stipulated settlement as a judgment
citations.quote: If parties to pending litigation stipulate, in a writing signed by the parties outside of the presence of the court or orally before the court, for settlement of the case, or part thereof, the court, upon motion, may enter judgment pursuant to the terms of the settlement.

clauses.title: Need-Based Attorney's Fees to Ensure Parity of Access
clauses.body: In a proceeding for dissolution, nullity, or legal separation, a court is directed to ensure that each party has access to legal representation, including early in the proceedings, by ordering one party, if necessary based on income and needs assessments, to pay the other party or the other party's attorney a reasonable amount for attorney's fees and costs of the proceeding.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a need-based attorney's-fee mechanism in dissolution proceedings — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marital settlement agreement. Whether such fee-shifting exists at all, and on what terms, varies by state; this clause states the statutory standard only and does not address whether it would apply to any specific case. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 2030(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2030(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the need-based attorney's fee standard
citations.quote: In a proceeding for dissolution of marriage, nullity of marriage, or legal separation of the parties, and in any proceeding subsequent to entry of a related judgment, the court shall ensure that each party has access to legal representation, including access early in the proceedings, to preserve each party's rights by ordering, if necessary based on the income and needs assessments, one party, except a governmental entity, to pay to the other party, or to the other party's attorney, whatever amount is reasonably necessary for attorney's fees and for the cost of maintaining or defending the proceeding during the pendency of the proceeding.

clauses.title: Interspousal Fiduciary Duty
clauses.body: In transactions between {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}, California law subjects spouses to the general rules governing fiduciary relationships that control persons in confidential relations with each other, including a duty of the highest good faith and fair dealing, a bar on either spouse taking unfair advantage of the other, and — as to community property — an obligation to give the other spouse access to books kept regarding a transaction, to render true and full information affecting a transaction on request, and to account for and hold as trustee any benefit or profit derived from a transaction made without the other spouse's consent.
clauses.gap: This is California's interspousal fiduciary-duty statute, used as real evidence of what a "confidential relationship" duty between spouses consists of under one state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific postnuptial agreement. California is a community-property state; most U.S. states use common-law/equitable-distribution property systems instead, and this duty framework is tied specifically to California's community-property structure. Separately: § 721 itself, read in full, does not contain the word "presumption" or state a burden-shifting rule for transactions that advantage one spouse — any such presumption is judicial doctrine, not statutory text, and no statutory citation is offered for it here. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 721(b)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 721(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the interspousal fiduciary duty and its specific obligations
citations.quote: (b) Except as provided in Sections 143, 144, 146, 16040, 16047, and 21385 of the Probate Code, in transactions between themselves, spouses are subject to the general rules governing fiduciary relationships that control the actions of persons occupying confidential relations with each other. This confidential relationship imposes a duty of the highest good faith and fair dealing on each spouse, and neither shall take any unfair advantage of the other. This confidential relationship is a fiduciary relationship subject to the same rights and duties of nonmarital business partners, as provided in Sections 16403, 16404, and 16503 of the Corporations Code, including, but not limited to, the following: (1) Providing each spouse access at all times to any books kept regarding a transaction for the purposes of inspection and copying. (2) Rendering upon request, true and full information of all things affecting any transaction that concerns the community property. Nothing in this section is intended to impose a duty for either spouse to keep detailed books and records of community property transactions. (3) Accounting to the spouse, and holding as a trustee, any benefit or profit derived from any transaction by one spouse without the consent of the other spouse that concerns the community property.

clauses.title: Transmutation Writing / Express Declaration Requirement
clauses.body: California law permits married persons to change ("transmute") the character of property between community and separate, or between the spouses, by agreement or transfer, with or without consideration. Such a change of character is not valid unless made in writing by an express declaration that is made, joined in, consented to, or accepted by the spouse whose interest in the property is adversely affected.
clauses.gap: This is California's transmutation statute, used as real evidence of one state's formal-validity rule for changing property character between spouses — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific postnuptial agreement. Community property (and its transmutation concept) is itself a minority framework among U.S. states; most states use common-law/equitable-distribution systems that do not use "transmutation" as a legal category at all. Separately, California courts have required specific, unambiguous language to satisfy the "express declaration" standard, but the statutory text itself does not spell out a required form of words beyond "express declaration... adversely affected" — that further specificity is judicial interpretation, not quoted here as statutory text.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 850 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the transmutation authorization
citations.quote: Subject to Sections 851 to 853, inclusive, married persons may by agreement or transfer, with or without consideration, do any of the following: (a) Transmute community property to separate property of either spouse. (b) Transmute separate property of either spouse to community property. (c) Transmute separate property of one spouse to separate property of the other spouse.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 852(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the writing/express declaration requirement
citations.quote: (a) A transmutation of real or personal property is not valid unless made in writing by an express declaration that is made, joined in, consented to, or accepted by the spouse whose interest in the property is adversely affected.

clauses.title: Personal-Gift Exception to the Writing Requirement
clauses.body: California's writing/express-declaration requirement for transmutations does not apply to a gift between spouses of clothing, wearing apparel, jewelry, or other tangible articles of a personal nature that is used solely or principally by the spouse receiving the gift, provided the gift is not substantial in value taking into account the circumstances of the marriage.
clauses.gap: This is a specific statutory carve-out within California's transmutation statute, used as real evidence that at least one state's transmutation-writing rule has a bounded gift exception — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific postnuptial agreement, and not a claim about what dollar or value threshold counts as "substantial" (the statute does not itself define that term numerically). Community property is a minority approach among U.S. states. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 852(c)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 852(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the personal-gift exception
citations.quote: (c) This section does not apply to a gift between the spouses of clothing, wearing apparel, jewelry, or other tangible articles of a personal nature that is used solely or principally by the spouse to whom the gift is made and that is not substantial in value taking into account the circumstances of the marriage.

clauses.title: Recording and Third-Party Effect of a Real Property Transmutation
clauses.body: Under California's transmutation statute, a transmutation of real property is not effective as to third parties without notice of it unless the transmutation instrument is recorded. This recording rule addresses effectiveness against third parties; it is a separate concept from the writing/express-declaration requirement that governs validity of the transmutation as between the spouses themselves.
clauses.gap: This is California's transmutation statute, used as real evidence of one state's third-party recording rule for a real-property transmutation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific postnuptial agreement, and not a claim that recording is required for the transmutation to be valid between the spouses themselves (the statute ties recording only to effect on third parties without notice). Community property is a minority approach among U.S. states, and a non-community-property state's recording/title rules for interspousal real property transfers may differ materially. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 852(b)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 852(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the third-party recording rule
citations.quote: (b) A transmutation of real property is not effective as to third parties without notice thereof unless recorded.

clauses.title: Default Community and Separate Property Characterization
clauses.body: Absent an agreement changing these defaults, California law characterizes property acquired by a married person during the marriage while domiciled in California as community property. Separate property, by contrast, includes property owned before marriage, property acquired during marriage by gift, bequest, devise, or descent, and the rents, issues, and profits of that separate property.
clauses.gap: These are California's default property-characterization statutes, used as real evidence of the specific default rules a California postnuptial agreement would exist to override — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific postnuptial agreement. Community property is itself a minority approach among U.S. states; most states are common-law/equitable-distribution states, where property acquired during marriage is not automatically split into "community" and "separate" categories in this way, and a postnuptial agreement drafted for a non-community-property state would be overriding a different set of default rules entirely.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 760 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the community property default
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided by statute, all property, real or personal, wherever situated, acquired by a married person during the marriage while domiciled in this state is community property.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 770(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the separate property definition
citations.quote: (a) Separate property of a married person includes all of the following: (1) All property owned by the person before marriage. (2) All property acquired by the person after marriage by gift, bequest, devise, or descent. (3) The rents, issues, and profits of the property described in this section.

clauses.title: Spousal Support Terms — Statutory Basis Differs From a Premarital Agreement
clauses.body: California's Uniform Premarital Agreement Act defines a "premarital agreement" as an agreement between prospective spouses made in contemplation of marriage and effective upon marriage. That Act's specific spousal-support-waiver conditions — independent counsel and non-unconscionability at enforcement — are stated as conditions on a "premarital agreement," by that definition. An agreement addressing spousal support entered into by people who are already married is not a "premarital agreement" under that definition; its validity is instead a function of the general interspousal fiduciary duty and transmutation rules described elsewhere in this document.
clauses.gap: This is California's statutory definition of "premarital agreement" and its spousal-support-waiver conditions, used as real evidence that one state's specific independent-counsel/unconscionability conditions for spousal-support waivers are, by the statute's own terms, tied to agreements made before marriage — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific postnuptial agreement, and not a claim that identical or similar conditions do or do not apply to a postnuptial spousal-support provision under California law generally. No statutory text extending § 1612(c)'s specific conditions to agreements entered into after marriage was located in the sections researched for this document; that gap is disclosed rather than assumed.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 1610(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the statutory definition of a premarital agreement
citations.quote: “Premarital agreement” means an agreement between prospective spouses made in contemplation of marriage and to be effective upon marriage.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 1612(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the spousal-support-waiver conditions, tied to a premarital agreement
citations.quote: (c) Any provision in a premarital agreement regarding spousal support, including, but not limited to, a waiver of it, is not enforceable if the party against whom enforcement of the spousal support provision is sought was not represented by independent counsel at the time the agreement containing the provision was signed, or if the provision regarding spousal support is unconscionable at the time of enforcement. An otherwise unenforceable provision in a premarital agreement regarding spousal support may not become enforceable solely because the party against whom enforcement is sought was represented by independent counsel.

clauses.title: Community Property Management, Gifts, and Disclosure Duty
clauses.body: Beyond the general interspousal fiduciary duty, California's community-property management statute states that a spouse may not make a gift of community personal property, or dispose of it for less than fair and reasonable value, without the other spouse's written consent — except that this rule does not apply to gifts one spouse gives directly to the other. The same statute also restates a full-disclosure obligation: each spouse must make full disclosure to the other of all material facts and information regarding the existence, characterization, and valuation of community assets and debts, and provide equal access to related information, records, and books on request.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory section (§ 1100, subdivisions (b) and (e)); no additional independent source was found for this beyond that one section — it is used as real evidence of a specific written-consent-for-gifts rule and a restated disclosure duty under one state's community-property management statute, not a claim about which state's law governs a specific postnuptial agreement. Community property is a minority framework among U.S. states.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 1100(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the written-consent-for-gifts rule
citations.quote: (b) A spouse may not make a gift of community personal property, or dispose of community personal property for less than fair and reasonable value, without the written consent of the other spouse. This subdivision does not apply to gifts mutually given by both spouses to third parties and to gifts given by one spouse to the other spouse.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 1100(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the restated disclosure duty
citations.quote: (e) Each spouse shall act with respect to the other spouse in the management and control of the community assets and liabilities in accordance with the general rules governing fiduciary relationships which control the actions of persons having relationships of personal confidence as specified in Section 721, until such time as the assets and liabilities have been divided by the parties or by a court. This duty includes the obligation to make full disclosure to the other spouse of all material facts and information regarding the existence, characterization, and valuation of all assets in which the community has or may have an interest and debts for which the community is or may be liable, and to provide equal access to all information, records, and books that pertain to the value and character of those assets and debts, upon request.

clauses.title: Transmutation's Interaction With a Will and Nonprobate Transfers
clauses.body: California's transmutation statute addresses two specific death-related scenarios. A statement in a will about the character of property is not admissible as evidence of a transmutation in a proceeding commenced before the death of the person who made the will. Separately, a written joinder or written consent to a nonprobate transfer of community property on death that satisfies the transmutation writing requirement is itself treated as a transmutation, governed by transmutation law rather than the Probate Code's nonprobate-transfer provisions.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory section (§ 853, subdivisions (a) and (c)); no additional independent source was found for this beyond that one section — it is used as real evidence of two specific, narrow statutory rules connecting transmutation to death-related proceedings under one state's law, not a claim about which state's law governs a specific postnuptial agreement, and not a claim that transmutation law generally displaces probate or divorce proceedings beyond what these two subdivisions state. Beyond these two rules, this document's research did not find a separate statutory mechanism for how a transmuted property's new character carries into probate or dissolution proceedings — the working assumption, not independently verified as a distinct statutory rule, is that reclassified property is simply treated according to its new character (separate or community) like any other property of that character. Community property is a minority approach among U.S. states.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 853(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a will statement isn't evidence of transmutation before death
citations.quote: (a) A statement in a will of the character of property is not admissible as evidence of a transmutation of the property in a proceeding commenced before the death of the person who made the will.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 853(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: written consent to a nonprobate transfer is itself a transmutation
citations.quote: (c) A written joinder or written consent to a nonprobate transfer of community property on death that satisfies Section 852 is a transmutation and is governed by the law applicable to transmutations and not by Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 5010) of Part 1 of Division 5 of the Probate Code.

clauses.title: Legal and Physical Custody: Joint and Sole, Defined
clauses.body: California law treats "custody" as two separate, independently-decided questions: legal custody (who has the right and responsibility to make decisions about a child's health, education, and welfare) and physical custody (with whom the child resides and who supervises the child day to day). Each question can be awarded jointly or solely, and the two axes can combine independently rather than as one all-or-nothing label. Joint legal custody means both {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}} share the right and responsibility to make decisions relating to {{childName}}'s health, education, and welfare. Sole legal custody means only one parent holds that right and responsibility. Joint physical custody means each parent has significant periods of physical custody, shared so as to assure {{childName}} of frequent and continuing contact with both parents. Sole physical custody means {{childName}} resides with and is supervised by one parent, subject to the court's power to order visitation for the other parent.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that legal custody and physical custody are two independently defined, independently awarded axes — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parenting plan or custody matter. Custody terminology and the joint/sole framework vary by state; some states use different labels (for example, "parenting time" rather than "physical custody") or a different default framework entirely. Each of the four definitions below comes from its own distinct Family Code section, not from subsections of a single section, so these four citations are independent of one another.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3003 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: joint legal custody, defined
citations.quote: “Joint legal custody” means that both parents shall share the right and the responsibility to make the decisions relating to the health, education, and welfare of a child.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3004 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: joint physical custody, defined
citations.quote: “Joint physical custody” means that each of the parents shall have significant periods of physical custody. Joint physical custody shall be shared by the parents in such a way so as to assure a child of frequent and continuing contact with both parents, subject to Sections 3011 and 3020.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3006 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: sole legal custody, defined
citations.quote: “Sole legal custody” means that one parent shall have the right and the responsibility to make the decisions relating to the health, education, and welfare of a child.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3007 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: sole physical custody, defined
citations.quote: “Sole physical custody” means that a child shall reside with and be under the supervision of one parent, subject to the power of the court to order visitation.

clauses.title: The Best-Interest-of-the-Child Standard and Its Statutory Factors
clauses.body: In making a custody determination, a California court is directed to consider — among any other factors it finds relevant — at least: the health, safety, and welfare of {{childName}}; any history of abuse by one parent or another person seeking custody against a child the person has cared for, against the other parent, or against certain other described household or relationship members; the nature and amount of {{childName}}'s contact with both parents; and the habitual or continual illegal use of controlled substances, habitual or continual abuse of alcohol, or habitual or continual abuse of prescribed controlled substances by either parent. The court does not consider a parent's, legal guardian's, or relative's sex, gender identity, gender expression, or sexual orientation in this determination.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific statutory best-interest factor list — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parenting plan or custody matter, and not a claim that this list is exhaustive (the statute itself invites the court to weigh "any other factors it finds relevant"). Best-interest standards, and the specific factors a state's statute names, vary significantly by state. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 3011); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3011(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the best-interest factors, part 1
citations.quote: (a) In making a determination of the best interests of the child in a proceeding described in Section 3021, the court shall, among any other factors it finds relevant and consistent with Section 3020, consider all of the following: (1) The health, safety, and welfare of the child. (2) (A) A history of abuse by one parent or any other person seeking custody against any of the following: (i) A child to whom the parent or person seeking custody is related by blood or affinity or with whom the parent or person seeking custody has had a caretaking relationship, no matter how temporary. (ii) The other parent. (iii) A parent, current spouse, or cohabitant, of the parent or person seeking custody, or a person with whom the parent or person seeking custody has a dating or engagement relationship.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3011(a)(3)-(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the best-interest factors, part 2
citations.quote: (3) The nature and amount of contact with both parents, including as provided in Sections 3046 and 3100. (4) The habitual or continual illegal use of controlled substances, the habitual or continual abuse of alcohol, or the habitual or continual abuse of prescribed controlled substances by either parent.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3011(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the sex/gender/orientation exclusion
citations.quote: (b) Notwithstanding subdivision (a), the court shall not consider the sex, gender identity, gender expression, or sexual orientation of a parent, legal guardian, or relative in determining the best interests of the child.

clauses.title: State Policy: Frequent and Continuing Contact, Subject to Child Safety
clauses.body: California's Family Code declares that the health, safety, and welfare of children is a court's primary concern in any custody or visitation order, and it is the state's public policy to ensure that {{childName}} has frequent and continuing contact with both {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}} after separation — except when that contact would not be in {{childName}}'s best interest. Where the safety-first policy and the frequent-contact policy point in different directions in a given case, the statute directs that the order be made in whatever manner ensures the health, safety, and welfare of the child and of all family members.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific, declared statutory priority ordering — child safety controls when it conflicts with the frequent-contact preference — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parenting plan or custody matter. Whether, and how, a state's law states this kind of priority ordering between contact and safety varies by state. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 3020); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3020(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: child safety as the court's primary concern
citations.quote: The Legislature finds and declares that it is the public policy of this state to ensure that the health, safety, and welfare of children shall be the court's primary concern in determining the best interests of children when making any orders regarding the physical or legal custody or visitation of children.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3020(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the frequent-and-continuing-contact policy
citations.quote: The Legislature finds and declares that it is the public policy of this state to ensure that children have frequent and continuing contact with both parents after the parents have separated or dissolved their marriage, or ended their relationship, and to encourage parents to share the rights and responsibilities of child rearing in order to effect this policy, except when the contact would not be in the best interests of the child, as provided in subdivisions (a) and (c) of this section and Section 3011.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3020(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: priority ordering when the two policies conflict
citations.quote: (c) When the policies set forth in subdivisions (a) and (b) of this section are in conflict, a court's order regarding physical or legal custody or visitation shall be made in a manner that ensures the health, safety, and welfare of the child and the safety of all family members.

clauses.title: Domestic Violence and Custody: The Rebuttable Presumption
clauses.body: Under California law, a court finding that a parent seeking custody has perpetrated domestic violence within the preceding five years — against the other parent seeking custody, against {{childName}} or {{childName}}'s siblings, or against certain other described persons connected to the parent — creates a rebuttable presumption that awarding that parent sole or joint physical or legal custody is detrimental to the child's best interest. The presumption can be rebutted only by a preponderance of the evidence, and the statute specifically states that the ordinary preference for frequent and continuing contact with both parents may not, by itself, be used to rebut it. To overcome the presumption, the court must find the parent has demonstrated that custody is in the child's best interest, and must weigh additional factors including: completion of a batterer's treatment program meeting statutory criteria; completion of alcohol or drug abuse counseling, where the court finds it appropriate; completion of a parenting class, where the court finds it appropriate; the parent's probation or parole status and compliance; compliance with any protective or restraining order; whether the parent has committed further acts of domestic violence; and whether the court has found the parent to be a restrained person unlawfully in possession of a firearm or ammunition.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific, heavily litigated rebuttable presumption — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific custody matter. Domestic-violence-related custody presumptions — including whether one exists at all, the look-back period, and the rebuttal factors — vary significantly by state. The version of this statute quoted here was enacted by Stats. 2024, Ch. 544 and became operative January 1, 2026; a document assembled from this text does not track future amendments to it. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 3044); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3044(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the rebuttable presumption itself
citations.quote: (a) Upon a finding by the court that a party seeking custody of a child has perpetrated domestic violence within the previous five years against the other party seeking custody of the child, or against the child or the child's siblings, or against a person in subparagraph (A) of paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3011 with whom the party has a relationship, there is a rebuttable presumption that an award of sole or joint physical or legal custody of a child to a person who has perpetrated domestic violence is detrimental to the best interest of the child, pursuant to Sections 3011 and 3020. This presumption may only be rebutted by a preponderance of the evidence.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3044(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the factors for overcoming the presumption
citations.quote: (b) To overcome the presumption set forth in subdivision (a), the court shall find that paragraph (1) is satisfied and shall find that the factors in paragraph (2), on balance, support the legislative findings in Section 3020. (1) The perpetrator of domestic violence has demonstrated that giving sole or joint physical or legal custody of a child to the perpetrator is in the best interest of the child pursuant to Sections 3011 and 3020. In determining the best interest of the child, the preference for frequent and continuing contact with both parents, as set forth in subdivision (b) of Section 3020, or with the noncustodial parent, as set forth in paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 3040, may not be used to rebut the presumption, in whole or in part. (2) Additional factors: (A) The perpetrator has successfully completed a batterer's treatment program that meets the criteria outlined in subdivision (c) of Section 1203.097 of the Penal Code. (B) The perpetrator has successfully completed a program of alcohol or drug abuse counseling, if the court determines that counseling is appropriate. (C) The perpetrator has successfully completed a parenting class, if the court determines the class to be appropriate. (D) The perpetrator is on probation or parole, and has or has not complied with the terms and conditions of probation or parole. (E) The perpetrator is restrained by a protective order or restraining order, and has or has not complied with its terms and conditions. (F) The perpetrator of domestic violence has committed further acts of domestic violence. (G) The court has determined, pursuant to Section 6322.5, that the perpetrator is a restrained person in possession or control of a firearm or ammunition in violation of Section 6389, Section 527.9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, or Section 18120 of the Penal Code.

clauses.title: A Parents' Custody Agreement Is Not Self-Executing
clauses.body: California law creates a presumption, affecting the burden of proof, that joint custody serves a minor child's best interest where the parents have agreed to joint custody or so agree in open court at a custody hearing — but that presumption is expressly made subject to the same best-interest factors the court otherwise applies. A parenting plan {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}} reach between themselves is therefore evidence the court considers alongside the statutory best-interest factors, not an order in itself; it takes legal effect for {{childName}} only once incorporated into an order entered by a court with jurisdiction over the matter.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a parents' custody agreement functions as a rebuttable presumption feeding into the court's own best-interest determination, rather than as an automatically binding private contract — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parenting plan or custody matter. How strongly, and whether, a state's law defers to parents' own custody agreements varies by state. This is a single statutory section (§ 3080); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3080 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the joint-custody agreement presumption
citations.quote: There is a presumption, affecting the burden of proof, that joint custody is in the best interest of a minor child, subject to Section 3011, where the parents have agreed to joint custody or so agree in open court at a hearing for the purpose of determining the custody of the minor child.

clauses.title: Modifying a Custody Order: Statute and Unwritten Doctrine
clauses.body: A joint custody order can be modified or terminated on the petition of either or both parents, or on the court's own motion, if it is shown that {{childName}}'s best interest requires the change; if either parent opposes the change, the statute requires the court to state its reasons for modifying or terminating the order.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the specific standard governing modification or termination of a joint custody order — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parenting plan or custody matter. Beyond this joint-custody-termination provision, California's general changed-circumstances practice for modifying custody orders is judicial doctrine developed by California courts, not codified in one clean statute; this research did not independently verify a case citation for that doctrine through the primary-source, twice-fetched discipline used elsewhere in this document, so none is offered here rather than presenting an unverified citation as verified. This is a single statutory section (§ 3087); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3087 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: modification or termination of a joint custody order
citations.quote: An order for joint custody may be modified or terminated upon the petition of one or both parents or on the court's own motion if it is shown that the best interest of the child requires modification or termination of the order. If either parent opposes the modification or termination order, the court shall state in its decision the reasons for modification or termination of the joint custody order.

clauses.title: Mediation Before a Contested Custody Hearing
clauses.body: Under California law, if it appears on the face of a petition, application, or other pleading seeking to obtain or modify a temporary or permanent custody or visitation order that custody, visitation, or both are contested, the court is required to set the contested issues for mediation.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific, mandatory pre-hearing mediation mechanism for contested custody or visitation matters — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parenting plan or custody dispute. Whether mediation is required, optional, or unavailable, and on what trigger, varies substantially by state. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 3170(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3170(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the mandatory mediation trigger
citations.quote: (a) If it appears on the face of a petition, application, or other pleading to obtain or modify a temporary or permanent custody or visitation order that custody, visitation, or both are contested, the court shall set the contested issues for mediation.

clauses.title: Equal Access to a Child's Records Regardless of Custody
clauses.body: Under California law, access to records and information about {{childName}} — including, but not limited to, medical, dental, and school records — is not to be denied to {{parent1Name}} or {{parent2Name}} merely because that parent does not hold custody. This rule applies notwithstanding other provisions of law.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific, self-executing records-access rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parenting plan or custody matter, and not a claim that no other statute or court order could ever limit this access. This research examined only the text of § 3025 itself and did not independently check for a separate statutory exception (for example, one tied to certain findings of abuse), so none is asserted here. This is a single statutory section (§ 3025); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3025 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the records-access rule
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other provision of law, access to records and information pertaining to a minor child, including, but not limited to, medical, dental, and school records, shall not be denied to a parent because that parent is not the child's custodial parent.

clauses.title: A Custodial Parent's Presumptive Right to Move a Child's Residence
clauses.body: In a different part of the Family Code than the custody chapter itself (Division 12, Parent and Child Relationship, rather than Division 8, Custody of Children), California law states that a parent entitled to custody of a child has a right to change the child's residence, subject to the power of the court to restrain a move that would prejudice the child's rights or welfare. The Legislature has stated its intent to affirm, and to declare as the public policy and law of the state, the California Supreme Court's decision in In re Marriage of Burgess (1996) 13 Cal.4th 25.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific presumptive relocation right for a custodial parent, expressly subject to a court's power to restrain a prejudicial move — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific relocation or parenting-plan dispute. This provision sits in a different Division of the Family Code than the custody definitions and best-interest standard cited elsewhere in this document, and its interaction with a joint-custody or shared-timeshare arrangement — along with the substantial body of California case law interpreting Burgess since 1996 — is not independently verified or restated here. Relocation and "move-away" rules vary widely by state, and some states codify a move-away standard directly rather than through a general residence-change provision like this one. This is a single statutory section (§ 7501); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7501(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the presumptive relocation right and the court's power to restrain it
citations.quote: (a) A parent entitled to the custody of a child has a right to change the residence of the child, subject to the power of the court to restrain a removal that would prejudice the rights or welfare of the child.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7501(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the legislative intent to affirm In re Marriage of Burgess
citations.quote: It is the intent of the Legislature to affirm the decision in In re Marriage of Burgess (1996) 13 Cal.4th 25, and to declare that ruling to be the public policy and law of this state.

clauses.title: Declaration of Parents and Child
clauses.body: This Parenting Plan is entered into by {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}} ("the parents") regarding their child, {{childName}}. This Plan sets out the parents' agreement regarding legal custody, physical custody, and a visitation and timeshare schedule for {{childName}}, subject to the review and approval of a court with jurisdiction over this matter.

clauses.title: Visitation and Timeshare Schedule
clauses.body:

Holiday, school-break, and other special-occasion schedules, where different from the regular schedule above, are set out separately below:

clauses.body:

This Parenting Plan becomes part of a court order only once reviewed and entered by a court with jurisdiction over {{childName}}'s custody.

clauses.title: Statewide Guideline Amount Is Presumptively Correct
clauses.body: Under California's child support statute, the amount produced by the statewide uniform guideline formula is presumed to be the correct amount of child support to be ordered. That presumption is rebuttable and affects the burden of proof — a party seeking a different amount carries the burden of showing, by admissible evidence, that applying the formula would be unjust or inappropriate given the specific circumstances. {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}} acknowledge that a support figure agreed between parents is not automatically the "correct" amount in the way this statute defines that term; it is an amount the parents propose regarding support for {{childName}}.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how a guideline-based child support system frames the relationship between an agreed number and a legally "correct" number — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific child support matter. Whether a guideline formula exists at all, whether it is rebuttable, and what burden of proof applies are all jurisdiction-specific and vary state to state. This is a single statutory section (§ 4057(a)-(b)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 4057(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the presumptive-correctness rule and its rebuttable burden
citations.quote: The amount of child support established by the formula provided in subdivision (a) of Section 4055 is presumed to be the correct amount of child support to be ordered.
