citations.quote: Any agreement by a lessee of a dwelling waiving or modifying his rights under Section 1941 or 1942 shall be void as contrary to public policy with respect to any condition which renders the premises untenantable, except that the lessor and the lessee may agree that the lessee shall undertake to improve, repair or maintain all or stipulated portions of the dwelling as part of the consideration for rental.

clauses.title: Commercial Security Deposits Are Regulated Differently, Not Left Unregulated
clauses.body: Commercial security deposits are governed by a separate, less protective statute than the residential one — Civil Code § 1950.7 — rather than being entirely unregulated. Section 1950.7 doesn't cap the amount a commercial landlord can charge as a deposit, and it doesn't require the itemized statement that Civil Code § 1950.5 requires for a residential deposit. But it does restrict what the deposit can be used for — unpaid rent, repairing tenant-caused damage, and cleaning at the end of the tenancy — and it does set return deadlines: if the landlord's only claim is for possible unpaid rent and the deposit (plus anything designated as last month's rent) is one month's rent or less, any unused balance must be returned within 30 days of the landlord regaining possession; if that rent-only deposit exceeds one month's rent, the excess over one month must be returned within two weeks, with the remainder returned or accounted for within 30 days; and if the landlord's claim includes damage repair or cleaning, any unused balance must be returned within 30 days. A landlord who retains a commercial deposit in bad faith is liable for the tenant's actual damages plus a statutory penalty of up to $200.
clauses.gap: This is worth stating precisely because it corrects a common assumption: California doesn't simply have no rule for commercial security deposits — it has a real statute, just a much thinner one than the residential statute. There is no deposit-amount cap, no photo-documentation duty, no pre-move-out inspection right, and the bad-faith penalty tops out at $200 rather than residential's up-to-double-the-deposit exposure. Because there's no statutory cap on amount, the deposit figure in a commercial lease is set entirely by negotiation. This is one state's statute; other states regulate commercial deposits differently, including some with no statute on the subject at all. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1950.7) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.7(a)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, scope of the commercial deposit statute
citations.quote: Any payment or deposit of money the primary function of which is to secure the performance of a rental agreement for other than residential property or any part of the agreement, other than a payment or deposit, including an advance payment of rent, made to secure the execution of a rental agreement, shall be governed by the provisions of this section. With respect to residential property, the provisions of Section 1950.5 shall prevail.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.7(c)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, permitted deductions and return deadlines
citations.quote: The landlord may claim of the payment or deposit only those amounts as are reasonably necessary to remedy tenant defaults in the payment of rent, to repair damages to the premises caused by the tenant, or to clean the premises upon termination of the tenancy, if the payment or deposit is made for any or all of those specific purposes. (1) If the claim of the landlord upon the payment or deposit is only for defaults in the payment of rent and the security deposit equals no more than one month's rent plus a deposit amount clearly described as the payment of the last month's rent, then any remaining portion of the payment or deposit shall be returned to the tenant at a time as may be mutually agreed upon by landlord and tenant, but in no event later than 30 days from the date the landlord receives possession of the premises.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.7(f)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, bad-faith retention penalty
citations.quote: The bad faith retention by a landlord or transferee of a payment or deposit or any portion thereof, in violation of this section, may subject the landlord or the transferee to damages not to exceed two hundred dollars ($200), in addition to any actual damages.

clauses.title: CASp Inspection Status Disclosure
clauses.body: A commercial property owner or lessor must state on every lease form or rental agreement executed on or after January 1, 2017, whether the premises have undergone inspection by a Certified Access Specialist (CASp). If the premises have not been issued a CASp disability access inspection certificate confirming compliance, the lease must include this exact statutory disclosure: "A Certified Access Specialist (CASp) can inspect the subject premises and determine whether the subject premises comply with all of the applicable construction-related accessibility standards under state law. Although state law does not require a CASp inspection of the subject premises, the commercial property owner or lessor may not prohibit the lessee or tenant from obtaining a CASp inspection of the subject premises for the occupancy or potential occupancy of the lessee or tenant, if requested by the lessee or tenant. The parties shall mutually agree on the arrangements for the time and manner of the CASp inspection, the payment of the fee for the CASp inspection, and the cost of making any repairs necessary to correct violations of construction-related accessibility standards within the premises."
clauses.gap: This applies to "commercial property" as this specific statute defines it — property offered for rent to someone operating, or intending to operate, a place of public accommodation, or a facility the general public is invited to — so it's aimed squarely at retail and public-facing space; the statute doesn't itself say whether it reaches every kind of non-public commercial lease (e.g., a private warehouse with no public access), and this document doesn't resolve that line. Separate rules apply if the premises have already been inspected and no impacting alterations have happened since (the CASp report must be shared with a confidentiality agreement, and a 72-hour rescission right applies if it isn't shared at least 48 hours before signing) — this clause's quoted paragraph is specifically for the no-certificate case. This is one state's statute; this particular pre-lease accessibility disclosure requirement is distinctive to California, not a nationwide practice. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1938) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1938(a)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the disclosure obligation
citations.quote: A commercial property owner or lessor shall state on every lease form or rental agreement executed on or after January 1, 2017, whether or not the subject premises have undergone inspection by a Certified Access Specialist (CASp).

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1938(e)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the required disclosure paragraph
citations.quote: If the subject premises have not been issued a disability access inspection certificate, as described in subdivision (e) of Section 55.53, the commercial property owner or lessor shall state the following on the lease form or rental agreement: "A Certified Access Specialist (CASp) can inspect the subject premises and determine whether the subject premises comply with all of the applicable construction-related accessibility standards under state law. Although state law does not require a CASp inspection of the subject premises, the commercial property owner or lessor may not prohibit the lessee or tenant from obtaining a CASp inspection of the subject premises for the occupancy or potential occupancy of the lessee or tenant, if requested by the lessee or tenant. The parties shall mutually agree on the arrangements for the time and manner of the CASp inspection, the payment of the fee for the CASp inspection, and the cost of making any repairs necessary to correct violations of construction-related accessibility standards within the premises."

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1938(f)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, definition of "commercial property" for this section
citations.quote: As used in this section, "commercial property" means property that is offered for rent or lease to persons operating, or intending to operate, a place of public accommodation as defined in Section 202 of Chapter 2 of Part 2 of Title 24 of the California Code of Regulations, or a facility to which the general public is invited, at those premises.

clauses.title: Tenant's Right to Request a CASp Inspection
clauses.body: Section 1938 doesn't just require a disclosure — it separately protects the tenant's ability to have the premises inspected. Even though state law doesn't require a CASp inspection, the statute states the landlord "may not prohibit the lessee or tenant from obtaining a CASp inspection of the subject premises for the occupancy or potential occupancy of the lessee or tenant, if requested by the lessee or tenant." The statute requires the parties to "mutually agree on the arrangements for the time and manner of the CASp inspection, the payment of the fee for the CASp inspection, and the cost of making any repairs necessary" — meaning the statute itself does not assign that cost to either party by default; it's left to negotiation. Separately, if a CASp inspection has already happened and turned up violations, the statute presumes the landlord bears the cost of fixing them, "unless otherwise mutually agreed upon by the commercial property owner or lessor and the lessee or tenant."
clauses.gap: The task of confirming "who bears the cost" of a tenant-requested inspection has an honest answer that cuts against a natural assumption: the statute does not say the tenant pays for it. It requires the landlord and tenant to mutually agree on the fee, the timing, and the manner of the inspection — cost-shifting isn't automatic in either direction under this statute. What the statute does presume by default is that the landlord bears the cost of fixing violations an inspection turns up, unless the parties agree otherwise. This is one state's statute. All citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1938) as the CASp disclosure clause elsewhere in this document; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1938(e) [inspection right]
citations.cite: California Civil Code, tenant's right to request an inspection and cost/time arrangements
citations.quote: the commercial property owner or lessor may not prohibit the lessee or tenant from obtaining a CASp inspection of the subject premises for the occupancy or potential occupancy of the lessee or tenant, if requested by the lessee or tenant. The parties shall mutually agree on the arrangements for the time and manner of the CASp inspection, the payment of the fee for the CASp inspection, and the cost of making any repairs necessary to correct violations of construction-related accessibility standards within the premises.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1938(c)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, default responsibility for repairs found in an existing CASp report
citations.quote: Making any repairs or modifications necessary to correct violations of construction-related accessibility standards that are noted in a CASp report is presumed to be the responsibility of the commercial property owner or lessor, unless otherwise mutually agreed upon by the commercial property owner or lessor and the lessee or tenant.

clauses.title: Notice to End a Commercial Tenancy
clauses.body: For a periodic (e.g., month-to-month) commercial tenancy with no fixed end date, Civil Code § 1946 sets a default notice period of 30 days from either party to terminate — the same general default statute that applies to any periodic tenancy of real property, residential or commercial, unless the parties agree in the lease to a shorter period (as little as seven days). A narrower statute, Civil Code § 1946.1, extends the longer, residential-style 60-day (or 30-day, for a tenancy under a year) notice period to a "qualified commercial tenant" specifically — defined as a tenant that is a microenterprise, a restaurant with fewer than 10 employees, or a nonprofit with fewer than 20 employees, that has given the landlord a required written self-attestation of that status. Outside that narrow category, an ordinary commercial tenant gets the 30-day default under § 1946, not the 60-day residential-style period. For ending a tenancy for cause — nonpayment of rent or a lease breach — the same unlawful detainer statute used for residential tenancies, Code of Civil Procedure § 1161, applies to commercial tenancies too: it requires three days' written notice (excluding judicial holidays) to pay rent or quit, or to cure a covenant breach or quit, before an unlawful detainer action can be filed, because § 1161 applies broadly to "a tenant of real property," not only a residential dwelling unit. California law even sets out a separate set of notice-service methods specifically for a "commercial tenant" under Code of Civil Procedure § 1162, confirming the legislature understands this statute to reach commercial tenancies directly.
clauses.gap: This describes the statutory floor, not the whole picture — a fixed-term commercial lease typically states its own notice-and-cure terms, and none of this analysis governs a fixed-term lease that simply expires by its own stated end date (though the lease may separately require notice of intent to renew or vacate). Whether a specific tenant actually qualifies as a "qualified commercial tenant" under § 1946.1 depends on facts (entity type, employee count, and whether the required written self-attestation was actually given) that this document doesn't evaluate. This is one state's statutes, current as of a January 1, 2025 amendment that extended § 1946.1 to qualified commercial tenants for the first time — notice requirements for ending a commercial tenancy vary significantly by state, and some states impose no statutory notice floor at all for a commercial periodic tenancy. Two of the citations below (§ 1946.1(b)-(c) and § 1946.1(k)(4)) are subsections of the same statutory section, as are two others (§ 1161(2) and § 1161(7)); together, the citations below draw from four independently enacted statutes — §§ 1946, 1946.1, 1161, and 1162 — not one source restated multiple times.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1946
citations.cite: California Civil Code, default 30-day notice to end a periodic tenancy of real property
citations.quote: A hiring of real property, for a term not specified by the parties, is deemed to be renewed as stated in Section 1945, at the end of the term implied by law unless one of the parties gives written notice to the other of that party's intention to terminate the same, at least as long before the expiration thereof as the term of the hiring itself, not exceeding 30 days; provided, however, that as to tenancies from month to month either of the parties may terminate the same by giving at least 30 days' written notice thereof at any time and the rent shall be due and payable to and including the date of termination. It shall be competent for the parties to provide by an agreement at the time the tenancy is created that a notice of the intention to terminate the same may be given at any time not less than seven days before the expiration of the term thereof.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.1(b)-(c)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, extended 60/30-day notice for a qualified commercial tenant
citations.quote: An owner of a residential dwelling or commercial real property hired by a qualified commercial tenant giving notice pursuant to this section shall give notice at least 60 days prior to the proposed date of termination. A tenant giving notice pursuant to this section shall give notice for a period at least as long as the term of the periodic tenancy prior to the proposed date of termination... an owner of a residential dwelling or commercial real property hired by a qualified commercial tenant giving notice pursuant to this section shall give notice at least 30 days prior to the proposed date of termination if a tenant or resident has resided in the dwelling or occupied the property for less than one year.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.1(k)(4)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, definition of "qualified commercial tenant"
citations.quote: "Qualified commercial tenant" means a tenant of commercial real property that meets both of the following requirements: (A) The tenant is a microenterprise, a restaurant with fewer than 10 employees, or a nonprofit organization with fewer than 20 employees. (B) (i) Subject to clause (ii), the tenant has provided the landlord, within the previous 12 months, a written notice that the tenant is a qualified commercial tenant and a self-attestation regarding the number of employees, at such time the protections under this section come into place.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161(2)
citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, three-day pay-rent-or-quit notice
citations.quote: When the tenant continues in possession, in person or by subtenant, without the permission of the landlord, or the successor in estate of the landlord, if applicable, after default in the payment of rent, pursuant to the lease or agreement under which the property is held, and three days' notice, excluding Saturdays and Sundays and other judicial holidays, in writing, requiring its payment, stating the amount that is due... or possession of the property, shall have been served upon the tenant and if there is a subtenant in actual occupation of the premises, also upon the subtenant.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161(7)
citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, this notice statute is not limited to dwellings
citations.quote: As used in this section, "tenant" includes any person who hires real property except those persons whose occupancy is described in subdivision (b) of Section 1940 of the Civil Code.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1162(b)-(c)
citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, separate service methods and definition for a commercial tenant
citations.quote: The notices required by Section 1161 may be served upon a commercial tenant by any of the following methods: (1) By delivering a copy to the tenant personally. (2) If he or she is absent from the commercial rental property, by leaving a copy with some person of suitable age and discretion at the property, and sending a copy through the mail addressed to the tenant at the address where the property is situated... For purposes of subdivision (b), "commercial tenant" means a person or entity that hires any real property in this state that is not a dwelling unit, as defined in subdivision (c) of Section 1940 of the Civil Code, or a mobilehome, as defined in Section 798.3 of the Civil Code.

clauses.title: Personal Guaranties Are General Contract Law, Not a Commercial-Lease-Specific Statute
clauses.body: California has no statute written specifically for a personal guaranty of a commercial lease. What applies instead is the general contract-law statute of frauds: Civil Code § 1624(a)(2) makes "a special promise to answer for the debt, default, or miscarriage of another" — which is what a personal guaranty of a tenant entity's lease obligations is — unenforceable "unless they, or some note or memorandum thereof, are in writing and subscribed by the party to be charged or by the party's agent." Separately, the lease itself, if for a term longer than one year, independently must be in writing under Civil Code § 1624(a)(3).
clauses.gap: This is an honest gap in the sense the task asked to check for: there is no commercial-lease-specific guaranty statute in California comparable to, say, the CASp disclosure requirement. A personal guaranty of a commercial lease is enforced, or not, under the same general statute-of-frauds and suretyship principles that apply to a personal guaranty of any other kind of debt or obligation — principles found in Civil Code § 1624 and in the general suretyship statutes (Civil Code §§ 2787 et seq.), which this document doesn't otherwise cover. This is one state's statute of frauds; every state has some version of a statute of frauds covering a promise to answer for another's debt, but the exact wording and exceptions vary. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1624) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1624(a)(2)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, statute of frauds for a promise to answer for another's debt
citations.quote: The following contracts are invalid, unless they, or some note or memorandum thereof, are in writing and subscribed by the party to be charged or by the party's agent... (2) A special promise to answer for the debt, default, or miscarriage of another, except in the cases provided for in Section 2794.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1624(a)(3)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, statute of frauds for a lease longer than one year
citations.quote: An agreement for the leasing for a longer period than one year, or for the sale of real property, or of an interest therein; such an agreement, if made by an agent of the party sought to be charged, is invalid, unless the authority of the agent is in writing, subscribed by the party sought to be charged.

clauses.title: Parties, Premises, and Rent
clauses.body: This is a commercial lease agreement between {{landlordName}} ("Landlord") and {{tenantName}} ("Tenant") for the commercial premises located at {{propertyAddress}}. The lease term runs from {{leaseStartDate}} to {{leaseEndDate}}. Tenant will pay Landlord base rent of ${{monthlyRent}} per month, due on the day of each month specified in this agreement, payable by the method specified in this agreement. This lease is for commercial, non-residential use of the premises only. It does not create a residential tenancy, and the statutory protections that apply specifically to residential tenancies under California law do not apply to it.

clauses.title: Use of Premises
clauses.body: Tenant may use the premises only for the following purpose(s): {{permittedUse}} (the "Permitted Use"), and for no other purpose without Landlord's prior written consent. Confirming that the Permitted Use complies with applicable zoning, building, health, safety, and accessibility requirements for the premises is Tenant's responsibility.

clauses.title: Signatures
clauses.body:
Signed:

Landlord: ☐ _________________________ Date: _______________

Tenant: ☐ _________________________ Date: _______________

Guarantor (if applicable): ☐ _________________________ Date: _______________

A personal guaranty of Tenant's obligations under this lease is a separate promise that California law requires to be set out in a signed writing of its own; an individual's signature on this lease in a representative capacity for a business-entity Tenant does not, by itself, create a personal guaranty of that entity's obligations.

clauses.title: The Settlor's Statutory Power to Modify a Revocable Trust
clauses.body: Once {{trustName}} exists as a trust revocable by {{settlorName}}, California's Probate Code gives {{settlorName}} an independent statutory power to modify it, separate from the power to revoke it outright. Unless {{trustName}}'s own instrument provides otherwise, {{settlorName}} may modify {{trustName}} by following the same procedure the Probate Code provides for revoking it.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual statutory basis for a settlor's power to modify a revocable trust -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. The statute's current text is a single sentence, and that sentence does not itself offer 'a signed writing delivered to the trustee' as one alternative among several, with an additional catch-all allowing modification by any method that shows clear and convincing evidence of the settlor's intent. That broader 'clear and convincing evidence of intent' standard appears in some other states' trust statutes and in the Restatement (Third) of Trusts, but was not found in the current text of California Probate Code section 15402 itself -- so this document does not attribute that language to section 15402. What the modification power actually incorporates is whatever procedure a separate statute sets out for revocation, quoted in a different clause of this document. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 15402); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15402 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the settlor's statutory power to modify a revocable trust
citations.quote: Unless the trust instrument provides otherwise, if a trust is revocable by the settlor, the settlor may modify the trust by the procedure for revocation.

clauses.title: The Procedure for Revocation, Incorporated by Reference for Modification
clauses.body: Because {{trustName}}'s modification power works 'by the procedure for revocation,' the specific procedure that power incorporates comes from a separate Probate Code section governing revocation. That section provides two routes: compliance with whatever revocation method {{trustName}}'s own instrument sets out, or -- if {{trustName}}'s instrument doesn't make its own method the exclusive one -- a writing, other than a will, signed by {{settlorName}} and delivered to {{trusteeName}} during {{settlorName}}'s lifetime.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual procedure California's modification statute incorporates by reference -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This same statutory section, Probate Code section 15401, is also the source for a separate clause of this document addressing a trust with more than one settlor; that clause quotes a different subdivision -- (b) -- of this same section, rather than an independent source, and this disclosure is made there as well. A further subdivision of this section, (e), also states that a trust created by an instrument executed before July 1, 1987 is governed by prior law rather than by this section; this document does not independently research what that prior law required.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15401(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the statutory methods of revocation, incorporated by section 15402 for modification
citations.quote: (a) A trust that is revocable by the settlor or any other person may be revoked in whole or in part by any of the following methods: (1) By compliance with any method of revocation provided in the trust instrument. (2) By a writing, other than a will, signed by the settlor or any other person holding the power of revocation and delivered to the trustee during the lifetime of the settlor or the person holding the power of revocation. If the trust instrument explicitly makes the method of revocation provided in the trust instrument the exclusive method of revocation, the trust may not be revoked pursuant to this paragraph.

clauses.title: When the Trust Instrument Makes Its Own Amendment Method Exclusive
clauses.body: If {{trustName}}'s own instrument states, in explicit terms, that its stated amendment or revocation method is the exclusive method, then the fallback method -- a signed writing delivered to {{trusteeName}} -- is not available; only the method the instrument itself specifies will do. A published California Court of Appeal decision, applying this same statutory framework, has summarized the rule this way: a trust may be revoked by complying with any method the trust instrument provides; if the instrument explicitly makes that method exclusive, the trust may be revoked only in that manner; if not, the trust may also be revoked by a writing, signed by the settlor and delivered to the trustee; and unless the trust provides otherwise, a trust may be modified by these same revocation procedures.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on the same Probate Code section 15401(a)(2) 'exclusive method' language already quoted in a separate clause of this document addressing the general revocation procedure, plus one independent source: a published California Court of Appeal decision, not a California Supreme Court decision. A search for a California Supreme Court decision squarely deciding whether a trust instrument's stated amendment method can be made exclusive did not turn up one on that specific question -- the most relevant California Supreme Court decision this search located, Donkin v. Donkin (2013) 58 Cal.4th 412, addresses a different question (how post-2010 no-contest-clause law applies to a trust amendment), not the exclusive-method question, so it is not cited here. The Court of Appeal decision quoted here, Huscher v. Wells Fargo Bank (2004) 121 Cal.App.4th 956, states the current-law rule in an overview passage, but the trust at issue in that case was created before July 1, 1987, so the court's actual holding turned on interpreting a prior Civil Code provision rather than on Probate Code sections 15401-15402 directly; the quoted passage is the court's own description of 'current law,' not the basis of its holding in that case. This is one state's case law and statute, used as real evidence -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust.

citations.case: Huscher v. Wells Fargo Bank (2004) 121 Cal.App.4th 956 (California Court of Appeal, Second Appellate District)
citations.cite: overview of the exclusive-method rule under Probate Code sections 15401-15402
citations.quote: Under current law, a trust may be revoked by complying with any method provided in the trust instrument. (Prob. Code, § 15401, subd. (a)(1).) If the trust explicitly makes that method exclusive, then it may be revoked only in that manner. If not, then the trust may also be revoked by a writing, other than a will, signed by the trustor and delivered to the trustee while the trustor is alive. (Prob. Code, § 15401, subd. (a)(2).) Unless the trust provides otherwise, the trust may be modified by the revocation procedures of Probate Code section 15401. (Prob. Code, § 15402.)

clauses.title: The Capacity Standard for Amending a Trust
clauses.body: The Probate Code sets a general legal-capacity standard that, by its own terms, applies to a person's capacity 'to execute trusts,' among other acts. That general standard applies 'except where otherwise provided by law' -- and the statute setting that general standard itself lists 'the statutory and decisional law of testamentary capacity' as an example of law that can displace it. A published California Court of Appeal decision has held that when a settlor's trust amendment, in its content and complexity, closely resembles a will or codicil, it is that lower, will-specific testamentary-capacity standard -- not the Probate Code's general capacity statute standing alone -- that a court should use to evaluate the settlor's capacity to make the amendment.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute and case law, used as real evidence of how California determines the capacity standard applicable to a trust amendment -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust amendment, or about the capacity of any specific person to amend a specific trust. The Court of Appeal decision quoted here, Andersen v. Hunt (2011) 196 Cal.App.4th 722, held that the will-specific standard (Probate Code section 6100.5) applies to a trust amendment only because it is incorporated through Probate Code section 811, subdivision (b) -- the court expressly said that section 6100.5 'is not directly applicable to determine competency to make or amend a trust' on its own, and that whether the will-specific standard controls a given amendment can depend on how closely, 'in its content and complexity,' that amendment resembles a will or codicil. This document does not attempt to resolve that content-and-complexity question for any particular amendment. This is a Court of Appeal decision, not a California Supreme Court decision; this search did not identify a California Supreme Court decision resolving the same question.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 812 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the general capacity standard and its carve-out for testamentary-capacity law
citations.quote: Except where otherwise provided by law, including, but not limited to, Section 813 and the statutory and decisional law of testamentary capacity, a person lacks the capacity to make a decision unless the person has the ability to communicate verbally, or by any other means, the decision, and to understand and appreciate, to the extent relevant, all of the following: (a) The rights, duties, and responsibilities created by, or affected by the decision. (b) The probable consequences for the decisionmaker and, where appropriate, the persons affected by the decision. (c) The significant risks, benefits, and reasonable alternatives involved in the decision.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 811(a), (b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the general-capacity evidentiary standard, expressly covering the act of executing a trust
citations.quote: (a) A determination that a person is of unsound mind or lacks the capacity to make a decision or do a certain act, including, but not limited to, the incapacity to contract, to make a conveyance, to marry, to make medical decisions, to execute wills, or to execute trusts, shall be supported by evidence of a deficit in at least one of the following mental functions, subject to subdivision (b), and evidence of a correlation between the deficit or deficits and the decision or acts in question: ... (b) A deficit in the mental functions listed above may be considered only if the deficit, by itself or in combination with one or more other mental function deficits, significantly impairs the person's ability to understand and appreciate the consequences of his or her actions with regard to the type of act or decision in question.

citations.case: Andersen v. Hunt (2011) 196 Cal.App.4th 722 (California Court of Appeal, Second Appellate District)
citations.cite: holding that the testamentary-capacity standard applies to a trust amendment resembling a will or codicil, via section 811(b)
citations.quote: When determining whether a trustor had capacity to execute a trust amendment that, in its content and complexity, closely resembles a will or codicil, we believe it is appropriate to look to section 6100.5 to determine when a person's mental deficits are sufficient to allow a court to conclude that the person lacks the ability 'to understand and appreciate the consequences of his or her actions with regard to the type of act or decision in question.' (§ 811, subd. (b).) In other words, while section 6100.5 is not directly applicable to determine competency to make or amend a trust, it is made applicable through section 811 to trusts or trust amendments that are analogous to wills or codicils.

clauses.title: A Trust With More Than One Settlor
clauses.body: If a trust has more than one settlor -- as is common for a married couple's joint trust -- the same statute that supplies the default modification procedure also addresses, separately from the single-settlor case, what each settlor may do on their own. Unless the trust instrument provides otherwise, where a trust is created by more than one settlor, each settlor may revoke -- and, through the modification statute's cross-reference, modify -- the trust as to the portion of the trust that settlor contributed, subject to a Family Code provision governing community property. A settlor may also grant another person, including a spouse, a power to revoke or modify all or part of that settlor's own contributed portion.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's revocation-and-modification statute addresses a trust with more than one settlor -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific joint trust, and not a claim about how any specific joint trust's own terms should be read. This clause quotes subdivision (b) of Probate Code section 15401, the same statutory section already quoted (subdivision (a)) in a separate clause of this document addressing the single-settlor default procedure; it is presented as its own clause because subdivision (b) addresses a distinct question. The statute's cross-reference to Family Code section 761, governing community property held in trust, is not independently quoted or researched here. Beyond this subdivision, no additional statute specific to joint or shared trusts addressing modification was located; whether unanimous consent, majority action, or some other rule applies to jointly contributed or community property held in a specific joint trust can depend on that trust's own terms and on the community-property characterization of the property involved, neither of which this document resolves.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15401(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: revocation and modification where a trust has more than one settlor
citations.quote: (b) (1) Unless otherwise provided in the instrument, if a trust is created by more than one settlor, each settlor may revoke the trust as to the portion of the trust contributed by that settlor, except as provided in Section 761 of the Family Code. (2) Notwithstanding paragraph (1), a settlor may grant to another person, including, but not limited to, his or her spouse, a power to revoke all or part of that portion of the trust contributed by that settlor, regardless of whether that portion was separate property or community property of that settlor, and regardless of whether that power to revoke is exercisable during the lifetime of that settlor or continues after the death of that settlor, or both.

clauses.title: 'Amendment' Versus 'Restatement' Is a Drafting Convention, Not a Separate Statute
clauses.body: California's Probate Code does not use or define the term 'restatement' anywhere in its trust-modification provisions. Whether a settlor changes a trust by executing a document labeled an 'amendment' that alters specific provisions, or by executing a document labeled an 'amendment and restatement' that replaces the entire body of the trust instrument while keeping the same underlying trust in existence, both are exercises of the same statutory modification power: the settlor's ability, unless the trust instrument provides otherwise, to modify the trust by the procedure for revocation. The choice between amending discrete provisions and restating the whole instrument is a drafting convention, not a distinct legal mechanism with its own statutory requirements.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California's trust-modification statute does not distinguish between an 'amendment' and a 'restatement' as separate legal categories -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This clause quotes the same single-sentence statute, Probate Code section 15402, already quoted in full in a separate clause of this document addressing the general statutory basis for modification; it is repeated here only because this clause makes a distinct point about that statute's scope -- that it does not carve out 'restatement' as something different from 'modification' -- and no independent second source using 'restatement' as a term of art was located in the statute itself.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15402 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the modification power, which does not distinguish 'amendment' from 'restatement'
citations.quote: Unless the trust instrument provides otherwise, if a trust is revocable by the settlor, the settlor may modify the trust by the procedure for revocation.

clauses.title: Declaration Identifying the Original Trust and the Amendment
clauses.body: I, {{settlorName}}, of {{settlorCounty}} County, California, as settlor, declare this instrument to be an amendment to the {{trustName}}, dated {{originalTrustDate}} (the "Trust"). I identify below the specific provision(s) of the Trust that this amendment adds, deletes, or amends, and the new text of each: ☐ _________________________. This amendment is effective as of {{amendmentDate}}.

clauses.title: Ratification of All Other Trust Provisions
clauses.body: Except as specifically changed by this amendment, I confirm that all other provisions of the Trust remain unchanged and in full force and effect. This amendment does not revoke the Trust; the Trust, as amended by this instrument and by any prior amendments, continues without interruption.

clauses.title: Signature and Notarization
clauses.body:
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, {{settlorName}}, as settlor, has signed this amendment to {{trustName}} on the date written below.

_________________________ Date: _________________________
{{settlorName}}, Settlor

Delivery of a signed writing to {{trusteeName}} is one of the statutory methods described elsewhere in this document for satisfying the procedure that California's modification statute incorporates, unless {{trustName}}'s own instrument makes a different method exclusive.

A notary public or other officer completing a notarial certificate for this instrument verifies only the identity of the individual who signed the document, not the truthfulness, accuracy, or validity of that document.

clauses.title: The Statutory Grant Deed Form and Fee-Simple Presumption
clauses.body: California's Civil Code sets out a statutory short form for "a grant of an estate in real property," built around the operative word "grant": "I, A B, grant to C D all that real property situated in (insert name of county) County, State of California, bounded (or described) as follows: ..." This deed, conveying the interest of {{grantorName}} to {{granteeName}} in the real property at {{propertyAddress}}, uses that same operative word "grant." Separately, California law presumes that a grant of real property is intended to pass fee simple title — full ownership, rather than some lesser interest such as a life estate or a term of years — unless the grant itself shows that a lesser estate was intended.
clauses.gap: §§ 1092 and 1105 are genuinely separate statutory sections within the same Civil Code chapter (Article 1, Mode of Transfer, and Article 2, Effect of Transfer, respectively), treated here as two independent sources. This is California's own statutory grant-deed form and fee-simple presumption, used as real evidence of how this state's law treats a conveyance that uses the word "grant" — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular transfer, or about whether another state uses the same terminology or presumption. § 1092's statutory form is optional wording ("may be made in substance as follows"); California law does not require a grant deed to track that exact form, only that it use operative language of grant, and this clause does not evaluate whether any particular deed's actual wording qualifies.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1092
citations.cite: California Civil Code, statutory form of a grant of an estate in real property
citations.quote: A grant of an estate in real property may be made in substance as follows: “I, A B, grant to C D all that real property situated in (insert name of county) County, State of California, bounded (or described) as follows: (here insert property description, or if the land sought to be conveyed has a descriptive name, it may be described by the name, as for instance, ‘The Norris Ranch.’) Witness my hand this (insert day) day of (insert month), 20___. _____ AB”

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1105
citations.cite: California Civil Code, fee-simple title presumed from a grant
citations.quote: A fee simple title is presumed to be intended to pass by a grant of real property, unless it appears from the grant that a lesser estate was intended.

clauses.title: Implied Statutory Covenants of a Grant Deed
clauses.body: Because this deed conveys {{grantorName}}'s interest in the real property at {{propertyAddress}} using the word "grant," California law implies two specific covenants on {{grantorName}}'s part, running to {{granteeName}} and to {{granteeName}}'s heirs and assigns, unless the deed's own express terms restrain them: first, that before signing this deed {{grantorName}} has not already conveyed the same estate, or any right, title, or interest in it, to anyone other than {{granteeName}}; and second, that the estate is, as of the date this deed is signed, free from encumbrances done, made, or suffered by {{grantorName}} or anyone claiming under {{grantorName}}. California law states that these are the only covenants implied from the word "grant" — "the following covenants, and none other" — and that they may be sued upon in the same manner as if they had been expressly written into the deed.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory section (§ 1113); no additional independent statutory source was found for these two implied covenants specifically, and that gap is disclosed here rather than filled with a second citation to a different subsection of the same section. This is California's own implied-covenant rule tied to the word "grant" — used as real evidence of what this state's law implies from that word — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular deed; which words of conveyance, if any, imply covenants of title, and what those covenants cover, vary from state to state. These statutory covenants are narrower than a general warranty of title: their text does not cover an encumbrance created by someone other than the grantor (for example, a prior owner), and it says nothing about matters of public record, boundary disputes, or title defects that do not arise from the grantor's own acts. This clause does not evaluate whether either covenant is in fact breached on the facts of any specific transfer.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1113
citations.cite: California Civil Code, covenants implied from the word "grant"
citations.quote: From the use of the word “grant” in any conveyance by which an estate of inheritance or fee simple is to be passed, the following covenants, and none other, on the part of the grantor for himself and his heirs to the grantee, his heirs, and assigns, are implied, unless restrained by express terms contained in such conveyance: 1. That previous to the time of the execution of such conveyance, the grantor has not conveyed the same estate, or any right, title, or interest therein, to any person other than the grantee; 2. That such estate is at the time of the execution of such conveyance free from incumbrances done, made, or suffered by the grantor, or any person claiming under him. Such covenants may be sued upon in the same manner as if they had been expressly inserted in the conveyance.

clauses.title: After-Acquired Title Passes Automatically
clauses.body: If {{grantorName}} signs this deed purporting to grant the real property at {{propertyAddress}} in fee simple, but does not yet hold full title to it at that time, and {{grantorName}} later acquires title or a claim of title to that property, California law passes that later-acquired title automatically — by operation of law — to {{granteeName}} or {{granteeName}}'s successors, without requiring {{grantorName}} to sign a new deed.
clauses.gap: The research brief that prompted this clause pointed to Civil Code § 1105 for the after-acquired-title rule. Direct review of the statutory text shows that citation is incorrect: § 1105 states a different rule — that a grant of real property is presumed to convey fee simple unless the grant shows a lesser estate was intended — and that rule is addressed in a separate clause. The after-acquired-title rule is instead stated in the next section, § 1106, quoted below; that correction is disclosed here rather than silently carried forward. This is a single statutory section (§ 1106); no additional independent statutory source was found for the after-acquired-title rule itself. This is California's own after-acquired-title rule, tied to an instrument that "purports to grant" property in fee simple, used as real evidence of how this state's law treats that situation — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular transfer or a particular grantor's later-acquired interest, and not every state applies an equivalent doctrine, or applies it identically, to every type of deed.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1106
citations.cite: California Civil Code, after-acquired title passes by operation of law
citations.quote: Where a person purports by proper instrument to grant real property in fee simple, and subsequently acquires any title, or claim of title thereto, the same passes by operation of law to the grantee, or his successors.

clauses.title: Granting Clause and Property Declaration
clauses.body: {{grantorName}} ("Grantor") hereby GRANTS to {{granteeName}} ("Grantee") all of Grantor's right, title, and interest in the real property located at {{propertyAddress}}, together with all improvements, tenements, hereditaments, and appurtenances belonging to it. This deed's use of the word "grant" carries the statutory covenants and fee-simple presumption described elsewhere in this document. It is not a general warranty of title, and it does not by itself guarantee that Grantor holds any particular interest in the property beyond what those statutory covenants state.

clauses.title: Legal Description and Assessor's Parcel Number
clauses.body: The real property this deed grants is more particularly described as follows, and this legal description controls if it differs from the street address given above: {{legalDescription}}. This deed also references Assessor's Parcel Number {{parcelNumber}}, provided for identification only and not as part of the legal description.

clauses.title: Signature, Notarial Acknowledgment, and Recording
clauses.body:
SIGNATURE AND DATE: {{grantorName}} signs and dates this deed below; the name should exactly match the name shown on the property's current title documents.

Signature of {{grantorName}}: _________________________ Date: _______________

ACKNOWLEDGMENT OF NOTARY: A notary public or other officer completing this certificate verifies only the identity of the individual who signed the document to which this certificate is attached, and not the truthfulness, accuracy, or validity of that document.

State of California ) County of _________________________ )

On _________________________ before me, _________________________ (here insert name and title of the officer), personally appeared _________________________, who proved to me on the basis of satisfactory evidence to be the person(s) whose name(s) is/are subscribed to the within instrument and acknowledged to me that they executed the same in their authorized capacity(ies), and that by their signature(s) on the instrument the person(s), or the entity upon behalf of which the person(s) acted, executed the instrument. I certify under PENALTY OF PERJURY under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing paragraph is true and correct.

WITNESS my hand and official seal.

Signature: _________________________ (Seal)

RECORDING: This deed transfers {{grantorName}}'s interest, together with the statutory covenants described above, to {{granteeName}} once it is validly signed and delivered; it is not recorded automatically upon signing. Recording is a separate step: presenting the signed, notarized deed to the county recorder in the county where the property is located, together with any required Preliminary Change of Ownership Report and any applicable documentary transfer tax.

clauses.title: This Petition Information Sheet Describes a Court Proceeding, Not a Nomination Document
clauses.body: A guardianship of the person of {{childName}} under California law is established only through an actual court proceeding under Probate Code Division 4, Part 2 — a filed petition, notice, and a hearing that ends in a court order — not by a private nomination document or affidavit. California Probate Code § 1510(a) authorizes "a relative or other person on behalf of the minor, or the minor if 12 years of age or older," to file the petition that starts that proceeding.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a guardianship of a minor's person is created only through an actual court proceeding — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. This document is informational: it describes the statutory guardianship-of-the-person petition process and does not itself appoint, nominate, or authorize anyone as guardian of the child named in this document. That distinction matters because a related, separately available document — a parent's own advance nomination of a guardian for their minor children, made in a will or a standalone signed writing under Probate Code §§ 1500 and 1502, or California's no-court Caregiver's Authorization Affidavit under Family Code §§ 6550–6552 — addresses a different mechanism entirely: a parent's advance designation, or a caregiver's limited authority without any court filing. This document instead addresses the separate, real court process by which a proposed guardian actually becomes a court-appointed guardian of a minor's person; it does not restate that companion document's content. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1510(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1510(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1510(a)
citations.quote: A relative or other person on behalf of the minor, or the minor if 12 years of age or older, may file a petition for the appointment of a guardian of the minor. A relative may file a petition for the appointment of a guardian under this section regardless of the relative’s immigration status.

clauses.title: What the Petition Must Say, and Who Must Be Notified
clauses.body: The petition to appoint a guardian of {{childName}}'s person must specify the proposed guardian's name and address and {{childName}}'s name and date of birth, and must state that the appointment is necessary or convenient. So far as known to the petitioner, the petition must also list the names and addresses of {{childName}}'s parents and of any person who has legal custody or care of {{childName}}. At least 15 days before the hearing, notice of the hearing's time and place — together with a copy of the petition — must be served on {{childName}} personally if {{childName}} is 12 years of age or older, on any person having legal custody of {{childName}} or serving as guardian of {{childName}}'s estate, on {{childName}}'s parents, and on any person previously nominated as guardian for {{childName}} under Probate Code § 1500 or § 1501.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the petition-content and notice requirements for a guardianship-of-the-person proceeding — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petition. Two of these citations (§ 1510(b) and § 1510(c)) are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1510); no additional independent source beyond § 1510 itself was found for the specific list of petition contents. The notice-recipient list is independently sourced from a separate section, § 1511, whose own two cited subsections — § 1511(a) and § 1511(b) — are likewise subsections of that single section (§ 1511); no additional independent source beyond § 1511 itself was found for that list. The statute also lets a court excuse notice to a specific person on findings this clause does not describe.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1510(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1510(b)
citations.quote: The petition shall request that a guardian of the person or estate of the minor, or both, be appointed, shall specify the name and address of the proposed guardian and the name and date of birth of the proposed ward, and shall state that the appointment is necessary or convenient.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1510(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1510(c)
citations.quote: The petition shall set forth, so far as is known to the petitioner, the names and addresses of all of the following: (1) The parents of the proposed ward. (2) The person having legal custody of the proposed ward and, if that person does not have the care of the proposed ward, the person having the care of the proposed ward.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1511(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1511(a)
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivisions (f) and (g), at least 15 days before the hearing on the petition for the appointment of a guardian, notice of the time and place of the hearing shall be given as provided in subdivisions (b), (c), (d), and (e) of this section. The notice shall be accompanied by a copy of the petition and shall include a copy of the form required by Section 68511.1 of the Government Code. The court shall not shorten the time for giving the notice of hearing under this section.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1511(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1511(b)
citations.quote: Notice shall be served in the manner provided in Section 415.10 or 415.30 of the Code of Civil Procedure, or in any manner authorized by the court, on all of the following persons: (1) The proposed ward if 12 years of age or older. (2) Any person having legal custody of the proposed ward, or serving as guardian of the estate of the proposed ward. (3) The parents of the proposed ward. (4) Any person nominated as a guardian for the proposed ward under Section 1500 or 1501.

clauses.title: The Court Investigator or Agency Report Required Before Appointment
clauses.body: Unless waived by the court for good cause, a court investigator, probation officer, or domestic relations investigator must investigate and file a report and recommendation on a proposed guardianship of {{childName}}'s person before the court rules on the petition. If the proposed guardian is a relative, a court investigator conducts the investigation; if the proposed guardian is not a relative, the county agency designated to investigate potential dependency conducts it instead. That report must discuss, among other required topics, a social history of the proposed guardian, a social history of {{childName}} including any identified developmental, emotional, psychological, or educational needs, the relationship between {{childName}} and the proposed guardian, and the duration of the guardianship anticipated by the parents and the proposed guardian.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a real pre-appointment investigation requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 1513(a)); no additional independent source was found for this. This corrects an initial research assumption in the task brief that framed the investigation requirement as arising under § 1514: on the actual statutory text, § 1513 is the investigation-and-report provision, while § 1514 instead sets out the standard the court applies in deciding whether, and whom, to appoint — covered in this document's companion clause on appointment priority. Separately, § 1513(b) describes a narrower, additional referral to the local child welfare agency when the proposed ward may be a dependent child described in Welfare and Institutions Code § 300; that narrower referral mechanism is not covered by this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1513(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1513(a)
citations.quote: Unless waived by the court for good cause, a court investigator, probation officer, or domestic relations investigator shall make an investigation and file with the court a report and recommendation concerning each proposed guardianship of the person or guardianship of the estate. Investigations where the proposed guardian is a relative shall be made by a court investigator. Investigations where the proposed guardian is a nonrelative shall be made by the county agency designated to investigate potential dependency. The report of the investigation for a guardianship of the person shall include, but need not be limited to, a discussion of all of the following: (1) A social history of the proposed guardian. (2) A social history of the proposed ward, including, to the extent feasible, an assessment of any identified developmental, emotional, psychological, or educational needs of the proposed ward and the capability of the proposed guardian to meet those needs. (3) The relationship of the proposed ward to the proposed guardian, including the duration and character of the relationship, the circumstances under which the proposed guardian took physical custody of the proposed ward, and a statement of the proposed ward’s wishes concerning the proposed guardianship, unless the proposed ward’s developmental, physical, or emotional condition prevents the proposed ward from forming or stating their wishes concerning the proposed guardianship. (4) The duration of the guardianship anticipated by the parents and the proposed guardian and the plans of each parent and the proposed guardian to provide a stable and permanent home for the child. The court may waive this requirement when no parent is available.

clauses.title: Who the Court May Appoint, and the Order of Priority
clauses.body: In deciding whom to appoint as guardian of {{childName}}'s person, the court is governed by the same statutory chapters that govern custody decisions generally. Except in the specific circumstances addressed by Probate Code § 1510.1 or § 2105, {{childName}}'s own parent may not be appointed as guardian of {{childName}}'s person. Where custody is not to be granted to a parent, California Family Code § 3040(a) directs a preference first to the person or persons in whose home the child has been living in a wholesome and stable environment, and then to any other person or persons the court deems suitable and able to provide adequate and proper care and guidance for the child.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the appointment standard and priority order for a guardian of a minor's person — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petition. Two of these citations (§ 1514(b)(1) and § 1514(b)(2)) are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1514); the substantive priority order itself is independently sourced from a separate code section, Family Code § 3040(a), which § 1514(b)(1) incorporates by cross-reference for guardian-of-the-person appointments. The way § 3040(a)'s parent-preference and § 1514(b)(2)'s bar on appointing a parent as guardian of their own child's person interact — meaning the operative preferences in a guardianship-of-the-person case are actually § 3040(a)'s second and third tiers — is this clause's own synthesis of the two statutes' text, not a quotation from either.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1514(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: In appointing a guardian of the person, the court is governed by Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 3020) and Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 3040) of Part 2 of Division 8 of the Family Code, relating to custody of a minor.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1514(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Except as provided in Section 1510.1 or 2105, a minor’s parent may not be appointed as a guardian of the person of the minor.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3040(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Custody should be granted in the following order of preference according to the best interest of the child as provided in Sections 3011 and 3020: (1) To both parents jointly pursuant to Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 3080) or to either parent. ... (2) If to neither parent, to the person or persons in whose home the child has been living in a wholesome and stable environment. (3) To any other person or persons deemed by the court to be suitable and able to provide adequate and proper care and guidance for the child.

clauses.title: A Guardianship of the Person Does Not Terminate Parental Rights
clauses.body: Appointing a guardian of {{childName}}'s person is a different legal act from terminating {{childName}}'s parent's parental rights, and this document does not purport to do either. California Family Code § 3041(c) confirms that a finding supporting a nonparent's custody — the same detriment standard incorporated into a guardianship-of-the-person appointment — "does not require a finding of unfitness of the parents." The guardianship itself also remains subject to court termination: California Probate Code § 1601 allows the guardian, a parent, or the minor ward to petition the court to terminate the guardianship whenever termination would be in the ward's best interest, and a ward who has reached 18 years of age is entitled to have the guardianship terminated on request.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a guardianship of a minor's person is legally distinct from, and does not itself terminate, parental rights — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case, and not a claim that a guardianship has no practical effect on a parent's day-to-day custody while it remains in place. These citations are two different code sections (Fam. C. § 3041(c) and Prob. C. § 1601); no single section is cited more than once in this clause. Neither section addresses the separate, and more severe, formal process for terminating parental rights entirely (e.g., Family Code § 7800 et seq., governing proceedings to free a child from a parent's custody and control), which this document does not cover and which is not the same proceeding as the guardianship petition described here. An earlier research assumption treated Probate Code § 1601 as a consent-to-appointment or relative-preference statute; on the actual statutory text, § 1601 is the guardianship-termination provision quoted above, not a consent or relative-preference rule — no such standalone "relative preference" statute for guardian-of-the-person appointments was located in the Probate Code itself (the closest analog is the custody-preference order in Family Code § 3040(a), covered in this document's companion clause).

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3041(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: As used in this section, “detriment to the child” includes the harm of removal from a stable placement of a child with a person who has assumed, on a day-to-day basis, the role of the child’s parent, fulfilling both the child’s physical needs and the child’s psychological needs for care and affection, and who has assumed that role for a substantial period of time. A finding of detriment does not require a finding of unfitness of the parents.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1601 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1601
citations.quote: Upon petition of the guardian, a parent, the minor ward, or, in the case of an Indian child custody proceeding, an Indian custodian or the ward’s tribe, the court may make an order terminating the guardianship if the court determines that it is in the ward’s best interest to terminate the guardianship. Upon petition of a ward who is 18 years of age or older, the court shall make an order terminating the guardianship. Notice of the hearing on the petition shall be given for the period and in the manner provided in Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 1460) of Part 1.

clauses.title: What a Court-Appointed Guardian of the Person May Do Once Appointed
clauses.body: Once a court appoints a guardian of {{childName}}'s person, California Probate Code § 2351(a) gives that guardian "the care, custody, and control of, and... charge of the education of," {{childName}}, subject to any limits the court's order states. Under § 2351(b), the court may, in its discretion, specifically limit the powers a particular guardian has, reserving certain powers or rights instead to someone else, such as the conservatee or, by analogy, to a parent whose rights the court's order does not displace.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a court-appointed guardian's default powers and duties over a minor's person — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific guardianship. This is a single statutory section (§ 2351), citing two of its subsections (§ 2351(a) and § 2351(b)); no additional independent source was found for this. These default powers arise only from an actual court order appointing a guardian of the child's person — nothing in this document creates, limits, or confirms the care, custody, or educational authority described here, and only a signed court order following the statutory petition process can do that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 2351(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 2351(a)
citations.quote: Subject to subdivision (b), the guardian or conservator, but not a limited conservator, has the care, custody, and control of, and has charge of the education of, the ward or conservatee. This control shall not extend to personal rights retained by the conservatee, including, but not limited to, the right to receive visitors, telephone calls, and personal mail, unless specifically limited by court order.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 2351(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 2351(b)
citations.quote: Where the court determines that it is appropriate in the circumstances of the particular conservatee, the court, in its discretion, may limit the powers and duties that the conservator would otherwise have under subdivision (a) by an order stating either of the following: (1) The specific powers that the conservator does not have with respect to the conservatee’s person and reserving the powers so specified to the conservatee. (2) The specific powers and duties the conservator has with respect to the conservatee’s person and reserving to the conservatee all other rights with respect to the conservatee’s person that the conservator otherwise would have under subdivision (a).

clauses.title: Proposed Guardian — Information and Declaration in Support of Petition
clauses.body: I, {{proposedGuardianName}}, am the person proposed to serve as guardian of the person of {{childName}}, a minor born {{childDOB}}. I state that my relationship to {{childName}} is: {{relationshipToChild}}. This declaration provides background information for use with an actual petition for appointment of a guardian of the person, to be filed in the California probate court under Probate Code Division 4, Part 2. This declaration is not itself a court filing, and signing it does not appoint, authorize, or confirm {{proposedGuardianName}} — or anyone else — as {{childName}}'s guardian. {{childName}}'s parent(s) of record, so far as known, are {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}}, where applicable. Only a court order issued after the statutory petition, notice, investigation, and hearing process can actually appoint a guardian of {{childName}}'s person.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment Block — Guardianship Petition Information Sheet
clauses.body:
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{proposedGuardianName}}: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet is prepared for use alongside an actual guardianship-of-the-person petition filed with the California probate court. It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete that petition, and it does not appoint a guardian; only a court order does that.]

clauses.title: Corporate Existence Begins Upon Filing
clauses.body: A California corporation may be formed by one or more natural persons, partnerships, associations, or corporations (domestic or foreign) who execute and file articles of incorporation with the Secretary of State. Corporate existence begins the moment the articles are filed — not on any earlier date the incorporators sign the document — and continues perpetually unless the law or the articles themselves provide otherwise. If the articles name the corporation's initial directors, each of those directors must personally sign and acknowledge the articles; if no initial directors are named, the articles are instead signed by the person or persons forming the corporation, who are then the incorporators.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of who may form a corporation and when a corporation's legal existence begins — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation's formation; who may form a corporation, and the moment its existence begins, vary by state. All three quotes below come from subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 200, so they are treated as one source, not three independent ones.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 200(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, who may form a corporation
citations.quote: One or more natural persons, partnerships, associations or corporations, domestic or foreign, may form a corporation under this division by executing and filing articles of incorporation.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 200(b)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, who signs the articles
citations.quote: If initial directors are named in the articles, each director named in the articles shall sign and acknowledge the articles; if initial directors are not named in the articles, the articles shall be signed by one or more persons described in subdivision (a) who thereupon are the incorporators of the corporation.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 200(c)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the moment corporate existence begins
citations.quote: The corporate existence begins upon the filing of the articles and continues perpetually, unless otherwise expressly provided by law or in the articles.

clauses.title: Required Content of the Articles of Incorporation
clauses.body: California's articles-of-incorporation statute requires the filed document to state: the corporation's name; one of two alternative purpose statements — either the general default that the corporation's purpose is to engage in any lawful act or activity for which a corporation may be organized under the General Corporation Law (other than the banking business, the trust-company business, or the practice of a licensed profession), or, for a corporation formed to practice a specific licensed profession, a statement naming that profession; the name and California street address of the corporation's initial agent for service of process; the initial street address of the corporation's principal office, plus a separate mailing address if it differs; and, because a California corporation exists by default as a stock corporation, a statement of its initial share structure — either the total number of shares authorized (if only one class of stock), or, if more than one class or series is authorized, the number, designation, and rights of each class and series.
clauses.gap: This is one state's list of required formation-document content, not a claim about what any other state's equivalent filing must contain — required content for a corporation's founding filing varies by state. The four citations below are all subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 202, so they are treated as one source, not four independent ones; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 202(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the corporation's name
citations.quote: The name of the corporation; provided, however, that in order for the corporation to be subject to the provisions of this division applicable to a close corporation (Section 158), the name of the corporation must contain the word “corporation,” “incorporated,” or “limited” or an abbreviation of one of such words.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 202(b)(1)(A)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the default lawful-purpose statement
citations.quote: The purpose of the corporation is to engage in any lawful act or activity for which a corporation may be organized under the General Corporation Law of California other than the banking business, the trust company business or the practice of a profession permitted to be incorporated by the California Corporations Code

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 202(c)-(e)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, agent for service of process and office addresses
citations.quote: (c) The name and street address in this state of the corporation’s initial agent for service of process in accordance with subdivision (b) of Section 1502. (d) The initial street address of its principal office. (e) The initial mailing address of the corporation, if different from the initial street address.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 202(f)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, initial authorized shares (single-class corporations)
citations.quote: If the corporation is authorized to issue only one class of shares, the total number of shares which the corporation is authorized to issue.

clauses.title: The Corporation Name Requirement
clauses.body: California's general naming statute for corporations does not, by default, require a corporation's name to include any particular word like "Corporation," "Incorporated," "Limited," or an abbreviation of one of those words — that designator requirement applies only to a corporation that elects to be governed by the state's close-corporation provisions. What the general naming statute actually restricts is different: the Secretary of State will not file articles using a name containing "bank," "trust," "trustee," or related words unless a specified financial regulator's certificate of approval is attached, and separately, a corporation's name cannot be one the Secretary of State determines is likely to mislead the public, or that isn't distinguishable in the Secretary of State's records from other registered or reserved entity names.
clauses.gap: This is one state's naming statute, not a claim about naming rules in any other state — restricted words, and whether any designator word must be included in an entity's name at all, vary by state.
