California's Judicial Council petition form for a domestic violence restraining order (Form DV-100) is signed under penalty of perjury; this block mirrors that requirement for informational purposes and is not itself a court filing or a substitute for a completed Judicial Council form. This document, including this signature block, does not itself grant a restraining order -- only a court, after applying the statutory process described in this document to the completed Judicial Council forms, can issue one.

clauses.title: What Governs Sublessor's Right to Sublet
clauses.body: California has a statutory chapter specifically addressing a landlord's ability to restrict a tenant from transferring the tenant's lease interest (by assignment or sublease), including a default rule that if the lease requires the landlord's consent but states no standard for it, that consent may not be unreasonably withheld. That chapter, by its own terms, applies only to a lease of real property for other than residential purposes. For a residential tenancy, whether {{sublessorName}} may sublet {{propertyAddress}} to {{subtenantName}}, and whether {{landlordName}}'s consent is required first, is controlled by the terms of the existing lease between {{landlordName}} and {{sublessorName}} (the "Master Lease") — not by that separate statutory chapter.
clauses.gap: This is a real, easy-to-miss gap rather than an assumption forced to fit: Civil Code Chapter 6 (Assignment and Sublease, §§ 1995.010-1995.340) — including its default rule that an unstandardized landlord-consent requirement may not be unreasonably withheld — is defined, by its own text, to cover only a lease of real property for other than residential purposes. There is no parallel Civil Code chapter creating a general residential right to sublet or a residential landlord-consent standard. That means a residential tenant's subletting rights genuinely are, in the main, a matter of what the Master Lease itself says: a typical residential lease either bars subletting outright, allows it only with the landlord's prior written consent, or is silent (in which case older common-law principles about a tenant's default freedom to transfer a leasehold interest can come into play). This document does not assume the Master Lease permits or forbids subletting, or that it requires consent — that has to be checked directly against the Master Lease's own text. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual scope of California's assignment/subletting statute — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific master lease. The first two citations are sections of the same statutory chapter (§§ 1995.010, 1995.020) defining that chapter's own scope; the third citation, § 1995.270's legislative findings, is an independent statutory source that separately corroborates the chapter's commercial-only focus and its historical basis in the Kendall v. Ernest Pestana litigation. The fourth citation goes further still: it's Kendall's own text (verified directly against CourtListener's opinion record, not a paraphrase), and in a footnote the California Supreme Court itself expressly declined to say whether the commercial-lease consent principles it was announcing in that case apply to residential leases at all — meaning even the single most important California case on landlord-consent standards pointedly leaves the residential question open, rather than answering it.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1995.010 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the assignment/sublease restrictions chapter is nonresidential-only
citations.quote: This chapter applies to transfer of a tenant’s interest in a lease of real property for other than residential purposes.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1995.020(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, "lease" is defined as nonresidential for this chapter
citations.quote: “Lease” means a lease or sublease of real property for other than residential purposes, and includes modifications and other agreements affecting a lease.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1995.270(a)(1)-(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, legislative findings confirming the chapter concerns commercial real property leases
citations.quote: (a) The Legislature finds and declares: (1) It is the public policy of the state and fundamental to the commerce and economic development of the state to enable and facilitate freedom of contract by the parties to commercial real property leases. (2) The parties to commercial real property leases must be able to negotiate and conduct their affairs in reasonable reliance on the rights and protections given them under the laws of the state. (3) Until the case of Kendall v. Ernest Pestana, Inc., 40 Cal. 3d 488 (1985), and its predecessor, Cohen v. Ratinoff, 147 Cal. App. 3d 321 (1983), the parties to commercial real property leases could reasonably rely on the law of the state to provide that if a lease restriction requires the landlord’s consent for transfer of the tenant’s interest in the lease but provides no standard for giving or withholding consent, the landlord’s consent may be unreasonably withheld.

citations.case: Kendall v. Ernest Pestana, Inc., 40 Cal.3d 488, 493 n.1 (1985) (opinion text via CourtListener)
citations.cite: California Supreme Court, expressly declining to decide whether its commercial-lease rule extends to residential leases
citations.quote: We are presented only with a commercial lease and therefore do not address the question whether residential leases are controlled by the principles articulated in this opinion.

clauses.title: Assignment vs. Sublease
clauses.body: Subletting {{propertyAddress}} to {{subtenantName}} is legally different from assigning the Master Lease to {{subtenantName}}, even though both are ways {{sublessorName}} can transfer some interest in the leased property to someone else. In a sublease, {{sublessorName}} transfers only part of its remaining interest under the Master Lease — for example, a shorter term than what remains, or only part of the space — and remains a tenant to {{landlordName}} while also taking on a landlord-like role toward {{subtenantName}}. In a full assignment, {{sublessorName}} would instead transfer its entire remaining interest under the Master Lease to the new party, who would then generally deal with {{landlordName}} directly going forward in {{sublessorName}}'s place. This document is a sublease, not an assignment: {{sublessorName}} keeps its position as tenant under the Master Lease and remains directly responsible to {{landlordName}} for compliance with it, as described elsewhere in this document.
clauses.gap: This distinction is confirmed directly against primary case text, not a secondary-source paraphrase. Kendall v. Ernest Pestana, Inc. (1985) 40 Cal.3d 488, 493 n.2, states it in so many words: "The difference between an assignment and a sublease is that an assignment transfers the lessee's entire interest in the property whereas a sublease transfers only a portion of that interest, with the original lessee retaining a right of reentry at some point during the unexpired term of the lease." Kendall cites, for that same point, Hartman Ranch Co. v. Associated Oil Co. (1937) 10 Cal.2d 232, 242-243 — an independent, older California Supreme Court decision (about an oil-and-gas lease, not real estate generally) that states the distinction on its own terms and explains the doctrine behind it: California follows the "Massachusetts rule" that a transferor who reserves a right of reentry for breach of conditions keeps a "contingent reversionary interest," which is what keeps the transfer from operating as a full assignment of the unexpired term — a sublease results instead. Both quotes below were read directly from each case's opinion text (via CourtListener), not assumed from a secondary summary. Neither case involved a residential tenancy — Kendall was a commercial hangar-space dispute and Hartman Ranch an oil-and-gas lease dispute — but the assignment/sublease distinction itself is treated in both opinions as general property-law doctrine rather than something specific to a commercial lease, and Civil Code § 1995.020(e) (part of the nonresidential-only Chapter 6 discussed under "What Governs Sublessor's Right to Sublet" above) independently confirms that California statutory law also recognizes assignment and sublease as distinct categories of lease transfer, even though it doesn't itself spell out the substantive test. That third citation quotes two subsections of the same statutory section, § 1995.020(a) and (e) — disclosed here because it is one section read twice, not two independent statutory sources, so the real independent authority for the doctrinal test itself is the case law above, with the statute offered only as corroboration that California law recognizes the two categories at all. This is one state's case law, used as real evidence of the actual doctrinal test — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific document.

citations.case: Kendall v. Ernest Pestana, Inc., 40 Cal.3d 488, 493 n.2 (1985) (opinion text via CourtListener)
citations.cite: California Supreme Court, the assignment/sublease distinction stated directly
citations.quote: Since the present case involves an assignment rather than a sublease, we will speak primarily in terms of assignments. However, our holding applies equally to subleases. The difference between an assignment and a sublease is that an assignment transfers the lessee's entire interest in the property whereas a sublease transfers only a portion of that interest, with the original lessee retaining a right of reentry at some point during the unexpired term of the lease.

citations.case: Hartman Ranch Co. v. Associated Oil Co., 10 Cal.2d 232, 242-243 (1937) (opinion text via CourtListener)
citations.cite: California Supreme Court, independently stating the same distinction and its doctrinal basis
citations.quote: The generally stated distinction between an assignment and a sublease is that an assignment transfers the entire unexpired term. ... [W]e are committed to the so-called Massachusetts rule that where the transferor reserves the right of reentry for breach of conditions he has a "contingent reversionary interest" which prevents his transfer from operating as an assignment of the whole of the unexpired term. Instead, a sublease arises.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1995.020(a), (e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, "transfer" is defined to include both assignment and sublease as distinct categories, and a sublease creates a "sublandlord"
citations.quote: (a) “Landlord” includes a tenant who is a sublandlord under a sublease. ... (e) “Transfer” of a tenant’s interest in a lease means an assignment, sublease, or other voluntary or involuntary transfer or encumbrance of all or part of a tenant’s interest in the lease.

clauses.title: Sublessor Remains Bound to Landlord
clauses.body: Entering into this sublease with {{subtenantName}} does not release {{sublessorName}} from any of its obligations to {{landlordName}} under the Master Lease. {{sublessorName}} remains fully responsible to {{landlordName}} for rent, upkeep, and all other Master Lease obligations for {{propertyAddress}}, regardless of whether {{subtenantName}} pays rent on time, complies with the Master Lease's terms, or vacates early. If {{subtenantName}} breaches this sublease or damages the property, {{sublessorName}} — not {{landlordName}} — bears that loss in the first instance, unless {{sublessorName}} separately recovers it from {{subtenantName}}. At the same time, under this sublease {{sublessorName}} effectively stands in {{landlordName}}'s shoes toward {{subtenantName}}, taking on landlord-like responsibilities to {{subtenantName}} while remaining, itself, a tenant to {{landlordName}}.
clauses.gap: This is a well-established rule of California landlord-tenant law, confirmed directly against primary case text. The California Supreme Court has stated it plainly: "the original lessee remains liable to the lessor as a surety even if the lessor consents to the assignment and the assignee expressly assumes the obligations of the lease" (Kendall v. Ernest Pestana, Inc. (1985) 40 Cal.3d 488, 500) — a sentence that itself cites, for that exact point, two of the Supreme Court's own earlier decisions, so the underlying rule rests on at least three independent sources, not one restated citation. One of those two, Peiser v. Mettler (1958) 50 Cal.2d 594, 602, was independently pulled and confirms the rule in even more direct language (quoting an earlier case, De Hart v. Allen): an assignment or sublease "does not release the lessee from his obligations even though the lessor consents to the assignment," and "the express assumption by the assignee of obligations under the lease" doesn't change that, because "as between the lessor and the lessee[,] the latter remains a primary obligor under his express contract to pay rent." All of this case law states the rule in the assignment context specifically, but nothing in the reasoning turns on the assignment/sublease distinction described elsewhere in this document — a sublessor, who transfers only part of the leasehold interest and keeps an ongoing tenancy relationship with the landlord, has at least as much of a continuing contractual relationship with the landlord as an assignor does, so the same primary-obligor/surety-liability logic applies with equal or greater force to a sublease. Separately, Civil Code § 1995.020(a), (d) — part of the nonresidential-only Chapter 6 discussed under "What Governs Sublessor's Right to Sublet" above — independently corroborates the underlying structure by defining a sublessor as simultaneously a "tenant" to the original landlord and a "sublandlord" to the subtenant, consistent with the sublessor's obligations to the landlord surviving the sublease. That statutory citation likewise quotes two subsections of the same section, § 1995.020(a) and (d) — disclosed here because it is one section read twice, not two independent statutory sources; the independent authority for the liability rule itself is the case law above, with the statute offered only as structural corroboration. This is one state's case law, used as real evidence of the actual liability rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific master lease — and it says nothing about whatever separate indemnity or reimbursement rights Sublessor may or may not have against Subtenant; the actual Master Lease's own default and remedies provisions, not this general default description, control the mechanics of any actual dispute.

citations.case: Kendall v. Ernest Pestana, Inc., 40 Cal.3d 488, 500 (1985) (opinion text via CourtListener)
citations.cite: California Supreme Court, original tenant remains liable as a surety after transferring the lease
citations.quote: The lessor's interests are also protected by the fact that the original lessee remains liable to the lessor as a surety even if the lessor consents to the assignment and the assignee expressly assumes the obligations of the lease. (Peiser v. Mettler (1958) 50 Cal.2d 594, 602 [328 P.2d 953, 74 A.L.R.2d 1]; Samuels v. Ottinger (1915) 169 Cal. 209, 212 [146 P. 638].)

citations.case: Peiser v. Mettler, 50 Cal.2d 594, 602 (1958) (opinion text via CourtListener)
citations.cite: California Supreme Court, independently stating the original tenant remains a primary obligor to the landlord
citations.quote: Ordinarily an assignment of a lease does not release the lessee from his obligations even though the lessor consents to the assignment. ... Nor does the express assumption by the assignee of obligations under the lease affect the liability of the lessee to the lessor. ... but as between the lessor and the lessee the latter remains a primary obligor under his express contract to pay rent.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1995.020(a), (d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, a sublessor is both a "tenant" to the landlord and a "sublandlord" (landlord) to the subtenant
citations.quote: (a) “Landlord” includes a tenant who is a sublandlord under a sublease. ... (d) “Tenant” includes a subtenant or assignee.

clauses.title: Subtenant Has No Direct Relationship with Landlord
clauses.body: As a general default rule, {{subtenantName}} does not step into a direct legal relationship with {{landlordName}} merely by virtue of this sublease. {{subtenantName}}'s rights and obligations run to {{sublessorName}}, not to {{landlordName}}, and {{landlordName}}'s remedies for a breach of the Master Lease generally run against {{sublessorName}}, not directly against {{subtenantName}}. This sublease does not, by itself, give {{subtenantName}} the right to enforce the Master Lease against {{landlordName}}, or give {{landlordName}} the right to collect rent or otherwise enforce lease terms directly against {{subtenantName}} for {{propertyAddress}}, unless the Master Lease, {{landlordName}}'s written consent to this sublease, or a separate agreement signed by all three parties provides otherwise.
clauses.gap: This no-privity default is a real, well-established rule of California property law, confirmed directly against primary case text. Hartman Ranch Co. v. Associated Oil Co. (1937) 10 Cal.2d 232, 242, states it directly: "This doctrine as to sublessees generally is well settled. ... A sublessee is liable only to his own lessor, that is, the sub-lessor, since he does not acquire the whole estate, but only a portion of the unexpired term." A few pages later the same opinion explains the doctrinal mechanism — that the sublessee's relationship with the original landlord lacks privity of estate (the property-law relationship that, for an assignee in full possession, makes the assignee directly answerable to the landlord on the lease covenants): "as to both sublessee in possession, and the assignee who has terminated his possession[,] there is no privity of estate with the lessor." Both quotes below are from the same 1937 case rather than independently authored sources; that case is, however, corroborated by a second, independent source: Civil Code § 822 extends a landlord's lease remedies — for breach of a lease agreement, or for recovery of possession — expressly to the tenant's "assignees," but its text never mentions subtenants or sublessees at all, which is consistent with (though not itself an express statement of) the same no-privity default for subtenants that Hartman Ranch states directly. Hartman Ranch was an oil-and-gas lease dispute, not a residential tenancy, but the privity principle it applies is general California property-law doctrine rather than something specific to that lease type. This is one state's case law, used as real evidence of the actual default rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific master lease. Nothing here should be read as guaranteeing that no direct relationship can ever arise in a particular deal — a landlord's written consent to a sublease, a separate non-disturbance or attornment agreement, or specific master lease language can each create direct rights or obligations between the landlord and the subtenant, and the actual Master Lease and any consent documents should be checked for that possibility.

citations.case: Hartman Ranch Co. v. Associated Oil Co., 10 Cal.2d 232, 242 (1937) (opinion text via CourtListener)
citations.cite: California Supreme Court, a subtenant is liable only to the sublessor, not the original landlord
citations.quote: Defendant contends that as a sublessee it is not liable to the original lessor in damages for breach of covenants in the parent lease. This doctrine as to sublessees generally is well settled. ... A sublessee is liable only to his own lessor, that is, the sub-lessor, since he does not acquire the whole estate, but only a portion of the unexpired term.

citations.case: Hartman Ranch Co. v. Associated Oil Co., 10 Cal.2d 232, 244 (1937) (opinion text via CourtListener)
citations.cite: California Supreme Court, a subtenant lacks privity of estate with the original landlord
citations.quote: An assignee in possession is liable to the parent lessor by virtue of privity of estate (covenants running with the land), and it is not ordinarily necessary to consider whether by virtue of an agreement of assumption there is also privity of contract between them. But where the assignee is no longer in possession, the privity of estate is terminated ..., and if he is liable to the lessor it is by virtue of his contract of assumption. Since as to both sublessee in possession, and the assignee who has terminated his possession there is no privity of estate with the lessor, cases involving an assignee who has assumed the parent lease, but is no longer in possession, will indicate the rule applicable also to sublessees who assume the parent lease.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 822 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, a landlord's lease remedies extend to the tenant's "assignees" — subtenants are not mentioned
citations.quote: Whatever remedies the lessor of any real property has against his immediate lessee for the breach of any agreement in the lease, or for recovery of the possession, he has against the assignees of the lessee, for any cause of action accruing while they are such assignees, except where the assignment is made by way of security for a loan, and is not accompanied by possession of the premises.

clauses.title: Who Owns the Work Before It's Assigned
clauses.body: Under federal copyright law, copyright in a work vests initially in the person who actually creates it — the author — the moment the work is fixed in a tangible form. When {{creatorName}} is an independent creator or freelancer rather than an employee of {{hiringPartyName}}, the employee branch of the work-made-for-hire doctrine does not apply, and {{creatorName}} is the initial copyright owner even though {{hiringPartyName}} commissioned and paid for the work. Ownership passes to {{hiringPartyName}} only through the assignment made in this agreement, or through one of the narrow work-made-for-hire exceptions described elsewhere in this document.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of how initial copyright ownership is allocated between an individual creator and a hiring party — not a claim that every commissioned work or every fact pattern is resolved the same way, since ownership can also be affected by joint-authorship rules, prior agreements, or other provisions of Title 17 not addressed here. The Effects Associates decision cited below is Ninth Circuit precedent; it is widely cited nationally on this point but is only binding within that circuit.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 201(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, initial ownership of copyright
citations.quote: Copyright in a work protected under this title vests initially in the author or authors of the work. The authors of a joint work are coowners of copyright in the work.

citations.case: Effects Associates, Inc. v. Cohen
citations.quote: Absent an express transfer of ownership, a contributor who is not an employee retains ownership of his copyright.

clauses.title: Why Most Freelance Work Isn't Automatically "Work Made for Hire"
clauses.body: Federal copyright law defines “work made for hire” in two ways: (1) work created by an employee within the scope of employment, or (2) work that is both specially ordered or commissioned for use in one of nine specific categories listed in the statute — a contribution to a collective work, a part of a motion picture or other audiovisual work, a translation, a supplementary work, a compilation, an instructional text, a test, answer material for a test, or an atlas — and that the parties expressly agree in a signed written instrument is a work made for hire. Work by an independent creator like {{creatorName}} does not fall within the first branch, and most freelance deliverables — things like a logo, most illustration and graphic design, most software, most photography, and most website or marketing copy — do not fall within any of the nine categories in the second branch either. For work outside those categories, no work-made-for-hire designation in a contract can make {{hiringPartyName}} the legal “author” of it; a separate written assignment, like this agreement, is what actually transfers ownership from {{creatorName}} to {{hiringPartyName}}.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the statutory definition of “work made for hire” directly and confirms the nine enumerated categories by checking the statutory text itself, rather than assuming the count or the list. Whether a specific piece of work fits (or doesn't fit) one of those categories is a fact-specific characterization this clause doesn't resolve for any particular work. This is federal law, used as real evidence of how the work-made-for-hire categories are defined — not a claim that every creative work, or every industry's customary way of describing its own output, has actually been tested against this list in litigation.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 101 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, definition of “work made for hire”
citations.quote: A “work made for hire” is— (1) a work prepared by an employee within the scope of his or her employment; or (2) a work specially ordered or commissioned for use as a contribution to a collective work, as a part of a motion picture or other audiovisual work, as a translation, as a supplementary work, as a compilation, as an instructional text, as a test, as answer material for a test, or as an atlas, if the parties expressly agree in a written instrument signed by them that the work shall be considered a work made for hire.

citations.case: Community for Creative Non-Violence v. Reid
citations.quote: Nor was the sculpture a “work made for hire” under the second subsection of § 101 (hereinafter § 101(2)): sculpture is not one of the nine categories of works enumerated in that subsection, and the parties had not agreed in writing that the sculpture would be a work for hire.

clauses.title: Copyright Transfers Must Be in Writing
clauses.body: Federal copyright law requires that a transfer of copyright ownership — other than by operation of law, such as through inheritance — be in a signed writing to be valid. An oral agreement, a handshake deal, or an implied understanding is generally not enough to transfer copyright ownership itself, even if it may create other rights (such as an implied license to use the work). This is part of why a signed assignment agreement like this one, rather than an invoice, a verbal agreement, or a course of dealing, is what's needed to actually move copyright ownership of {{workDescription}} from {{creatorName}} to {{hiringPartyName}}.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the signed-writing requirement for copyright transfers — not a claim that every method of communicating agreement (email, a signed purchase order, electronic signature) satisfies it in every circumstance, which can depend on facts not addressed here. The cited Effects Associates decision is Ninth Circuit precedent; it is frequently cited nationally on this point but is only binding within that circuit.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 204(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, execution of transfers of copyright ownership
citations.quote: A transfer of copyright ownership, other than by operation of law, is not valid unless an instrument of conveyance, or a note or memorandum of the transfer, is in writing and signed by the owner of the rights conveyed or such owner’s duly authorized agent.

citations.case: Effects Associates, Inc. v. Cohen
citations.quote: The rule is really quite simple: If the copyright holder agrees to transfer ownership to another party, that party must get the copyright holder to sign a piece of paper saying so. It doesn't have to be the Magna Charta; a one-line pro forma statement will do.

clauses.title: The Statutory Right to Terminate This Assignment Later
clauses.body: Assigning copyright ownership does not necessarily last forever, no matter what the assignment agreement says. Federal copyright law gives an individual author — or, after the author's death, certain statutorily defined heirs — the right to terminate a copyright transfer or license during a five-year window that begins 35 years after the grant was signed (or, for a grant covering publication rights, the earlier of 35 years from publication or 40 years from execution). This termination right exists notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary, including language in the assignment itself purporting to waive it, but it does not apply to a work made for hire. To exercise it, the author or heirs must serve an advance written notice stating the effective termination date, served not less than two nor more than ten years before that date, and a copy of the notice must be recorded with the U.S. Copyright Office before termination takes effect.
clauses.gap: This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (17 U.S.C. § 203(a)(3) and § 203(a)(4)); no additional independent source was found for this, since both describe requirements of the same termination mechanism. The statute, by its own terms, applies only to a transfer or license “executed by the author on or after January 1, 1978” and expressly excludes a work made for hire — a status this document's other clauses address separately. This is federal law, used as real evidence of how the termination right and its timing work — not a claim that any specific assignment made under this agreement will in fact be eligible for termination, since eligibility depends on facts (such as whether the party assigning the work is an individual human author, as opposed to, for example, a company, and when the assignment was signed) that this clause doesn't resolve.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 203(a)(3) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, termination of transfers — timing
citations.quote: Termination of the grant may be effected at any time during a period of five years beginning at the end of thirty-five years from the date of execution of the grant; or, if the grant covers the right of publication of the work, the period begins at the end of thirty-five years from the date of publication of the work under the grant or at the end of forty years from the date of execution of the grant, whichever term ends earlier.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 203(a)(4) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, termination of transfers — notice requirements
citations.quote: The notice shall state the effective date of the termination, which shall fall within the five-year period specified by clause (3) of this subsection, and the notice shall be served not less than two or more than ten years before that date. A copy of the notice shall be recorded in the Copyright Office before the effective date of termination, as a condition to its taking effect.

clauses.title: Moral Rights Are Separate From Copyright Ownership
clauses.body: Separately from copyright ownership itself, federal law gives the author of certain “works of visual art” personal rights of attribution and integrity — the right to be credited (or not falsely credited) as the work's author, and the right to object to certain distortions, mutilations, or destruction of the work. These rights, sometimes called “moral rights,” belong to the individual human author and cannot be sold or transferred, even by an assignment like this one. They can only be waived, and only if the author expressly agrees to the waiver in a written instrument, signed by the author, that specifically identifies the work and the particular uses the waiver covers. Assigning copyright ownership of {{workDescription}} to {{hiringPartyName}} does not, by itself, waive any moral rights {{creatorName}} may have in it.
clauses.gap: Moral rights under 17 U.S.C. § 106A apply only to a narrow statutory category called a “work of visual art” — in general, a single copy or a signed, numbered limited edition of 200 copies or fewer of a painting, drawing, print, or sculpture, or a still photograph produced for exhibition purposes only — and the definition expressly excludes posters, maps, applied art, most merchandising and advertising or promotional material, and any work made for hire. Most freelance deliverables (logos, software, written content, and most commercial illustration or photography) fall outside that definition and so are not affected by § 106A at all; this clause is included because it may be relevant to a narrower category of assigned work, not because it applies to every work this document could be used for. This is federal law, used as real evidence of how moral rights and their waiver requirements work under the one federal statute (the Visual Artists Rights Act) that creates them — not a claim that any particular work assigned under this agreement qualifies as a “work of visual art,” or that state-law moral-rights doctrines, which some states separately recognize, work the same way.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 106A(e)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, rights of certain authors to attribution and integrity — transfer and waiver
citations.quote: The rights conferred by subsection (a) may not be transferred, but those rights may be waived if the author expressly agrees to such waiver in a written instrument signed by the author. Such instrument shall specifically identify the work, and uses of that work, to which the waiver applies, and the waiver shall apply only to the work and uses so identified.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 101 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, definition of “work of visual art”
citations.quote: A “work of visual art” is— (1) a painting, drawing, print, or sculpture, existing in a single copy, in a limited edition of 200 copies or fewer that are signed and consecutively numbered by the author... or (2) a still photographic image produced for exhibition purposes only, existing in a single copy that is signed by the author, or in a limited edition of 200 copies or fewer that are signed and consecutively numbered by the author. A work of visual art does not include— ...any merchandising item or advertising, promotional, descriptive, covering, or packaging material or container... (B) any work made for hire...

clauses.title: Assignment of Copyright
clauses.body: {{creatorName}} hereby assigns and transfers to {{hiringPartyName}} all right, title, and interest in and to the copyright in the following work: {{workDescription}}, including the exclusive rights to reproduce, distribute, publicly display, publicly perform, and prepare derivative works based on it, for the full term of copyright and any renewals or extensions available under law. This assignment is effective as of the date this agreement is signed. {{creatorName}} agrees to sign any additional documents reasonably requested by {{hiringPartyName}} to confirm, record, or perfect this assignment.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
When Final Wages Become Due Under California Law
clauses.body: California law sets a specific deadline for paying an employee's final wages, and which deadline applies depends on how the employment ended. If an employer discharges an employee, the wages earned and unpaid at the time of discharge are due and payable immediately. If an employee quits without giving the employer at least 72 hours' notice, final wages are due within 72 hours of the quit; if the employee gives at least 72 hours' notice, final wages are due at the time of quitting. This letter treats {{terminationDate}} as the date {{employeeName}}'s employment with {{companyName}} ended, based on a separation described here as: {{separationType}}.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of when final wages become due on a discharge or a quit — not a claim about which state's law governs this particular separation. These are the general discharge-and-quit deadlines (Labor Code sections 201(a) and 202(a)); California law contains additional, narrower deadlines for other circumstances not addressed here (for example, a longer same-day-equivalent window for certain seasonal employees in the perishable-food industry, and separate provisions that apply only to state-government employers). Which deadline actually governed this particular separation, and whether the separation is correctly characterized as a discharge or a quit with or without notice, are factual questions this clause does not resolve.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 201(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: If an employer discharges an employee, the wages earned and unpaid at the time of discharge are due and payable immediately.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 202(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: If an employee not having a written contract for a definite period quits his or her employment, his or her wages shall become due and payable not later than 72 hours thereafter, unless the employee has given 72 hours previous notice of his or her intention to quit, in which case the employee is entitled to his or her wages at the time of quitting.

clauses.title: The Waiting-Time Penalty: How It Accrues and Its Cap
clauses.body: When an employer willfully fails to pay final wages on time, California law imposes a separate penalty on top of the unpaid wages themselves. Under this rule, wages continue to accrue as a penalty at the same daily rate of pay, starting from the original due date, until they are paid in full or until a lawsuit to collect them is filed — whichever happens first. That penalty cannot exceed 30 days of wages. An employee who deliberately avoids payment, or who refuses a payment that is fully and properly offered (including any penalty already accrued), is not entitled to a penalty for the period during which they did so.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how a waiting-time penalty accrues and is capped — not a claim about which state's law governs this particular unpaid-wage dispute. This penalty requires that the employer's failure to pay be ‘willful,’ a legal standard with its own body of case law addressed in a separate clause; an employer whose failure to pay was not willful is not liable under this section even if wages were, in fact, paid late. This clause states the general accrual and cap rule; it does not work through how the daily rate is calculated for pay that is not a fixed daily wage (for example, commission-based or highly variable pay). This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 203(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 203(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: If an employer willfully fails to pay, without abatement or reduction, in accordance with Sections 201, 201.3, 201.5, 201.6, 201.8, 201.9, 202, and 205.5, any wages of an employee who is discharged or who quits, the wages of the employee shall continue as a penalty from the due date thereof at the same rate until paid or until an action therefor is commenced; but the wages shall not continue for more than 30 days. An employee who secretes or absents themselves to avoid payment to them, or who refuses to receive the payment when fully tendered to them, including any penalty then accrued under this section, is not entitled to any benefit under this section for the time during which the employee so avoids payment.

clauses.title: What “Willful” Means for the Waiting-Time Penalty
clauses.body: The waiting-time penalty does not apply automatically just because final wages were paid late — it applies only if the employer's failure to pay was “willful.” California courts have held that this does not require proof that the employer deliberately set out to cheat the employee out of money it knew was owed. It means only that the employer intentionally failed or refused to do an act that was legally required, as opposed to a failure caused by something genuinely outside the employer's control. Courts have also recognized that when an employer has a genuine, good-faith dispute about whether it is legally required to pay the wages at issue, that good-faith dispute can defeat a finding of willfulness — even if the employer later turns out to be wrong about the underlying legal question.
clauses.gap: This is one state's case law, used as real evidence of how ‘willful’ has been interpreted for this specific penalty — not a claim about which state's law governs this particular dispute, and not a claim that any dispute an employer raises will succeed in defeating the penalty. Both quotations below come from the same California Court of Appeal decision (which in turn quotes a still-earlier appellate decision for the core definition of ‘willful’); this research session's case-law lookups were rate-limited, and no independent second case was verified for this specific point — that gap is disclosed here rather than papered over. It's also worth being precise about what the cited case actually decided: the good-faith defense that succeeded there involved a good-faith dispute over the employer's legal right to a wage setoff, and the court was explicit that there was no dispute about the amount of wages owed. Whether a good-faith factual dispute over the amount owed would be treated the same way is a related but distinct question this clause does not resolve; the same opinion notes, without deciding, that some other jurisdictions have recognized a defense along those lines.

citations.case: Barnhill v. Robert Saunders & Co.
citations.quote: As used in section 203, ‘willful’ merely means that the employer intentionally failed or refused to perform an act which was required to be done. (Davis v. Morris (1940) 37 Cal.App.2d 269, 274 [99 P.2d 345].)

citations.case: Barnhill v. Robert Saunders & Co.
citations.quote: We conclude that given that uncertainty, appellant should not be penalized for believing that setoff was proper and payment of wages not required. Accordingly, appellant's attempt to exercise a right to setoff was not wilful nonpayment of wages within the meaning of Labor Code section 203, and the imposition of penalties was inappropriate.

clauses.title: The Filing Deadline for a Waiting-Time Penalty Claim
clauses.body: California's waiting-time penalty statute does not set its own fixed, standalone number of years within which a claim for the penalty must be filed. Instead, it ties the filing deadline for the penalty to whatever statute of limitations applies to the underlying unpaid-wage claim the penalty is based on: a lawsuit for waiting-time penalties may be filed at any time before that underlying wage claim's own statute of limitations runs out.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how the filing deadline for a waiting-time-penalty claim is structured — not a claim about which state's law governs this particular claim, and not a claim about exactly how many years apply here. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 203(b)); this research session's CourtListener case-law lookups were rate-limited at the point this clause's authority was being verified, so no case law interpreting or applying this cross-reference (for example, on which limitations period applies to the underlying wage claim once it has already been paid) was independently verified, and that gap is disclosed here rather than assumed away. Figuring out the actual filing deadline requires first identifying the limitations period that applies to the underlying wage claim itself — which under California law can differ depending on how that claim is legally characterized — and that threshold question is not answered by this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 203(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Suit may be filed for these penalties at any time before the expiration of the statute of limitations on an action for the wages from which the penalties arise.

clauses.title: Accrued Vacation and PTO as Part of Final Wages
clauses.body: Where California's rule that vested, unused vacation or PTO must be paid out as wages at termination applies, that payout is treated as part of the final wages covered by the deadlines and the waiting-time penalty described in this letter — not as a separate category of pay with its own separate due date.
clauses.gap: This is one state's rule, used as real evidence that accrued vacation/PTO payout is legally treated as final wages — not a claim about which state's law governs this particular payout, and not a claim that any particular accrued balance is actually owed here. This clause deliberately does not re-derive the underlying vacation/PTO payout rule or its authority (California Labor Code section 227.3 and the case law interpreting it) because this document set already contains a dedicated, separately verified clause covering that rule in full, including its own citations and its own disclosed limits (for example, the distinction between a no-forfeiture rule and a permissible accrual cap). This clause exists only to connect that already-covered rule to the waiting-time-penalty mechanics described elsewhere in this letter. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 227.3); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 227.3 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Unless otherwise provided by a collective-bargaining agreement, whenever a contract of employment or employer policy provides for paid vacations, and an employee is terminated without having taken off his vested vacation time, all vested vacation shall be paid to him as wages at his final rate in accordance with such contract of employment or employer policy respecting eligibility or time served; provided, however, that an employment contract or employer policy shall not provide for forfeiture of vested vacation time upon termination.

clauses.title: Demand for Payment of Final Wages and Waiting-Time Penalty
clauses.body:
Re: Demand for Payment of Final Wages — {{employeeName}}

To {{companyName}}:

This letter concerns the employment of {{employeeName}}, whose employment with {{companyName}} ended on {{terminationDate}}. The separation is described here as: {{separationType}}.

California Labor Code sections 201 and 202 set deadlines for paying an employee's final wages depending on how the employment ended. As of the date of this letter, {{employeeName}} has not received full payment of final wages owed, including all earned and unpaid wages and any accrued, unused vacation or paid time off required to be paid out as wages at termination. The unpaid amount is currently identified as approximately {{unpaidWagesAmount}}.

Because final wages were not paid by the applicable statutory deadline, California Labor Code section 203 provides that unpaid wages continue as a penalty at {{employeeName}}'s daily rate of pay — {{dailyWageRate}} per day — for each day payment remains outstanding, up to a maximum of 30 days.

Payment in full of the unpaid final wages described above, together with all waiting-time penalties accrued as of the date payment is made, is demanded.

clauses.title: Closing, Reservation of Rights, and Signature
clauses.body:
Please direct payment, and any response to this letter, to {{employeeName}} at the address below.

If full payment — including all waiting-time penalties accrued under California Labor Code section 203 — is not received, {{employeeName}} reserves all rights and remedies available under California law, including further accrual of statutory penalties up to the applicable cap, and any other remedy available for unpaid final wages.

Sincerely,

{{employeeName}}
Date: _______________

clauses.title: Recitals — Dissolution and Winding Up
clauses.body: {{companyName}} was dissolved effective {{dissolutionDate}}, based on {{dissolutionReason}}. This document records the winding up of {{companyName}}'s affairs and the filing that formally cancels {{companyName}}'s existence with the California Secretary of State. It addresses the statutory winding-up and cancellation process itself — a separate matter from whatever dissolution triggers and buyout terms appear in {{companyName}}'s own operating agreement, which govern only when and how dissolution happens under the operating agreement's own terms, not how the company's existence is actually wound up and canceled with the state.

clauses.title: Who Conducts the Winding Up
clauses.body: Once an LLC is dissolved, state law puts someone in charge of winding up its affairs by default: the managers who did not wrongfully cause the dissolution, or if there are none, the members, or if there are none of those either, the person or a majority of the people who signed the articles of organization. Whoever ends up in that role must give written notice, by mail, of the start of winding up to every known creditor and claimant whose address appears in the company's own records. If a court instead orders the winding up — on a manager's, member's, or three-or-more-creditors' petition — the court's decree controls who does it. Absent a contrary provision in the articles of organization or a written operating agreement, the people conducting the winding up are entitled to reasonable compensation for doing so.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of who conducts an LLC's winding up by default and what notice duty attaches — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC. This document doesn't identify who is actually conducting a given LLC's winding up, or confirm that the right people signed the notices — that's a matter of fact for the company's own records, not something this statute settles on its own. Both quotes below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.04, so they are treated as one source, not two independent ones.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.04(a)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, default winding-up authority and creditor notice
citations.quote: The managers who have not wrongfully dissolved the limited liability company, or, if none, the members, or, if none, the person or a majority of the persons signing the articles of organization, may wind up the affairs of the limited liability company, unless the dissolution occurs pursuant to Section 17707.03, in which event the winding up shall be conducted in accordance with the decree of dissolution. The persons winding up the affairs of the limited liability company shall give written notice of the commencement of winding up by mail to all known creditors and claimants whose addresses appear on the records of the limited liability company.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.04(c)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, compensation for winding up
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided in the articles of organization or a written operating agreement, the persons winding up the affairs of the limited liability company pursuant to this section shall be entitled to reasonable compensation.

clauses.title: Priority Order for Distributing Remaining Assets
clauses.body: Once an LLC's known debts and liabilities have been paid or adequately provided for — including debts owed to members who are themselves creditors of the company — state law sets a specific default order for distributing whatever assets remain, unless the articles of organization or a written operating agreement says otherwise: first, to members to satisfy any liabilities for distributions the company already owed them; second, to members for the return of their capital contributions; and only after that, to members in the proportions in which they otherwise share in distributions. If the winding up is happening through a court proceeding or under court supervision, no distribution can be made until any court-ordered period for creditors to present claims has expired.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual default priority order for distributing an LLC's remaining assets on winding up — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC. This order applies only 'except as otherwise provided' in the articles of organization or a written operating agreement — the company's own governing documents can set a different order, and this document doesn't say whether a given LLC's documents do that. Both quotes below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.05, so they are treated as one source, not two independent ones.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.05(a)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, default distribution priority on winding up
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided in the articles of organization or the written operating agreement, after determining that all the known debts and liabilities of a limited liability company in the process of winding up, including, without limitation, debts and liabilities to members who are creditors of the limited liability company, have been paid or adequately provided for, the remaining assets shall be distributed among the members according to their respective rights and preferences as follows: (1) To members in satisfaction of liabilities for distributions pursuant to Sections 17704.04, 17704.05, and 17704.06. (2) To members of the limited liability company for the return of their contributions. (3) To members in the proportions in which those members share in distributions.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.05(b)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, distribution timing when winding up is court-supervised
citations.quote: If the winding up is by court proceeding or subject to court supervision, the distribution shall not be made until after the expiration of any period for the presentation of claims that has been prescribed by order of the court.

clauses.title: The Certificate of Dissolution and Certificate of Cancellation
clauses.body: Formally ending an LLC's existence with the California Secretary of State generally takes two filings. First, on dissolution, the managers — or, if the 90-consecutive-days-with-no-members event is what triggered dissolution, whoever is conducting the winding up — must sign and file a certificate of dissolution stating the LLC's name, its Secretary of State file number, and which statutory dissolution event actually triggered it. Second, once winding up is complete and assets have been distributed, that same person must sign and file a certificate of cancellation of articles of organization, which must state the LLC's name and file number, that a final franchise or annual tax return has been or will be filed with the Franchise Tax Board, and that filing the certificate cancels the LLC and ends its powers, rights, and privileges. If dissolution happened by the vote of all the members and the certificate of cancellation itself includes a statement saying so, a separate certificate of dissolution is not required — the two filings can merge into one.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual two-filing cancellation mechanism and what each filing must contain — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC, and not a claim that every state uses a two-document process like this one. Both quotes below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.08, so they are treated as one source, not two independent ones. A narrow exception to 'powers, rights, and privileges cease' on cancellation is addressed separately in this document, in the clause on continued existence after cancellation.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.08(a)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, the certificate of dissolution
citations.quote: (1) The managers shall sign and cause to be filed in the office of, and on a form prescribed by, the Secretary of State, a certificate of dissolution upon the dissolution of the limited liability company pursuant to this article unless the event causing the dissolution is that specified in subdivision (c) of Section 17707.01, in which case the persons conducting the winding up of the limited liability company’s affairs pursuant to Section 17707.04 shall have the obligation to sign and cause to be filed the certificate of dissolution. (2) The certificate of dissolution shall set forth all of the following: (A) The name of the limited liability company and the Secretary of State’s file number. (B) Any other information the persons filing the certificate of dissolution determine to include. (C) The event listed in Section 17707.01 causing dissolution. (3) If a dissolution pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 17707.01 is made by the vote of all of the members and a statement to that effect is added to the certificate of cancellation of articles of organization pursuant to subdivision (b), the separate filing of a certificate of dissolution pursuant to this subdivision is not required.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.08(b)-(c)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, the certificate of cancellation and its effect
citations.quote: (b) (1) The managers shall sign and cause to be filed in the office of, and on a form prescribed by, the Secretary of State, a certificate of cancellation of articles of organization upon the completion of the winding up of the affairs of the limited liability company pursuant to Section 17707.04 and distribution of its assets pursuant to Section 17707.05... (2) The certificate of cancellation of articles of organization shall set forth all of the following: (A) The name of the limited liability company and the Secretary of State’s file number. (B) That a final franchise tax return, as described by Section 23332 of the Revenue and Taxation Code, or a final annual tax return, as described by Section 17947 of the Revenue and Taxation Code, has been or will be filed with the Franchise Tax Board... (C) That upon the filing of the certificate of cancellation, except as provided in Section 17707.06, the limited liability company shall be canceled and its powers, rights, and privileges shall cease... (c) Upon filing a certificate of cancellation pursuant to subdivision (b), except as provided in Section 17707.06, a limited liability company shall be canceled and its powers, rights, and privileges shall cease.

clauses.title: Limited Existence After Cancellation
clauses.body: Filing the certificate of cancellation does not erase an LLC out of existence entirely. State law lets a canceled LLC continue to exist afterward, but only for a narrow set of purposes: winding up its affairs, prosecuting or defending lawsuits by or against it in order to collect and pay off what it owes, disposing of and conveying its property, and collecting and dividing its remaining assets — it cannot continue conducting business beyond what winding up actually requires. No lawsuit involving the LLC is dismissed just because a certificate of cancellation was filed while the case was pending. And if an asset gets missed during winding up, it does not disappear — it stays with the canceled LLC for whoever is entitled to it, to be used first to pay off any liabilities the company still owes, with anything left over going to the members.
clauses.gap: This corrects a framing this research started with: the relevant statute does not say an LLC's existence continues for limited purposes 'until' cancellation is filed. Verified directly, Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.06 says the opposite — the LLC's existence becomes limited to specific enumerated purposes starting after a certificate of cancellation is filed, not before it. Before cancellation (while merely dissolved and winding up), the company has not yet lost its powers, rights, and privileges under § 17707.08(c); those cease on cancellation, subject to this narrower continued-existence carve-out. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine post-cancellation continued-existence rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC. Both quotes below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.06, so they are treated as one source, not two independent ones.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.06(a)-(b)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, continued existence for winding-up purposes after cancellation
citations.quote: (a) A limited liability company that has filed a certificate of cancellation nevertheless continues to exist for the purpose of winding up its affairs, prosecuting and defending actions by or against it in order to collect and discharge obligations, disposing of and conveying its property, and collecting and dividing its assets. A limited liability company shall not continue business except so far as necessary for its winding up. (b) No action or proceeding to which a limited liability company is a party abates by the filing of a certificate of cancellation for the limited liability company or by reason of proceedings for its winding up and dissolution.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.06(c)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, assets omitted from winding up
citations.quote: Any assets inadvertently or otherwise omitted from the winding up continue in the canceled limited liability company for the benefit of the persons entitled to those assets upon cancellation and on realization shall be used to discharge unsatisfied liabilities, if any, known to the company, and any excess shall be distributed to the members.

clauses.title: The Short-Form Cancellation Option
clauses.body: California law provides a separate, simplified cancellation path for an LLC that meets a specific, narrow set of conditions, letting it skip the certificate-of-dissolution-then-certificate-of-cancellation sequence described elsewhere in this document. To use it, all of the following must be true: the LLC has not conducted any business at all since its articles of organization were filed; the certificate of cancellation is filed within 12 months of that filing date; the LLC has no debts or other liabilities, apart from the requirement that a final franchise or annual tax return be filed with the Franchise Tax Board; the LLC's known assets, if it has any, have already been distributed to whoever is entitled to them, or it never acquired any known assets in the first place; 50% or more of the voting interests of the managers (or, if there are none, the members, or if there are neither, the person or persons who signed the articles of organization) voted to dissolve; and, if the LLC took in any payments from investors in exchange for an interest, those payments have been returned to those investors. If all of that is true, the relevant people may execute and file a single certificate of cancellation without a separate certificate of dissolution.
clauses.gap: This clause corrects two assumptions this research started with. First, the short-form cancellation eligibility rules are not found in Cal. Corp. Code § 17713.04 — verified directly, that section is a transition and applicability provision governing which LLCs the 2014 recodification (RULLCA) covers versus 'prior law,' with nothing about short-form dissolution or cancellation at all. The actual short-form provision, verified directly, is Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.02. Second, the eligibility test is not that the LLC 'commenced business within the last 12 months' — the verified statutory text requires the opposite: the LLC must have conducted no business whatsoever since filing its articles of organization, not merely recently-commenced business. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a genuine short-form cancellation shortcut exists with real, specific conditions — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC, and not a claim that any other state offers a comparable shortcut. This is a single statutory section (§ 17707.02); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.02(a)-(b)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, short-form cancellation eligibility and filing deadline
citations.quote: (a) Notwithstanding any other provision of this title, if a domestic limited liability company has not conducted any business, 50 percent or more of the voting interests of the members, or, if there are no members, 50 percent or more of the voting interests of the managers, if any, or if no members or managers, the person or 50 percent or more of the persons signing the articles of organization, may execute and acknowledge a certificate of cancellation of articles of organization... stating all of the following: (1) The name of the domestic limited liability company and the Secretary of State’s file number. (2) That the certificate of cancellation is being filed within 12 months from the date the articles of organization was filed. (3) That the limited liability company does not have any debts or other liabilities, except as provided in paragraph (4). (4) That a final franchise tax return... or a final annual tax return... has been or will be filed with the Franchise Tax Board... (5) That the known assets of the limited liability company remaining after payment of, or adequately providing for, known debts and liabilities have been distributed to the persons entitled thereto or that the limited liability company acquired no known assets, as the case may be. (6) That the limited liability company has not conducted any business from the time of the filing of the articles of organization. (7) That 50 percent or more of the voting interests of the managers or members voted, or, if no managers or members, the person or 50 percent or more of the persons signing the articles of organization, voted to dissolve the limited liability company. (8) If the limited liability company has received payments for interests from investors, that those payments have been returned to those investors. (b) A certificate of cancellation executed and acknowledged pursuant to subdivision (a) shall be filed with the Secretary of State within 12 months from the date that the articles of organization was filed.

clauses.title: Stopping the Annual LLC Tax on Cancellation
clauses.body: Filing a certificate of cancellation (or dissolution) does not, by itself, stop the state's ongoing annual LLC tax. Under California's Revenue and Taxation Code, an LLC owes no further annual tax for a given taxable year only if it does all three of the following: files a timely final annual tax return with the Franchise Tax Board for the preceding taxable year; does no further business in California after that taxable year ends; and files a certificate of dissolution or certificate of cancellation with the Secretary of State within 12 months of the date that final return was filed.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a genuine, checkable tax-clearance mechanism ties the annual LLC tax to the cancellation filing — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC, and not tax advice about any particular LLC's own filings or filing deadlines. This statute cross-references the certificate-of-cancellation filing under Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.08 by name, which is independently verified elsewhere in this document. It also cross-references, by number only, Cal. Corp. Code § 17708.06 as an alternate certificate-of-cancellation provision and Rev. & Tax. Code § 18633.5's definition of a 'final annual tax return'; neither of those two specifically cross-referenced provisions was independently fetched and verified as part of this research, so their text is not relied on beyond what this section itself states. This is a single statutory section (Rev. & Tax. Code § 17947); no additional independent source was found for this specific tax-clearance mechanism.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 17947(a)
citations.cite: Tax and Fees on Limited Liability Companies, relief from the annual tax on timely final return and cancellation
citations.quote: A limited liability company shall not be subject to the taxes imposed by this chapter for a taxable year if the limited liability company does all of the following: (1) Files with the Franchise Tax Board a timely final annual tax return for the preceding taxable year. (2) Does not do business in this state after the end of the taxable year for which the final annual tax return was filed. (3) Files a certificate of dissolution with the Secretary of State, pursuant to Section 17707.08 of the Corporations Code, or a certificate of cancellation with the Secretary of State pursuant to Section 17708.06 of the Corporations Code, before the end of the 12-month period beginning with the date the final annual tax return was filed.

clauses.title: Winding-Up Declaration and Signatures
clauses.body:
