clauses.title: Tenant's Default 30-Day Notice to End a Periodic (Month-to-Month) Tenancy
clauses.body: For a periodic tenancy — one with no specified end date, such as a month-to-month tenancy — California statute lets either party end it by giving at least 30 days' written notice, at any time, with rent due and payable through the termination date. This is a two-way default rule: a tenant ending the tenancy on the tenant's own initiative gives the same 30-day notice a landlord would give. The statute lets the parties shorten this by their own agreement, made when the tenancy was created, to as little as seven days. The notice may be served the same way an unlawful-detainer notice is served under a separate statute, or by certified or registered mail to the other party — and a tenant giving notice has one further option not available to a landlord: mailing (by certified or registered mail) or personally delivering a copy to the landlord's own agent, specifically the agent to whom the tenant has been paying rent for the month before the notice. Separately, a landlord or the landlord's agent may not charge a tenant a fee for serving, posting, or otherwise delivering this notice.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California), used as real evidence of what notice a tenant ending a periodic tenancy must give under this state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's tenancy; default notice periods for ending a periodic tenancy vary by state, and some states use a different default length entirely. Three of the four citations below come from the same statutory section (Civil Code section 1946, subdivisions (a) and (b)); Code of Civil Procedure section 1162 is the only independently enacted source among them, and even that section is drawn in only by cross-reference — section 1162's own text says it governs the notices required by Code of Civil Procedure sections 1161 and 1161a (the unlawful-detainer notices), not section 1946 by its own terms; section 1946 separately borrows 'the manner prescribed in Section 1162' for its own periodic-tenancy notice, so this document treats section 1162 as incorporated authority for this purpose rather than a source that independently addresses this notice on its own terms. This document addresses only the statewide default period; it says nothing about any city or county's own rent-control or just-cause ordinance, and many California cities layer additional notice or documentation requirements on top of this statewide floor. Neither this statute nor any published California case this research located addresses whether a tenant may unilaterally rescind or withdraw a notice of intent to vacate once it has been validly given; this document does not state a rule on that question because none was found, and nothing here should be read to say rescission is either freely available or unavailable.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1946(a)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the two-way 30-day default notice for a periodic tenancy
citations.quote: provided, however, that as to tenancies from month to month either of the parties may terminate the same by giving at least 30 days' written notice thereof at any time and the rent shall be due and payable to and including the date of termination.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1946(a)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the tenant's own alternative way of serving this notice
citations.quote: The notice herein required shall be given in the manner prescribed in Section 1162 of the Code of Civil Procedure or by sending a copy by certified or registered mail addressed to the other party. In addition, the lessee may give the notice by sending a copy by certified or registered mail addressed to the agent of the lessor to whom the lessee has paid the rent for the month prior to the date of the notice or by delivering a copy to the agent personally.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1946(b)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, no fee may be charged to serve this notice
citations.quote: A landlord or its agent shall not charge a tenant a fee for serving, posting, or otherwise delivering any notice, as described in this section.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1162(a)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, the general service methods incorporated by reference into Section 1946's notice
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivision (b), the notices required by Sections 1161 and 1161a may be served by any of the following methods: (1) By delivering a copy to the tenant personally. (2) If he or she is absent from his or her place of residence, and from his or her usual place of business, by leaving a copy with some person of suitable age and discretion at either place, and sending a copy through the mail addressed to the tenant at his or her place of residence. (3) If such place of residence and business cannot be ascertained, or a person of suitable age or discretion there can not be found, then by affixing a copy in a conspicuous place on the property, and also delivering a copy to a person there residing, if such person can be found; and also sending a copy through the mail addressed to the tenant at the place where the property is situated. Service upon a subtenant may be made in the same manner.

clauses.title: A Fixed-Term Lease That Simply Ends: No Statutory Notice Required — Unless the Tenant Holds Over
clauses.body: California's periodic-tenancy notice statute, by its own text, applies only to 'a hiring of real property, for a term not specified by the parties' — that is, a periodic tenancy such as a month-to-month tenancy. A lease for a fixed term, with a stated start date and a stated end date, is not a hiring for a term left unspecified, so this statute's notice-to-terminate requirement does not apply to it: the tenancy simply ends on the date the lease itself states, without either party needing to give any additional written notice under this statute for the tenancy to end on time. That changes if the tenant remains in possession after the fixed term's stated end date and the landlord accepts rent for a further period: California law then presumes the parties have renewed the hiring on the same terms, for a period not exceeding one month if rent is paid monthly (and not exceeding one year in any case) — converting what had been a fixed-term tenancy into a periodic one going forward, at which point the 30-day notice requirement described elsewhere in this document would then govern ending it.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California), used as real evidence of what this state's law requires (and does not require) for a fixed-term tenancy's own expiration — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's tenancy, and other states' rules on this point vary. This document addresses only the statewide statutory floor; a specific fixed-term lease's own text may separately require the tenant to give the landlord advance notice of an intent to vacate, or of an intent not to renew, as a matter of the parties' private agreement rather than statute — this document does not have that lease's specific language and does not attempt to evaluate it. The two citations below come from two separately enacted Civil Code sections (sections 1945 and 1946), not the same section restated twice.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1946(a)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the notice requirement is limited by its own text to a hiring for an unspecified term
citations.quote: A hiring of real property, for a term not specified by the parties, is deemed to be renewed as stated in Section 1945, at the end of the term implied by law unless one of the parties gives written notice to the other of that party's intention to terminate the same, at least as long before the expiration thereof as the term of the hiring itself, not exceeding 30 days

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1945
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the holdover presumption that converts a fixed-term tenancy into a periodic one
citations.quote: If a lessee of real property remains in possession thereof after the expiration of the hiring, and the lessor accepts rent from him, the parties are presumed to have renewed the hiring on the same terms and for the same time, not exceeding one month when the rent is payable monthly, nor in any case one year.

clauses.title: Civil Code § 1946.1: Mostly a Landlord-Side Duty, With One Narrow Tenant Role
clauses.body: A separate statute, Civil Code section 1946.1, requires an owner of a residential dwelling (and, since a 2025 amendment, an owner leasing to a 'qualified commercial tenant') to give a longer notice than section 1946's default when the owner ends a periodic tenancy: at least 60 days, or 30 days if the tenant has occupied for less than a year. That extended notice duty runs to the landlord, as the party required to give it — it does not lengthen the period a tenant must give under section 1946 when the tenant is the one initiating the end of the tenancy. Section 1946.1 does give the tenant one narrow, secondary role: once a landlord has already given a notice to terminate under this section, the tenant may also give the tenant's own notice under this same section, provided the tenant's notice covers a period at least as long as the periodic tenancy's own term and proposes a termination date earlier than the landlord's. Outside that specific after-the-landlord's-notice scenario, a tenant ending a periodic tenancy on the tenant's own initiative gives the ordinary 30-day notice described elsewhere in this document under section 1946, not a notice under section 1946.1.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, and both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Civil Code section 1946.1, subdivisions (a) and (e)); no independent second source was used for this specific point. The surrounding landlord-side 60/30-day notice duty itself is separately sourced to this same section elsewhere in this project's corpus — the Commercial Lease Agreement document's commlease_notice_to_terminate clause already quotes section 1946.1(b)-(c) and (k)(4) for that duty and for the definition of 'qualified commercial tenant' — and this clause does not re-quote that material; it adds only the scope-defining subdivision (a) and the tenant-facing subdivision (e), which that other clause does not cover. Whether a specific tenancy is subject to section 1946.1's landlord-side duty at all, or is instead governed by a purely local rent-control or just-cause ordinance with its own notice rules, depends on facts (property type, tenant category, and any applicable city or county ordinance) this document does not evaluate.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.1(a)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, this section's scope — it supersedes Section 1946 for the tenancies it covers
citations.quote: Notwithstanding Section 1946, a hiring of residential real property or commercial real property by a qualified commercial tenant for a term not specified by the parties, is deemed to be renewed as stated in Section 1945, at the end of the term implied by law unless one of the parties gives written notice to the other of the party's intention to terminate the tenancy, as provided in this section.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.1(e)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the tenant's narrow right to give a competing, earlier-dated notice after the landlord has already given one
citations.quote: After an owner has given notice of the owner's intention to terminate the tenancy pursuant to this section, a tenant may also give notice of the tenant's intention to terminate the tenancy pursuant to this section, provided that the tenant's notice is for a period at least as long as the term of the periodic tenancy and the proposed date of termination occurs before the owner's proposed date of termination.

clauses.title: What Giving This Notice Triggers: The Landlord's Separate Pre-Move-Out Inspection Duty
clauses.body: Separately from the notice requirements described elsewhere in this document, California law ties a landlord's duty to offer a pre-move-out inspection to the moment either party gives notice of an intention to end the tenancy (or, for a fixed-term lease, to a point before the lease term ends, notice or not). Once a tenant delivers a notice like this one, the landlord must, within a reasonable time afterward, notify the tenant in writing of the tenant's option to request that inspection and of the tenant's right to be present for it. The full mechanics of that inspection right — when it must occur, the 48-hour scheduling notice, and its effect on what the landlord can later deduct from the security deposit — are addressed elsewhere in this project's corpus (the Security Deposit Itemization document's pre-move-out inspection clause) and are not repeated here; this clause identifies only that giving this notice is the event, on the tenant's side, that starts that separate clock.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Civil Code section 1950.5(f)(1)), used as real evidence of what a tenant's notice of intent to vacate triggers under this state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's tenancy, and not every state ties an inspection right to the giving of notice at all. This is a single statutory subsection; no additional independent source was found for this specific triggering point, and this document deliberately does not re-derive the inspection right's own substance, already sourced elsewhere in this project's corpus, in order to avoid duplicating that content.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(f)(1)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the landlord's duty triggered by a party's notice of intent to terminate
citations.quote: Within a reasonable time after notification of either party's intention to terminate the tenancy, or before the end of the lease term, the landlord shall notify the tenant in writing of the tenant's option to request an initial inspection and of the tenant's right to be present at the inspection.

clauses.title: What Counts as a "Trademark" Under Federal Law
clauses.body: Federal trademark law (the Lanham Act) defines a “trademark” broadly, as any word, name, symbol, or device — or combination of these — used by a person, or that a person has a bona fide intention to use, to identify and distinguish that person's goods from goods made or sold by others and to indicate the source of the goods, even if the source is unknown to the public. This statutory definition is what makes {{trademarkDescription}} the kind of thing federal trademark law protects and regulates, and it is the backdrop against which a license — permission from {{licensorName}}, as the mark's owner, for {{licenseeName}} to use it — operates.
clauses.gap: This is federal law (the Lanham Act, which applies nationwide, not just in California), used as real evidence of the statutory definition of "trademark" — not a claim that the mark described in this agreement has been examined here for whether it actually qualifies for trademark protection or registration, which depends on facts such as distinctiveness and actual use in commerce that this clause does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 1127); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: 15 U.S.C. § 1127 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Lanham Act definitions — "trademark"
citations.quote: The term “trademark” includes any word, name, symbol, or device, or any combination thereof— (1) used by a person, or (2) which a person has a bona fide intention to use in commerce and applies to register on the principal register established by this chapter, to identify and distinguish his or her goods, including a unique product, from those manufactured or sold by others and to indicate the source of the goods, even if that source is unknown.

clauses.title: Why a Licensee's Use Can Benefit the Licensor — Only With Quality Control
clauses.body: Under federal trademark law, a licensee's use of a mark can legally count as the trademark owner's own use — meaning it can support and benefit the owner's trademark rights, rather than creating a separate, competing claim to the mark — but only where that use is by a “related company,” a term the statute defines as a person whose use of the mark is controlled by the owner with respect to the nature and quality of the goods or services the mark is used on. A separate statutory provision confirms that where a mark is used by such related companies, that use inures to the benefit of the registrant, provided the mark is not used in a way that deceives the public. This is the statutory basis for allowing {{licenseeName}}'s use of {{trademarkDescription}} to support, rather than undermine, {{licensorName}}'s trademark rights — and it is expressly conditioned on {{licensorName}} actually controlling the nature and quality of what {{licenseeName}} sells or offers under the mark.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the statutory “related company” and inurement mechanism — not a claim that any particular licensing arrangement in fact involves the level of control the statute requires, which is a fact question this clause does not resolve. This clause cites two provisions of the same Lanham Act definitional/inurement scheme (15 U.S.C. § 1127's definition of "related company" and 15 U.S.C. § 1055's inurement rule); they are cited together because § 1055 uses the term § 1127 defines, and no independent second source exists for a two-provision statutory mechanism like this one. This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule.

citations.case: 15 U.S.C. § 1127 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Lanham Act definitions — "related company"
citations.quote: The term “related company” means any person whose use of a mark is controlled by the owner of the mark with respect to the nature and quality of the goods or services on or in connection with which the mark is used.

citations.case: 15 U.S.C. § 1055 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, use by related companies
citations.quote: Where a registered mark or a mark sought to be registered is or may be used legitimately by related companies, such use shall inure to the benefit of the registrant or applicant for registration, and such use shall not affect the validity of such mark or of its registration, provided such mark is not used in such manner as to deceive the public.

clauses.title: "Naked Licensing" and the Risk of Losing the Mark
clauses.body: Courts have held that a trademark owner who licenses a mark without exercising adequate quality control over the licensee's use of it risks losing rights in the mark altogether, through a doctrine commonly called “naked licensing.” The Ninth Circuit has explained that a trademark owner may grant a license and remain protected only if quality control over the goods or services sold under the mark by the licensee is maintained; uncontrolled, or “naked,” licensing can result in the mark ceasing to function as a symbol of consistent quality and a controlled source, and where a licensor fails to exercise adequate quality control, a court may find that the owner has abandoned the mark — an involuntary forfeiture that does not require any intent by the owner to give up the mark. In the case the Ninth Circuit was deciding, the trademark owner's licensing agreements contained no quality-control provisions, and the owner's evidence of any actual control over the licensee's product — occasional informal tastings and reliance on a now-deceased winemaker's reputation — was held insufficient, resulting in cancellation of the registration for abandonment. This is why {{licensorName}} exercising, and being able to show it exercised, real quality control over {{licenseeName}}'s use of {{trademarkDescription}} is treated by courts as more than a formality.
clauses.gap: "Naked licensing" is not itself a phrase used in the Lanham Act; it is a judicial doctrine that courts have built on the Act's statutory definition of "abandoned" (15 U.S.C. § 1127), which includes when a mark owner's course of conduct causes a mark to lose its significance as a mark, and on 15 U.S.C. § 1064(3), which allows a registration to be cancelled at any time on abandonment grounds. This clause cites Ninth Circuit precedent (Barcamerica), which is binding only within that circuit; other circuits apply the same general naked-licensing doctrine but the exact standard for how much control is "adequate" can vary and is decided case by case on the specific facts of the licensing relationship, none of which this clause resolves for any particular license.

citations.case: Barcamerica International USA Trust v. Tyfield Importers, Inc.
citations.quote: A trademark owner may grant a license and remain protected provided quality control of the goods and services sold under the trademark by the licensee is maintained. But uncontrolled or naked licensing may result in the trademark ceasing to function as a symbol of quality and controlled source. Consequently, where the licensor fails to exercise adequate quality control over the licensee, a court may find that the trademark owner has abandoned the trademark, in which case the owner would be estopped from asserting rights to the trademark.

citations.case: 15 U.S.C. § 1127 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, definition of "abandoned"
citations.quote: A mark shall be deemed to be “abandoned” if either of the following occurs: ... (2) When any course of conduct of the owner, including acts of omission as well as commission, causes the mark to become the generic name for the goods or services on or in connection with which it is used or otherwise to lose its significance as a mark.

clauses.title: Abandonment as a Ground for Cancelling a Registered Mark
clauses.body: Federal trademark law allows a petition to cancel a registered mark to be filed at any time — with no time limit — if the registered mark has been abandoned, among other grounds such as the mark becoming generic or its registration having been obtained fraudulently. Because abandonment includes the naked-licensing scenario courts have recognized, an uncontrolled license of {{trademarkDescription}} is not merely a private contract problem between {{licensorName}} and {{licenseeName}}; it can expose the underlying registration itself to a cancellation proceeding brought by a third party, at any time, regardless of how long the registration has otherwise stood unchallenged.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence that abandonment (of which naked licensing is one judicially recognized species, per the clause above) is a codified cancellation ground with no time limit — not a claim that any particular license under this agreement will in fact be challenged, or that a cancellation petition would succeed, which depends on facts about actual quality control this clause does not resolve. The task brief that prompted this research guessed this ground might appear at 15 U.S.C. § 1064(5); on checking the statutory text directly, the "at any time" abandonment ground is actually in § 1064(3), not § 1064(5) — this clause cites the section as verified, not as assumed. This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 1064(3)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: 15 U.S.C. § 1064(3) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, grounds for cancellation of a registered mark
citations.quote: A petition to cancel a registration of a mark ... may ... be filed as follows by any person who believes that he is or will be damaged ... by the registration of a mark on the principal register ...: ... (3) At any time if the registered mark becomes the generic name for the goods or services, or a portion thereof, for which it is registered, or is functional, or has been abandoned, or its registration was obtained fraudulently ...

clauses.title: Trademark Licenses Have No Statutory Writing Requirement
clauses.body: Unlike a copyright transfer, which federal copyright law requires to be in a signed writing to be valid, the Lanham Act contains no comparable statutory provision requiring a trademark license to be in writing. The Lanham Act does require an assignment of a registered mark — an outright transfer of ownership — to be by a written instrument, but that writing requirement applies to assignments of ownership, not to licenses, which merely grant permission to use a mark the owner continues to own. Putting a license like this one for {{trademarkDescription}} in writing is common practice, and is generally the only practical way to establish and prove the quality-control terms the naked-licensing doctrine looks for, but doing so is a matter of prudence and contract practice, not a freestanding federal statutory mandate the way it is for a copyright transfer.
clauses.gap: This clause reports an absence — the lack of a statutory writing requirement for trademark licenses specifically — confirmed by reviewing the relevant Lanham Act provisions (15 U.S.C. §§ 1055, 1060, 1127) directly rather than assuming it; it does not cite a provision imposing a writing requirement because none was found for licenses. This is federal law that applies nationwide; it does not address whether any state's general contract-law statute of frauds might separately require a writing for an agreement like this one depending on its terms or duration, which is a separate body of law this clause does not cover.

citations.case: 15 U.S.C. § 1060(a)(3) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, assignment of marks — writing requirement (contrast with licenses)
citations.quote: Assignments shall be by instruments in writing duly executed.

clauses.title: Grant of License
clauses.body: {{licensorName}} ("Licensor") owns the trademark described as follows: {{trademarkDescription}} (the "Mark"). Licensor grants to {{licenseeName}} ("Licensee") a license to use the Mark solely in connection with the goods and/or services, and within the geographic territory, described in this agreement. This license is personal to Licensee and may not be assigned, sublicensed, or transferred without Licensor's prior written consent. All use of the Mark by Licensee, and all goodwill arising from that use, shall inure to the benefit of Licensor.

clauses.title: Quality Control
clauses.body: Licensee agrees that all goods and/or services offered under the Mark will meet quality standards materially consistent with those Licensor has established for goods and/or services bearing the Mark. Licensor, or its designated representative, may request samples of Licensee's goods or services bearing the Mark and may inspect Licensee's use of the Mark on reasonable notice, to confirm this standard is being met. If Licensor reasonably determines that Licensee's use of the Mark fails to meet this standard, Licensor may notify Licensee in writing, and Licensee shall correct the deficiency within the time period stated in that notice. Nothing in this agreement transfers ownership of the Mark to Licensee, and Licensee's use of the Mark, and any goodwill it generates, exists solely for Licensor's benefit and reverts fully to Licensor upon termination of this agreement.

clauses.title: Blacklisting Prohibition
clauses.body: California makes it a crime for a former employer, or its agent or officer, to prevent or attempt to prevent a former employee from obtaining employment elsewhere by misrepresentation. If {{companyName}} communicates with {{inquiringPartyName}} about {{employeeName}}'s former employment, that communication is the kind of act this statute reaches. A violation is a misdemeanor.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a blacklisting prohibition of this kind exists in at least one jurisdiction — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular employer-employee relationship. Coverage turns on the word “misrepresentation”: the statute reaches false or misleading communications intended to prevent re-employment, not merely negative-but-truthful ones, a line its companion provision (Labor Code section 1053) draws directly by carving out truthful statements furnished on request. Whether any given communication crosses that line is a fact-specific question this document does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1050); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1050 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Any person, or agent or officer thereof, who, after having discharged an employee from the service of such person or after an employee has voluntarily left such service, by any misrepresentation prevents or attempts to prevent the former employee from obtaining employment, is guilty of a misdemeanor.

clauses.title: Truthful Statement on Request
clauses.body: The same chapter of California's Labor Code that makes blacklisting a crime also protects a truthful statement about why {{employeeName}}'s employment with {{companyName}} ended, when that statement is given upon a special request for it — such as a request from {{inquiringPartyName}}. The statute adds an evidentiary rule of its own: if the statement conveys information through a mark, sign, code, or other means different from what its words say, or if information of that kind is given without having been specially requested, that fact is itself prima facie evidence of a violation.
clauses.gap: This clause corrects a common mislabeling: Labor Code section 1053 is not itself the criminal-penalty provision for blacklisting — the misdemeanor penalty is written into section 1050. Section 1053 instead operates as a safe harbor, affirmatively permitting a truthful, specially-requested statement about the reason for separation, while also creating a specific evidentiary trap for coded or unsolicited signals. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a safe-harbor and evidentiary rule of this kind exists — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reference request. Whether a specific communication was “specially requested,” or used a “mark, sign, or other means” conveying different information, are fact-specific questions this document does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1053); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1053 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Nothing in this chapter shall prevent an employer or an agent, employee, superintendent or manager thereof from furnishing, upon special request therefor, a truthful statement concerning the reason for the discharge of an employee or why an employee voluntarily left the service of the employer. If such statement furnishes any mark, sign, or other means conveying information different from that expressed by words therein, such fact, or the fact that such statement or other means of furnishing information was given without a special request therefor is prima facie evidence of a violation of sections 1050 to 1053.

clauses.title: Civil Treble-Damages Remedy
clauses.body: Beyond misdemeanor criminal exposure, a person, or agent or officer, who violates the blacklisting provisions is also civilly liable in a private lawsuit for treble damages — three times the actual damages of the party aggrieved. If {{employeeName}} believes a communication from {{companyName}} to {{inquiringPartyName}} crossed that line, this civil remedy can be pursued without first establishing criminal liability.
clauses.gap: The civil treble-damages remedy applies, by its own text, to violations of sections 1050 through 1052 — not section 1053, which (as the surrounding clause explains) is a safe-harbor provision rather than a prohibition. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a private treble-damages remedy for this kind of misconduct exists in at least one jurisdiction — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular dispute, and not a calculation of what damages, if any, would be available in a specific case. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1054); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1054 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: In addition to and apart from the criminal penalty provided any person or agent or officer thereof, who violates any provision of sections 1050 to 1052, inclusive, is liable to the party aggrieved, in a civil action, for treble damages. Such civil action may be brought by such aggrieved person or his assigns, or successors in interest, without first establishing any criminal liability under this article.

clauses.title: Qualified Privilege for Employer Communications
clauses.body: Separately, California's Civil Code gives {{companyName}} a qualified legal privilege for a communication about {{employeeName}}'s job performance or qualifications. The privilege covers a communication made without malice, based on credible evidence, by {{companyName}} to {{inquiringPartyName}} when {{companyName}} reasonably believes {{inquiringPartyName}} is a prospective employer of {{employeeName}} and the communication is made at {{inquiringPartyName}}'s request. The same provision also lets {{companyName}} state, without malice, whether it would rehire {{employeeName}}, and whether a decision not to rehire rests on a determination that {{employeeName}} engaged in sexual harassment.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a qualified reference privilege of this kind exists — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular communication. The privilege is conditional, not absolute: by its own terms it applies only “without malice,” so a communication made with malice falls outside it. Independent case law addressing exactly what conduct defeats this privilege was not verified for this clause: CourtListener research for that case law was rate-limited during drafting and was not pursued further past that point, so that gap is disclosed here rather than filled with an unverified case citation. Whether any particular communication is privileged, or was made with malice, is a fact-specific question this document does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 47(c)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 47(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code
citations.quote: In a communication, without malice, to a person interested therein, (1) by one who is also interested, or (2) by one who stands in such a relation to the person interested as to afford a reasonable ground for supposing the motive for the communication to be innocent, or (3) who is requested by the person interested to give the information. This subdivision applies to and includes a communication concerning the job performance or qualifications of an applicant for employment, based upon credible evidence, made without malice, by a current or former employer of the applicant to, and upon request of, one whom the employer reasonably believes is a prospective employer of the applicant. ... This subdivision authorizes a current or former employer, or the employer’s agent, to answer, without malice, whether or not the employer would rehire a current or former employee and whether the decision to not rehire is based upon the employer’s determination that the former employee engaged in sexual harassment.

clauses.title: No Statutory Mandate for a Neutral-Reference Format
clauses.body: California law does not require {{companyName}} to limit what it tells {{inquiringPartyName}} to only {{employeeName}}'s dates of employment and job title. A strict “neutral reference” policy of that kind is a risk-management practice some employers choose to adopt — it is not a rule California statute imposes. Nor does the statute discussed above set a specific deadline for responding to {{inquiringPartyName}}'s request, or require the request to be in writing.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of what these specific provisions do and do not require — not an exhaustive survey of every California statute that could conceivably touch reference requests, and not a claim about which state's law governs any particular employer's practice. A “neutral reference” policy limiting responses to dates and title is a widely adopted risk-management practice precisely because it avoids the fact-specific line-drawing the statutes above require — but adopting it is a choice, not a legal obligation, under California law. No specific California statute setting a response-time deadline or a writing requirement for reference requests was located during this research; that absence is reported honestly rather than assumed away. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1053); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1053 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Nothing in this chapter shall prevent an employer or an agent, employee, superintendent or manager thereof from furnishing, upon special request therefor, a truthful statement concerning the reason for the discharge of an employee or why an employee voluntarily left the service of the employer.

clauses.title: Reference Request Overview
clauses.body: {{inquiringPartyName}} has asked {{companyName}} for information about {{employeeName}}'s former employment. This document sets out the California legal framework that applies to how {{companyName}} responds to a reference or verification request — it states the law and does not tell {{companyName}} what to say in any particular case.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
This Petition Information Sheet Describes a Court Proceeding, Not a Grant of Visitation
clauses.body: California law lets a grandparent seek court-ordered visitation with {{childName}} only through one of several distinct statutory pathways in the Family Code's chapter on visitation rights (Fam. Code §§ 3100-3105) — not through a private agreement, letter, or this information sheet itself. The general, freestanding pathway, Family Code § 3104(a), provides: "On petition to the court by a grandparent of a minor child, the court may grant reasonable visitation rights to the grandparent if the court" makes certain findings described in this document's companion clauses. Completing this information sheet does not itself grant {{grandparentName}} — or any grandparent — visitation rights with {{childName}}; only a court order issued after a petition, notice, and hearing under the applicable statute can do that.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that grandparent visitation in California arises only from an actual court petition and order, never from a private document — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. California actually provides three distinct statutory pathways for grandparent visitation depending on the family's circumstances (a deceased parent under § 3102, a pending custody proceeding between the parents under § 3103, or a freestanding petition under § 3104), each with its own requirements; this clause describes only the shared framework, and this document's companion clauses address each pathway's specific requirements separately. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 3104(a)); no additional independent source was found for this framing.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3104(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: On petition to the court by a grandparent of a minor child, the court may grant reasonable visitation rights to the grandparent if the court does both of the following: (1) Finds that there is a preexisting relationship between the grandparent and the grandchild that has engendered a bond such that visitation is in the best interest of the child. (2) Balances the interest of the child in having visitation with the grandparent against the right of the parents to exercise their parental authority.

clauses.title: Grandparent Visitation When a Parent Has Died — Family Code § 3102
clauses.body: If a parent of {{childName}}, an unemancipated minor, is deceased, California Family Code § 3102(a) allows not only the deceased parent's own parents (that is, {{childName}}'s grandparents) but also the deceased parent's children, siblings, and other parent to petition for reasonable visitation with {{childName}} during {{childName}}'s minority, upon a finding that the visitation would be in {{childName}}'s best interest. Where the court grants visitation under this section to someone other than a grandparent of the child, § 3102(b) directs the court to consider the amount of personal contact that person had with the child before the visitation application was filed. Under § 3102(c), this section does not apply — and any visitation rights already granted under it automatically terminate — if the child has been adopted by someone other than a stepparent or grandparent of the child.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's deceased-parent grandparent (and other-relative) visitation mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petition. This clause cites three subsections of the same statutory section (§ 3102(a), (b), and (c)); no additional independent source beyond § 3102 itself was found for this. This corrects an assumption embedded in the research request that prompted this clause: § 3102's petitioning class is broader than grandparents alone — its actual text also reaches the deceased parent's own children, siblings, and surviving parent (so, for example, a minor child's aunts, uncles, or adult siblings could also qualify to petition under this same section) — so a description of this section as reaching only grandparents would understate who it actually authorizes to petition.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3102(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: If either parent of an unemancipated minor child is deceased, the children, siblings, parents, and grandparents of the deceased parent may be granted reasonable visitation with the child during the child's minority upon a finding that the visitation would be in the best interest of the minor child.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3102(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: In granting visitation pursuant to this section to a person other than a grandparent of the child, the court shall consider the amount of personal contact between the person and the child before the application for the visitation order.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3102(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: This section does not apply if the child has been adopted by a person other than a stepparent or grandparent of the child. Any visitation rights granted pursuant to this section before the adoption of the child automatically terminate if the child is adopted by a person other than a stepparent or grandparent of the child.

clauses.title: Grandparent Visitation Within a Pending Custody Proceeding — Family Code § 3103
clauses.body: Separately from a freestanding petition, California Family Code § 3103(a) provides: "Notwithstanding any other provision of law, in a proceeding described in Section 3021, the court may grant reasonable visitation to a grandparent of a minor child of a party to the proceeding if the court determines that visitation by the grandparent is in the best interest of the child." This pathway is available only inside an already-pending proceeding of the kind described in § 3021 (for example, a dissolution, legal separation, or other custody-related proceeding between {{childName}}'s parents) — not as its own standalone filing. Under § 3103(c), the person petitioning must give notice of the petition to each of {{childName}}'s parents, any stepparent, and any person who has physical custody of {{childName}}, by certified mail, return receipt requested, to that person's last known address, or to the parties' attorneys of record. Under § 3103(d), a rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of proof applies that grandparent visitation is not in {{childName}}'s best interest if {{childName}}'s parents agree that the grandparent should not be granted visitation rights.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's separate, pending-custody-proceeding grandparent visitation mechanism (distinct from the freestanding petition addressed in this document's other clauses) — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific proceeding. This clause cites three subsections of the same statutory section (§ 3103(a), (c), and (d)); no additional independent source beyond § 3103 itself was found for this. The cross-referenced definition of a "proceeding described in Section 3021" is not independently restated in full here.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3103(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other provision of law, in a proceeding described in Section 3021, the court may grant reasonable visitation to a grandparent of a minor child of a party to the proceeding if the court determines that visitation by the grandparent is in the best interest of the child.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3103(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The petitioner shall give notice of the petition to each of the parents of the child, any stepparent, and any person who has physical custody of the child, by certified mail, return receipt requested, postage prepaid, to the person's last known address, or to the attorneys of record of the parties to the proceeding.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3103(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: There is a rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of proof that the visitation of a grandparent is not in the best interest of a minor child if the child's parents agree that the grandparent should not be granted visitation rights.

clauses.title: The General Grandparent Visitation Petition and Its Two Required Findings — Family Code § 3104(a)
clauses.body: California's most frequently used grandparent-visitation mechanism, Family Code § 3104(a), lets a grandparent petition the court directly, without any other custody proceeding pending between {{childName}}'s parents. The court may grant reasonable visitation to {{grandparentName}} only if it makes both of two required findings: first, that there is a preexisting relationship between {{grandparentName}} and {{childName}} that has engendered a bond such that visitation is in {{childName}}'s best interest; and second, a balancing of {{childName}}'s interest in having visitation with {{grandparentName}} against the right of {{childName}}'s parents to exercise their parental authority. Family Code § 3104(c) requires {{grandparentName}}, as petitioner, to give notice of the petition to each of {{childName}}'s parents, any stepparent, and any person with physical custody of {{childName}}, by personal service under Code of Civil Procedure § 415.10.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the two-finding standard and notice requirement governing California's general, freestanding grandparent visitation petition — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petition, and not a claim that meeting these two findings alone is sufficient to obtain visitation. A separate statutory filing restriction and separate rebuttable presumptions — addressed in this document's companion clauses — can bar this petition from being filed at all, or can reverse the burden of proof, even where these two findings would otherwise be met. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 3104(a) and (c)); no additional independent source beyond § 3104 itself was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3104(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: On petition to the court by a grandparent of a minor child, the court may grant reasonable visitation rights to the grandparent if the court does both of the following: (1) Finds that there is a preexisting relationship between the grandparent and the grandchild that has engendered a bond such that visitation is in the best interest of the child. (2) Balances the interest of the child in having visitation with the grandparent against the right of the parents to exercise their parental authority.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3104(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The petitioner shall give notice of the petition to each of the parents of the child, any stepparent, and any person who has physical custody of the child, by personal service pursuant to Section 415.10 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

clauses.title: The Statutory Bar on Filing a § 3104 Petition While Parents Are Married and Living Together
clauses.body: Family Code § 3104(b) states that "A petition for visitation under this section shall not be filed while the natural or adoptive parents are married," unless one or more of six specific circumstances exist: the parents are currently living separately and apart on a permanent or indefinite basis; one parent has been absent for more than a month without the other spouse knowing that parent's whereabouts; one parent joins in the petition with the grandparent; the child is not residing with either parent; the child has been adopted by a stepparent; or one parent is incarcerated or involuntarily institutionalized. If a change of circumstances occurs such that none of these six circumstances any longer exist, § 3104(b) directs that a parent may move the court to terminate grandparental visitation, and the court "shall grant the termination." The U.S. Supreme Court's decision in Troxel v. Granville (2000) 530 U.S. 57 held that a state visitation statute affording no deference at all to a fit parent's own decision about a child's visitation can violate that parent's substantive due process right under the Fourteenth Amendment.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, together with a real U.S. Supreme Court decision, used as real evidence of a specific statutory filing restriction and of the constitutional backdrop against which it operates — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petition, and not a claim that Troxel itself construed or struck down this particular California provision (it did not; Troxel addressed a Washington statute, Wash. Rev. Code § 26.10.160(3), not this one). This corrects a framing assumption in the research request that prompted this clause: California's actual text does not describe the married-and-living-together scenario as a "rebuttable presumption" against visitation — it is a flat bar on filing the § 3104 petition at all while the parents are married, subject to the six listed exceptions above. The distinct rebuttable presumptions that do exist under § 3104 apply to different fact patterns (the parents agreeing that visitation should not be granted, or a sole-custody parent objecting to it) and are addressed in this document's companion clause, together with the case law actually construing those presumptions. This clause's two citations — a single statutory subsection, § 3104(b), and the Troxel opinion — are independent of one another.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3104(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: A petition for visitation under this section shall not be filed while the natural or adoptive parents are married, unless one or more of the following circumstances exist: (1) The parents are currently living separately and apart on a permanent or indefinite basis. (2) One of the parents has been absent for more than one month without the other spouse knowing the whereabouts of the absent spouse. (3) One of the parents joins in the petition with the grandparents. (4) The child is not residing with either parent. (5) The child has been adopted by a stepparent. (6) One of the parents is incarcerated or involuntarily institutionalized. At any time that a change of circumstances occurs such that none of these circumstances exist, the parent or parents may move the court to terminate grandparental visitation and the court shall grant the termination.

citations.case: Troxel v. Granville, 530 U.S. 57 (2000) (U.S. Supreme Court, plurality opinion of O'Connor, J.)
citations.quote: In light of this extensive precedent, it cannot now be doubted that the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment protects the fundamental right of parents to make decisions concerning the care, custody, and control of their children.

clauses.title: The Rebuttable Presumptions Against Grandparent Visitation Under Section 3104(e)-(f), and California's Application of Troxel
clauses.body: Beyond the filing restriction described in this document's companion clause, Family Code § 3104 creates two further, distinct rebuttable presumptions against grandparent visitation. Under § 3104(e), there is a rebuttable presumption that grandparent visitation is not in {{childName}}'s best interest if {{childName}}'s natural or adoptive parents agree that {{grandparentName}} should not be granted visitation rights. Under § 3104(f), a separate rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of proof applies if the parent who has been awarded sole legal and physical custody of {{childName}} in another proceeding — or the parent with whom {{childName}} resides if there is currently no operative custody order — objects to visitation by {{grandparentName}}. In Troxel v. Granville (2000) 530 U.S. 57, the U.S. Supreme Court's plurality opinion cited California's § 3104(e) presumption approvingly, contrasting it with the Washington statute struck down in that case, as an example of a state law that gives a fit parent's own decision a "presumption of validity." The California Supreme Court later confirmed, in In re Marriage of Harris (2004) 34 Cal.4th 210, that where a sole-custody parent objects to grandparent visitation, § 3104(f)'s presumption controls, is constitutional both on its face and as applied, and requires the trial court to actually apply it rather than simply asking what visitation schedule serves the child's best interest.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute and two real appellate decisions, used as real evidence of the specific rebuttable presumptions Family Code § 3104 creates and of how California courts have applied Troxel's constitutional floor to them — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petition. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 3104(e) and (f)); the Troxel and Harris citations are independent of that statutory source and of each other. This clause corrects a further assumption in the research request that prompted it: no single statutory or case-law "presumption against grandparent visitation when the parents are married and living together and object" was located as such. Troxel's own opinion cites § 3104(e) — the parents-agree presumption — and Harris's holding addresses § 3104(f) — the sole-custody-parent-objects presumption; both are materially different fact patterns from two married, cohabiting parents who both object to a petition, which instead falls under the flat filing bar in § 3104(b) addressed in this document's companion clause, not under either presumption described here.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3104(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: There is a rebuttable presumption that the visitation of a grandparent is not in the best interest of a minor child if the natural or adoptive parents agree that the grandparent should not be granted visitation rights.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3104(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: There is a rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of proof that the visitation of a grandparent is not in the best interest of a minor child if the parent who has been awarded sole legal and physical custody of the child in another proceeding, or the parent with whom the child resides if there is currently no operative custody order objects to visitation by the grandparent.

citations.case: Troxel v. Granville, 530 U.S. 57 (2000) (U.S. Supreme Court, plurality opinion of O'Connor, J.)
citations.quote: Cf., e.g., Cal. Fam. Code Ann. § 3104(e) (West 1994) (rebuttable presumption that grandparent visitation is not in child's best interest if parents agree that visitation rights should not be granted)

citations.case: In re Marriage of Harris, 34 Cal.4th 210 (2004) (California Supreme Court, majority opinion of Moreno, J.)
citations.quote: Because the mother had sole custody of the child and objected to grandparent visitation, Family Code section 3104, subdivision (f), imposed a rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of proof that grandparent visitation was not in the child's best interest. The superior court did not utilize this presumption.

clauses.title: Petitioning Grandparent — Information and Declaration in Support of Petition
clauses.body: I, {{grandparentName}}, am the grandparent of {{childName}}, a minor born {{childDOB}}. My relationship to {{childName}} is: {{relationshipToChild}}. This declaration provides background information for use with an actual grandparent-visitation petition, to be filed in California superior court under Family Code § 3102, § 3103, or § 3104, whichever applies to this family's circumstances. This declaration is not itself a court filing, and signing it does not grant {{grandparentName}} — or any grandparent — visitation rights with {{childName}}. {{childName}}'s parent(s) of record, so far as known, are {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}}, where applicable. Only a court order issued after the applicable statutory petition, notice, and hearing process can actually grant grandparent visitation.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment Block — Grandparent Visitation Petition Information Sheet
clauses.body:
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{grandparentName}}: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet is prepared for use alongside an actual grandparent-visitation petition filed with the California superior court. It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete that petition, and it does not grant visitation rights; only a court order does that.]

clauses.title: Target Housing and Regulatory Exemptions (Lead-Based Paint)
clauses.body: The federal lead-based paint disclosure requirement applies to "target housing" — any housing constructed prior to 1978, except housing for the elderly or persons with disabilities, or any 0-bedroom dwelling, unless a child under 6 resides or is expected to reside there (in a jurisdiction that banned lead-based paint before 1978, HUD's Secretary may designate an earlier cutoff date at the Secretary's discretion). Separately, the implementing regulation excludes four categories of transaction from the disclosure subpart entirely, even where the housing would otherwise be "target housing": sales of target housing at foreclosure; leases of housing found lead-based-paint-free by a certified inspector; short-term leases of 100 days or less where no renewal or extension can occur; and renewals of an existing lease where the lessor already made the required disclosures and no new information has come into the lessor's possession.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of how target housing and its exemptions are defined nationwide — not a claim that every property or transaction is covered, since these exemptions apply on their own terms and a specific property's or transaction's classification isn't resolved by this document. Three of the citations below (40 C.F.R. § 745.101(a), (b), and (c)) are subsections of the same regulatory section; the statutory definition (a separate U.S. Code section) is an independently authored source. Separately, the statute and the EPA regulation place the "(unless any child... resides)" parenthetical immediately after "0-bedroom dwelling," while HUD's parallel regulation (24 C.F.R. § 35.86) places the identical parenthetical immediately after "housing for the elderly or persons with disabilities" instead — a genuine wording difference between the two agencies' codifications of the same joint rule that this document doesn't resolve.

citations.cite: Federal law, definition of "target housing"
citations.quote: The term “target housing” means any housing constructed prior to 1978, except housing for the elderly or persons with disabilities or any 0-bedroom dwelling (unless any child who is less than 6 years of age resides or is expected to reside in such housing). In the case of jurisdictions which banned the sale or use of lead-based paint prior to 1978, the Secretary, at the Secretary’s discretion, may designate an earlier date.

citations.cite: Federal regulation, foreclosure-sale exemption
citations.quote: This subpart applies to all transactions to sell or lease target housing, including subleases, with the exception of the following: (a) Sales of target housing at foreclosure.

citations.cite: Federal regulation, certified lead-free lease exemption
citations.quote: (b) Leases of target housing that have been found to be lead-based paint free by an inspector certified under the Federal certification program or under a federally accredited State or tribal certification program.

citations.cite: Federal regulation, short-term-lease exemption
citations.quote: (c) Short-term leases of 100 days or less, where no lease renewal or extension can occur.

clauses.title: Lead Hazard Disclosure Duties (Sale or Lease)
clauses.body: Before a purchaser or lessee of target housing becomes obligated under a contract to purchase or lease, the seller or lessor must provide the purchaser or lessee an EPA-approved lead hazard information pamphlet — such as the EPA document "Protect Your Family From Lead in Your Home" (EPA #747-K-94-001) or an equivalent pamphlet approved for use in that state; disclose the presence of any known lead-based paint or lead-based paint hazards, along with any additional information available (such as the basis for the determination, the location of the paint or hazard, and the condition of painted surfaces); and provide any records or reports available concerning lead-based paint or hazards, including records regarding common areas. The seller or lessor must make the same known-hazard and records disclosure to any agent involved in the transaction. If any required disclosure activity happens after the purchaser or lessee has already made an offer, the seller or lessor must complete it before accepting that offer and allow the purchaser or lessee an opportunity to review the information and possibly amend the offer.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the disclosure duties that apply nationwide to a sale or lease of target housing — not a claim that every property or transaction is covered, since target-housing exemptions apply. Three of the citations below (40 C.F.R. § 745.107(a)(1), (a)(2), and (b)) are subsections of the same regulatory section; the statutory citation (42 U.S.C. § 4852d(a)(1)) is the independently authored source the regulation implements.

citations.cite: Federal law, pamphlet/disclosure/records requirement
citations.quote: The regulations shall require that, before the purchaser or lessee is obligated under any contract to purchase or lease the housing, the seller or lessor shall— (A) provide the purchaser or lessee with a lead hazard information pamphlet, as prescribed by the Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency under section 406 of the Toxic Substances Control Act [15 U.S.C. 2686]; (B) disclose to the purchaser or lessee the presence of any known lead-based paint, or any known lead-based paint hazards, in such housing and provide to the purchaser or lessee any lead hazard evaluation report available to the seller or lessor; and (C) permit the purchaser a 10-day period (unless the parties mutually agree upon a different period of time) to conduct a risk assessment or inspection for the presence of lead-based paint hazards.

citations.cite: Federal regulation, EPA-approved pamphlet requirement
citations.quote: The seller or lessor shall provide the purchaser or lessee with an EPA-approved lead hazard information pamphlet. Such pamphlets include the EPA document entitled Protect Your Family From Lead in Your Home (EPA #747-K-94-001) or an equivalent pamphlet that has been approved for use in that State by EPA.

citations.cite: Federal regulation, known-hazard disclosure requirement
citations.quote: The seller or lessor shall disclose to the purchaser or lessee the presence of any known lead-based paint and/or lead-based paint hazards in the target housing being sold or leased. The seller or lessor shall also disclose any additional information available concerning the known lead-based paint and/or lead-based paint hazards, such as the basis for the determination that lead-based paint and/or lead-based paint hazards exist, the location of the lead-based paint and/or lead-based paint hazards, and the condition of the painted surfaces.

citations.cite: Federal regulation, post-offer disclosure timing
citations.quote: If any of the disclosure activities identified in paragraph (a) of this section occurs after the purchaser or lessee has provided an offer to purchase or lease the housing, the seller or lessor shall complete the required disclosure activities prior to accepting the purchaser's or lessee's offer and allow the purchaser or lessee an opportunity to review the information and possibly amend the offer.

clauses.title: Ten-Day Inspection Opportunity (Sale Transactions Only)
clauses.body: For a purchase (as distinct from a lease) of target housing, before the purchaser becomes obligated under the contract, the seller must permit the purchaser a 10-day period — unless the parties mutually agree in writing to a different period — to conduct a risk assessment or inspection for lead-based paint hazards; the purchaser may waive this opportunity by so indicating in writing. Every contract for the purchase and sale of an interest in target housing must contain a Lead Warning Statement and a statement signed by the purchaser confirming having read and understood the Lead Warning Statement, received the pamphlet, and either had the 10-day (or agreed) opportunity or waived it. By its own terms, this inspection-opportunity requirement runs to a "purchaser," not a "lessee" — the parallel disclosure duties that apply to a lease do not include a counterpart risk-assessment or inspection-opportunity provision.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of a requirement that, on its face, applies to a purchase and not to a lease of target housing — not a claim about how a specific transaction is or should be structured. The two regulatory citations below (40 C.F.R. § 745.110(a) and (b)) are subsections of the same regulatory section; the statutory citation (42 U.S.C. § 4852d(a)(2)) is the independently authored source the regulation implements.

citations.cite: Federal law, purchase-contract certification requirement
citations.quote: Regulations promulgated under this section shall provide that every contract for the purchase and sale of any interest in target housing shall contain a Lead Warning Statement and a statement signed by the purchaser that the purchaser has— (A) read the Lead Warning Statement and understands its contents; (B) received a lead hazard information pamphlet; and (C) had a 10-day opportunity (unless the parties mutually agreed upon a different period of time) before becoming obligated under the contract to purchase the housing to conduct a risk assessment or inspection for the presence of lead-based paint hazards.

citations.cite: Federal regulation, the 10-day opportunity (purchaser only)
citations.quote: Before a purchaser is obligated under any contract to purchase target housing, the seller shall permit the purchaser a 10-day period (unless the parties mutually agree, in writing, upon a different period of time) to conduct a risk assessment or inspection for the presence of lead-based paint and/or lead-based paint hazards.

citations.cite: Federal regulation, written waiver
citations.quote: Not withstanding paragraph (a) of this section, a purchaser may waive the opportunity to conduct the risk assessment or inspection by so indicating in writing.

clauses.title: Civil Penalties and Private Liability for Lead Disclosure Violations
clauses.body: A knowing violation of the federal lead-based paint disclosure requirement carries several distinct consequences. It exposes the violator to civil money penalties under a separate cross-referenced HUD penalty statute, and HUD's Secretary is authorized to seek an injunction against any violation in federal district court. Independently of any government enforcement action, a person who knowingly violates the disclosure requirement is jointly and severally liable to the purchaser or lessee for treble damages — three times the amount of the damages the purchaser or lessee incurred — and a court may award the prevailing plaintiff court costs, reasonable attorney fees, and expert witness fees in a suit for those damages. Failing or refusing to comply is also a prohibited act under the Toxic Substances Control Act, subjecting the violator to a civil penalty of not more than $10,000 per violation under that Act's separate enforcement provisions.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence that this federal disclosure duty carries enforcement teeth — both a private damages remedy and government penalty authority — not a claim about what penalty a specific violation would draw, since that depends on facts (knowledge, actual damages, and how a court or agency exercises its discretion) this document doesn't resolve. Three of the citations below (42 U.S.C. § 4852d(b)(1), (b)(3), and (b)(5)) are subsections of the same statutory section; the regulatory citation (24 C.F.R. § 35.96(c)) is HUD's independently codified restatement of the treble-damages rule. One correction worth flagging: the treble-damages private-liability provision is at § 4852d(b)(3), not (b)(5) — (b)(5) is instead the provision making noncompliance a "prohibited act" enforceable under the Toxic Substances Control Act's separate, capped civil-penalty scheme; the two are easy to conflate but are legally distinct remedies. This document also does not independently verify the substance of 42 U.S.C. § 3545 (the cross-referenced HUD civil-penalty statute) or its current penalty amounts, which weren't part of this research pass.

citations.cite: Federal law, HUD civil money penalty cross-reference
citations.quote: Any person who knowingly violates any provision of this section shall be subject to civil money penalties in accordance with the provisions of section 3545 of this title.

citations.cite: Federal law, treble-damages private civil liability
citations.quote: Any person who knowingly violates the provisions of this section shall be jointly and severally liable to the purchaser or lessee in an amount equal to 3 times the amount of damages incurred by such individual.

citations.cite: Federal law, TSCA prohibited-act enforcement and penalty cap
citations.quote: It shall be a prohibited act under section 409 of the Toxic Substances Control Act [15 U.S.C. 2689] for any person to fail or refuse to comply with a provision of this section or with any rule or order issued under this section. For purposes of enforcing this section under the Toxic Substances Control Act [15 U.S.C. 2601 et seq.], the penalty for each violation applicable under section 16 of that Act [15 U.S.C. 2615] shall not be more than $10,000.

citations.cite: Federal regulation (HUD), parallel treble-damages codification
citations.quote: Any person who knowingly violates the provisions of this subpart shall be jointly and severally liable to the purchaser or lessee in an amount equal to 3 times the amount of damages incurred by such individual.

clauses.title: Required Lead Warning Statement (Sale and Lease Versions)
clauses.body:
For the sale of {{propertyAddress}}, the following Lead Warning Statement is the exact statutorily and regulatorily required text for a purchase-and-sale contract, printed in large type on a separate attached sheet:

"Every purchaser of any interest in residential real property on which a residential dwelling was built prior to 1978 is notified that such property may present exposure to lead from lead-based paint that may place young children at risk of developing lead poisoning. Lead poisoning in young children may produce permanent neurological damage, including learning disabilities, reduced intelligence quotient, behavioral problems, and impaired memory. Lead poisoning also poses a particular risk to pregnant women. The seller of any interest in residential real property is required to provide the buyer with any information on lead-based paint hazards from risk assessments or inspections in the seller's possession and notify the buyer of any known lead-based paint hazards. A risk assessment or inspection for possible lead-based paint hazards is recommended prior to purchase."

For the lease of {{propertyAddress}}, the following is the separate, shorter Lead Warning Statement the regulation prescribes for a lease contract:

"Housing built before 1978 may contain lead-based paint. Lead from paint, paint chips, and dust can pose health hazards if not managed properly. Lead exposure is especially harmful to young children and pregnant women. Before renting pre-1978 housing, lessors must disclose the presence of known lead-based paint and/or lead-based paint hazards in the dwelling. Lessees must also receive a federally approved pamphlet on lead poisoning prevention."

Only the version matching the actual transaction type — sale or lease — applies to a given transaction; the two are not interchangeable.

clauses.body:
