clauses.title: Who Owns a Patent Before It's Assigned
clauses.body: Under federal patent law, the right to a patent vests initially in the individual human inventor — not automatically in an employer, a company that funded the research, or anyone else — unless and until the inventor actually assigns those rights away. The U.S. Supreme Court confirmed this default in a case involving a university, a research company, and a scientist who had signed two different agreements about the same line of research: one merely promising to assign future inventions, the other actually assigning them outright. The Court held that even federal funding of the underlying research didn't change this default; rights in an invention belong to the inventor unless the inventor signs them away. Where {{assignorName}} holds an existing patent, or has invented something covered by {{patentDescription}}, that ownership belongs to {{assignorName}} personally unless and until {{assignorName}} signs an assignment — like this one — transferring it to {{assigneeName}}.
clauses.gap: This is federal law — patent ownership is governed exclusively by the Patent Act and federal case law nationwide, with no state-by-state variation on this initial-ownership question to resolve. This clause states the default rule from Board of Trustees of the Leland Stanford Junior University v. Roche Molecular Systems, Inc., a U.S. Supreme Court decision binding nationwide. That case's underlying facts illustrate two related points this document addresses separately rather than resolving here: an employer can still end up owning an inventor's rights through an actual signed assignment (the subject of this document), and — in a narrower category of case — a court may find an inventor's rights were never entirely under the inventor's own control to begin with, where the inventor's engagement was specifically to solve the problem the invention solves. That narrower doctrine, sometimes called "hired to invent," is addressed in a separate clause. This clause also doesn't resolve joint-inventorship questions — where more than one person contributed to conceiving an invention, ownership can be shared among them in ways not addressed here.

citations.case: Board of Trustees of the Leland Stanford Junior University v. Roche Molecular Systems, Inc.
citations.quote: Since 1790, the patent law has operated on the premise that rights in an invention belong to the inventor.

citations.case: United States v. Dubilier Condenser Corp.
citations.quote: A patent is property and title to it can pass only by assignment.

clauses.title: The "Hired to Invent" Exception to Inventor Ownership
clauses.body: Patent case law recognizes a narrow exception to the default rule that an invention belongs to the person who conceived it: where an individual was specifically engaged — not just employed in a general capacity — to solve the particular problem that resulted in the invention, courts have held that the resulting patent belongs to the employer even without a separate written assignment, because the individual has, as the U.S. Supreme Court put it, "only produced that which he was employed to invent." This is different from general employment during which someone happens to conceive something inventive along the way; courts have held that general employment alone, without a specific engagement to solve that problem, does not transfer patent rights to the employer by itself. Whether {{assignorName}}'s relationship to {{assigneeName}} was general employment or a specific engagement to solve the problem addressed by {{patentDescription}} is a factual question this document doesn't resolve — which is a central reason a written assignment, rather than reliance on this exception, is the reliable way to establish {{assigneeName}}'s ownership.
clauses.gap: A sourcing note worth being direct about: this doctrine is sometimes assumed to be a matter of state law, but the authority actually verified for this clause is federal — two U.S. Supreme Court decisions (United States v. Dubilier Condenser Corp. and Standard Parts Co. v. Peck) applying what those opinions describe as the implied terms of "the contract of employment" as a matter of patent case law, not a distinct state statute. No independent state statute or state appellate decision establishing a separately-sourced state-law version of this doctrine was located in this research. That said, because the doctrine turns on interpreting the implied terms of an employment relationship, some modern courts analyze the same question under state contract-law principles rather than as freestanding federal common law; both Supreme Court decisions cited here predate Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins' curtailment of general federal common law in ordinary contract disputes, and how a court today would characterize the doctrine's legal source was not resolved by anything found in this research. This clause states federal patent-law authority for the existence of the doctrine, applicable nationwide; it does not determine how any particular court would characterize that authority's source, or whether any specific employment relationship actually fits it.

citations.case: United States v. Dubilier Condenser Corp.
citations.quote: One employed to make an invention, who succeeds, during his term of service, in accomplishing that task, is bound to assign to his employer any patent obtained. The reason is that he has only produced that which he was employed to invent. His invention is the precise subject of the contract of employment. A term of the agreement necessarily is that what he is paid to produce belongs to his paymaster.

citations.case: Standard Parts Co. v. Peck
citations.quote: Whose property was the 'process and machinery' to be when developed? The answer would seem to be inevitable and resistless — of him who engaged the services and paid for them, they being his inducement and compensation.

clauses.title: Patents Are Property, and Assignments Must Be in Writing
clauses.body: Federal patent law treats a patent, and an interest in one, as personal property. That property interest — including an interest in a patent application that hasn't yet issued as a patent — can be transferred only by an instrument in writing. The statute is explicit that this covers not just an already-issued patent but also applications for patent, meaning rights in an invention can be assigned before the patent office has acted on an application, or even before any application has been filed at all. This is part of why a written, signed assignment like this one — rather than a verbal understanding or an informal exchange of messages — is what's needed to actually transfer {{assignorName}}'s ownership interest in {{patentDescription}} to {{assigneeName}}.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on two sentences of the same federal statute, 35 U.S.C. § 261, rather than two independent sources. Both were checked directly against the U.S. Code text at Cornell's Legal Information Institute, fetched twice with different request headers to confirm the returned text was byte-identical both times, rather than assumed from memory or a summary. This is federal law, uniform nationwide — patent assignment law doesn't vary state to state the way many of this project's other clauses do, since patents are exclusively a creature of federal statute. This clause doesn't resolve what specific form of signature (a handwritten signature, a scanned signature, or a fully electronic signature under the federal E-SIGN Act or a state UETA-equivalent statute) satisfies the "instrument in writing" requirement in every circumstance — that question wasn't independently verified here.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 261 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, ownership; assignment of patents and applications
citations.quote: Subject to the provisions of this title, patents shall have the attributes of personal property.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 261 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, ownership; assignment of patents and applications
citations.quote: Applications for patent, patents, or any interest therein, shall be assignable in law by an instrument in writing.

clauses.title: Recording the Assignment With the USPTO
clauses.body: Federal law permits — but doesn't require — an assignment like this one to be recorded with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office. Recording matters because of a specific consequence for not doing so: an assignment is void as against a later, good-faith purchaser or mortgagee who pays valuable consideration for the same patent rights without notice of this assignment, unless this assignment is recorded with the USPTO within three months of its date, or before the date of that later purchase. In other words, an unrecorded assignment remains fully valid as between {{assignorName}} and {{assigneeName}} — the three-month window doesn't affect that — but it can lose its priority against a specific kind of later, unaware buyer if it isn't recorded in time. A federal appellate court has described this rule as adapting to patents the same basic idea used in real-estate recording statutes.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, uniform nationwide; the only registry involved is the USPTO's own, and there's no state recording system in play. This clause doesn't resolve whether recording actually occurs for any particular signed copy of this agreement — that's a ministerial step the parties would need to take themselves, and this document doesn't track it. It also doesn't address the separate rules governing recordal of ownership changes for patents in other countries, which fall outside the U.S. statute cited here. And it states the general recording rule and its "subsequent purchaser" consequence only; the Federal Circuit decision cited below also describes evidentiary requirements — paying real value, and actually lacking notice of the earlier assignment — to qualify as a protected subsequent purchaser in the first place, which go beyond what's summarized above.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 261 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, ownership; assignment of patents and applications
citations.quote: An interest that constitutes an assignment, grant or conveyance shall be void as against any subsequent purchaser or mortgagee for a valuable consideration, without notice, unless it is recorded in the Patent and Trademark Office within three months from its date or prior to the date of such subsequent purchase or mortgage.

citations.case: FilmTec Corp. v. Allied-Signal, Inc.
citations.quote: Section 261 of Title 35 goes a step further. It adopts the principle of the real property recording acts, and provides that the bona fide purchaser for value cuts off the rights of a prior assignee who has failed to record the prior assignment in the Patent and Trademark Office by the dates specified in the statute.

clauses.title: Why This Agreement Uses "Hereby Assigns," Not "Agrees to Assign"
clauses.body: The exact words a patent assignment uses can determine whether it transfers ownership immediately or merely creates an obligation to transfer it later. Federal appellate courts have distinguished contract language promising to assign rights in the future — which courts have read as creating only a future obligation, not an immediate transfer — from language that assigns rights immediately, in the present tense, sometimes called a present assignment. In one closely watched case, a research scientist signed one agreement in which he merely "agree[d] to assign" future inventions to his university, and a separate agreement in which he stated he "will assign and do[es] hereby assign" his rights to a company; a federal appellate court held that only the second agreement's present-tense language actually transferred his rights — automatically, without any further paperwork, the moment the invention came into existence. This agreement is written to use present-tense assignment language for that reason: to transfer {{assignorName}}'s rights in {{patentDescription}} to {{assigneeName}} immediately upon signing, rather than merely promising a future transfer.
clauses.gap: This describes Federal Circuit precedent — the federal appellate court with exclusive jurisdiction over patent appeals nationwide — on how courts interpret assignment language. Courts treat this specific question as a matter of federal law even though contract interpretation is usually governed by state law, because whether an assignment clause creates an automatic transfer or merely an obligation to assign later directly affects who has standing to sue for patent infringement. This clause doesn't guarantee that the language used elsewhere in this document achieves a present assignment under every possible reading a court might give it — it explains the reasoning behind using that language, not the outcome of any future dispute over it. It's also worth being precise about what was and wasn't decided in the related U.S. Supreme Court appeal arising from the same underlying dispute: the question of which agreement's wording created a present assignment was resolved by the Federal Circuit below and was not the question the Supreme Court took up (the Supreme Court's opinion addressed a different statute, the Bayh-Dole Act). The present-assignment holding cited here is Federal Circuit authority, not Supreme Court authority, even though it comes out of the same litigation.

citations.case: Board of Trustees of the Leland Stanford Junior University v. Roche Molecular Systems, Inc.
citations.quote: We have held that the contract language "agree to assign" reflects a mere promise to assign rights in the future, not an immediate transfer of expectant interests.

citations.case: Board of Trustees of the Leland Stanford Junior University v. Roche Molecular Systems, Inc.
citations.quote: In contrast to the CPA, the VCA's language of "do hereby assign" effected a present assignment of Holodniy's future inventions to Cetus.

citations.case: FilmTec Corp. v. Allied-Signal, Inc.
citations.quote: Ordinarily, no further act would be required once an invention came into being; the transfer of title would occur by operation of law.

clauses.title: Assignment of Patent Rights
clauses.body: {{assignorName}} hereby assigns and transfers to {{assigneeName}} all right, title, and interest in and to {{patentDescription}}, including all rights to file, prosecute, and obtain patents based on it in the United States and elsewhere, all rights to sue for and collect damages for past, present, and future infringement, and all rights of priority under any earlier-filed application. This assignment is effective as of the date this agreement is signed and applies whether {{patentDescription}} is an issued patent, a pending application, or an invention for which no application has yet been filed. {{assignorName}} agrees to sign any additional documents, and to cooperate with any further steps, reasonably requested by {{assigneeName}} to confirm, record, or perfect this assignment, including recording it with the United States Patent and Trademark Office.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Board Action Without a Meeting
clauses.body: A corporation's board of directors can take action without holding a meeting at all, but the bar for doing so is higher than at a meeting: every director then serving must individually or collectively consent in writing to the specific action, and the number of directors serving at the time must be enough to constitute a quorum. A meeting only needs a majority of directors present to vote yes; written consent in place of a meeting needs all of them to sign. The signed consent (or consents) must be filed with the minutes of the board's proceedings, the same as if the action had been taken at an actual meeting.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine formal requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. The statute contains a specific carve-out for an “interested director” or “common director” (as those terms are defined in a separate conflict-of-interest statute, Section 310): such a director can be counted among “all members of the board” for unanimity purposes by abstaining in writing from the consent, if the required conflict-of-interest disclosures were made first and are included in the consent — a real but narrow exception this clause does not attempt to fully restate. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 307) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 307(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, board action without a meeting requires unanimous written consent
citations.quote: An action required or permitted to be taken by the board may be taken without a meeting, if all members of the board shall individually or collectively consent in writing to that action and if the number of members of the board serving at the time constitutes a quorum. The written consent or consents shall be filed with the minutes of the proceedings of the board.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 307(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, meeting and written-consent rules extend to board committees and incorporators
citations.quote: This section applies also to committees of the board and incorporators and action by those committees and incorporators, mutatis mutandis.

clauses.title: The Meeting Alternative: Notice and Waiver
clauses.body: A board can also act the traditional way, at a meeting, rather than by written consent. A regular meeting needs no notice at all if its time and place were already fixed by the bylaws or the board. A special meeting is different — it requires at least four days' notice by mail, or 48 hours' notice delivered personally, by telephone (including voicemail), or electronically — and the articles or bylaws cannot eliminate that requirement. But a director can waive that notice: by signing a written waiver, a written consent to holding the meeting, or a written approval of the minutes afterward, or simply by attending the meeting without objecting, before or at its start, to the lack of notice. Any such waiver, consent, or approval has to be filed with the corporate records or made part of the meeting minutes.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine formal requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 307) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this. Note for anyone tracing this research: an early research plan for this document guessed the notice requirement might live in § 311 and the waiver mechanism in § 307(a)(8). Both guesses were wrong when checked against the actual statute — § 311 turns out to govern board committees and their authority (see the companion clause on committee delegation), and the waiver mechanism is actually § 307(a)(3), not (a)(8) (which instead sets the majority-vote rule for acts done at a meeting).

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 307(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, notice for regular vs. special board meetings
citations.quote: Regular meetings of the board may be held without notice if the time and place of the meetings are fixed by the bylaws or the board. Special meetings of the board shall be held upon four days’ notice by mail or 48 hours’ notice delivered personally or by telephone, including a voice messaging system or by electronic transmission by the corporation (Section 20). The articles or bylaws may not dispense with notice of a special meeting.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 307(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, how notice of a board meeting is waived
citations.quote: Notice of a meeting need not be given to a director who provides a waiver of notice or a consent to holding the meeting or an approval of the minutes thereof in writing, whether before or after the meeting, or who attends the meeting without protesting, prior thereto or at its commencement, the lack of notice to that director. These waivers, consents and approvals shall be filed with the corporate records or made a part of the minutes of the meeting.

clauses.title: Notice and Revocation Around a Shareholder Written Consent
clauses.body: When shareholders act by written consent instead of a meeting, two mechanical rules apply on top of the vote-count requirement itself. First, unless literally every shareholder entitled to vote signed the consent, shareholders who didn't sign are entitled to notice afterward that the action was taken — prompt notice for most actions, but at least 10 days before the action is carried out for a defined set of more sensitive actions (including certain conflict-of-interest approvals, indemnification approvals, and reorganizations). Second, a shareholder who signs a written consent can revoke it, but only up until the point enough consents to actually authorize the action have been filed with the corporation's secretary — not after.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine formal requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 603) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this. This document's authority clause on the general shareholder written-consent vote-count rule and the director-election unanimity exception (§ 603(a) and (d)) already appears elsewhere in this collection, in the Corporate Bylaws document's “Acting Without a Meeting” clause; this clause instead covers the two mechanical points — post-consent notice and revocation — that clause's own gap note flagged but did not cite.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 603(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, notice to shareholders who didn't sign a written consent
citations.quote: Unless the consents of all shareholders entitled to vote have been solicited in writing, both of the following shall apply: ... (2) Prompt notice shall be given of the taking of any other corporate action approved by shareholders without a meeting by less than unanimous written consent, to those shareholders entitled to vote who have not consented in writing. Notice shall be given as provided in subdivision (b) of Section 601.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 603(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, revoking a written consent
citations.quote: Any shareholder giving a written consent, or the shareholder’s proxyholders, or a transferee of the shares or a personal representative of the shareholder or their respective proxyholders, may revoke the consent personally or by proxy by a writing received by the corporation prior to the time that written consents of the number of shares required to authorize the proposed action have been filed with the secretary of the corporation, but may not do so thereafter. The revocation is effective upon its receipt by the secretary of the corporation.

clauses.title: Delegating Board Authority to a Committee
clauses.body: A board of directors can, by resolution passed by a majority of the authorized number of directors, create a committee of two or more directors and give it some or all of the board's own authority to act — including, by the same logic as board action generally, the ability for that committee to act by the committee members' unanimous written consent instead of a meeting. That delegation has real, fixed limits: a committee can never approve anything that itself requires shareholder approval, fill a board or committee vacancy, set director compensation, adopt or amend bylaws, amend an unamendable board resolution, authorize a distribution outside board-set parameters, or appoint other committees.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine formal requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. No additional independent source was found restating this specific committee-authority boundary. An earlier research plan for this document assumed this statutory section dealt with notice of board meetings; on direct review of the statutory text, that assumption was wrong — this section governs the scope of authority a board may delegate to a committee, not meeting notice (which is instead § 307(a)(2), covered in the companion clause on the meeting alternative).

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 311 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, board committees and the limits on delegated authority
citations.quote: The board may, by resolution adopted by a majority of the authorized number of directors, designate one or more committees, each consisting of two or more directors, to serve at the pleasure of the board. ... Any such committee, to the extent provided in the resolution of the board or in the bylaws, shall have all the authority of the board, except with respect to: (a) The approval of any action for which this division also requires shareholders’ approval (Section 153) or approval of the outstanding shares (Section 152).

clauses.title: Why Written Consent Needs More Signatures Than a Meeting Vote
clauses.body: There's a real structural gap, under this state's corporate law, between what it takes to skip a board meeting and what it takes to skip a shareholder meeting. Board written consent has no lesser-vote option at all — the statute requires every director then serving to sign, full stop, with no stated mechanism for the articles or bylaws to authorize anything less. Shareholder written consent, by contrast, generally only needs signatures from shareholders holding at least the number of votes that action would need to pass at a fully-attended meeting — which, for an ordinary majority-vote matter, is a majority of the outstanding voting shares, not every share. The one place shareholder written consent does require true unanimity is electing directors, which cannot be done by written consent at all unless every share entitled to vote on it signs on (subject to a narrow exception for filling a vacancy other than one created by removal).
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine structural feature of its corporate law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and not a claim about how any other state's law treats written consent. An initial research plan for this document assumed that this state's default rule requires unanimity for both board AND shareholder written consent, by analogy to how some other states are commonly described as treating the two differently. On direct review of the actual statutory text, that assumption held for board consent but did not hold for shareholder consent generally — only the director-election consent is truly unanimous; other shareholder action by written consent uses the same vote count that would carry at a meeting, which is often well short of unanimous. This clause does not attempt to verify or characterize any other state's statute, and no comparison to another state's law is made or implied.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 307(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, board written consent requires every director serving to sign
citations.quote: An action required or permitted to be taken by the board may be taken without a meeting, if all members of the board shall individually or collectively consent in writing to that action and if the number of members of the board serving at the time constitutes a quorum.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 603(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, shareholder written consent needs only a meeting-equivalent vote count, not unanimity
citations.quote: Unless otherwise provided in the articles, any action that may be taken at any annual or special meeting of shareholders may be taken without a meeting and without prior notice, if a consent in writing, as specified in Section 195, setting forth the action so taken, shall be provided by the holders of outstanding shares having not less than the minimum number of votes that would be necessary to authorize or take that action at a meeting at which all shares entitled to vote thereon were present and voted.

clauses.title: Written Consent Heading
clauses.body:
Action by Unanimous Written Consent of the Board of Directors of {{companyName}}, in Lieu of a Meeting

The undersigned, being all of the directors of {{companyName}}, a corporation organized under the laws of {{stateOfFormation}}, presently serving on the board and constituting a quorum, do hereby consent in writing to the adoption of the following resolution(s) without a meeting, effective as of {{resolutionDate}}.

clauses.title: Resolution Text
clauses.body:
RESOLVED, that {{resolutionDescription}}; and it is further

RESOLVED, that any officer of {{companyName}} is authorized to take any further action necessary or appropriate to carry out the foregoing resolution.

This consent may be executed in counterparts, each of which is deemed an original, and all of which together constitute one instrument. This consent, and any counterparts, shall be filed with the minutes of the proceedings of the board of {{companyName}}.

clauses.title: Director Signatures
clauses.body:
The undersigned directors of {{companyName}} — {{directorNames}} — each sign below to evidence their unanimous written consent:

Director: _______________________ Date: _______________
Director: _______________________ Date: _______________
(Every director then serving must sign for this consent to be effective in place of a meeting. Add additional signature lines as needed.)

clauses.title: Who May Claim a Mechanics Lien
clauses.body: California law gives a mechanics lien right to a person who provides work authorized for a work of improvement, including — without limitation — a direct contractor, a subcontractor, a material supplier, an equipment lessor, a laborer, or a design professional (such as a licensed architect, landscape architect, engineer, or land surveyor who provides professional design services). A separate statute extends the same lien right to a person who provides authorized work for a site improvement (such as street, drainage, or utility work related to a subdivision) even where that work isn't part of a building's construction.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of who California law recognizes as a potential lien claimant — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular project or contract. It states only that these categories of persons have a lien right; it doesn't state whether a specific person's work actually qualifies, whether that person is licensed as required for the work performed, or what amount, if any, that person could lawfully claim. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 8400); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 8400 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, persons who may claim a mechanics lien
citations.quote: A person that provides work authorized for a work of improvement, including, but not limited to, the following persons, has a lien right under this chapter: (a) Direct contractor. (b) Subcontractor. (c) Material supplier. (d) Equipment lessor. (e) Laborer. (f) Design professional.

clauses.title: Who Must Give a Preliminary Notice
clauses.body: Before recording a lien claim, giving a stop payment notice, or asserting a claim against a payment bond, California law generally requires a claimant to give a preliminary notice to the property's owner (or reputed owner), to the direct contractor (or reputed direct contractor) for the work — even if the claimant's own contract is with a subcontractor rather than the direct contractor — and to the construction lender, if any. Two categories of claimants are treated differently: a laborer is not required to give a preliminary notice at all, and a claimant who has a direct contractual relationship with the owner (which includes a direct contractor working directly for the owner) is required to give a preliminary notice only to the construction lender, if one exists — not to the owner or to a direct contractor.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of who this state's law requires to give preliminary notice — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular project. The two quotes below are both subsections of the same statutory section (§ 8200) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this. It states the categories of required recipients and the two statutory exceptions; it doesn't state whether a specific claimant's contractual relationship with the owner is 'direct' for this purpose, whether a construction lender exists on a particular project, or what the consequence is for a specific claimant who omits a required recipient (that consequence is addressed in a separate section on lien-claim prerequisites, not restated here).

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 8200(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, required recipients of a preliminary notice
citations.quote: before recording a lien claim, giving a stop payment notice, or asserting a claim against a payment bond, a claimant shall give preliminary notice to the following persons: (1) The owner or reputed owner. (2) The direct contractor or reputed direct contractor to which the claimant provides work, either directly or through one or more subcontractors. (3) The construction lender or reputed construction lender, if any.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 8200(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, exceptions for laborers and claimants in direct contractual privity with the owner
citations.quote: Notwithstanding the foregoing subdivisions: (1) A laborer is not required to give preliminary notice. (2) A claimant with a direct contractual relationship with an owner or reputed owner is required to give preliminary notice only to the construction lender or reputed construction lender, if any.

clauses.title: Deadline to Give a Preliminary Notice — and the Partial-Recovery Rule for a Late Notice
clauses.body: California law requires a preliminary notice to be given no later than 20 days after the claimant first furnishes work on the work of improvement. A claimant who misses that 20-day deadline is not permanently barred from giving a preliminary notice — the claimant may still give one at any time afterward. But a late notice limits recovery: the claimant may record a lien claim, give a stop payment notice, or assert a claim against a payment bond only for work performed within the 20 days immediately before the late notice was served, plus any work performed after that point. Work performed more than 20 days before a late preliminary notice is not recoverable through these remedies.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual, non-uniform preliminary-notice deadline and its partial-recovery consequence for a late notice — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular project's notice deadline. It doesn't state how 'first furnished work' is determined on a specific project, or address the separate rule for a design professional's preliminary notice (a design professional who notices within 20 days after the work of improvement commences is deemed compliant as to design services), which this document doesn't cover. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 8204(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 8204(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, 20-day preliminary notice deadline and partial-recovery rule for a late notice
citations.quote: A preliminary notice shall be given not later than 20 days after the claimant has first furnished work on the work of improvement. If work has been provided by a claimant who did not give a preliminary notice, that claimant shall not be precluded from giving a preliminary notice at any time thereafter. The claimant shall, however, be entitled to record a lien, give a stop payment notice, and assert a claim against a payment bond only for work performed within 20 days prior to the service of the preliminary notice, and at any time thereafter.

clauses.title: Required Content of a Preliminary Notice, and How It Must Be Served
clauses.body: A preliminary notice must include a general description of the work to be provided and an estimate of the total price of the work provided and to be provided, along with the general notice information California law requires (the owner's and direct contractor's names and addresses, the construction lender's name and address if any, a description of the site, and the person giving notice's name, address, and relationship to the parties). The notice must also include a specific boldface statutory warning addressed to the property owner, beginning 'NOTICE TO PROPERTY OWNER,' explaining that even full payment to the contractor doesn't protect against a lien for the claimant's unpaid work, and describing steps the owner may take to protect against that risk. Separately, California law specifies how notice under this part of the mechanics lien law must be given by mail: by registered mail, certified mail, express mail, or overnight delivery by an express service carrier.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of this state's preliminary-notice content and mail-service requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular notice. The two citations below are from different statutory sections (§ 8202 and § 8110), not subsections of the same section. This document doesn't reproduce the complete boldface statutory warning text (see the drafting clause for that), doesn't address service methods other than mail (such as personal delivery, which this part also permits under a different section this document doesn't cover), and doesn't state when notice is deemed complete once sent (a separate section addresses that).

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 8202(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, required content of a preliminary notice
citations.quote: The preliminary notice shall comply with the requirements of Section 8102, and shall also include: (1) A general description of the work to be provided. (2) An estimate of the total price of the work provided and to be provided. (3) The following statement in boldface type: NOTICE TO PROPERTY OWNER EVEN THOUGH YOU HAVE PAID YOUR CONTRACTOR IN FULL, if the person or firm that has given you this notice is not paid in full for labor, service, equipment, or material provided or to be provided to your construction project, a lien may be placed on your property.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 8110 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, method of notice by mail
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided by this part, notice by mail under this part shall be given by registered or certified mail, express mail, or overnight delivery by an express service carrier.

clauses.title: Deadline to Record a Mechanics Lien Claim
clauses.body: The deadline to record a mechanics lien claim depends on the type of claimant. A direct contractor may not enforce a lien unless the claim of lien is recorded after the direct contract is completed and before the earlier of: 90 days after completion of the work of improvement, or 60 days after the owner records a notice of completion or notice of cessation. A claimant other than a direct contractor (a subcontractor, material supplier, equipment lessor, laborer, or design professional) may not enforce a lien unless the claim of lien is recorded after that claimant ceases to provide work and before the earlier of: 90 days after completion of the work of improvement, or 30 days after the owner records a notice of completion or notice of cessation. For this purpose, 'completion' of the work of improvement is a defined term with several possible triggers — including actual completion, the owner's occupation or use of the property together with cessation of labor, or a continuous 60-day cessation of labor — not simply the date construction work visibly ends.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of this state's lien-recording deadlines — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular project's deadline. The recording deadlines quoted are from two different sections (§ 8412 for a direct contractor, § 8414 for every other claimant) and the completion definition from a third (§ 8180); none are subsections of the same section. It states the general deadlines only; it doesn't state the deadline for a work of improvement performed under two or more separate direct contracts, which a different section addresses, and it doesn't state whether a notice of completion or notice of cessation was actually recorded on a particular project, which changes which of the alternative deadlines applies.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 8412 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, direct contractor's deadline to record a lien claim
citations.quote: A direct contractor may not enforce a lien unless the contractor records a claim of lien after the contractor completes the direct contract, and before the earlier of the following times: (a) Ninety days after completion of the work of improvement. (b) Sixty days after the owner records a notice of completion or cessation.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 8414 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, other claimants' deadline to record a lien claim
citations.quote: A claimant other than a direct contractor may not enforce a lien unless the claimant records a claim of lien within the following times: (a) After the claimant ceases to provide work. (b) Before the earlier of the following times: (1) Ninety days after completion of the work of improvement. (2) Thirty days after the owner records a notice of completion or cessation.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 8180(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, definition of 'completion' of a work of improvement
citations.quote: For the purpose of this title, completion of a work of improvement occurs upon the occurrence of any of the following events: (1) Actual completion of the work of improvement. (2) Occupation or use by the owner accompanied by cessation of labor. (3) Cessation of labor for a continuous period of 60 days. (4) Recordation of a notice of cessation after cessation of labor for a continuous period of 30 days.

clauses.title: Required Content, Verification, and Service of a Mechanics Lien Claim
clauses.body: A claim of mechanics lien must be a written statement, signed and verified (made under oath) by the claimant, stating: the claimant's demand after deducting all just credits and offsets; the owner's or reputed owner's name, if known; a general statement of the kind of work furnished; the name of the person by whom the claimant was employed or to whom the claimant furnished work; a description of the site sufficient for identification; the claimant's address; a proof-of-service affidavit for service of the lien claim on the owner; and a specific boldface 'NOTICE OF MECHANICS LIEN' statutory warning. A copy of the recorded lien claim, including that warning, must also be served on the owner or reputed owner — generally by registered mail, certified mail, or first-class mail evidenced by a certificate of mailing, addressed to the owner's residence or place of business or to the address on file with the building permit authority (with an alternate method available if the owner cannot be served that way).
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of this state's mechanics lien claim content and service requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular lien claim. The two citations below are both subsections of the same statutory section (§ 8416) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this. It doesn't reproduce the full boldface statutory warning text, doesn't state the amount a specific claimant may lawfully claim, and doesn't address the separate consequences of an inaccurate or overstated lien claim.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 8416(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, required content of a mechanics lien claim
citations.quote: A claim of mechanics lien shall be a written statement, signed and verified by the claimant, containing all of the following: (1) A statement of the claimant's demand after deducting all just credits and offsets. (2) The name of the owner or reputed owner, if known. (3) A general statement of the kind of work furnished by the claimant. (4) The name of the person by whom the claimant was employed or to whom the claimant furnished work. (5) A description of the site sufficient for identification. (6) The claimant's address.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 8416(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, service of the recorded lien claim on the owner
citations.quote: A copy of the claim of mechanics lien, which includes the Notice of Mechanics Lien required by paragraph (8) of subdivision (a), shall be served on the owner or reputed owner. Service shall be made as follows: (1) For an owner or reputed owner to be notified who resides in or outside this state, by registered mail, certified mail, or first-class mail, evidenced by a certificate of mailing, postage prepaid, addressed to the owner or reputed owner at the owner's or reputed owner's residence or place of business address or at the address shown by the building permit on file with the authority issuing a building permit for the work, or as otherwise provided in Section 8174.

clauses.title: Preliminary Notice — Parties, Property, and Work Furnished
Preliminary Notice — Statutory Warning and Proof of Service
clauses.body:
NOTICE TO PROPERTY OWNER

EVEN THOUGH YOU HAVE PAID YOUR CONTRACTOR IN FULL, if the person or firm that has given you this notice is not paid in full for labor, service, equipment, or material provided or to be provided to your construction project, a lien may be placed on your property. Foreclosure of the lien may lead to loss of all or part of your property. You may wish to protect yourself against this by (1) requiring your contractor to provide a signed release by the person or firm that has given you this notice before making payment to your contractor, or (2) any other method that is appropriate under the circumstances.

This notice is required by law to be served by the undersigned as a statement of your legal rights. This notice is not intended to reflect upon the financial condition of the contractor or the person employed by you on the construction project.

If you record a notice of cessation or completion of your construction project, you must within 10 days after recording, send a copy of the notice of completion to your contractor and the person or firm that has given you this notice. The notice must be sent by registered or certified mail. Failure to send the notice will extend the deadline to record a claim of lien. You are not required to send the notice if you are a residential homeowner of a dwelling containing four or fewer units.

Claimant: {{claimantName}}
Signature: _______________________ Date: _______________

PROOF OF SERVICE
This notice was served on {{ownerName}} on _______________, by (check one):
☐ Registered mail   ☐ Certified mail   ☐ Express mail   ☐ Overnight delivery by an express service carrier
addressed to: _______________________________________________

Served by: _______________________________________________

clauses.title: Response to Notice of Claim Filed
clauses.body: {{companyName}} submits this response to the Notice of Claim Filed that the California Employment Development Department (EDD) mailed regarding a claim for unemployment insurance benefits filed by {{employeeName}}, a former employee of {{companyName}} whose employment with {{companyName}} ended on {{separationDate}}. The EDD's notice was mailed on {{claimDate}}.

clauses.title: The Notice of Claim Filed and the Employer's 10-Day Window to Respond
clauses.body: When a former employee files a new or additional unemployment insurance claim, California law requires the EDD to give notice of the filing to the employing unit that last employed the claimant immediately before the claim was filed. That employer must, within 10 days after the notice is mailed, submit to the EDD any facts then known that may affect the claimant's eligibility for benefits — a duty the statute's own text says expressly includes facts relevant to the misconduct/voluntary-quit disqualification standard described below. A related, more specific statute independently gives an employer entitled under that same notice provision up to 10 days after the notice is mailed to submit facts showing that the claimant left employment voluntarily without good cause, was discharged for misconduct connected with the work, or left under several other listed circumstances (for example, to accompany a spouse or domestic partner, or to escape domestic violence abuse). Both 10-day periods described here may be extended by the EDD's director for good cause, and if an employer learns relevant facts only after its 10-day period has run, it has a further 10 days from acquiring that knowledge to submit them.
clauses.gap: This task's research brief asked this document's drafter to verify, rather than assume, which statute sets the commonly-cited 10-day employer response deadline, expecting it to be Unemployment Insurance Code § 1032. That expectation does not match the statutory text: § 1032 was checked directly and contains no response deadline at all — it addresses whether benefits paid are charged to the employer's reserve account, which is a separate, later-in-the-process question addressed in a separate clause below. The real 10-day deadline is set by two overlapping provisions: § 1327 (the general duty on the claimant's last employer to report any fact affecting eligibility) and § 1030(a) (a more specific right, for an employer entitled under § 1327 to receive notice, to submit facts on the voluntary-quit-without-good-cause and misconduct issues listed in that subsection). The commonly-cited '10 days' figure itself is accurate; the section number commonly associated with it in this project's prior assumptions was not. Separately, the brief also asked this drafter to verify whether § 1327 establishes that a non-responding employer loses its status as an 'interested party' to the claim, along with related appeal or relief-from-charges rights. No such text was found: neither § 1327 nor § 1030 uses the phrase 'interested party' to describe an employer's status, and the one appearance of that phrase in § 1030 (subdivision (c)) describes the EDD director's own status on an appeal, not any employer's. This document therefore does not state that an employer forfeits 'interested party' status for a late or missing response; the real, verified consequence of an untimely or missing response — loss of the reserve-account non-charging protection — is described in a separate clause below. This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code §§ 1327 and 1030(a)), used as real evidence of the notice-and-response mechanism a state can build into its unemployment insurance claims process — not a claim about which state's law governs a given employer or claim.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1327 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: The department shall give a notice of the filing of a new or additional claim to the employing unit by which the claimant was last employed immediately preceding the filing of the claim unless the additional claim is the result of the filing of a partial claim as defined by the department, there has not been a subsequent employing unit which is designated as the last employer, and there is no separation issue. The employing unit so notified shall submit within 10 days after the mailing of the notice any facts then known that may affect the claimant’s eligibility for benefits, including, but not limited to, facts pertaining to eligibility under Section 1256. The 10-day period may be extended for good cause. If after the 10-day period the employing unit acquires knowledge of facts that may affect the eligibility of the claimant and facts could not reasonably have been known within the period, the employing unit shall, within 10 days of acquiring the knowledge, submit the facts to the department, and the 10-day period may also be extended for good cause.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1030(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: (a) An employer that is entitled under Section 1327 to receive notice of the filing of a new or additional claim may, within 10 days after mailing of the notice, submit to the department any facts within its possession disclosing whether the claimant left the employer’s employ voluntarily and without good cause or left under one of the following circumstances: (1) The claimant was discharged from the employment for misconduct connected with their work. … The period during which the employer may submit these facts may be extended by the director for good cause.

clauses.title: Reason for Separation: The Misconduct / Voluntary-Quit Standard
clauses.body: A separate statute states the substantive standard the EDD applies in deciding whether a claimant's own reason for leaving disqualifies the claimant from unemployment insurance benefits: an individual is disqualified if the director finds that the individual left the most recent work voluntarily without good cause, or was discharged for misconduct connected with the most recent work. The same statute creates a rebuttable presumption running in the claimant's favor: an individual is presumed to have been discharged for reasons other than misconduct, and not to have voluntarily left without good cause, unless the employer has given written notice to the contrary to the EDD (as provided in the notice-and-response statute described above), setting out facts sufficient to overcome that presumption.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1256), used as real evidence of the substantive eligibility standard and burden-shifting structure a state can attach to an employer's separation-response duty — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular claimant's eligibility, and not a statement about how a specific claimant's separation should be characterized. Neither 'misconduct' nor 'good cause' is defined within the statutory text quoted here; both terms have been the subject of extensive EDD precedent decisions and California appellate case law construing their meaning, which this document does not survey or attempt to summarize. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1256); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1256 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: An individual is disqualified for unemployment compensation benefits if the director finds that he or she left his or her most recent work voluntarily without good cause or that he or she has been discharged for misconduct connected with his or her most recent work. An individual is presumed to have been discharged for reasons other than misconduct in connection with his or her work and not to have voluntarily left his or her work without good cause unless his or her employer has given written notice to the contrary to the department as provided in Section 1327, setting forth facts sufficient to overcome the presumption. The presumption provided by this section is rebuttable.

clauses.title: Reserve-Account Charging Consequence of an Untimely or Missing Response
clauses.body: A further statute ties the outcome of the misconduct/voluntary-quit ruling described above to the employer's own unemployment insurance reserve account. If it is ruled that the claimant left voluntarily without good cause, was discharged for misconduct, or left under one of several other listed circumstances, benefits later paid to the claimant based on wages earned from that employer are, subject to certain exceptions, not charged to the employer's reserve account. That protection from charging does not apply, however, if the employer failed to furnish the facts described above within the applicable time limit, or if the ruling is later reversed on reconsideration.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1032), used as real evidence that a state can condition an employer's protection from reserve-account charging on a timely factual response to a notice of claim — not a claim about which state's law governs a given employer's account or charges. This clause quotes § 1032's operative sentence, which itself cross-references Unemployment Insurance Code §§ 1026, 1026.1, 1030, and 1328; this document does not independently verify the content of §§ 1026, 1026.1, or 1328, and describes only what § 1032's own text says about the consequence of an untimely or missing § 1030 response. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1032); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1032 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: If it is ruled under Section 1030 or 1328 that the claimant left the employer’s employ voluntarily and without good cause, or left under one of the following circumstances, benefits paid to the claimant subsequent to the termination of employment that are based upon wages earned from the employer prior to the date of the termination of employment shall not be charged to the account of the employer, except as provided by Section 1026 or if the department determines pursuant to Section 1026.1 that the employer’s reserve account should not be credited, unless the employer failed to furnish the information specified in Section 1030 within the time limit prescribed in that section or unless that ruling is reversed by a reconsidered ruling: (a) The claimant was discharged by reason of misconduct connected with his or her work.

clauses.title: How Reserve-Account Charges Connect to the Employer's Contribution Rate
clauses.body: A separate statute sets each employer's UI contribution (payroll tax) rate from a statutory schedule keyed to the employer's own 'reserve ratio' — the employer's net reserve-account balance measured against its average base payroll — with rate lines that, depending on which statewide schedule is in effect for the year and where the employer's reserve ratio falls on it, run from a small fraction of a percent up to a statutory maximum of 5.4% of the wage base described in the statute. Because a benefit charge that is not excluded from charging under the provision described in the previous clause is charged to the employer's reserve account, and because that account's balance is a direct input to this rate-setting formula, a charge to the account is capable of moving an employer to a different line on this statutory schedule, and therefore a different contribution rate, in a later year.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 977(a)), used as real evidence that California ties an employer's own future UI contribution rate to that employer's reserve-account balance through a statutory experience-rating formula — not a claim about which state's law governs a given employer's rate, and not a prediction of what will happen to any particular employer's rate. The statute itself sets out the rate-schedule mechanics; it does not contain a sentence stating that a single unanswered claim will raise a given employer's rate, and this document does not calculate or predict the size, timing, or existence of any rate effect for any specific employer — that depends on the employer's full reserve-account history, the statewide schedule in effect for the relevant year, and other statutory provisions (including § 1032, described in the preceding clause) that are not independently modeled here. § 977(a) also incorporates a lengthy numeric rate table with dozens of lines; this clause quotes only the table's structural, operative sentence and does not reproduce the table itself. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 977(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 977(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: (a) Except as provided in subdivision (c), if, as of the computation date, the employer’s net balance of reserve equals or exceeds that percentage of his or her average base payroll which appears on any line in column 1 of the following table, but is less than that percentage of his or her average base payroll which appears on the same line in column 2 of that table, his or her contribution rate shall be the figure appearing on that same line in the appropriate schedule, as defined in subdivision (b), which shall be a percentage of the wages specified in Section 930.

clauses.title: Statement of Facts Regarding Separation
clauses.body: {{companyName}} states that {{employeeName}}'s employment ended for the following reason: {{separationReason}}. In support of this response, {{companyName}} submits the following facts within its knowledge concerning the separation: {{supportingFacts}}. {{companyName}} is submitting this statement within the time period stated in the EDD's notice.

clauses.title: License Versus Sale: Why the Distinction Matters
clauses.body: Federal copyright law treats a license and a sale of software very differently. Under the Copyright Act, the owner of copyright in a work has the exclusive rights to reproduce it, prepare derivative works from it, distribute copies of it, and to authorize others to do those things. This document grants {{licenseeName}} permission to use {{softwareDescription}} under some of {{licensorName}}'s exclusive rights — it is a license, not a sale, and {{licensorName}} retains ownership of the copyright in {{softwareDescription}} unless a separate agreement transfers that ownership. This distinction matters because federal law also gives the owner of a lawfully made copy — someone who bought that copy outright — the right to resell or otherwise dispose of that particular copy without needing the copyright owner's permission, a rule known as the first sale doctrine. Whether {{licenseeName}} qualifies as an "owner" of a copy for purposes of that rule, given that this document is a license rather than a sale, is addressed elsewhere in this document.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, uniform nationwide. The exclusive-rights list in 17 U.S.C. § 106 is itself expressly made "subject to sections 107 through 122" of the Copyright Act — including fair use and other statutory limitations not addressed by this clause. This clause states the general license/sale distinction and the existence of the first sale doctrine; it does not resolve whether any particular transaction under this agreement will be characterized as a license or a sale, which depends on the specific terms of the agreement and is addressed in the next clause.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 106 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, exclusive rights in copyrighted works
citations.quote: Subject to sections 107 through 122, the owner of copyright under this title has the exclusive rights to do and to authorize any of the following: (1) to reproduce the copyrighted work in copies or phonorecords; (2) to prepare derivative works based upon the copyrighted work; (3) to distribute copies or phonorecords of the copyrighted work to the public by sale or other transfer of ownership, or by rental, lease, or lending...

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 109(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, limitations on exclusive rights — effect of transfer of particular copy or phonorecord (first sale doctrine)
citations.quote: Notwithstanding the provisions of section 106(3), the owner of a particular copy or phonorecord lawfully made under this title, or any person authorized by such owner, is entitled, without the authority of the copyright owner, to sell or otherwise dispose of the possession of that copy or phonorecord.

clauses.title: The Ninth Circuit Test for Whether Software Is Licensed or Sold
clauses.body: The label a software agreement uses for itself is not necessarily the last word on whether the transaction is legally a license or a sale. The Ninth Circuit has articulated a specific test: a software user is a licensee, rather than an owner of a copy — meaning the first sale doctrine does not apply to that copy — where the copyright owner (1) specifies that the user is granted a license, (2) significantly restricts the user's ability to transfer the software, and (3) imposes notable use restrictions. In the case establishing this test, the software publisher's agreement retained title to the software, barred the customer from renting, leasing, or transferring it without consent, barred transfer outside a defined geographic area, and restricted the customer's ability to modify or reverse-engineer the software — and the court held that because of those provisions, the customer was a licensee, not an owner, so a person who later acquired copies from that customer could not invoke the first sale doctrine to justify reselling them. A consequence the same court identified is that a licensee who is not an "owner" of a copy also cannot invoke the separate statutory defense that lets an owner of a copy make the essential copies needed just to run software on a computer.
clauses.gap: This is Ninth Circuit precedent (Vernor v. Autodesk); it is binding within that circuit, including on courts sitting in California, but other federal circuits have not uniformly adopted this same three-factor test for distinguishing a software license from a sale, and the question can be analyzed differently outside the Ninth Circuit. This clause states the three-factor test and its stated consequences as articulated in that case; it does not resolve how any particular license's actual terms would be evaluated under that test, since that depends on close review of the specific provisions at issue — something this clause does not do for this agreement.

citations.case: Vernor v. Autodesk, Inc.
citations.quote: We hold today that a software user is a licensee rather than an owner of a copy where the copyright owner (1) specifies that the user is granted a license; (2) significantly restricts the user's ability to transfer the software; and (3) imposes notable use restrictions.

citations.case: Vernor v. Autodesk, Inc.
citations.quote: CTA was a licensee rather than an “owner of a particular copy” of Release 14, and it was not entitled to resell its Release 14 copies to Vernor under the first sale doctrine. 17 U.S.C. § 109(a). Therefore, Vernor did not receive title to the copies from CTA and accordingly could not pass ownership on to others.

clauses.title: Clickwrap and Browsewrap: What Makes an Online Agreement Enforceable
clauses.body: When a software license is presented to a user online rather than signed on paper, courts distinguish between two common formats. In a "clickwrap" (or "click-through") agreement, the user must click an "I agree" button after being shown the terms; in a "browsewrap" agreement, the terms are simply posted, often via a hyperlink, and the site states that continuing to use it counts as agreement, without requiring the user to take any affirmative step. The Ninth Circuit has explained that ordinary contract-formation principles — including that mutual assent is the touchstone of a contract — apply to both formats, but they are not treated the same in practice: because a browsewrap agreement doesn't require the user to expressly manifest assent, its enforceability turns on whether the user had actual notice of the terms, or whether the design and placement of the notice would put a reasonably prudent user on inquiry notice of them, and courts have refused to enforce browsewrap terms that were buried or easy to miss. A clickwrap agreement's affirmative "I agree" step is what distinguishes it and is why courts have been more willing to find assent where a browsewrap-style notice resembles a clickwrap flow — for example, requiring an affirmative acknowledgment before proceeding.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on Ninth Circuit case law (Nguyen v. Barnes & Noble); it is binding within that circuit and is frequently cited by California federal and state courts on this point, but it applied New York law under the parties' contractual choice-of-law clause in that specific case (the court noted California and New York law reached the same result on the facts before it, so it did not need to resolve which applied). This clause describes the general clickwrap/browsewrap distinction and the reasoning courts have used; it does not evaluate whether any specific online presentation of this license's terms to the software's licensee would in fact be found enforceable, which depends on the actual design, placement, and required steps of that specific presentation.

citations.case: Nguyen v. Barnes & Noble Inc.
citations.quote: Contracts formed on the Internet come primarily in two flavors: “clickwrap” (or “click-through”) agreements, in which website users are required to click on an “I agree” box after being presented with a list of terms and conditions of use; and “browsewrap” agreements, where a website's terms and conditions of use are generally posted on the website via a hyperlink at the bottom of the screen.

citations.case: Nguyen v. Barnes & Noble Inc.
citations.quote: Because no affirmative action is required by the website user to agree to the terms of a contract other than his or her use of the website, the determination of the validity of the browsewrap contract depends on whether the user has actual or constructive knowledge of a website's terms and conditions.

clauses.title: Exclusive Licenses Are Treated as Ownership Transfers — and Must Be in Writing
clauses.body: Federal copyright law draws a sharp line between an exclusive license and a nonexclusive one. An exclusive license — one where {{licensorName}} promises not to grant the same rights to anyone else, including {{licensorName}} itself in some cases — is legally treated as a "transfer of copyright ownership," the same category that includes an outright assignment. A nonexclusive license is expressly excluded from that definition. This distinction has a real consequence: like other transfers of copyright ownership, an exclusive license is not valid unless there is a signed writing — an instrument of conveyance, or at least a note or memorandum of the transfer, signed by {{licensorName}} or {{licensorName}}'s authorized agent. A nonexclusive license carries no equivalent federal writing requirement and, under general contract-law principles, can in some circumstances be granted orally or implied from conduct.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, uniform nationwide. This clause cites two provisions that work together — the Copyright Act's definition of "transfer of copyright ownership" in 17 U.S.C. § 101 and its writing requirement for such transfers in 17 U.S.C. § 204(a) — rather than two independent sources, since the definition is what makes the writing requirement apply to an exclusive license in the first place. This clause does not determine whether any particular license granted under this agreement is exclusive or nonexclusive; that depends on the license's actual terms, addressed elsewhere in this document.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 101 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, definitions — "transfer of copyright ownership"
citations.quote: A “transfer of copyright ownership” is an assignment, mortgage, exclusive license, or any other conveyance, alienation, or hypothecation of a copyright or of any of the exclusive rights comprised in a copyright, whether or not it is limited in time or place of effect, but not including a nonexclusive license.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 204(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, execution of transfers of copyright ownership
citations.quote: A transfer of copyright ownership, other than by operation of law, is not valid unless an instrument of conveyance, or a note or memorandum of the transfer, is in writing and signed by the owner of the rights conveyed or such owner's duly authorized agent.

clauses.title: Whether an Implied Warranty Applies to Licensed Software Is Unsettled
clauses.body: California's Commercial Code implies a warranty that goods are merchantable — fit for their ordinary purpose, among other things — in a contract for the sale of goods, when the seller is a merchant dealing in goods of that kind, unless that warranty is excluded or modified. This warranty, by its own terms, is tied to a "contract for sale" of "goods." Whether software delivered under a license, rather than sold outright, counts as a "sale" of "goods" for purposes of this warranty is a genuinely unsettled and contested question: software is intangible information rather than a tangible item in the traditional sense, and courts in different jurisdictions have not converged on a single answer, including on whether the analysis differs depending on how the software is delivered (for example, on physical media versus downloaded or accessed remotely) or on whether a transaction that bundles software with services is treated under a "predominant purpose" test that looks at the transaction as a whole. This is why software license agreements, including this one, commonly include an express warranty disclaimer: to state the parties' agreement plainly rather than depend on how an unresolved threshold question about the Commercial Code's scope would eventually be answered.
clauses.gap: California's Commercial Code Article 2 (Cal. Com. Code §§ 2101 et seq.) is a state statute; other states' versions of the Uniform Commercial Code contain similar merchantability language, and the same scope question exists under those states' laws as well, so this clause's description of the underlying provision is specific to California but the unresolved-scope problem is not unique to it. This clause is deliberately conservative: it identifies a real, cited textual hook (the "contract for sale" of "goods" limitation in Cal. Com. Code § 2314) and honestly states that whether software licensing satisfies that hook is contested, rather than asserting a definitive answer either way — a case-law search for on-point California and Ninth Circuit authority on this specific question was attempted but could not be completed and quote-verified before this session's legal-research tool access was rate-limited, so no case citation is included here for that narrower question, only the statutory hook itself. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 2314); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Com. Code § 2314 (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Commercial Code, implied warranty of merchantability
citations.quote: Unless excluded or modified (Section 2316), a warranty that the goods shall be merchantable is implied in a contract for their sale if the seller is a merchant with respect to goods of that kind.
