clauses.title: Required Content of Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Articles
clauses.body: California's Nonprofit Corporation Law contains its own, separate required-content statute for a nonprofit public benefit corporation's articles of incorporation, distinct from the required-content statute that governs an ordinary for-profit corporation. The nonprofit statute requires the filed articles to state: the corporation's name; a specific statutorily prescribed statement that the corporation "is a nonprofit public benefit corporation and is not organized for the private gain of any person" and is organized under the Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law for "public" or "charitable" purposes (or both) — with a further description of the corporation's purposes mandatory if "public" purposes are elected and optional in all other cases (a narrow exception substitutes a different, Government Code-prescribed purpose statement for a corporation that is itself a public bank); the name and California street address of the corporation's initial agent for service of process; the corporation's initial street address; and its initial mailing address, if that differs from the street address. Unlike the required content for an ordinary for-profit corporation's articles, nothing in this list calls for a statement of authorized shares — a nonprofit public benefit corporation has no shareholders and issues no stock.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what one state's required formation-document content for this specific type of nonprofit corporation looks like — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation's formation, and required content for a nonprofit corporation's founding filing varies by state. The two citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 5130, so they are treated as one source, not two independent ones.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 5130(a)-(b)(1)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, the required name and statutory purpose statement
citations.quote: The articles of incorporation of a corporation formed under this part shall set forth: (a) The name of the corporation. (b) (1) Except as provided in paragraph (2), the following statement: “This corporation is a nonprofit public benefit corporation and is not organized for the private gain of any person. It is organized under the Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law for (public or charitable [insert one or both]) purposes.” [If the purposes include “public” purposes, the articles shall, and in all other cases the articles may, include a further description of the corporation’s purposes.]

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 5130(c)-(e)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, agent for service of process and required addresses
citations.quote: (c) The name and street address in this state of the corporation’s initial agent for service of process in accordance with subdivision (b) of Section 6210. (d) The initial street address of the corporation. (e) The initial mailing address of the corporation, if different from the initial street address.

clauses.title: State Purpose Statement vs. the Federal 501(c)(3) Organizational Test
clauses.body: California's required purpose statement for a nonprofit public benefit corporation's articles and the Internal Revenue Code's tax-exemption purpose language are two different legal requirements from two different governments, layered on top of each other rather than one flowing from the other. The state formation statute requires only the fixed statutory sentence that the corporation "is a nonprofit public benefit corporation... organized under the Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law for (public or charitable) purposes" — it does not use the word "exclusively," and it does not itself require the specific language the IRS looks for. That more specific language comes from federal law: 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(3) grants tax-exempt status only to corporations "organized and operated exclusively for religious, charitable, scientific, testing for public safety, literary, or educational purposes" (among a few other listed purposes), and a federal Treasury regulation implementing that statute — the "organizational test" — requires an organization's articles to limit its purposes to one or more of those exempt purposes and not expressly empower it to engage, beyond an insubstantial part of its activities, in activities that are not in furtherance of an exempt purpose. A California nonprofit public benefit corporation's articles can fully satisfy the state's own formation statute while still needing additional, more specific purpose language to satisfy this separate federal test — the state statute does not require that federal-test language, and satisfying the state statute is not the same as satisfying the federal one.
clauses.gap: This clause deliberately mixes two different sources of law and discloses that mixing rather than hiding it: the California statute is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what that one state's formation law actually requires — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation — while the federal statute and regulation are evidence of a separate, nationwide requirement layered on top of state law for any organization (in any state) that wants federal 501(c)(3) recognition. These are not the same authority and are not being treated as such. This clause is also a direct, load-bearing correction of an assumption worth stating plainly: the specific IRS 501(c)(3)-track "organized and operated exclusively for" language is not required by California's nonprofit formation statute at all — it is purely a federal requirement, found in 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(3) itself and in the Treasury regulation's organizational test, not in Cal. Corp. Code § 5130.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 5130(b)(1)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, the state's own purpose-statement requirement
citations.quote: “This corporation is a nonprofit public benefit corporation and is not organized for the private gain of any person. It is organized under the Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law for (public or charitable [insert one or both]) purposes.”

citations.cite: Internal Revenue Code, the federal tax-exemption purpose requirement
citations.quote: Corporations, and any community chest, fund, or foundation, organized and operated exclusively for religious, charitable, scientific, testing for public safety, literary, or educational purposes, or to foster national or international amateur sports competition... or for the prevention of cruelty to children or animals, no part of the net earnings of which inures to the benefit of any private shareholder or individual...

citations.cite: Federal tax regulation, the organizational test articles-of-organization requirement
citations.quote: An organization is organized exclusively for one or more exempt purposes only if its articles of organization... (a) Limit the purposes of such organization to one or more exempt purposes; and (b) Do not expressly empower the organization to engage, otherwise than as an insubstantial part of its activities, in activities which in themselves are not in furtherance of one or more exempt purposes.

clauses.title: The Dissolution-of-Assets Clause: Not a California Filing Requirement
clauses.body: The specific, dedicated-assets dissolution clause that commonly appears in nonprofit articles of incorporation — stating that upon dissolution the corporation's remaining assets will be distributed to another nonprofit organization, or to a federal, state, or local government, for a public purpose — is not one of the items California's own nonprofit-articles content statute (Cal. Corp. Code § 5130, covered above) requires. That statute's required-content list runs to five items — name, purpose statement, agent, street address, mailing address — and a dissolution or asset-distribution clause is not among them. A dissolution-related provision does appear in California's Nonprofit Corporation Law, but only as an optional clause available in one narrow situation: for a subordinate corporation created under a head organization's authority, the articles may (not must) provide that the corporation dissolves when the head organization revokes its charter, and that upon such a dissolution its assets will be distributed to that head organization. Separately, when a nonprofit public benefit corporation actually dissolves for any reason, a different statute governs how its assets are in fact disposed of: in conformity with the corporation's own articles or bylaws, subject to the terms of any trust under which the assets are held, and ordinarily only by a superior court decree issued in a proceeding to which the California Attorney General is a party (or, alternatively, upon the Attorney General's written waiver of objection). The specific "distribute to another exempt organization or government entity, never to members" language is instead a federal tax-law requirement: a Treasury regulation implementing 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(3) treats an organization's assets as properly "dedicated to an exempt purpose" — a condition of the same organizational test discussed above — only if, on dissolution, they would go by the articles or by operation of law to another exempt purpose, to a government for a public purpose, or to a court-selected organization; that same regulation states the test fails outright if the articles or state law would let dissolution assets go to the organization's own members or shareholders.
clauses.gap: This clause corrects, directly and specifically, an assumption behind the original research question: Cal. Corp. Code § 5134 does not impose a dissolution-clause requirement. On the actual statutory text, § 5134 addresses something unrelated — it lets the incorporator or incorporators act on the corporation's behalf (adopting and amending bylaws, electing directors and officers) before any initial directors are named or elected; it has nothing to do with dissolution or asset distribution. This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of what that one state's formation and dissolution law actually require — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and the mandatory content of a nonprofit's dissolution provisions, if any, varies by state. Separately, the Treasury regulation cited is evidence of a distinct federal requirement layered on top of (not required by) the state statutes; it is not being treated as California authority. The two California citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 5132 and Cal. Corp. Code § 6716, and are treated as two independent sources, not subsections of one section.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 5132(a)(2)(B)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, the narrow optional dissolution provision for subordinate corporations
citations.quote: That in the event of its dissolution pursuant to an article provision allowed by subparagraph (A) or in the event of its dissolution for any reason, any assets of the corporation after compliance with the applicable provisions of Chapters 15 (commencing with Section 6510), 16 (commencing with Section 6610) and 17 (commencing with Section 6710) shall be distributed to the head organization.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 6716(a)-(b)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, how assets are actually disposed of upon dissolution
citations.quote: (a) Except as provided in Section 6715, all of a corporation’s assets shall be disposed of on dissolution in conformity with its articles or bylaws subject to complying with the provisions of any trust under which such assets are held. (b) Except as provided in subdivision (c), the disposition required in subdivision (a) shall be made by decree of the superior court of the proper county in proceedings to which the Attorney General is a party.

citations.cite: Federal tax regulation, the organizational test's dissolution-of-assets requirement
citations.quote: An organization is not organized exclusively for one or more exempt purposes unless its assets are dedicated to an exempt purpose... However, an organization does not meet the organizational test if its articles or the law of the State in which it was created provide that its assets would, upon dissolution, be distributed to its members or shareholders.

clauses.title: Statutory Prohibition on Distributions
clauses.body: California's Nonprofit Corporation Law contains a distinct, freestanding statutory prohibition that has no counterpart in the state's general for-profit corporation statute: "No corporation shall make any distribution," subject only to a narrow carve-out for the purchase of a membership in a limited-equity housing cooperative organized as a public benefit corporation. This sits in its own chapter of the Nonprofit Corporation Law titled "Distributions," under an article titled "Limitations." A separate section of the same law gives specific people standing to go to court over a violation of a nonprofit's charitable character: the corporation itself (or a member suing in the corporation's name), an officer, a director, a person with a reversionary, contractual, or property interest in trust-held assets, or the California Attorney General, may bring an action to enjoin, correct, obtain damages for, or otherwise remedy a breach of a charitable trust, and the Attorney General must be given notice of any such action brought by the other listed parties and may intervene in it.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of a genuine, distinct nonprofit-specific prohibition and its enforcement mechanism in that one state — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and whether a state imposes a no-distribution rule on nonprofit corporations, and how it is enforced, varies by state. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 5410 and Cal. Corp. Code § 5142, and are treated as two independent sources, not subsections of one section.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 5410
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, the prohibition on distributions
citations.quote: No corporation shall make any distribution. This section shall not apply to the purchase of a membership in a limited-equity housing cooperative, as defined in Section 33007.5 of the Health and Safety Code, which is organized as a public benefit corporation.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 5142(a)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, who may sue to enforce a charitable trust
citations.quote: Notwithstanding Section 5141, any of the following may bring an action to enjoin, correct, obtain damages for or to otherwise remedy a breach of a charitable trust: (1) The corporation, or a member in the name of the corporation pursuant to Section 5710. (2) An officer of the corporation. (3) A director of the corporation. (4) A person with a reversionary, contractual, or property interest in the assets subject to such charitable trust. (5) The Attorney General, or any person granted relator status by the Attorney General. The Attorney General shall be given notice of any action brought by the persons specified in paragraphs (1) through (4), and may intervene.

clauses.title: Nonprofit Corporation Naming Rules Mirror the General Corporation Law
clauses.body: California's Nonprofit Corporation Law has its own naming statute for a nonprofit public benefit corporation, separate from the naming statute that governs an ordinary for-profit corporation — but on the actual statutory text, the two impose essentially the same restrictions rather than materially different ones. The nonprofit statute provides that the Secretary of State will not file articles setting forth a name containing "bank," "trust," "trustee," or related words unless a certificate of approval from the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation is attached, and that a nonprofit corporation's name cannot be one the Secretary of State determines is likely to mislead the public, and must be distinguishable in the Secretary of State's records from the names of other corporations, qualified foreign corporations, and reserved or registered names. Those are the same two substantive restrictions — the financial-institution-word restriction and the misleading/distinguishability restriction — that apply to an ordinary for-profit corporation's name. The one naming feature that does not carry over is not, on inspection, a nonprofit-specific difference either: the for-profit statute's requirement that a name include "corporation," "incorporated," or "limited" (or an abbreviation) applies only to a for-profit corporation that elects close-corporation status under a share-structure-based statute that has no nonprofit counterpart — a nonprofit public benefit corporation, having no shares and no close-corporation election available to it, was never within reach of that requirement in the first place.
clauses.gap: This is one state's naming statute, not a claim about naming rules in any other state — restricted words, and whether any designator word must be included in a nonprofit corporation's name at all, vary by state. This clause is also a direct correction of an assumption worth stating plainly: on the statutory text actually found, California's nonprofit naming rules do not differ in substance from the state's general for-profit corporation naming rules — both restrict the same categories of names for the same reasons, and the one difference initially expected (a designator-word requirement) turns out never to have applied to nonprofit corporations under either statute. The two citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 5122, and are treated as one source, not two independent ones.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 5122(a)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, the bank/trust name restriction
citations.quote: The Secretary of State shall not file articles setting forth a name in which “bank,” “trust,” “trustee,” or related words appear, unless the certificate of approval of the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation is attached thereto.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 5122(b)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, the misleading-name and distinguishability requirement
citations.quote: The name of a corporation shall not be a name that the Secretary of State determines is likely to mislead the public and shall be distinguishable in the records of the Secretary of State from all of the following: (1) The name of any corporation. (2) The name of any foreign corporation authorized to transact intrastate business in this state.

clauses.title: Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Purpose Declaration
clauses.body: The name of the corporation is {{companyName}}. {{companyName}} is a nonprofit public benefit corporation and is not organized for the private gain of any person. It is organized under the Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law for the following purposes: {{nonprofitPurpose}}. The initial street address of {{companyName}} is {{principalOfficeAddress}}.

clauses.title: Nonprofit Agent for Service of Process Designation
clauses.body: The name of {{companyName}}'s initial agent for service of process in California is {{agentName}}. The agent's street address in California is {{agentAddress}}.

clauses.title: Nonprofit Incorporator Signature
HOA/CC&R Disclosure — Introduction
clauses.body: This HOA/CC&R Disclosure is provided in connection with the sale of {{propertyAddress}} by {{sellerName}} to {{buyerName}}. The property is a separate interest in {{hoaName}}, a common interest development. This disclosure is furnished under California's Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act and is separate from, and in addition to, any Transfer Disclosure Statement provided elsewhere in connection with this sale.

clauses.title: Documents the Seller Must Provide Before Transfer
clauses.body: Before the transfer of title to a separate interest in a common interest development, or the execution of a real property sales contract, the owner must provide the prospective purchaser with: a copy of all governing documents (including, if the association is unincorporated, a written statement to that effect); a copy of the association's most recent annual budget report and related financial documents; a true written statement of the association's current regular and special assessments and fees, any assessments or monetary fines against the owner's interest that remain unpaid as of the date of the statement, and related late-charge, interest, and collection-cost information; a copy or summary of any notice of an unresolved alleged violation of the governing documents previously sent to the owner; a copy of the initial list of construction defects provided to association members, unless the matter has since been resolved and the association has complied with the applicable settlement-disclosure requirements; and, if requested by the purchaser, the minutes of the board's regular meetings for the preceding 12 months. The owner must also provide a copy of the association's most recent exterior elevated elements inspection report.
clauses.gap: The statutory list in Civil Code § 4525(a) has eleven numbered items; the body above summarizes the most transaction-relevant ones and omits two narrower items (an age-restriction statement keyed to Civil Code § 51.3, and a rental/lease-prohibition statement) that only apply if the governing documents contain those specific restrictions. The task assumption that this list includes a general 'statement regarding pending legal claims/litigation involving the HOA' does not hold up against the statutory text as fetched: § 4525(a) requires disclosure of the initial list of construction defects under the association's builder-defect process (§§ 6000, 6100), which is narrower than a general litigation disclosure, but there is no separate line item in § 4525(a) requiring disclosure of the HOA's pending or threatened litigation generally. All six citations below are to subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code § 4525(a); they are not independent sections corroborating each other. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Davis-Stirling document-disclosure scheme — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific HOA sale; common-interest-development disclosure regimes vary by state.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4525(a)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, Davis-Stirling Act, seller's document-disclosure obligation and timing
citations.quote: The owner of a separate interest shall provide the following documents to a prospective purchaser of the separate interest, as soon as practicable before the transfer of title or the execution of a real property sales contract, as defined in Section 2985:

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4525(a)(1)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, governing documents
citations.quote: A copy of all governing documents. If the association is not incorporated, this shall include a statement in writing from an authorized representative of the association that the association is not incorporated.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4525(a)(3)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, most recent annual budget report documents
citations.quote: A copy of the most recent documents distributed pursuant to Article 7 (commencing with Section 5300) of Chapter 6.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4525(a)(4)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, assessment and unpaid-amount statement
citations.quote: A true statement in writing obtained from an authorized representative of the association as to the amount of the association's current regular and special assessments and fees, any assessments levied upon the owner's interest in the common interest development that are unpaid on the date of the statement, and any monetary fines or penalties levied upon the owner's interest and unpaid on the date of the statement.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4525(a)(5)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, unresolved violation notice
citations.quote: A copy or a summary of any notice previously sent to the owner pursuant to Section 5855 that sets forth any alleged violation of the governing documents that remains unresolved at the time of the request.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4525(a)(11)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, exterior elevated elements inspection report
citations.quote: A copy of the report issued pursuant to the most recent inspection conducted pursuant to Section 5551.

clauses.title: HOA's Deadline and Fee for Providing Requested Documents
clauses.body: Upon a seller's written request, the association must provide copies of the documents listed above within 10 days of the mailing or delivery of the request. The association may charge the seller a fee for the documents, but only a reasonable fee based on the association's actual cost to procure, prepare, reproduce, and deliver them; no additional fee may be charged for electronic delivery instead of a hard copy. The seller must provide the prospective purchaser, at no cost, with any of these documents the seller already has in the seller's possession.
clauses.gap: The task brief assumed a specific dollar cap on the fee an HOA may charge for compiling these documents. That assumption does not hold up against the statutory text as fetched: Civil Code § 4530(b)(1) authorizes only a 'reasonable fee' tied to the association's actual cost of procurement, preparation, reproduction, and delivery — there is no fixed dollar ceiling in the statute. The three citations below are all to subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code § 4530; they are not independent sections corroborating each other. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Davis-Stirling document-disclosure scheme — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific HOA sale; common-interest-development disclosure regimes vary by state.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4530(a)(1)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, 10-day deadline to provide requested documents
citations.quote: Upon written request, the association shall, within 10 days of the mailing or delivery of the request, provide the owner of a separate interest, or any other recipient authorized by the owner, with a copy of all of the requested documents specified in Section 4525.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4530(b)(1)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, fee limited to actual cost — no fixed dollar cap
citations.quote: The association may collect a reasonable fee from the seller based upon the association's actual cost for the procurement, preparation, reproduction, and delivery of the documents requested pursuant to this section. An additional fee shall not be charged for the electronic delivery in lieu of a hard copy delivery of the documents requested.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4530(b)(6)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, seller must provide documents already in seller's possession at no cost
citations.quote: A seller shall provide to the prospective purchaser, at no cost, current copies of any documents specified by Section 4525 that are in the possession of the seller.

clauses.title: Itemized Fee Disclosure Form for Requested Documents
clauses.body: When the association delivers the requested documents, it must also provide a completed copy of the statutory billing-disclosure form, which itemizes each document the seller may be charged for, the Civil Code section requiring it, whether it was included, and the fee charged for it. A seller may request to purchase some or all of the listed documents but cannot be required to purchase all of them.
clauses.gap: The task brief assumed Civil Code § 4528 creates a distinct, separately defined 'Assessment and Reserve Funding Disclosure Summary' document. That assumption does not hold up against the statutory text as fetched: § 4528 is the template for the itemized billing-disclosure form required by § 4530(d) — an invoice-style checklist of the documents an association may charge for. 'Assessment and reserve funding disclosure summary' appears on that form only as the label of one line item (cross-referencing Sections 5300 and 4525(a)(4)), not as a freestanding document with its own separately defined statutory content. Both citations below are to the same statutory section, Civil Code § 4528; they are not independent sections corroborating each other. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Davis-Stirling document-disclosure scheme — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific HOA sale; common-interest-development disclosure regimes vary by state.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4528
citations.cite: California Civil Code, billing-disclosure form is an itemized checklist tied to § 4525 documents
citations.quote: The form for billing disclosures required by Section 4530 shall be in at least 10-point type and substantially the following form: CHARGES FOR DOCUMENTS PROVIDED AS REQUIRED BY SECTION 4525

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4528
citations.cite: California Civil Code, 'Assessment and reserve funding disclosure summary' is one line item on the form
citations.quote: Annual budget report or summary, including reserve study Sections 5300 and 4525(a)(3) Assessment and reserve funding disclosure summary Sections 5300 and 4525(a)(4)

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4530(d)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, association must deliver the § 4528 form with the requested documents
citations.quote: The association shall also provide a recipient authorized by the owner of a separate interest with a copy of the completed form specified in Section 4528 at the time the required documents are delivered.

clauses.title: Consequence of a Seller's Failure to Disclose
clauses.body: A transfer is not invalidated solely because a party failed to comply with this disclosure article, and title to the transferred property remains valid. A person who willfully violates this article is liable to the purchaser for the purchaser's actual damages, plus a civil penalty of up to five hundred dollars, and the prevailing party in an action to enforce this liability is entitled to reasonable attorney's fees.
clauses.gap: The task brief asked whether § 4525(f) or a nearby subsection creates a buyer's right of rescission for a seller's failure to provide these HOA documents. That assumption does not hold up against the statutory text as fetched: current Civil Code § 4525 has only subsections (a) and (b) — there is no subsection (f). More importantly, the article's own remedy section, Civil Code § 4540, provides only a damages remedy (actual damages, a civil penalty capped at $500, and fee-shifting to the prevailing party) for a willful violation, and the immediately following section, § 4545, expressly states that a violation does not affect the validity of title. Read together, these two sections affirmatively rule out rescission or invalidation of the sale as a remedy under this article — the opposite of what the brief assumed. This is a different remedial structure than the Transfer Disclosure Statement scheme addressed elsewhere in this corpus (Civil Code § 1102.13), which similarly provides only a non-invalidation/actual-damages remedy rather than rescission, for a related but separate disclosure obligation. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Davis-Stirling document-disclosure scheme — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific HOA sale; common-interest-development disclosure regimes vary by state.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4540
citations.cite: California Civil Code, willful-violation damages remedy, capped civil penalty, and fee-shifting
citations.quote: Any person who willfully violates this article is liable to the purchaser of a separate interest that is subject to this section for actual damages occasioned thereby and, in addition, shall pay a civil penalty in an amount not to exceed five hundred dollars ($500). In an action to enforce this liability, the prevailing party shall be awarded reasonable attorney's fees.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4545
citations.cite: California Civil Code, a violation does not affect the validity of title — no rescission remedy
citations.quote: Nothing in this article affects the validity of title to real property transferred in violation of this article.

clauses.title: This Disclosure Is Separate From, and Cumulative With, the Transfer Disclosure Statement
clauses.body: The Davis-Stirling document-disclosure obligation applies to the sale of a 'separate interest' in a common interest development, which includes a condominium unit, a lot or parcel in a planned development, an apartment in a community apartment project, or a unit in a stock cooperative. This obligation arises from a different statutory article than the Transfer Disclosure Statement requirement, which applies to transfers of single-family residential property generally. Where a sale involves a separate interest that also qualifies as single-family residential property, both disclosure obligations can apply to the same transaction, and satisfying one does not by itself satisfy the other.
clauses.gap: This clause draws a distinction between two separate California statutory articles cited elsewhere in this corpus (the Transfer Disclosure Statement clauses under Civil Code § 1102 et seq.) and the Davis-Stirling document-disclosure obligation addressed by this document (Civil Code § 4525 et seq.). It does not resolve, for any specific transaction, whether a given common-interest-development unit meets the 'single-family residential property' scope language used in § 1102(a); that scope question is separately flagged, and left unresolved for the same reason, in this corpus's existing Transfer Disclosure Statement Requirement clause. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Davis-Stirling document-disclosure scheme — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific HOA sale; common-interest-development disclosure regimes vary by state.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4185(a)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, 'separate interest' includes condominium units and planned-development lots
citations.quote: In a condominium project, “separate interest” means a separately owned unit, as specified in Section 4125. (3) In a planned development, “separate interest” means a separately owned lot, parcel, area, or space.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1102(a)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, Transfer Disclosure Statement applies to single-family residential property
citations.quote: Except as provided in Section 1102.2, this article applies to any transfer by sale, exchange, real property sales contract as defined in Section 2985, lease with an option to purchase, any other option to purchase, or ground lease coupled with improvements of any single-family residential property.

clauses.title: Buyer's Acknowledgment of Receipt
clauses.body: Buyer acknowledges receipt of the governing documents, financial and assessment information, and other documents described in this HOA/CC&R Disclosure for {{hoaName}}, including a statement of the association's current regular assessment of ${{monthlyAssessment}} per month, before the transfer of title to {{propertyAddress}}. Seller: {{sellerName}}. Buyer: {{buyerName}}.

clauses.title: "Business" and "Service Provider" Are Defined Terms
clauses.body: California's Consumer Privacy Act uses "business" and "service provider" as specific, defined terms — not every company that hires a vendor is a "business" under this statute, and not every vendor is a "service provider" under it. A "business" is a for-profit entity that does business in California, collects or directs the collection of consumers' personal information, and meets at least one of three thresholds: annual gross revenue above $25,000,000, annually buying, selling, or sharing the personal information of 100,000 or more consumers or households, or deriving 50% or more of annual revenue from selling or sharing personal information. A "service provider" is a person that processes personal information on {{businessName}}'s behalf and receives it for a business purpose under a written contract that meets specific statutory conditions described elsewhere in this document. Whether {{businessName}} meets the statutory revenue or volume thresholds, and whether {{serviceProviderName}}'s processing arrangement meets the statutory conditions for "service provider" status, are factual questions this document does not resolve.
clauses.gap: This clause cites two subsections of the same statute, Civil Code § 1798.140 — subdivision (d)(1) ("business") and subdivision (ag)(1) ("service provider") — because both definitions come from the same statutory definitions section and are necessary to explain who this document's two defined roles correspond to. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Consumer Privacy Act (as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act) — not a claim about which state's law governs this document or any party's obligations under it. This document addresses only California's CCPA/CPRA framework; it does not address the EU/UK GDPR, other states' privacy statutes (e.g., Virginia, Colorado, Connecticut, Utah, or the many other state privacy laws now in force), or any other jurisdiction's data-processing requirements, which use different definitions and impose different or additional contract terms. The "business" definition's full text also includes an alternate "controlled entity" category (§ 1798.140(d)(2)), a joint-venture category (§ 1798.140(d)(3)), and a voluntary-certification category (§ 1798.140(d)(4)) not quoted here because they describe corporate-structure edge cases outside this document's two-party scope. No case law interpreting these definitions was checked; the statute's own text is unambiguous, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(d)(1) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Consumer Privacy Act, definition of "business"
citations.quote: “Business” means:(1) A sole proprietorship, partnership, limited liability company, corporation, association, or other legal entity that is organized or operated for the profit or financial benefit of its shareholders or other owners, that collects consumers’ personal information, or on the behalf of which such information is collected and that alone, or jointly with others, determines the purposes and means of the processing of consumers’ personal information, that does business in the State of California, and that satisfies one or more of the following thresholds:(A) As of January 1 of the calendar year, had annual gross revenues in excess of twenty-five million dollars ($25,000,000) in the preceding calendar year, as adjusted pursuant to subdivision (d) of Section 1798.199.95.(B) Alone or in combination, annually buys, sells, or shares the personal information of 100,000 or more consumers or households.(C) Derives 50 percent or more of its annual revenues from selling or sharing consumers’ personal information.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(ag)(1) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Consumer Privacy Act, definition of "service provider"
citations.quote: “Service provider” means a person that processes personal information on behalf of a business and that receives from or on behalf of the business consumer’s personal information for a business purpose pursuant to a written contract, provided that the contract prohibits the person from:(A) Selling or sharing the personal information.(B) Retaining, using, or disclosing the personal information for any purpose other than for the business purposes specified in the contract for the business, including retaining, using, or disclosing the personal information for a commercial purpose other than the business purposes specified in the contract with the business, or as otherwise permitted by this title.(C) Retaining, using, or disclosing the information outside of the direct business relationship between the service provider and the business.(D) Combining the personal information that the service provider receives from, or on behalf of, the business with personal information that it receives from, or on behalf of, another person or persons, or collects from its own interaction with the consumer, provided that the service provider may combine personal information to perform any business purpose as defined in regulations adopted pursuant to paragraph (9) of subdivision (a) of Section 1798.185, except as provided for in paragraph (6) of subdivision (e) of this section and in regulations adopted by the California Privacy Protection Agency.

clauses.title: Two Separate Statutory Sources of Required Contract Terms
clauses.body: The CCPA imposes required contract terms in two separate places, not one, and a compliant agreement needs to satisfy both. First, Civil Code § 1798.140(ag)(1) makes these terms part of the definition of "service provider" itself: a written contract only creates "service provider" status if it prohibits the recipient from (A) selling or sharing the personal information; (B) retaining, using, or disclosing the personal information for any purpose other than the business purposes specified in the contract; (C) retaining, using, or disclosing the information outside the direct business relationship between the recipient and the business; and (D) combining the personal information with personal information the recipient receives from other sources, except as separately permitted by regulation. Second, and independently, Civil Code § 1798.100(d) imposes a general duty on any business that discloses personal information to a service provider or contractor for a business purpose: the business "shall enter into an agreement" that (1) specifies the information is disclosed only for limited and specified purposes; (2) obligates the recipient to comply with the CCPA and to provide the same level of privacy protection the statute requires; (3) grants the business rights to take reasonable and appropriate steps to help ensure the recipient's compliant use of the information; (4) requires the recipient to notify the business if it determines it can no longer meet its CCPA obligations; and (5) grants the business the right, on notice, to take reasonable and appropriate steps to stop and remediate unauthorized use.
clauses.gap: This clause cites four subparagraphs of one subdivision of Civil Code § 1798.140 (§ 1798.140(ag)(1)(A)-(D)) and five paragraphs of one subdivision of Civil Code § 1798.100 (§ 1798.100(d)(1)-(5)); both groupings are quoted in full because each is a single integrated list in the statute's own text. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Consumer Privacy Act (as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act) — not a claim about which state's law governs this document or any party's obligations under it. This document addresses only California's CCPA/CPRA framework; it does not address the EU/UK GDPR, other states' privacy statutes (e.g., Virginia, Colorado, Connecticut, Utah, or the many other state privacy laws now in force), or any other jurisdiction's data-processing requirements, which use different definitions and impose different or additional contract terms. Correction to this document's working assumption: the task brief that prompted this research treated § 1798.100(d) and § 1798.140(ag) as alternative possible locations for the required contract terms ("§ 1798.100(d) or § 1798.140(ag) or similar"). Checking the actual statutory text shows they are not alternatives — both provisions impose real, independent, and only partly overlapping contract-term requirements, and this document's operative contract-terms clause is drafted to satisfy both lists rather than treating either one as sufficient by itself. Separately, § 1798.140(ag)(1) — the service-provider definition used here — does not itself include an explicit certification requirement; the parallel "contractor" definition at § 1798.140(j)(1)(B) does ("Includes a certification made by the contractor that the contractor understands the restrictions in subparagraph (A) and will comply with them."). This document's drafting clause includes a certification for the service provider as a matter of drafting practice, not because § 1798.140(ag) itself requires one by its own text; whether the California Privacy Protection Agency's regulations separately require a service-provider certification was not checked here and is outside this clause's statutory-text-only scope. No case law was checked on either provision; both provisions' own text is unambiguous, so the statutes stand as the source here without a corroborating case.

clauses.title: Why a Compliant Service-Provider Transfer Is Not a "Sale" or "Share"
clauses.body: The CCPA defines "sell" as disclosing a consumer's personal information "to a third party for monetary or other valuable consideration," and defines "share" as disclosing personal information "to a third party for cross-context behavioral advertising," whether or not for consideration. Both definitions depend on the recipient being a "third party." The statute's definition of "third party" expressly excludes two categories of recipient: "(2) A service provider to the business," and "(3) A contractor." Read together, these three definitions are the statutory mechanism this document relies on: a disclosure of personal information to a recipient who meets the statutory definition of "service provider" is, by the statute's own definitional structure, not a disclosure "to a third party" at all — and because both "sell" and "share" are defined only as disclosures to a third party, such a disclosure falls outside both definitions.
clauses.gap: This clause cites three subsections of the same statute, Civil Code § 1798.140 — subdivision (ad)(1) ("sell"), subdivision (ah)(1) ("share"), and subdivision (ai) ("third party") — because the exemption mechanism only becomes visible by reading all three together; no single sentence in the statute states "a compliant service-provider transfer is not a sale" in so many words. This clause's conclusion is this researcher's own structural reading of how the three definitions interlock, not a quotation of an express statutory statement to that effect — flagged here so the reader can verify the chain of definitions independently rather than relying on a paraphrase. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Consumer Privacy Act (as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act) — not a claim about which state's law governs this document or any party's obligations under it. This document addresses only California's CCPA/CPRA framework; it does not address the EU/UK GDPR, other states' privacy statutes (e.g., Virginia, Colorado, Connecticut, Utah, or the many other state privacy laws now in force), or any other jurisdiction's data-processing requirements, which use different definitions and impose different or additional contract terms. Neither definition's own list of what does NOT count as a sale or share (§ 1798.140(ad)(2), § 1798.140(ah)(2)) mentions service providers or contractors at all — those carve-outs cover consumer-directed disclosures, opt-out identifiers, and mergers/acquisitions, which is a further sign that the service-provider exemption operates through the "third party" definition rather than through a sale/share carve-out provision. No case law was checked on how courts have applied this definitional chain; the statute's own text was treated as the source here without a corroborating case.

clauses.title: Audit Rights Are Permissive, Not a Statutory Mandate
clauses.body: The CCPA does not require every service-provider contract to include an audit clause. Civil Code § 1798.140(ag)(1) states that the contract "may, subject to agreement with the service provider, permit the business to monitor the service provider's compliance with the contract through measures, including, but not limited to, ongoing manual reviews and automated scans and regular assessments, audits, or other technical and operational testing at least once every 12 months" — permissive language ("may... permit"), conditioned on the service provider's own agreement, that sets a minimum once-per-12-months cadence only if an audit mechanism is included at all. Separately, Civil Code § 1798.100(d)(3) and (d)(5) do impose a mandatory (not optional) requirement that the business's agreement with the service provider grant the business "rights to take reasonable and appropriate steps to help ensure" the service provider's compliant use of the information, and the right, on notice, "to take reasonable and appropriate steps to stop and remediate unauthorized use." That mandatory language requires some mechanism for the business to police compliance, but its own text does not specify that the mechanism must be an audit right, on-site inspection, or any particular verification procedure.
clauses.gap: This clause cites one subsection of Civil Code § 1798.140 (subdivision (ag)(1), specifically its monitoring sentence) together with two paragraphs of one subdivision of Civil Code § 1798.100 (§ 1798.100(d)(3) and (d)(5)) to contrast the statute's optional audit language with its separate mandatory "reasonable steps" language. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Consumer Privacy Act (as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act) — not a claim about which state's law governs this document or any party's obligations under it. This document addresses only California's CCPA/CPRA framework; it does not address the EU/UK GDPR, other states' privacy statutes (e.g., Virginia, Colorado, Connecticut, Utah, or the many other state privacy laws now in force), or any other jurisdiction's data-processing requirements, which use different definitions and impose different or additional contract terms. The task brief that prompted this research asked whether the statute imposes "a specific contractual audit-rights or verification requirement" — checking the text directly shows the answer is qualified rather than a simple yes or no: no specific audit mechanism is mandated, but a general (non-audit-specific) compliance-assurance term is mandatory under § 1798.100(d)(3). This document does not represent that an audit clause is legally required; it includes one in its drafting clauses as a common contracting practice for satisfying the mandatory "reasonable steps" requirement, not as a quotation of a statutory mandate. No case law was checked on this distinction; both provisions' own text is unambiguous, so the statutes stand as the source here without a corroborating case.

clauses.title: What Follows, Under the Statute's Own Definitions, if the Contract Terms Are Missing
clauses.body: The statute's definitions are structured so that a written contract lacking the terms described in Civil Code § 1798.140(ag)(1)(A)-(D) has a specific definitional consequence. "Service provider" status under § 1798.140(ag)(1) exists only "provided that the contract prohibits the person from" the four listed things. A recipient processing personal information under a contract that does not meet that condition does not fall within the statutory definition of "service provider." Because § 1798.140(ai) defines "third party" as a person who is not a service provider or a contractor, a recipient who is not a "service provider" and not a "contractor" falls within the definition of "third party" instead. And because "sell" (§ 1798.140(ad)(1)) and "share" (§ 1798.140(ah)(1)) are both defined as disclosures of personal information "to a third party" — for consideration in the case of a sale, for cross-context behavioral advertising in the case of a share — a disclosure to a recipient who is a "third party" for lack of a compliant contract can fall within the statutory definition of a sale or a share of personal information, depending on the nature of the disclosure and the consideration or purpose involved.
clauses.gap: This clause cites the same cluster of Civil Code § 1798.140 subsections as the sell/share/third-party clause above — subdivisions (ag)(1), (ad)(1), (ah)(1), and (ai) — because the reclassification consequence follows from tracing the same definitional chain in the reverse direction (starting from a noncompliant contract rather than a compliant one). This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Consumer Privacy Act (as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act) — not a claim about which state's law governs this document or any party's obligations under it. This document addresses only California's CCPA/CPRA framework; it does not address the EU/UK GDPR, other states' privacy statutes (e.g., Virginia, Colorado, Connecticut, Utah, or the many other state privacy laws now in force), or any other jurisdiction's data-processing requirements, which use different definitions and impose different or additional contract terms. This clause states a logical consequence of how the definitions interlock, not a quotation of an express statutory sentence saying "a noncompliant contract makes the transfer a sale" — the statute's own text was checked directly and contains no single provision phrased that way, so this is disclosed as this researcher's structural reading rather than forced into an unqualified statutory holding. This clause does not describe what a business must then do as a result (for example, any opt-out-of-sale or opt-out-of-sharing notice and link obligations elsewhere in the CCPA, such as at Civil Code §§ 1798.120 and 1798.135) — those provisions were not fetched or verified for this research and are outside this document's scope, which addresses the service-provider contract terms only. No case law was checked on this reclassification consequence; the statute's own definitional text was treated as the source here without a corroborating case.

clauses.title: Recitals and Business Purpose
clauses.body: This CCPA Service Provider Data Processing Agreement ("Agreement") is entered into between {{businessName}} ("Business") and {{serviceProviderName}} ("Service Provider"). Business discloses personal information to Service Provider so that Service Provider can process it on Business's behalf for the following business purpose: {{businessPurpose}}. This Agreement sets out the terms Business and Service Provider intend to satisfy the requirements described in California Civil Code §§ 1798.100(d) and 1798.140(ag) for disclosures of personal information to a service provider under the California Consumer Privacy Act, as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act.

clauses.title: Service Provider's Restrictions on Use of Personal Information
clauses.body: In processing personal information that {{businessName}} discloses to it, {{serviceProviderName}} shall not: (a) sell or share the personal information; (b) retain, use, or disclose the personal information for any purpose other than the business purpose described in this Agreement ({{businessPurpose}}), including for any commercial purpose other than that business purpose, except as otherwise permitted by the California Consumer Privacy Act; (c) retain, use, or disclose the personal information outside the direct business relationship between {{serviceProviderName}} and {{businessName}}; or (d) combine the personal information it receives from {{businessName}} with personal information it receives from or on behalf of any other person, or collects from its own interaction with the consumer, except as permitted by applicable regulations. {{serviceProviderName}} certifies that it understands the restrictions in this clause and will comply with them. If {{serviceProviderName}} engages another person to assist in processing personal information for the business purpose described in this Agreement, {{serviceProviderName}} shall notify {{businessName}} of that engagement and shall bind that other person, by written contract, to observe the same restrictions set out in this clause. {{businessName}} may take reasonable and appropriate steps to help ensure that {{serviceProviderName}} uses the personal information consistently with this Agreement, including through periodic assessments, audits, or other technical and operational testing, and {{serviceProviderName}} shall notify {{businessName}} if it determines that it can no longer meet the restrictions in this clause.

clauses.title: Declaration and Scope of This Statement
clauses.body: This Statement of Earned but Unpaid Commissions is prepared by {{employeeName}}, a former employee of {{companyName}}, whose employment ended on {{terminationDate}}. It identifies a commission that {{employeeName}} contends was already earned, under the terms of the commission agreement between {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}}, before employment ended — as distinct from a commission that was merely anticipated or still contingent on something that had not yet occurred as of {{terminationDate}} — and that remains unpaid as of the date of this statement.

clauses.title: Commissions Are "Wages" Under California Law
clauses.body: California law defines "wages" to expressly include amounts computed on a commission basis, alongside amounts computed by time, task, or piece. Because an earned commission is legally a "wage" and not some separate, lesser category of pay, a commission that {{employeeName}} actually earned while employed by {{companyName}} is subject to the same statutory protections that apply to wages generally — including the final-pay-timing and waiting-time-penalty rules that already govern when other wages must be paid out at termination.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that an earned commission is legally a "wage" — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific commission arrangement, and not a claim that other states classify commissions the same way. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 200(a)); the second citation below is a California Court of Appeal decision quoting and applying that same subsection to commissions specifically, not an independent statutory source. This clause does not re-derive the final-pay-timing deadlines or the waiting-time-penalty mechanics themselves — this document set already contains dedicated, separately verified clauses covering those rules in full (in the Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter document); this clause exists only to establish the threshold premise that an earned commission counts as a "wage" those rules reach in the first place.

citations.cite: the statutory definition of "wages"
citations.quote: “Wages” includes all amounts for labor performed by employees of every description, whether the amount is fixed or ascertained by the standard of time, task, piece, commission basis, or other method of calculation.

citations.case: Steinhebel v. Los Angeles Times Communications, LLC
citations.quote: Section 200, subdivision (a) defines “wages” to include “all amounts for labor performed by employees of every description, whether the amount is fixed or ascertained by the standard of time, task, piece, commission basis, or other method of calculation.” (Italics added; see Reid v. Overland Machined Products (1961) 55 Cal.2d 203, 207-208 [commissions are wages].)

clauses.title: The Commission-Writing Statute Sets No Separate Payout Rule for Termination
clauses.body: The California statute that requires a commission arrangement to be in writing does not, on its own text, set out any separate rule for what happens to an unpaid commission when an employee's employment ends. Its requirements are about the writing itself — that the contract be in writing, that it state how commissions are computed and paid, that a signed copy be given to the employee, and that a signed receipt be obtained — not about a payout deadline or a special termination-triggered rule. Whether a specific commission was earned before {{terminationDate}}, and when an earned commission must be paid out once employment with {{companyName}} ends, are questions this statute leaves to be answered elsewhere: by the commission agreement's own terms (which control what "earned" means) and by the general wage statutes that apply once a commission is properly classified as an earned wage.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what this specific statutory section does and does not address — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific commission arrangement. This clause makes a negative claim (that § 2751 contains no termination-specific default rule); that negative claim was checked by reading the section's full text directly rather than assumed, and the full text of subsections (a) through (c) is what supports it. This document deliberately does not re-derive the written-contract, signed-copy, signed-receipt, or expired-contract-continuation requirements of this same statute in general, since this document set already contains dedicated, separately verified clauses covering each of those (in the Commission Agreement document); this clause exists only to make clear, for a reader assembling this specific termination-focused document, that this well-known commission statute does not itself supply a termination payout rule, so one should not be inferred from it.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2751 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the full written-commission-contract statute, subsections (a) through (c)
citations.quote: (a) Whenever an employer enters into a contract of employment with an employee for services to be rendered within this state and the contemplated method of payment of the employee involves commissions, the contract shall be in writing and shall set forth the method by which the commissions shall be computed and paid. (b) The employer shall give a signed copy of the contract to every employee who is a party thereto and shall obtain a signed receipt for the contract from each employee. In the case of a contract that expires and where the parties nevertheless continue to work under the terms of the expired contract, the contract terms are presumed to remain in full force and effect until the contract is superseded or employment is terminated by either party. (c) As used in this section, “commissions” has the meaning set forth in Section 204.1.

clauses.title: What Makes a Commission "Earned": The Condition-Precedent Distinction
clauses.body: California courts have held that a commission is not automatically "earned," as a matter of law, simply because the underlying sale or transaction that will eventually generate it has occurred. An employer may lawfully condition an employee's right to a commission on a further contingency — something in addition to the sale itself — and until that contingency actually occurs, the commission is not yet an earned wage. A payment made to the employee before the contingency occurs is legally an advance, not a wage, precisely because the employer cannot yet determine whether the commission will ever actually be earned. Whether a specific commission that {{employeeName}} points to was actually earned before {{terminationDate}}, or was instead still subject to an unsatisfied contingency as of that date, depends on what the commission agreement between {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}} itself identifies as the condition for earning it.
clauses.gap: This is one state's case law, used as real evidence of how California courts have drawn the earned-versus-contingent line for commissions — not a claim about which state's law governs this particular commission arrangement, and not a claim that any particular contingency in any particular agreement is enforceable. Both quotations below come from the same California Court of Appeal decision; this research session was rate-limited on CourtListener's general search and API-lookup tools (125 requests/day, exhausted before this clause was verified, with the daily quota not resetting until roughly 16 hours later), so a second, independent case was not located and read in full this session — that gap is disclosed here rather than papered over. A second frequently-cited California case on this same question, Neisendorf v. Levi Strauss & Co., 143 Cal.App.4th 509 (2006), was identified through secondary sources (law-firm summaries and case-database listings) but its primary opinion text could not be located or read this session because CourtListener's search tool was rate-limited and direct fetches to courtlistener.com, justia.com, findlaw.com, leagle.com, and scholar.google.com were all blocked by this environment's network egress controls when tested directly; it is deliberately not cited here with any quoted language, since its holding was not independently verified against the primary opinion text this session.

citations.case: Steinhebel v. Los Angeles Times Communications, LLC
citations.quote: The essence of an advance is that at the time of payment the employer cannot determine whether the commission will eventually be earned because a condition to the employee’s right to the commission has yet to occur or its occurrence as yet is otherwise unascertainable. An advance, therefore, by definition is not a wage because all conditions for performance have not been satisfied.

citations.case: Steinhebel v. Los Angeles Times Communications, LLC
citations.quote: In the present case, under the stipulated facts, appellants’ commission was contingent upon two general conditions... Unless both conditions were met, there was no “commissionable sale.” Appellants’ commissions were predicated on a successful sale, and unless a sale met both conditions, there was in fact no sale.

clauses.title: The Commission Agreement's Own Terms Control What Counts as "Earned"
clauses.body: California courts have held that there is no single, universal legal trigger — such as the date of the sale, the date of a customer's order, or the date of a customer's payment — that automatically determines when a commission is "earned" in every case. Instead, an employee's right to a commission is governed by whatever the commission agreement between the employee and the employer itself specifies as the earning trigger. This is why the method-of-computation-and-payment language in a written commission agreement, of the kind California law already separately requires be in writing, is central to answering whether a particular commission was earned before {{terminationDate}}: {{commissionStructure}}
clauses.gap: This is one state's case law, used as real evidence that contract terms (not a single universal rule) determine when a commission is earned — not a claim about which state's law governs this particular commission agreement, and not a claim that the specific commission structure quoted into this document's placeholder is enforceable as written. This clause quotes a passage from Commeford v. Baker, 127 Cal.App.2d 111, 118 (1954), but only as that passage is quoted and relied upon within the Steinhebel opinion below; Commeford's own opinion text was not independently located and read this session, for the same CourtListener rate-limiting reason disclosed in this document's clause on the earned-versus-contingent distinction, so this citation should be understood as "Commeford as quoted by the Steinhebel court," not as independent verification of Commeford's full text or holding.

citations.case: Steinhebel v. Los Angeles Times Communications, LLC, quoting Commeford v. Baker, 127 Cal.App.2d 111, 118 (1954)
citations.quote: Appellants’ right to commissions therefore must be governed by the provisions of the Agreement. ... “[T]he right of a salesman or any other person to commissions under given circumstances depends upon the terms of his contract for compensation.” (Commeford, at p. 118.)

clauses.title: Once a Commission Is Actually Earned, It Cannot Be Taken Back as a Wage
clauses.body: Separately from the question of when a commission becomes earned in the first place, California law makes it unlawful for an employer to collect or receive back any part of wages it has already paid an employee. California courts have read this rule together with the earned-versus-contingent distinction described elsewhere in this document: an employer may lawfully make an earlier payment contingent on something not yet satisfied (so that no wage has been earned yet), but once a commission has actually been earned by the employee's completion of everything the agreement required for it to be earned, that protection against employers clawing back already-paid wages applies to it like any other wage.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute and case law, used as real evidence of the legal line between a lawful earning-contingency and an unlawful clawback of an already-earned wage — not a claim about which state's law governs this particular commission or clawback, and not a claim that any specific deduction, chargeback, or clawback arrangement in any particular agreement is lawful or unlawful. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 221) and a single Court of Appeal decision applying it to a commission chargeback scheme; the case addressed an advance-and-chargeback arrangement where the court found no wage had yet been earned (so § 221 was not implicated), not a case where an employer took back a commission the court found to be already earned — so this clause states the general principle the court articulated rather than an outcome directly forfeiting an earned commission. This research session's CourtListener search and API-lookup tools were rate-limited (disclosed in full in this document's clause on the earned-versus-contingent distinction), so no additional independent case specifically striking down a termination-triggered forfeiture of an already-earned commission was located and read this session; that gap is disclosed here rather than assumed away.
