clauses.title: Who Owns Copyright by Default in a Contractor Relationship
clauses.body: Under federal copyright law, copyright in a work vests initially in the person who actually creates it — the author — the moment the work is fixed in a tangible form. When {{contractorName}} creates {{workDescription}} for {{companyName}} as an independent contractor rather than as an employee, {{contractorName}} is, by default, both the author and the copyright owner of that work, even though {{companyName}} commissioned and paid for it. That default changes only if the work qualifies as a “work made for hire” under federal copyright law's specific definition of that term, or if {{contractorName}} separately assigns ownership to {{companyName}} in a signed writing.
clauses.gap: This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (17 U.S.C. § 201(a) and § 201(b)); no additional independent source was found for this point beyond the statute itself and the Supreme Court's own restatement of it, since both subsections describe the same initial-ownership rule and its work-for-hire exception. This is federal law, used as real evidence of how copyright ownership is allocated by default between an independent creator and the party that commissioned the work — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a reader's specific situation, or about whether any particular work or relationship actually qualifies as independent-contractor work under this rule.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 201(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, initial ownership of copyright
citations.quote: Copyright in a work protected under this title vests initially in the author or authors of the work. The authors of a joint work are coowners of copyright in the work.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 201(b) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, ownership of work made for hire
citations.quote: In the case of a work made for hire, the employer or other person for whom the work was prepared is considered the author for purposes of this title, and, unless the parties have expressly agreed otherwise in a written instrument signed by them, owns all of the rights comprised in the copyright.

citations.case: Community for Creative Non-Violence v. Reid
citations.quote: As a general rule, the author is the party who actually creates the work, that is, the person who translates an idea into a fixed, tangible expression entitled to copyright protection.

clauses.title: The Statutory Definition of “Work Made for Hire” Has Two Separate Branches
clauses.body: Federal copyright law defines “work made for hire” in exactly two ways: work created by an employee within the scope of employment, or work that is both specially ordered or commissioned for use in one of nine enumerated categories — a contribution to a collective work, a part of a motion picture or other audiovisual work, a translation, a supplementary work, a compilation, an instructional text, a test, answer material for a test, or an atlas — and made the subject of an express written agreement, signed by both parties, that the work is a work made for hire. Work {{contractorName}} creates for {{companyName}} as an independent contractor, rather than as an employee, can only ever fall within the second of these two definitions; the first branch applies only to an actual employment relationship as federal law defines it, a status independent contractor status is legally distinct from.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of how the two branches of the “work made for hire” definition are structured — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a reader's specific situation, or about whether the contractor's relationship with the hiring party named in this agreement is, in fact, an independent-contractor relationship rather than an employment relationship (a separate, fact-specific question this clause does not resolve). This clause quotes the same statutory text (17 U.S.C. § 101) already quoted elsewhere in this project's corpus, in this project's Invention Assignment & Confidentiality Agreement and Copyright Assignment Agreement documents; it is repeated here, in a document specifically about the independent-contractor branch of the definition, because that document's own framing centers on the employee branch and does not itself state the independent-contractor branch's requirements.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 101 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, definition of “work made for hire”
citations.quote: A “work made for hire” is— (1) a work prepared by an employee within the scope of his or her employment; or (2) a work specially ordered or commissioned for use as a contribution to a collective work, as a part of a motion picture or other audiovisual work, as a translation, as a supplementary work, as a compilation, as an instructional text, as a test, as answer material for a test, or as an atlas, if the parties expressly agree in a written instrument signed by them that the work shall be considered a work made for hire.

clauses.title: Work-for-Hire Status for a Contractor Does Not Arise Automatically
clauses.body: Unlike the employee branch of the work-made-for-hire doctrine, the independent-contractor branch does not attach automatically just because {{companyName}} hired {{contractorName}} to create {{workDescription}} and paid for it. Both of two separate conditions have to be satisfied: the work has to actually fall within one of the statute's nine enumerated categories, and the parties have to expressly agree, in a written instrument signed by both of them, that the work is a work made for hire. If either condition is missing, the work is not a “work made for hire” under federal law — regardless of what a contract calls it, what the parties intended, or how the parties otherwise describe their working relationship.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of how the independent-contractor branch of the work-made-for-hire definition actually functions when applied — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a reader's specific situation, or about whether any particular commissioned work satisfies these conditions. Both citations below are drawn from the same Supreme Court opinion (different passages of it), applying the statute to the facts before the Court; that opinion is also cited elsewhere in this project's corpus for a related but distinct point (the common-law agency factors used to decide who counts as an “employee” under the first branch), which this clause does not repeat.

citations.case: Community for Creative Non-Violence v. Reid
citations.quote: Sculpture does not fit within any of the nine categories of “specially ordered or commissioned” works enumerated in that subsection, and no written agreement between the parties establishes “Third World America” as a work for hire.

citations.case: Community for Creative Non-Violence v. Reid
citations.quote: Because Reid was an independent contractor, whether “Third World America” is a work for hire depends on whether it satisfies the terms of § 101(2). This petitioners concede it cannot do. Thus, CCNV is not the author of “Third World America” by virtue of the work for hire provisions of the Act.

clauses.title: Work Outside the Nine Categories Can Still Be Transferred by a Separate Assignment
clauses.body: Work commissioned from an independent contractor that does not fall within one of the statute's nine enumerated categories cannot become {{companyName}}'s property through a “work made for hire” designation, no matter how an agreement describes it — federal law does not let parties expand the nine categories by private agreement. That does not mean ownership of such work is stuck with {{contractorName}} regardless of the parties' intentions, though: federal law separately allows a contractor to transfer copyright ownership to the hiring party through an ordinary assignment, which is valid as long as it is set out in a signed writing. A work-for-hire clause that does not legally qualify as a work-for-hire designation is not, for that reason alone, void or without effect — when the same agreement also includes assignment language, that language can still operate as a valid transfer of ownership.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of how a signed writing actually transfers copyright ownership, separately from (and as a backstop to) any work-for-hire designation — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a reader's specific situation, or that any particular contract's language is effective to accomplish either an assignment or a work-for-hire designation, which depends on the document's actual wording. The Effects Associates quote below is reused, not independently re-verified in this research session, from this project's already-verified Copyright Assignment Agreement document (checked 2026-09-01): CourtListener's search tool returned a daily rate-limit error ("429 — Rate limit exceeded: 125/day") when this research attempted to re-fetch it directly, so that specific citation is disclosed as reused rather than freshly re-confirmed this session. The 17 U.S.C. § 204(a) statutory quote below, by contrast, was independently fetched and verified fresh in this research session. Effects Associates is Ninth Circuit precedent; it is frequently cited nationally on this point but is only binding within that circuit.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 204(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, execution of transfers of copyright ownership
citations.quote: A transfer of copyright ownership, other than by operation of law, is not valid unless an instrument of conveyance, or a note or memorandum of the transfer, is in writing and signed by the owner of the rights conveyed or such owner’s duly authorized agent.

citations.case: Effects Associates, Inc. v. Cohen
citations.quote: The rule is really quite simple: If the copyright holder agrees to transfer ownership to another party, that party must get the copyright holder to sign a piece of paper saying so. It doesn't have to be the Magna Charta; a one-line pro forma statement will do.

clauses.title: Work Made for Hire Designation
clauses.body: {{contractorName}} and {{companyName}} agree that {{workDescription}} is specially ordered and commissioned by {{companyName}}, that it falls within the following category under 17 U.S.C. § 101: {{categoryOfWork}}, and that it shall be considered a “work made for hire” as that term is defined under federal copyright law. This designation is made in the written instrument signed by both parties below.

clauses.title: Backup Assignment of Ownership
clauses.body: To the extent {{workDescription}} is determined not to qualify as a “work made for hire” under federal copyright law — whether because it does not fall within one of the statutory categories described above, because the designation above is found deficient for any reason, or otherwise — {{contractorName}} hereby assigns to {{companyName}} all right, title, and interest in and to the copyright in {{workDescription}}, effective as of the date this agreement is signed. {{contractorName}} agrees to sign any additional documents reasonably requested by {{companyName}} to confirm, record, or perfect this assignment.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes the federal Form I-9 employment eligibility verification process that the Immigration Reform and Control Act (IRCA) requires an employer to complete for a new hire, in connection with {{companyName}}'s hiring of {{employeeName}} with a start date of {{startDate}}. It summarizes selected requirements of 8 U.S.C. § 1324a and its implementing federal regulations. It is not the Form I-9 itself, does not complete, replace, or substitute for that form, and does not state, verify, or determine {{employeeName}}'s actual identity, employment authorization, or immigration status.

clauses.title: Federal Prohibition on Knowingly Hiring or Continuing to Employ an Unauthorized Alien
clauses.body: Federal law makes it unlawful for a person or entity to hire an alien for employment in the United States knowing the alien is an unauthorized alien, and separately makes it unlawful, once an alien has been hired, to continue employing that alien knowing the alien is or has become unauthorized to work. {{companyName}}'s hiring process, including the hiring of {{employeeName}}, operates within this federal framework.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the federal prohibition on knowingly hiring or continuing to employ an unauthorized alien — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about any specific individual's actual work authorization status. The statute does not state this prohibition as a single unified rule covering both hiring and continued employment in one sentence or subsection, as is sometimes assumed; it is split across two separate paragraphs of the same section — 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(a)(1)(A) (the hiring prohibition) and 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(a)(2) (the separate continuing-employment prohibition, which applies only once an employer already knows, after the fact, that a previously hired alien is or has become unauthorized). Both citations below are to different subsections of this same statutory section (§ 1324a); this clause draws no conclusion from that structure other than that they are two distinct prohibitions. Separately, § 1324a(a)(3) provides an affirmative defense to the hiring prohibition — not quoted or relied on here — for a person or entity that establishes good-faith compliance with the verification requirements of subsection (b).

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(a)(1)(A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Immigration Reform and Control Act, hiring prohibition
citations.quote: It is unlawful for a person or other entity— (A) to hire, or to recruit or refer for a fee, for employment in the United States an alien knowing the alien is an unauthorized alien (as defined in subsection (h)(3)) with respect to such employment

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(a)(2) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Immigration Reform and Control Act, continuing-employment prohibition
citations.quote: It is unlawful for a person or other entity, after hiring an alien for employment in accordance with paragraph (1), to continue to employ the alien in the United States knowing the alien is (or has become) an unauthorized alien with respect to such employment.

clauses.title: The Federal Employment Verification Requirement (Form I-9 Attestation)
clauses.body: Federal law requires an employer to attest, under penalty of perjury on a federally designated form, that it has verified a new hire is not an unauthorized alien by examining specified documents establishing identity and employment authorization. {{companyName}} completes this attestation for {{employeeName}} using Form I-9.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the federal Form I-9 attestation and document-examination requirement — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about any specific individual's actual identity or work authorization status. All four citations below are to different subsections of the same statutory paragraph, 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(b)(1); none is cited more than once, and this clause draws no conclusion from the fact that they share a common paragraph other than that they are components of one attestation-and-documentation scheme. Separately: the statute itself organizes acceptable documents into three categories — documents establishing both identity and employment authorization (subparagraph (B)), documents evidencing employment authorization only (subparagraph (C)), and documents establishing identity only (subparagraph (D)) — so this three-way structure is genuinely in the statutory text, not only in agency guidance. The specific labels "List A," "List B," and "List C" that appear on the Form I-9 and in USCIS's Handbook for Employers (Form M-274), however, are not the statute's own subparagraph labels — the statute uses lettered subparagraphs, not numbered "Lists." The implementing regulation examined for this clause, 8 C.F.R. § 274a.2, restates the same three-way document structure at § 274a.2(b)(1)(v) and separately uses the term "List B" once, in a specific provision about how a minor's Form I-9 is completed — so the List A/B/C terminology has at least partial regulatory and form-instruction pedigree, but this clause did not find "List A," "List B," and "List C" used as formal headings within the regulatory text itself, only within that one incidental reference.

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(b)(1)(A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, employment verification system, attestation requirement
citations.quote: The person or entity must attest, under penalty of perjury and on a form designated or established by the Attorney General by regulation, that it has verified that the individual is not an unauthorized alien by examining

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(b)(1)(B) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, employment verification system, documents establishing both identity and authorization
citations.quote: Documents establishing both employment authorization and identity

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(b)(1)(C) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, employment verification system, documents evidencing employment authorization only
citations.quote: Documents evidencing employment authorization

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(b)(1)(D) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, employment verification system, documents establishing identity only
citations.quote: Documents establishing identity of individual

clauses.title: Timing of Employment Verification
clauses.body: Federal regulations set a deadline, measured from the date of hire, for completing the employment-verification examination and Form I-9 documentation, with a different, same-day deadline for a hire expected to last less than three business days.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of a federal verification-timing deadline — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about any specific individual's actual hire date or work authorization status. This clause corrects an assumption worth stating directly: the "three business days" deadline is not located in 8 U.S.C. § 1324a itself. This clause's drafter read the full statutory text of § 1324a(a) and (b) directly and found no specific number-of-days deadline for completing verification after hire anywhere in the statute; § 1324a(b)(3), in particular, addresses retention of the completed form, not the deadline for completing it. The three-business-day deadline exists only in the implementing regulation, 8 C.F.R. § 274a.2(b)(1)(ii)-(iii) — a distinction that matters because a regulation can be amended by the agency through notice-and-comment rulemaking without a change to the underlying statute. Both regulatory citations below are to the same C.F.R. section, § 274a.2(b)(1); this clause draws no conclusion from that overlap other than that they are the general rule and its short-hire exception.

citations.case: 8 C.F.R. § 274a.2(b)(1)(ii) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Electronic Code of Federal Regulations, general verification deadline
citations.quote: an employer, his or her agent, or anyone acting directly or indirectly in the interest thereof, must within three business days of the hire

citations.case: 8 C.F.R. § 274a.2(b)(1)(iii) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Electronic Code of Federal Regulations, short-duration-hire exception
citations.quote: An employer who hires an individual for employment for a duration of less than three business days must comply with paragraphs (b)(1)(ii)(A) and (b)(1)(ii)(B) of this section at the time of the hire.

clauses.title: Federal Civil Penalties for Violations
clauses.body: Federal law authorizes civil monetary penalties, after notice and an opportunity for a hearing, against an employer found to have knowingly hired or continued to employ an unauthorized alien, in one statutory dollar range, and authorizes a separate, lower statutory dollar range of civil penalties for paperwork or documentation violations of the Form I-9 verification requirement.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the existence and structure of two distinct federal civil-penalty ranges — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about any specific individual's or employer's actual liability or work authorization status. Both citations below are to different paragraphs of the same statutory subsection, 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(e) — paragraph (4) (hiring and continuing-employment violations) and paragraph (5) (paperwork violations); this clause draws no conclusion from that shared subsection other than that they set different penalty ranges for different kinds of violations. The dollar figures quoted below are the amounts as codified in the U.S. Code text itself (originally set in 1986 and last amended in the statute in 1996). This clause did not independently verify the current, inflation-adjusted penalty amounts that DHS actually assesses today: those base statutory dollar amounts are subject to periodic upward adjustment under a separate law, the Federal Civil Penalties Inflation Adjustment Act, implemented through DHS rulemaking (codified at 8 C.F.R. § 274a.10) rather than through amendment of § 1324a(e) itself, and this clause's drafter did not fetch or verify that separate inflation-adjustment regulation or its current dollar figures — an honest gap, disclosed rather than guessed at.

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(e)(4)(A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, civil penalty for hiring and continuing-employment violations
citations.quote: With respect to a violation of subsection (a)(1)(A) or (a)(2), the order under this subsection— (A) shall require the person or entity to cease and desist from such violations and to pay a civil penalty in an amount of— (i) not less than $250 and not more than $2,000 for each unauthorized alien with respect to whom a violation of either such subsection occurred, (ii) not less than $2,000 and not more than $5,000 for each such alien in the case of a person or entity previously subject to one order under this paragraph, or (iii) not less than $3,000 and not more than $10,000 for each such alien in the case of a person or entity previously subject to more than one order under this paragraph

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(e)(5) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, civil penalty for paperwork violations
citations.quote: With respect to a violation of subsection (a)(1)(B), the order under this subsection shall require the person or entity to pay a civil penalty in an amount of not less than $100 and not more than $1,000 for each individual with respect to whom such violation occurred.

clauses.title: Retention of Form I-9 — No Filing With a Government Agency
clauses.body: Federal law does not require an employer to submit or file a completed Form I-9 with any government agency at the time it is completed. Instead, federal law requires the employer to retain the completed form for a set period and make it available for inspection by specified federal officials if asked. {{companyName}} retains Form I-9 for {{employeeName}} accordingly.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the federal retain-and-make-available (rather than routinely file) structure for a completed Form I-9, and of the statutory retention period — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about any specific individual's actual work authorization status. The retention period under § 1324a(b)(3)(B), quoted below, is three years after the date of hiring, or one year after the date employment is terminated, whichever is later. The statute names the officials who may inspect the retained form as officers of "the Service," the Special Counsel for Immigration-Related Unfair Employment Practices, and the Department of Labor. This clause's drafter did not independently re-verify, against a separate reorganization statute, exactly how "the Service" (the former Immigration and Naturalization Service) maps onto current DHS component agencies after the 2003 creation of DHS and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement; the codified text of § 1324a itself still uses "the Service" and "the Attorney General" throughout, which this clause quotes as written rather than substituting current agency names.

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(b)(3) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, retention of verification form
citations.quote: After completion of such form in accordance with paragraphs (1) and (2), the person or entity must retain a paper, microfiche, microfilm, or electronic version of the form and make it available for inspection by officers of the Service, the Special Counsel for Immigration-Related Unfair Employment Practices, or the Department of Labor during a period beginning on the date of the hiring, recruiting, or referral of the individual and ending— (A) in the case of the recruiting or referral for a fee (without hiring) of an individual, three years after the date of the recruiting or referral, and (B) in the case of the hiring of an individual— (i) three years after the date of such hiring, or (ii) one year after the date the individual’s employment is terminated, whichever is later.

clauses.title: Separate Federal Prohibition on Discrimination in the Verification Process
clauses.body: A separate federal statute prohibits an employer from discriminating against an individual, in hiring or in discharge, because of national origin or, for a protected individual, because of citizenship status, including when the employer is carrying out the employment-verification process described above. This prohibition exists independently of, and in addition to, the employment-verification requirement itself, and it does not apply to every employer.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence that a distinct anti-discrimination protection is layered on top of the employment-verification requirement, not that the verification requirement itself is a discrimination statute — and not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, or about any specific individual's actual national origin, citizenship status, or work authorization status. Both citations below are to different paragraphs of the same statutory subsection, 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(a) — paragraph (1) (the general prohibition) and paragraph (2)(A) (an exception to it); this clause draws no conclusion from that shared subsection other than that the exception qualifies the general rule. The general prohibition, § 1324b(a)(1), does not apply to a person or entity that employs three or fewer employees, under § 1324b(a)(2)(A) — so, as quoted below, this protection has a small-employer carve-out that this clause's body does not itself state. § 1324b(a)(2) also contains two further exceptions not quoted here: one for national-origin discrimination already covered by Title VII of the Civil Rights Act as applied to a given employer, and one for citizenship-status discrimination that is otherwise required by law, regulation, executive order, or government contract.

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(a)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, general prohibition on national-origin and citizenship-status discrimination
citations.quote: It is an unfair immigration-related employment practice for a person or other entity to discriminate against any individual (other than an unauthorized alien, as defined in section 1324a(h)(3) of this title) with respect to the hiring, or recruitment or referral for a fee, of the individual for employment or the discharging of the individual from employment— (A) because of such individual’s national origin, or (B) in the case of a protected individual (as defined in paragraph (3)), because of such individual’s citizenship status.

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(a)(2)(A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, small-employer exception
citations.quote: Paragraph (1) shall not apply to— (A) a person or other entity that employs three or fewer employees

clauses.title: About This Document
clauses.body: This information sheet summarizes selected federal requirements under the Immigration Reform and Control Act. It is not the Form I-9, USCIS's Handbook for Employers (Form M-274), or any other official government form, and reading or retaining it does not by itself satisfy {{companyName}}'s obligation to complete an actual Form I-9 for {{employeeName}}. The current Form I-9 and its instructions are published by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

clauses.title: Declaration and Scope of This Notice
clauses.body: This 401(k)/Retirement Plan Distribution Notice at Termination concerns {{employeeName}}, whose employment with {{companyName}} ended on {{terminationDate}}, and {{employeeName}}'s account under {{companyName}}'s {{planName}}. It states general rules of federal law that govern what happens to a former employee's account balance under an employer-sponsored retirement plan such as a 401(k) once employment ends: the tax treatment available for a distribution from the plan, the right to have a distribution transferred directly to another eligible retirement plan, the mandatory withholding that applies when a distribution is instead paid to the former employee, the plan administrator's obligation to explain these rules in writing before making a distribution, and the vesting rules that determine what portion of the account balance is the former employee's to keep. This notice states rules of general federal law. It does not state the terms of {{planName}} itself, which can vary within what federal law permits, and it does not state what {{employeeName}} should do about any distribution, rollover, or election.

clauses.title: Tax-Free Rollover of an Eligible Rollover Distribution Within 60 Days
clauses.body: Federal tax law allows an "eligible rollover distribution" from a qualified retirement plan to be excluded from an employee's gross income for the year paid, if the recipient transfers the distributed property to an eligible retirement plan such as an IRA or another qualified employer plan. That transfer generally must happen no later than the 60th day after the day the distributee received the distributed property, subject to a narrow hardship waiver of that 60-day rule that the Secretary of the Treasury may grant. Whether a distribution {{employeeName}} receives from {{planName}} qualifies as an eligible rollover distribution in the first place, and whether a transfer of it is completed within the applicable time limit, are separate questions this clause does not resolve for {{employeeName}}'s specific distribution.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the general tax-free-rollover mechanism and the 60-day time limit under 26 U.S.C. § 402(c) — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs the reader's situation, and not a claim about the terms of any specific retirement plan, which can vary within what federal law permits. This clause is not a claim about whether any particular distribution qualifies as an eligible rollover distribution (a separate clause in this document addresses that definition) or about whether the Secretary would grant a hardship waiver of the 60-day rule in any specific case. Both citations below are to different subsections of the same statutory section, 26 U.S.C. § 402(c) — paragraph (1) (the exclusion-from-income rule) and paragraph (3)(A) (the 60-day time limit) — and are disclosed together here rather than presented as independent sources.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 402(c)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, exclusion from income for a rolled-over eligible rollover distribution
citations.quote: If— (A) any portion of the balance to the credit of an employee in a qualified trust is paid to the employee in an eligible rollover distribution, (B) the distributee transfers any portion of the property received in such distribution to an eligible retirement plan, and (C) in the case of a distribution of property other than money, the amount so transferred consists of the property distributed, then such distribution (to the extent so transferred) shall not be includible in gross income for the taxable year in which paid.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 402(c)(3)(A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, 60-day time limit on rollover transfers
citations.quote: Except as provided in subparagraphs (B) and (C), paragraph (1) shall not apply to any transfer of a distribution made after the 60th day following the day on which the distributee received the property distributed.

clauses.title: What Counts as an "Eligible Rollover Distribution" Under Federal Tax Law
clauses.body: Not every payment out of a qualified retirement plan is an "eligible rollover distribution." Federal tax law defines the term broadly, as any distribution to an employee of all or any portion of the balance credited to the employee in a qualified trust, but then carves out three specific categories that are not eligible rollover distributions: (1) a distribution that is one of a series of substantially equal periodic payments made at least annually, for the life or life expectancy of the employee (or the joint lives or joint life expectancies of the employee and a designated beneficiary), or for a specified period of 10 years or more; (2) a distribution required under the federal minimum-distribution rules; and (3) a distribution made on account of the employee's hardship. Whether a specific payment {{employeeName}} may receive from {{planName}} falls within the general definition or within one of these three carve-outs depends on the nature of that specific payment, which this clause does not determine.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the statutory definition of "eligible rollover distribution" and its three carve-outs under 26 U.S.C. § 402(c)(4) — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs the reader's situation, and not a claim about the terms of any specific retirement plan, which can vary within what federal law permits. This clause cites a single statutory paragraph (§ 402(c)(4)); it does not restate the separate 2020-specific transition rule that appears later in the same paragraph, which is no longer of current relevance and was not carried into this clause's body text.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 402(c)(4) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, definition of "eligible rollover distribution"
citations.quote: For purposes of this subsection, the term “eligible rollover distribution” means any distribution to an employee of all or any portion of the balance to the credit of the employee in a qualified trust; except that such term shall not include— (A) any distribution which is one of a series of substantially equal periodic payments (not less frequently than annually) made— (i) for the life (or life expectancy) of the employee or the joint lives (or joint life expectancies) of the employee and the employee's designated beneficiary, or (ii) for a specified period of 10 years or more, (B) any distribution to the extent such distribution is required under section 401(a)(9), and (C) any distribution which is made upon hardship of the employee.

clauses.title: The Right to a Direct Rollover to Another Eligible Retirement Plan
clauses.body: Separately from the tax-free-rollover mechanism itself, federal tax law imposes a qualification requirement on the plan: a trust cannot be a "qualified trust" — meaning the tax-favored retirement plan status {{planName}} depends on — unless the plan gives a distributee who is entitled to an eligible rollover distribution the option to have that distribution paid directly to an eligible retirement plan the distributee specifies, made as a direct trustee-to-trustee transfer, rather than paid to the distributee first. This direct-rollover option is what allows a distributee to receive an eligible rollover distribution without the distribution passing through the distributee's own hands at all.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the statutory direct-rollover requirement under 26 U.S.C. § 401(a)(31)(A) — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs the reader's situation, and not a claim about the terms of any specific retirement plan, which can vary within what federal law permits. This clause cites a single statutory subparagraph (§ 401(a)(31)(A)); it does not restate the separate automatic-cash-out / mandatory-distribution rule in the neighboring subparagraph (§ 401(a)(31)(B)), which applies only to certain small mandatory distributions and is not addressed in this document.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 401(a)(31)(A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, qualified-trust requirement to offer a direct rollover
citations.quote: A trust shall not constitute a qualified trust under this section unless the plan of which such trust is a part provides that if the distributee of any eligible rollover distribution— (i) elects to have such distribution paid directly to an eligible retirement plan, and (ii) specifies the eligible retirement plan to which such distribution is to be paid (in such form and at such time as the plan administrator may prescribe), such distribution shall be made in the form of a direct trustee-to-trustee transfer to the eligible retirement plan so specified.

clauses.title: Mandatory 20% Withholding When a Distribution Is Paid Directly to the Employee
clauses.body: If an eligible rollover distribution is paid to the distributee rather than transferred directly to an eligible retirement plan, federal tax law requires the payor to withhold federal income tax from the distribution at a mandatory rate of 20 percent, regardless of the distributee's actual income tax liability for the year. This mandatory 20% withholding does not apply, however, to any distribution that the distributee elects to have paid directly to an eligible retirement plan under the direct-rollover provision described elsewhere in this document. In other words, the 20% withholding is specifically tied to the choice between a direct trustee-to-trustee transfer and a payment made to the distributee personally.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the mandatory 20% withholding rule and its direct-rollover exception under 26 U.S.C. § 3405(c) — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs the reader's situation, and not a claim about the terms of any specific retirement plan, which can vary within what federal law permits, and not a claim about any specific reader's actual federal income tax liability, which this withholding amount does not determine. Both citations below are to different subsections of the same statutory section, 26 U.S.C. § 3405(c) — paragraph (1) (the 20%-withholding rule) and paragraph (2) (the direct-rollover exception) — and are disclosed together here rather than presented as independent sources.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 3405(c)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, mandatory 20% withholding on an eligible rollover distribution
citations.quote: In the case of any designated distribution which is an eligible rollover distribution— (A) subsections (a) and (b) shall not apply, and (B) the payor of such distribution shall withhold from such distribution an amount equal to 20 percent of such distribution.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 3405(c)(2) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, exception for a direct rollover election
citations.quote: Paragraph (1)(B) shall not apply to any distribution if the distributee elects under section 401(a)(31)(A) to have such distribution paid directly to an eligible retirement plan.

clauses.title: The Plan Administrator's Written Explanation Before a Distribution: the Section 402(f) Notice
clauses.body: Before making an eligible rollover distribution, federal tax law itself — not merely a regulation implementing it — requires the plan administrator to give the recipient a written explanation covering: the recipient's right to have the distribution directly transferred to an eligible retirement plan (and that automatic direct transfer applies to certain distributions); the withholding of tax that applies if the distribution is not directly transferred; the conditions under which the distribution will not be taxed if transferred to an eligible retirement plan within 60 days of receipt; certain special tax-computation provisions, where applicable; and the fact that the receiving plan may impose restrictions or tax consequences different from those of the distributing plan. This written explanation is commonly referred to as a "402(f) notice," after the Internal Revenue Code section that requires it, and it must be provided within a reasonable period of time before the distribution is made.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the written-explanation requirement under 26 U.S.C. § 402(f)(1) — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs the reader's situation, and not a claim about the terms of any specific retirement plan, which can vary within what federal law permits. This clause cites a single statutory paragraph (§ 402(f)(1)); it does not address the separate cross-referenced provisions of §§ 402(d) or (e), which the notice must also cover "if applicable" but which are not otherwise addressed in this document. This requirement is set out directly in the Internal Revenue Code itself, at 26 U.S.C. § 402(f) — it is not solely a creature of Treasury regulations, and this clause does not rely on, or cite, 29 U.S.C. § 1132 (ERISA's civil-enforcement provision), which is a different statute addressing who may sue to enforce ERISA rights rather than the content of this notice.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 402(f)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, written explanation before an eligible rollover distribution
citations.quote: The plan administrator of any plan shall, within a reasonable period of time before making an eligible rollover distribution, provide a written explanation to the recipient— (A) of the provisions under which the recipient may have the distribution directly transferred to an eligible retirement plan and that the automatic distribution by direct transfer applies to certain distributions in accordance with section 401(a)(31)(B), (B) of the provision which requires the withholding of tax on the distribution if it is not directly transferred to an eligible retirement plan, (C) of the provisions under which the distribution will not be subject to tax if transferred to an eligible retirement plan within 60 days after the date on which the recipient received the distribution, (D) if applicable, of the provisions of subsections (d) and (e) of this section, and (E) of the provisions under which distributions from the eligible retirement plan receiving the distribution may be subject to restrictions and tax consequences which are different from those applicable to distributions from the plan making such distribution.

clauses.title: Vesting: Employee Contributions Are Always Fully Vested; Employer Contributions May Vest on a Schedule
clauses.body: Federal law draws a sharp line between two sources of money inside a retirement plan account like {{planName}}. An employee's own contributions to the plan — such as elective deferrals from {{employeeName}}'s own pay — are always fully, immediately nonforfeitable ("vested"): federal law requires that a plan treat an employee's rights in the portion of the account derived from the employee's own contributions as nonforfeitable, with no waiting period at all. Employer contributions, such as an employer match or profit-sharing contribution, are different: federal law permits a plan to vest that portion of the account on a schedule instead of immediately. For a 401(k) or similar individual-account (defined-contribution) plan specifically, federal law permits, at most, a schedule under which an employee becomes 100% vested in employer contributions after completing 3 years of service (with nothing vested before that point), or, alternatively, a graded schedule of at least 20% after 2 years of service, 40% after 3, 60% after 4, 80% after 5, and 100% after 6 years of service. A plan may vest employer contributions faster than these schedules — including immediately — but federal law does not allow a 401(k)-type plan to vest more slowly than whichever of these two schedules it has adopted. Whether {{employeeName}}'s specific account under {{planName}} uses the 3-year-cliff schedule, the graded schedule, faster vesting, or some other permitted combination, and how many years of vesting service {{employeeName}} had completed as of {{terminationDate}}, are questions this clause does not answer; they depend on {{planName}}'s own terms and {{employeeName}}'s own service record.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the vesting rules under 29 U.S.C. § 1053(a) — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs the reader's situation, and not a claim about the terms of any specific retirement plan, which can vary within what federal law permits. Two of the citations below are to different subsections of the same statutory section, 29 U.S.C. § 1053(a) — paragraph (1) (full vesting of an employee's own contributions) and paragraph (2)(B) (the two permitted maximum vesting schedules for an individual account plan) — and are disclosed together here rather than presented as independent sources. This clause states the individual-account-plan vesting schedules in § 1053(a)(2)(B), because a 401(k) is an individual account (defined contribution) plan; § 1053(a)(2)(A), a separate, slightly longer schedule (a 5-year cliff, or a 3-through-7-year graded schedule) that applies specifically to defined benefit plans, is not restated here because it does not govern a 401(k)-type account. The third citation, to 29 U.S.C. § 1002(34), a different statutory section defining "individual account plan," supports that classification and is cited as a separate, independent source rather than folded into the § 1053(a) disclosure above.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 1053(a)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, full vesting of an employee's own contributions
citations.quote: A plan satisfies the requirements of this paragraph if an employee's rights in his accrued benefit derived from his own contributions are nonforfeitable.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 1053(a)(2)(B) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, maximum permitted vesting schedules for an individual account plan
citations.quote: (i) In the case of an individual account plan, a plan satisfies the requirements of this paragraph if it satisfies the requirements of clause (ii) or (iii). (ii) A plan satisfies the requirements of this clause if an employee who has completed at least 3 years of service has a nonforfeitable right to 100 percent of the employee's accrued benefit derived from employer contributions. (iii) A plan satisfies the requirements of this clause if an employee has a nonforfeitable right to a percentage of the employee's accrued benefit derived from employer contributions determined under the following table: Years of service: The nonforfeitable percentage is: 2 20 3 40 4 60 5 80 6 or more 100.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 1002(34) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, definition of "individual account plan" / "defined contribution plan"
citations.quote: The term “individual account plan” or “defined contribution plan” means a pension plan which provides for an individual account for each participant and for benefits based solely upon the amount contributed to the participant's account, and any income, expenses, gains and losses, and any forfeitures of accounts of other participants which may be allocated to such participant's account.

clauses.title: Statement of Plan and Account Information, and Signature
Declaration of Parents and the Order Sought to Be Modified
clauses.body: This Post-Judgment Modification of Child Custody/Support — Information Sheet concerns an existing California custody, visitation, or support order regarding {{childName}} (date of birth: {{childDOB}}), whose parents are {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}}. The order sought to be modified was entered on {{originalOrderDate}} in {{countyOfFiling}}. This information sheet is prepared for use alongside an actual noticed motion or order to show cause to modify or terminate that order, filed in the California superior court that entered it. It is not itself a court filing, and completing it does not modify, terminate, or otherwise change the existing custody, visitation, or support order concerning {{childName}}. Only a new order signed by the court can do that.

clauses.title: The Court's Continuing Jurisdiction to Modify Custody and Support — Two Different Statutes
clauses.body: A California court's authority to change a custody or support order it has already entered does not expire once the original judgment becomes final. As to custody, the court "may, during the pendency of a proceeding or at any time thereafter, make an order for the custody of a child during minority that seems necessary or proper." As to support, a support order "may be modified or terminated at any time as the court determines to be necessary," subject to statutory limits described elsewhere in this document. In each case, that continuing authority belongs to the court, not to {{parent1Name}} or {{parent2Name}} acting alone.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's post-judgment custody/support modification process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific order. This document is informational: it does not itself modify or terminate any custody, visitation, or support order concerning this document's parents; only a court order can do that. These two citations are to two different Family Code sections (§ 3022, governing custody, and § 3651(a), governing support), not subsections of the same section. This corrects an initial research assumption in the task brief that treated § 3651 as the statutory basis for modifying custody as well as support: on the fetched statutory text, § 3651 addresses only support orders (child and spousal) and never uses the word "custody"; the custody-specific continuing-jurisdiction statute is instead § 3022, cited separately here.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3022 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the court's continuing jurisdiction over custody
citations.quote: The court may, during the pendency of a proceeding or at any time thereafter, make an order for the custody of a child during minority that seems necessary or proper.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3651(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the court's continuing jurisdiction over support
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivisions (c) and (d) and subject to Article 3 (commencing with Section 3680) and Sections 3552, 3587, and 4004, a support order may be modified or terminated at any time as the court determines to be necessary.

clauses.title: Modifying a Final Custody Order: A Judicially Developed Stability Standard
clauses.body: Beyond that bare continuing-jurisdiction statute, California's appellate courts have described a further, judicially developed limit on reopening a final custody judgment: before the court will revisit custody terms already decided, the parent seeking the change is ordinarily described as needing to show some significant change in circumstances since the prior custody order, tied to the child's welfare — a doctrine aimed at protecting the stability of a final custody judgment rather than allowing it to be relitigated on demand. That doctrine is not written into one clean Family Code section. The reason-stating and best-interest showing the Legislature did codify for one particular kind of custody order — a joint-custody order — reflects the same protective posture in narrower, statutory form: an order for joint custody "may be modified or terminated upon the petition of one or both parents or on the court's own motion if it is shown that the best interest of the child requires modification or termination of the order," and if either parent opposes the change, "the court shall state in its decision the reasons for modification or termination of the joint custody order."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's post-judgment custody modification process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific custody order. This document is informational: it does not itself modify or terminate any custody order named in this document; only a court order can do that. This is a single statutory section (§ 3087); no additional independent source was found for this. This same section is independently cited in this corpus's Parenting Plan document (clause parenting_modification_standard); it is cited again here, independently re-verified against the statute's live text, for this document's distinct post-judgment-modification purpose. Honest gap on the broader doctrine: the changed-circumstances rule described in this clause's body — commonly associated with the California Supreme Court's decision in Montenegro v. Diaz, 26 Cal.4th 249 (2001) — is judge-made doctrine, not directly codified in one statute. This research attempted to independently verify that case's actual holding through CourtListener, the case-law source this corpus's verification discipline requires, but CourtListener's daily request cap (125 requests/day) had already been exhausted by earlier calls in this same research session before that attempt, with the next availability roughly 13.6 hours out at the time of the attempt. Rather than presenting an unverified case citation as verified, or waiting out the rate limit, this clause describes the doctrine's substance in general terms and does not cite Montenegro or any other case for it; that description should be read as unverified case law, not as an independently confirmed holding.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3087 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: modification or termination of a joint custody order
citations.quote: An order for joint custody may be modified or terminated upon the petition of one or both parents or on the court’s own motion if it is shown that the best interest of the child requires modification or termination of the order. If either parent opposes the modification or termination order, the court shall state in its decision the reasons for modification or termination of the joint custody order.

clauses.title: Modifying Support to Match the Guideline: A More Permissive Standard Than Custody's
clauses.body: The standard governing a support-order modification is not identical to the judicially developed stability standard described elsewhere in this document for custody. On its face, the support-modification statute asks only whether the change is something "the court determines to be necessary"; it contains no "changed circumstances" language of its own. California's guideline-conformity rule goes further still in one specific circumstance: where {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}} earlier stipulated to a child support order below the amount the statewide guideline formula would produce, "no change of circumstances need be demonstrated to obtain a modification of the child support order to the applicable guideline level or above." A request to raise support to the guideline amount in that circumstance does not require the kind of threshold showing California courts describe before reopening a final custody judgment.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California applies a different, and in this specific circumstance more permissive, standard to a child-support modification than the judicially developed changed-circumstances doctrine described in this document's companion clause on custody modification — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific support order, and not a claim that every support modification requires no showing at all: this statutory rule applies specifically to raising a below-guideline stipulated order up to the guideline level. A downward modification, a modification of an order that was not originally stipulated below guideline, or a modification unrelated to guideline conformity is not addressed by this subsection and may be subject to other standards this document does not describe. This document is informational: it does not itself modify or terminate any support order named in this document; only a court order can do that. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 4065(d)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 4065(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: no change-of-circumstances showing to modify up to the guideline level
citations.quote: If the parties to a stipulated agreement stipulate to a child support order below the amount established by the statewide uniform guideline, no change of circumstances need be demonstrated to obtain a modification of the child support order to the applicable guideline level or above.

clauses.title: How Far Back a Support Modification Can Reach
clauses.body: California law limits how far back in time a support modification can reach. A support order "may not be modified or terminated as to an amount that accrued before the date of the filing of the notice of motion or order to show cause to modify or terminate," subject to narrow exceptions this document does not describe. Consistent with that limit, an order modifying or terminating support "may be made retroactive to the date of the filing of the notice of motion or order to show cause to modify or terminate, or to any subsequent date" — but not earlier, except as federal law or a narrow statutory exception separately provides.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a real retroactivity limit tied to the date a party files a request to modify — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific support order, and not an exhaustive statement of the exceptions to that limit (§ 3651(c)(2)-(4) separately addresses a servicemember's activation and deployment, and § 3653(b)-(c) separately address retroactivity following unemployment or military deployment; none of those narrower exceptions is described in this clause). These two citations are to two different Family Code sections (§ 3651(c)(1) and § 3653(a)), not subsections of the same section; § 3651(c)(1) itself cross-references § 3653 only in the narrower military-deployment context this clause does not quote. This document is informational: it does not itself modify or terminate any support order named in this document; only a court order can do that. This clause does not address whether, or on what showing, a custody order may likewise be given retroactive effect; no equivalent custody-retroactivity statute was independently verified for this document, so none is offered here rather than presenting an unverified rule as verified.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3651(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: no modification of amounts that accrued before the filing
citations.quote: Except as provided in paragraph (2) and subdivision (b), a support order may not be modified or terminated as to an amount that accrued before the date of the filing of the notice of motion or order to show cause to modify or terminate.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3653(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: retroactivity to the date of filing, or later
citations.quote: An order modifying or terminating a support order may be made retroactive to the date of the filing of the notice of motion or order to show cause to modify or terminate, or to any subsequent date, except as provided in subdivision (b) or by federal law (42 U.S.C. Sec. 666(a)(9)).

clauses.title: A Parents' Agreement to Change Support Is Not, By Itself, a Modified Order
clauses.body: {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}} can agree between themselves that a support amount should change, but that agreement does not, by itself, become the legally operative support order. California's child-support-stipulation statute allows parties to "stipulate to a child support amount subject to approval of the court" — meaning court approval, not the parents' agreement alone, is what makes a stipulated amount an enforceable order. The support-modification statute confirms the same point from a different angle: it "applies whether or not the support order is based upon an agreement between the parties," so even an order that originated in the parties' own agreement is changed only through the same court process described elsewhere in this document, not by a later, private agreement to change it.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that even an agreed change to a support order requires court approval to take legal effect — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific order. This document is informational: it does not itself modify or terminate any custody, visitation, or support order named in this document, and a parents' private agreement on that subject does not do so either; only a court order can do that. These two citations are to two different Family Code sections (§ 4065(a) and § 3651(e)), not subsections of the same section. § 4065(a) is also independently cited, for a different point (the specific findings required for a below-guideline stipulation), in this corpus's Child Support Agreement document (clause childsupport_stipulation_conditions); it is re-verified here against the statute's live text and quoted only for its opening sentence, for the narrower point that court approval — not agreement alone — is what makes a stipulated support figure operative. This document's research did not separately verify an equivalent single statutory statement that a custody order likewise cannot be changed by private agreement alone; that conclusion is drawn here from this document's companion clause on the court's continuing custody jurisdiction (Family Code § 3022), which describes only the court as empowered to "make an order" for custody, rather than from an independently cited custody-specific analogue to § 4065(a).

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 4065(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a stipulated support amount is subject to court approval
citations.quote: Unless prohibited by applicable federal law, the parties may stipulate to a child support amount subject to approval of the court.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3651(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the modification statute applies regardless of the parties' agreement
citations.quote: This section applies whether or not the support order is based upon an agreement between the parties.

clauses.title: The Guideline Presumption Applies to a Modified Amount, Not Only a First-Time Order
clauses.body: Whenever a California court sets a child support amount — including in ruling on a request to modify an existing order — the amount produced by the statewide guideline formula "is presumed to be the correct amount of child support to be ordered." That presumption is rebuttable: a parent seeking a different, modified amount carries the burden of showing, by admissible evidence, that applying the formula would be unjust or inappropriate given the case's specific circumstances.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a guideline-based presumption governs any court-ordered child support figure, not only a first-time order — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific support modification. This is a single statutory section (§ 4057(a)-(b)); no additional independent source was found for this. This same section is independently cited in this corpus's Child Support Agreement document (clause childsupport_guideline_presumption) for the initial-order context; it is cited again here, independently re-verified against the statute's live text, to state that the presumption applies to a modified amount as well — a reading drawn from § 4057(a)'s own unrestricted "to be ordered" language, since the statute does not separately limit the presumption to a first-time order, rather than from a sentence in the statute that names modification specifically. This document is informational: it does not itself modify or terminate any support order named in this document; only a court order can do that.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 4057(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the presumptive-correctness rule and its rebuttable burden
citations.quote: The amount of child support established by the formula provided in subdivision (a) of Section 4055 is presumed to be the correct amount of child support to be ordered. (b) The presumption of subdivision (a) is a rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of proof and may be rebutted by admissible evidence showing that application of the formula would be unjust or inappropriate in the particular case, consistent with the principles set forth in Section 4053, because one or more of the following factors is found to be applicable by a preponderance of the evidence, and the court states in writing or on the record the information required in subdivision (a) of Section 4056:

clauses.title: Description of the Alleged Changed Circumstance and Modification Sought
clauses.body: For reference in connection with a request to modify the {{originalOrderDate}} custody, visitation, or support order concerning {{childName}}, entered in {{countyOfFiling}}: the circumstance identified as having changed since that order is: {{allegedChangedCircumstance}}. The modification described as being sought is: {{proposedModification}}. This description is background information only; it is not a declaration filed with any court, and it does not itself change the existing order.
