clauses.title: Federal Civil Cause of Action for Trade Secret Misappropriation
clauses.body: Federal law gives the owner of a trade secret a private civil cause of action for misappropriation, but only where the trade secret is related to a product or service used in, or intended for use in, interstate or foreign commerce. A civil action under this federal law generally must be brought within three years after the misappropriation is discovered, or after it should have been discovered through reasonable diligence; a misappropriation that continues over time counts as a single claim for this purpose, not a separate claim each time it recurs.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the existence and scope of the federal private civil cause of action for trade secret misappropriation — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs this letter or any dispute related to it, and not a claim that the interstate-or-foreign-commerce requirement is met for any specific trade secret. This clause cites two provisions of the same statutory section, 18 U.S.C. § 1836 — subsection (b)(1) (the cause of action itself) and subsection (d) (the three-year limitations period) — grouped together because both define the outer boundaries of the same federal claim. A CourtListener case-law search for this clause was attempted but returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, daily limit reported as exhausted) before any case could be retrieved, so no case law on how courts apply the interstate-commerce requirement in practice is included here; only the statutory text is quoted.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, private civil action
citations.quote: An owner of a trade secret that is misappropriated may bring a civil action under this subsection if the trade secret is related to a product or service used in, or intended for use in, interstate or foreign commerce.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1836(d) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, period of limitations
citations.quote: A civil action under subsection (b) may not be commenced later than 3 years after the date on which the misappropriation with respect to which the action would relate is discovered or by the exercise of reasonable diligence should have been discovered. For purposes of this subsection, a continuing misappropriation constitutes a single claim of misappropriation.

clauses.title: Federal Definition of "Misappropriation" and "Improper Means"
clauses.body: Federal law defines "misappropriation" of a trade secret to cover two distinct situations: acquiring a trade secret while knowing or having reason to know it was acquired by improper means, and disclosing or using a trade secret without consent under specified circumstances — including where the person used improper means to acquire it, or knew or had reason to know they owed a duty to keep it secret or limit its use. "Improper means" is itself a separately defined term; it includes theft, bribery, misrepresentation, breach or inducement of breach of a duty to maintain secrecy, and espionage, but it specifically excludes reverse engineering, independent derivation, and other lawful means of acquiring the same information.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the statutory definitions of "misappropriation" and "improper means" — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs this letter or any dispute related to it, and not a claim that misappropriation, as this statute defines it, occurred in any specific case. This clause cites two provisions of the same statutory section, 18 U.S.C. § 1839 — paragraph (5) (misappropriation) and paragraph (6) (improper means). The statutory definition of "trade secret" itself, 18 U.S.C. § 1839(3), is not requoted here because it is already covered as an authority clause elsewhere in this tool's confidentiality-agreement documents; this clause adds the misappropriation and improper-means definitions, which those other documents do not cover. A CourtListener case-law search for this clause was attempted but returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429) before any case could be retrieved, so no corroborating case law is included here; only the statutory text is quoted.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1839(5) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, definition of "misappropriation"
citations.quote: the term "misappropriation" means— (A) acquisition of a trade secret of another by a person who knows or has reason to know that the trade secret was acquired by improper means; or (B) disclosure or use of a trade secret of another without express or implied consent by a person who— (i) used improper means to acquire knowledge of the trade secret; (ii) at the time of disclosure or use, knew or had reason to know that the knowledge of the trade secret was— (I) derived from or through a person who had used improper means to acquire the trade secret; (II) acquired under circumstances giving rise to a duty to maintain the secrecy of the trade secret or limit the use of the trade secret; or (III) derived from or through a person who owed a duty to the person seeking relief to maintain the secrecy of the trade secret or limit the use of the trade secret; or (iii) before a material change of the position of the person, knew or had reason to know that— (I) the trade secret was a trade secret; and (II) knowledge of the trade secret had been acquired by accident or mistake

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1839(6) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, definition of "improper means"
citations.quote: the term "improper means"— (A) includes theft, bribery, misrepresentation, breach or inducement of a breach of a duty to maintain secrecy, or espionage through electronic or other means; and (B) does not include reverse engineering, independent derivation, or any other lawful means of acquisition

clauses.title: Federal Civil Remedies for Trade Secret Misappropriation
clauses.body: In a federal civil action for trade secret misappropriation, a court may grant injunctive relief; award damages for the trade secret owner's actual loss and for the misappropriator's unjust enrichment not already captured in that loss figure, or, in place of those damages, impose a reasonable royalty for the unauthorized disclosure or use; and, where the trade secret was willfully and maliciously misappropriated, award exemplary damages of up to two times the damages awarded, plus reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing party. Federal law separately authorizes an extraordinary, ex parte civil seizure remedy in limited circumstances; that seizure remedy is a different provision and isn't addressed by this clause.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the remedies a court may award in a federal civil action for trade secret misappropriation — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs this letter or any dispute related to it, and not a claim about what remedy, if any, a court would award for any specific conduct. This clause quotes a single statutory provision, 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3), covering injunctive relief, damages, and exemplary damages/attorney's fees together (with the injunctive-relief detail abridged); it does not separately quote the civil-seizure provision, § 1836(b)(2), which is only mentioned by name here. A CourtListener case-law search for this clause was attempted but returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429) before any case could be retrieved, so no case law on how courts apply these remedy provisions is included here; only the statutory text is quoted.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, civil remedies
citations.quote: In a civil action brought under this subsection with respect to the misappropriation of a trade secret, a court may— (A) grant an injunction ... ; (B) award— (i) (I) damages for actual loss caused by the misappropriation of the trade secret; and (II) damages for any unjust enrichment caused by the misappropriation of the trade secret that is not addressed in computing damages for actual loss; or (ii) in lieu of damages measured by any other methods, the damages caused by the misappropriation measured by imposition of liability for a reasonable royalty for the misappropriator’s unauthorized disclosure or use of the trade secret; (C) if the trade secret is willfully and maliciously misappropriated, award exemplary damages in an amount not more than 2 times the amount of the damages awarded under subparagraph (B); and (D) if a claim of the misappropriation is made in bad faith, which may be established by circumstantial evidence, a motion to terminate an injunction is made or opposed in bad faith, or the trade secret was willfully and maliciously misappropriated, award reasonable attorney’s fees to the prevailing party.

clauses.title: California's Definition of Misappropriation
clauses.body: California's Uniform Trade Secrets Act separately defines "misappropriation." Under that statute, misappropriation includes acquiring a trade secret while knowing or having reason to know it was acquired by improper means, and it also includes disclosing or using a trade secret without express or implied consent under specified circumstances — including where the person used improper means to acquire it, or knew or had reason to know they owed a duty to keep it secret or limit its use. This definition is substantively similar to the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act's own misappropriation definition, though the two statutes use some different phrasing, and both a federal DTSA claim and a California UTSA claim can potentially be based on the same underlying conduct.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own definition of "misappropriation" — not a claim about which state's law governs this letter or any dispute related to it, and not a claim that misappropriation, as this statute defines it, occurred in any specific case. This clause cites a single statutory subsection, Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.1(b); no additional independent source was found for this. The observation that California's definition is substantively similar to the federal definition is this researcher's own side-by-side comparison of the two statutes' text (compare 18 U.S.C. § 1839(5), quoted in a separate authority clause in this document), not a holding from any case that has compared them; no case law testing that comparison is included, since a CourtListener search attempted for this clause returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429) before any case could be retrieved.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.1(b) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Uniform Trade Secrets Act, definition of "misappropriation"
citations.quote: "Misappropriation" means: (1) Acquisition of a trade secret of another by a person who knows or has reason to know that the trade secret was acquired by improper means; or (2) Disclosure or use of a trade secret of another without express or implied consent by a person who: (A) Used improper means to acquire knowledge of the trade secret; or (B) At the time of disclosure or use, knew or had reason to know that his or her knowledge of the trade secret was: (i) Derived from or through a person who had utilized improper means to acquire it; (ii) Acquired under circumstances giving rise to a duty to maintain its secrecy or limit its use; or (iii) Derived from or through a person who owed a duty to the person seeking relief to maintain its secrecy or limit its use; or (C) Before a material change of his or her position, knew or had reason to know that it was a trade secret and that knowledge of it had been acquired by accident or mistake.

clauses.title: California's Remedies for Trade Secret Misappropriation
clauses.body: California's Uniform Trade Secrets Act allows a complainant to recover damages for actual loss caused by misappropriation, plus damages for unjust enrichment caused by the misappropriation that isn't already counted in the actual-loss figure. If neither actual loss nor unjust enrichment can be proven, the statute instead allows a court to order payment of a reasonable royalty for no longer than the period the use could have been prohibited. If the misappropriation was willful and malicious, the statute allows a court to award exemplary damages of up to twice the damages otherwise awarded. Separately, California's statute allows a court to award reasonable attorney's fees and costs to the prevailing party where a misappropriation claim (or a motion to terminate an injunction) is made or opposed in bad faith, or where willful and malicious misappropriation exists. This overall structure closely parallels the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act's own remedy structure, including the same two-times cap on exemplary damages for willful and malicious misappropriation, though the two statutes are independent of each other and a court would apply each on its own terms.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own remedy structure for trade secret misappropriation — not a claim about which state's law governs this letter or any dispute related to it, and not a claim about what remedy, if any, a court would award for any specific conduct. This clause cites two different statutory sections, Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.3 (damages, royalty, and exemplary damages) and § 3426.4 (attorney's fees and costs) — these are separate sections of the same title, not different subsections of one section. The observation that California's two-times exemplary-damages cap parallels the federal cap is this researcher's own comparison of the two statutes' text (compare 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(C), quoted in a separate authority clause in this document), not a holding from any case; no case law on how courts apply either cap in practice is included, since a CourtListener search attempted for this clause returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429) before any case could be retrieved.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.3 (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Uniform Trade Secrets Act, damages
citations.quote: (a) A complainant may recover damages for the actual loss caused by misappropriation. A complainant also may recover for the unjust enrichment caused by misappropriation that is not taken into account in computing damages for actual loss. (b) If neither damages nor unjust enrichment caused by misappropriation are provable, the court may order payment of a reasonable royalty for no longer than the period of time the use could have been prohibited. (c) If willful and malicious misappropriation exists, the court may award exemplary damages in an amount not exceeding twice any award made under subdivision (a) or (b).

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.4 (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Uniform Trade Secrets Act, attorney's fees
citations.quote: If a claim of misappropriation is made in bad faith, a motion to terminate an injunction is made or resisted in bad faith, or willful and malicious misappropriation exists, the court may award reasonable attorney’s fees and costs to the prevailing party.

clauses.title: Fictitious Business Name Statement — Purpose and Scope
clauses.body: This Fictitious Business Name Statement Information Sheet relates to the fictitious business name "{{fictitiousBusinessName}}" used by {{registrantName}}, a {{entityType}} with a principal place of business at {{principalOfficeAddress}}, in connection with a filing made with the Clerk of {{filingCounty}} County. California law treats the use of a business name other than a person's or entity's own true legal name as a distinct filing event, addressed in Business and Professions Code Chapter 5 (Sections 17900 through 17930), commonly called a fictitious business name statement or, informally, a "DBA" filing. This is a county-level filing made with the clerk of the county where the business's principal place of business is located — it is not a state-level filing with the California Secretary of State. It is separate from, and does not substitute for, the state-level filings involved in forming a corporation or LLC (articles of incorporation or articles of organization) or in that entity's periodic Statement of Information filed with the Secretary of State after formation. An entity can complete all of those state-level filings and still separately need to file a fictitious business name statement at the county level if it uses a name other than the name already on file with the Secretary of State, just as an individual sole proprietor who has made no state-level filing at all can independently be required to file one. This document's research addressed only this county-level fictitious business name filing requirement under California's Business and Professions Code; it did not research the filing requirements of any other state, or any additional local business license or tax registration requirement that a county or city may separately impose on the same business.

clauses.title: The Statutory Definition of a 'Fictitious Business Name'
clauses.body: California's fictitious business name statute defines what counts as a "fictitious business name" separately for each type of registrant — it is not simply any name a business chooses to operate under. For an individual, a name is fictitious if it does not include that individual's own surname, or if it suggests the existence of additional owners the individual does not actually have. For a partnership or other association of persons (with statutory exceptions for certain limited partnerships and registered limited liability partnerships that separately register with the Secretary of State), a name is fictitious if it does not include the surname of each general partner, or if it suggests additional owners beyond those partners. For a domestic or foreign corporation, any name other than the exact corporate name stated in its articles of incorporation on file with the Secretary of State is a fictitious business name. For a limited liability company, any name other than the exact name stated in its articles of organization on file with the Secretary of State is a fictitious business name. A name "suggests the existence of additional owners" if it includes words such as "Company," "& Company," "& Son," "& Sons," "& Associates," or "Brothers," though not words that merely describe the business being conducted. The statute states its own purpose directly: to protect people dealing with a business operating under a name other than its true name, by making the identity of the people or entity behind that name a matter of public record — and the statute expressly states it is not intended to confer any right or advantage on a business that files, or on one that fails to.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's fictitious business name requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific business; other states impose different DBA/assumed-name requirements with different names, deadlines, and forms. All three citations below are to subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17900 — subdivisions (a)(1), (b), and (c) — and are treated as one source, not three independent statutes. This clause's research also confirmed the statute contains additional categories not summarized above: separate definitions for limited partnerships and foreign limited partnerships that have filed with the Secretary of State (subdivision (b)(4)), which this document's fields do not separately address because this project's scope, per its research request, targeted individuals, partnerships, corporations, and LLCs rather than limited partnerships specifically.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17900(a)(1)
citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, statement of statutory purpose
citations.quote: The purpose of this section is to protect those dealing with individuals or partnerships doing business under fictitious names, and it is not intended to confer any right or advantage on individuals or firms that fail to comply with the law. The filing of a fictitious business name certificate is designed to make available to the public the identities of persons doing business under the fictitious name.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17900(b)
citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, statutory definition by registrant type
citations.quote: As used in this chapter, “fictitious business name” means: (1) In the case of an individual, a name that does not include the surname of the individual or a name that suggests the existence of additional owners, as described in subdivision (c). (2) In the case of a partnership or other association of persons, other than a limited partnership that has filed a certificate of limited partnership with the California Secretary of State pursuant to Section 15902.01 of the Corporations Code, a foreign limited partnership that has filed an application for registration with the California Secretary of State pursuant to Section 15909.02 of the Corporations Code, a registered limited liability partnership that has filed a registration pursuant to Section 16953 of the Corporations Code, or a foreign limited liability partnership that has filed an application for registration pursuant to Section 16959 of the Corporations Code, a name that does not include the surname of each general partner or a name that suggests the existence of additional owners, as described in subdivision (c) and in Section 17901. (3) In the case of a domestic or foreign corporation, any name other than the corporate name stated in its articles of incorporation filed with the California Secretary of State, in accordance with subdivision (a) of Section 17910.5. (4) In the case of a limited partnership that has filed a certificate of limited partnership with the California Secretary of State pursuant to Section 15902.01 of the Corporations Code and in the case of a foreign limited partnership that has filed an application for registration with the California Secretary of State pursuant to Section 15902.02 of the Corporations Code, any name other than the name of the limited partnership as on file with the California Secretary of State. (5) In the case of a limited liability company, any name other than the name stated in its articles of organization and in the case of a foreign limited liability company that has filed an application for registration with the California Secretary of State pursuant to Section 17708.02 of the Corporations Code, any name other than the name of the limited liability company as on file with the California Secretary of State, in accordance with subdivision (b) of Section 17910.5.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17900(c)
citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, what it means for a name to 'suggest additional owners'
citations.quote: A name that suggests the existence of additional owners within the meaning of subdivision (b) is one that includes such words as “Company,” “& Company,” “& Son,” “& Sons,” “& Associates,” “Brothers,” and the like, but not words that merely describe the business being conducted.

clauses.title: Filing Deadline and Where the Statement Is Filed
clauses.body: A person or entity that regularly transacts business in California for profit under a fictitious business name is statutorily required to file a fictitious business name statement, and the statute sets a deadline measured from when that business under the name actually began: the statement must be filed not later than 40 days from the time the registrant commences transacting business under the fictitious name. The statement is not filed with the California Secretary of State. It is filed at the county level, with the clerk of the county in which the registrant has its principal place of business in California; if the registrant has no place of business in California, the statement is instead filed with the Clerk of Sacramento County. California law also permits, without requiring, filing in a county other than the county of the principal place of business, so long as the filing in the principal-place-of-business county is also separately made.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's fictitious business name requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific business; other states impose different DBA/assumed-name requirements with different names, deadlines, and forms. This clause cites two different statutory sections, not subsections of one section: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17910(a) sets the 40-day filing deadline, and Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17915 sets the county-level place of filing; each is an independent source.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17910(a)
citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, the 40-day filing deadline
citations.quote: Every person who regularly transacts business in this state for profit under a fictitious business name shall do all of the following: (a) File a fictitious business name statement in accordance with this chapter not later than 40 days from the time the registrant commences to transact such business.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17915
citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, county of filing
citations.quote: A fictitious business name statement shall be filed with the clerk of the county in which the registrant has his or her principal place of business in this state or, if the registrant has no place of business in this state, with the Clerk of Sacramento County. This chapter does not preclude a person from filing a fictitious business name statement in a county other than that where the principal place of business is located, as long as the requirements of this section are also met.

clauses.title: Required Content of the Statement
clauses.body: California's statute prescribes a specific form of content for a fictitious business name statement rather than leaving the content to the filer's discretion. The statement must identify the fictitious business name or names used, the street address and county of the registrant's principal place of business, and — depending on what kind of registrant is filing — specific identifying information: an individual's full name; the full name of each general partner for a partnership; or, for an LLC or corporation, the entity's name and address exactly as stated in its articles of organization or articles of incorporation on file with the Secretary of State, together with its state of organization or incorporation. The statement must also state the nature of the business (for example, that the registrant is an individual, a partnership, an LLC, or a corporation) and the date the registrant commenced transacting business under the fictitious name. The registrant must sign a declaration that all information in the statement is true and correct, and the prescribed form itself states — as a matter of statute, not merely as boilerplate — that a registrant who declares as true a material matter under this statute knowing it to be false is guilty of a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $1,000.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's fictitious business name requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific business; other states impose different DBA/assumed-name requirements with different names, deadlines, and forms. This clause cites two different subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17913 — subdivisions (a) and (b)(3) — and treats them as one source, not two independent statutes. The quoted subdivision (b)(3) excerpt below also names trusts as a distinct registrant category with their own content requirement (naming each trustee), which this document's fields do not separately collect because trusts as fictitious-name registrants were outside this research's requested scope.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17913(a)
citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, prescribed statutory form and the false-declaration misdemeanor
citations.quote: The fictitious business name statement shall contain all of the information required by this subdivision and shall be substantially in the following form: FICTITIOUS BUSINESS NAME STATEMENT The following person (persons) is (are) doing business as * at ** : *** This business is conducted by **** The registrant commenced to transact business under the fictitious business name or names listed above on ***** I declare that all information in this statement is true and correct. (A registrant who declares as true any material matter pursuant to Section 17913 of the Business and Professions Code that the registrant knows to be false is guilty of a misdemeanor punishable by a fine not to exceed one thousand dollars ($1,000).)

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17913(b)(3)
citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, registrant-identifying information by entity type
citations.quote: If the registrant is a limited liability company, insert the name and business mailing address of the limited liability company, as set out in its articles of organization on file with the California Secretary of State, and the state of organization. If the registrant is a trust, insert the full name and business mailing address of each trustee. If the registrant is a corporation, insert the name and address of the corporation, as set out in its articles of incorporation on file with the California Secretary of State, and the state of incorporation.

clauses.title: The Newspaper Publication Requirement
clauses.body: Filing a fictitious business name statement with the county clerk is not, by itself, the end of the statutory process — California also requires the statement to be published. Within 45 days after the statement has been filed, the registrant must cause it to be published in a newspaper of general circulation in the county where the statement was filed (or, if no such newspaper exists in that county, in an adjoining county; or, for a registrant with no California place of business, in a newspaper of general circulation in Sacramento County). The publication itself must run once a week for four successive weeks, under the state's general publication-of-notice statute, which specifies that four weekly publications with at least five days between each publication date are sufficient, with the notice period running from the first day of publication through the twenty-eighth day. After publication is complete, an affidavit showing that the statement was published must be filed with the same county clerk within 45 days after the publication is finished. A refiling made because a prior statement expired does not have to be republished, provided the information has not changed and the refiling is made within 40 days of the prior statement's expiration.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's fictitious business name requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific business; other states impose different DBA/assumed-name requirements with different names, deadlines, and forms. This clause cites material from two different codes and, within one of them, two different subsections of the same section: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17917, subdivisions (a) and (d), are subsections of one statutory section and are treated as one source, not two; separately, Cal. Gov. Code § 6064 is an independent source from a different code altogether, incorporated by cross-reference into § 17917(a) rather than restated there, which is why this clause cites it directly rather than assuming its content.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17917(a)
citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, publication deadline and newspaper selection
citations.quote: Within 45 days after a fictitious business name statement has been filed pursuant to this chapter, the registrant shall cause a statement in the form prescribed by subdivision (a) of Section 17913 to be published pursuant to Section 6064 of the Government Code in a newspaper of general circulation in the county where the fictitious business name statement was filed or, if there is no such newspaper in that county, in a newspaper of general circulation in an adjoining county. If the registrant does not have a place of business in this state, the notice shall be published in a newspaper of general circulation in Sacramento County.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17917(d)
citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, filing the affidavit of publication
citations.quote: An affidavit showing the publication of the statement shall be filed with the county clerk where the fictitious business name statement was filed within 45 days after the completion of the publication.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 6064
citations.cite: General Provisions Relating to Publication of Notice, the once-a-week-for-four-weeks requirement
citations.quote: Publication of notice pursuant to this section shall be once a week for four successive weeks. Four publications in a newspaper regularly published once a week or oftener, with at least five days intervening between the respective publication dates not counting such publication dates, are sufficient. The period of notice commences with the first day of publication and terminates at the end of the twenty-eighth day, including therein the first day.

clauses.title: Expiration and Refiling
clauses.body: A fictitious business name statement does not remain effective indefinitely. Absent an earlier expiration, it expires five years from the date it was filed with the county clerk. It can expire sooner: it expires 40 days after any change occurs in the facts originally set forth in the statement, and it also expires whenever the registrant files a statement of abandonment of the fictitious business name it covered. The statutorily prescribed form itself is required to state the statement's expiration date. Filing a new fictitious business name statement before an existing one expires is how a registrant continues its filing.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's fictitious business name requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific business; other states impose different DBA/assumed-name requirements with different names, deadlines, and forms. This clause cites four subsections/sections together: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17920(a), (b), and (c) are three subsections of the same statutory section and are treated as one source, not three; Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17921, requiring the expiration date to appear on the form, is a separate, independent section.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17920(a)
citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, the five-year expiration
citations.quote: Unless the statement expires earlier under subdivision (b) or (c), a fictitious business name statement expires five years from the date it was filed in the office of the county clerk.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17920(b)
citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, early expiration on a change of facts
citations.quote: Except as provided in Section 17923, a fictitious business name statement expires 40 days after any change in the facts set forth in the statement pursuant to Section 17913.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17920(c)
citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, expiration on a statement of abandonment
citations.quote: A fictitious business name statement expires when the registrant files a statement of abandonment of the fictitious business name described in the statement.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17921
citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, expiration date required on the form
citations.quote: Notice of the date of expiration shall be on the fictitious business name statement form.

clauses.title: Filing Does Not Create Exclusive Rights to the Name
clauses.body: Filing a fictitious business name statement does not, by itself, authorize the use of that name in violation of another person's or entity's rights under federal, state, or common law — the statutorily prescribed form itself states this directly, in a notice that is required to appear on the form. Filing does have one narrower, related legal effect: California law establishes a rebuttable presumption that the first registrant to file a fictitious business name statement containing a given name in a particular county has the exclusive right to use that name, and any confusingly similar name, as a trade name within that county — but only for a registrant who is actually engaged in a trade or business using the name in that county, and only as a presumption affecting the burden of producing evidence, not a conclusive or automatic right. This presumption is a creature of this specific filing statute; it operates county by county rather than statewide, and it is separate from, and not a substitute for, federal or state trademark registration or the common-law trademark rights that can arise independently from a business's actual use of a name in commerce.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's fictitious business name requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific business; other states impose different DBA/assumed-name requirements with different names, deadlines, and forms. This clause cites two different statutory sections, not subsections of one section: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17913(a), quoted for the notice printed on the prescribed statutory form, and Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 14411, which creates the rebuttable presumption; each is an independent source. This document's research addressed only these two California statutes; it did not independently research federal trademark law (including the Lanham Act) or California common-law trademark doctrine, and any statement above about trademark rights existing independently of this filing describes only the fact that such rights can exist and does not characterize their scope, requirements, or how they would interact with a specific name in a specific case.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17913(a)
citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, statutory notice that filing does not authorize infringing use
citations.quote: THE FILING OF THIS STATEMENT DOES NOT OF ITSELF AUTHORIZE THE USE IN THIS STATE OF A FICTITIOUS BUSINESS NAME IN VIOLATION OF THE RIGHTS OF ANOTHER UNDER FEDERAL, STATE, OR COMMON LAW (SEE SECTION 14411 ET SEQ., BUSINESS AND PROFESSIONS CODE).

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 14411
citations.cite: Trade Name Registration, the rebuttable presumption created by first-to-file
citations.quote: The filing of any fictitious business name statement by a person required to file such statement pursuant to Section 17910 shall establish a rebuttable presumption that the registrant has the exclusive right to use as a trade name the fictitious business name, as well as any confusingly similar trade name, in the county in which the statement is filed, if the registrant is the first to file such a statement containing the fictitious business name in that county, and is actually engaged in a trade or business utilizing such fictitious business name or a confusingly similar name in that county. The rebuttable presumption created by this section shall be one affecting the burden of producing evidence.

clauses.title: Consequences of Transacting Business Without a Valid Statement on File
clauses.body: California law attaches two distinct consequences to the fictitious business name filing requirement. The first is civil: a person transacting business under a fictitious business name contrary to the statute may not maintain any action in a California court on a contract made, or a transaction had, in that fictitious business name, until the fictitious business name statement has been executed, filed, and published as the statute requires. The statute carves out one specific exception: failing to satisfy the newspaper-selection preference in a different subdivision of the publication statute does not, by itself, count as "transacting business contrary to" the chapter for purposes of this civil consequence. The second consequence is criminal: any person who executes, files, or publishes a statement under this statutory chapter knowing that the statement is false, in whole or in part, is guilty of a misdemeanor, punishable upon conviction by a fine of up to $1,000 — the same $1,000 figure the prescribed statement form separately references for a registrant who knowingly declares false material information.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's fictitious business name requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific business; other states impose different DBA/assumed-name requirements with different names, deadlines, and forms. This clause cites two different statutory sections, not subsections of one section: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17918, the civil bar on maintaining a court action, and Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17930, the misdemeanor for a knowingly false statement; each is an independent source. An honest limit on what this clause verified: § 17918 states only that a noncomplying registrant "may [not] maintain any action" in a California court until the statement is executed, filed, and published, without further specifying whether or how that bar can be cured mid-litigation, whether it applies to actions other than those on a contract or transaction, or how courts have applied it in practice — this research did not independently fetch and verify any court opinion interpreting the scope of this bar, so this clause states only the statute's own text and does not characterize its practical litigation consequences beyond that text.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17918
citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, bar on maintaining a court action while noncompliant
citations.quote: No person transacting business under a fictitious business name contrary to the provisions of this chapter, or his assignee, may maintain any action upon or on account of any contract made, or transaction had, in the fictitious business name in any court of this state until the fictitious business name statement has been executed, filed, and published as required by this chapter. For the purposes of this section, the failure to comply with subdivision (b) of Section 17917 does not constitute transacting business contrary to the provisions of this chapter.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17930
citations.cite: Fictitious Business Names, misdemeanor for a knowingly false statement
citations.quote: Any person who executes, files, or publishes any statement under this chapter, knowing that such statement is false, in whole or in part, shall be guilty of a misdemeanor and upon conviction thereof shall be punished by a fine not to exceed one thousand dollars ($1,000).

clauses.title: Background Information — Trustee's Notification to Beneficiaries and Heirs
clauses.body: I, {{trusteeName}}, am serving, or have been asked to serve, as trustee of {{trustName}}, executed {{originalTrustDate}}, following the death of {{decedentName}} on {{dateOfDeath}}. This information sheet describes California's statutory trustee-notification requirement as background in connection with {{trustName}}. My address as trustee, for purposes of any actual notification, is: {{trusteeAddress}}. This information sheet is not itself the notification a trustee must serve on a trust's beneficiaries and heirs under California Probate Code § 16061.7; preparing, reviewing, or signing it does not satisfy {{trusteeName}}'s notice obligation, if any, for {{trustName}} or for any other trust. Only actual service of a notification that satisfies § 16061.7's required content, service method, and timing does that.

clauses.title: The Statutory Duty to Notify, and the Three Events That Trigger It
clauses.body: A trustee's duty to serve the statutory notification described in this document arises only upon one of three specific events: (1) a revocable trust, or a portion of it, becomes irrevocable because of the death of one or more of its settlors, or becomes irrevocable within one year of a settlor's death because of a contingency related to that death; (2) there is a change of trustee of an irrevocable trust; or (3) a power of appointment a settlor retained becomes effective or lapses upon the settlor's death, for an inter vivos trust that was, or was purported to be, irrevocable when created — with an exception for a charitable remainder annuity trust or unitrust. Where {{trustName}} became irrevocable following {{decedentName}}'s death on {{dateOfDeath}}, that is an instance of the first event; the same statute imposes an identical duty for the other two events even when no settlor has just died. The duty to serve the notification belongs to the continuing or successor trustee of {{trustName}}, and if {{trustName}} has more than one trustee, any one cotrustee may serve it.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's trustee notification requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This document is informational: it does not itself satisfy any trustee's notice obligation for any specific trust — only actual, compliant service of the statutory notification does that. This corrects an assumption in the original research brief: the duty to notify is not triggered by a settlor's death alone. Section 16061.7(a) lists three independent triggering events, and only one of them — irrevocability caused by, or within one year of, a settlor's death — involves a settlor's death at all; a change of trustee of an already-irrevocable trust, or the lapse of a power of appointment retained over an irrevocable inter vivos trust, each independently triggers the same duty even where no settlor has just died. This clause cites a single statutory subdivision (§ 16061.7(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16061.7(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the trustee's duty to serve notification and its three triggering events
citations.quote: (a) A trustee shall serve a notification by the trustee as described in this section in the following events:(1) When a revocable trust or any portion thereof becomes irrevocable because of the death of one or more of the settlors of the trust, or because, by the express terms of the trust, the trust becomes irrevocable within one year of the death of a settlor because of a contingency related to the death of one or more of the settlors of the trust.(2) Whenever there is a change of trustee of an irrevocable trust.(3) Whenever a power of appointment retained by a settlor is effective or lapses upon death of the settlor with respect to an inter vivos trust which was, or was purported to be, irrevocable upon its creation. This paragraph shall not apply to a charitable remainder trust. For purposes of this paragraph, “charitable remainder trust” means a charitable remainder annuity trust or charitable remainder unitrust as defined in Section 664(d) of the Internal Revenue Code.(4) The duty to serve the notification by the trustee pursuant to this subdivision is the duty of the continuing or successor trustee, and any one cotrustee may serve the notification.

clauses.title: Who Must Receive the Notification — Beneficiaries, Heirs, and the Attorney General
clauses.body: The notification described in this document must be served on each beneficiary of the irrevocable trust or irrevocable portion of the trust (subject to the limitations of a separate Probate Code section governing notice to a person who may represent and bind another); on each heir of the deceased settlor, if the triggering event is a settlor's death or irrevocability within one year of it; and, if the trust is a charitable trust subject to the Attorney General's supervision, on the Attorney General. For determining who {{decedentName}}'s heirs are, a trustee may rely on any final judicial determination of heirship known to the trustee, and otherwise has discretion to make a good-faith determination by any reasonable means. A trustee need not provide the notification to a beneficiary or heir who is known to the trustee but cannot be located after reasonable diligence, or who is unknown to the trustee.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's trustee notification requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This document is informational: it does not itself satisfy any trustee's notice obligation for any specific trust, and it does not identify the actual beneficiaries or heirs of any specific decedent — only actual, compliant service of the statutory notification, addressed to the actual persons the statute requires, does that. This clause cites three different subdivisions of the same statutory section (§ 16061.7(b), (c), and (d)); no single subdivision is cited more than once in this clause. The beneficiary-notice requirement is itself made 'subject to the limitations of Section 15804' — a separate Probate Code section permitting certain persons (for example, a parent representing a minor beneficiary in specified circumstances) to receive notice on another person's behalf; this document does not independently quote or fully research that representation mechanism, and does not determine whether it applies to any specific beneficiary.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16061.7(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: who the notification must be served on
citations.quote: (b) The notification by the trustee required by subdivision (a) shall be served on each of the following:(1) Each beneficiary of the irrevocable trust or irrevocable portion of the trust, subject to the limitations of Section 15804.(2) Each heir of the deceased settlor, if the event that requires notification is the death of a settlor or irrevocability within one year of the death of the settlor of the trust by the express terms of the trust because of a contingency related to the death of a settlor.(3) If the trust is a charitable trust subject to the supervision of the Attorney General, to the Attorney General.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16061.7(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: how a trustee determines the heirs of a deceased settlor
citations.quote: (c) A trustee shall, for purposes of this section, rely upon any final judicial determination of heirship, known to the trustee, but the trustee shall have discretion to make a good faith determination by any reasonable means of the heirs of a deceased settlor in the absence of a final judicial determination of heirship known to the trustee.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16061.7(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the exception for a beneficiary or heir who cannot be located or is unknown
citations.quote: (d) The trustee need not provide a copy of the notification by trustee to any beneficiary or heir (1) known to the trustee but who cannot be located by the trustee after reasonable diligence or (2) unknown to the trustee.

clauses.title: The 60-Day Deadline to Serve the Notification, and How It Must Be Served
clauses.body: The notification described in this document — including any actual notification a trustee of {{trustName}} may need to serve — must be served by one of the methods a separate Probate Code section (§ 1215) authorizes, sent to the recipient's last known address. As a general rule, it must be served not later than 60 days following the occurrence of the event that requires it. A second, separate 60-day period applies only to a person entitled to the notification who was not known to the trustee when the triggering event occurred: for that person, the deadline instead runs 60 days from the date the trustee became aware of that person's existence. If there is a vacancy in the office of trustee on the date of the triggering event, or if that event itself causes the vacancy, the 60-day period does not begin to run until the date the new trustee commences to serve as trustee.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's trustee notification requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This document is informational: it does not itself serve any notification, and preparing it does not start, toll, or satisfy the 60-day deadline described here for any specific trust — only actual, compliant service of the statutory notification does that. This clause cites two different subdivisions of the same statutory section (§ 16061.7(e) and (f)); no single subdivision is cited more than once in this clause. This confirms the assumption in the original research brief that the deadline is commonly understood as 60 days: the statute's text sets that figure directly, both for the general case and for the previously-unknown-person exception, rather than deriving it by cross-reference to some other number of days.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16061.7(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the required method of service
citations.quote: (e) The notification by trustee shall be served by any of the methods described in Section 1215 to the last known address.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16061.7(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the 60-day deadline, its previously-unknown-person exception, and the trustee-vacancy rule
citations.quote: (f) The notification by trustee shall be served not later than 60 days following the occurrence of the event requiring service of the notification by trustee, or 60 days after the trustee became aware of the existence of a person entitled to receive notification by trustee, if that person was not known to the trustee on the occurrence of the event requiring service of the notification. If there is a vacancy in the office of the trustee on the date of the occurrence of the event requiring service of the notification by trustee, or if that event causes a vacancy, then the 60-day period for service of the notification by trustee commences on the date the new trustee commences to serve as trustee.

clauses.title: What the Notification Must Contain
clauses.body: California Probate Code § 16061.7(g) requires the notification described in this document to contain five specific items: the identity of the settlor or settlors of {{trustName}} and the date {{trustName}}'s instrument was executed; the name, address, and telephone number of each trustee of {{trustName}}, including {{trusteeName}} at {{trusteeAddress}}; the address of the physical location of {{trustName}}'s principal place of administration; any additional information the trust instrument itself expressly requires; and a notification that the recipient is entitled, upon reasonable request to the trustee, to receive from the trustee a true and complete copy of the terms of the trust.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's trustee notification requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This document is informational: it does not itself constitute a notification that satisfies § 16061.7(g) for any specific trust — only an actual notification containing all five required items, properly served, does that. This corrects an assumption in the original research brief: the statute's required-content list has five items, not the four the brief anticipated. Beyond settlor identity and the trust's date of execution, trustee name/address/telephone, and the reasonable-request entitlement to a full copy of the trust's terms, the statute also requires the address of the trust's principal place of administration and any additional information the trust instrument itself expressly requires. This clause cites a single statutory subdivision (§ 16061.7(g)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16061.7(g) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the five required contents of the notification
citations.quote: (g) The notification by trustee shall contain the following information:(1) The identity of the settlor or settlors of the trust and the date of execution of the trust instrument.(2) The name, address, and telephone number of each trustee of the trust.(3) The address of the physical location where the principal place of administration of the trust is located, pursuant to Section 17002.(4) Any additional information that may be expressly required by the terms of the trust instrument.(5) A notification that the recipient is entitled, upon reasonable request to the trustee, to receive from the trustee a true and complete copy of the terms of the trust.

clauses.title: Confidentiality of Trust Terms — Available on Request, Not Automatically Disclosed
clauses.body: Neither the notification described in this document nor the statute requiring it obligates a trustee to send a copy of {{trustName}}'s actual terms to every beneficiary or heir automatically. Instead, § 16061.7(g)(5) requires only that the notification tell the recipient that they are entitled, upon reasonable request to the trustee, to receive a true and complete copy of the terms of {{trustName}} from {{trusteeName}} — for example, if {{beneficiaryName}} makes that request. A separate statute governing a trustee's general reporting duty confirms the same 'on request' structure outside the notification context: on a beneficiary's reasonable request, a trustee must report to that beneficiary by providing information relating to the trust's administration that is relevant to the beneficiary's interest.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's trustee notification requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This document is informational: it does not itself notify anyone of anything, and it does not determine what any specific trust's terms say or who is entitled to see them — only an actual, compliant § 16061.7 notification, followed by the trustee's response (if any) to an actual reasonable request, does that. This clause quotes subdivision (g)(5) of Probate Code section 16061.7, already quoted in full as part of a separate clause of this document addressing all five required contents of the notification; it is repeated here, rather than only cross-referenced, because this clause makes a distinct point about that subdivision — that it authorizes withholding the trust's actual terms absent a request — that the required-contents clause does not itself draw out. The clause's second citation is to a different statutory section (§ 16061), not a repetition of § 16061.7.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16061.7(g)(5) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the recipient is entitled to a copy only upon reasonable request
citations.quote: (5) A notification that the recipient is entitled, upon reasonable request to the trustee, to receive from the trustee a true and complete copy of the terms of the trust.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16061 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the trustee's general duty to report on a beneficiary's reasonable request
citations.quote: Except as provided in Section 16069, on reasonable request by a beneficiary, the trustee shall report to the beneficiary by providing requested information to the beneficiary relating to the administration of the trust relevant to the beneficiary’s interest.

clauses.title: The Mandatory Contest Warning and the 120-Day Limitations Period It Describes
clauses.body: When the notification described in this document is served because a trust became irrevocable due to a settlor's death (or within one year of it, under a contingency tied to that death), § 16061.7(h) requires the notification to include a specific warning, set out in a separate paragraph in at least 10-point boldface type (or a reasonable equivalent), stating: 'You may not bring an action to contest the trust more than 120 days from the date this notification by the trustee is served upon you or 60 days from the date on which a copy of the terms of the trust is delivered to you during that 120-day period, whichever is later.' A separate statute, § 16061.8, makes that warning an accurate statement of law for a person actually served with the notification under this trigger: that person may not bring an action to contest the trust more than 120 days from the date the notification is served, or 60 days from the date a copy of the trust's terms is delivered during that 120-day period, whichever is later — and this rule applies whether the notification was served within or after the ordinary 60-day service deadline described elsewhere in this document.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's trustee notification requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This document is informational: it does not itself serve any notification and does not determine the limitations period applicable to any specific person's ability to contest any specific trust — only actual, compliant service of the statutory notification, described here, starts the period this clause addresses. This corrects an assumption in the original research brief: delivering a copy of the trust's terms along with, or shortly after, the notification does not shorten the 120-day period to 60 days. The statute takes 'whichever is later' of two figures — 120 days from service of the notification, or 60 days from delivery of a copy of the trust's terms during that 120-day period — so the period can only be extended beyond 120 days by a copy delivered late in that window; it is never cut below 120 days by delivering a copy sooner. This document does not resolve whether § 16061.8's 120-day bar applies to a person who is never served the notification at all: the statute's own text limits the bar to 'a person upon whom the notification by the trustee is served,' which on its face does not reach someone never served, but a search for a published California appellate decision confirming that reading returned a rate-limit error from the case-law search tool used for this research (CourtListener: '429 Rate limit exceeded, 125/day') rather than a completed search; that search was not repeated or worked around, and no case-law citation is offered on this specific point as a result. This clause cites two different statutory sections (§ 16061.7(h) and § 16061.8); no single section is cited more than once in this clause. Separately, § 16061.8's 120-day bar applies, by its own terms, only to a notification served under paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of § 16061.7 — the death-of-settlor trigger — not to a notification served because of a change of trustee or a lapsed power of appointment; this document does not address what limitations period, if any, applies to a contest following those other two triggers.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16061.7(h) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the required boldface contest-deadline warning
citations.quote: If the notification by the trustee is served because a revocable trust or any portion of it has become irrevocable because of the death of one or more settlors of the trust, or because, by the express terms of the trust, the trust becomes irrevocable within one year of the death of a settlor because of a contingency related to the death of one or more of the settlors of the trust, the notification by the trustee shall also include a warning, set out in a separate paragraph in not less than 10-point boldface type, or a reasonable equivalent thereof, that states as follows:“You may not bring an action to contest the trust more than 120 days from the date this notification by the trustee is served upon you or 60 days from the date on which a copy of the terms of the trust is delivered to you during that 120-day period, whichever is later.”

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16061.8 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the 120-day/60-day limitations period on contesting the trust
citations.quote: A person upon whom the notification by the trustee is served pursuant to paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 16061.7, whether the notice is served on the person within or after the time period set forth in subdivision (f) of Section 16061.7, shall not bring an action to contest the trust more than 120 days from the date the notification by the trustee is served upon the person, or 60 days from the date on which a copy of the terms of the trust is delivered pursuant to Section 1215 to the person during that 120-day period, whichever is later.

clauses.title: A Settlor Cannot Waive This Notice Requirement; a Trustee May Notify Additional Persons
clauses.body: Any waiver by a settlor of the requirement that a trustee serve the notification described in this document is against public policy and void — a settlor cannot use {{trustName}}'s own terms to excuse {{trusteeName}}, or any successor trustee, from this statutory duty. Separately, a trustee may serve the notification, in the form the statute requires, on any person in addition to those the statute requires it be served on, and is not liable to any person for serving, or for not serving, the notification on someone beyond that required group. The statute also does not require a trustee to serve a notification for a triggering event that occurred before January 1, 1998.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's trustee notification requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This document is informational: it does not itself waive, satisfy, or excuse any trustee's notice obligation for any specific trust — only actual, compliant service of the statutory notification does that, and this clause's own subject matter confirms that no provision of a trust instrument can lawfully excuse that obligation either. This clause cites two different subdivisions of the same statutory section (§ 16061.7(i) and (j)); no single subdivision is cited more than once in this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16061.7(i) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a settlor's waiver of the notice requirement is void
citations.quote: (i) Any waiver by a settlor of the requirement of serving the notification by trustee required by this section is against public policy and shall be void.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16061.7(j) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: optional notification to additional persons and the pre-1998 exception
citations.quote: (j) A trustee may serve a notification by trustee in the form required by this section on any person in addition to those on whom the notification by trustee is required to be served. A trustee is not liable to any person for serving or for not serving the notice on any person in addition to those on whom the notice is required to be served. A trustee is not required to serve a notification by trustee if the event that otherwise requires service of the notification by trustee occurs before January 1, 1998.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment Block — Trustee's Notification to Beneficiaries Information Sheet
