clauses.title: Information and Background — Alleged Public-Policy Termination
clauses.body: I, {{employeeName}}, am completing this information sheet in connection with the ending of my employment with {{companyName}}, which this document treats as having ended on {{terminationDate}}. The activity or report I believe may be legally protected is described here as: {{allegedProtectedActivity}}. The law, regulation, or public policy I believe may have been implicated is described here as: {{allegedPolicyViolated}}. This information sheet provides background for someone evaluating whether a termination may have violated public policy under California law. It is not a court filing, a demand letter, an employer policy, or a legal determination of any kind, and completing it does not establish, prove, or determine that {{employeeName}}'s termination by {{companyName}} violated any public policy, statute, or law, or that any claim described in this document is valid. Only a court, or another body with legal authority to decide the question, can determine whether a specific termination was unlawful.

clauses.title: California's At-Will Default — And Its Statutory Limits
clauses.body: California law presumes that employment with no specified term may be ended by either the employer or the employee at will, for any reason or no reason, on notice to the other. That default is not absolute: California has enacted specific statutes making it unlawful for an employer to end someone's employment, or take other adverse action against them, for defined reasons — including some of the reasons described elsewhere in this document.
clauses.gap: This is California's own general at-will statute, used here as real evidence of the default rule against which the statutory exceptions described in this document operate — not a claim about which state's law actually governs a specific employment relationship, and not a claim that any specific termination was, or was not, lawful. Beyond this statutory default, California courts have long recognized a separate, judicially created exception to at-will employment for termination that violates a fundamental public policy — commonly discussed under the case name Tameny v. Atlantic Richfield Co., 27 Cal.3d 167 (1980) — along with a multi-part test courts use to decide whether a particular policy is sufficiently "fundamental" to support that kind of claim, commonly discussed under cases including Gantt v. Sentry Insurance, 1 Cal.4th 1083 (1992), and Stevenson v. Superior Court, 16 Cal.4th 880 (1997). This research session's CourtListener case-law lookups returned a daily-rate-limit error on every attempt (across its search, endpoint, and item-lookup tools), and a direct fetch to courtlistener.com was separately blocked by this environment's network egress controls; as a result, this document does not state the holding of Tameny, the exact formulation of the fundamental-policy test, or any other case-law point as verified fact, and cites no case law for any of it. That is disclosed here as an honest gap rather than filled with an unverified citation. This clause cites a single statutory section (Labor Code § 2922); no additional independent source was sought for the at-will default itself. This document is informational: it does not itself determine that any specific termination violated public policy or that a wrongful termination occurred in this or any specific case.

clauses.title: Statutory Protection for Reporting a Suspected Legal Violation
clauses.body: California law prohibits an employer from making, adopting, or enforcing any rule, regulation, or policy that would prevent an employee from disclosing information to a government or law enforcement agency, to a person with authority over the employee, or to another employee with authority to investigate, discover, or correct a violation, where the employee has reasonable cause to believe the information discloses a violation of a state or federal statute, or a violation of or noncompliance with a local, state, or federal rule or regulation. Separately, the same statute prohibits an employer from retaliating against an employee for making that kind of disclosure, or because the employer believes the employee disclosed or may disclose that kind of information. This protection applies regardless of whether making the disclosure is part of the employee's own job duties.
clauses.gap: Both citations in this clause are to different subsections of the same statutory section — Labor Code § 1102.5(a) and § 1102.5(b), as amended effective January 1, 2024 — which is disclosed here explicitly rather than presented as two independent sources. This is California's own statute, used as real evidence of a specific, currently operative statutory anti-retaliation protection — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employment relationship, and not a claim that any particular disclosure actually qualifies for this protection or that any particular termination was retaliatory. Whether an employee in fact had "reasonable cause to believe" the disclosed information showed a legal violation, and whether the disclosure was actually made to one of the specific recipients this statute covers, are fact-specific questions this document does not resolve. This document is informational: it does not itself determine that a termination violated public policy or that a wrongful termination occurred in this or any specific case.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: An employer, or any person acting on behalf of the employer, shall not make, adopt, or enforce any rule, regulation, or policy preventing an employee from disclosing information to a government or law enforcement agency, to a person with authority over the employee, or to another employee who has authority to investigate, discover, or correct the violation or noncompliance, or from providing information to, or testifying before, any public body conducting an investigation, hearing, or inquiry, if the employee has reasonable cause to believe that the information discloses a violation of state or federal statute, or a violation of or noncompliance with a local, state, or federal rule or regulation, regardless of whether disclosing the information is part of the employee’s job duties.

clauses.title: Refusing to Break the Law, Protection Carried From a Prior Job, and Government-Employee Reports
clauses.body: The same statute also prohibits an employer from retaliating against an employee for refusing to participate in an activity that would violate a state or federal statute, or that would violate or fail to comply with a local, state, or federal rule or regulation. It separately prohibits retaliation against an employee for having exercised these same protections in a former job, not only the current one. And it specifically treats a report made by a government employee to their own employer as a covered disclosure under this statute.
clauses.gap: All three citations in this clause are to different subsections of the same statutory section — Labor Code § 1102.5(c), (d), and (e) — which is disclosed here explicitly rather than presented as independent sources. This is California's own statute, used as real evidence of the scope of this specific statutory protection — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employment relationship, and not a claim that any particular refusal, prior-job activity, or report actually falls within this statute's coverage in a specific case. This document is informational: it does not itself determine that a termination violated public policy or that a wrongful termination occurred in this or any specific case.

clauses.title: Civil Penalty and Attorney's Fees Under This Statute
clauses.body: In addition to any other available remedy, California law makes an employer who violates this statute liable for a civil penalty of up to $10,000 per employee for each violation, awarded to the employee who was retaliated against. In assessing the amount of that penalty, the Labor Commissioner considers the nature and seriousness of the violation, including the type of violation, the economic or mental harm suffered, and the chilling effect on the exercise of employment rights in the workplace. Separately, a court may award reasonable attorney's fees to a plaintiff who brings a successful lawsuit for a violation of this statute.
clauses.gap: All three citations in this clause are to different subdivisions of the same statutory section — Labor Code § 1102.5(f)(1), (f)(2), and (j) — which is disclosed here explicitly rather than presented as independent sources. This is California's own statute, used as real evidence of the specific civil-penalty and fee-shifting structure this particular statute carries — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employment relationship, and not a claim that any specific violation occurred or that any specific penalty or fee award would result. The $10,000 figure is a per-employee, per-violation cap the Labor Commissioner may assess after considering the listed factors; it is not an amount awarded automatically or in every case. This document is informational: it does not itself determine that a termination violated public policy or that a wrongful termination occurred in this or any specific case.

The Labor Commissioner’s consideration of the nature and seriousness of the violation shall include, but is not limited to, the type of violation, the economic or mental harm suffered, and the chilling effect on the exercise of employment rights in the workplace, and shall be considered to the extent evidence obtained during the investigation concerned any of these or other relevant factors.

citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: The court is authorized to award reasonable attorney’s fees to a plaintiff who brings a successful action for a violation of these provisions.

clauses.title: A Separate Statute Protecting Wage Claims and Labor Commissioner Complaints
clauses.body: A different California statute separately prohibits an employer from discharging an employee, or otherwise discriminating or retaliating against them, because the employee filed a bona fide complaint or claim relating to rights under the Labor Commissioner's jurisdiction, made a written or oral complaint that they are owed unpaid wages, or exercised certain other rights this statute covers. An employee retaliated against for one of these reasons is entitled to reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits, and if the employer's adverse action happens within 90 days of the protected activity, the law creates a rebuttable presumption in the employee's favor. This statute also carries its own civil penalty of up to $10,000 per employee for each violation.
clauses.gap: The citations in this clause are to different subdivisions of the same statutory section — Labor Code § 98.6(a), (b)(1), and (b)(3) — which is disclosed here explicitly rather than presented as independent sources. This is California's own statute, used as real evidence of a second, separate statutory anti-retaliation protection distinct from Labor Code § 1102.5 addressed elsewhere in this document — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employment relationship, and not a claim that any particular complaint or activity actually falls within this statute's coverage, or that any specific employer action was retaliatory. The 90-day presumption described here is rebuttable, not conclusive — an employer can offer a non-retaliatory explanation for its action within that window. This document is informational: it does not itself determine that a termination violated public policy or that a wrongful termination occurred in this or any specific case.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 98.6(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: A person shall not discharge an employee or in any manner discriminate, retaliate, or take any adverse action against any employee or applicant for employment because the employee or applicant engaged in any conduct delineated in this chapter, including the conduct described in subdivision (k) of Section 96, and Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 1101) of Part 3 of Division 2, or because the employee or applicant for employment has filed a bona fide complaint or claim or instituted or caused to be instituted any proceeding under or relating to their rights that are under the jurisdiction of the Labor Commissioner, made a written or oral complaint that they are owed unpaid wages, or because the employee has initiated any action or notice pursuant to Section 2699, or has testified or is about to testify in a proceeding pursuant to that section, or because of the exercise by the employee or applicant for employment on behalf of themselves or others of any rights afforded them.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 98.6(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Any employee who is discharged, threatened with discharge, demoted, suspended, retaliated against, subjected to an adverse action, or in any other manner discriminated against in the terms and conditions of their employment because the employee engaged in any conduct delineated in this chapter, including the conduct described in subdivision (k) of Section 96, and Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 1101) of Part 3 of Division 2, or because the employee has made a bona fide complaint or claim to the division pursuant to this part, or because the employee has initiated any action or notice pursuant to Section 2699 shall be entitled to reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by those acts of the employer. If an employer engages in any action prohibited by this section within 90 days of the protected activity specified in this section, there shall be a rebuttable presumption in favor of the employee’s claim.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 98.6(b)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: In addition to other remedies available, an employer who violates this section is liable for a civil penalty not exceeding ten thousand dollars ($10,000) per employee for each violation of this section, to be awarded to the employee or employees who suffered the violation.

clauses.title: A Different Kind of Filing Deadline — And What Wasn't Verified Here
clauses.body: Separately from the wage-claim and civil-penalty statutes described elsewhere in this document, California law sets a two-year filing deadline for an action for injury to, or the death of, an individual caused by the wrongful act or neglect of another — the general statute of limitations that applies to an ordinary personal-injury tort claim. This is a different kind of deadline, tied to a different kind of claim, than the wage-claim deadlines and statutory penalty provisions addressed elsewhere in this document.
clauses.gap: This is California's own general personal-injury tort statute of limitations, used here as real evidence of how California law structures an ordinary tort claim's filing deadline — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employment relationship, and not a claim that any specific termination was wrongful. Two related points this clause does not establish, and could not verify in this research session: first, whether a common-law wrongful-termination-in-violation-of-public-policy claim — the kind of claim this document is named for, commonly discussed under the case name Tameny v. Atlantic Richfield Co., 27 Cal.3d 167 (1980) — is treated by California courts as the kind of personal-injury tort this two-year deadline covers, as opposed to some other claim classification with a different deadline; second, whether such a claim is treated as carrying tort remedies (potentially including emotional-distress and punitive damages) as distinct from the narrower remedies available on a straightforward unpaid-wage claim. Both are case-law questions. CourtListener, the case-law research tool used throughout this research session, returned a daily-rate-limit error ("Rate limit exceeded: 125/day") on every attempt made during this session — across its search tool, its call_endpoint tool (tried against the clusters and courts endpoints), and its get_endpoint_item tool — and a direct fetch to courtlistener.com was separately blocked by this environment's network egress controls. As a result, no case law confirming either point was independently verified, and none is cited here; that is disclosed honestly as a gap rather than filled in with an unverified citation or an assumed holding. This clause cites a single statutory section (Code of Civil Procedure § 335.1); no additional independent source was sought for the general tort deadline itself. This document is informational: it does not itself determine that a termination violated public policy, that any wrongful-termination claim exists, or that any specific remedy would be available in this or any specific case.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 335.1 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure
citations.quote: Within two years: An action for assault, battery, or injury to, or for the death of, an individual caused by the wrongful act or neglect of another.

clauses.title: About This Wage Theft Prevention Act Notice Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes the written hiring-time notice that California Labor Code § 2810.5 requires many employers to give many new employees, in connection with {{companyName}}'s hiring of {{employeeName}} with a start date of {{startDate}}. It summarizes selected requirements of that statute: who the statute's notice duty reaches and does not reach, what categories of information the notice must contain, and the separate duty to notify an employee in writing of later changes to that information. It is not the Labor Commissioner's own "Notice to Employee" template, does not itself serve as the written notice the statute requires, and does not state, verify, or determine {{employeeName}}'s actual pay rate, payday, exempt or non-exempt status, or any other term of {{employeeName}}'s employment with {{companyName}}.

clauses.title: The Hiring-Time Written Notice Requirement
clauses.body: California law requires an employer to give each employee a written notice at the time of hiring, in the language the employer normally uses to communicate employment-related information to that employee, containing a specified list of categories of information. {{companyName}}'s hiring of {{employeeName}} falls within the timing this statute describes.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(1)), used as real evidence of California's hiring-time written-notice requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's actual situation. The statute's own definition of "employee" for this section excludes several categories of workers, described in a separate clause of this information sheet; this clause states only the general notice duty and does not by itself establish that any particular worker is or is not within the statute's coverage. This clause, and this document as a whole, is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific notice given (or not given) by any particular employer complied with Section 2810.5, and does not determine that any particular employer's practices are compliant or noncompliant with it.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, hiring-time written notice requirement
citations.quote: At the time of hiring, an employer shall provide to each employee a written notice, in the language the employer normally uses to communicate employment-related information to the employee, containing the following information:

clauses.title: Categories of Information the Notice Must Contain
clauses.body: The statute lists specific categories of information the hiring-time notice must contain, including the employee's rate or rates of pay and the basis for that rate (such as hourly, shift, day, week, salary, piece, or commission, including any overtime rate), any allowances claimed as part of the minimum wage, the regular payday, the employer's name (including any "doing business as" names), the employer's physical and mailing address, the employer's telephone number, the name, address, and telephone number of the employer's workers' compensation insurance carrier, specified information about paid sick leave rights, specified information about certain recent federal or state emergency or disaster declarations affecting the county of employment, and any other information the Labor Commissioner deems material and necessary.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(1)(A)-(J)), used as real evidence of what California's hiring-time notice must contain — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. All ten citations below are to subparagraphs (A) through (J) of a single statutory paragraph, Section 2810.5(a)(1); they are treated here as one source describing one list, not as independent corroborating sources. Two of these required categories — subparagraph (H), on paid sick leave rights, and subparagraph (I), on certain recent emergency or disaster declarations — are easy to omit from an informal summary of this statute because they were added by later amendments rather than appearing in the section's original 2011 enactment; this clause's drafter confirms both are present in the current, amended text quoted below. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific notice given (or not given) by any particular employer included every required category, and does not determine that any employer's practices are compliant or noncompliant with Section 2810.5.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(1)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, rate(s) of pay and basis
citations.quote: The rate or rates of pay and basis thereof, whether paid by the hour, shift, day, week, salary, piece, commission, or otherwise, including any rates for overtime, as applicable.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(1)(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, minimum-wage allowances
citations.quote: Allowances, if any, claimed as part of the minimum wage, including meal or lodging allowances.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(1)(C) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, regular payday
citations.quote: The regular payday designated by the employer in accordance with the requirements of this code.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(1)(D) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, employer name and DBAs
citations.quote: The name of the employer, including any “doing business as” names used by the employer.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(1)(E) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, employer physical and mailing address
citations.quote: The physical address of the employer’s main office or principal place of business, and a mailing address, if different.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(1)(F) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, employer telephone number
citations.quote: The telephone number of the employer.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(1)(G) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, workers' compensation carrier information
citations.quote: The name, address, and telephone number of the employer’s workers’ compensation insurance carrier.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(1)(H) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, paid sick leave rights
citations.quote: That an employee: may accrue and use sick leave; has a right to request and use accrued paid sick leave; may not be terminated or retaliated against for using or requesting the use of accrued paid sick leave; and has the right to file a complaint against an employer who retaliates.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(1)(I) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, emergency or disaster declaration disclosure
citations.quote: The existence of a federal or state emergency or disaster declaration applicable to the county or counties where the employee is to be employed, and that was issued within 30 days before the employee’s first day of employment, that may affect their health and safety during their employment.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(1)(J) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Labor Commissioner catch-all
citations.quote: Any other information the Labor Commissioner deems material and necessary.

clauses.title: Employees the Statute's Definition Excludes
clauses.body: For purposes of this notice requirement, the statute defines "employee" to exclude three categories of workers: an employee directly employed by the state or a political subdivision of the state (such as a city, county, city and county, or special district); an employee who is exempt from the payment of overtime wages by statute or by an Industrial Welfare Commission wage order; and an employee covered by a qualifying collective bargaining agreement that expressly provides for wages, hours, and working conditions and that meets specified premium overtime-pay and minimum regular-hourly-rate conditions set out in the statute.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 2810.5(c)), used as real evidence of which categories of workers this particular notice statute's own definition excludes — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that a collective-bargaining agreement covering any particular reader does or does not meet the specific premium-pay and minimum-rate conditions the statute sets out. All four citations below are to the introductory clause and paragraphs (1) through (3) of a single statutory subdivision, Section 2810.5(c); they are treated here as one source describing one exclusion list, not as independent corroborating sources. The third exclusion is narrower than a blanket exemption for any employee covered by any collective bargaining agreement: the statute requires the agreement itself to expressly address wages, hours, and working conditions, and to provide a premium overtime rate and a regular hourly rate at least 30 percent above the state minimum wage; this clause does not determine whether any specific collective bargaining agreement meets that test. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any particular individual worker falls inside or outside this statute's definition of "employee," and does not determine that any particular employer's notice practices are compliant or noncompliant with Section 2810.5.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, definition-of-employee introductory clause
citations.quote: For purposes of this section, “employee” does not include any of the following:

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, state and political-subdivision employees excluded
citations.quote: An employee directly employed by the state or any political subdivision thereof, including any city, county, city and county, or special district.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, overtime-exempt employees excluded
citations.quote: An employee who is exempt from the payment of overtime wages by statute or the wage orders of the Industrial Welfare Commission.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(c)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, qualifying collective-bargaining-agreement employees excluded
citations.quote: An employee who is covered by a valid collective bargaining agreement if the agreement expressly provides for the wages, hours of work, and working conditions of the employee, and if the agreement provides premium wage rates for all overtime hours worked and a regular hourly rate of pay for those employees of not less than 30 percent more than the state minimum wage.

clauses.title: Duty to Notify Employees in Writing of Later Changes
clauses.body: Separately from the hiring-time notice itself, the statute requires an employer to notify its employees in writing of any changes to the information set forth in the notice, within seven calendar days after the time of the change, unless the change is reflected on a timely wage statement furnished to the employee, or is provided in another writing the employer is otherwise required by law to give the employee within seven days of the change.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 2810.5(b)), used as real evidence of California's update-notice requirement and its two stated exceptions — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. All three citations below are to the introductory clause and paragraphs (1) and (2) of a single statutory subdivision, Section 2810.5(b); they are treated here as one source describing one requirement and its exceptions, not as independent corroborating sources. The seven-calendar-day period runs from the time of the change itself, not from when the employer discovers or acts on it, and the statute measures it in calendar days rather than business days. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific update notice given (or not given) by any particular employer, or any specific wage statement, satisfied this requirement, and does not determine that any employer's practices are compliant or noncompliant with Section 2810.5(b).

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, seven-day update notice requirement
citations.quote: An employer shall notify their employees in writing of any changes to the information set forth in the notice within seven calendar days after the time of the changes, unless one of the following applies:

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, timely-wage-statement exception
citations.quote: All changes are reflected on a timely wage statement furnished in accordance with Section 226.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, other-required-writing exception
citations.quote: Notice of all changes is provided in another writing required by law within seven days of the changes.

clauses.title: Labor Commissioner Template, and Additional Content for Temporary Services Employers
clauses.body: The statute directs the Labor Commissioner to prepare templates for the required hiring-time notice and to make those templates available to employers. Separately, if the employer is a "temporary services employer" as statutorily defined, the notice must also include the name, physical and mailing address, and telephone number of the client legal entity for which the employee will actually perform work, along with any other information the Labor Commissioner deems material and necessary — a requirement that itself does not apply to a security services company licensed by the Department of Consumer Affairs that solely provides security services.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(2) and (a)(3)), used as real evidence that a Labor Commissioner template exists and that temporary services employers face an additional content requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. Both citations below are to different paragraphs of the same statutory subdivision, Section 2810.5(a); they are treated here as one source describing two related administrative provisions, not as independent corroborating sources. This clause does not reproduce the Labor Commissioner's template itself and did not fetch or verify the template document's current content or web location; it relies only on the statutory text's own description that such a template must be prepared and made available. The statute also contains a further, separate content requirement for notices given to employees admitted under the federal H-2A agricultural visa program, in Section 2810.5(a)(4); that H-2A-specific provision is not quoted or summarized in this clause, an honest gap disclosed rather than covered. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any particular employer is or is not a "temporary services employer" as the statute defines that term, and does not determine that any employer's practices are compliant or noncompliant with Section 2810.5.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Labor Commissioner template requirement
citations.quote: The Labor Commissioner shall prepare templates for the required notices that comply with the requirements of paragraphs (1) and (4). The templates shall be made available to employers in a manner as determined by the Labor Commissioner, and as set forth in subdivision (d).

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.5(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, temporary services employer additional content
citations.quote: If the employer is a temporary services employer, as defined in Section 201.3, the notice described in paragraph (1) shall also include the name, the physical address of the main office, the mailing address if different from the physical address of the main office, and the telephone number of the legal entity for whom the employee will perform work, and any other information the Labor Commissioner deems material and necessary.

clauses.title: No Penalty Provision Specific to This Section Found in Its Own Text
clauses.body: The text of Labor Code § 2810.5 itself, in subdivisions (a) through (d), does not state a civil penalty, fine, or other sanction tied specifically to an employer's failure to provide the hiring-time notice or the update notice the section describes. Two other California Labor Code sections that create civil penalties for related pay-practice failures — Section 1197.1, addressing paying an employee less than the applicable minimum wage, and Section 226.3, addressing failure to provide a compliant itemized wage statement or to keep required payroll records — do not, in their current codified text, name Section 2810.5 or its hiring-time or update-notice requirements.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory text, used as real evidence that these three specific sections do not on their face state a penalty tied to Section 2810.5 — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that no California law of any kind provides any consequence for a failure to give this notice. This clause's drafter checked only these three sections (2810.5 itself, 1197.1, and 226.3) directly against their current statutory text; it did not exhaustively check every other Labor Code provision that could conceivably bear on enforcement, such as the Labor Commissioner's general citation and hearing authority under Section 98, or a representative action under the Labor Code Private Attorneys General Act — an honest gap, disclosed rather than resolved by assumption. An absence found across three checked sections is evidence of an absence, not proof that no enforcement mechanism exists anywhere in California law for a Section 2810.5 violation. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any particular employer's failure (or compliance) has any particular legal consequence, and does not determine that any employer's practices are compliant or noncompliant with Section 2810.5.

citations.quote: Any employer or other person acting either individually or as an officer, agent, or employee of another person, who pays or causes to be paid to any employee a wage less than the minimum fixed by an applicable state or local law, or by an order of the commission, shall be subject to a civil penalty, restitution of wages, liquidated damages payable to the employee, and any applicable penalties imposed pursuant to Section 203 as follows:

clauses.title: Foreign Qualification Information Sheet — Purpose and Scope
clauses.body: This information sheet relates to {{companyName}}, a {{entityType}} originally formed under the law of {{stateOfFormation}}, with a principal office at {{principalOfficeAddress}}. It describes California's statutory requirement that an out-of-state ("foreign") corporation or limited liability company register with the California Secretary of State before transacting intrastate business in California, along with the meaning of that phrase and the consequences California law attaches to transacting business here without first registering. This document is not this project's LLC Articles of Organization, Articles of Incorporation, or Statement of Information document. Those documents concern an entity being formed under California law in the first place, or an already-California-qualified entity's periodic reporting to the Secretary of State after formation or qualification. This document instead concerns an entity formed under the law of another state or jurisdiction that is separately registering to transact business in California without becoming a California entity. California maintains two distinct statutory frameworks for this registration, one in the General Corporation Law for foreign corporations and one in the California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act for foreign limited liability companies; this document addresses both. This information sheet is educational only. It does not itself register {{companyName}}, or any other entity, with the California Secretary of State, and it does not determine whether {{companyName}}'s specific activities in California do or do not constitute "transacting intrastate business" within the meaning of California law.

clauses.title: Requirement for a Foreign Corporation to Obtain a Certificate of Qualification
clauses.body: California's General Corporation Law states that a foreign corporation shall not transact intrastate business in California without first having obtained a certificate of qualification from the Secretary of State. That certificate is obtained by filing a statement and designation by foreign corporation, on a form the Secretary of State prescribes, signed by a corporate officer or, for a foreign association that has no officers, by a trustee. This filing requirement applies to a corporation formed under the law of another U.S. state, another country, or any jurisdiction other than California, once that corporation is transacting intrastate business in California, a term California law defines separately.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's foreign-corporation qualification requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific corporation's obligations; other states impose their own, differently worded foreign-qualification requirements. This clause quotes a single subsection, Cal. Corp. Code § 2105(a), so no same-section multiple-subsection issue arises here. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself obtain a certificate of qualification or file the statement and designation described here on behalf of any entity, and it does not determine whether any specific corporation's activities in California constitute "transacting intrastate business."

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2105(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, Chapter 21 (Foreign Corporations), certificate-of-qualification requirement
citations.quote: A foreign corporation shall not transact intrastate business without having first obtained from the Secretary of State a certificate of qualification. To obtain that certificate it shall file, on a form prescribed by the Secretary of State, a statement and designation signed by a corporate officer or, in the case of a foreign association that has no officers, signed by a trustee stating:

clauses.title: Required Content of a Foreign Corporation's Statement and Designation
clauses.body: The statement and designation a foreign corporation files to obtain its certificate of qualification must state: the corporation's name (and, if that name does not comply with California's naming rules, an alternate name adopted for use in California); the state or place of its incorporation and a statement that it is authorized to exercise its powers and privileges there; the street address of its principal office; the street address of its principal office in California, if it has one; its mailing address, if different from those addresses; and the name of an agent in California upon whom process directed to the corporation may be served. California also requires the statement and designation to include the corporation's irrevocable consent to service of process on that designated agent, and on the Secretary of State if the agent cannot be found, and a disclosure if the corporation will be subject to the Insurance Code as an insurer. Separately, the corporation must annex to the statement and designation a certificate from an authorized public official of its state or place of incorporation confirming that it is an existing corporation in good standing there.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's foreign-corporation application requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific corporation's obligations; other states impose their own, differently worded application requirements. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 2105(a) for the content of the statement and designation itself and § 2105(b) for the annexed certificate of good standing, and treats them as one source, not as two independent corroborating sources. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself prepare, sign, or file the statement and designation described here on behalf of any entity, and it does not determine whether any specific corporation's activities in California constitute "transacting intrastate business."

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2105(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, content required in a foreign corporation's statement and designation
citations.quote: (1) The name of the corporation, and, if the name does not comply with Section 201, an alternate name adopted pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 2106. (2) The state or place of its incorporation or organization and a statement that the foreign corporation is authorized to exercise its powers and privileges in that state or place of its incorporation or organization. (3) The street address of its principal office. (4) The street address of its principal office in California, if any. (5) The mailing address of its principal office, if different from the addresses specified pursuant to paragraphs (3) and (4). (6) The name of an agent upon whom process directed to the corporation may be served within this state.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2105(b)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, annexed certificate of good standing requirement
citations.quote: (b) Annexed to the statement and designation shall be a certificate by an authorized public official of the state or place of incorporation of the corporation to the effect that the corporation is an existing corporation in good standing in that state or place or, in the case of an association, an officers’ certificate stating that it is a validly organized and existing business association under the laws of a specified foreign jurisdiction.

clauses.title: Statutory Definition of "Transacting Intrastate Business"
clauses.body: California defines "transacting intrastate business" separately for foreign corporations and for foreign limited liability companies, in near-identical terms. For a foreign corporation, and only for purposes of the chapter of the General Corporation Law governing foreign corporations, "transact intrastate business" means entering into repeated and successive transactions of the corporation's business in California, other than interstate or foreign commerce. For a foreign limited liability company, and only within the meaning of the article of the Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act governing foreign limited liability companies, a company that enters into repeated and successive transactions of business in California, other than in interstate or foreign commerce, is considered to be transacting intrastate business. Under both definitions, a single or isolated transaction, and business conducted across state lines rather than within California, are treated differently from a repeated, ongoing pattern of business conducted within the state.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California defines this term for its own foreign-qualification statutes — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific entity's activities, and not a claim that other states, or other California statutes, use this identical definition. This clause cites two different statutory sections, not subsections of one section: Cal. Corp. Code § 191(a) defines the term for foreign corporations, and Cal. Corp. Code § 17708.03(a) defines it, in separately worded but substantively similar terms, for foreign limited liability companies. These are treated as two independent, entity-type-specific sources, not as one source standing in for the other. This information sheet is informational only: it does not determine whether any specific entity's activities in California constitute "transacting intrastate business" under either definition.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 191(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, statutory definition of "transact intrastate business" for foreign corporations
citations.quote: (a) For the purposes of Chapter 21 (commencing with Section 2100), “transact intrastate business” means entering into repeated and successive transactions of its business in this state, other than interstate or foreign commerce.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17708.03(a)

citations.quote: (a) A foreign limited liability company that enters into repeated and successive transactions of business in this state, other than in interstate or foreign commerce, is considered to be transacting intrastate business in this state within the meaning of this article.

clauses.title: Activities That Do Not Constitute Transacting Intrastate Business
clauses.body: California's statutes list specific activities that, without excluding other activities that might also fall outside the definition, do not by themselves make a foreign corporation or foreign limited liability company one that is "transacting intrastate business" in California. For a foreign corporation, that list covers: maintaining or defending any action, suit, or administrative or arbitration proceeding, or settling claims or disputes; holding board or shareholder meetings or otherwise carrying on activities concerning its internal affairs; maintaining bank accounts; maintaining offices or agencies for the transfer, exchange, and registration of its own securities; effecting sales through independent contractors; soliciting or procuring orders that require acceptance outside California before becoming binding contracts; creating evidences of debt or liens or security interests on property; and conducting a single, isolated transaction completed within 180 days that is not part of a number of repeated transactions of a similar nature. The parallel list for a foreign limited liability company is substantively similar and adds two further items not listed for corporations: securing or collecting debts or enforcing security interests in property securing those debts, and transacting business in interstate commerce. Separately, both statutes state that merely holding a status — being a shareholder of a corporation, a limited partner of a limited partnership, or a member or manager of a limited liability company that itself transacts intrastate business — does not, by itself, make the shareholder, partner, member, or manager a transactor of intrastate business.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own carve-out list for this term — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific entity's activities, and not a claim that any other jurisdiction recognizes the same carve-outs. This clause cites two different statutory sections, not subsections of one section: Cal. Corp. Code § 191(c) lists the carve-out activities for foreign corporations, and Cal. Corp. Code § 17708.03(b) lists the separately worded, substantially parallel carve-out activities for foreign limited liability companies; they are treated as two independent, entity-type-specific sources. Each statute also states expressly that its list does not exclude other activities that may likewise fall outside the definition, so an activity's absence from this list does not mean it constitutes transacting intrastate business. This information sheet is informational only: it does not determine whether any specific entity's specific activities in California fall within or outside this carve-out list.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, activities that do not constitute transacting intrastate business for foreign corporations
citations.quote: (c) Without excluding other activities that may not constitute transacting intrastate business, a foreign corporation shall not be considered to be transacting intrastate business within the meaning of subdivision (a) solely by reason of carrying on in this state any one or more of the following activities: (1) Maintaining or defending any action or suit or any administrative or arbitration proceeding, or effecting the settlement thereof or the settlement of claims or disputes. (2) Holding meetings of its board or shareholders or carrying on other activities concerning its internal affairs. (3) Maintaining bank accounts. (4) Maintaining offices or agencies for the transfer, exchange, and registration of its securities or depositaries with relation to its securities. (5) Effecting sales through independent contractors. (6) Soliciting or procuring orders, whether by mail or through employees or agents or otherwise, where those orders require acceptance outside this state before becoming binding contracts. (7) Creating evidences of debt or mortgages, liens or security interests on real or personal property. (8) Conducting an isolated transaction completed within a period of 180 days and not in the course of a number of repeated transactions of like nature.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17708.03(b)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, parallel activities list for foreign limited liability companies
citations.quote: (b) Without excluding other activities that may not be considered to be transacting intrastate business in this state within the meaning of this article, activities of a foreign limited liability company that do not constitute transacting intrastate business in this state include all of the following: (1) Maintaining or defending any action or suit or any administrative or arbitration proceeding, or effecting the settlement of those, or the settlement of claims or disputes. (2) Carrying on any activity concerning its internal affairs, including holding meetings of its members or managers. (3) Maintaining accounts in financial institutions. (4) Maintaining offices or agencies for the transfer, exchange, and registration of the limited liability company’s own securities or maintaining trustees or depositories with respect to those securities. (5) Selling through independent contractors. (6) Soliciting or procuring orders, whether by mail or electronic means or through employees or agents or otherwise, if the orders require acceptance outside this state before they become contracts. (7) Creating or acquiring indebtedness, evidences of indebtedness, mortgages, liens, or security interests in real or personal property. (8) Securing or collecting debts or enforcing mortgages or other security interests in property securing the debts and holding, protecting, or maintaining property so acquired. (9) Conducting an isolated transaction that is completed within 180 days and is not in the course of a number of repeated transactions of a like nature. (10) Transacting business in interstate commerce.

clauses.title: Required Content of a Foreign LLC's Application for Certificate of Registration
clauses.body: A foreign limited liability company registers to transact business in California by delivering an application for a certificate of registration to the Secretary of State, on a form the Secretary of State prescribes. The application must state: the company's name (and, if that name does not comply with California's naming rules, an alternate name adopted for use in California); the state or other jurisdiction under whose law the company is organized and a statement that it is authorized to exercise its powers and privileges there; and the street address of the company's principal office, and of its principal office in California, if it has one. California's Limited Liability Company Act does not, at this section, contain a single sentence stating outright that a foreign LLC "shall not" transact intrastate business without registering, the way the corporation statute does; instead, the obligation to register functions through the application requirements described here together with the litigation-related and injunctive consequences described elsewhere in this document. Separately, the company must deliver with its application a certificate of existence, status, or good standing (or a record of similar import), issued within the past six months, from the official who has custody of its public records in its home jurisdiction. California law also makes clear that receiving a certificate of registration does not authorize a foreign limited liability company to engage in any business, or exercise any power, that a California limited liability company itself could not engage in or exercise here.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's foreign-LLC application requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific limited liability company's obligations; other states impose their own, differently worded application requirements. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 17708.02(a) for the content of the application and § 17708.02(b) for the accompanying certificate of existence or good standing, and treats them as one source, not as two independent corroborating sources; it separately cites Cal. Corp. Code § 17708.01(c), a different section, for the limited scope of what a certificate of registration authorizes. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself prepare or file the application described here on behalf of any entity, and it does not determine whether any specific limited liability company's activities in California constitute "transacting intrastate business."

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17708.02(a)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, content required in a foreign LLC's application for a certificate of registration
citations.quote: (a) A foreign limited liability company may apply for a certificate of registration to transact business in this state by delivering an application to the Secretary of State for filing on a form prescribed by the Secretary of State. The application shall state all of the following: (1) The name of the foreign limited liability company, and, if the name does not comply with Section 17701.08, an alternate name adopted pursuant to subdivision (a) of Section 17708.05. (2) The state or other jurisdiction under whose law the foreign limited liability company is organized and a statement that the foreign limited liability company is authorized to exercise its powers and privileges in that state or other jurisdiction. (3) The street address of the foreign limited liability company’s principal office and of its principal office in California, if any.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17708.02(b)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, certificate of existence or good standing requirement
citations.quote: (b) A foreign limited liability company shall deliver with a completed application under subdivision (a) a certificate of existence, status, or good standing or a record of similar import, issued within the past six months from the submission of the application for filing in California, signed by the Secretary of State or other official having custody of the foreign limited liability company’s publicly filed records in the state or other jurisdiction under whose law the foreign limited liability company is formed.

citations.quote: (c) A certificate of registration does not authorize a foreign limited liability company to engage in any business or exercise any power that a limited liability company shall not engage in or exercise in this state.

clauses.title: Consequences for a Foreign Corporation Transacting Business Without Qualifying
clauses.body: California law attaches several distinct consequences to a foreign corporation transacting intrastate business without holding a valid certificate of qualification. First, the corporation may be subject to a civil penalty of $20 for each day that unauthorized intrastate business is transacted, and by transacting that unauthorized business, the corporation is deemed to consent to the jurisdiction of California's courts in any civil action arising in California in which it is named a defendant. Second, and separately, a corporation that transacts intrastate business without complying with the certificate-of-qualification requirement is barred from maintaining any action or proceeding, in a California court, upon the intrastate business it transacted — but only for an action or proceeding commenced before it complies. That bar lifts once the corporation has complied with the qualification requirement, paid a $250 penalty to the Secretary of State (in addition to the filing fees otherwise due), and filed with the court receipts showing payment of that penalty, those fees, and any franchise or other taxes on business or property that should have been paid for the period it transacted business unqualified. The statute barring the corporation from maintaining an action does not, by its terms, prevent other parties from suing the unqualified corporation, and does not state that the underlying business the corporation transacted is void or unenforceable — only that the corporation itself cannot affirmatively maintain an action on it until it complies. Third, transacting intrastate business without complying with the qualification requirement is separately a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of not less than $500 and not more than $1,000, prosecuted by the Attorney General or a district attorney.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own consequences for a foreign corporation's noncompliance — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific corporation's obligations, and not a claim that other states attach the same consequences to the same conduct. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 2203(a) for the per-day penalty and deemed consent to jurisdiction, and § 2203(c) for the bar on maintaining an action until compliance, and treats them as one source, not as two independent corroborating sources; it separately cites Cal. Corp. Code § 2258, a different section in a different chapter, for the misdemeanor criminal penalty. This information sheet is informational only: it does not determine whether any specific corporation has transacted intrastate business without a certificate of qualification, or what penalty, if any, would apply to any specific corporation's conduct.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2203(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, per-day monetary penalty and deemed consent to California court jurisdiction
citations.quote: (a) Any foreign corporation which transacts intrastate business and which does not hold a valid certificate from the Secretary of State may be subject to a penalty of twenty dollars ($20) for each day that unauthorized intrastate business is transacted; and the foreign corporation, by transacting unauthorized intrastate business, shall be deemed to consent to the jurisdiction of the courts of California in any civil action arising in this state in which the corporation is named a party defendant.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2203(c)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, bar on maintaining an action until compliance
citations.quote: (c) A foreign corporation subject to the provisions of Chapter 21 (commencing with Section 2100) which transacts intrastate business without complying with Section 2105 shall not maintain any action or proceeding upon any intrastate business so transacted in any court of this state, commenced prior to compliance with Section 2105, until it has complied with the provisions thereof and has paid to the Secretary of State a penalty of two hundred fifty dollars ($250) in addition to the fees due for filing the statement and designation required by Section 2105 and has filed with the clerk of the court in which the action is pending receipts showing the payment of the fees and penalty and all franchise taxes and any other taxes on business or property in this state that should have been paid for the period during which it transacted intrastate business.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, misdemeanor criminal penalty for transacting business without complying with Chapter 21
citations.quote: Any foreign corporation subject to the provisions of Chapter 21 which transacts intrastate business without complying therewith is guilty of a misdemeanor, punishable by fine of not less than five hundred dollars ($500) nor more than one thousand dollars ($1,000), to be recovered in any court of competent jurisdiction.

clauses.title: Consequences for a Foreign LLC Transacting Business Without Registering
clauses.body: California's Limited Liability Company Act attaches its own set of consequences to a foreign limited liability company transacting intrastate business without a certificate of registration, and those consequences are not identical to the corporation statute's. A foreign limited liability company transacting intrastate business in California may not maintain an action or proceeding in California unless it holds a certificate of registration — but lacking a certificate does not prevent the company from defending an action or proceeding brought against it. The statute also states expressly that a member or manager of the company is not personally liable for the company's debts, obligations, or other liabilities solely because the company transacted intrastate business without a certificate of registration. And if the company transacts intrastate business without a certificate, or cancels a certificate it previously held, it is deemed to have appointed the Secretary of State as its agent for service of process for rights of action arising out of that intrastate business. Unlike the corporation statute, this article does not itself set out a specific per-day or fixed-dollar civil penalty, or a separate misdemeanor criminal penalty, for a foreign limited liability company that transacts intrastate business without registering. It does, however, give the Attorney General a separate enforcement tool: the Attorney General may bring an action to enjoin a foreign limited liability company from transacting intrastate business in California in violation of the Act.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own consequences for a foreign LLC's noncompliance — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific limited liability company's obligations, and not a claim that other states attach the same consequences to the same conduct. This clause cites four subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 17708.07(a) through (d), and treats them as one source, not as four independent corroborating sources; it separately cites Cal. Corp. Code § 17708.09, a different section, for the Attorney General's injunctive remedy. The observation that this article does not itself set out a per-day or fixed-dollar civil penalty, or a criminal penalty, parallel to the corporation statute's is a statement about the absence of such a provision in the specific sections reviewed for this document, not a survey of every provision anywhere in California law that could conceivably apply to an unregistered foreign LLC's conduct. This information sheet is informational only: it does not determine whether any specific limited liability company has transacted intrastate business without a certificate of registration, or what consequence, if any, would apply to any specific company's conduct.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17708.07(a)-(d)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, consequences of transacting intrastate business without a certificate of registration
citations.quote: (a) A foreign limited liability company transacting intrastate business in this state shall not maintain an action or proceeding in this state unless it has a certificate of registration to transact intrastate business in this state. (b) The failure of a foreign limited liability company to have a certificate of registration to transact intrastate business in this state does not prevent the foreign limited liability company from defending an action or proceeding in this state. (c) A member or manager of a foreign limited liability company is not liable for the debts, obligations, or other liabilities of the foreign limited liability company solely because the foreign limited liability company transacted intrastate business in this state without a certificate of registration. (d) If a foreign limited liability company transacts intrastate business in this state without a certificate of registration or cancels its certificate of registration, it shall be deemed to have appointed the Secretary of State as its agent for service of process for rights of action arising out of the transaction of intrastate business in this state.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17708.09
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, Attorney General's authority to enjoin unauthorized intrastate business
citations.quote: The Attorney General may maintain an action to enjoin a foreign limited liability company from transacting intrastate business in this state in violation of this title.

clauses.body: Author/copyright claimant: {{claimantName}}. Title of the work: {{workTitle}}. Description of the work: {{workDescription}}. Date the work was created (completed): {{creationDate}}. Date of first publication, if the work has been published: {{firstPublicationDate}}. clauses.title: What Copyright Protects, and the Idea/Expression Distinction
clauses.body: Federal copyright law defines what copyright protects, and where that protection stops, in a single statutory provision. Under 17 U.S.C. § 102(a), copyright protection "subsists, in accordance with this title, in original works of authorship fixed in any tangible medium of expression, now known or later developed, from which they can be perceived, reproduced, or otherwise communicated, either directly or with the aid of a machine or device," and the statute lists eight illustrative categories, including literary, musical, dramatic, choreographic, pictorial/graphic/sculptural, audiovisual, sound-recording, and architectural works. The same section immediately limits that protection: under § 102(b), "[i]n no case does copyright protection for an original work of authorship extend to any idea, procedure, process, system, method of operation, concept, principle, or discovery, regardless of the form in which it is described, explained, illustrated, or embodied in such work." Copyright can accordingly protect the particular expression fixed in a work — the specific words, images, or sounds an author actually created — without protecting the underlying idea, method, system, or discovery that expression describes, no matter how that idea or method is written down. The work identified in this document, {{workTitle}}, is described here as: {{workDescription}}.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of what 17 U.S.C. § 102 protects and where its idea/expression line falls — not a claim about whether the work identified in this document is in particular original, fixed in a tangible medium of expression, or otherwise qualifies for copyright protection, and not a claim about which specific elements of that work, if any, are unprotectable idea, procedure, process, system, method of operation, concept, principle, or discovery under § 102(b). This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, § 102(a) and § 102(b); they are treated here as one source describing one integrated statutory scheme, not as two independent corroborating sources. This document is informational only: it does not itself register any copyright with the U.S. Copyright Office, does not determine that the work identified in this document or any other work is protectable subject matter, and does not determine the term of protection for any specific work.

citations.quote: Copyright protection subsists, in accordance with this title, in original works of authorship fixed in any tangible medium of expression, now known or later developed, from which they can be perceived, reproduced, or otherwise communicated, either directly or with the aid of a machine or device.

clauses.title: The Basic Term of Copyright Protection
clauses.body: Federal copyright law fixes the basic term of protection based on when a work was created and, for certain categories, on how the work is attributed rather than on who the individual human author is. Under 17 U.S.C. § 302(a), for a work created on or after January 1, 1978, copyright "subsists from its creation and, except as provided by the following subsections, endures for a term consisting of the life of the author and 70 years after the author's death." A joint work created by co-authors who did not work for hire instead runs for the life of the last surviving co-author plus 70 years, under § 302(b). A different, fixed-duration rule applies to three specific categories the statute treats alike: under § 302(c), "[i]n the case of an anonymous work, a pseudonymous work, or a work made for hire, the copyright endures for a term of 95 years from the year of its first publication, or a term of 120 years from the year of its creation, whichever expires first." Which of these rules actually measures the term of a given work's copyright turns on how that work is attributed and, for a work made for hire, on whether it in fact qualifies as one under the statutory definition of that term — a categorization this document does not make for {{workTitle}}.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of how 17 U.S.C. § 302 measures the basic term of copyright — not a claim about how long copyright protection actually lasts for the work identified in this document specifically, which the term-measuring facts (the identity and death dates of any human author, whether the work is anonymous or pseudonymous, and whether it in fact qualifies as a work made for hire under the statute's own definition of that term) would have to establish. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, § 302(a) and § 302(c); they are treated here as one source describing one integrated statutory scheme, not as two independent corroborating sources. (§ 302(b)'s joint-work rule is described narratively above without a separate quotation, for the same reason.) § 302 also contains additional subsections on recording an author's date of death and a resulting presumption of death after 95/120 years, which this clause does not address because they concern proving the term's endpoint rather than stating the term itself. This document is informational only: it does not itself register any copyright, does not determine that the work identified in this document or any other work is protectable, and does not determine the term of protection that actually applies to that work or any other specific work.

clauses.title: Registration Is Optional, Not a Condition of Copyright Protection
clauses.body: Federal law makes registering a copyright with the U.S. Copyright Office optional, not a prerequisite to copyright existing in the first place. Under 17 U.S.C. § 408(a), the owner of copyright in a work "may obtain registration of the copyright claim" at any time during the copyright's subsistence, by delivering the required deposit, application, and fee to the Copyright Office — and the statute states directly that "[s]uch registration is not a condition of copyright protection." Copyright itself arises automatically, under the originality and fixation rules described elsewhere in this document, the moment an eligible work is created and fixed in a tangible medium; registering it with the Copyright Office afterward is a separate, optional step, taken (or not taken) for reasons — including the benefits and deadlines described in the other clauses of this document — that are independent of whether the copyright itself exists.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence that registration under 17 U.S.C. § 408(a) is optional rather than a condition of copyright's existence — not a claim about whether the work identified in this document in fact qualifies for copyright protection, or about whether registering it would be advisable. This clause cites a single statutory subsection, § 408(a); no additional independent source was located for this specific point. This document is informational only: it does not itself register any copyright with the U.S. Copyright Office, does not determine that the work identified in this document or any other work is protectable, and does not determine the term of protection for any specific work.

clauses.title: Deposit and Application Requirements for Registration
clauses.body: Registering a copyright requires delivering specific physical or digital material to the Copyright Office, not just completing a form. Under 17 U.S.C. § 408(b), the material that must be deposited for registration depends on the work's publication status: "the material deposited for registration shall include" — for an unpublished work, one complete copy or phonorecord; for a published work, two complete copies or phonorecords of the best edition; for a work first published outside the United States, one complete copy or phonorecord as so published; and for a contribution to a collective work, one complete copy or phonorecord of the best edition of the collective work. This deposit requirement applies in addition to the application and fee that § 408(a) separately requires before the Copyright Office will register a claim. The Register of Copyrights is separately authorized to adjust these default deposit requirements by regulation for particular administrative classes of works.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the deposit categories 17 U.S.C. § 408(b) sets by default — not a claim about what deposit the work identified in this document specifically would require, which depends on facts (whether and where it has been published, and whether it falls into an administrative class for which the Register of Copyrights has adopted different deposit regulations under § 408(c)) this document does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory subsection, § 408(b); it does not independently verify the optional-deposit regulations authorized under § 408(c), the correction procedure under § 408(d), or the preregistration procedure under § 408(f), each of which is a related but separate part of the same section. This document is informational only: it does not itself register any copyright, does not deposit any copy of the work identified in this document with the Copyright Office, and does not determine the term of protection for any specific work.
