clauses.title: Introduction and Scope
clauses.body:
This information sheet describes California's statewide Tenant Protection Act of 2019 (AB 1482), which consists of two related but separate statutory requirements that apply to many, but not all, California residential tenancies: a cap on how much rent may be increased over a 12-month period (Civil Code section 1947.12), and a requirement that a landlord have "just cause," stated in the written termination notice itself, before ending certain tenancies (Civil Code section 1946.2). It concerns the property commonly known as {{propertyAddress}}, the tenancy of {{tenantName}}, and the landlord {{landlordName}}. If a current monthly rent figure is relevant, it is stated here as: {{monthlyRent}}.

This document is distinct from a specific eviction notice -- such as a three-day notice to pay rent or quit for nonpayment, or a three-day notice to perform covenant or quit for another lease violation -- and describes instead the broader statewide statutory framework of occupancy thresholds, just-cause categories, rent-increase limits, and exemptions within which those specific notices operate. This information sheet does not itself determine whether this or any other specific tenancy is covered by, or exempt from, the statewide rent cap or the statewide just-cause requirement, and it does not calculate the legality of any specific rent increase or termination.

clauses.title: The 12-Month Occupancy Threshold and What "Just Cause" Means
clauses.body: California's Tenant Protection Act sets an occupancy-based threshold before its just-cause requirement attaches to a residential tenancy, and then defines just cause as one of two statutory categories. Once a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a unit for 12 months, the landlord may not terminate the tenancy without just cause stated in the written termination notice. If an additional adult tenant is added to the lease before an existing tenant reaches that 12-month mark, the threshold instead requires either that all tenants have occupied the unit for 12 months or more, or that at least one tenant has occupied it for 24 months or more. The statute defines "just cause" as being either "at-fault just cause" or "no-fault just cause," each broken into specific, enumerated grounds addressed in other clauses of this document. As currently enacted, this just-cause requirement is scheduled to expire and be repealed on January 1, 2030.

citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other law, after a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy. If any additional adult tenants are added to the lease before an existing tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied the residential real property for 24 months, then this subdivision shall only apply if either of the following are satisfied: (1) All of the tenants have continuously and lawfully occupied the residential real property for 12 months or more. (2) One or more tenants have continuously and lawfully occupied the residential real property for 24 months or more.

clauses.title: The Enumerated "At-Fault" Just-Cause Grounds
clauses.body: Civil Code section 1946.2(b)(1) lists eleven specific grounds that qualify as "at-fault just cause" for terminating a tenancy that has crossed the occupancy threshold. Four of them are quoted below: default in the payment of rent; a breach of a material term of the lease (the same kind of breach addressed by Code of Civil Procedure section 1161(3)), including violating a lease provision after a written notice to correct it; maintaining or permitting a nuisance; and committing waste. The statute separately lists (among others) a tenant's refusal, after written demand, to sign a renewal or extension lease of similar duration and terms; criminal activity by the tenant on the property, or criminal activity or a criminal threat directed at the owner or the owner's agent; an unauthorized assignment or sublease; refusing to allow the owner lawful entry; using the premises for an unlawful purpose; an employee, agent, or licensee's failure to vacate after that relationship ends; and a tenant's failure to deliver possession after the tenant's own notice of intent to terminate, or an accepted written offer to surrender. For a curable lease violation, the statute separately requires the landlord to first give the tenant a notice of the violation with an opportunity to cure -- specifically cross-referenced to Code of Civil Procedure section 1161(3) -- before a termination notice for that violation may be served.

If the violation is not cured within the time period set forth in the notice, a three-day notice to quit without an opportunity to cure may thereafter be served to terminate the tenancy.

clauses.title: The Enumerated "No-Fault" Just-Cause Grounds
clauses.body: Civil Code section 1946.2(b)(2) lists four grounds that qualify as "no-fault just cause" -- reasons for ending a tenancy that do not depend on anything the tenant did. They are: (1) intent to occupy the property, for at least 12 continuous months as a primary residence, by the owner or the owner's spouse, domestic partner, child, grandchild, parent, or grandparent, subject to detailed conditions on timing, required notice content, and what happens if the intended occupant does not actually move in; (2) withdrawal of the property from the rental market; (3) the owner's compliance with a government agency or court order relating to habitability, a government agency or court order to vacate, or a local ordinance that necessitates vacating; and (4) intent to demolish, or to substantially remodel, the property, where "substantially remodel" is itself statutorily defined and requires the tenant to vacate for at least 30 consecutive days, and a termination notice on this ground must include a specific statutory statement about the tenant's right to re-rent the unit if the remodel or demolition is not carried out. Each no-fault ground listed above triggers the relocation-assistance-or-rent-waiver requirement described in a separate clause of this document.

clauses.title: Relocation Assistance or a Rent Waiver Required for No-Fault Terminations
clauses.body: When a landlord terminates a covered tenancy for one of the no-fault just-cause grounds described elsewhere in this document, Civil Code section 1946.2(d) requires the landlord -- regardless of the tenant's income, and at the landlord's own election -- to do one of two things: either pay the tenant direct relocation assistance, or waive in writing the rent for the final month of the tenancy before that rent becomes due. The amount, whichever form is chosen, is set by statute as equal to one month of the tenant's rent in effect when the termination notice was issued, and if relocation assistance is paid rather than the rent waived, it must be paid within 15 calendar days of the notice being served. The statute states expressly that a landlord's failure to strictly comply with this relocation-assistance-or-rent-waiver requirement renders the termination notice void.

clauses.title: The Statewide Rent-Increase Cap Formula
clauses.body: Civil Code section 1947.12(a) caps how much a covered landlord may increase rent over any 12-month period. The cap is 5 percent plus the percentage change in the applicable regional consumer price index, or 10 percent, whichever is lower, applied to the lowest gross rental rate charged for the unit at any time during the 12 months before the increase takes effect (with any rent discounts, incentives, or concessions offered and accepted excluded from that baseline figure). If the same tenant remains in the unit over a 12-month period, the rent may not be increased more than twice within that period, even if each individual increase would otherwise fit within the percentage cap. The "percentage change in the cost of living" figure used in the formula is tied to the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers for a specific metropolitan area (or a statewide substitute where no regional index exists), not a single statewide number. The cap applies only to increases on an existing tenancy: for a new tenancy in which no tenant from the prior tenancy remains in lawful possession, the landlord may set the initial rental rate without regard to this cap, and the cap applies again only to increases after that initial rate is set. If a current monthly rent figure for this tenancy is relevant, it is stated here as: {{monthlyRent}}.

clauses.title: Exemptions from the Statewide Rent Cap
clauses.body: Civil Code section 1947.12(d) lists six categories of residential real property to which the statewide rent cap does not apply. They are: (1) housing that is deed-restricted, or otherwise subject to a recorded document or government agreement, as affordable housing for very low, low, or moderate income persons and families; (2) dormitories owned and operated by a college, university, or K-12 school; (3) housing already subject to a local rent- or price-control ordinance that restricts annual increases to an amount less than this statute's own cap; (4) housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years, unless it is a mobilehome; (5) certain residential property alienable separate from any other dwelling unit, subject to non-corporate-ownership conditions and a required exemption notice described in a separate clause of this document; and (6) a two-unit property in which the owner occupies one unit as a principal residence, so long as the owner continues to occupy it and neither unit is an accessory dwelling unit.

clauses.title: Exemptions from the Statewide Just-Cause Requirement
clauses.body: Civil Code section 1946.2(e) lists nine categories of residential real property or residential circumstances to which the statewide just-cause requirement does not apply. Among them: transient and tourist hotel occupancy; housing in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended care facility, or licensed elder- or adult-care facility; dormitories owned and operated by a college, university, or K-12 school; housing where the tenant shares a bathroom or kitchen with an owner who maintains a principal residence there; a single-family owner-occupied residence in which the owner-occupant rents or leases no more than two units or bedrooms; a two-unit property where the owner occupies one unit as a principal residence; housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years, unless it is a mobilehome; certain property alienable separate from any other dwelling unit, subject to non-corporate-ownership conditions and a required exemption notice addressed in a separate clause of this document; and housing that is deed-restricted, or otherwise subject to a recorded document or government agreement, as affordable housing for very low, low, or moderate income persons and families. This statewide just-cause requirement is also displaced, rather than layered on top of, certain local just-cause ordinances: a property already subject to a local just-cause ordinance adopted on or before September 1, 2019, is governed by that local ordinance instead, and a property subject to a local just-cause ordinance adopted or amended after that date is likewise governed by the local ordinance instead of this section, but only if the local ordinance meets the statute's own definition of "more protective."

clauses.title: The Alienable-Title Exemption's Required Statutory Notice Language
clauses.body: Both the rent-cap statute and the just-cause statute exempt the same category of property -- residential real property (including a mobilehome under the just-cause statute) that is alienable separate from the title to any other dwelling unit, commonly including many single-family homes and some condominiums -- but only if the owner is not a real estate investment trust, a corporation, a corporation-containing limited liability company, or mobile home park management, and only if the tenants have been given a specific written exemption notice. Each statute requires the notice to use a statutorily prescribed statement, quoted below, that expressly cites both Civil Code section 1947.12(d)(5) and Civil Code section 1946.2(e)(8). For a tenancy commenced or renewed on or after July 1, 2020 (or July 1, 2022, for a mobilehome tenancy under the just-cause statute), the notice must be included in the rental agreement itself, not merely delivered separately; for a tenancy that predates those dates, including the notice in the rental agreement is permitted but not required.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Elder and Dependent Adult Financial Abuse Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Information Sheet describes California's Elder Abuse and Dependent Adult Civil Protection Act (Welfare and Institutions Code section 15600 et seq.) as it applies to financial abuse specifically — the statutory definitions of “elder” and “dependent adult,” the statutory definition of “financial abuse” and its three alternative prongs, the related statutory definition of “undue influence,” the civil remedies the Act makes available for a financial-abuse claim, the mandated-reporter framework (including a category specific to financial institutions), and the statute of limitations that applies to a financial-abuse damages claim under the Act. It is prepared by {{preparerName}}, whose relationship to {{personOfConcernName}} is: {{relationshipToPersonOfConcern}}. This Information Sheet is a general informational reference, not a private designation, court filing, petition, or report of abuse, and completing it does not itself determine that {{personOfConcernName}} is an “elder” or “dependent adult” within the meaning of the Act, that any specific conduct constitutes financial abuse, or that any specific person committed or suffered financial abuse. This document is also distinct from, and does not overlap with, a conservatorship petition: a conservatorship is a court proceeding that appoints a substitute decision-maker for a person going forward, while the Elder Abuse and Dependent Adult Civil Protection Act instead defines a category of wrongful conduct and civil remedies for it — a distinct legal question that can arise whether or not anyone is, or ever becomes, subject to a conservatorship.

clauses.title: Statutory Definitions of "Elder" and "Dependent Adult"
clauses.body: The Elder Abuse and Dependent Adult Civil Protection Act applies only to conduct directed at a person who meets one of two defined statutory categories. Welfare and Institutions Code section 15610.27 defines “elder” as any person residing in California who is 65 years of age or older — an age-based, residency-based definition with no additional requirement of incapacity, disability, or vulnerability. Section 15610.23 separately defines “dependent adult” in two independent ways: first, as a person between the ages of 18 and 64 who resides in California and who has physical or mental limitations that restrict their ability to carry out normal activities or to protect their rights — expressly including, without limitation, people with physical or developmental disabilities or people whose physical or mental abilities have diminished because of age; and second, regardless of any disability finding, as any person between 18 and 64 who is admitted as an inpatient to a 24-hour health facility as defined in specified sections of the Health and Safety Code. Whether {{personOfConcernName}} meets either statutory definition depends on {{personOfConcernName}}'s age, California residency, and, for the dependent-adult category, the nature of any limitations or inpatient admission — facts this Information Sheet does not evaluate.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California defines "elder" and "dependent adult" for purposes of its Elder Abuse and Dependent Adult Civil Protection Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person or situation. This clause cites two different code sections (§ 15610.27, a single subsection, and § 15610.23(a)-(b), two subsections of the same section); the two subsections of § 15610.23 are treated here as one source, not independent corroborating sources. This clause states only the statutory definitions; it does not itself determine that any specific person is an "elder" or "dependent adult" under California law, and it is not a substitute for that determination.

clauses.title: Statutory Definition of "Financial Abuse" — Three Alternative Prongs
clauses.body: Welfare and Institutions Code section 15610.30(a) defines “financial abuse” of an elder or dependent adult as occurring when a person or entity does any one of three alternative things: (1) takes, secretes, appropriates, obtains, or retains the elder or dependent adult's real or personal property for a wrongful use or with intent to defraud, or both; (2) assists another person or entity in taking, secreting, appropriating, obtaining, or retaining that property for a wrongful use or with intent to defraud, or both; or (3) takes, secretes, appropriates, obtains, or retains — or assists in doing so — the elder or dependent adult's property by undue influence, as separately defined in section 15610.70. These three prongs are independent alternatives; a claim of financial abuse rests on establishing any one of them, not all three. Section 15610.30(b) further provides that a person or entity is deemed to have acted for a wrongful use, for purposes of the first two prongs, if the person or entity took, secreted, appropriated, obtained, or retained the property while knowing or having reason to know that doing so was likely to be harmful to the elder or dependent adult — meaning proof of actual intent to defraud is not the only route to a wrongful-use finding.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California defines "financial abuse" of an elder or dependent adult, including its three alternative statutory prongs — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific set of facts. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 15610.30(a) and (b)); they are treated here as one source, not independent corroborating sources. Subsections (c) and (d) of the same section, defining when property is "taken" for purposes of the statute and defining "representative," are not quoted or described in this clause. This clause states only the statutory definition; it does not itself determine that any specific conduct constitutes financial abuse or that any specific person committed or suffered financial abuse.

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15610.30(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) “Financial abuse” of an elder or dependent adult occurs when a person or entity does any of the following: (1) Takes, secretes, appropriates, obtains, or retains real or personal property of an elder or dependent adult for a wrongful use or with intent to defraud, or both. (2) Assists in taking, secreting, appropriating, obtaining, or retaining real or personal property of an elder or dependent adult for a wrongful use or with intent to defraud, or both. (3) Takes, secretes, appropriates, obtains, or retains, or assists in taking, secreting, appropriating, obtaining, or retaining, real or personal property of an elder or dependent adult by undue influence, as defined in Section 15610.70.

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15610.30(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Welf. & Inst. C. § 15610.30(b)
citations.quote: (b) A person or entity shall be deemed to have taken, secreted, appropriated, obtained, or retained property for a wrongful use if, among other things, the person or entity takes, secretes, appropriates, obtains, or retains the property and the person or entity knew or should have known that this conduct is likely to be harmful to the elder or dependent adult.

clauses.title: Statutory Definition of "Undue Influence" and Its Enumerated Factors
clauses.body: Where a claim of financial abuse rests on the third statutory prong — taking property “by undue influence” — Welfare and Institutions Code section 15610.70, added in 2013, supplies the governing definition; the Act does not leave “undue influence” to be defined by cross-reference to a different code. Section 15610.70(a) defines “undue influence” as “excessive persuasion that causes another person to act or refrain from acting by overcoming that person's free will and results in inequity,” and directs that four categories of evidence be considered in determining whether a result was produced by undue influence: the victim's vulnerability (including incapacity, illness, disability, injury, age, education, impaired cognitive function, emotional distress, isolation, or dependency, and whether the influencer knew or should have known of it); the influencer's apparent authority (including status as a fiduciary, family member, care provider, health care professional, legal professional, or spiritual adviser); the actions or tactics the influencer used (including controlling necessaries of life or access to information, use of affection, intimidation, or coercion, and haste or secrecy in effecting changes); and the equity of the result (including the economic consequences to the victim and any divergence from the victim's prior intent or course of conduct). Section 15610.70(b) adds an express limit: evidence that a result was inequitable, standing alone, is not sufficient to prove undue influence — the other statutory factors must also be considered.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California defines "undue influence" for purposes of a financial-abuse claim, and of the factors the statute directs be considered — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific set of facts. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 15610.70(a) and (b)); they are treated here as one source, not independent corroborating sources. Research-tool limitation: this clause was researched together with an attempt to locate a citable, verifiable published California appellate decision applying this statutory undue-influence factor list to a financial-abuse claim; the case-law research tool used for this project (CourtListener) returned a daily rate-limit error (125 requests/day exceeded) before any case could be located and independently verified, so no case-law citation is included here — this clause rests on the statutory text alone, and no case law should be assumed to have been checked. This clause states only the statutory definition and factors; it does not itself determine that any specific person exercised undue influence over any other specific person, or that any specific result was produced by undue influence.

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15610.70(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Welf. & Inst. C. § 15610.70(a)
citations.quote: (a) “Undue influence” means excessive persuasion that causes another person to act or refrain from acting by overcoming that person’s free will and results in inequity. In determining whether a result was produced by undue influence, all of the following shall be considered: (1) The vulnerability of the victim. Evidence of vulnerability may include, but is not limited to, incapacity, illness, disability, injury, age, education, impaired cognitive function, emotional distress, isolation, or dependency, and whether the influencer knew or should have known of the alleged victim’s vulnerability. (2) The influencer’s apparent authority. Evidence of apparent authority may include, but is not limited to, status as a fiduciary, family member, care provider, health care professional, legal professional, spiritual adviser, expert, or other qualification. (3) The actions or tactics used by the influencer. Evidence of actions or tactics used may include, but is not limited to, all of the following: (A) Controlling necessaries of life, medication, the victim’s interactions with others, access to information, or sleep. (B) Use of affection, intimidation, or coercion. (C) Initiation of changes in personal or property rights, use of haste or secrecy in effecting those changes, effecting changes at inappropriate times and places, and claims of expertise in effecting changes. (4) The equity of the result. Evidence of the equity of the result may include, but is not limited to, the economic consequences to the victim, any divergence from the victim’s prior intent or course of conduct or dealing, the relationship of the value conveyed to the value of any services or consideration received, or the appropriateness of the change in light of the length and nature of the relationship.

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15610.70(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Welf. & Inst. C. § 15610.70(b)
citations.quote: (b) Evidence of an inequitable result, without more, is not sufficient to prove undue influence.

clauses.title: Civil Remedies for Financial Abuse — Attorney's Fees and the Different Proof Standards That Apply
clauses.body: Welfare and Institutions Code section 15657.5 supplies the civil remedies specific to a financial-abuse claim under the Act. This is a separate remedy provision from the Act's general elder-abuse remedy statute, section 15657, which by its own terms applies only to claims of physical abuse, neglect, or abandonment — not financial abuse. Under section 15657.5(a), where a defendant's liability for financial abuse is proven merely by a preponderance of the evidence, the court shall award the plaintiff reasonable attorney's fees and costs, in addition to compensatory damages and all other remedies otherwise provided by law. A higher proof standard applies to one additional, separate remedy: under section 15657.5(b), where financial-abuse liability is proven by a preponderance of the evidence and it is separately proven by clear and convincing evidence that the defendant acted with recklessness, oppression, fraud, or malice in committing the abuse, the damages limitations that Code of Civil Procedure section 377.34 would otherwise impose on a claim that survives the plaintiff's death do not apply. Attorney's fees and costs under the Act are thus available on an ordinary preponderance-of-the-evidence standard; it is only the removal of the survival-action damages cap that requires clear and convincing evidence of aggravated conduct.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the civil remedies California makes available for a financial-abuse claim under the Act and the proof standards that attach to each — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific claim. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 15657.5(a) and (b)); they are treated here as one source, not independent corroborating sources. Correction to an initial research assumption: section 15657 does carry a clear-and-convincing evidentiary standard and a structure that resembles section 15657.5's, but section 15657 governs only physical abuse, neglect, and abandonment claims under the Act — as stated on the face of section 15657 itself — and is not an available remedy provision for a financial-abuse claim, which is instead governed exclusively by section 15657.5. This clause does not attach the general section 15657 text as an independent citation because it is describing what section 15657.5, not section 15657, provides; the contrast is stated only in this gap note, drawn from the same verified fetch of section 15657 described in this project's research. Section 15657.5(c)-(e), addressing the separate standard for punitive damages against an employer and a required statement in any resulting money judgment, are not quoted or described in this clause. This clause states only the statutory remedies and proof standards; it does not itself determine that any specific defendant is liable for financial abuse, that any specific defendant acted with recklessness, oppression, fraud, or malice, or that any specific plaintiff is entitled to any remedy.

citations.cite: Welf. & Inst. C. § 15657.5(a)
citations.quote: (a) Where it is proven by a preponderance of the evidence that a defendant is liable for financial abuse, as defined in Section 15610.30, in addition to compensatory damages and all other remedies otherwise provided by law, the court shall award to the plaintiff reasonable attorney’s fees and costs.

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15657.5(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Welf. & Inst. C. § 15657.5(b)
citations.quote: (b) Where it is proven by a preponderance of the evidence that a defendant is liable for financial abuse, as defined in Section 15610.30, and where it is proven by clear and convincing evidence that the defendant has been guilty of recklessness, oppression, fraud, or malice in the commission of the abuse, in addition to reasonable attorney’s fees and costs set forth in subdivision (a), compensatory damages, and all other remedies otherwise provided by law, the limitations imposed by Section 377.34 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the damages recoverable shall not apply.

clauses.title: Statute of Limitations for a Financial-Abuse Damages Claim — Four Years From Discovery
clauses.body: Welfare and Institutions Code section 15657.7 sets a limitations period specific to a financial-abuse damages claim under the Act, distinct from the limitations periods that apply to ordinary tort or contract claims. An action for damages under sections 15657.5 and 15657.6 for financial abuse of an elder or dependent adult, as defined in section 15610.30, must be commenced within four years after the plaintiff discovers, or through the exercise of reasonable diligence should have discovered, the facts constituting the financial abuse. This is a discovery-based period, not a fixed period running automatically from the date of the underlying conduct — the four years runs from when the facts constituting the abuse were, or reasonably should have been, discovered.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the limitations period that applies to a financial-abuse damages claim under California's Elder Abuse and Dependent Adult Civil Protection Act — not a claim about which state's law, or which limitations period, governs a specific claim, and not a claim about the limitations period for any non-financial-abuse claim (including physical abuse, neglect, or abandonment claims, which section 15657.7 does not govern). This is a single statutory section, and no subsection of it is cited more than once in this clause. This clause states only the statutory limitations period; it does not itself determine when any specific plaintiff discovered or should have discovered any specific facts, or that any specific claim is or is not time-barred.

citations.cite: Welf. & Inst. C. § 15657.7
citations.quote: An action for damages pursuant to Sections 15657.5 and 15657.6 for financial abuse of an elder or dependent adult, as defined in Section 15610.30, shall be commenced within four years after the plaintiff discovers or, through the exercise of reasonable diligence, should have discovered, the facts constituting the financial abuse.

clauses.title: General Mandated-Reporter Categories and Reporting Duty (Financial Abuse Included)
clauses.body: Welfare and Institutions Code section 15630 designates broad categories of people as mandated reporters of suspected elder and dependent adult abuse, and financial abuse is expressly included among the abuse types those reporters must report — within section 15630 itself, financial abuse is not treated as a narrower category than physical abuse. Section 15630(a) designates as a mandated reporter any person who has assumed full or intermittent responsibility for the care or custody of an elder or dependent adult, whether or not compensated, including administrators, supervisors, and licensed staff of a facility that provides care or services for elder or dependent adults, any elder or dependent adult care custodian, health practitioner, clergy member, or employee of a county adult protective services agency or a local law enforcement agency. Under section 15630(b)(1), a mandated reporter who, in a professional capacity or within the scope of employment, observes or has knowledge of an incident that reasonably appears to be financial abuse (among other listed abuse types), or reasonably suspects it, must report the known, suspected, or alleged instance by telephone or through a confidential internet reporting tool immediately or as soon as practicably possible; if the report is made by telephone, a written or internet report must follow within two working days. Where the suspected abuse occurred outside a long-term care facility, a state mental hospital, or a state developmental center, section 15630(b)(1)(F) directs that the report be made to the county adult protective services agency or the local law enforcement agency.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's general mandated-reporter categories and reporting duty for suspected elder and dependent adult abuse, including financial abuse — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific reporter's obligations. This clause cites three subsections of the same statutory section (§ 15630(a), (b)(1), and (b)(1)(F)); they are treated here as one source, not independent corroborating sources. Section 15630 is substantially longer than what is quoted or described here — it separately addresses reporting within long-term care facilities, state mental hospitals, and state developmental centers; a narrow exception for clergy members receiving a penitential communication; a narrow exception for certain physicians, registered nurses, and psychotherapists; permissive (non-mandatory) reporting of other abuse types; and criminal penalties for a mandated reporter's willful failure to report — none of which this clause fully describes. A distinct and narrower mandated-reporter category that applies specifically to financial abuse — officers and employees of financial institutions — is addressed separately in this document's companion clause on section 15630.1. This clause does not itself determine that any specific person is a mandated reporter or that any specific reporter's duty has or has not been triggered.

citations.quote: (a) A person who has assumed full or intermittent responsibility for the care or custody of an elder or dependent adult, whether or not they receive compensation, including administrators, supervisors, and any licensed staff of a public or private facility that provides care or services for elder or dependent adults, or any elder or dependent adult care custodian, health practitioner, clergy member, or employee of a county adult protective services agency or a local law enforcement agency, is a mandated reporter.

citations.quote: (b) (1) A mandated reporter who, in their professional capacity, or within the scope of their employment, has observed or has knowledge of an incident that reasonably appears to be physical abuse, as defined in Section 15610.63, abandonment, abduction, isolation, financial abuse, or neglect, or is told by an elder or dependent adult that they have experienced behavior, including an act or omission, constituting physical abuse, as defined in Section 15610.63, abandonment, abduction, isolation, financial abuse, or neglect, or reasonably suspects that abuse, shall report the known, suspected, or alleged instance of abuse by telephone or through a confidential internet reporting tool, as authorized by Section 15658, immediately or as soon as practicably possible. If reported by telephone, a written report shall be sent, or an internet report shall be made through the confidential internet reporting tool established in Section 15658, within two working days.

citations.quote: (F) If the abuse has occurred in any place other than a long-term care facility, a state mental hospital, or a state developmental center, the report shall be made to the adult protective services agency or the local law enforcement agency.

clauses.title: A Narrower, Financial-Abuse-Specific Mandated-Reporter Category: Financial Institution Officers and Employees
clauses.body: Separate from the general mandated-reporter categories in section 15630, Welfare and Institutions Code section 15630.1 — part of the Financial Elder Abuse Reporting Act of 2005 — creates a mandated-reporter category and reporting duty that exist only for suspected financial abuse, not for other abuse types. Section 15630.1(a) defines a “mandated reporter of suspected financial abuse of an elder or dependent adult” as all officers and employees of financial institutions, a term section 15630.1(b) defines to include depository institutions, institution-affiliated parties, and federal or state credit unions. Under section 15630.1(d)(1), a financial institution officer or employee who has direct contact with an elder or dependent adult, or who reviews or approves that person's financial documents, records, or transactions, and who, within the scope of that employment, observes, has knowledge of, or reasonably suspects an incident of financial abuse, must report the known or suspected instance by telephone or through a confidential internet reporting tool immediately or as soon as practicably possible; a telephone report must be followed by a written or internet report within two working days, to the local adult protective services agency or the local law enforcement agency. Enforcement of this financial-institution duty differs from enforcement of the general mandated-reporter statute: section 15630.1(f) makes a financial institution's failure to report a civil penalty of up to $1,000 (up to $5,000 if the failure is willful), recoverable only in a civil action brought by the Attorney General, a district attorney, or county counsel — not the misdemeanor criminal penalty that section 15630(h) attaches to a mandated reporter's failure to report under the general statute.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California's Financial Elder Abuse Reporting Act of 2005 creates a mandated-reporter category and reporting duty that exist specifically for financial abuse and apply only to financial institution officers and employees — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific reporter's obligations. This clause cites three subsections of section 15630.1 (§ 15630.1(a), (d)(1), and (f)), treated here as one source rather than independent corroborating sources; it also cites one subsection of the separate section 15630 (§ 15630(h)) solely for contrast with section 15630.1(f)'s civil-penalty enforcement mechanism — that single citation is not treated as independent corroboration of anything this clause states about section 15630.1 itself. This clause does not itself determine that any specific officer or employee is a mandated reporter under this section, that any specific transaction or conduct constitutes suspected financial abuse, or that any specific report was or was not required.

clauses.title: Federal Infringement of a Registered Mark: The Likelihood-of-Confusion Standard
clauses.body: Federal law creates civil liability for a person who, without the consent of the registrant, uses in commerce a reproduction, counterfeit, copy, or colorable imitation of a registered mark in connection with the sale, offering for sale, distribution, or advertising of goods or services, where that use is likely to cause confusion, mistake, or deception. This "likelihood of confusion" standard — not proof of actual confusion, and not proof of an intent to confuse — is the statutory trigger for civil liability under this provision. The statute states the standard itself but does not enumerate the factors a court weighs in deciding whether a likelihood of confusion exists in a given case; that multi-factor analysis has instead been developed by courts. Whether any particular use meets this standard depends on comparison of the marks, the goods or services involved, and other marketplace facts that this clause does not evaluate.
clauses.gap: This is federal law (the Lanham Act, which applies nationwide), used as real evidence of the statutory likelihood-of-confusion standard for infringement of a registered mark — not a claim that the recipient's use, or any other specific use, of the mark described on this sheet is likely to cause confusion or otherwise meets this standard, which this clause does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (15 U.S.C. § 1114(1)(a)); no additional independent statutory source was needed for it. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific use of a mark infringes, dilutes, or otherwise violates any right, and completing or sending this information sheet does not itself send any cease-and-desist letter. A CourtListener case-law search for the multi-factor test courts use to assess likelihood of confusion (for example, the Ninth Circuit's factors) was attempted for this clause but returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, daily limit reported as exhausted) before any case could be retrieved, so no case citation for that multi-factor test is included here — only the statutory text, which does not itself list the factors, is quoted.

clauses.title: Federal Cause of Action for an Unregistered Mark: False Designation of Origin
clauses.body: Federal trademark protection is not limited to marks that have been federally registered. A separate federal statute creates civil liability for any person who, on or in connection with goods or services, uses in commerce any word, term, name, symbol, or device — or any false designation of origin, or false or misleading description or representation of fact — that is likely to cause confusion, mistake, or deception as to the affiliation, connection, or association of that person with another person, or as to the origin, sponsorship, or approval of goods, services, or commercial activities. By its own terms, this cause of action does not require that the mark at issue be registered with the USPTO; it protects a mark based on its use in commerce. This is the statutory basis for what is often described as "unregistered" or "common-law" federal trademark protection, and it means that a person's belief that a mark infringes is not automatically wrong merely because that mark, or the person's own mark, has never been registered.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence that a federal civil cause of action for use of an unregistered mark exists and of what that cause of action requires — not a claim that the mark described on this sheet, or any specific use of it, satisfies this standard, which this clause does not resolve. clauses.title: Federal Dilution: Blurring, Tarnishment, and the "Famous Mark" Requirement
clauses.body: Federal law provides a separate cause of action for "dilution," distinct from ordinary infringement, available only to the owner of a mark that is "famous." Unlike an ordinary infringement claim, a dilution claim does not require any showing of actual or likely confusion, competition, or economic injury. The statute sets a demanding definition of "famous": a mark is famous only if it is widely recognized by the general consuming public of the United States as a designation of the source of the mark owner's goods or services — a nationwide, general-public standard, not fame within a niche market, region, or industry alone, though the statute lists factors (including the extent of advertising, sales volume, and actual recognition) a court may consider in that inquiry. The statute defines two distinct forms of dilution: "dilution by blurring," which is association arising from similarity between another mark or trade name and the famous mark that impairs the famous mark's distinctiveness, and "dilution by tarnishment," which is association arising from that similarity that harms the famous mark's reputation. These are separate theories, and a dilution claim can rest on either one.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the federal dilution cause of action, the statutory definition of a "famous" mark, and the distinction between blurring and tarnishment — not a claim that any specific mark is famous, or that any specific use dilutes it by blurring or tarnishment, all of which this clause does not resolve. This clause cites four provisions of the same statutory subsection, 15 U.S.C. § 1125(c) — paragraph (1) (the injunctive-relief cause of action and its confusion-independent nature), paragraph (2)(A) (the definition of "famous"), and paragraphs (2)(B) and (2)(C) (the definitions of blurring and tarnishment) — and they are not independent sources; all four are grouped together here because they define a single statutory dilution framework. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific use of a mark infringes, dilutes, or otherwise violates any right, and completing or sending this information sheet does not itself send any cease-and-desist letter.

clauses.title: Federal Monetary Remedies: Profits, Damages, Costs, Enhanced Damages, and Attorney's Fees
clauses.body: Where a violation described in the federal trademark statute has been established, the statute allows the plaintiff, subject to the principles of equity, to recover the defendant's profits, the plaintiff's own damages, and the costs of the action. Separately, the statute gives a court discretion to enhance a damages award: in assessing damages, a court may enter judgment for any sum above actual damages, up to three times that amount, and this enhancement is treated as compensation rather than a penalty. The statute allows an award of reasonable attorney's fees, but only in "exceptional cases" and only to the prevailing party — fee-shifting is the exception, not the default. The statute also contains a separate, more specific rule for counterfeit-mark cases: where a violation involves intentionally using a mark known to be a counterfeit, or providing goods or services to enable such use, the statute requires the court to enter judgment for three times the profits or damages, whichever is greater, plus a reasonable attorney's fee, unless the court finds extenuating circumstances — a mandatory treble-damages-and-fee rule distinct from the general, discretionary enhancement described above.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the monetary remedies available in a federal trademark action and of the "exceptional cases" standard for attorney's fees — not a claim about what remedy, if any, a court would award for any specific conduct. This clause cites two different subsections of the same statutory section, 15 U.S.C. § 1117(a) (the general profits/damages/costs/enhancement/fees provision) and § 1117(b) (the separate, mandatory treble-damages-and-fee rule for certain counterfeit-mark violations); they are not independent sources of law, and this clause treats them together as describing one remedies section with a general rule and a more specific counterfeiting rule, not as two corroborating authorities. clauses.title: Federal Injunctive Relief for Trademark Infringement
clauses.body: Federal law gives courts with jurisdiction over trademark actions the power to grant injunctions, according to the principles of equity and on terms the court deems reasonable, to prevent violation of a registered mark owner's rights or a violation of the separate false-designation-of-origin or dilution provisions described in this document's companion clauses. This injunctive-relief power is a distinct remedy from the monetary remedies described elsewhere in this document; a plaintiff can seek an injunction, monetary relief, or both, depending on the circumstances and the court's discretion.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence that federal courts have statutory power to grant injunctions in trademark actions — not a claim that any court would grant, or that the sender of this letter is entitled to, an injunction with respect to any specific use of the mark described on this sheet. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (15 U.S.C. § 1116(a)); no additional independent source was needed for it. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific use of a mark infringes, dilutes, or otherwise violates any right, and completing or sending this information sheet does not itself send any cease-and-desist letter or request any injunction from any court.

clauses.title: Sending a Cease-and-Desist Letter Is Not a Federal Statutory Prerequisite to Filing Suit
clauses.body: Federal law gives district and territorial courts original jurisdiction over actions arising under the federal trademark statute, without regard to the amount in controversy or the parties' citizenship. This jurisdictional grant, and the separate provisions creating the causes of action described in this document's other clauses (registered-mark infringement, false designation of origin, and dilution) and the provision authorizing injunctive relief, do not condition a plaintiff's ability to bring a civil action on first sending a cease-and-desist letter or any other pre-suit notice to the person whose use is at issue. Sending a letter like this one before filing suit is a common business and litigation practice — it can create a documented record, and it may prompt a response without litigation — but it is not itself a federal statutory requirement that must be satisfied before a mark owner may sue.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence that the trademark statute's jurisdictional grant does not itself impose a notice precondition on filing suit — this clause reports an absence, confirmed by reviewing this jurisdictional provision together with the cause-of-action and injunctive-relief provisions cited in this document's other authority clauses (15 U.S.C. §§ 1114, 1116, 1125(a), 1125(c)) directly, rather than assuming it; none of those provisions mentions or requires a pre-suit demand letter, so no statutory citation requiring one is given and none should be inferred to exist. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (15 U.S.C. § 1121(a)) as its affirmative source; no additional independent statutory source was needed. This is federal law that applies nationwide; it does not describe any state's court-filing procedures. clauses.title: California Common-Law Trademark Rights Exist Independently of Registration
clauses.body: California's own trademark registration statute expressly preserves common-law trademark rights: the statute states that nothing in it adversely affects the rights, or the enforcement of rights, in marks acquired in good faith at any time within common law. This means that neither federal nor California state registration is the exclusive source of enforceable trademark rights in California; rights can also arise, and be enforced, based on a mark's actual good-faith use, independent of any registration with the USPTO or the California Secretary of State.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California law itself preserves common-law trademark rights alongside its own registration scheme — not a claim about the scope or strength of any common-law rights in the mark described on this sheet specifically, which depends on facts about use, reputation, and geographic scope this clause does not resolve, and not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs this letter or any dispute related to it. This clause cites a single statutory section (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 14259); no additional independent source was needed for it. This is distinct from, and does not duplicate, this tool's existing Fictitious Business Name (DBA) Statement document, whose own authority clause on this topic addresses a different statute (the FBN filing law's county-level rebuttable presumption of exclusive use of a registered fictitious business name) rather than California's trademark statute's preservation of common-law trademark rights; it is also distinct from this tool's Trademark Registration (USPTO Application) Information Sheet, whose authority clause on unregistered rights addresses the federal statute rather than California's state trademark statute. clauses.title: About This Pay Scale Disclosure and Salary History Ban Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes two related California Labor Code requirements that can arise in {{companyName}}'s hiring process for {{employeeName}} in connection with the position of {{jobTitle}}: the statutory ban on relying on, or asking about, an applicant's salary history, and the statutory duty to disclose a position's pay scale under specified circumstances, including in job postings. It summarizes selected requirements of California Labor Code section 432.3, and, where relevant, section 1197.5. It is not a determination that any specific question asked, information sought, pay scale disclosed or withheld, or job posting drafted by {{companyName}} in connection with {{employeeName}} or the {{jobTitle}} position complies or fails to comply with either statute, and it does not itself satisfy any notice, posting, or recordkeeping duty either statute may impose.

clauses.title: The Salary History Ban: Two Separate Prohibitions, Applicable to All Employers
clauses.body: California law imposes two separate prohibitions on an employer in connection with an applicant's salary history: an employer may not rely on an applicant's salary history information as a factor in deciding whether to offer employment or what salary to offer, and, separately, an employer may not seek salary history information about an applicant, whether orally or in writing, and whether personally or through an agent. The statute states that it applies to all employers, including state and local government employers and the Legislature, without any numerical size threshold.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 432.3(a), (b), and (g)), used as real evidence of California's salary-history-ban requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's actual situation. All three citations below are to subdivisions (a), (b), and (g) of a single statutory section, Section 432.3; they are treated here as one source describing the ban and its scope, not as independent corroborating sources. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific question asked or not asked, or any specific hiring decision made, by any particular employer complied or failed to comply with Section 432.3(a) or (b), and does not determine that any particular employer's practices toward any particular applicant or employee are compliant or noncompliant with it.

clauses.title: Exceptions: Voluntary Disclosure, Salary-Expectation Questions, and the Link to the Equal Pay Act
clauses.body: The salary-history ban does not prohibit an applicant from voluntarily and without prompting disclosing salary history information to a prospective employer, and if an applicant does so, the statute does not prohibit that employer from considering or relying on that voluntarily disclosed information in determining the applicant's salary. Separately, the statute does not prohibit an employer from asking an applicant about the applicant's salary expectation for the position being applied for. The statute also cross-references California's Equal Pay Act, stating that, consistent with Labor Code section 1197.5, nothing in the salary-history-ban statute is to be construed to allow prior salary to justify any disparity in compensation.

All four citations below are to subdivisions (h) through (k) of a single statutory section, Section 432.3; they are treated here as one source describing related exceptions and a cross-reference, not as independent corroborating sources. The fourth citation, subdivision (k), points to Labor Code section 1197.5 rather than restating its text; a separate clause in this information sheet addresses what Section 1197.5 itself says and, as importantly, what it does not say about job postings. This clause does not determine whether any particular disclosure by any particular applicant to any particular employer was, in fact, voluntary and without prompting, and is informational only: it does not determine that any particular employer's practices are compliant or noncompliant with Section 432.3.

clauses.title: Duty to Disclose Pay Scale on Request — Applicants and Current Employees, No Size Threshold
clauses.body: Separately from any job posting, California law requires an employer, upon reasonable request, to provide the pay scale for a position to an applicant applying for that position, and requires an employer, upon request, to provide a current employee the pay scale for the position in which that employee is currently employed. By their own text, neither of these two request-triggered disclosure duties is limited to employers of any particular size.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 432.3(c)(1) and (c)(2)), used as real evidence of these request-triggered pay-scale disclosure duties — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. Both citations below are to paragraphs (1) and (2) of a single statutory subdivision, Section 432.3(c); they are treated here as one source describing two related disclosure duties, not as independent corroborating sources. A separate clause in this information sheet addresses the different, proactive job-posting disclosure duty in Section 432.3(c)(3) and (c)(5), which does carry a 15-employee threshold; this clause does not state that the two duties are identical in scope. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific request made or not made, or any specific pay-scale figure disclosed or withheld, by any particular employer toward any particular applicant or employee satisfied or failed to satisfy Section 432.3(c)(1) or (c)(2).

clauses.title: Job-Posting Pay Scale Requirement and the 15-Employee Threshold
clauses.body: California law requires an employer with 15 or more employees to include the pay scale for a position in any job posting for that position. If such an employer engages a third party to announce, post, publish, or otherwise make known a job posting, the employer must provide the pay scale to that third party, and the third party must include the pay scale in the job posting.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 432.3(c)(3) and (c)(5)), used as real evidence of the job-posting pay-scale requirement and its numerical threshold — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. Both citations below are to paragraphs (3) and (5) of a single statutory subdivision, Section 432.3(c); they are treated here as one source describing a proactive posting duty and its extension to third-party postings, not as independent corroborating sources. This 15-employee threshold applies specifically to these two paragraphs; a separate clause in this information sheet addresses the request-triggered disclosure duties in Section 432.3(c)(1) and (c)(2), which by their own text carry no such threshold, and this clause does not state or imply that every duty this statute creates shares the same size threshold. The statute does not itself define how an employer's number of employees is counted (for example, whether part-time employees, employees outside California, or a particular measurement date are included), and this clause does not resolve that question or determine that any particular employer does or does not meet the threshold. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific job posting used by any particular employer for any particular position complied or failed to comply with Section 432.3(c)(3) or (c)(5).

clauses.title: Statutory Definitions: “Pay Scale” and “Applicant”
clauses.body: The statute defines "pay scale" to mean a good faith estimate of the salary or hourly wage range that the employer reasonably expects to pay for the position upon hire. It defines "applicant" or "applicant for employment" to mean an individual who is seeking employment with the employer and who is not currently employed with that employer in any capacity or position.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 432.3(m)(1) and (m)(2)), used as real evidence of these two statutory definitions — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. Both citations below are to paragraphs (1) and (2) of a single statutory subdivision, Section 432.3(m); they are treated here as one source, not as independent corroborating sources. The pay-scale definition turns on the employer's own good faith estimate of a range it reasonably expects to pay, rather than on any fixed formula, and this clause does not determine what dollar figures any particular employer does or should reasonably expect to pay for any particular position. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any particular figure or range disclosed by any particular employer does or does not meet this statutory definition of "pay scale."

clauses.title: Recordkeeping Duty, Civil Penalties, and Enforcement Procedure
clauses.body: The statute requires an employer to maintain records of a job title and wage rate history for each employee for the duration of that employment plus three years after the employment ends, so that the Labor Commissioner can determine whether a pattern of wage discrepancy still exists; these records must be open to inspection by the Labor Commissioner. A person claiming to be aggrieved by a violation of the statute may file a written complaint with the Labor Commissioner within one year after learning of the violation, stating the employer's name and address and a detailed account of the alleged violation, and may separately bring a civil action for injunctive relief and any other relief the court deems appropriate. The Labor Commissioner must promptly investigate complaints alleging a violation, and upon finding a violation, may order the employer to pay a civil penalty of not less than $100 and not more than $10,000 per violation, with the amount based on the totality of the circumstances, including whether the employer has previously violated the section; for a first violation of the job-posting subdivision specifically, no penalty is assessed if the employer demonstrates that all job postings for open positions have been updated to include the required pay scale. If an employer fails to keep the required records, the statute creates a rebuttable presumption in favor of the employee's claim.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 432.3(c)(4) and (d)(1) through (d)(5)), used as real evidence of California's recordkeeping duty, complaint and civil-action procedures, civil penalty range, and adverse-inference-style presumption — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. All six citations below are to a single paragraph, (c)(4), and paragraphs (1) through (5) of a single statutory subdivision, (d), of one section, Section 432.3; they are treated here as one source describing one connected recordkeeping-and-enforcement scheme, not as independent corroborating sources. By its own text, the recordkeeping duty in paragraph (c)(4) carries no 15-employee threshold and so is not, on its face, limited to the same employers as the job-posting duty in (c)(3); this clause does not resolve any tension that might arise from that reading. The first-violation cure applies, by its own text, only to a violation "of subdivision (c)" — the pay-scale provisions — and this clause does not state that the same cure applies to a violation of the separate salary-history-ban provisions in subdivisions (a) or (b). This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any particular employer has or has not kept the required records for any particular employee, and does not determine that any employer's practices are compliant or noncompliant with Section 432.3.

For a first violation of subdivision (c), no penalty shall be assessed upon demonstration by the employer that all job postings for open positions have been updated to include the pay scale as required by this section.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 432.3(d)(5) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, rebuttable presumption for failure to keep records
citations.quote: If an employer fails to keep records in violation of this section, there shall be a rebuttable presumption in favor of the employee’s claim.

clauses.title: Labor Code § 1197.5: California's Equal Pay Act, Not the Source of the Job-Posting Duty
clauses.body: Labor Code section 1197.5 is California's Equal Pay Act. Its own text prohibits paying an employee at a wage rate less than the rate paid to an employee of another sex (and, separately, another race or ethnicity) for substantially similar work, unless the employer demonstrates that the entire wage differential is accounted for by specified factors, and it states that prior salary alone shall not justify a pay disparity. It also requires every employer to maintain records of the wages and wage rates, job classifications, and other terms and conditions of employment of its employees, on file for three years. Section 1197.5's own text does not contain a requirement that an employer include a pay scale in a job posting; the job-posting pay-scale requirement, its 15-employee threshold, and the related third-party-posting duty appear in Labor Code section 432.3, not in section 1197.5.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 1197.5(a) and (e)), used as real evidence of what Section 1197.5 itself requires and does not require — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. Both citations below are to subdivisions (a) and (e) of a single statutory section, Section 1197.5; they are treated here as one source, not as independent corroborating sources. This clause's drafter read Section 1197.5 in full, subdivisions (a) through (l), and confirmed that no part of its current codified text imposes a job-posting pay-scale disclosure duty of the kind found in Section 432.3(c)(3) and (c)(5); this is an absence found by reading the entire section, not an absence inferred from a partial reading. This clause does not restate every element of the Equal Pay Act's burden-shifting framework in subdivision (a), and does not determine whether any specific pay differential between any particular employees is or is not justified under Section 1197.5. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any particular employer's pay practices toward any particular employee are compliant or noncompliant with Section 1197.5.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1197.5(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Equal Pay Act sex-based wage-differential prohibition and prior-salary limitation
citations.quote: Prior salary shall not justify any disparity in compensation. Nothing in this section shall be interpreted to mean that an employer may not make a compensation decision based on a current employee’s existing salary, so long as any wage differential resulting from that compensation decision is justified by one or more of the factors in this subdivision.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1197.5(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Equal Pay Act general wage/job-classification recordkeeping duty
citations.quote: Every employer shall maintain records of the wages and wage rates, job classifications, and other terms and conditions of employment of the persons employed by the employer. All of the records shall be kept on file for a period of three years.
