It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete that petition, and it does not emancipate any minor or determine that any minor meets the statutory eligibility requirements; only a court declaration issued under Family Code § 7122 can do that.]

clauses.title: The Emancipation of Minors Law, and the Three Statutory Paths to Emancipated Status
clauses.body: California's Emancipation of Minors Law states that its purpose is to provide a clear statement defining emancipation and its consequences, and to permit an emancipated minor to obtain a court declaration of the minor's status. Under Family Code § 7002, a person under 18 is an emancipated minor if any one of three conditions is satisfied: the person has entered a valid marriage or established a valid domestic partnership, regardless of whether it has since been dissolved; the person is on active duty with the Armed Forces of the United States; or the person has received a court declaration of emancipation under Family Code § 7122. Only the third path involves the court petition process this document describes; the first two occur by operation of the statute itself, without any court filing.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own statutory definition of emancipated status — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific minor's status, and not a claim that any specific minor has taken either of the non-judicial paths described here. This clause cites two sections: § 7001 (a single citation, standing alone) and § 7002, whose three subsections — § 7002(a), § 7002(b), and § 7002(c) — are all part of the same statutory section and are treated here as one source for the three-paths framework, not as three independently corroborating sources. This document is informational only: it does not itself emancipate any minor by any of the three paths it describes, and does not determine that any specific minor has married, entered a domestic partnership, entered active-duty military service, or received a court declaration.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7001 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: It is the purpose of this part to provide a clear statement defining emancipation and its consequences and to permit an emancipated minor to obtain a court declaration of the minor’s status.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7002(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The person has entered into a valid marriage, or has established a valid domestic partnership, regardless of whether the marriage or the domestic partnership has been dissolved.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7002(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The person is on active duty with the Armed Forces of the United States.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7002(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The person has received a declaration of emancipation pursuant to Section 7122.

clauses.title: Who May Petition, and the Facts the Petition Must Allege
clauses.body: Family Code § 7120(a) allows a minor to petition the superior court of the county in which the minor resides or is temporarily domiciled for a declaration of emancipation. Under § 7120(b), the petition must set forth with specificity four facts: that the minor is at least 14 years of age; that the minor willingly lives separate and apart from the minor's parents or guardian with the consent or acquiescence of the minor's parents or guardian; that the minor is managing their own financial affairs, evidenced by a completed declaration of income and expenses on Judicial Council form FL-150; and that the source of the minor's income is not derived from any activity declared a crime under the laws of California or the United States.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the facts California law requires a petition to allege — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific minor's situation. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 7120(a) and § 7120(b)); they are treated as one source, not as independently corroborating sources. This document is informational only: it does not itself allege, verify, or determine that any specific minor — including a minor identified elsewhere in this document — actually satisfies any of these four statutory facts, is at least 14, lives apart from a parent or guardian with that parent's or guardian's consent, manages their own finances, or has a lawful source of income. Whether a particular minor's actual circumstances meet these requirements is a factual and legal question for the minor's petition and the court, not a determination this document makes.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7120(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: A minor may petition the superior court of the county in which the minor resides or is temporarily domiciled for a declaration of emancipation.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7120(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The petition shall set forth with specificity all of the following facts: (1) The minor is at least 14 years of age. (2) The minor willingly lives separate and apart from the minor’s parents or guardian with the consent or acquiescence of the minor’s parents or guardian. (3) The minor is managing their own financial affairs. As evidence of this, the minor shall complete and attach a declaration of income and expenses as provided in Judicial Council form FL-150. (4) The source of the minor’s income is not derived from any activity declared to be a crime by the laws of this state or the laws of the United States.

clauses.title: Notice to Parents, Guardian, and Public Agencies Before the Hearing
clauses.body: Before a petition for a declaration of emancipation is heard, Family Code § 7121(a) requires that notice the court determines reasonable be given to the minor's parents, guardian, or other person entitled to the minor's custody — or that proof be made to the court that their addresses are unknown or that notice cannot otherwise be given. Under § 7121(b), the clerk of the court must also notify the local child support agency of the county where the matter will be heard, and, depending on the minor's status, the probation department if the minor is a ward of the court, or the county welfare department if the minor is a dependent child of the court. Section 7121(c) requires the notice to include a form by which the parents or guardian may consent in writing to the emancipation, together with a warning that a court may later void or rescind the declaration and that the parents may become liable for the minor's support and medical insurance coverage.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the notice California law requires before a petition is heard — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petition. This clause cites three subsections of the same statutory section (§ 7121(a), § 7121(b), and § 7121(c)); they are treated as one source, not as independently corroborating sources. This document is informational only: it does not itself give notice to anyone, does not determine that notice to any specific parent or guardian named elsewhere in this document is required, excused, or has been given, and does not itself create any consent or liability the statute describes.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7121(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Before the petition for a declaration of emancipation is heard, notice the court determines is reasonable shall be given to the minor’s parents, guardian, or other person entitled to the custody of the minor, or proof shall be made to the court that their addresses are unknown or that for other reasons the notice cannot be given.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7121(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The clerk of the court shall also notify the local child support agency of the county in which the matter is to be heard of the proceeding. If the minor is a ward of the court, notice shall be given to the probation department. If the child is a dependent child of the court, notice shall be given to the county welfare department.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7121(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The notice shall include a form whereby the minor’s parents, guardian, or other person entitled to the custody of the minor may give their written consent to the petitioner’s emancipation. The notice shall include a warning that a court may void or rescind the declaration of emancipation and the parents may become liable for support and medical insurance coverage pursuant to Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 4000) of Part 2 of Division 9 and Sections 17400, 17402, 17404, and 17422.

clauses.title: The Court's Findings, and the Legal Effect of a Declaration
clauses.body: Family Code § 7122(a) directs the court to sustain the petition if it finds that the minor is a person described by § 7120 and that emancipation would not be contrary to the minor's best interest. Under § 7122(b), if the petition is sustained, the court must forthwith issue a declaration of emancipation, which the clerk of the court then files. Section 7122(c) makes the resulting declaration conclusive evidence that the minor is emancipated.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the finding a California court must make and the legal effect of the resulting declaration — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petition. This clause cites three subsections of the same statutory section (§ 7122(a), § 7122(b), and § 7122(c)); they are treated as one source, not as independently corroborating sources. This document is informational only: it does not itself find that any specific minor is a person described by § 7120, does not find that emancipation would or would not be contrary to any specific minor's best interest, and does not itself issue, and cannot substitute for, a court's declaration of emancipation.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7122(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The court shall sustain the petition if it finds that the minor is a person described by Section 7120 and that emancipation would not be contrary to the minor’s best interest.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7122(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: If the petition is sustained, the court shall forthwith issue a declaration of emancipation, which shall be filed by the clerk of the court.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7122(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: A declaration is conclusive evidence that the minor is emancipated.

clauses.title: What Emancipation Changes Once a Declaration Is Granted
clauses.body: Once emancipated — whether by court declaration or by one of the two other statutory paths — Family Code § 7050 treats the minor as an adult for a defined list of purposes. These include ending the minor's right to support from the minor's parents; ending the parents' right to the minor's earnings and to control the minor; the application of Welfare and Institutions Code §§ 300 and 601; and ending vicarious or imputed liability of the minor's parents or guardian for the minor's torts, subject to statutory exceptions for liability imposed by the Vehicle Code or arising from an agency relationship. Section 7050(e) also gives the minor an adult's capacity for a further, statutorily enumerated list of acts — among them consenting to medical, dental, or psychiatric care without parental consent, knowledge, or liability; entering a binding contract; suing or being sued in the minor's own name; establishing the minor's own residence; and enrolling in a school or college.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the legal effects California law attaches to emancipated status — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific minor's status. Both citations in this clause are drawn from the same statutory section (§ 7050, subsections (a)-(d) and (e)); they are treated as one source, not as independently corroborating sources. An earlier research assumption in the task brief framed the effects provisions as falling within Family Code §§ 7120-7143; on the actual statutory text, the effects of emancipation are instead set out in a separate chapter, §§ 7050-7052 (Chapter 2, "Effect of Emancipation"), which precedes the court-declaration procedure in §§ 7110-7143 (Chapter 3) and is not part of the range the brief identified — this clause corrects that gap. This document is informational only: it does not itself confer any of these effects on any specific minor, and describes them only as consequences the statute attaches to a person who has actually become an emancipated minor under § 7002 — not as a statement that any specific minor identified in this document has become emancipated.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7050(a)-(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: An emancipated minor shall be considered as being an adult for the following purposes: (a) The minor’s right to support by the minor’s parents. (b) The right of the minor’s parents to the minor’s earnings and to control the minor. (c) The application of Sections 300 and 601 of the Welfare and Institutions Code. (d) Ending all vicarious or imputed liability of the minor’s parents or guardian for the minor’s torts. Nothing in this section affects any liability of a parent, guardian, spouse, or employer imposed by the Vehicle Code, or any vicarious liability that arises from an agency relationship.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7050(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (e) The minor’s capacity to do any of the following: (1) Consent to medical, dental, or psychiatric care, without parental consent, knowledge, or liability. (2) Enter into a binding contract or give a delegation of power. (3) Buy, sell, lease, encumber, exchange, or transfer an interest in real or personal property, including, but not limited to, shares of stock in a domestic or foreign corporation or a membership in a nonprofit corporation. (4) Sue or be sued in the minor’s own name. (5) Compromise, settle, arbitrate, or otherwise adjust a claim, action, or proceeding by or against the minor. (6) Make or revoke a will. (7) Make a gift, outright or in trust. (8) Convey or release contingent or expectant interests in property, including marital property rights and any right of survivorship incident to joint tenancy, and consent to a transfer, encumbrance, or gift of marital property. (9) Exercise or release the minor’s powers as donee of a power of appointment unless the creating instrument otherwise provides. (10) Create for the minor’s own benefit or for the benefit of others a revocable or irrevocable trust. (11) Revoke a revocable trust. (12) Elect to take under or against a will. (13) Renounce or disclaim any interest acquired by testate or intestate succession or by inter vivos transfer, including exercise of the right to surrender the right to revoke a revocable trust. (14) Make an election referred to in Section 13502 of, or an election and agreement referred to in Section 13503 of, the Probate Code. (15) Establish the minor’s own residence. (16) Apply for a work permit pursuant to Section 49110 of the Education Code without the request of the minor’s parents. (17) Enroll in a school or college.

clauses.title: Voiding a Declaration for Fraud, and Rescinding One for Indigency
clauses.body: A declaration of emancipation is not necessarily permanent. Family Code § 7130(a) makes a declaration obtained by fraud or by withholding material information voidable, while § 7130(b) makes a declaration of an indigent minor with no means of support subject to rescission — two distinct grounds, each with its own standard. Under § 7131, a petition to void a declaration for fraud or withheld information may be filed by any person or by any public or private agency, in the court that issued the declaration. A petition to rescind a declaration for indigency, by contrast, may under § 7132(a) be filed only by the minor, the minor's conservator, or the district attorney of the county where the minor resides, and must be filed in the county where the minor or conservator resides; § 7132(b) lets the court treat a minor as indigent if the minor's only income is public assistance benefits, and requires the court to find that rescission would not be contrary to the minor's best interest before granting it. Before either kind of petition is heard, § 7133(a) requires notice the court determines reasonable to the minor's parents or guardian, or proof that notice cannot be given. Finally, § 7135 provides that voiding or rescinding a declaration does not alter any contractual obligation, right, or property interest that arose while the declaration was in effect.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how a California declaration of emancipation may later be voided or rescinded — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific declaration. Two pairs of these citations are subsections of the same statutory section and are each treated as one source rather than independently corroborating sources: § 7130(a) and § 7130(b) (the two grounds), and § 7132(a) and § 7132(b) (the rescission-petition procedure and standard). Section 7131, § 7133(a), and § 7135 are each drawn from separate, independently numbered sections. This document is informational only: it does not itself void, rescind, or otherwise affect any declaration of emancipation, and does not determine that any specific declaration was or was not obtained by fraud or that any specific minor is or is not indigent within the meaning of § 7132(b).

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7130(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: A declaration of emancipation obtained by fraud or by the withholding of material information is voidable.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7130(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: A declaration of emancipation of a minor who is indigent and has no means of support is subject to rescission.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7131 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: A petition to void a declaration of emancipation on the ground that the declaration was obtained by fraud or by the withholding of material information may be filed by any person or by any public or private agency. The petition shall be filed in the court that made the declaration.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7132(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: A petition to rescind a declaration of emancipation on the ground that the minor is indigent and has no means of support may be filed by the minor declared emancipated, by the minor’s conservator, or by the district attorney of the county in which the minor resides. The petition shall be filed in the county in which the minor or the conservator resides.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7132(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The minor may be considered indigent if the minor’s only source of income is from public assistance benefits. The court shall consider the impact of the rescission of the declaration of emancipation on the minor and shall find the rescission of the declaration of emancipation will not be contrary to the best interest of the minor before granting the order to rescind.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7133(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Before a petition under this article is heard, notice the court determines is reasonable shall be given to the minor’s parents or guardian, or proof shall be made to the court that their addresses are unknown or that for other reasons the notice cannot be given.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7135 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Voiding or rescission of the declaration of emancipation does not alter any contractual obligation or right or any property right or interest that arose during the period that the declaration was in effect.

clauses.title: How Emancipation Affects an Existing Guardianship of the Person
clauses.body: California's guardianship-termination statute cross-references the Emancipation of Minors Law directly. Probate Code § 1600(b) provides that a guardianship of the person terminates upon the death of the ward, the adoption of the ward, or upon the emancipation of the ward under Section 7002 of the Family Code — meaning an existing guardianship of a minor's person ends once that minor becomes an emancipated minor within the meaning of Family Code § 7002, by any of that section's three statutory paths, and not only through the court-declaration path this document otherwise describes. Probate Code § 1600(c) addresses termination of a guardianship of the estate separately, on its own terms, and does not list emancipation among the events that terminate a guardianship of the estate.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's guardianship-termination statute treats emancipation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific guardianship. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1600(b) and § 1600(c)); they are treated as one source, not as independently corroborating sources. No separate statutory provision was located that bars a court from being asked to appoint a new guardian for a minor who is already emancipated, or that otherwise addresses guardian eligibility specifically in light of a minor's emancipated status; this clause describes only the one express cross-reference this research located — automatic termination of an existing guardianship of the person under § 1600(b) — and does not assert a broader rule beyond that text. This document is informational only: it does not itself terminate any guardianship, and does not determine that any specific minor named elsewhere in this document, or any guardianship concerning that minor, is affected by § 1600(b).

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1600(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1600(b)
citations.quote: A guardianship of the person terminates upon the death of the ward, the adoption of the ward, or upon the emancipation of the ward under Section 7002 of the Family Code.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1600(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1600(c)
citations.quote: A guardianship of the estate terminates upon the death of the ward, except as provided by Section 2467 and Article 4 (commencing with Section 2630) of Chapter 7 of Part 4, and except as otherwise provided by law.

clauses.title: Declaration and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Bonus and Incentive Compensation at Termination — Information Sheet is prepared with respect to {{employeeName}}'s employment with {{companyName}}, which ended on {{terminationDate}}. It describes how California law treats bonus, incentive, and similar variable pay when employment ends — including the legal line California authorities draw between a bonus the employer retains discretion to pay or withhold, which is not itself a legally owed wage, and a bonus tied to an objective formula, quota, or other criteria the employee has already satisfied, which can be. This document addresses bonus and incentive compensation generally; it is separate from, and does not repeat, this project's Commission Payout Upon Termination document, which addresses commissions specifically — a form of pay tied to a written commission agreement governed by its own statute, Labor Code section 2751. The bonus or incentive arrangement addressed here is described as: {{bonusType}}, covering the period {{bonusPeriodCovered}}, under plan terms described as: {{bonusPlanTerms}}.

clauses.title: "Wages" Is a General Definition — It Does Not Expressly Mention Bonuses
clauses.body: California's core statutory definition of "wages" is general: it covers "all amounts for labor performed by employees of every description," measured by the standard of time, task, piece, commission basis, "or other method of calculation" — a catch-all that does not, on its own text, use the word "bonus" or "incentive," or list bonus pay among its examples. Whether a bonus counts as a "wage" under this definition is instead something California's own labor enforcement agency has interpreted, not something the statute spells out for bonuses by name: the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's published glossary states that a bonus may be "a contractually required payment where a promise is made that a bonus will be paid in return for a specific result, such as exceeding a minimum sales figure or piece quota, or as an inducement to remain in the employ of the employer for a certain period of time," and that "[s]ums earned as bonuses are wages under the definition found in Labor Code Section 200." A bonus or incentive payment that {{employeeName}} contends was earned before {{terminationDate}} is, on this interpretation, a "wage" reached by the same statutory protections that apply to wages generally — but only once, and to the extent, it was actually earned.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute and labor-agency interpretation, used as real evidence of how California treats bonus pay under its general wage definition — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific bonus arrangement, and not a claim that this same catch-all wording appears, or is interpreted the same way, in every other state's wage statute. The statutory text quoted below (Labor Code section 200(a)) was fetched twice this session, directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, using two different User-Agent headers, and found byte-identical both times; the DLSE glossary entry for "bonus" was fetched twice this session, directly from dir.ca.gov, using two different User-Agent headers, and found byte-identical both times. This clause and this document are informational only: this clause does not itself determine that any specific payment described in this document is a bonus, is a wage, or was actually earned before termination, and it does not determine that any specific amount is owed — that depends on the terms of the specific plan and the facts of the specific arrangement, addressed in this document's other clauses.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 200(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the statutory definition of "wages"
citations.quote: “Wages” includes all amounts for labor performed by employees of every description, whether the amount is fixed or ascertained by the standard of time, task, piece, commission basis, or other method of calculation.

citations.case: California DLSE, Glossary of Terms — "bonus" (California Department of Industrial Relations text)
citations.cite: DLSE Glossary, entry for "bonus"
citations.quote: A bonus may be in the form of a gratuity where there is no promise for their payment, for example, a holiday bonus at the end of the year. Additionally, a bonus may be a contractually required payment where a promise is made that a bonus will be paid in return for a specific result, such as exceeding a minimum sales figure or piece quota, or as an inducement to remain in the employ of the employer for a certain period of time. Sums earned as bonuses are wages under the definition found in Labor Code Section 200.

clauses.title: A Genuinely Discretionary Bonus Is Not, By Itself, an Owed Wage
clauses.body: No section of the California Labor Code itself codifies a rule that a "discretionary" bonus is not a wage while a "nondiscretionary" bonus is. That specific vocabulary, and the line it draws, comes instead from the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's own sub-regulatory interpretation of the general wage statute, reflected in the agency's published Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual: "Bonuses which are completely discretionary, based on no objective criteria and are not routine, would not, of course, give rise to an implied bonus contract." On this interpretation, an employer's retained discretion over whether to pay a bonus at all, and how much to pay if it does, means no legal obligation to pay any particular amount has yet arisen — so there is nothing yet for a departing employee to have "earned" as a wage, unless and until the employer actually exercises that discretion in the employee's favor.
clauses.gap: This is one state's labor-agency interpretation, used as real evidence that California's discretionary-bonus principle is agency guidance rather than codified statutory text — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific bonus arrangement. The quoted manual section comes from the DLSE's 2002 Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual (Section 35.4.3), fetched directly from dir.ca.gov and confirmed byte-identical (by file checksum) across two fetches with different User-Agent headers; the same agency's own website states, on the page linking to this manual, that "[p]ursuant to Executive Order S-2-03, the DLSE opinion letters and the Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual are currently under review to determine their legal force and effect and to ensure compliance with the requirements of the Administrative Procedures Act" — meaning DLSE's own site flags this manual's binding legal weight as unresolved, and this particular section has not been revised since June 2002, so it does not reflect any California case law decided after that date. This research session's CourtListener case-law tools were rate-limited (125 requests/day, exhausted before this document's research began) and direct fetches to individual case pages on courtlistener.com, law.justia.com, and caselaw.findlaw.com were each blocked or returned no usable text when tested this session, so no case applying the discretionary-bonus principle directly, independent of the DLSE Manual's own description of it, was independently read this session; that gap is disclosed here rather than papered over. This clause and this document are informational only: this clause does not itself determine that any specific bonus or incentive arrangement described in this document is actually discretionary, nondiscretionary, or owed — that depends on the plan's own terms and the facts of the specific arrangement.

citations.cite: DLSE Enforcement Manual § 35.4.3
citations.quote: Discretionary Bonus. Bonuses which are completely discretionary, based on no objective criteria and are not routine, would not, of course, give rise to an implied bonus contract.

clauses.title: A Bonus Tied to a Quota, Formula, or Objective Criteria Can Become an Earned Wage
clauses.body: Where a bonus is not left to the employer's unfettered discretion, but is instead promised in return for meeting an objective, ascertainable condition — a sales figure, a production quota, or simply remaining employed through a stated period, without the employer having reserved discretion over whether to pay it — California's labor enforcement agency has taken the position that the bonus can become earned by the employee's satisfaction of that condition, independent of any further discretionary act by the employer. The agency's Enforcement Manual illustrates this with a California Court of Appeal decision it describes as holding that, where a bonus was part of the inducement for continuing employment and the employer's plan did not expressly condition payment on continued employment through some later date, "the bonus is earned by the employee remaining in the employment of the employer." California's labor agency uses closely related language — "nondiscretionary bonus" — in a different but conceptually related context: computing the "regular rate of pay" used for overtime, where a bonus that compensates "for hours worked, production or proficiency, or as an incentive to remain employed by the same employer" must be folded into that calculation precisely because it is not discretionary.
clauses.gap: This is one state's labor-agency interpretation and case description, used as real evidence of California's approach to a formula- or quota-based bonus — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific bonus arrangement, and not a claim that any specific bonus described in this document actually meets this standard. The Chinn v. China Nat. Aviation Corp. (1955) 138 Cal.App.2d 98 discussion quoted below is reused as the DLSE Enforcement Manual (§ 35.4.1, June 2002) describes and quotes it, not independently verified against Chinn's own opinion text this session; this session's CourtListener access was rate-limited and direct fetches to case-law sites were blocked, as disclosed in this document's clause on discretionary bonuses, so that gap applies here as well and is not papered over. The DLSE "nondiscretionary bonus" language quoted below (from the agency's Overtime FAQ) is offered honestly for what it is: guidance developed for the different question of calculating the regular rate of pay for overtime, not guidance written specifically to answer whether a bonus must be paid out at termination — it is cited here only as further evidence that California's labor agency treats a formula- or quota-tied bonus as categorically different from a discretionary one, not as a holding about termination payout timing. This clause and this document are informational only: this clause does not itself determine that any specific bonus or incentive arrangement described in this document is actually nondiscretionary or owed — that depends on the plan's own terms and the facts of the specific arrangement.

citations.case: California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 35.4.1, describing Chinn v. China Nat. Aviation Corp. (1955) 138 Cal.App.2d 98 (June 2002; California Department of Industrial Relations text)
citations.cite: DLSE Enforcement Manual § 35.4.1
citations.quote: In Chinn v. China Nat. Aviation Corp. (1955) 138 Cal.App.2d 98, 291 P.2d 91 the court held that if the bonus is part of the inducement for the initial or continuing employment (see also Sabatini v. Hensley (1958) 161 Cal.App.2d 172, 326 P.2d 622; Hunter v. Ryan (1930) 109 Cal.App. 736, 293 P. 825) and where the employer, in announcing the plan, did not expressly qualify his promise to pay on any requirement of continued employment, the bonus is earned by the employee remaining in the employment of the employer.

citations.quote: A nondiscretionary bonus is included in determining the regular rate of pay for computing overtime when the bonus is compensation for hours worked, production or proficiency, or as an incentive to remain employed by the same employer.

clauses.title: A "Must Be Employed on the Payment Date" Condition: Enforceable Sometimes, Contested Often
clauses.body: California authorities do not resolve, by a single clean rule, whether a bonus condition requiring the employee to still be employed on a future payment date is enforceable against an employee terminated before that date. The DLSE's Enforcement Manual describes the result as turning on how the condition was written: where the employer has "expressly qualified its promise of a bonus on a requirement of continued employment," an employee who leaves before the bonus calculation date is not entitled to receive it — a rule the manual traces to Lucien v. All States Trucking (1981) 116 Cal.App.3d 972, 975, and further back to Peterson v. California Shipbuilding Corp. (1947) 80 Cal.App.2d 827, 831. But where the bonus plan does not expressly condition payment on continued employment through that date, the same manual describes a different result: it discusses Hill v. Kaiser Aetna (1982) 130 Cal.App.3d 188, where an employee who resigned before a bonus's calculation date was nonetheless held to be vested in the prior year's bonus because the plan did not expressly require continued employment and the bonus itself was an inducement for continued employment. Which of these two lines of description applies to a specific bonus plan depends on the plan's own written terms — described here as: {{bonusPlanTerms}} — and on whether {{terminationDate}} fell before or after whatever date, if any, that plan specifies.
clauses.gap: This is one state's labor-agency description of case law, used as real evidence that California's treatment of an employment-through-the-payment-date condition is fact- and plan-specific rather than resolved by one clean statutory rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific bonus plan, and not a claim about how any particular plan would actually be characterized. The two citations below are both drawn from the same document — Section 35 of the DLSE Enforcement Manual — describing two different cases with two different outcomes; they are presented here as one source's account of a split in outcomes, not as two independent corroborating sources for a single rule. The descriptions of Lucien v. All States Trucking, Peterson v. California Shipbuilding Corp., and Hill v. Kaiser Aetna are reused as the DLSE Enforcement Manual (§ 35.2-35.3, June 2002) describes them, not independently verified against each case's own opinion text this session; this session's CourtListener access was rate-limited and direct fetches to individual case pages were blocked, as disclosed in this document's clause on discretionary bonuses, and that same gap applies to all three cases named in this clause. This document set's Commission Payout Upon Termination document separately covers a related but distinct earned-versus-contingent distinction for commissions specifically, verified there against the commission case Steinhebel v. Los Angeles Times Communications, LLC directly; this clause does not repeat that verification because commissions and bonuses are governed by different lines of authority, as this document's declaration clause explains. This clause and this document are informational only: this clause does not itself determine that any specific bonus condition in any specific plan is enforceable or unenforceable, or that any specific amount is owed — that depends on the plan's own written terms and the facts of the specific arrangement.

citations.case: California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 35.2, describing Lucien v. All States Trucking (1981) 116 Cal.App.3d 972 and Peterson v. California Shipbuilding Corp. (1947) 80 Cal.App.2d 827 (June 2002; California Department of Industrial Relations text)
citations.cite: DLSE Enforcement Manual § 35.2
citations.quote: An employee who voluntarily leaves his employment before the bonus calculation date is not entitled to receive it if the employer has expressly qualified its promise of a bonus on a requirement of continued employment. Lucien v. All States Trucking (1981) 116 Cal.App.3d 972, 975. This has been the rule ever since Peterson v. California Shipbuilding Corp. (1947) 80 Cal.App.2d 827, 831, 183 P.2d 56.

citations.case: California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 35.3, describing Hill v. Kaiser Aetna (1982) 130 Cal.App.3d 188 (June 2002; California Department of Industrial Relations text)
citations.cite: DLSE Enforcement Manual § 35.3
citations.quote: Where the promise of a bonus is not expressly conditioned on continued employment an employee who voluntarily leaves employment may be entitled to the bonus if other applicable conditions have been satisfied. Thus, in Hill v. Kaiser Aetna (1982) 130 Cal.App.3d 188, an employee who resigned on January 3, 1978, was held to be vested in his right to a bonus for calendar year 1977 where: (1) the bonus plan did not expressly require continued employment, and (2) the bonus was an inducement for continued employment.

clauses.title: Employer-Initiated Discharge Before a Bonus Period Ends: A Different Question from a Voluntary Quit
clauses.body: The DLSE Enforcement Manual treats an employer-initiated discharge, before the terms of a bonus arrangement have been completed, as a legally different situation from an employee's own voluntary departure. Under common-law contract principles the manual applies, one party to a contract may not use its own act to prevent the other party from completing the conditions that would have entitled that party to performance: "If the employee is discharged before completion of all of the terms of the bonus agreement, and there is not valid cause, based on conduct of the employee, for the discharge, the employee may be entitled to recover at least a pro-rata share of the promised bonus." This is a distinct question from the discretionary-versus-nondiscretionary line addressed elsewhere in this document: it applies even to a bonus that would otherwise have required the employee to remain employed through a later date, where the reason employment did not continue was the employer's own decision to discharge the employee for reasons unrelated to the employee's conduct.
clauses.gap: This is one state's labor-agency interpretation of common-law contract principles, used as real evidence of how California's enforcement agency approaches a discharge-before-completion scenario for bonus pay — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific separation, and not a claim that any specific termination was, in fact, a discharge without cause as opposed to a voluntary quit or a discharge for cause. The quoted manual section (§ 35.4.4, June 2002) cites only an internal DLSE opinion letter (O.L. 1987.06.03) as its authority, not a published court decision; that opinion letter itself was not independently located or read this session, so this clause is disclosed as agency guidance describing a common-law contract principle, not as a case holding. This session's CourtListener case-law tools were rate-limited and direct case-page fetches were blocked, as disclosed in this document's clause on discretionary bonuses, and the same gap applies here: no independent published California decision squarely addressing pro-rata bonus recovery on a for-cause-less discharge was located and read this session. This clause and this document are informational only: this clause does not itself determine that any specific separation was, or was not, a discharge without cause, or that any specific pro-rata amount is owed — those are factual questions this clause does not resolve.

citations.case: California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 35.4.4, "Termination Of The Employment By The Employer" (June 2002; California Department of Industrial Relations text)
citations.cite: DLSE Enforcement Manual § 35.4.4
citations.quote: Termination Of The Employment By The Employer. Common law contract theories will not allow one party to the contract to prevent the other party from completing the contract. If the employee is discharged before completion of all of the terms of the bonus agreement, and there is not valid cause, based on conduct of the employee, for the discharge, the employee may be entitled to recover at least a pro-rata share of the promised bonus.

clauses.title: Not Every Bonus-Forfeiture Condition Is Enforceable — Even Beyond the Discretionary/Nondiscretionary Line
clauses.body: Even where a bonus plan expressly conditions payment on some fact about the employee's later status, California authorities have recognized that not every such condition will be enforced. The DLSE Enforcement Manual describes a California Court of Appeal decision striking down a bonus- and profit-sharing forfeiture condition that penalized an employee for going to work for a competitor after leaving, on the ground that the condition was "contrary to the strong public policy against contracts by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade or business" — the same public policy embodied in California's statute voiding most non-compete restrictions. This illustrates that the discretionary/nondiscretionary distinction addressed elsewhere in this document is not the only limit California law places on bonus-forfeiture conditions; a condition can be independently unenforceable for a reason unrelated to discretion, such as conflicting with a separate California public policy.
clauses.gap: This is one state's labor-agency description of case law and a related statute, used as real evidence that a bonus-forfeiture condition can be independently unenforceable on grounds unrelated to the discretionary/nondiscretionary line — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific bonus plan, and not a claim that any particular condition in any particular plan is, or is not, enforceable. The Ware v. Merrill Lynch, Pierce, Fenner & Smith, Inc. (1972) 24 Cal.App.3d 35 discussion quoted below is reused as the DLSE Enforcement Manual (§ 35.4.2, June 2002) describes it, not independently verified against the case's own opinion text this session, for the same CourtListener rate-limiting and blocked-direct-fetch reasons disclosed in this document's clause on discretionary bonuses. The underlying statute the manual cross-references, Business and Professions Code section 16600, is not itself independently fetched or quoted in this clause; it is named only as the manual names it, as the statutory embodiment of the public policy the described case applied. This clause and this document are informational only: this clause does not itself determine that any specific condition in any specific bonus plan is lawful or unlawful — that depends on the condition's own terms and the facts of the specific arrangement.

citations.case: California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 35.4.2, describing Ware v. Merrill Lynch, Pierce, Fenner & Smith, Inc. (1972) 24 Cal.App.3d 35 (June 2002; California Department of Industrial Relations text)
citations.cite: DLSE Enforcement Manual § 35.4.2
citations.quote: Illegal Conditions. Ware v. Merrill Lynch, Pierce, Fenner & Smith, Inc. (1972) 24 Cal.App.3d 35, 100 Cal.Rptr. 791, involved a profit-sharing plan containing a provision that an employee who voluntarily terminated his employment and went to work for a competitor forfeited his rights to benefits under the plan. The court held that the forfeiture clause was invalid as it was contrary to the strong public policy against contracts by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade or business.

clauses.title: An Earned, Unpaid Bonus Rides on the Same Final-Pay Deadlines and Waiting-Time Penalty as Other Wages
clauses.body: Once a bonus or incentive payment is properly classified as an earned wage — as distinct from a still-discretionary or not-yet-earned amount — California law does not carve out a separate payment deadline or a separate penalty scheme for it. It is folded into the same final-wage-payment deadlines, and the same willful-nonpayment penalty, that apply to wages generally: where an employer willfully fails to pay wages due to a discharged or quitting employee, "the wages of the employee shall continue as a penalty from the due date thereof at the same rate until paid or until an action therefor is commenced," up to a cap of 30 days. Whether that penalty actually applies to a specific unpaid bonus depends on the same final-pay-timing and willfulness questions this project's Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter document already addresses for unpaid wages generally.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that an earned bonus is folded into the same final-wage deadlines and waiting-time-penalty framework as other wages — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific separation, and not a claim that any specific bonus amount was actually earned, unpaid, or subject to a willful violation. This clause deliberately does not re-derive the specific final-pay deadlines of Labor Code sections 201 and 202, the full mechanics and 30-day cap of the waiting-time penalty, or the case law defining "willful" for this purpose, because this project's Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter document already contains dedicated, separately verified clauses covering those in full; this clause exists only to connect an earned bonus, once recognized as a wage under this document's other clauses, to that already-covered framework rather than to duplicate it. The statutory text quoted below (Labor Code section 203(a)) was fetched twice this session, directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, using two different User-Agent headers, and found byte-identical both times, independently of that same section's earlier verification for this project's Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter document — this is honestly the same statutory section already cited elsewhere in this corpus, re-verified rather than newly discovered, not a second independent source. This clause and this document are informational only: this clause does not itself determine that any specific bonus described in this document was actually earned, unpaid as of the termination date, or that the employer's failure to pay it, if any, was willful — those are factual and legal questions this clause does not resolve.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 203(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: If an employer willfully fails to pay, without abatement or reduction, in accordance with Sections 201, 201.3, 201.5, 201.6, 201.8, 201.9, 202, and 205.5, any wages of an employee who is discharged or who quits, the wages of the employee shall continue as a penalty from the due date thereof at the same rate until paid or until an action therefor is commenced; but the wages shall not continue for more than 30 days.

clauses.title: Summary of the Bonus or Incentive Arrangement and Signature
Purpose of This Digital Assets and Online Account Access Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act (Probate Code sections 870 through 884), the statutory framework governing when and how a fiduciary — an executor or other personal representative, a trustee, an agent acting under a power of attorney, or a conservator — may obtain access to a person's digital assets and online accounts from the company or platform that holds them (the “custodian”), such as an email provider, a social media platform, or a cloud storage service. It is prepared by {{preparerName}} concerning the digital assets and online accounts of {{accountHolderName}}, in connection with {{fiduciaryName}}'s prospective or actual role as {{fiduciaryRole}}. This statutory framework operates alongside — not in place of — the general authority a will, trust, or power of attorney already grants a fiduciary over a person's property; it supplies the specific rules a custodian and a fiduciary must follow for digital assets and online accounts specifically, including what document a fiduciary must produce, how and when a custodian must respond, and the different rules that apply depending on whether the fiduciary is asking for the content of a user's electronic communications (such as the text of emails or messages) or only a catalogue of them (such as sender, recipient, and timestamp information without message content). This information sheet does not itself grant {{fiduciaryName}} access to any digital asset or online account belonging to {{accountHolderName}}, does not itself constitute the will, trust, power of attorney, court order, or other record a custodian may require, and does not determine what any specific custodian will disclose in any specific case.

clauses.title: Statutory Definitions: “Digital Asset,” “Custodian,” and the Content/Catalogue Distinction
clauses.body: California's Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act defines the terms that determine what it reaches and how. A “digital asset” is defined broadly: “Digital asset” means an electronic record in which an individual has a right or interest. — meaning the term covers essentially any electronic record a person has a right or interest in, not a fixed list of specific account types, though the statute separately clarifies that an underlying asset or liability isn't itself a “digital asset” merely because it is recorded electronically, unless that asset or liability is itself an electronic record. The “custodian” is the company or platform on the other side of the relationship: “Custodian” means a person who carries, maintains, processes, receives, or stores a digital asset of a user. — for example, an email provider, a social media platform, or a cloud storage service holding {{accountHolderName}}'s account. The Act also draws a sharp line between two kinds of information a custodian might disclose about an account. A “catalogue of electronic communications” is limited to envelope-level information: “Catalogue of electronic communications” means information that identifies each person with which a user has had an electronic communication, the time and date of the communication, and the electronic address of the person.. “Content of an electronic communication,” by contrast, reaches the substance of what was actually said: “Content of an electronic communication” means information concerning the substance or meaning of the communication, which meets all of the following requirements:(1) Has been sent or received by a user.(2) Is in electronic storage by a custodian providing an electronic communication service to the public or is carried or maintained by a custodian providing a remote-computing service to the public.(3) Is not readily accessible to the public. As the clauses below describe, which document a fiduciary must produce, and how specifically a will, trust, or power of attorney must address digital assets, differs depending on whether a fiduciary is requesting a catalogue or content.

clauses.gap: This is California's own statute, used here as real evidence of what California's Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act actually provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific fiduciary's access to any specific account. Most states have enacted some version of the Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act, but the details — including document requirements, timeframes, and liability protections — can differ from state to state, and this document describes California's version only. This clause cites four subsections of the same statutory section, § 871(c), (d), (f), and (h); they are treated here as one source describing that one section's definitions, not as four independent corroborating sources. One correction to an initial research assumption: the content-versus-catalogue distinction is defined here, in § 871(c) and (d), but the specific document requirements that turn on that distinction appear in later, separate sections (§§ 876-877 for a personal representative, §§ 878-879 for a trustee, and §§ 879.1-879.2 for an agent) rather than in § 875, which instead concerns a custodian's own discretion over the degree and format of access it grants and permits a reasonable administrative charge for disclosure — not the content/catalogue split itself. No published California case law interpreting these definitions was located or relied on for this document; it is based on the statutory text alone. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself grant any fiduciary access to any digital asset or online account, does not itself constitute the will, trust, power of attorney, court order, or other record a custodian may require, and does not determine what any specific custodian will provide, require, or accept in response to any specific request.

clauses.title: Which Fiduciaries, Time Periods, and Accounts This Act Covers
clauses.body: The Act applies broadly across fiduciary roles and across time: (a) This part shall apply to all of the following:(1) A fiduciary acting under a will executed before, on, or after January 1, 2017.(2) A personal representative acting for a decedent who died before, on, or after January 1, 2017.(3) A trustee acting under a trust created before, on, or after January 1, 2017.(4) A custodian of digital assets for a user if the user resides in this state or resided in this state at the time of the user’s death.(5) A conservator appointed before, on, or after January 1, 2025.(6) A fiduciary acting under a power of attorney executed before, on, or after January 1, 2025. Read together, this reaches a fiduciary acting under a will, a personal representative administering a decedent's estate, a trustee, a conservator, and — as of a 2024 amendment effective January 1, 2025 — an agent acting under a power of attorney, regardless of when the underlying document was executed or the relevant appointment made, and regardless of whether {{accountHolderName}}'s account predates the statute. It also reaches any custodian of digital assets for a user who resides, or resided at death, in California. The Act carves out one category from its coverage entirely: (b) This part does not apply to a digital asset of an employer used by an employee in the ordinary course of the employer’s business. — meaning a workplace email or file-storage account {{accountHolderName}} used only in the ordinary course of an employer's business is not covered by this framework at all, whatever role {{fiduciaryName}} holds.

clauses.gap: This is California's own statute, used here as real evidence of what California's Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act actually provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific fiduciary's access to any specific account. Most states have enacted some version of the Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act, but the details — including document requirements, timeframes, and liability protections — can differ from state to state, and this document describes California's version only. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, § 872(a) and (b); they are treated here as one source, not independent corroborating sources. A correction to an initial research assumption: this Act did not always reach an agent acting under a power of attorney, or a conservator, on the same footing as a personal representative or trustee — coverage of those two roles, and the disclosure procedures specific to them described elsewhere in this document, were added to the Act only by a 2024 amendment (Stats. 2024, Ch. 799) effective January 1, 2025; the Act as originally enacted in 2016 already covered fiduciaries acting under a will, personal representatives, and trustees. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself grant any fiduciary access to any digital asset or online account, does not itself constitute the will, trust, power of attorney, court order, or other record a custodian may require, and does not determine what any specific custodian will provide, require, or accept in response to any specific request.

clauses.title: The Three-Tier Priority System: Online Tool, Then Estate-Planning Document, Then Terms of Service
clauses.body: The Act establishes a specific order of priority for who controls disclosure of a user's digital assets. First, a custodian-provided online tool controls if the user used one: (a) A user may use an online tool to direct the custodian to disclose to a designated recipient or not disclose some or all of the user’s digital assets, including the content of electronic communications. If the online tool allows the user to modify or delete a direction at all times, a direction regarding disclosure using an online tool overrides a contrary direction by the user in a will, trust, power of attorney, or other record. — meaning a service like an account's own built-in legacy-contact or inactive-account-management feature, where one exists and {{accountHolderName}} used it to give a direction that could be changed or deleted at any time, overrides anything {{accountHolderName}} said in a will, trust, power of attorney, or other record. Second, only if {{accountHolderName}} did not use such a tool, or the custodian never offered one, does a will, trust, power of attorney, or other record control: (b) If a user has not used an online tool to give direction under subdivision (a) or if a custodian has not provided an online tool, a user may allow or prohibit in a will, trust, power of attorney, or other record the disclosure to a fiduciary of some or all of the user’s digital assets, including the contents of electronic communications sent or received by the user. Third, absent both of the above, the custodian's own terms-of-service agreement governs by default: (c) A fiduciary’s or designated recipient’s access to digital assets may be modified or eliminated by a user, by federal law, or by a terms-of-service agreement when the user has not provided any direction that is recognized in Section 873. — meaning where {{accountHolderName}} used no online tool and left no direction in a will, trust, power of attorney, or other record, {{fiduciaryName}}'s access to a given account depends on whatever the custodian's own terms of service, or federal law, otherwise allow.

clauses.title: What a Personal Representative Must Give a Custodian — and Why Content Requires More Than a Catalogue Does
clauses.body: Where {{fiduciaryName}} acts as personal representative of {{accountHolderName}}'s estate, the Act sets different requirements depending on whether the request is for content or only a catalogue. To obtain the catalogue of a deceased user's electronic communications, and any digital assets other than content, a personal representative generally need only establish the standard facts of the appointment: Unless the user prohibited disclosure of digital assets or the court directs otherwise, a custodian shall disclose to the personal representative of the estate of a deceased user a catalogue of electronic communications sent or received by the user and digital assets, other than the content of electronic communications, of the user, if the personal representative gives to the custodian all of the following:(a) A written request for disclosure in physical or electronic form.(b) A certified copy of the death certificate of the user.(c) A certified copy of the letter of appointment of the representative, a small-estate affidavit under Section 13101, or court order. To obtain the content of a deceased user's electronic communications instead, the Act requires the same threshold documents plus something more specific: If a deceased user consented to or a court directs disclosure of the content of electronic communications of the user, the custodian shall disclose to the personal representative of the estate of the user the content of an electronic communication sent or received by the user if the personal representative gives to the custodian all of the following: (d) Unless the user provided direction using an online tool, a copy of the user’s will, trust, power of attorney, or other record evidencing the user’s consent to disclosure of the content of electronic communications. In other words, a document that generally authorizes a personal representative to administer an estate is enough by itself for the catalogue tier, but obtaining actual message content requires a will, trust, power of attorney, or other record that specifically evidences {{accountHolderName}}'s consent to disclosure of content — not merely a general grant of estate-administration authority. The content provision also lets a custodian, before disclosing, require a court finding that disclosure would not violate the federal Stored Communications Act (18 U.S.C. § 2701 et seq.) — a reminder that this state statute operates alongside, and does not override, that separate federal constraint on a custodian's disclosure of communications content.

clauses.title: What a Trustee Must Give a Custodian — the Same Content/Catalogue Split, Tied to the Settlor's Consent
clauses.body: The Act imposes a parallel structure on a trustee seeking digital assets held in a trust's account, again splitting catalogue from content. For the catalogue of electronic communications sent or received through the trust's account, and other digital assets short of content, a trustee generally need only certify its status and the settlor's death: a custodian shall disclose, to a trustee that is not an original user of an account, the catalogue of electronic communications sent or received by an original or successor user and stored, carried, or maintained by the custodian in an account of the trust and any digital assets, other than the content of electronic communications, in which the trust has a right or interest if the settlor of the trust is deceased and the trustee gives the custodian all of the following:(a) A written request for disclosure in physical or electronic form.(b) A certified copy of the death certificate of the settlor.(c) A certified copy of the trust instrument or a certification of trust under Section 18100.5. For content, the Act again requires something beyond the trustee's basic authority: a custodian shall disclose to a trustee that is not an original user of an account the content of an electronic communication sent or received by an original or successor user and carried, maintained, processed, received, or stored by the custodian in the account of the trust if the trustee gives to the custodian all of the following: (c) A certified copy of the trust instrument, or a certification of trust under Section 18100.5, evidencing the settlor’s consent to disclosure of the content of electronic communications to the trustee. As with a personal representative, a trust instrument that generally names {{fiduciaryName}} as trustee and describes ordinary trustee powers is not, by its terms, described by the statute as sufficient for content; the trust instrument or certification of trust must evidence the settlor's consent to disclosure of content specifically.

clauses.title: What an Agent Under a Power of Attorney Must Give a Custodian — Content Requires an Express Grant
clauses.body: For an agent acting under a power of attorney — a role this Act only reached starting with a 2024 amendment effective January 1, 2025 — the statute states its general-versus-specific requirement more explicitly than it does for a personal representative or trustee. For the catalogue of a principal's electronic communications and non-content digital assets, either a specific or a general grant of authority in the power of attorney is enough: a custodian shall disclose to an agent with specific authority over digital assets or general authority to act on behalf of a principal a catalogue of electronic communications sent or received by the principal and digital assets, other than the content of electronic communications, of the principal if the agent gives the custodian all of the following: (a) A written request for disclosure in physical or electronic form. (b) An original or copy of the power of attorney that gives the agent specific authority over digital assets or general authority to act on behalf of the principal. For content, the statute requires more: To the extent a power of attorney expressly grants an agent authority over the content of electronic communications sent or received by the principal, and unless directed otherwise by the principal or the court, a custodian shall disclose the content of electronic communications to the agent if the agent gives the custodian all of the following: (a) A written request for disclosure in physical or electronic form. (b) An original or copy of the power of attorney expressly granting the agent authority over the content of electronic communications of the principal. Unlike the catalogue tier, the power of attorney must expressly grant {{fiduciaryName}} authority over content specifically; a power of attorney that only grants an agent general authority to act on {{accountHolderName}}'s behalf, without expressly addressing the content of electronic communications, does not by its terms satisfy this requirement, even though that same general grant is enough for the catalogue tier.

clauses.title: The Custodian's 60-Day Response Deadline, and the Good-Faith Liability Shield
clauses.body: Once a fiduciary or designated recipient has given a custodian the information the Act requires, the custodian is on a statutory clock: (a) Not later than 60 days after receipt of the information required under Sections 876 to 879.3, inclusive, a custodian shall comply with a request under this part from a fiduciary or designated recipient to disclose digital assets or terminate an account. If the custodian fails to comply with a request, the fiduciary or designated recipient may apply to the court for an order directing compliance. The Act also protects a custodian that complies: (f) (1) A custodian and its officers, employees, and agents are immune from liability for an act or omission done in good faith and in compliance with this part.(2) The protections specified in paragraph (1) do not apply in a case of gross negligence or willful or wanton misconduct of the custodian or its officers, employees, or agents. — meaning a custodian that discloses digital assets, or declines to, in a good-faith, compliant response to a request under this Act is shielded from liability for that act or omission, except where the custodian or its officers, employees, or agents acted with gross negligence or willful or wanton misconduct. A custodian is not without options if it questions a request: the same section lets a custodian require a fiduciary or designated recipient to first obtain a court order making specific findings, including that the account belongs to the decedent, principal, conservatee, or trustee in question, and that compliance would not violate the federal Stored Communications Act (18 U.S.C. § 2702) — another point at which this state statute is written to operate alongside, not in place of, that separate federal constraint.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California statutory law on the disclosure of real estate agency relationships in a transaction involving the real property at {{propertyAddress}}, where {{sellerName}} is named as seller and {{buyerName}} is named as buyer. It states what California law provides about the kinds of agency relationships a real estate agent may have in a real property transaction — seller's agent, buyer's agent, or dual agent — and about the disclosures the law requires concerning those relationships. It is separate from, and in addition to, any Transfer Disclosure Statement, HOA/CC&R disclosure, or lead-based paint disclosure provided in connection with this transaction, each of which concerns different subject matter. This information sheet does not itself identify, establish, or confirm which agency relationship exists in this transaction, and it does not tell {{sellerName}}, {{buyerName}}, or any real estate agent involved what agency relationship to choose or how to proceed.

clauses.title: What Kinds of Property and Transactions This Disclosure Law Covers
clauses.body: The statutes governing agency-relationship disclosure define "real property," for purposes of that disclosure duty, to include not only single-family residential property but also multiunit residential property with more than four dwelling units, commercial real property, vacant land, a ground lease coupled with improvements, and certain manufactured or mobile homes sold through an agent. "Real property transaction" is defined broadly as any transaction for the sale of real property in which a buyer, a seller, or both retain an agent, including a listing or an offer to purchase. Within that broader scope, "single-family residential property" is itself a defined term that reaches beyond a simple one-to-four-unit house: it includes real property improved with one to four dwelling units, a unit in a residential stock cooperative, condominium, or planned unit development, and certain mobilehomes or manufactured homes sold through a real estate broker. A separate and narrower statute in this same article — the broker's duty to conduct a reasonably competent and diligent visual inspection and disclose what it would reveal — is expressly limited to a prospective buyer of residential real property improved with one to four dwelling units or a qualifying manufactured home; that narrower unit-count trigger belongs to that separate visual-inspection duty, not to the agency-relationship disclosure and confirmation duties described elsewhere in this information sheet.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of how California defines the scope of its real estate agency-disclosure law — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific transaction; other states regulate real estate agency relationships differently. The agency-relationship disclosure and confirmation duties described in this document are not limited to a sale of residential real property comprising one to four dwelling units — that unit-count trigger applies to a different, narrower duty (the broker's visual-inspection duty) codified in a separate section of the same article, quoted here only for contrast. The three citations to § 2079.13 below are subsections of the same statutory section and are treated here as one source, not as independent corroborating sources; the citation to § 2079 is an independent section addressing a different duty, included to show the contrast in scope rather than to corroborate the § 2079.13 definitions. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine which scope definition applies to any specific transaction, and it does not satisfy any disclosure or confirmation that the statutes described here require.

clauses.title: Seller's Agent, Buyer's Agent, and Dual Agent — Statutory Definitions
clauses.body: California statutory law recognizes three distinct agency roles a real estate agent can occupy in a real property transaction. A seller's agent is a person who has obtained a listing of real property to act as agent for compensation. A buyer's agent is an agent who represents a buyer in a real property transaction. A dual agent is an agent acting, either directly or through a salesperson or broker associate, as agent for both the seller and the buyer in the same real property transaction. An agent may lawfully act as a dual agent, but only with the knowledge and consent of both the seller and the buyer.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of how California defines these three agency roles — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific transaction. The three citations to § 2079.13 below are subsections of the same statutory section and are treated here as one source, not as independent corroborating sources; the citation to § 2079.16 is an independent, separately enacted section used as a second, distinct source for the dual-agency consent requirement. This document is informational only: it does not itself identify which of these three roles any specific agent occupies in any specific transaction, and it does not satisfy any disclosure or confirmation that the statutes described here require.

clauses.title: When the General Agency Disclosure Form Must Be Given
clauses.body: California statutory law fixes when the general agency-relationship disclosure form must be provided, and to whom, and the timing differs by which agent is providing it. A seller's agent, if any, must provide the disclosure form to the seller before entering into the listing agreement with the seller — not merely "as soon as practicable" before an offer. A buyer's agent must provide the disclosure form to the buyer as soon as practicable, before execution of a buyer-broker representation agreement and before execution of the buyer's offer to purchase; if the buyer's agent did not prepare the offer to purchase, that agent must present the disclosure form to the buyer no later than the next business day after receiving the offer from the buyer. Whichever agent provides the disclosure form must obtain a signed acknowledgment of its receipt from the buyer or seller, subject to a statutory exception.

The three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 2079.14) and are treated here as one source, not as independent corroborating sources. The statutory exception to the signed-acknowledgment requirement, referenced in subdivision (b) as "except as provided in Section 2079.15," is noted but not itself researched or quoted in this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether the disclosure form was, or was not, timely provided or acknowledged in any specific transaction, and it does not satisfy any disclosure or confirmation that the statutes described here require.

clauses.title: Required Text of the Agency Disclosure Form — Duties Described
clauses.body: California statutory law prescribes the actual text that must appear on the general agency-relationship disclosure form, captioned "Disclosure Regarding Real Estate Agency Relationship (As required by the Civil Code)." That prescribed text separates two kinds of duty. A seller's agent owes the seller a fiduciary duty of utmost care, integrity, honesty, and loyalty — a duty owed only to the agent's own client. A buyer's agent owes that same fiduciary duty of utmost care, integrity, honesty, and loyalty to the buyer only. Separately, the same prescribed text describes duties that a seller's agent or a buyer's agent owes to both the buyer and the seller — including the non-client party, who is not that agent's fiduciary client: diligent exercise of reasonable skill and care in performance of the agent's duties; a duty of honest and fair dealing and good faith; and a duty to disclose all facts known to the agent materially affecting the value or desirability of the property that are not known to, or within the diligent attention and observation of, the parties. In a dual agency, the prescribed text states that the agent owes the fiduciary duty of utmost care, integrity, honesty, and loyalty to both the seller and the buyer at once, while also providing that a dual agent may not, without the express permission of the respective party, disclose to the other party confidential information such as either party's financial position, motivations, bargaining position, or willingness to accept a lower or pay a higher price than currently offered.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's prescribed agency-disclosure form text — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific transaction; other states use different disclosure forms or none at all. All five citations below quote different portions of the same statutory section (§ 2079.16), and are treated here as one source, not as independent corroborating sources. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine which of these duties applies to any specific agent in any specific transaction, and it does not satisfy the statute's requirement that this actual prescribed form — not this information sheet — be delivered and acknowledged.
