citations.quote: The term “ newly hired employee ” means an employee who— (i) has not previously been employed by the employer ; or (ii) was previously employed by the employer but has been separated from such prior employment for at least 60 consecutive days.

clauses.title: Information a New Hire Report Must Contain
clauses.body: California law specifies what a new hire report must contain: (A) the employee's name, address, and Social Security number; (B) the employer's name, address, state employer identification number (if one has been issued), and the identifying number assigned to the employer under Internal Revenue Code § 6109 (its federal EIN); and (C) the first date the employee worked. An employer may satisfy this reporting duty by submitting a copy of the employee's completed Form W-4, a form the department itself provides, or any other hiring document already being transmitted — by first-class mail, magnetically, or electronically.
clauses.gap: This is California law, used as evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific employer's situation. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself file a new-hire report with the California Employment Development Department or any other agency, and it does not itself fulfill any employer's reporting duty. All four citations below are to different paragraphs of the same statutory subdivision, Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5(d) — paragraph (4)'s subparagraphs (A), (B), and (C) (the three required content items) and paragraph (5) (the permitted reporting formats) — and are treated as one source, not independent. The statute's list of required content is exactly these three items; it does not separately require, for example, the employee's date of birth or job title as part of this report. This clause does not independently verify the current name or number of any specific EDD-provided reporting form (the statute itself does not name one), so no form name is stated here.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5(d)(4)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code, required employee information
citations.quote: The name, address, and social security number of the employees.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5(d)(4)(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code, required employer information
citations.quote: The employer’s name, address, state employer identification number (if one has been issued), and identifying number assigned to the employer under Section 6109 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5(d)(4)(C) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code, the first-date-worked requirement
citations.quote: The first date the employee worked.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5(d)(5) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code, permitted reporting formats (W-4 or equivalent)
citations.quote: Employers may report pursuant to this section by submitting a copy of the employee’s W-4 form, a form provided by the department, or any other hiring document transmitted by first-class mail, magnetically, or electronically.

clauses.title: Penalties for Failing to Report
clauses.body: California law authorizes the Employment Development Department to assess a penalty of $24 for each failure to report the hiring of an employee as required and within the time required, unless the failure is due to good cause; the penalty rises to $490 if the failure results from a conspiracy between the employer and the employee not to supply the required report, or to supply a false or incomplete one. These amounts are not California's own invention set independent of federal law: the federal statute underlying this program caps what a state may set its new-hire-reporting civil penalty at — no more than $25 per failure, or $500 for a conspiracy — and California's own codified penalty amounts sit at or under that federal ceiling.
clauses.gap: This is California and federal law, used as evidence of what California and the federal government requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific employer's situation. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself file a new-hire report with the California Employment Development Department or any other agency, and it does not itself fulfill any employer's reporting duty. The two citations below are to genuinely independent, separately numbered sources — California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5(e) and federal 42 U.S.C. § 653a(d) — not subsections of a single section, so no same-source caveat applies. This clause states the penalty amounts as codified in the statutory text itself; it does not independently verify whether either figure has since been adjusted for inflation by regulation or administrative action outside the statute, and does not state that these are the only consequences an employer could face (for example, the statute is silent on any private right of action, and this clause takes no position on whether one might exist under some other law). "Good cause" is not defined in the statutory text reviewed.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code, the codified penalty amounts
citations.quote: For each failure to report the hiring of an employee, as required and within the time required by this section, unless the failure is due to good cause, the department may assess a penalty of twenty-four dollars ($24), or four hundred ninety dollars ($490) if the failure is the result of conspiracy between the employer and employee not to supply the required report or to supply a false or incomplete report.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 653a(d) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Federal statute, the ceiling on a state's new-hire-reporting civil penalty
citations.quote: The State shall have the option to set a State civil money penalty which shall not exceed— (1) $25 per failure to meet the requirements of this section with respect to a newly hired employee ; or (2) $500 if, under State law, the failure is the result of a conspiracy between the employer and the employee to not supply the required report or to supply a false or incomplete report.

clauses.title: Separate Reporting Duty for Certain Independent Contractors
clauses.body: California law imposes a second, independent reporting duty distinct from the employee new-hire reporting duty described above: a "service-recipient" — defined to include an individual, corporation, association, or partnership doing business in the state — that makes or is required to make an information return to the IRS under Internal Revenue Code § 6041A for payments to a "service-provider" (an individual who is not its employee for California purposes) must also report specified information to the Employment Development Department. That duty is triggered within 20 days of the earlier of two events: the service-recipient's aggregate payments to that service-provider first reaching $600 in a calendar year, or the service-recipient entering into a contract or contracts with that service-provider providing for aggregate payments of $600 or more in a calendar year. The required report includes the service-provider's full name, address, and Social Security number, among other identifying information.
clauses.gap: This is California law, used as evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific employer's situation. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself file a new-hire report with the California Employment Development Department or any other agency, and it does not itself fulfill any employer's reporting duty. This is a real, and easy to miss, feature of California's program: it is not limited to common-law employees the way the federal underlying statute, 42 U.S.C. § 653a, is. All four citations below are to different subdivisions of the same statutory section, Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.8 — subdivisions (a) and (b)(2) (who is covered) and subdivision (c) and its paragraph (1) (the trigger and required content) — and are treated as one source, not independent. This clause does not summarize § 1088.8(c)'s remaining required-content items (the service-recipient's own identifying information, the contract date, and the contract's dollar amount), nor § 1088.8(d)'s retention period for the department, nor § 1088.8(f)'s limits on how the department may use information collected under this section. Section 1088.8(e) sets the same $24/$490 penalty structure described in this information sheet's penalties clause, applied here to a service-recipient's own failure to comply with subdivision (c).

citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code, the independent-contractor reporting trigger (IRC § 6041A)
citations.quote: Effective January 1, 2001, any service-recipient, as defined in subdivision (b), who makes or is required to make a return to the Internal Revenue Service, in accordance with subdivision (a) of Section 6041A of the Internal Revenue Code (relating to payments made to a service-provider as compensation for services) shall file with the department information as required under subdivision (c).

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.8(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code, definition of "service-provider"
citations.quote: “Service-provider” means an individual who is not an employee of the service-recipient for California purposes and who received compensation or executes a contract for services performed for that service-recipient within or without the state.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.8(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code, the $600 aggregate-payment reporting trigger and 20-day deadline
citations.quote: Each service-recipient shall report all of the following information to the department, within 20 days of the earlier of first making payments that in the aggregate equal or exceed six hundred dollars ($600) in any year to a service-provider, or entering into a contract or contracts with a service-provider providing for payments that in the aggregate equal or exceed six hundred dollars ($600) in any year:

clauses.title: About This New Hire Reporting Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This New Hire Reporting — Information Sheet describes the federal and California legal framework requiring an employer to report a newly hired or rehired employee to a state new-hire reporting agency, in connection with {{companyName}}'s hiring of {{employeeName}}, whose first date of work is {{startDate}}. It summarizes selected requirements of the federal Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996 (42 U.S.C. § 653a) and California's implementing statute, Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5: what counts as a reportable "new employee" or "rehire," the reporting deadline, the information a report must contain, and the statute's own reporting penalties. It also summarizes California's separate reporting duty for certain independent contractors, Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.8.

This information sheet is not the new-hire report itself, does not submit any report to the California Employment Development Department or any other agency on {{companyName}}'s behalf, and does not determine whether {{companyName}}'s own reporting practices for {{employeeName}} are or are not compliant with California law.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Declaration of Partners and Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Domestic Partnership Dissolution — Information Sheet concerns the registered domestic partnership of {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}, who registered as domestic partners in California on {{registrationDate}}. It is prepared for background use in connection with the possible filing of a Notice of Termination of Domestic Partnership with the California Secretary of State, or a petition for dissolution, nullity, or legal separation of the domestic partnership in the Superior Court of California, County of {{countyOfFiling}}. This information sheet describes California's statutory framework for ending a registered domestic partnership — the administrative and judicial paths, the same-as-marriage standards that apply to the judicial path, and the community-property default — as background for that filing. It is not itself a Notice of Termination or a court filing, and completing it does not terminate, dissolve, or otherwise change the legal status of the domestic partnership of {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}. Only the Secretary of State's processing of a qualifying Notice of Termination, or a court judgment, can do that.

clauses.title: Administrative Termination — Eligibility for the Secretary of State's Notice of Termination
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} state that California law allows a registered domestic partnership to be terminated without any court dissolution proceeding, by filing a Notice of Termination of Domestic Partnership with the Secretary of State, but only if all of the following conditions exist at the time of filing: the Notice is signed by both registered domestic partners; there are no children of the relationship, born or adopted before or after registration, and neither partner knows themselves to be pregnant; the partnership is not more than five years in duration; neither partner has any interest in real property, subject to a narrow exception for a short-term residential lease that includes no purchase option and ends within a year of filing; neither partner has unpaid obligations, or the partners' community-property assets do not exceed, the statutory dollar thresholds set by Family Code Section 2400 (thresholds that are periodically adjusted and are not restated here); the partners have executed an agreement dividing their community-property assets and liabilities; both partners waive any right to support from the other; both partners have read and understand the Secretary of State's brochure describing the requirements, nature, and effect of terminating a domestic partnership; and both partners desire the termination.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California), used as evidence of what that state's law provides for ending a registered domestic partnership — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific partnership. This document is informational only: it does not itself terminate any partnership or resolve any dissolution, nullity, or legal-separation matter; only the Secretary of State's processing of a qualifying Notice of Termination, or a court judgment, can do that. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 299(a)); no additional independent source was found for this. The specific current dollar thresholds referenced by Family Code Section 2400 are indexed and adjusted by the Judicial Council roughly every two years and were not independently re-verified as of any particular current date; this clause states only that such thresholds exist and are cross-referenced, not their present dollar amounts.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 299(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the ten conditions for administrative termination by Notice of Termination
citations.quote: (a) A registered domestic partnership may be terminated without filing a proceeding for dissolution of domestic partnership by the filing of a Notice of Termination of Domestic Partnership with the Secretary of State pursuant to this section, provided that all of the following conditions exist at the time of the filing: (1) The Notice of Termination of Domestic Partnership is signed by both registered domestic partners. (2) There are no children of the relationship of the parties born before or after registration of the domestic partnership or adopted by the parties after registration of the domestic partnership, and neither of the registered domestic partners, to their knowledge, is pregnant. (3) The registered domestic partnership is not more than five years in duration. (4) Neither party has any interest in real property wherever situated, with the exception of the lease of a residence occupied by either party which satisfies the following requirements: (A) The lease does not include an option to purchase. (B) The lease terminates within one year from the date of filing of the Notice of Termination of Domestic Partnership. (5) There are no unpaid obligations in excess of the amount described in paragraph (6) of subdivision (a) of Section 2400, as adjusted by subdivision (b) of Section 2400, incurred by either or both of the parties after registration of the domestic partnership, excluding the amount of any unpaid obligation with respect to an automobile. (6) The total fair market value of community property assets, excluding all encumbrances and automobiles, including any deferred compensation or retirement plan, is less than the amount described in paragraph (7) of subdivision (a) of Section 2400, as adjusted by subdivision (b) of Section 2400, and neither party has separate property assets, excluding all encumbrances and automobiles, in excess of that amount. (7) The parties have executed an agreement setting forth the division of assets and the assumption of liabilities of the community property, and have executed any documents, title certificates, bills of sale, or other evidence of transfer necessary to effectuate the agreement. (8) The parties waive any rights to support by the other domestic partner. (9) The parties have read and understand a brochure prepared by the Secretary of State describing the requirements, nature, and effect of terminating a domestic partnership. (10) Both parties desire that the domestic partnership be terminated.

clauses.title: Effective Date, Revocation, and Court Challenge of an Administrative Termination
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} state that filing a Notice of Termination of Domestic Partnership with the Secretary of State does not end the partnership immediately: termination becomes effective six months after the date of filing, unless either partner files a notice of revocation with the Secretary of State and mails a copy of it to the other partner before that date. Once effective, the termination is treated for all purposes as the entry of a judgment of dissolution of the domestic partnership. Terminating a partnership this way does not bar either partner from later asking the superior court to set the termination aside and declare it null and void, on proof that the partners did not actually meet the eligibility conditions at the time of filing, or on a showing of fraud, duress, mistake, or another ground recognized at law or in equity.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California), used as evidence of what that state's law provides for ending a registered domestic partnership — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific partnership. This document is informational only: it does not itself terminate any partnership or resolve any dissolution, nullity, or legal-separation matter; only the Secretary of State's processing of a qualifying Notice of Termination, or a court judgment, can do that. This is a single statutory section, two contiguous subsections (§ 299(b)-(c)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 299(b)-(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the six-month effective date, revocation procedure, and grounds to set aside the termination
citations.quote: (b) The registered domestic partnership shall be terminated effective six months after the date of filing of the Notice of Termination of Domestic Partnership with the Secretary of State pursuant to this section, provided that neither party has, before that date, filed with the Secretary of State a notice of revocation of the termination of domestic partnership, in the form and content as shall be prescribed by the Secretary of State, and sent to the other party a copy of the notice of revocation by first-class mail, postage prepaid, at the other party’s last known address. The effect of termination of a domestic partnership pursuant to this section shall be the same as, and shall be treated for all purposes as, the entry of a judgment of dissolution of a domestic partnership. (c) The termination of a domestic partnership pursuant to subdivision (b) does not prejudice nor bar the rights of either of the parties to institute an action in the superior court to set aside the termination for fraud, duress, mistake, or any other ground recognized at law or in equity. A court may set aside the termination of domestic partnership and declare the termination of the domestic partnership null and void upon proof that the parties did not meet the requirements of subdivision (a) at the time of the filing of the Notice of Termination of Domestic Partnership with the Secretary of State.

clauses.title: Judicial Dissolution for Partnerships That Don't Qualify — Same Procedures as Marriage, Plus One Added Exception
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} state that a domestic partnership that does not meet every condition for administrative termination can be ended only through a proceeding in California Superior Court, which has jurisdiction over the dissolution, nullity, and legal separation of registered domestic partnerships. Except as provided for administrative termination, that judicial proceeding follows the same procedures, and the partners possess the same rights, protections, and benefits, and are subject to the same responsibilities, obligations, and duties, as apply respectively to the dissolution, nullity, or legal separation of a marriage. California law adds one further, partnership-specific rule on top of that equivalence: because a domestic partner's consent to it is built into the Declaration of Domestic Partnership filed at registration, a proceeding to dissolve, void, or legally separate a domestic partnership registered in California may be filed in California's superior courts even if, at the time of filing, neither partner resides in or is domiciled in California — a jurisdictional allowance that does not depend on either partner's sex or on the marriage-specific residency exception that otherwise applies to some marriage-dissolution proceedings under California law.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California), used as evidence of what that state's law provides for ending a registered domestic partnership — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific partnership. This document is informational only: it does not itself terminate any partnership or resolve any dissolution, nullity, or legal-separation matter; only the Secretary of State's processing of a qualifying Notice of Termination, or a court judgment, can do that. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 299(d)); no additional independent source was found for this. The comparison drawn here to marriage's ordinary residency requirement is general background only, drawn from this corpus's own separately and independently verified citation to Family Code § 2320 in its Petition for Dissolution of Marriage document (clause dissolution_residency_requirement); § 2320 was not independently re-fetched for this document, and no citation to it is included here.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 299(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the same-procedures rule for judicial dissolution and its added jurisdictional exception
citations.quote: (d) The superior courts shall have jurisdiction over all proceedings relating to the dissolution of domestic partnerships, nullity of domestic partnerships, and legal separation of partners in a domestic partnership. The dissolution of a domestic partnership, nullity of a domestic partnership, and legal separation of partners in a domestic partnership shall follow the same procedures, and the partners shall possess the same rights, protections, and benefits, and be subject to the same responsibilities, obligations, and duties, as apply to the dissolution of marriage, nullity of marriage, and legal separation of spouses in a marriage, respectively, except as provided in subdivision (a), and except that, in accordance with the consent acknowledged by domestic partners in the Declaration of Domestic Partnership form, proceedings for dissolution, nullity, or legal separation of a domestic partnership registered in this state may be filed in the superior courts of this state even if neither domestic partner is a resident of, or maintains a domicile in, the state at the time the proceedings are filed.

clauses.title: Effective Date of the Current Termination Rules, and a Pre-2005 Transition Rule
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} state that the version of Family Code Section 299 described in this document — including the five-year duration limit and the other conditions for administrative termination — took its current form through a 2010 amendment that became effective January 1, 2011, and applies to terminations filed on or after that date. Separately, California law carries a narrow transition rule for partnerships registered before January 1, 2005: for those partnerships, an agreement between the partners intended to be governed by California's premarital-agreement statutes, and complying with those statutes apart from its effective date, remains enforceable under those statutes if it was fully executed and in force by June 30, 2005 — even though it was necessarily signed before the partnership's registration rather than before a marriage.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California), used as evidence of what that state's law provides for ending a registered domestic partnership — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific partnership. This document is informational only: it does not itself terminate any partnership or resolve any dissolution, nullity, or legal-separation matter; only the Secretary of State's processing of a qualifying Notice of Termination, or a court judgment, can do that. These two citations are to two different Family Code provisions — § 299's own legislative history note and § 297.5(k)(2) — not subsections of the same section, so each is independent of the other. This clause does not address whether, or how, the current five-year duration limit applied to partnerships that had already exceeded five years' duration as of the 2011 effective date; that transitional question was not researched here.

citations.cite: the effective date of the current administrative-termination criteria
citations.quote: (Amended by Stats. 2010, Ch. 397, Sec. 1. (AB 2700) Effective January 1, 2011.)

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 297.5(k)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the pre-2005-registration premarital-agreement transition rule
citations.quote: (2) Notwithstanding paragraph (1), for domestic partnerships registered with the state before January 1, 2005, an agreement between the domestic partners that the partners intend to be governed by the requirements set forth in Sections 1600 to 1620, inclusive, and which complies with those sections, except for the agreement’s effective date, shall be enforceable as provided by Sections 1600 to 1620, inclusive, if that agreement was fully executed and in force as of June 30, 2005.

clauses.title: Same Rights and Duties as Spouses — During the Partnership and After
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} state that, under California law, registered domestic partners have the same rights, protections, and benefits, and are subject to the same responsibilities, obligations, and duties under law — whether arising from statutes, administrative regulations, court rules, government policies, common law, or any other source of law — as are granted to and imposed upon spouses, and that this same-treatment rule continues in parallel form for former registered domestic partners once a partnership ends, matching how the law treats former spouses.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California), used as evidence of what that state's law provides for ending a registered domestic partnership — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific partnership. This document is informational only: it does not itself terminate any partnership or resolve any dissolution, nullity, or legal-separation matter; only the Secretary of State's processing of a qualifying Notice of Termination, or a court judgment, can do that. This is a single statutory section, two contiguous subsections (§ 297.5(a)-(b)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 297.5(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the same-rights-and-duties statute, for current and former partners
citations.quote: (a) Registered domestic partners shall have the same rights, protections, and benefits, and shall be subject to the same responsibilities, obligations, and duties under law, whether they derive from statutes, administrative regulations, court rules, government policies, common law, or any other provisions or sources of law, as are granted to and imposed upon spouses. (b) Former registered domestic partners shall have the same rights, protections, and benefits, and shall be subject to the same responsibilities, obligations, and duties under law, whether they derive from statutes, administrative regulations, court rules, government policies, common law, or any other provisions or sources of law, as are granted to and imposed upon former spouses.

clauses.title: Standards Governing a Partner's Rights and Obligations Regarding a Child
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} state that California law makes a registered domestic partner's rights and obligations with respect to a child of either partner the same as a spouse's rights and obligations, and makes a former or surviving registered domestic partner's rights and obligations with respect to such a child the same as a former or surviving spouse's — so that the custody and child-related support standards applied on the dissolution of a marriage with children apply in the same way to the dissolution of a domestic partnership with children, rather than under a separate, partnership-specific standard.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California), used as evidence of what that state's law provides for ending a registered domestic partnership — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific partnership. This document is informational only: it does not itself terminate any partnership or resolve any dissolution, nullity, or legal-separation matter; only the Secretary of State's processing of a qualifying Notice of Termination, or a court judgment, can do that. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 297.5(d)); no additional independent source was found for this. This clause states that the same legal standards apply; it does not restate the substance of California's child custody or child support statutes themselves, which this document does not otherwise cover.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 297.5(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the same rights-and-obligations rule regarding a partner's or former partner's children
citations.quote: (d) The rights and obligations of registered domestic partners with respect to a child of either of them shall be the same as those of spouses. The rights and obligations of former or surviving registered domestic partners with respect to a child of either of them shall be the same as those of former or surviving spouses.

clauses.title: Community Property Division and Spousal Support — the Marital Default, Applied Through the Registration Date
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} state that California law ties community-property division and support rules for a domestic partnership to the date the partnership was registered, in the same way those rules turn on the date of marriage for spouses: for community property, mutual responsibility for debts to third parties, and either partner's right to seek support from the other after dissolution, any statute referring to "the date of a marriage" is read to mean the date of registration of the domestic partnership. Because a judicial dissolution of a domestic partnership otherwise follows the same procedures as a marital dissolution, the community-property default a court applies absent the partners' own written agreement or oral stipulation in open court — dividing the community estate equally — applies to a domestic partnership's community estate in the same way it applies to a marriage's, even though that default rule's own text refers only to "dissolution of marriage" and "legal separation," not to domestic partnerships by name.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California), used as evidence of what that state's law provides for ending a registered domestic partnership — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific partnership. This document is informational only: it does not itself terminate any partnership or resolve any dissolution, nullity, or legal-separation matter; only the Secretary of State's processing of a qualifying Notice of Termination, or a court judgment, can do that. These two citations are to two different Family Code sections (§ 297.5(k)(1) and § 2550), not subsections of the same section, so each is independent of the other. Section 2550 reaches domestic partnership dissolution only indirectly — through § 299(d)'s same-procedures rule and § 297.5(k)(1)'s registration-date-as-marriage-date rule — not because § 2550 itself mentions domestic partnerships; this clause states that chain of cross-reference explicitly rather than assuming it. This clause does not address spousal/partner support amount or duration standards, which this document does not otherwise cover.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 297.5(k)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the registration-date-as-marriage-date rule for property and support
citations.quote: (k) (1) For purposes of the statutes, administrative regulations, court rules, government policies, common law, and any other provision or source of law governing the rights, protections, and benefits, and the responsibilities, obligations, and duties of registered domestic partners in this state, as effectuated by this section, with respect to community property, mutual responsibility for debts to third parties, the right in particular circumstances of either partner to seek financial support from the other following the dissolution of the partnership, and other rights and duties as between the partners concerning ownership of property, any reference to the date of a marriage shall be deemed to refer to the date of registration of a domestic partnership with the state.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2550 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the equal-division default a court applies absent a settlement agreement
citations.quote: 2550. Except upon the written agreement of the parties, or on oral stipulation of the parties in open court, or as otherwise provided in this division, in a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or for legal separation of the parties, the court shall, either in its judgment of dissolution of the marriage, in its judgment of legal separation of the parties, or at a later time if it expressly reserves jurisdiction to make such a property division, divide the community estate of the parties equally.

clauses.title: One Express Statutory Carve-Out: Long-Term Care Plan Eligibility
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} state that California's same-rights-and-duties statute contains at least one express, narrow carve-out from the general rule that registered domestic partners are treated the same as spouses: that statute does not apply to modify eligibility for long-term care plans made available under a specific chapter of the Government Code governing long-term care benefits for state employees and annuitants.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California), used as evidence of what that state's law provides for ending a registered domestic partnership — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific partnership. This document is informational only: it does not itself terminate any partnership or resolve any dissolution, nullity, or legal-separation matter; only the Secretary of State's processing of a qualifying Notice of Termination, or a court judgment, can do that. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 297.5(g)); no additional independent source was found for this. This clause identifies the one express carve-out this document's research located within § 297.5 and § 299 themselves; it is not the product of an exhaustive survey of every other Family Code or Government Code provision, and it does not state whether other, narrower differences between domestic-partner and spousal treatment exist elsewhere in California law.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 297.5(g) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the express long-term-care-plan-eligibility carve-out
citations.quote: (g) No public agency in this state may discriminate against any person or couple on the ground that the person is a registered domestic partner rather than a spouse or that the couple are registered domestic partners rather than spouses, except that nothing in this section applies to modify eligibility for long-term care plans pursuant to Chapter 15 (commencing with Section 21660) of Part 3 of Division 5 of Title 2 of the Government Code.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment — Not a Notice of Termination or a Court Filing
clauses.body:
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing background information is true and correct.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{party1Name}}: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet is prepared for background use in connection with ending a registered domestic partnership under California law. It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete a Notice of Termination of Domestic Partnership filed with the Secretary of State, or a petition filed with the California superior court, and it does not terminate, dissolve, void, or legally separate a domestic partnership; only the Secretary of State's processing of a qualifying Notice of Termination, or a court judgment, can do that.]

clauses.title: The Surviving Spouse's Own One-Half Already Belongs to Them
clauses.body: Under California Probate Code § 100, when a person who is married or in a registered domestic partnership dies, one-half of the community property already belongs to the surviving spouse or surviving registered domestic partner by operation of law, and the other one-half belongs to the decedent. Probate Code § 101 applies the same one-half/one-half division to quasi-community property, but only when the decedent was domiciled in California at death. Both statutes describe the surviving spouse's own one-half as already belonging to them, not as property the decedent's estate passes or transfers to them at death — for that half-interest, the surviving spouse is not a successor of the decedent, and confirming it is a matter of documenting an existing ownership interest rather than of receiving a bequest or inheritance.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides for a decedent domiciled in, or with property characterized under, California law — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific decedent's marital property or estate. Sections 100 and 101 are separately numbered Probate Code sections addressing community and quasi-community property respectively, not subsections of one section, so they are independent sources. This document is informational only; it does not itself confirm title to any property or resolve any probate matter.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 100(a)-(b)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, division of community property on death of a married person or registered domestic partner
citations.quote: (a) Upon the death of a person who is married or in a registered domestic partnership, one-half of the community property belongs to the surviving spouse and the other one-half belongs to the decedent. (b) Notwithstanding subdivision (a), spouses may agree in writing to divide their community property on the basis of a non pro rata division of the aggregate value of the community property or on the basis of a division of each individual item or asset of community property, or partly on each basis. Nothing in this subdivision shall be construed to require this written agreement in order to permit or recognize a non pro rata division of community property.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 101(a)-(b)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, division of quasi-community property on death of a married person or registered domestic partner domiciled in California
citations.quote: (a) Upon the death of a person who is married or in a registered domestic partnership, and is domiciled in this state, one-half of the decedent's quasi-community property belongs to the surviving spouse and the other one-half belongs to the decedent. (b) Notwithstanding subdivision (a), spouses may agree in writing to divide their quasi-community property on the basis of a non pro rata division of the aggregate value of the quasi-community property, or on the basis of a division of each individual item or asset of quasi-community property, or partly on each basis. Nothing in this subdivision shall be construed to require this written agreement in order to permit or recognize a non pro rata division of quasi-community property.

clauses.title: Property Passing to the Surviving Spouse Needs No Administration
clauses.body: California Probate Code § 13500 provides that when a spouse or registered domestic partner dies intestate leaving property that passes to the surviving spouse under Probate Code § 6401, or dies testate and by will devises all or part of their property to the surviving spouse, that property passes to the survivor and no administration is necessary, subject to the surviving spouse's power to dispose of community or quasi-community real property and to the surviving spouse's liability for the decedent's debts (both described elsewhere in this document). Section 13500's own text is not limited to community or quasi-community property — by its terms it covers whatever property the will devises to the surviving spouse outright, separate property included. Where the decedent dies intestate rather than leaving a will, though, § 6401(a)-(b) confines the surviving spouse's intestate share of community and quasi-community property to the one-half that belonged to the decedent under §§ 100 and 101; a different share applies to the decedent's separate property depending on what other relatives survive.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides for property passing to a surviving spouse or registered domestic partner under a will or by intestate succession — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific decedent's estate. Sections 13500 and 6401 are separately numbered, independently enacted Probate Code sections in different divisions of the code, not subsections of one section. This document is informational only; it does not itself confirm title to any property or resolve any probate matter.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13500
citations.cite: California Probate Code, passage of property to a surviving spouse without administration
citations.quote: Except as provided in this chapter, when a spouse dies intestate leaving property that passes to the surviving spouse under Section 6401, or dies testate and by his or her will devises all or a part of his or her property to the surviving spouse, the property passes to the survivor subject to the provisions of Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 13540) and Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 13550), and no administration is necessary.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6401(a)-(b)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, surviving spouse's intestate share of community and quasi-community property
citations.quote: (a) As to community property, the intestate share of the surviving spouse is the one-half of the community property that belongs to the decedent under Section 100. (b) As to quasi-community property, the intestate share of the surviving spouse is the one-half of the quasi-community property that belongs to the decedent under Section 101.

clauses.title: What Doesn't Pass Without Administration
clauses.body: Probate Code § 13501 identifies property that remains subject to full administration despite § 13500's general no-administration rule: property passing under the decedent's will or by intestate succession to someone other than the surviving spouse; property the will disposes of in trust; and property in which the will limits the surviving spouse to a "qualified ownership" (for example, a devise conditioned on the spouse surviving the decedent by a stated period, once that period has expired). This means § 13500 reaches only the interest the will or the intestate succession rules give to the surviving spouse outright — not property left to other heirs or beneficiaries, and not property left in trust for the spouse's benefit rather than to the spouse directly.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific decedent's estate. This document is informational only; it does not itself confirm title to any property or resolve any probate matter.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13501
citations.cite: California Probate Code, property remaining subject to administration despite Section 13500
citations.quote: Except as provided in Chapter 6 (commencing with Section 6600) of Division 6 and in Part 1 (commencing with Section 13000) of this division, the following property of the decedent is subject to administration under this code: (a) Property passing to someone other than the surviving spouse under the decedent's will or by intestate succession. (b) Property disposed of in trust under the decedent's will. (c) Property in which the decedent's will limits the surviving spouse to a qualified ownership. For the purposes of this subdivision, a devise to the surviving spouse that is conditioned on the spouse surviving the decedent by a specified period of time is not a "qualified ownership" interest if the specified period of time has expired.

clauses.title: The Surviving Spouse's Election to Have Property Administered Anyway
clauses.body: Probate Code § 13502 lets the surviving spouse — or the surviving spouse's personal representative, guardian, or conservator — elect to have all or part of the community or quasi-community property, and the decedent's separate property, administered through the probate estate instead of relying on § 13500's automatic passage rule. The election can reach the decedent's one-half of the community and quasi-community property plus the decedent's separate property, the surviving spouse's own one-half of the community and quasi-community property, or both. It must be made in a writing specifically evidencing the election, filed in the decedent's probate proceeding within four months after letters issue (or later, if the court allows more time for good cause), and before an order is entered under Probate Code § 13656.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific decedent's estate, and not advice about whether a specific surviving spouse should or should not make this election. This document is informational only; it does not itself confirm title to any property or resolve any probate matter.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13502
citations.cite: California Probate Code, surviving spouse's election to have community/quasi-community and separate property administered
citations.quote: (a) Upon the election of the surviving spouse or the personal representative, guardian of the estate, or conservator of the estate of the surviving spouse, all or a portion of the following property may be administered under this code: (1) The one-half of the community property that belongs to the decedent under Section 100, the one-half of the quasi-community property that belongs to the decedent under Section 101, and the separate property of the decedent. (2) The one-half of the community property that belongs to the surviving spouse under Section 100 and the one-half of the quasi-community property that belongs to the surviving spouse under Section 101. (b) The election shall be made by a writing specifically evidencing the election filed in the proceedings for the administration of the estate of the deceased spouse within four months after the issuance of letters, or within any further time that the court may allow upon a showing of good cause, and before entry of an order under Section 13656.

clauses.title: The Surviving Spouse's Power to Sell Community Real Property After 40 Days
clauses.body: Separately from the no-administration rule, Probate Code § 13540 gives the surviving spouse (or the surviving spouse's personal representative, guardian, or conservator) full power, beginning 40 days after the other spouse's death, to sell, convey, lease, mortgage, or otherwise dispose of community or quasi-community real property, with any resulting buyer's, lender's, or lessee's interest free of claims by the deceased spouse's estate, devisees, or creditors — the same as if the surviving spouse had owned the property as separate property all along. The surviving spouse may record an affidavit of the facts establishing this right before or together with the instrument that makes the disposition. This power does not affect or limit the surviving spouse's own liability for the decedent's debts.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific decedent's estate. This document is informational only; it does not itself confirm title to any property or resolve any probate matter.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13540(a)-(c)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, surviving spouse's power to dispose of community or quasi-community real property after 40 days
citations.quote: (a) Except as provided in Section 13541, after 40 days from the death of a spouse, the surviving spouse or the personal representative, guardian of the estate, or conservator of the estate of the surviving spouse has full power to sell, convey, lease, mortgage, or otherwise deal with and dispose of the community or quasi-community real property, and the right, title, and interest of any grantee, purchaser, encumbrancer, or lessee shall be free of rights of the estate of the deceased spouse or of devisees or creditors of the deceased spouse to the same extent as if the property had been owned as the separate property of the surviving spouse. (b) The surviving spouse or the personal representative, guardian of the estate, or conservator of the estate of the surviving spouse may record, prior to or together with the instrument that makes a disposition of property under this section, an affidavit of the facts that establish the right of the surviving spouse to make the disposition. (c) Nothing in this section affects or limits the liability of the surviving spouse under Sections 13550 to 13553, inclusive, and Chapter 3.5 (commencing with Section 13560).

clauses.title: The Spousal or Domestic Partner Property Petition — A Separate Court Procedure
clauses.body: Beyond the automatic passage rule, Probate Code §§ 13650-13660 create a separate, optional court procedure: a surviving spouse (or the surviving spouse's personal representative, guardian, or conservator) may petition the superior court in the county where the decedent's estate could be administered for an order that administration is unnecessary because the property passes to the surviving spouse, and/or for an order confirming the surviving spouse's ownership of property belonging to them under § 100 or § 101. This petition does not reach property the surviving spouse has separately elected, under § 13502, to have administered as part of the estate, and a guardian or conservator may file it without separate court authorization in the guardianship or conservatorship proceeding. Because it produces a recordable court order rather than a private declaration, this petition is the mechanism typically used to clear title to real property or resolve a dispute about how property should be characterized — something an unrecorded declaration like this document cannot do on its own. Attorney's fees for the petition are set by private agreement between attorney and client, not by court approval, unless the client and attorney dispute the fee or its meaning, in which case either may ask the court to resolve that dispute in the same proceeding.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific decedent's estate, and not advice about whether a specific surviving spouse needs to file this petition. Sections 13650 and 13660 are separately numbered sections within the same chapter, not subsections of one section. This document is informational only; it does not itself confirm title to any property, constitute this petition, or resolve any probate matter.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13650(a)-(c)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, petition for order confirming property passing or belonging to surviving spouse
citations.quote: (a) A surviving spouse or the personal representative, guardian of the estate, or conservator of the estate of the surviving spouse may file a petition in the superior court of the county in which the estate of the deceased spouse may be administered requesting an order that administration of all or part of the estate is not necessary for the reason that all or part of the estate is property passing to the surviving spouse. The petition may also request an order confirming the ownership of the surviving spouse of property belonging to the surviving spouse under Section 100 or 101. (b) To the extent of the election, this section does not apply to property that the petitioner has elected, as provided in Section 13502, to have administered under this code. (c) A guardian or conservator may file a petition under this section without authorization or approval of the court in which the guardianship or conservatorship proceeding is pending.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13660
citations.cite: California Probate Code, attorney's fees for a spousal or domestic partner property petition
citations.quote: The attorney's fees for services performed in connection with the filing of a petition and obtaining of a court order under this chapter shall be determined by private agreement between the attorney and the client and are not subject to approval by the court.

clauses.title: What Counts as Community Property and Quasi-Community Property
clauses.body: Family Code § 760 defines community property, for property acquired during marriage, as all property, real or personal, wherever situated, acquired by a married person during the marriage while domiciled in California, unless a statute provides otherwise. Family Code § 125 defines quasi-community property as property acquired by either spouse while domiciled elsewhere that would have been community property had the acquiring spouse been domiciled in California at the time of acquisition, or property acquired in exchange for such property. In short: community property is generally marital or domestic-partnership property acquired while the couple lived in California; quasi-community property is property that would have been community property had the couple lived in California when it was acquired, typically because it was acquired while domiciled in another state or country. Separate property — owned before the marriage or partnership, or acquired during it by gift or inheritance — is neither, and is governed by different rules not addressed in this document.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides for characterizing marital property — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific couple's property or any specific decedent's estate; a couple who lived in more than one state may have property characterized differently depending on where and when it was acquired. Sections 760 and 125 are separately numbered Family Code sections in different parts of the code, not subsections of one section. This document is informational only; it does not itself characterize any specific item of property or resolve any dispute about characterization.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 760
citations.cite: California Family Code, definition of community property
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided by statute, all property, real or personal, wherever situated, acquired by a married person during the marriage while domiciled in this state is community property.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 125
citations.cite: California Family Code, definition of quasi-community property
citations.quote: "Quasi-community property" means all real or personal property, wherever situated, acquired before or after the operative date of this code in any of the following ways: (a) By either spouse while domiciled elsewhere which would have been community property if the spouse who acquired the property had been domiciled in this state at the time of its acquisition. (b) In exchange for real or personal property, wherever situated, which would have been community property if the spouse who acquired the property so exchanged had been domiciled in this state at the time of its acquisition.

clauses.title: The Surviving Spouse Remains Personally Liable for the Decedent's Debts
clauses.body: Receiving or confirming property under this mechanism does not extinguish the decedent's debts. Probate Code § 13550 makes the surviving spouse personally liable, upon the other spouse's death, for the deceased spouse's debts chargeable against the property described in § 13551, to the extent § 13551 provides (subject to a short list of exceptions in §§ 11446, 13552, 13553, and 13554). Section 13551 caps that liability at the fair market value, less liens and encumbrances, measured at the date of death, of three categories of property: the surviving spouse's own one-half of the community and quasi-community property (to the extent it is not exempt from enforcement of a money judgment and not administered in the estate); the decedent's one-half of the community and quasi-community property that passes to the surviving spouse without administration; and the decedent's separate property that passes to the surviving spouse without administration. In other words, the surviving spouse's exposure for the decedent's debts is capped at the value of what passed to or already belonged to them through this mechanism — not their own separate assets held apart from it.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides for a surviving spouse's liability for a deceased spouse's debts — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific decedent's estate or debts. Sections 13550 and 13551 are separately numbered sections within the same chapter, not subsections of one section. This document is informational only; it does not itself determine any specific debt, its amount, or any specific surviving spouse's liability for it.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13550
citations.cite: California Probate Code, surviving spouse's personal liability for the deceased spouse's debts
citations.quote: Except as provided in Sections 11446, 13552, 13553, and 13554, upon the death of a married person, the surviving spouse is personally liable for the debts of the deceased spouse chargeable against the property described in Section 13551 to the extent provided in Section 13551.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13551(a)-(c)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, cap on the surviving spouse's liability for the deceased spouse's debts
citations.quote: The liability imposed by Section 13550 shall not exceed the fair market value at the date of the decedent's death, less the amount of any liens and encumbrances, of the total of the following: (a) The portion of the one-half of the community and quasi-community property belonging to the surviving spouse under Sections 100 and 101 that is not exempt from enforcement of a money judgment and is not administered in the estate of the deceased spouse. (b) The portion of the one-half of the community and quasi-community property belonging to the decedent under Sections 100 and 101 that passes to the surviving spouse without administration under this part. (c) The separate property of the decedent that passes to the surviving spouse without administration under this part.

clauses.title: How This Differs From the Small Estate Affidavit and From Formal Probate
clauses.body: The small estate affidavit procedure of Probate Code §§ 13100-13106 is available only if the gross value of the decedent's real and personal property in California does not exceed a periodically-adjusted dollar ceiling ($166,250 as of the most recent adjustment reflected in the statute's text) and 40 days have passed since death. The no-administration rule for property passing to a surviving spouse or registered domestic partner under Probate Code § 13500 carries no comparable dollar ceiling in its own text; it turns on the couple's marital or registered-domestic-partnership status, on how the property was characterized (community, quasi-community, or property the decedent's will devises outright to the spouse), and on how the property passed (by will or by intestate succession) — not on the estate's total value. The two procedures also differ in scope: the small estate affidavit is available to any successor of the decedent for the decedent's personal property (and, in a separate affidavit form, certain real property), while § 13500 and the related sections described in this document are available only to a surviving spouse or registered domestic partner, for property passing to that survivor specifically. Both procedures avoid a full probate administration in the ordinary case, but under § 13502 the surviving spouse can still elect to bring the property into a formal probate administration, and a formal administration remains available or required for any property that does not qualify for either procedure.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific decedent's estate, and not a claim about which procedure (if any) is appropriate for a specific estate. The two citations here are drawn from two different Probate Code sections addressing two different statutory procedures (Part 1's small estate affidavit and Part 2's spousal passage rule), not subsections of one section; the quote from Section 13500 also appears in this document's clause on the no-administration rule, since both clauses draw on the same verified source. This document is informational only; it does not itself determine which procedure applies to any specific estate or resolve any probate matter.

clauses.title: California's Settlement-Agreement Disclosure Ban (Sexual Harassment, Discrimination, Retaliation)
clauses.body: California law prohibits including, in a settlement agreement resolving a claim filed in a civil action or an administrative complaint, any provision that prevents or restricts disclosure of factual information related to a claim of: sexual assault; sexual harassment; workplace harassment or discrimination, an employer's failure to prevent it, or retaliation against a person for reporting or opposing it; or harassment, discrimination, or retaliation by the owner of a housing accommodation. A court also can't enter an order, by stipulation or otherwise, that restricts disclosure of that same information. For an agreement entered into on or after January 1, 2019, a provision that violates this rule is void as a matter of law and against public policy, not merely voidable or unenforceable by one side.
clauses.gap: This statute (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1001) applies specifically to a settlement agreement resolving a claim already filed in court or with an administrative agency — it is not a general rule for every severance or separation agreement, including one offered before any claim is filed. A separate, broader California statute reaches ordinary separation agreements themselves; it's covered in this document's next clauses. A correction to a common assumption: California Civil Code § 1670.8 is sometimes assumed to be the state's employment non-disparagement statute, but it is not — it's an unrelated consumer-protection statute that bars a contract for the sale or lease of consumer goods or services from waiving a consumer's right to make statements about the seller or the goods or services (commonly discussed as an anti-"gag clause" rule for online reviews). It has nothing to do with employment, severance, or settlement agreements; it is quoted below only to make this correction concrete and verifiable, not as authority for anything else in this document. Separately, this clause's description of the covered claim categories relies on § 1001(a)'s own cross-references to Civil Code § 51.9 (defining sexual harassment) and Government Code §§ 12940 and 12955 (defining the covered forms of discrimination, harassment, and retaliation); those cross-referenced definitions were not separately fetched or independently verified in this research — only § 1001's own text, which names them, was fetched and confirmed. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's current rule on this point — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person's situation. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific non-disparagement clause is enforceable in a specific case.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1001(a) (Leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, Confidential Settlement Agreements, covered claims and disclosure-restriction ban
citations.quote: a provision within a settlement agreement that prevents or restricts the disclosure of factual information related to a claim filed in a civil action or a complaint filed in an administrative action, regarding any of the following, is prohibited: (1) An act of sexual assault that is not governed by subdivision (a) of Section 1002. (2) An act of sexual harassment, as defined in Section 51.9 of the Civil Code. (3) An act of workplace harassment or discrimination, failure to prevent an act of workplace harassment or discrimination, or an act of retaliation against a person for reporting or opposing harassment or discrimination, as described in subdivisions (a), (h), (i), (j), and (k) of Section 12940 of the Government Code.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1001(b), (d) (Leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, Confidential Settlement Agreements, court-order limit and void-as-a-matter-of-law rule
citations.quote: in a civil matter described in paragraphs (1) to (4), inclusive, of subdivision (a), a court shall not enter, by stipulation or otherwise, an order that restricts the disclosure of information in a manner that conflicts with subdivision (a). ... a provision within a settlement agreement that prevents or restricts the disclosure of factual information related to the claim described in subdivision (a) that is entered into on or after January 1, 2019, is void as a matter of law and against public policy.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1670.8(a)(1) (Leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, consumer-contract gag-clause ban — an unrelated statute, cited here only to correct a common misattribution
citations.quote: A contract or proposed contract for the sale or lease of consumer goods or services may not include a provision waiving the consumer’s right to make any statement regarding the seller or lessor or its employees or agents, or concerning the goods or services.

clauses.title: Carve-Outs: Compensation Confidentiality and Claimant Identity
clauses.body: The same statute preserves two things a settlement agreement can still keep confidential even though the underlying facts of a covered claim can't be gagged. First, at the claimant's own request (not the other side's), the agreement may shield the claimant's identity and any facts that would reveal it, including court pleadings — unless a government agency or public official is a party to the settlement, in which case this identity-shielding option isn't available. Second, and separately, the statute doesn't prohibit a provision that keeps confidential the amount paid in settlement of the claim — the dollar figure can still be kept confidential even where the facts underlying the claim cannot.
clauses.gap: Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section as the previous clause (nondisparagement_ccp_1001_scope) — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1001(c) and (e) — so they are treated as one source with that clause, not independent corroboration of each other or of it. The identity-shielding carve-out is the claimant's option to invoke, not the other side's to impose; nothing in this subsection lets an employer or defendant demand that the claimant's identity be hidden. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's current rule on this point — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person's situation. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific non-disparagement clause is enforceable in a specific case.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1001(c) (Leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, Confidential Settlement Agreements, claimant-identity-shielding option
citations.quote: a provision that shields the identity of the claimant and all facts that could lead to the discovery of the claimant’s identity, including pleadings filed in court, may be included within a settlement agreement at the request of the claimant. This subdivision does not apply if a government agency or public official is a party to the settlement agreement.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1001(e) (Leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, Confidential Settlement Agreements, settlement-amount confidentiality carve-out
citations.quote: This section does not prohibit the entry or enforcement of a provision in any agreement that precludes the disclosure of the amount paid in settlement of a claim.

clauses.title: California's Broader Ban on Silencing Workplace-Unlawful-Acts Disclosures
clauses.body: A separate California statute reaches beyond litigated settlements to ordinary employment and separation agreements generally. It is an unlawful employment practice for an employer to require an employee, as a condition of employment, continued employment, a raise, or a bonus, to sign a nondisparagement agreement or other document to the extent it has the purpose or effect of denying the employee the right to disclose information about unlawful acts in the workplace — defined to include, but not be limited to, information about harassment, discrimination, or any other conduct the employee has reasonable cause to believe is unlawful. The same rule separately applies to any agreement related to an employee's separation from employment: it's an unlawful employment practice for an employer or former employer to include a provision there that prohibits disclosing information about unlawful acts in the workplace. Any nondisparagement or other contractual provision restricting an employee's ability to disclose information about workplace conditions must include specific statutory notice language, in substantial form: "Nothing in this agreement prevents you from discussing or disclosing information about unlawful acts in the workplace, such as harassment or discrimination or any other conduct that you have reason to believe is unlawful." A provision that violates this rule is against public policy and unenforceable.
clauses.gap: All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Gov't Code § 12964.5 — (a)(1), (b)(1), and the shared notice-language requirement in (a)(1)(B)/(b)(1)(B) — so they are treated as one source, not independent corroboration of each other. Separately, this statute's own 5-business-day attorney-consultation requirement for a separation agreement (subdivision (b)(4), not quoted here) is a distinct, narrower notice period from the OWBPA's 21/45-day consideration periods for age-discrimination releases covered elsewhere in this corpus's severance-agreement document — the two periods arise under different statutes, serve different purposes, and don't substitute for each other where both independently apply to the same agreement. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's current rule on this point — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person's situation. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific non-disparagement clause is enforceable in a specific case.

clauses.title: Carve-Outs and Boundaries of the Broader California Rule
clauses.body: This broader rule has stated limits. It doesn't apply to a negotiated settlement agreement resolving an underlying claim that has already been filed in court, before an administrative agency, in alternative dispute resolution, or through an employer's internal complaint process — "negotiated" there means voluntary, deliberate, and informed, with consideration of value to the employee and notice of the opportunity to retain an attorney. It does not prohibit a provision that keeps confidential the amount paid in a severance agreement. And it does not stop an employer from protecting its trade secrets, proprietary information, or confidential information that doesn't involve unlawful acts in the workplace. Where a covered separation agreement is offered, the employer must also notify the employee of the right to consult an attorney about it and give at least five business days to do so, though the employee may sign sooner if that shortening is knowing and voluntary and not induced by fraud, misrepresentation, or a threat to withdraw or alter the offer.
clauses.gap: All citations below are subsections of the same statutory section as the previous clause (nondisparagement_gov_12964_5_prohibition) — Cal. Gov't Code § 12964.5(d), (e), (f), and (b)(4) — so they are treated as one source with it, not independent corroboration. The negotiated-settlement carve-out in subdivision (d) is what keeps this statute from duplicating or conflicting with the separate settlement-specific statute (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1001) covered earlier in this document: an already-filed claim resolved by a negotiated settlement falls under § 1001's own, narrower rule instead of this one, rather than under both at once. The five-business-day consultation period in (b)(4) applies to a covered separation agreement regardless of the employee's age; it is a different notice period, arising under a different statute, from the OWBPA's 21- or 45-day consideration periods for a valid age-discrimination release. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's current rule on this point — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person's situation. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific non-disparagement clause is enforceable in a specific case.
