clauses.title: The Putative Spouse Doctrine and Quasi-Marital Property
clauses.body: California law softens the consequences of a void or voidable marriage for a party who did not know the marriage was legally defective. When a marriage is determined to be void or voidable and the court finds that either party, or both, believed in good faith that the marriage was valid, the court must declare that party or those parties a 'putative spouse.' If property division is in issue, the court then divides — under the same property-division rules that apply to a community-property estate — the property acquired during the union that would have been community or quasi-community property had the marriage not been void or voidable, but only upon the request of a party who has been declared a putative spouse. This property is called 'quasi-marital property.' A party who lacked a good-faith belief the marriage was valid is not entitled to this treatment. The court may also expressly reserve jurisdiction and divide this quasi-marital property at a later time rather than in the nullity judgment itself.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's nullity-of-marriage process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage. This document is informational: it does not itself determine whether a specific party held a good-faith belief the marriage was valid, or divide any specific property; only a court can make that determination. Both citations are to subsections of the same Family Code section (§ 2251(a)(1) and § 2251(a)(2)) and are treated as one source, not independent. This clause does not independently verify the substance of Division 7 (commencing with Section 2500) of the Family Code, the community-property division rules that § 2251 cross-references and applies to quasi-marital property. No case law was independently verified for this clause; it rests on the statutory text alone.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2251(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: mandatory putative-spouse declaration on a good-faith finding
citations.quote: Declare the party or parties, who believed in good faith that the marriage was valid, to have the status of a putative spouse.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2251(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: quasi-marital property, divided as community property would be, only on a putative spouse's request
citations.quote: divide, in accordance with Division 7 (commencing with Section 2500), that property acquired during the union that would have been community property or quasi-community property if the union had not been void or voidable, only upon request of a party who is declared a putative spouse under paragraph (1). This property is known as “quasi-marital property.”

clauses.title: Support and Custody Consequences of a Nullity Judgment — Where Nullity Differs From, and Matches, Dissolution
clauses.body: A nullity judgment's practical consequences do not track dissolution's default rules uniformly — some are conditioned on putative-spouse status and some are not. Spousal support is conditioned: the court may order support during the pendency of a nullity proceeding or upon the nullity judgment, in the same manner as if the marriage had not been void or voidable, but only if the party who would benefit from the order is found to be a putative spouse. A party without a good-faith belief the marriage was valid is not eligible for support under this provision, which is a real point of divergence from an ordinary dissolution, where spousal support is not conditioned on a party's good-faith belief in the marriage's validity in the first place. Property division is likewise conditioned on putative-spouse status, as described in a separate clause of this document, and property divided as quasi-marital property remains liable for the parties' debts to the same extent as if it had been community or quasi-community property. Child custody, by contrast, is not conditioned on putative-spouse status or treated any differently at all: in a nullity proceeding, custody of the children is determined according to the same Family Code division that governs custody in a dissolution proceeding, so a marriage's nullity does not itself change how a court approaches custody.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's nullity-of-marriage process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage. This document is informational: it does not itself order support, divide property, or determine custody; only a court can do that. These two citations are to two different Family Code sections (§ 2254 and § 2253), not subsections of the same section, so they are independent sources. This clause's property-division statements rely on Cal. Fam. Code §§ 2251 and 2252, cited and verified in a separate clause of this document rather than re-cited here; its statement that dissolution's spousal-support rules are not conditioned on a good-faith belief in the marriage's validity is drawn from the absence of any such condition in § 2254, not from an independent verification of the dissolution spousal-support statutes (addressed, if at all, in this document's companion dissolution document). This clause does not independently verify the substance of Division 8 (commencing with Section 3000) of the Family Code, the custody statutes that § 2253 cross-references. No case law was independently verified for this clause; it rests on the statutory text alone.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2254 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: support conditioned on putative spouse status
citations.quote: The court may, during the pendency of a proceeding for nullity of marriage or upon judgment of nullity of marriage, order a party to pay for the support of the other party in the same manner as if the marriage had not been void or voidable if the party for whose benefit the order is made is found to be a putative spouse.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2253 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: custody determined under the same division that governs dissolution
citations.quote: In a proceeding under this part, custody of the children shall be determined according to Division 8 (commencing with Section 3000).

clauses.title: The Legal Effect of Any Nullity Judgment, and a Fault-Based Limit on Attorney's Fees Unique to Nullity
clauses.body: Whether a marriage is void or voidable, a judgment of nullity has the same basic legal effect: it restores the parties to the status of unmarried persons, and it is conclusive only as to the parties to the proceeding and those claiming under them — not conclusive against the whole world. California law also allows a court to grant attorney's fees and costs in a nullity proceeding, but attaches a fault-based limitation that has no counterpart in an ordinary dissolution proceeding: in a proceeding based on a voidable marriage, a party may recover fees and costs only if that party is found innocent of fraud or wrongdoing in inducing or entering into the marriage, and free from knowledge, at the time, of a prior marriage or other impediment to the marriage for which nullity is sought. A party who was at fault in bringing about the very defect that makes the marriage voidable — for example, the party who committed the fraud, rather than the party who was defrauded — is therefore not eligible for a fee award under this provision, even though either party could otherwise be a party to the proceeding.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's nullity-of-marriage process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage. This document is informational: it does not itself enter a judgment or award fees; only a court can do that. These two citations are to two different Family Code sections (§ 2212 and § 2255), not subsections of the same section, so they are independent sources. This clause's comparison to dissolution's fee statute (which § 2255 itself cross-references, as Chapter 3.5 commencing with Section 2030) was not independently re-verified with a second fetch in this research; it rests on the absence of an equivalent fault-based limitation in that cross-referenced chapter's general framing, not on this document's own verification of that chapter's text. No case law was independently verified for this clause; it rests on the statutory text alone.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2212 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a nullity judgment restores unmarried status and binds only the parties and their privies
citations.quote: The effect of a judgment of nullity of marriage is to restore the parties to the status of unmarried persons. (b) A judgment of nullity of marriage is conclusive only as to the parties to the proceeding and those claiming under them.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2255 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: attorney's fees in a voidable-marriage proceeding limited to a party innocent of fraud or wrongdoing
citations.quote: The court may grant attorney’s fees and costs in accordance with Chapter 3.5 (commencing with Section 2030) of Part 1 in proceedings to have the marriage adjudged void and in those proceedings based upon voidable marriage in which the party applying for attorney’s fees and costs is found to be innocent of fraud or wrongdoing in inducing or entering into the marriage, and free from knowledge of the then existence of any prior marriage or other impediment to the contracting of the marriage for which a judgment of nullity is sought.

clauses.title: The Agreed-Boundary Doctrine: A Common-Law Rule for Fixing an Uncertain Line
clauses.body: California recognizes a doctrine, developed by California courts rather than set out in a statute, under which adjoining landowners who are uncertain where the true boundary line between their parcels actually lies may fix that line by their own agreement. Secondary legal commentary describing this doctrine (identified in this clause's gap, since the underlying case law itself could not be independently verified in this research session) states it as requiring three things: (1) an uncertainty as to the true boundary line between the parcels, as distinct from a mere disagreement about a boundary both parties otherwise know the true location of; (2) an agreement, express or implied, between the adjoining owners fixing where the line is; and (3) acceptance and acquiescence in the line so fixed, described in that commentary either as lasting for a period equal to the applicable statute of limitations, or as arising under circumstances where changing the line's position would cause substantial loss. California's general statute of limitations for an action to recover real property, or its possession, is five years, running from when the plaintiff (or the plaintiff's predecessor or grantor) was last seized or possessed of the property. Where this doctrine applies, secondary commentary states that the agreed line becomes the boundary between the parcels, even if a survey conducted from the calls in the parties' deeds would show a different line. This document's boundary line agreement declaration does not itself transfer, convey, or grant any interest in real property from one party to the other; it records the parties' own statement of where an existing, but previously uncertain, boundary line lies.
clauses.gap: The core content of this clause is case law, not statute, and that case law could not be independently verified in this research session. CourtListener searches for the California case law establishing and restating this doctrine (commonly discussed under case names including Bryant v. Blevins and Ernie v. Trinity Lutheran Church) returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit error on the first attempt, reporting CourtListener's 125-request daily cap already exhausted with the next availability roughly ten hours out; no further CourtListener attempts were made after that response. Direct fetches to courtlistener.com, law.justia.com, caselaw.findlaw.com, and scocal.stanford.edu were separately attempted for the same case law and were each blocked by this environment's own network egress controls before any opinion text could be read. As a result, no case is cited in this clause's citations, no quotation is attributed to any case, and the case names appearing in this paragraph are given for identification only, drawn from secondary legal-commentary sources located through general web search (real-estate-law-firm client alerts and similar secondary writing describing these cases), not from independently fetched and read opinion text. The doctrine's existence, its three elements as stated in the body above, and the description of the acquiescence element as alternatively satisfiable by a statute-of-limitations-length period or by circumstances of substantial loss, should all be read as an unverified description of case law drawn from that secondary commentary, not as an independently confirmed holding of any court. This clause does independently verify, through Cal. Code Civ. Proc. §§ 318 and 319 (genuinely separate statutory sections, treated here as two independent sources), that California's general statute of limitations for an action to recover real property or its possession is five years; what is not independently verified is whether, or exactly how, the case law actually ties the agreed-boundary doctrine's acquiescence element to that particular period, or whether and when any court decision relaxed that period into the disjunctive test described above. This clause does not evaluate whether any particular boundary line, or any particular period of acceptance, would in fact satisfy this doctrine on the facts of a specific dispute. This is one state's common-law doctrine and statute, used as real evidence of California's law on fixing an uncertain boundary — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of real property; other states' rules for resolving uncertain boundaries by agreement, if any, may differ.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 318
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, five-year limitations period for an action to recover real property
citations.quote: No action for the recovery of real property, or for the recovery of the possession thereof, can be maintained, unless it appear that the plaintiff, his ancestor, predecessor, or grantor, was seized or possessed of the property in question, within five years before the commencement of the action.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 319
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, parallel five-year limitations period for a cause of action or defense arising out of title to real property
citations.quote: No cause of action, or defense to an action, arising out of the title to real property, or to rents or profits out of the same, can be effectual, unless it appear that the person prosecuting the action, or making the defense, or under whose title the action is prosecuted, or the defense is made, or the ancestor, predecessor, or grantor of such person was seized or possessed of the premises in question within five years before the commencement of the Act in respect to which such action is prosecuted or defense made.

clauses.title: Distinct From Adverse Possession: A Different Legal Theory for a Boundary Dispute
clauses.body: California's Code of Civil Procedure separately sets out a statutory basis on which a person may establish adverse possession of land, a legal theory analytically distinct from the agreed-boundary doctrine described elsewhere in this document. Under that statute, land is deemed to have been possessed and occupied, for adverse-possession purposes, only where it has been protected by a substantial enclosure or has been usually cultivated or improved; and in no case is adverse possession established unless the land has been occupied and claimed continuously for five years, with the claimant, or the claimant's predecessors and grantors, having timely paid all state, county, or municipal taxes levied and assessed on the land during that five-year period. This statutory test centers on a claimant's own possession, improvement, and tax payment with respect to land, regardless of whether the claimant and the neighboring owner ever agreed on, or were ever uncertain about, where the true boundary line lay. The agreed-boundary doctrine addresses a different starting condition: the adjoining owners' shared uncertainty about where the true boundary line is, resolved by their own agreement fixing it, rather than one owner's occupation of land the parties know, or could know, belongs to someone else. A landowner facing a boundary encroachment or dispute may have more than one potentially available legal theory on a given set of facts, of which adverse possession and the agreed-boundary doctrine are two; this clause states each as a distinct, separately sourced fact about California law, not as a determination of which theory, if any, applies to a specific dispute.
clauses.gap: § 325(a) and § 325(b) are subsections of the same statutory section, treated here as one source, not as two independent sources. Adverse possession is also commonly described, including in case law and secondary commentary, using terms such as "open," "notorious," "hostile," and "continuous" possession; none of those specific words appears in § 325's own text, which instead speaks of a "substantial enclosure," land "usually cultivated or improved," and land "occupied and claimed" for five years with taxes paid. This clause treats those common-law descriptive terms as conventional shorthand for how courts have construed § 325's own language, but that construction is itself case law, and this research session's CourtListener attempts were rate-limited before any case law on this statute's construction could be independently verified (see the companion clause on the agreed-boundary doctrine's sourcing limitations for the specific rate-limit and network-access details, which apply equally here). This clause does not evaluate whether any specific claimant's possession or tax payments in fact satisfy § 325, and does not determine which of the two theories described in this clause, if either, would apply to any specific encroachment or boundary dispute. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a distinct legal theory California law recognizes — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of real property; other states' adverse possession statutes differ in their required possession period and other elements.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 325(a)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, the manner of possession required to constitute adverse possession
citations.quote: (a) For the purpose of constituting an adverse possession by a person claiming title, not founded upon a written instrument, judgment, or decree, land is deemed to have been possessed and occupied in the following cases only: (1) Where it has been protected by a substantial enclosure. (2) Where it has been usually cultivated or improved.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 325(b)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, treated as one source with § 325(a) above, not an independent source
citations.quote: (b) In no case shall adverse possession be considered established under the provision of any section of this code, unless it shall be shown that the land has been occupied and claimed for the period of five years continuously, and the party or persons, their predecessors and grantors, have timely paid all state, county, or municipal taxes that have been levied and assessed upon the land for the period of five years during which the land has been occupied and claimed.

clauses.title: No Boundary-Specific Recording Statute; General Recording Rules Apply
clauses.body: California does not have a statute that specifically addresses a "boundary line agreement," or a boundary line agreement's recordation, as its own distinct category of instrument; the agreed-boundary doctrine described elsewhere in this document is a common-law doctrine, not a creature of statute. A written agreement fixing a previously uncertain boundary line is, like other written instruments affecting an interest in real property, recorded under California's general recording statutes rather than any boundary-specific one. Once validly signed, such an agreement is effective as between the parties who signed it whether or not it is ever recorded; recording is not a condition of its validity between those parties. Recording matters for what it does against later claimants: California law states that every conveyance of real property, once acknowledged, certified, and recorded as prescribed by law, serves from the time it is filed with the recorder as constructive notice of its contents to subsequent purchasers and mortgagees, and California is a "race-notice" state, under which an earlier, unrecorded conveyance of the same property is void against a later purchaser or mortgagee who takes in good faith, for valuable consideration, and records first. Separately, California law provides a specific exemption, under the Subdivision Map Act, for a "lot line adjustment" between four or fewer existing adjoining parcels, subject to local agency or advisory agency approval limited to a determination of conformance with the local general plan and zoning and building ordinances. That lot line adjustment process is a different statutory mechanism, addressing a deliberate reconfiguration of recorded lot lines for land-use and mapping purposes; it is not the common-law agreed-boundary doctrine described elsewhere in this document, and this document's boundary line agreement declaration is not drafted to accomplish, and does not substitute for, a Subdivision Map Act lot line adjustment.
clauses.gap: Cal. Civ. Code §§ 1213 and 1214 are genuinely separate statutory sections within the same chapter and article (Civil Code, Effect of Recording, or the Want Thereof), treated here as two independent sources. Cal. Gov't Code § 66412(d) is a third, independently verified source from a different code entirely, cited here only to establish that a differently named statutory process (a lot line adjustment under the Subdivision Map Act) exists and is analytically distinct from the common-law agreed-boundary doctrine; this clause does not otherwise research or describe that adjustment process's own approval procedure, certificate-of-compliance requirements, or recording mechanics beyond noting that it exists, so as not to conflate the two. California's race-notice recording rule is stated here as evidence of how one state resolves competing claims to the same property, not as a claim about which state's recording rule governs a particular property or agreement — recording statutes vary by state, including "pure race" and "pure notice" states. This clause treats a boundary line agreement as a "conveyance of real property" within §§ 1213 and 1214's own words for purposes of the general recording rule; it does not independently verify, through case law, every circumstance in which an unrecorded boundary line agreement in fact binds or does not bind a later purchaser of either parcel. This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of California's general recording framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of real property.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1213
citations.cite: California Civil Code, recording gives constructive notice
citations.quote: Every conveyance of real property or an estate for years therein acknowledged or proved and certified and recorded as prescribed by law from the time it is filed with the recorder for record is constructive notice of the contents thereof to subsequent purchasers and mortgagees

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1214
citations.cite: California Civil Code, race-notice recording rule
citations.quote: Every conveyance of real property or an estate for years therein, other than a lease for a term not exceeding one year, is void as against any subsequent purchaser or mortgagee of the same property, or any part thereof, in good faith and for a valuable consideration, whose conveyance is first duly recorded, and as against any judgment affecting the title, unless the conveyance shall have been duly recorded prior to the record of notice of action.

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 66412(d)
citations.cite: California Government Code, Subdivision Map Act exemption for a lot line adjustment, a distinct statutory process
citations.quote: A lot line adjustment between four or fewer existing adjoining parcels, where the land taken from one parcel is added to an adjoining parcel, and where a greater number of parcels than originally existed is not thereby created, if the lot line adjustment is approved by the local agency, or advisory agency.

clauses.title: Legal Description Sufficiency for Recording and Notice to Later Purchasers
clauses.body: California law requires a county recorder to accept for recordation an instrument affecting real property, on payment of proper fees and taxes, if the instrument contains sufficient information to be indexed as provided by statute, meets state and local recording requirements, and is photographically reproducible; the recorder may not refuse to record it on the basis of the instrument's "lack of legal sufficiency." Because both indexing and constructive notice to later purchasers depend on a recorded document identifying the real property it affects, a boundary line agreement that is meant to describe a specific, locatable line, and to give notice of that line to anyone who later takes an interest in either parcel, typically references a legal description sufficient to locate the agreed line on the ground, rather than relying on a street address alone. As a practical matter, describing a boundary line's specific location is often accompanied by a survey or other technical description prepared for that purpose. This is a factual point about what makes a recorded instrument identify real property adequately for indexing and later notice under California's general recording statutes; it is not a determination that a survey is required by statute in every case, and it does not evaluate the adequacy of any specific legal description.
clauses.gap: This clause cites a single statutory provision, Cal. Gov't Code § 27201(a)(1)(A); no additional independent statutory source was found requiring a "sufficient" legal description specifically for a boundary line agreement, so this clause's practical point about legal descriptions is drawn from § 27201(a)(1)(A)'s general indexing requirement, read together with the constructive-notice rule of Cal. Civ. Code § 1213 (independently cited and verified in a separate clause of this document, and not re-cited here as a second source for this clause). This is California's own recording-formalities framework; acknowledgment, indexing, and recording mechanics are not uniform across states, and this is not a claim about which state's law governs a particular boundary line agreement or parcel. This clause does not address any particular county recorder's additional local formatting requirements (margins, page size, first-page content, and similar mechanics), which § 27201(a)(1)(A) itself contemplates may exist on top of this statewide framework.

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 27201(a)(1)(A)
citations.cite: California Government Code, recorder's duty to accept a conforming instrument that contains sufficient information to be indexed
citations.quote: The recorder shall, upon payment of proper fees and taxes, accept for recordation any instrument, paper, or notice that is authorized or required by statute, or court order to be recorded, or authorized or required to be recorded by a local ordinance that relates to the recordation of any instrument, paper, or notice that relates to real property, if the instrument, paper, or notice contains sufficient information to be indexed as provided by statute, meets recording requirements of state statutes and local ordinances, and is photographically reproducible. The county recorder shall not refuse to record any instrument, paper, or notice that is authorized or required by statute, court order, or local ordinance that relates to the recordation of any instrument, paper, or notice that relates to real property to be recorded on the basis of its lack of legal sufficiency.

clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes E-Verify, a federal electronic employment eligibility verification system operated by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), and California's specific statutory restrictions on an employer's use of it, in connection with {{companyName}}'s employment of {{employeeName}} with a start date of {{startDate}}. E-Verify is a separate system from, though it draws information from, the Form I-9 employment eligibility verification process that federal law requires for every new hire; this sheet does not restate the Form I-9 requirements themselves, which are addressed in a separate information sheet. This document is not the Form I-9, does not enroll {{companyName}} in E-Verify or submit any query to it, and does not state, verify, or determine {{employeeName}}'s actual identity, employment authorization, or immigration status.

clauses.title: What E-Verify Is and Its Legal Basis
clauses.body: E-Verify is an internet-based federal program, administered by DHS/USCIS, that allows an enrolled employer to electronically confirm the employment eligibility of a worker against Social Security Administration and DHS records. It traces its legal basis to a set of federal "pilot programs of employment eligibility confirmation" that Congress established in 1996 as Subtitle A of Title IV of Division C of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act (IIRIRA), codified as a note under 8 U.S.C. § 1324a rather than as freestanding numbered sections of the U.S. Code. One of those three original pilot programs was itself named the "E-Verify Program" and was later expanded to all 50 states; California's own Labor Code separately confirms that the electronic system it regulates traces to this same 1996 federal enactment, renamed "E-Verify" in 2007.
clauses.gap: This is federal and California law, used as real evidence of E-Verify's identity as a federal pilot-program system and its statutory point of origin — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about any specific individual's actual work authorization status. The federal citation below is to a statutory note set out under 8 U.S.C. § 1324a (Pub. L. 104-208, div. C, title IV, subtitle A, as subsequently amended), not to numbered subsections of § 1324a itself — this note-versus-codified-section distinction matters because a note is set out by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel as historical/uncodified text rather than as the operative U.S. Code section, even though it remains legally operative. Separately, this clause's drafter found, in the course of reading that note, that the pilot programs' nominal sunset date has been repeatedly extended by later appropriations-related public laws that amend only the sunset date (most recently to September 30, 2026, by Pub. L. 119-75, div. I, § 5014, enacted Feb. 3, 2026) rather than by any permanent reauthorization — an honest, undisclosed-until-now gap in the premise that E-Verify's authorization is settled or permanent: as of this clause's checked date, the current extension is due to lapse September 30, 2026, absent a further extension. The California citation is to Cal. Lab. Code § 2813(a), a definitions provision from a different jurisdiction than the federal citation, so the two are independent sources of each other, not the same source viewed twice.

citations.case: Pilot Programs for Employment Eligibility Confirmation, Pub. L. 104-208, div. C, title IV, subtitle A, § 401(a) (set out as a note under 8 U.S.C. § 1324a) (uscode.house.gov text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, statutory note under 8 U.S.C. § 1324a, establishment of pilot programs
citations.quote: The Secretary of Homeland Security shall conduct 3 pilot programs of employment eligibility confirmation under this subtitle.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 2813(a) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, definition of "electronic employment verification system"
citations.quote: This includes the Basic Pilot Program, enacted by Section 404 of Public Law 104-208 and renamed in 2007 as the E-Verify Program, and other pilot programs for electronic employment eligibility confirmation.

clauses.title: E-Verify Use Is Voluntary for Most Employers, With Federal-Government Exceptions
clauses.body: As a general federal rule, participation in E-Verify is voluntary: an employer may elect to use it, but the federal government may not require an employer to participate, except in specifically enumerated categories. The statutory note establishing the program identifies its own carve-outs from that voluntary default, including a requirement that each department of the federal executive branch elect to participate. Whether a particular non-federal employer instead falls under a mandatory-use category — such as the federal-contractor mandate described in a separate clause of this information sheet, or a state-law mandate — is a separate question this general voluntariness rule does not resolve.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of E-Verify's default voluntary status and of the existence of specific federal-government exceptions to it — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about whether any particular reader's employer falls into a mandatory-use category. Both citations below are to different subsections of the same statutory note (Pub. L. 104-208, div. C, title IV, subtitle A, § 402) — subsection (a) (the general voluntariness rule) and subsection (e)(1)(A)(i) (the federal-executive-department exception); they are treated as one source, not independent, disclosed together here rather than presented as though they corroborate each other from separate origins. This clause does not attempt to catalog every category the note lists in subsection (e) — it also covers the legislative branch and certain parties already found to have violated federal immigration-related employment law under a formal order — and states only the general shape of the exception, not its full scope.

clauses.title: Mandatory E-Verify Use for Certain Federal Contractors
clauses.body: Federal acquisition regulations require an employer awarded a covered federal contract to enroll in and use E-Verify, both for its new hires generally and for employees specifically assigned to the contract, and to flow the same requirement down to certain subcontractors. This requirement is implemented through a standard clause that a contracting officer must insert into qualifying solicitations and contracts above a stated dollar threshold, subject to stated exceptions (including contracts performed entirely outside the United States, short-duration contracts, and certain purchases of commercial off-the-shelf items). Whether {{companyName}} holds a contract that includes this clause, and is therefore subject to this mandate, is a separate question this clause does not resolve.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of a specific, currently codified category of employer for whom E-Verify use is mandatory rather than voluntary — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about any specific employer's own contract status. This clause's drafter traced the mandate to its currently codified regulatory text, in the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) at 48 C.F.R. §§ 22.1802-22.1803 (agency policy and the instruction to insert the contract clause) and 48 C.F.R. § 52.222-54 (the clause itself, in its January 2025 form as reflected in the eCFR). The FAR text itself states that this requirement rests on "[s]tatutes and Executive orders" generally, without citing a specific executive order by number in the subpart text this clause read; this clause's drafter is aware, from general background knowledge rather than from a citation verified against a primary source in this research pass, that the commonly cited executive-order lineage for the federal-contractor E-Verify mandate is Executive Order 12989 (1996) as amended by Executive Order 13465 (2008), but did not independently fetch and verify the text of either order against a primary source in this research pass (an outbound fetch to a federal-register source was blocked in this environment) — so that specific EO citation is disclosed here as unverified background, not asserted as verified. The two FAR citations below are to different parts of the FAR (subpart 22.18 and the standalone clause at 52.222-54); they are independent regulatory citations, not two views of the same provision.

citations.quote: This subpart prescribes policies and procedures requiring contractors to utilize the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), United States Citizenship and Immigration Service's employment eligibility verification program (E-Verify) as the means for verifying employment eligibility of certain employees.

clauses.title: California Restriction on a State or Local Agency Mandating E-Verify
clauses.body: Under California law, except as required by federal law or as a condition of receiving federal funds, neither the state nor a city, county, city and county, or special district may require an employer to use an electronic employment verification system such as E-Verify — including as a condition of a government contract, as a condition of obtaining or keeping a business license, or as a penalty for a licensing violation.
clauses.gap: This is California law, used as real evidence of a specific statutory restriction on California state and local government agencies (not on private employers directly) — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about whether any specific state or local requirement a particular employer may separately encounter is, in fact, an unlawful E-Verify mandate under this section. This section, Cal. Lab. Code § 2812, restricts what government bodies may require of an employer; it is a distinct provision from Cal. Lab. Code § 2814, addressed in separate clauses of this information sheet, which instead restricts what an employer may do with E-Verify on its own initiative. This clause corrects a plausible mis-citation: the state/local-mandate prohibition is codified at § 2812, not at § 2814.

citations.quote: neither the state nor a city, county, city and county, or special district shall require an employer to use an electronic employment verification system, including under the following circumstances

clauses.title: California Restriction on an Employer's Own Use of E-Verify
clauses.body: Separately from the restriction on government mandates, California law makes it unlawful for an employer to use E-Verify to check the employment authorization status of an existing employee, or of an applicant who has not yet been offered employment, at a time or in a manner not required under federal law or authorized under a federal E-Verify memorandum of understanding — except as required by federal law or as a condition of receiving federal funds. The same California statute makes clear that this restriction does not prohibit an employer from using E-Verify, in accordance with federal law, to check a person who has already been offered employment.
clauses.gap: This is California law, used as real evidence of a specific statutory restriction on an employer's own, self-initiated use of E-Verify — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about whether any particular employer's use of E-Verify would in fact fall outside what federal law requires or a governing E-Verify memorandum of understanding authorizes (a fact-specific question this clause does not resolve). Both citations below are to different paragraphs of the same statutory subsection, Cal. Lab. Code § 2814(a) — paragraph (1) (the restriction) and paragraph (2) (the post-offer carve-out) — and are treated as one source, not independent, disclosed together here rather than presented as though they corroborate each other from separate origins.

citations.quote: it shall be unlawful for an employer, or any other person or entity to use the federal electronic employment verification system known as E-Verify to check the employment authorization status of an existing employee or an applicant who has not been offered employment at a time or in a manner not required under subsection (b) of Section 1324a of Title 8 of the United States

citations.quote: Nothing in this section shall prohibit an employer from utilizing the federal E-Verify system, in accordance with federal law, to check the employment authorization status of a person who has been offered employment.

clauses.title: California Notice Requirement Upon a Tentative Nonconfirmation
clauses.body: California law requires that, upon using E-Verify to check a person's employment authorization status, if the employer receives a tentative nonconfirmation from the Social Security Administration or DHS indicating the information entered did not match federal records, the employer must comply with the notification procedures required under the governing E-Verify memorandum of understanding, and must furnish to the employee any notification issued by the Social Security Administration or DHS containing information specific to that employee's E-Verify case, or any tentative nonconfirmation notice, as soon as practicable.
clauses.gap: This is California law, used as real evidence of a specific statutory notice requirement tied to E-Verify use — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about whether any specific individual has received or will receive a tentative nonconfirmation. The statute ties the substance of the required notification procedures to a separate federal document (the E-Verify memorandum of understanding) rather than specifying those procedures itself; this clause's drafter did not independently fetch or verify the current text of that memorandum of understanding in this research pass, and discloses that as an honest gap rather than describing its contents.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, notice of tentative nonconfirmation
citations.quote: The employer shall furnish to the employee any notification issued by the Social Security Administration or the United States Department of Homeland Security containing information specific to the employee’s E-Verify case or any tentative nonconfirmation notice.

clauses.title: California Civil Penalty for an Unlawful Use of E-Verify
clauses.body: California law makes an employer that violates this E-Verify restriction liable for a civil penalty of up to $10,000 for each violation, in addition to other available remedies, and treats each unlawful use of E-Verify on an employee or applicant as a separate violation. The same statute states that this section is intended to prevent discrimination in employment, not to sanction the potential hiring or employment of a person not authorized to work under federal law.
clauses.gap: This is California law, used as real evidence of the specific civil-penalty mechanism this statute creates for a violation of the employer-use restriction described in a separate clause of this information sheet — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about any specific employer's actual liability. This clause's drafter read the full text of Cal. Lab. Code § 2814 and found this civil penalty, capped per violation, to be the only enforcement mechanism the statute itself states; the statute does not, in the text this clause's drafter reviewed, create an explicit private right of action naming who may bring an action to recover the penalty or specifying an enforcing agency, and this clause does not assert that either exists.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 2814(c) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)

citations.quote: an employer who violates this section is liable for a civil penalty not to exceed ten thousand dollars ($10,000) for each violation of this section. Each unlawful use of the E-Verify system on an employee or applicant constitutes a separate violation.

clauses.title: Relationship to the Form I-9 Process and E-Verify Timing
clauses.body: E-Verify draws on information an employee and employer already recorded on Form I-9, but it is a separate system layered on top of the mandatory I-9 process, not a substitute for it, and California's own statutory definition expressly excludes the Form I-9 itself from the category of "electronic employment verification system" it regulates. Where E-Verify use applies — such as under the federal-contractor mandate described elsewhere in this information sheet — federal contracting rules require the E-Verify query for a new hire to be initiated within a set number of business days of the date of hire, on a timetable distinct from the separate Form I-9 completion deadline addressed in this office's I-9 information sheet.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on both federal regulatory law and California statutory law, used as real evidence that E-Verify and Form I-9 are legally distinct, and of one specific, currently codified E-Verify timing rule — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about any specific individual's hire date or the Form I-9 deadline (addressed in a separate document). The "3 business days after the date of hire" figure quoted in the federal-contractor-mandate clause of this information sheet is codified, for federal contractors specifically, at 48 C.F.R. § 52.222-54(b)(1)(ii) — a regulation, not a statute. This clause's drafter was unable to independently verify, against a primary source, whether an identical or different business-day timing rule applies to E-Verify participants generally (that is, non-federal-contractor employers who elect to use E-Verify voluntarily): outbound fetches to e-verify.gov and uscis.gov, which would ordinarily carry the E-Verify memorandum of understanding and User Manual describing that general timing rule, were blocked in this environment, and this clause does not assert a specific timing figure for that broader population beyond what the FAR text itself establishes for federal contractors. The Form I-9 timing deadline itself (three business days of hire, with a same-day exception for very short hires) is addressed with its own citations in a separate I-9 information sheet clause (id: i9_verification_timing) and is not re-derived here.

clauses.title: The Wage Garnishment Law and How an Employer Becomes Obligated to Withhold
clauses.body: California's Wage Garnishment Law generally makes the earnings withholding order the exclusive judicial procedure for requiring an employer to withhold an employee's earnings to pay a debt — the one stated exception is an earning assignment order for support. Once a judgment creditor has an earnings withholding order issued and it is served on {{companyName}} as {{employeeName}}'s employer, {{companyName}} is required by statute to comply with it; if {{companyName}} is served with more than one earnings withholding order, the statute requires compliance with whichever order was served first (subject to separate priority rules for support and tax orders and certain elder-financial-abuse orders).
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutory framework (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. §§ 706.020, 706.023(a)), offered as documented evidence of what California's Wage Garnishment Law says — not a claim about which state's procedure governs a specific employer or employee; wage garnishment procedure varies significantly by state, and federal law separately governs garnishment for certain federal debts (e.g., student loans, taxes) outside this state framework entirely. The two citations are from different sections of the same chapter (§ 706.020 and § 706.023), not subsections of one section, so they are treated as independent sources. Separately, California's primary mechanism for collecting child or spousal support from wages is not this earnings-withholding-order framework but a distinct 'earnings assignment order' issued under the Family Code, which by statute takes priority over an ordinary earnings withholding order (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.031) — that separate framework was not independently verified for this clause set and is not the subject of this document. No case law was researched for this clause; the proposition is stated directly from statutory text.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.020 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.020
citations.quote: Except for an earning assignment order for support, the earnings of an employee shall not be required to be withheld by an employer for payment of a debt by means of any judicial procedure other than pursuant to this chapter.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.023(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.023, subd. (a)
citations.quote: An employer shall comply with the first earnings withholding order served upon the employer.

clauses.title: The General Withholding Limit: The Lesser-of Formula
clauses.body: For a general (non-support) earnings withholding order, California law caps the amount that may be withheld from {{employeeName}}'s disposable earnings for any workweek at the lesser of two figures: 20% of {{employeeName}}'s disposable earnings for that week, or 40% of the amount by which {{employeeName}}'s disposable earnings for that week exceed 48 times the state minimum hourly wage in effect when the earnings are payable (or 48 times the local minimum hourly wage, if the applicable local minimum wage is higher than the state minimum wage). Separate multipliers apply to convert this weekly formula to daily, biweekly, semimonthly, and monthly pay periods.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.050(a)), offered as documented evidence of what that provision currently says — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. The federal default limit under the Consumer Credit Protection Act is materially different and less protective of the debtor: 25% of disposable earnings, or the amount by which disposable earnings exceed 30 times the federal minimum hourly wage, whichever is less (15 U.S.C. § 1673(a)) — California's 20%/48-times formula supersedes the federal default for debts collected in California courts because federal law expressly permits a state to impose a lower maximum. The current California formula (20% / 48-times-minimum-wage) took effect operatively on September 1, 2023, under a 2022 amendment (Stats. 2022, Ch. 849 (SB 1477)), which repealed and replaced a prior version of this section that had tied the exempt amount to federal poverty guidelines rather than to a multiple of the minimum wage; a document or calculation relying on the pre-September-2023 formula is relying on superseded law. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 706.050(a)); no additional independent source was found for this specific text. This clause states the general, non-support limit only; a materially different and generally higher cap applies where the order is a withholding order for support, addressed in a separate clause. No case law was researched for this clause; the proposition is stated directly from statutory text.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.050(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.050, subd. (a)
citations.quote: the maximum amount of disposable earnings of an individual judgment debtor for any workweek that is subject to levy under an earnings withholding order shall not exceed the lesser of the following: (1) Twenty percent of the individual’s disposable earnings for that week. (2) Forty percent of the amount by which the individual’s disposable earnings for that week exceed 48 times the state minimum hourly wage in effect at the time the earnings are payable.

clauses.title: The Different, Higher Cap for a Withholding Order for Support
clauses.body: Where the earnings withholding order served on {{companyName}} is a withholding order for support (a distinct sub-type of earnings withholding order used to collect delinquent child or spousal support), the general 20%-or-40%-over-the-minimum-wage limit does not apply. Instead, California law exempts one-half of {{employeeName}}'s disposable earnings from levy under this framework, and any interested party may move the court for an equitable division of {{employeeName}}'s earnings that accounts for the needs of everyone {{employeeName}} is required to support — but a court-ordered division under that equitable-division authority cannot exceed the cap set by federal law, which permits withholding up to 50% of disposable earnings (or 55% if the arrears being collected are more than twelve weeks old) where {{employeeName}} is supporting a current spouse or dependent child, and up to 60% (or 65% for arrears more than twelve weeks old) where {{employeeName}} is not.
clauses.gap: This clause combines one state statute (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.052(a)) and one federal statute (15 U.S.C. § 1673(b)(2)) — different sovereigns and different code sections, so they are independent sources, not duplicates of a single source. This is one state's mechanism for the specific 'withholding order for support' sub-type defined within the Wage Garnishment Law (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.030) — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific support obligation, and not a description of California's more commonly used child/spousal support collection tool. That more commonly used tool is the Family Code 'earnings assignment order for support,' which is a separate mechanism that, by statute, takes priority over any earnings withholding order (including a withholding order for support) when both reach an employer (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.031) — the Family Code provisions governing that separate mechanism were not independently verified for this clause set. The federal statute quoted here is a nationwide ceiling on support garnishment generally, applicable regardless of which state-law collection mechanism is used; it does not by itself specify which mechanism a given support order proceeds through. No case law was researched for this clause; the proposition is stated directly from statutory text.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.052(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.052, subd. (a)
citations.quote: one-half of the disposable earnings (as defined by Section 1672 of Title 15 of the United States Code) of the judgment debtor, plus any amount withheld from the judgment debtor’s earnings pursuant to any earnings assignment order for support, is exempt from levy under this chapter where the earnings withholding order is a withholding order for support under Section 706.030.

citations.case: 15 U.S.C. § 1673(b)(2) (Cornell Legal Information Institute text)
citations.quote: The maximum part of the aggregate disposable earnings of an individual for any workweek which is subject to garnishment to enforce any order for the support of any person shall not exceed— (A) where such individual is supporting his spouse or dependent child (other than a spouse or child with respect to whose support such order is used), 50 per centum of such individual’s disposable earnings for that week; and (B) where such individual is not supporting such a spouse or dependent child described in clause (A), 60 per centum of such individual’s disposable earnings for that week

clauses.title: When Withholding Must Begin and When Withheld Amounts Must Be Remitted
clauses.body: Under California law, the withholding period generally begins on the 30th day after an earnings withholding order is served on {{companyName}}; if a claim of exemption is filed with the levying officer and {{companyName}} receives actual notice of it before the close of business on the 29th day after service, the withholding period instead begins on the 45th day after service. Once the withholding period has begun, {{companyName}} must withhold the required amount from all of {{employeeName}}'s earnings payable for any pay period ending within that period. California law separately requires {{companyName}} to pay the amounts withheld to the levying officer monthly, no later than the 15th day of each month, unless {{companyName}} elects to pay more frequently, in which case payment for a given pay period is due within 10 days after that pay period closes.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. §§ 706.022(a), 706.025), offered as documented evidence of what that provision says — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer's payroll timing; other states set different deadlines for withholding to begin and for remitting withheld amounts. The two citations are from different sections of the same chapter (§ 706.022 and § 706.025), not subsections of one section, so they are treated as independent sources. This clause states the general timing rule; it does not address the separate rules governing when a withholding period may be dormant, suspended, or terminated, or the priority rules that apply when more than one order or assignment reaches the same employer. No case law was researched for this clause; the proposition is stated directly from statutory text.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.022(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.022, subd. (a)
citations.quote: As used in this section, “withholding period” means the period which commences on the 30th day after service of an earnings withholding order upon the judgment debtor’s employer. If a claim of exemption is filed with the levying officer, and the employer is given actual notice before the close of business on the 29th day after the service of the earnings withholding order on the judgment debtor’s employer, the withholding period commences on the 45th day after service of the earnings withholding order on the judgment debtor’s employer.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.025(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.025, subd. (a)
citations.quote: the amount required to be withheld pursuant to an earnings withholding order shall be paid monthly to the levying officer not later than the 15th day of each month

clauses.title: Anti-Retaliation Protection: Discharge Based on Garnishment
clauses.body: California law prohibits {{companyName}} from discharging {{employeeName}} because {{employeeName}}'s wages have been threatened with garnishment, and separately prohibits {{companyName}} from discharging {{employeeName}} because {{employeeName}}'s wages have been garnished for the payment of one judgment; an employment contract term giving {{employeeName}} less protection than this statute provides is void as against public policy. Federal law contains a related but differently worded protection: it prohibits an employer from discharging an employee because the employee's earnings have been garnished for any one indebtedness, and makes a willful violation punishable by a fine, imprisonment, or both.
clauses.gap: This clause combines one state statute (Cal. Lab. Code § 2929(b)) and one federal statute (15 U.S.C. § 1674(a)) — different sovereigns, so they are independent sources. California's statute expressly states it is intended to aid enforcement of, and to be interpreted consistently with, the federal Consumer Credit Protection Act's anti-discharge provisions (Cal. Lab. Code § 2929(e)), but the two statutes are not identically worded: California's protects against discharge for garnishment 'for the payment of one judgment,' while the federal provision protects against discharge for garnishment 'for any one indebtedness.' Neither statute's quoted text expressly extends this specific protection to discharge based on multiple garnishments for different debts arriving at or near the same time — that scenario is simply not addressed by the text quoted here, and this clause does not assert that either statute resolves it. This is a general statement of what these two statutes say; it is not a case-by-case assessment of whether a particular discharge was lawful. No case law was researched for this clause given CourtListener's daily rate limit and the statutory clarity of the text itself; the proposition is stated directly from statutory text.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 2929(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 2929, subd. (b)
citations.quote: No employer may discharge any employee by reason of the fact that his wages have been subjected to garnishment for the payment of one judgment. A provision of a contract of employment that provides an employee with less protection than is provided by this subdivision is against public policy and void.

citations.case: 15 U.S.C. § 1674(a) (Cornell Legal Information Institute text)
citations.quote: No employer may discharge any employee by reason of the fact that his earnings have been subjected to garnishment for any one indebtedness.

clauses.title: Employer Liability to the Judgment Creditor for Noncompliance
clauses.body: If {{companyName}} fails to withhold, or fails to pay over to the levying officer, an amount {{companyName}} is required to withhold and pay over under a validly served earnings withholding order, California law allows the judgment creditor to bring a civil action against {{companyName}} to recover that amount, and this remedy is not the judgment creditor's exclusive one. The same statute also protects an employer on the other side of this rule: an employer that complies with a written order or written notice that purports to have been given or served under this chapter is not subject to civil or criminal liability for that compliance, unless the employer actively participated in a fraud.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.154). Both citations in this clause come from subdivisions (a) and (b) of that same statutory section and are treated as one source, not independent, sources for verification purposes. The statutory text authorizes the judgment creditor to recover 'such amount' — meaning the amount the employer failed to withhold and pay over — from the employer; it does not itself state a separate fixed statutory penalty on top of that amount, so a document or calculation assuming a specific additional penalty figure beyond the shortfall amount is going beyond what this text says. This clause is not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer's liability, and it does not address any separate liability an employer might have under other law (for example, wage-and-hour statutes) for the same underlying failure. No case law was researched for this clause; the proposition is stated directly from statutory text.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.154(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.154, subd. (a)
citations.quote: If an employer fails to withhold or to pay over the amount the employer is required to withhold and pay over pursuant to this chapter, the judgment creditor may bring a civil action against the employer to recover such amount. The remedy provided by this subdivision is not exclusive.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.154(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.154, subd. (b)
citations.quote: an employer who complies with any written order or written notice which purports to be given or served in accordance with the provisions of this chapter is not subject to any civil or criminal liability for such compliance unless the employer has actively participated in a fraud.

Ex Parte Application Procedure and Standard Under California Rules of Court, Rule 5.151
clauses.body: California Rules of Court, rule 5.151 governs applications for emergency orders -- also called ex parte applications -- in family law cases. Rule 5.151(b) states that the purpose of a request for emergency orders is to address matters that cannot wait for the court's regular hearing calendar, that notice to the other party is shorter than in other family law proceedings, and that notice can be waived under exceptional and other circumstances stated in the rule. An ex parte request for emergency orders is not limited to custody; rule 5.151(b) describes its use to prevent immediate danger or irreparable harm to a party or to the children involved, to prevent immediate loss or damage to property subject to disposition in the case, and to address certain procedural matters such as shortening time for a hearing. Rule 5.151(d)(2) states the general factual showing required: the declarations supporting the application must contain facts within the declarant's personal knowledge that demonstrate why the matter is appropriately handled as an emergency, and the applicant must make an affirmative factual showing of irreparable harm, immediate danger, or another statutory basis for granting relief without notice or with shortened notice. Rule 5.151(d)(5) states that an application for emergency orders granting or modifying child custody or visitation must specifically be made under Family Code section 3064 and must include a full, detailed description of the most recent incidents showing immediate harm to the child (as defined in section 3064(b)) or immediate risk that the child will be removed from California, the date of each such incident, the existing custody and visitation arrangements and how the request would change them, a copy of any current custody order (or an explanation of where and with whom the child currently lives if none exists), and a completed UCCJEA declaration (form FL-105). Rule 5.151(c) lists the required documents for any request for emergency orders, including a Request for Order (form FL-300), a proposed order (form FL-305), and a written declaration regarding notice (form FL-303 or its equivalent).

clauses.title: Family Code Section 3064: The Immediate-Harm Standard for an Ex Parte Custody Order
clauses.body: Family Code section 3064(a) states the specific limiting standard for ex parte custody relief: the court shall refrain from granting or modifying a custody order on an ex parte basis unless there has been a showing of immediate harm to the child or immediate risk that the child will be removed from the State of California. Section 3064(b)(1) defines "immediate harm to the child" to include, without limitation, having a parent who has committed acts of domestic violence of recent origin or as part of a demonstrated and continuing pattern, or sexual abuse of the child of recent origin or as part of a demonstrated and continuing pattern. Section 3064(b)(2)(A) additionally requires the court, in determining whether immediate harm has been shown, to consider a parent's illegal access to firearms and ammunition, including whether that parent is prohibited from having firearms and ammunition. As fetched and verified, section 3064's text does not condition ex parte custody relief on a finding that the request is not sought merely to alter jurisdiction or venue; no such jurisdiction- or venue-focused limitation appears anywhere in the statutory text of section 3064.

This is one state's statute, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches (different User-Agent strings), used as real evidence of California's own immediate-harm standard for ex parte custody relief -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific applicant's request, or that an equivalent standard exists in any other state. Whether a specific set of facts meets this immediate-harm-or-immediate-risk-of-removal standard is a determination the court makes on the application before it; this clause does not make that determination for any individual case. citations.quote: The court shall refrain from making an order granting or modifying a custody order on an ex parte basis unless there has been a showing of immediate harm to the child or immediate risk that the child will be removed from the State of California.

clauses.title: The Follow-Up Noticed Hearing After an Ex Parte Custody Order
clauses.body: Family Code section 3062, not section 3066, is the provision requiring a further noticed hearing after an ex parte custody order. Section 3062(a) states that, absent an agreement, understanding, or stipulation between the parties, the court may -- if jurisdiction is appropriate -- enter an ex parte temporary custody order, set a hearing date within 20 days, and issue an order to show cause on the responding party; if the responding party does not appear or respond within the time set, the temporary order may be extended as necessary pending termination of the proceedings. Section 3062(b) states that if service of the ex parte order and order to show cause has not been timely effected despite good-faith efforts, and there is reason to believe the responding party has possession of the child and seeks to avoid the court's jurisdiction or is concealing the child's whereabouts, the hearing date may be reset and the ex parte order extended up to an additional 90 days; after service is effected, either party may request ex parte that the hearing date be advanced or the ex parte order be dissolved or modified. Family Code section 3063 separately states that in conjunction with any ex parte order seeking or modifying custody, the court shall enter an order restraining the person receiving custody from removing the child from the state, pending notice and a hearing on the underlying custody request. Both section 3062 and section 3064 (the immediate-harm standard) sit within the same statutory chapter, Family Code chapter 3 of division 8, part 2, titled 'Temporary Custody Order During Pendency of Proceeding,' spanning sections 3060 through 3064.
clauses.gap: Family Code section 3062 and section 3063, cited together above, are two separate, independently numbered statutory sections rather than subsections of one section, so no single-section source-independence disclosure applies to that pairing. A fetch for 'Family Code section 3066' -- the section number initially assumed to govern this follow-up hearing requirement -- returned no code section content from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, confirmed consistently across two independent fetches (different User-Agent strings); the custody-related chapter in which section 3064 sits runs only from section 3060 through section 3064, with no section 3066 in it. This document relies instead on section 3062(a), which was independently fetched, verified identical across two User-Agent strings, and does state a specific follow-up-hearing timing rule (a hearing date within 20 days). This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own follow-up-hearing mechanism -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case, or that an equivalent mechanism exists in any other state. Whether a specific ex parte custody order in fact triggers the 20-day hearing-setting requirement, and how it interacts with any parallel Domestic Violence Prevention Act proceeding, are determinations the court makes on the case before it.

clauses.title: Notice of the Ex Parte Application Itself: California Rules of Court, Rule 5.165
clauses.body: Ex parte does not mean no notice at all under California's general emergency-orders rules; California Rules of Court, rule 5.165(b) states that a party seeking emergency orders under this chapter must give notice to all parties or their attorneys so that it is received no later than 10:00 a.m. on the court day before the matter is to be considered by the court. If notice is given later than that deadline, rule 5.165(b)(1) requires the party to request, in a declaration regarding notice, that the court approve the shortened notice, supported by facts showing exceptional circumstances. Separately, rule 5.165(b)(2) allows a party to ask the court to waive notice entirely, by filing a written declaration signed under penalty of perjury showing good cause; the rule lists five categories of good cause a judicial officer may rely on: that giving notice would frustrate the purpose of the order; that giving notice would result in immediate and irreparable harm to the applicant or the children who may be affected; that giving notice would result in immediate and irreparable damage to or loss of property subject to disposition in the case; that the parties agreed in advance that notice would not be necessary; or that the party made reasonable, good-faith efforts to give notice and further efforts would probably be futile or unduly burdensome. Rule 5.165(b) also states that this notice rule does not apply to a party seeking emergency orders under the Domestic Violence Prevention Act.
clauses.gap: Rule 5.165(b) and its subdivisions (b)(1) and (b)(2), cited together above, are subdivisions of a single California Rule of Court and are treated as one source, not independent. This is one state's court rule, fetched directly from the Judicial Branch of California's own publication at courts.ca.gov and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches (different User-Agent strings), used as real evidence of California's own notice regime for ex parte applications -- not a claim about which state's rules govern a specific applicant's case, or that an equivalent notice regime exists in any other state. Correction of an initial research assumption: the rule's good-cause grounds for waiving notice altogether are broader than a single scenario of the other party being frightened into fleeing with the child -- the rule lists five distinct good-cause categories (frustrating the order's purpose, irreparable harm to the applicant or children, irreparable damage to or loss of property, an advance agreement dispensing with notice, or futile/unduly burdensome further efforts), only some of which could overlap with a flight-risk fact pattern. Whether a specific applicant's facts satisfy the shortened-notice or notice-waiver standard is a determination the court makes on the declaration before it; this clause does not make that determination for any individual case.

clauses.title: Relationship to a Domestic Violence Restraining Order: A Separate Procedural Track
clauses.body: An ex parte request for emergency custody orders in a family law case under California Rules of Court, rule 5.151 and Family Code section 3064 is a separate procedural track from a request for a domestic violence restraining order under the Domestic Violence Prevention Act (DVPA), which this corpus's separate Domestic Violence Restraining Order (Request for Order) Information Sheet document describes. Rule 5.151(a) states directly that the rules governing ex parte applications in family law cases -- described in this document -- do not apply to ex parte applications for domestic violence restraining orders under the DVPA, unless specifically stated otherwise. Rule 5.165(b) states the same distinction for its notice requirements: that rule does not apply to a party seeking emergency orders under the DVPA. The two tracks use different Judicial Council forms, different statutory standards (Family Code section 3064's immediate-harm-or-immediate-risk-of-removal standard for a custody-focused ex parte order under this document, versus the DVPA's own statutory abuse definition and ex parte mechanism for a DVRO), and different notice rules. The underlying facts prompting either request can overlap -- for example, a recent act of domestic violence can be relevant to both an ex parte custody request under section 3064(b)(1)(A) and a DVPA petition -- and a party may pursue either track, or both, depending on the circumstances of a specific case. Which track, or combination of tracks, applies to a specific set of facts is a legal determination; this document states the factual distinction between the two tracks and does not make that determination for any individual case.

This is one state's court rules, used as real evidence of how California itself structures these two ex parte tracks as procedurally distinct -- not a claim about which state's rules govern a specific party's situation, or that an equivalent dual-track structure exists in any other state, and not a claim about which track (if either) fits any specific reader's facts. This document does not restate the DVPA's own substantive standards, forms, or process, which this corpus's separate Domestic Violence Restraining Order (Request for Order) Information Sheet document addresses; nothing here duplicates that document's content.

These rules may be referred to as "the emergency orders rules." Unless specifically stated, these rules do not apply to ex parte applications for domestic violence restraining orders under the Domestic Violence Prevention Act.

clauses.title: Brief Distinction: The Law-Enforcement-Initiated Emergency Protective Order
clauses.body: A further, distinct emergency mechanism exists outside both tracks described above: the Emergency Protective Order (EPO) under Family Code section 6250. Section 6250 states that a judicial officer may issue an ex parte emergency protective order where a law enforcement officer asserts reasonable grounds to believe, among other things, that a person is in immediate and present danger of domestic violence, that a child is in immediate and present danger of abuse by a family or household member, or that a child is in immediate and present danger of being abducted by a parent or relative. Unlike the family-court ex parte custody procedure described in this document, an EPO is requested by a law enforcement officer, typically responding to an incident, directly to a judicial officer -- often by telephone -- rather than filed as a written application by a party or attorney in a pending or new family law case. An EPO is also short in duration: Family Code section 6256 states that an EPO expires at the earlier of two points, one measured in court days and one in calendar days from issuance.
