How a Testamentary Trust Is Created
clauses.body: A testamentary trust is a trust created by the terms of {{testatorName}}'s own will, rather than by a separate trust instrument executed during {{testatorName}}'s lifetime. California Probate Code § 15200 lists a transfer of property "by will or by other instrument taking effect upon the death of the owner, to another person as trustee" as one of the statutory methods of creating a trust, alongside a lifetime declaration of trust and a lifetime transfer to a trustee. Because that transfer takes effect only upon {{testatorName}}'s death, the trust it creates does not exist, and holds no property, while {{testatorName}} is alive; it comes into existence only once {{testatorName}}'s will takes legal effect.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual statutory basis for a will's ability to create a trust — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will or trust. This clause quotes a single subsection of Cal. Prob. Code § 15200(c); no additional independent source was found for this. This document does not restate the general requirements for a valid trust — settlor intent, a lawful purpose, and an ascertainable beneficiary — which apply to a trust created this way exactly as they would to a trust created any other way; see this corpus's Revocable Living Trust document for those requirements, sourced separately from the same Probate Code chapter (§§ 15201, 15203, 15205).

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15200(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a will is a statutory method of creating a trust
citations.quote: (c) A transfer of property by the owner, by will or by other instrument taking effect upon the death of the owner, to another person as trustee.

clauses.title: Why Probate Applies to a Testamentary Trust — the Key Difference From a Living Trust
clauses.body: Because a testamentary trust is created by {{testatorName}}'s will rather than by a lifetime trust instrument, the property that funds it is, at the moment of {{testatorName}}'s death, still {{testatorName}}'s own property passing under the will — not property already held by a trustee. California Probate Code § 7000 provides that title to a decedent's property passes at death to the person to whom it is devised by the decedent's will, but § 7001 immediately qualifies that: the decedent's property remains "subject to administration under this code" and to the rights of beneficiaries, creditors, and other persons as provided by law. That administration is the probate process — a court proceeding, not an automatic transfer. This is the structural difference from a properly funded revocable living trust, which already holds title to its property through a lifetime transfer and so does not depend on probate administration to give the trustee that property.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual mechanics of how a decedent's property passes and is administered — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate or trust. § 7000 and § 7001 are two different, adjacent statutory sections within the same short chapter (Chapter 1 of Division 7, Part 1); they are cited together because § 7001's administration language directly qualifies § 7000's passage-of-title rule, not as two unrelated sources. This document does not restate this corpus's separate Petition for Probate Information Sheet, which describes the actual probate court proceeding (petition, notice, hearing, and appointment of a personal representative) in full; see that document's clauses for those mechanics. Nor does it restate the corpus's Revocable Living Trust document's own funding disclosure, which addresses the parallel point for a lifetime trust: that a trust holds only property actually, correctly transferred into it during the settlor's life, and that property never transferred stays outside the trust and subject to probate. This document's companion drafting clause on a pour-over will's relationship to a living trust (`trust_pour_over_will`, Cal. Prob. Code § 6300(a)-(b)) addresses a related but distinct mechanism: a will provision that routes probate property into a trust the testator already created during life. Property left this way is not deemed to be held under a testamentary trust of the testator; a testamentary trust — the subject of this document — is a different mechanism, one where the will itself is the trust instrument, not a delivery vehicle to a separately-existing trust.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 7000 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: title to a decedent's property passes at death to the will's devisee
citations.quote: Subject to Section 7001, title to a decedent’s property passes on the decedent’s death to the person to whom it is devised in the decedent’s last will or, in the absence of such a devise, to the decedent’s heirs as prescribed in the laws governing intestate succession.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 7001 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: that property remains subject to probate administration
citations.quote: The decedent’s property is subject to administration under this code, except as otherwise provided by law, and is subject to the rights of beneficiaries, creditors, and other persons as provided by law.

clauses.title: A Common Use: Holding Property for a Minor or Other Beneficiary Until a Stated Age
clauses.body: One reason a will creates a trust, rather than simply giving property outright, is that a will's ordinary gifts vest immediately — a will has no built-in mechanism to hold and manage property for a beneficiary over time the way a trust does. This matters in particular for a beneficiary who is a minor at {{testatorName}}'s death: California Probate Code § 3401 lets money or property belonging to a minor be paid directly to a parent to hold in trust for the minor without a court-appointed guardian of the estate, but only where the minor's total estate — as defined in § 3400, and net of certain deductions such as custodial property already held under the California Uniform Transfers to Minors Act — does not exceed $5,000 in value. Above that threshold, this simplified route is unavailable on its own terms.
clauses.gap: Sourcing tier, disclosed honestly: the statutory citations below verify a real, specific fact — that California's simplified mechanism for handling a minor's inherited property without a guardian of the estate is capped at $5,000 — but they do not themselves say that testators commonly respond to that cap, or to a beneficiary's youth or vulnerability generally, by writing a testamentary trust into their wills. That broader claim is common estate-planning practice and professional convention, not a proposition independently stated by any single California statute this project verified; it's presented here as informed context, not as a specific state law creates it. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one concrete, verifiable trigger point — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific minor's inheritance. § 3400 and § 3401 are two different sections within the same short article; § 3401's dollar threshold is the operative fact, and § 3400 is cited only because it defines the "total estate of the minor" figure that threshold is measured against. This document does not address the California Uniform Transfers to Minors Act (Prob. Code §§ 3900-3925) itself, a separate, simpler mechanism for holding property for a minor that this document's drafting clauses do not use.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 3401(a), (c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the $5,000 cap on paying a minor's property to a parent to hold in trust without a guardian of the estate
citations.quote: (a) Where a minor does not have a guardian of the estate, money or other property belonging to the minor may be paid or delivered to a parent of the minor entitled to the custody of the minor to be held in trust for the minor until the minor reaches majority if the requirements of subdivision (c) are satisfied.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 3400(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: how the minor's "total estate" is defined and calculated for that cap
citations.quote: (a) As used in this article, “total estate of the minor” includes both the money and other property belonging to the minor and the money and other property belonging to the guardianship estate, if any, of the minor. (b) In computing the “total estate of the minor” for the purposes of this article, all of the following shall be deducted: (1) “Custodial property” held pursuant to the California Uniform Transfers to Minors Act, Part 9 (commencing with Section 3900).

clauses.title: How a Testamentary Trust Is Funded — Through the Probate Distribution Process
clauses.body: A testamentary trust does not receive its property automatically or immediately at {{testatorName}}'s death. Once {{testatorName}}'s estate is in a condition to be closed, California Probate Code § 11640(a) requires the personal representative to file a petition for, and the court to make, an order for final distribution of the estate; § 11641 then allows the personal representative to immediately distribute the estate property to the persons — including a testamentary trustee — entitled to it under that order, without further notice or proceedings. It is that court-ordered distribution, carried out by the personal representative during and at the conclusion of probate administration, that actually delivers property from {{testatorName}}'s estate into {{trustName}}'s hands as trustee.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual mechanics by which a testamentary trust is funded — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate. No provision specific to testamentary trusts was found for this step; funding a testamentary trust simply uses the same general order-for-distribution machinery that applies to any estate distribution, whether the ultimate recipient is an individual devisee or a trustee named in the will. § 11640 and § 11641 are two different sections within the same three-section article (Article 3, Final Distribution); no single section is cited more than once in this clause. This document does not address preliminary distribution before an estate is fully closed, or the separate procedures that apply if a distribution order fails to dispose of after-discovered property (Cal. Prob. Code § 11642) — a scenario in which a testamentary trust named in the will could still later receive property distributed under a supplemental court order.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 11640(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the personal representative must petition for, and the court must make, an order of final distribution
citations.quote: (a) When all debts have been paid or adequately provided for, or if the estate is insolvent, and the estate is in a condition to be closed, the personal representative shall file a petition for, and the court shall make, an order for final distribution of the estate.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 11641 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the personal representative then distributes the property under that order
citations.quote: When an order settling a final account and for final distribution is entered, the personal representative may immediately distribute the property in the estate to the persons entitled to distribution, without further notice or proceedings.

clauses.title: Trustee Obligations Once the Trust Is Funded — the Same Trust Law That Governs Any Trust
clauses.body: Once funded, {{trustName}} is administered under the same body of law that governs a trust created any other way. California Probate Code § 15001(a) provides that the Trust Law (Probate Code Division 9) "applies to all trusts," without limiting that coverage by how the trust was created; and § 16000 provides that on accepting the trust, {{trusteeName}} has a duty to administer it according to the trust instrument — here, {{testatorName}}'s will — and, except as the trust instrument itself provides otherwise, according to that same Division. The specific duties this generally imposes on a trustee — among them, the duty of loyalty and the duty to account to beneficiaries — apply to {{trusteeName}} exactly as they would to the trustee of a lifetime trust; this document does not restate them.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual, general scope of California's Trust Law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. No statutory provision was found that says, in so many words, that Division 9 applies "regardless of a trust's creation method"; that specific phrasing does not appear in the Probate Code. § 15001(a)'s "applies to all trusts" language and § 16000's unqualified reference to "the trustee" are the actual statutory basis for the inference stated in this clause's body, and that inference — not an express creation-method-neutrality rule — is what this clause relies on; it is not invented beyond what these two sections say. § 15001 and § 16000 are two different sections in two different parts of the same division (Part 1, General Provisions, and Part 4, Trust Administration); no single section is cited more than once in this clause. This document does not restate the specific trustee duties sourced elsewhere in this corpus's Revocable Living Trust document — the duty of loyalty and duty to keep trust property separate (Cal. Prob. Code § 16002(a), § 16009), and the duty to account (§ 16062(a), § 16069(a)(1)) — which apply here in the same way; see that document's clauses for the sourced text of those specific duties.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15001(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the Trust Law applies to all trusts
citations.quote: (a) This division applies to all trusts regardless of whether they were created before, on, or after July 1, 1987.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16000 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the trustee's general duty to administer the trust according to trust law
citations.quote: On acceptance of the trust, the trustee has a duty to administer the trust according to the trust instrument and, except to the extent the trust instrument provides otherwise, according to this division.

clauses.title: Revocability — Why a Testamentary Trust Becomes Irrevocable at the Testator's Death
clauses.body: A testamentary trust does not exist, and so is not itself capable of being revoked, until {{testatorName}}'s death — it is created by {{testatorName}}'s will, and that will has no effect until then. Before death, what can be changed is the will itself: California Probate Code § 6120 lets {{testatorName}} revoke the will (and with it, any trust the will would otherwise have created) by a later will, or by a physical act done with the intent to revoke — but only {{testatorName}}, or someone acting in {{testatorName}}'s presence and at {{testatorName}}'s direction, can do that. Once {{testatorName}} has died, § 6120 no longer offers any living person a way to revoke the will. California's default trust-revocation rule works the same way for the trust itself: § 15400 makes a trust revocable by the settlor by default, and § 15401(a)(2) requires that a settlor's chosen method of revocation, absent the trust's own exclusive method, be exercised by a signed writing delivered to the trustee "during the lifetime of the settlor." With {{testatorName}} deceased once {{trustName}} takes effect, no one remains who can exercise a settlor's power to revoke it under that rule.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual mechanics that make a testamentary trust irrevocable in practice once it takes effect — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will or trust, and not a claim that any single statute says in so many words that "a testamentary trust is irrevocable." That conclusion is this clause's own inference from § 6120 (which requires the testator's living act to revoke a will) and § 15400/§ 15401(a) (which condition a settlor's default revocation power on the settlor being alive to exercise it) — not an independently stated rule. Honest qualification: § 15401(b)(2) separately allows a settlor to grant another person a power to revoke that continues even after the settlor's death; on its text this provision is not limited to multi-settlor trusts, though it appears in a subdivision otherwise concerned with revocation of a specific settlor's contributed portion of a multi-settlor trust, and no source reviewed for this document applies it to a testamentary trust specifically. This document does not independently verify whether or how that narrow provision could apply to a testamentary trust naming someone other than the deceased testator as a revocation-power holder. § 6120 is sourced from Probate Code Division 6 (Wills) and § 15400/§ 15401 from Division 9 (Trust Law) — two different divisions of the code, not the same source; § 15400 and § 15401 are, however, adjacent sections of the same statutory chapter and are treated as one source, not independent, for purposes of this clause's revocable-trust half of the argument. This corpus's Last Will and Testament document independently sources § 6120's two revocation methods in its own `will_revocation` clause; this clause relies on, and does not restate, that same statutory text rather than duplicating it here as an unrelated finding.

citations.quote: A will or any part thereof is revoked by any of the following: (a) A subsequent will which revokes the prior will or part expressly or by inconsistency. (b) Being burned, torn, canceled, obliterated, or destroyed, with the intent and for the purpose of revoking it, by either (1) the testator or (2) another person in the testator’s presence and by the testator’s direction.

clauses.title: Testamentary Trust Declaration
clauses.body: If {{beneficiaryName}} has not reached the age of {{distributionAge}} at the time of my death, I direct that the share of my estate otherwise passing to {{beneficiaryName}} be held in trust rather than distributed outright, to be known as the {{trustName}}. I nominate {{trusteeName}} to serve as trustee of the {{trustName}}. If {{trusteeName}} is unable or unwilling to serve, I nominate {{successorTrusteeName}} to serve as successor trustee. The trustee shall hold, manage, and apply the trust property for {{beneficiaryName}}'s health, education, maintenance, and support until {{beneficiaryName}} reaches the age of {{distributionAge}}, at which time the trustee shall distribute the remaining trust property outright to {{beneficiaryName}}. The {{trustName}} is created by this will; it does not exist, and holds no property, unless and until this will is admitted to probate.

clauses.title: Trustee Acceptance
Two Statutory Categories of Time-Share Interest: Time-Share Estate and Time-Share Use
clauses.body: California's Vacation Ownership and Time-Share Act of 2004 (Bus. & Prof. Code § 11210 et seq., within the Business and Professions Code's Real Estate division) defines the terms it uses in Bus. & Prof. Code § 11212. A "time-share interest" is not one uniform kind of right — the statute defines it to mean either of two distinct things. A "time-share estate" is the right to occupy a time-share property coupled with a freehold estate, or an estate for years with a future interest, in the time-share property or a specified portion of it — an actual interest in real property. A "time-share use," by contrast, is the same right to occupy a time-share property, but a right that is not coupled with a freehold interest or with an estate for years with a future interest — a right to occupy without an accompanying real-property interest. The statute separately defines a "time-share plan" as the broader arrangement, scheme, or device — whether by membership agreement, sale, lease, deed, license, right-to-use agreement, or other means — under which a purchaser, in exchange for consideration, obtains ownership rights in, or the right to use, accommodations for a period of less than a full year during a given year, on a recurring basis for more than one year (not necessarily consecutive years). A time-share plan can be a "single site time-share plan" (rights at one property) or a "multisite time-share plan" (rights across more than one component site, as either a specific or a nonspecific interest); which category describes a particular offering determines which of the Act's registration and disclosure rules described elsewhere in this information sheet apply to it.
clauses.gap: This document is informational only: it does not itself determine which statutory category — time-share estate or time-share use, single-site or multisite — describes any specific timeshare interest or plan; that depends on the actual time-share instrument and disclosures for that offering, which this information sheet does not supply. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual statutory categories California uses for a time-share interest — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific timeshare purchase, or that every state draws the same estate/use distinction; some states use different terminology (for example, describing all timeshares as a form of membership or club interest) or regulate timeshares primarily as securities rather than as real property or contract interests. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, Bus. & Prof. Code § 11212 — treated as one source, not independent.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11212(x) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, definitions of "time-share estate" and "time-share use"
citations.quote: “Time-share interest” means and includes either of the following:(1) A “time-share estate,” which is the right to occupy a time-share property, coupled with a freehold estate or an estate for years with a future interest in a time-share property or a specified portion thereof.(2) A “time-share use,” which is the right to occupy a time-share property, which right is neither coupled with a freehold interest, nor coupled with an estate for years with a future interest, in a time-share property.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11212(z) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, definition of "time-share plan"
citations.quote: “Time-share plan” means any arrangement, plan, scheme, or similar device, other than an exchange program, whether by membership agreement, sale, lease, deed, license, right to use agreement, or by any other means, whereby a purchaser, in exchange for consideration, receives ownership rights in or the right to use accommodations for a period of time less than a full year during any given year, on a recurring basis for more than one year, but not necessarily for consecutive years.

clauses.title: The Statutory Right to Cancel a Time-Share Purchase Contract Without Penalty
clauses.body: California law gives a purchaser who has made an offer to purchase a time-share interest a specific statutory right to void the purchase contract. Under Bus. & Prof. Code § 11238(a), the purchase contract is voidable by the purchaser, without penalty, within seven calendar days — or a longer period if the contract itself provides one — after the later of (1) the purchaser's receipt of the public report for the time-share plan, or (2) the execution of the purchase contract. This same seven-calendar-day right, running from that same later-of trigger, also extends to an offer to purchase an incidental benefit, and to rights under an exchange program, when either is made on the same day as, or within seven calendar days after, a sales presentation for the time-share interest. The statute requires the purchase contract itself to state the seven-day cancellation period and the name and mailing address to which a cancellation notice must be delivered. A cancellation notice is deemed timely if given not later than midnight of the seventh calendar day measured from that later trigger date.
clauses.gap: This document is informational only: it does not itself void or rescind any specific purchase contract, and it does not calculate an actual cancellation deadline for any specific purchase — that deadline depends on the actual dates a specific purchaser received the public report and executed the contract, which this information sheet does not have. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's specific rescission-right structure for a time-share purchase — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific timeshare purchase; rescission periods, if any, and their triggering events vary by state, and some states measure a shorter or longer period running only from contract signing rather than from the later of signing or receipt of a disclosure document. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, Bus. & Prof. Code § 11238(a) — treated as one source, not independent.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11238(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, the seven-calendar-day time-share purchase rescission right and its trigger
citations.quote: (a) The purchase contract entered into by any person who has made an offer to purchase a time-share interest or interests, any incidental benefit, made on the same day or within seven calendar days after the person attended a sales presentation for a time-share interest, or any right under an exchange program, made on the same day or within seven calendar days after the person attended a sales presentation for a time-share interest, shall be voidable by the purchaser, without penalty, within seven calendar days, or a longer period as provided in the contract, after the receipt of the public report or the execution of the purchase contract, whichever is later.

citations.quote: (1) The purchase contract for the time-share interest shall provide notice of the seven-day cancellation period, together with the name and mailing address to which any notice of cancellation shall be delivered.

citations.quote: (2) Notice of cancellation shall be deemed timely if given not later than midnight of the seventh calendar day.

clauses.title: Registration and the Public Report: What Must Happen Before a Purchaser Is Bound
clauses.body: Before a developer may sell, offer, or dispose of a time-share interest to a purchaser located in California (or offer an accommodation located in California), the developer generally must register the time-share plan with the Real Estate Commissioner, and Bus. & Prof. Code § 11226 provides that a developer, or its agents, shall not sell, offer, or dispose of a time-share interest in the state unless the necessary registration requirements have been provided and approved by the Commissioner, or the sale is otherwise permitted under the Act. As part of registration, the developer must prepare a public report — for issuance by the Commissioner — that fully and accurately discloses the facts about the developer and the time-share plan that the Act and its regulations require. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11234 requires the developer to provide that public report to each purchaser, in writing or, at the purchaser's discretion, in digital format, dated, and requires the purchaser to certify in writing that they received it. A statutory receipt form set out at Bus. & Prof. Code § 11236, which the developer must obtain from each purchaser, states that the commissioner's law and regulations require a prospective purchaser be given the opportunity to read the public report before executing a contract to purchase or lease a time-share interest, or before any money or other consideration toward the purchase is accepted.
clauses.gap: This document is informational only: it does not itself register any time-share plan, does not issue or supply any public report, and does not determine whether registration or a public report was in fact obtained for any specific time-share plan or purchase. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own pre-sale registration and public-report disclosure structure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific timeshare purchase; many states have a comparable public-report or registration scheme, but the specific agency, procedure, and required content vary by state, and some jurisdictions regulate timeshare sales primarily under general real-estate or securities law instead. The three citations below are drawn from three separate, independently enacted statutory sections (§§ 11226, 11234, and 11236), not subsections of a single section. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11225 — which its position early in this same article might suggest states the general public-report requirement — in fact does the opposite: it lists specific transactions exempt from the registration requirement (for example, an owner reselling a time-share interest the owner originally acquired for their own use); the general registration and public-report duty is instead stated in the separate §§ 11226 and 11234 cited here, a correction to that assumption. This document also does not independently verify the state real estate agency's historical name changes; it reports only that the Act's own definitions section, Bus. & Prof. Code § 11212(e) (quoted in a separate clause of this document), currently defines "Department" to mean the "Department of Real Estate."

citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, prohibition on selling or offering a time-share interest without approved registration
citations.quote: (b) A developer, or any of its agents, shall not sell, offer, or dispose of a time-share interest in the state unless all necessary registration requirements are provided and approved by the commissioner, or the sale, offer, or disposition is otherwise permitted by this chapter, or while an order revoking or suspending a registration is in effect.

citations.quote: The developer shall provide the public report to each purchaser of a time-share interest in a time-share plan at the time of purchase. The public report shall be in writing or in a digital format at the discretion of the purchaser and dated and shall require the purchaser to certify in writing the receipt thereof.

clauses.title: The Cancellation Notice Must Be Conspicuous and Placed Immediately Before the Purchaser's Signature
clauses.body: California law does not leave the format of the required cancellation notice to a developer's discretion. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11238(d)(7) requires the developer to disclose, in conspicuous type, immediately prior to the space reserved in the purchase contract for the purchaser's signature, substantially a specific statutory notice of cancellation — set out in the statute itself — stating that the purchaser may cancel the contract without penalty or obligation within seven calendar days of receipt of the public report or after the date the contract is signed, whichever is later, explaining how to give notice of cancellation, and stating that any attempt to obtain a waiver of the cancellation right is void and of no effect. The Act separately defines what makes type "conspicuous" for this purpose: under Bus. & Prof. Code § 11212(h), conspicuous type means type in upper- and lower-case letters two point sizes larger than the nearest nonconspicuous type on the same page (excluding headings), and in any event at least 10-point type.
clauses.gap: This document is informational only: it quotes the statutory notice language as the Act itself states it, but it does not draft or supply an actual, contract-specific cancellation notice for any particular time-share purchase contract, and it does not determine whether any specific contract's typography or placement in fact satisfies this requirement — that is a fact-specific determination this document does not make. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California imposes a specific placement and typography requirement for a time-share cancellation notice, rather than a general "clear and conspicuous" standard left to case-by-case interpretation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific purchase contract, or that every state imposes a comparable formatting rule. The two citations below are drawn from two separate, independently enacted statutory sections, Bus. & Prof. Code § 11212(h) and § 11238(d)(7), not subsections of a single section.

citations.quote: “Conspicuous type” means either of the following:(1) Type in upper and lower case letters two point sizes larger than the nearest nonconspicuous type, exclusive of headings, on the page on which it appears but in at least 10-point type.

If you decide to cancel this contract, you must notify the developer in writing of your intent to cancel. Your notice of cancellation may also be sent by facsimile to (facsimile number of the developer) or by hand-delivery. Any attempt to obtain a waiver of your cancellation right is void and of no effect.

clauses.title: The Court Remedy for a Developer That Wrongfully Denies a Rescission
clauses.body: The Act provides a specific, if narrow, court remedy tied to the rescission right described elsewhere in this information sheet. Under Bus. & Prof. Code § 11238(e), if a purchaser seeks rescission under that section and a court finds that the developer denied the rescission in violation of that section, the court may also award reasonable attorneys' fees and costs to the prevailing purchaser. The statute frames this as a remedy a court may award once a purchaser has prevailed in litigation over a wrongfully denied rescission — a fee- and cost-shifting provision contingent on a court's ruling, not an automatically-triggered civil penalty, fine, or liquidated-damages amount that arises the moment a developer fails to honor a rescission request.
clauses.gap: This document is informational only: it does not evaluate whether any specific denial of any specific rescission request would be found to violate Bus. & Prof. Code § 11238, and it does not itself constitute, transmit, or enforce a rescission notice. This is one state's statutory remedy, used as real evidence of what the Act itself provides for a wrongfully denied rescission — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific dispute, or that every state gives a time-share purchaser a comparable remedy; some states provide a specific statutory penalty or damages multiplier for this kind of violation, and some provide no remedy beyond ordinary contract law. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 11238(e)); no additional independent statutory source was found for this specific remedy. Business and Professions Code Division 4 (Real Estate) separately contains general real-estate-licensee discipline provisions (for example, grounds for suspending or revoking a real estate license) that could potentially also apply to conduct by a licensed developer or its agents; this document did not independently research or verify those general provisions, and does not assert that any specific licensing consequence attaches to a denied rescission beyond the fee-shifting remedy quoted here.

citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, attorneys' fees and costs remedy for a wrongfully denied rescission
citations.quote: (e) If rescission is sought by the purchaser in accordance with this section, and a court finds the developer denied the rescission in violation of this section, the court may also award reasonable attorneys’ fees and costs to the prevailing purchaser.

clauses.title: Ongoing Assessments Are a Separate, Recurring Obligation Controlled by the Plan's Own Governing Documents
clauses.body: A time-share purchase is not limited to the one-time purchase price. The Act defines an "assessment," under Bus. & Prof. Code § 11212(d), as the share of funds required for the payment of common expenses that is assessed from time to time against each purchaser by the plan's managing entity — a recurring obligation distinct from the price paid to acquire the time-share interest itself. The Act requires this recurring obligation to be disclosed before a purchaser is bound: under Bus. & Prof. Code § 11238(d)(3), the purchase contract must state the initial purchase price and any additional recurring or nonrecurring charges the purchaser will be required to pay in connection with the purchase — including, but not limited to, the current year's annual assessment for common expenses and any financing charges — or, if the amount cannot then be determined, a good-faith estimate. Beyond requiring that current-year figure to be disclosed at the time of purchase, no provision of the Act located for this document sets, caps, or guarantees any future assessment amount, increase, or formula; the amount and any future increases are matters governed by the time-share plan's own governing instrument and budget, administered by its managing entity or association, not by a fixed statutory rate or ceiling.
clauses.gap: This document is informational only: it does not state, calculate, or guarantee the assessment amount for any specific time-share plan, and it does not itself supply or describe that plan's governing instrument or budget. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California requires disclosure of the current year's assessment amount before a purchaser is bound, while leaving the amount itself statutorily unfixed — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific timeshare, or that every state imposes even this disclosure duty. The two citations below are drawn from two separate, independently enacted statutory sections, Bus. & Prof. Code § 11212(d) and § 11238(d)(3), not subsections of a single section. This document did not locate, and does not assert the existence of, any provision of the Act capping future assessment increases or otherwise substantively regulating the amount of ongoing assessments beyond the point-of-sale disclosure duty described here; whether such limits exist for a specific time-share plan depends on that plan's own time-share instrument and governing documents, which this document does not have and does not describe.

clauses.title: Registering an Out-of-State Support Order for Enforcement
clauses.body: California law allows a child- or spousal-support order issued by another state, or a foreign support order, to be registered in a California tribunal for enforcement. Registration is accomplished by sending specific records to the appropriate California tribunal: (1) a letter of transmittal requesting registration and enforcement; (2) two copies of the order to be registered, including any modification of the order, one of which must be a certified copy; (3) a sworn statement by the person requesting registration, or a certified statement by the custodian of the records, showing the amount of any arrearage; (4) the obligor's name and, if known, the obligor's address and Social Security number, the obligor's employer and other income sources, and a description and location of the obligor's property in California; and (5) the obligee's name and address (or, if applicable, the person to whom payments are to be remitted). If two or more orders are in effect for the same obligor and obligee, additional filings are required identifying every order asserted to be in effect and specifying which order is claimed to control.
clauses.gap: Note on citation form: California's UIFSA is NOT codified at Family Code § 4900 et seq. -- that was the pre-2016 codification. Effective January 1, 2016, Stats. 2015, Ch. 493 (SB 646) repealed the former UIFSA part and recodified it, without substantive change to the numbering scheme used here, into Division 9, Part 6, at Family Code §§ 5700.101-5700.905. This was confirmed directly: a fetch of the old § 4900 on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov returns an empty code-text body (no text at that section number), while § 5700.101 et seq. contains the full current UIFSA text. All citations below use the current, correct §5700.xxx numbering. This clause cites two different statutory sections, not subsections of one section: Cal. Fam. Code §§ 5700.601 and 5700.602(a), both within the same 2015 enactment (Stats. 2015, Ch. 493) that added this entire part, so they are not independent sources in the sense of separately-enacted law, only in the sense of being separately numbered provisions. This clause states the mechanics of registration only; it does not state whether a particular order is eligible for registration, does not itself accomplish registration, and does not address registration for modification (a meaningfully different process, covered in a separate clause in this document). This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's enactment of the Uniform Interstate Family Support Act (UIFSA) actually works -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific support order. Every U.S. state, the District of Columbia, and U.S. territories have enacted some version of UIFSA (the 2008 Act, as amended, per the federal mandate at 42 U.S.C. § 666(f)), but the codification location, section numbers, specific deadlines, and some procedural details differ state to state; this document describes California's specific enactment only. This document is informational only: it does not itself register, enforce, confirm, contest, or modify any support order, and does not determine whether a specific order or party qualifies for any of these procedures. No case law is cited in this clause; this topic is governed almost entirely by statutory text rather than by litigated interpretation, and CourtListener was not queried for it this session, given the statutory nature of the topic and CourtListener's limited daily quota.

clauses.title: Continuing, Exclusive Jurisdiction: Only One Order Controls
clauses.body: UIFSA's central organizing principle is that, at any given time, only one state's child-support order controls, and the state that issued the controlling order generally keeps sole ('continuing, exclusive') jurisdiction to modify it. For a child-support order, a California tribunal that issued the order and whose order is the controlling order retains this jurisdiction only if, at the time a modification request is filed, California remains the residence of the obligor, the individual obligee, or the child, or the parties otherwise consent (in a record or in open court) to California continuing to exercise jurisdiction. If none of those conditions holds -- most notably, if none of the obligor, the obligee, or the child still lives in California -- California's basis for continuing, exclusive jurisdiction to modify its own child-support order no longer exists, and (as addressed in a separate clause) another state where a party resides may then be able to take up modification. Spousal-support orders work differently: the issuing state's continuing, exclusive jurisdiction to modify a spousal-support order it issued lasts for the entire existence of the support obligation, with no equivalent residency condition -- a real, non-obvious distinction from the child-support rule.

clauses.title: Registration for Modification Is Not the Same as Registration for Enforcement
clauses.body: UIFSA treats registering an out-of-state child-support order to enforce it (collect ongoing payments or existing arrears under the order as written) differently from registering it to seek a modification of its terms. A party or support enforcement agency seeking to modify, or to modify and enforce, another state's child-support order must first register that order using the same enforcement-registration procedure described above; a petition for modification may then be filed with, or after, that registration, and the petition must state the grounds for modification. Registering the order, by itself, does not give a California tribunal the power to change its terms: California may modify a registered child-support order issued by another state only if, after notice and hearing, additional jurisdictional prerequisites are met -- either (1) none of the child, the individual obligee, or the obligor still resides in the issuing state, the party petitioning for modification is not a California resident, and the other party is subject to California's personal jurisdiction; or (2) California is the child's residence, or a party is subject to California's personal jurisdiction, and all individual parties have filed a record consenting to have California modify the order and assume continuing, exclusive jurisdiction over it. Absent one of those two pathways, a California tribunal that has registered another state's child-support order may enforce it but may not modify it.

clauses.title: Contesting a Registered Support Order: Limited, Enumerated Defenses
clauses.body: A party who did not register the order (the nonregistering party) may contest its validity or enforcement, but only by requesting a hearing within a deadline set by a separate statute, and only on specific, enumerated grounds -- the contest right is not open-ended. If the nonregistering party does not timely request a hearing, the order is confirmed by operation of law without any further proceeding. A party who does request a hearing has the burden of proving one or more of eight listed defenses: (1) the issuing tribunal lacked personal jurisdiction over the contesting party; (2) the order was obtained by fraud; (3) the order has been vacated, suspended, or modified by a later order; (4) the issuing tribunal has stayed the order pending appeal; (5) there is a defense under California law to the specific remedy being sought; (6) full or partial payment has already been made; (7) a statute of limitations bars enforcement of some or all of the alleged arrears; or (8) the order asserted to be the controlling order is not actually the controlling order. This list is longer, and more specific, than a bare 'the order is wrong' objection -- a contest that does not fit one of these eight grounds does not defeat registration.

clauses.title: Effect of Registration and Confirmation
clauses.body: Once an out-of-state or foreign support order is registered in California, it becomes enforceable in the same manner, and subject to the same procedures, as an order that a California tribunal issued itself -- California courts recognize and enforce it, but (subject to the separate modification pathway addressed elsewhere in this document) may not modify it, as long as the issuing tribunal had jurisdiction when it issued the order. Confirmation of the registered order -- whether that happens automatically by operation of law because no timely contest was filed, or affirmatively after a contest hearing -- has a further, distinct effect: it forecloses raising, in any later proceeding, any matter that could have been raised as a defense at the time of registration. In other words, confirmation is not merely a formality; it operates as a final determination that cuts off previously-available objections.

clauses.title: Choice of Law for Arrears and Interest Versus California's Own Enforcement Procedures
clauses.body: UIFSA splits which state's law applies to a registered support order along substance-versus-procedure lines. The substantive law of the issuing state (or foreign country) governs the nature, extent, amount, and duration of current payments; the computation of arrearages and the accrual of interest on those arrearages; and the existence and satisfaction of other obligations under the order. For the statute of limitations specifically, whichever period is longer -- California's or the issuing state's -- applies to an arrears proceeding, a pro-enforcement rule rather than a strict issuing-state-controls rule. At the same time, the California tribunal enforcing the order applies California's own procedures and remedies to enforce current support and collect arrears and interest -- the forum state's procedural law governs the mechanics of enforcement even though the issuing state's substantive law governs the amounts owed. Once a tribunal determines which of two or more competing orders controls and consolidates the arrears, a California tribunal must then prospectively apply the controlling order's state's law -- including its interest-on-arrears rules -- going forward for current, future, and consolidated support.

clauses.title: Required Content of Nonprofit Religious Corporation Articles
clauses.body: California's Nonprofit Religious Corporation Law contains its own required-content statute for a religious corporation's articles of incorporation, separate from the required-content statutes that govern a nonprofit public benefit corporation and a nonprofit mutual benefit corporation. The religious-corporation statute requires the filed articles to state: the corporation's name; a specific, statutorily prescribed statement that the corporation “is a religious corporation and is not organized for the private gain of any person” and is organized under the Nonprofit Religious Corporation Law “(primarily or exclusively [insert one or both])” for religious purposes, with a further description of the corporation's purpose always optional and never mandatory; the name and California street address of the corporation's initial agent for service of process; the corporation's initial street address; and its initial mailing address, if that differs from the street address. Two features distinguish this required-content list from the nonprofit public benefit corporation's: first, the prescribed statement does not offer a choice between two different kinds of purpose (“public” or “charitable,” as the public benefit statute does) but instead asks only how exclusively religious the corporation's purpose is (“primarily”, “exclusively”, or both); second, a further description of purpose is optional in every case for a religious corporation, where the public benefit statute makes a further description mandatory whenever “public” purposes are elected. Third, and more a structural quirk than a substantive difference, the religious-corporation statute's agent-for-service-of-process requirement is not itself a direct grant of the general corporation law's agent statute; it cross-references “Section 6210 (made applicable pursuant to Section 9660)” — the same underlying agent-designation rule public and mutual benefit corporations use, but adopted into the religious corporation law by a separate incorporating statute rather than cited directly. As with the other two nonprofit corporation types, nothing in this list calls for a statement of authorized shares — a nonprofit religious corporation has no shareholders and issues no stock.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what one state's required formation-document content for this specific type of nonprofit corporation looks like — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation's formation, and required content for a nonprofit corporation's founding filing varies by state. The three citations below are all subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 9130, so they are treated as one source, not independent ones. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any corporation, file anything with the California Secretary of State, or determine whether any corporation qualifies for federal tax-exempt status, which is a separate determination made by the Internal Revenue Service under federal law, not by this document or by the California statute it describes.

clauses.title: Eligibility Standard: “Primarily or Exclusively... Religious Purposes”
clauses.body: California's Nonprofit Corporation Law sets a genuinely different eligibility standard for a religious corporation than it sets for a nonprofit public benefit corporation, and each standard appears in its own dedicated “Title and Purposes” article at the head of the respective part of the statute. The religious-corporation statute provides that, subject to other law applying to a particular class of corporation or line of activity, “a corporation may be formed under this part primarily or exclusively for any religious purposes.” The nonprofit public benefit statute uses the identical opening structure but a different substantive standard: “a corporation may be formed under this part for any public or charitable purposes.” The two standards are not the same text with different labels substituted in — the religious-corporation statute alone builds in the “primarily or exclusively” qualifier that describes how completely religious the corporation's purposes must be, and that qualifier is what the required purpose statement in the corporation's articles (covered above) later asks the incorporator to elect between. A corporation eligible to form under the religious-corporation statute is accordingly one formed primarily or exclusively for religious purposes — not, as with a public benefit corporation, one formed for public or charitable purposes more broadly, of which a religious purpose could be only one example.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of how that one state's Corporations Code itself sets a different formation-eligibility standard for a religious corporation than for a nonprofit public benefit corporation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and the eligibility standard and vocabulary used for a religious nonprofit corporation vary by state. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 9111 and Cal. Corp. Code § 5111, and are treated as two independent sources, not subsections of one section. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any corporation, does not determine which nonprofit category best fits a specific organization's activities, and does not determine federal tax-exempt status, which is a separate IRS determination this document does not make.

clauses.title: Reduced Attorney General Oversight of Religious Corporations
clauses.body: California law imposes a specific, statute-based limit on the Attorney General's power over an entity “incorporated or classified as a religious corporation” that has no equivalent stated so broadly for a nonprofit public benefit corporation. The religious-corporation statute provides that, apart from the Attorney General's ordinary criminal-law-enforcement role, “the Attorney General shall have no powers with respect to any corporation incorporated or classified as a religious corporation under or pursuant to this code” except as expressly granted by three narrow, listed carve-outs: authority to bring a declaratory-relief action to determine that an entity is not properly qualified or classified as a religious corporation in the first place; the specific authority separately granted over the religious-corporation law's own filing, sale-of-assets, merger, and dissolution provisions (covered elsewhere in this document); the ordinary authority to prosecute crimes; authority to represent other state agencies with their own express authority over religious corporations; and a narrow authority to sue only where property was solicited from the general public for a specific charitable purpose and then diverted from that purpose. A separate statute confirms the same reduced role from another angle: the Attorney General's Registry of Charitable Trusts filing, registration, and reporting regime — the ongoing state charity-oversight filings that apply generally to entities holding charitable assets — by its own terms “do[es] not apply to... any religious corporation sole or other religious corporation or organization that holds property for religious purposes,” a categorical exemption not extended in that same provision to a nonprofit public benefit corporation generally (the statute separately exempts only certain other categories, such as an educational institution, a hospital, or a charitable organization “organized and operated primarily as a religious organization” — an ordinary public benefit charity outside those categories remains subject to the filing and reporting regime). This combination — a narrow, enumerated list of the Attorney General's powers over religious corporations specifically, plus a separate exemption from the ongoing charitable-registry filings — is commonly discussed as reflecting First Amendment church-autonomy concerns, though the statutory text itself does not state that rationale; this document reports what the statutes say, not why the Legislature enacted them.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of a genuine, statute-based reduction in Attorney General oversight of this one specific type of nonprofit corporation in that one state — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and whether and how a state limits its Attorney General's oversight of religious nonprofit corporations varies by state. clauses.title: The No-Distributions Rule Applies by Cross-Reference, With a Narrower Enforcement List
clauses.body: Unlike a nonprofit public benefit corporation and a nonprofit mutual benefit corporation, each of which has its own freestanding “Distributions” chapter stating the no-distribution rule in its own words, the Nonprofit Religious Corporation Law does not restate that rule at all — it adopts the public benefit corporation's distributions chapter by cross-reference instead. The religious corporation statute provides: “The provisions of Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 5410) of Part 2 apply to religious corporations except for subdivision (b) of Section 5420.” Chapter 4 of Part 2 is the same public benefit corporation distributions chapter already covered elsewhere in this project's public benefit corporation document, whose central rule is: “No corporation shall make any distribution,” subject to a narrow carve-out for limited-equity housing cooperative memberships. Because the religious-corporation statute imports that rule by reference rather than granting an outright exemption from it, a religious corporation is, on this point, subject to essentially the same substantive no-distributions rule as a public benefit corporation. The one piece the cross-reference deliberately excludes — subdivision (b) of Section 5420, the public benefit statute's own provision on who may sue over a wrongful distribution — is replaced with the religious corporation law's own, narrower version, and the difference between the two lists is specific: the public benefit provision states that “suit may be brought in the name of a corporation by a creditor, a director, the Attorney General, or... a member,” while the religious corporation's own replacement provision states that “suit may be brought in the name of the corporation by a creditor, a director, or the authorized number of members” — omitting the Attorney General from the list of people who may sue to enforce the no-distributions rule against a religious corporation, a further, specific instance of the reduced Attorney General enforcement role addressed in the clause above.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of how that one state's Corporations Code applies a shared substantive rule to two different nonprofit corporation types through a cross-reference, and of a specific difference in who may enforce it — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and whether a state applies a no-distribution rule to a religious nonprofit corporation, and how it is enforced, varies by state. The citations to Cal. Corp. Code § 9610(a) and § 9610(b) are subsections of the same statutory section and are treated as one source; the citation to Cal. Corp. Code § 5420(b) is drawn from an independently enacted section and is treated as a second, independent source, used for direct textual contrast with § 9610(b). clauses.title: Dissolution: Assets Disposed of Under the Corporation's Own Articles, With a Weaker Attorney General Role
clauses.body: California's dissolution statutes give a religious corporation a genuinely different, and lighter, Attorney General role in the final disposition of its assets than the role a nonprofit public benefit corporation faces. The religious-corporation statute again proceeds by cross-reference and exclusion: it provides that the public benefit corporation law's winding-up and dissolution chapters “apply to religious corporations except for Sections 6610, 6614, 6710, 6711 and 6716” — an express carve-out of Section 6716, which is the public benefit corporation's own asset-disposition statute (already covered in this project's public benefit corporation document). In its place, the religious corporation statute supplies its own, separately worded disposition rule: assets are disposed of “in conformity with its articles or bylaws subject to complying with the provisions of any trust under which such assets are held,” and that disposition “shall be made by decree of the superior court of the proper county. The decree shall be made upon petition therefor, upon 30 days' notice to the Attorney General, by any person concerned in the dissolution.” The excluded public benefit statute, by contrast, requires that the disposition “be made by decree of the superior court of the proper county in proceedings to which the Attorney General is a party.” The substance of the two rules is otherwise close — both look first to the corporation's own articles or bylaws, both route the actual disposition through a superior court decree, and both give the Attorney General a role — but the religious-corporation version's role for the Attorney General is notice and an opportunity to object, not formal party status in the court proceeding itself, which is exactly what the excluded public benefit statute requires.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of that state's own, differently calibrated dissolution-disposition procedure for this specific type of nonprofit corporation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation's dissolution, and default asset-disposition procedures on a nonprofit's dissolution vary by state. This clause is a direct, load-bearing correction of an assumption worth stating plainly: on the statutory text, a religious corporation's assets on dissolution are not shown by these sections to be required to pass specifically to another religious or charitable organization by name — the operative rule, like the public benefit corporation's, defers first to whatever the corporation's own articles or bylaws provide, subject to any trust under which the assets are held; this document did not locate a religious-corporation-law counterpart to the federal 501(c)(3) organizational test's dissolution requirement, which is a separate, federal-law constraint addressed in the cross-referenced clause on federal tax-exempt status. clauses.title: Governance Flexibility: Articles or Bylaws May Override the Members' Statutory Removal Power
clauses.body: California's default rule letting members remove a director without cause is worded differently, and is more freely displaceable, for a religious corporation than the corresponding default rule is for either a nonprofit public benefit corporation or a nonprofit mutual benefit corporation. The religious-corporation statute provides: “Except as provided in the articles or bylaws and subject to subdivision (b) of this section, any or all directors may be removed without cause if the removal is approved by the members.” The opening qualifier — “Except as provided in the articles or bylaws” — gives a religious corporation's own governing documents a general power to displace or modify this default in whatever way they choose. The corresponding public benefit corporation statute states the same basic default — members may remove a director without cause — but opens instead with “Subject to subdivisions (b) and (f) of this section,” not with any general “except as provided in the articles or bylaws” carve-out; its only built-in flexibility is the specific cumulative-voting protection in subdivision (b) and the specific designator-consent mechanism in subdivision (f), not a general license for the articles or bylaws to override the members' removal power itself. The nonprofit mutual benefit corporation's parallel removal statute is worded the same restrictive way as the public benefit corporation's. On this specific point — whether the corporation's own articles or bylaws may override the members' statutory power to remove a director without cause — the religious-corporation statute is the only one of the three that says so in its own opening text.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of a genuine, textually verifiable difference in how much governance flexibility this one state's law gives a religious corporation on this one specific point, compared to a public benefit corporation under the same state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, not a claim that religious corporations have greater flexibility on every governance point, and not a claim about any other state's law. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 9222 and Cal. Corp. Code § 5222, and are treated as two independent sources, not subsections of one section; this document separately confirmed, but does not separately cite, that the nonprofit mutual benefit corporation's parallel removal statute, Cal. Corp. Code § 7222, opens with the same restrictive “Subject to subdivisions (b) and (f)” language as § 5222 rather than the religious corporation statute's “Except as provided in the articles or bylaws” language. This document is informational only: it does not itself draft or adopt any corporation's articles or bylaws, does not determine whether a specific proposed governance provision is enforceable, and does not determine federal tax-exempt status, which is a separate IRS determination this document does not make.

clauses.title: Federal Tax-Exempt Status Remains a Separate Question, Where “Religious” Is Itself a Listed IRC Purpose
clauses.body: The same point already made in this project's Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation and Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation documents applies here without needing to be re-derived: California's formation statute for a religious corporation — including the required purpose statement covered above — governs only what must appear in the articles filed with the California Secretary of State, and does not itself confer, guarantee, or evaluate federal tax-exempt status, which is a separate determination made by the Internal Revenue Service under federal law. One detail is specific to a religious corporation, however: the federal statute those other two documents already identify as the source of the 501(c)(3) organizational test lists “religious” purposes by name, on equal footing with “charitable,” “scientific,” and “educational” purposes, as one of the purposes for which a corporation must be “organized and operated exclusively” to qualify for exemption under 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(3). That federal statutory alignment between the word “religious” in California's own formation statute and the word “religious” in the federal exemption statute does not collapse the two determinations into one — satisfying California's state-law purpose statement is still not the same thing as satisfying the IRS's separate organizational and operational tests under federal law, for the same reasons already given in this project's other two nonprofit corporation documents.
clauses.gap: This clause deliberately cross-references, rather than re-deriving, the state-law-versus-federal-law distinction already established in this project's nonprofit_purpose_state_vs_federal and mutualbenefit_federal_tax_status_separate_question clauses; readers should consult those clauses for the fuller discussion of the federal organizational test and Treasury regulation. The single citation below, to 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(3), is federal law, not California law; it is cited here as evidence of a separate, nationwide requirement layered on top of state law for any organization, in any state, that wants federal tax-exempt recognition — not as evidence of what California itself requires. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any corporation and does not determine federal tax-exempt status for any organization under any Internal Revenue Code provision — that determination is made by the IRS, not by this document or by the California statutes it describes.

Statutory Basis: Trade Dress Claims Under the General Lanham Act False-Designation-of-Origin Provision
clauses.body: Federal law does not contain a standalone statute captioned "trade dress." A claim that another person's product packaging, product design, or décor infringes protectable trade dress is instead brought under the same general federal unfair-competition provision, 15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(1)(A), that creates civil liability for use in commerce of "any word, term, name, symbol, or device, or any combination thereof" likely to cause confusion as to the origin, sponsorship, or approval of goods or services. That statutory text — the same general false-designation-of-origin provision already addressed in this tool's Trademark Infringement Cease and Desist Letter Information Sheet and Trademark Registration Information Sheet documents for word marks and logos — does not itself use the words "trade dress," "packaging," "product design," or "décor," and it does not single out a product's overall appearance as an example of a protectable "symbol" or "device." Courts and the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office have long read this general confusion-based language to extend to a product's or service's overall look and feel — this reading is a judicial and administrative gloss on the statutory text, developed through case law, not language Congress wrote into this specific provision. Confirming that Congress itself has since treated "trade dress" as a recognized category of claim arising under this same statutory chapter, a separate provision in this same section — 15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(3), addressed in this document's companion clause on functionality — expressly uses the phrase "trade dress" when allocating the burden of proof in an infringement action, even though the general cause-of-action language quoted above does not contain that phrase.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the general statutory cause of action under which trade dress claims are brought, and of the fact that this specific statutory text does not itself use the words "trade dress" — not a claim that any specific product's or service's appearance is protectable trade dress, or that any specific use of it is likely to cause confusion, both of which this clause does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(1)(A)); no additional independent statutory source was needed for it. The statement that courts and the USPTO have applied this general language to product appearance describes a widely reported feature of trademark practice; it is not supported here by a citation to any specific court decision or USPTO guidance, because a CourtListener case-law search for a foundational trade dress decision (for example, Two Pesos, Inc. v. Taco Cabana, Inc.) was not attempted this session given CourtListener's confirmed exhaustion of its 125/day rate limit at the time of drafting (see this document's other authority clauses for the same disclosure), and no USPTO Trademark Manual of Examining Procedure page was independently fetched and verified this session. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific product's, package's, or service's appearance is protectable trade dress, that it is federally registered or registrable, or that any specific use of it infringes, and completing this information sheet does not itself assert or waive any right. This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule.

clauses.title: The Functionality Doctrine: A Categorical Bar to Trade Dress Protection
clauses.body: Even if a product's or service's overall appearance is otherwise distinctive, federal law bars trade dress protection for any feature that is "functional." The functionality doctrine operates as a categorical limit: a functional feature is not protectable as trade dress no matter how distinctive it has become, because trade dress law protects source-identifying appearance, not useful product features — those are instead the subject of patent law, which has its own, time-limited protections. The statute itself does not define "functional" or list the specific facts a court weighs in deciding functionality (for example, whether a feature is "essential to the use or purpose of the article" or "affects the cost or quality of the article" — a formulation widely attributed to the courts and discussed further in this clause's gap note); what the statute does provide, expressly using the phrase "trade dress," is a burden-of-proof rule: in a civil action for trade dress infringement brought under this chapter, where the trade dress at issue is not registered on the principal register, the party asserting trade dress protection bears the burden of proving that the matter it seeks to protect is not functional. This means that, for unregistered trade dress, the burden of proof on functionality is placed on the person claiming trade dress rights, not on the person accused of infringing them.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the statutory functionality bar to trade dress protection and of the burden-of-proof allocation for unregistered trade dress that the statute itself expressly places on the party asserting protection — not a claim that any specific product feature described on this sheet is or is not functional, which this clause does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(3)); no additional independent statutory source was needed for it. The often-cited two-part judicial description of functionality — that a feature is functional if it is essential to the use or purpose of the article or if it affects the cost or quality of the article — is widely reported to originate in Supreme Court case law (commonly associated with Inwood Laboratories, Inc. v. Ives Laboratories, Inc., 456 U.S. 844 (1982), and TrafFix Devices, Inc. v. Marketing Displays, Inc., 532 U.S. 23 (2001)); it is described here only as a widely-reported judicial formulation, not independently verified against either opinion this session, because CourtListener case-law search returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, 125/day daily limit, confirmed exhausted with hours remaining before reset) before either case could be retrieved. No quotation from, or citation entry for, either decision is included in this clause's citations array as a result. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific feature is functional or non-functional, and completing this information sheet does not itself assert or waive any right. This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule.

clauses.title: Distinctiveness Requirement: Inherent Distinctiveness and Secondary Meaning
clauses.body: Trade dress, like other trademarks, is protectable only if it is distinctive — capable of identifying and distinguishing the source of goods or services, rather than merely decorating or describing them. Federal trademark law recognizes two routes to distinctiveness: a mark or trade dress can be "inherently distinctive" (distinctive from the moment of first use, without any need to show that consumers have come to associate it with a particular source), or it can acquire distinctiveness over time through use — commonly called "secondary meaning." The general federal registration statute expressly recognizes the secondary-meaning route: except for marks expressly excluded on other statutory grounds, nothing in the statute prevents registration of a mark that "has become distinctive of the applicant's goods in commerce," and the statute allows proof of substantially exclusive and continuous use for the five years before the distinctiveness claim as prima facie evidence of that distinctiveness. It is widely reported in trade dress case law — most significantly, the Supreme Court's decision in Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Samara Brothers, Inc., 529 U.S. 205 (2000) — that this general distinctiveness framework applies differently to different categories of trade dress: product packaging can potentially qualify as inherently distinctive, while product design (the shape or configuration of the product itself) is widely reported to never be inherently distinctive and to require proof of secondary meaning in every case. This document reports that distinction here because it is a significant, non-obvious feature of trade dress law that differs from ordinary word-mark or logo analysis, but the underlying case law establishing it was not independently verified this session (see this clause's gap note), and it should not be treated as a verified quotation from that decision.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the general two-route distinctiveness framework (inherent distinctiveness and secondary meaning) that federal registration law applies to trademarks generally, including the statutory secondary-meaning provision quoted here — not a claim about whether any specific trade dress described on this sheet is inherently distinctive or has acquired secondary meaning, which this clause does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (15 U.S.C. § 1052(f)); no additional independent statutory source was needed for it. The product-packaging-versus-product-design distinction described in this clause's body — that product packaging can be inherently distinctive while product design cannot — is reported as a widely-known feature of trade dress case law commonly attributed to Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Samara Brothers, Inc., 529 U.S. 205 (2000), but that decision was not independently fetched or verified this session: CourtListener case-law search returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, 125/day daily limit, reported as exhausted with hours remaining before reset) before the case could be retrieved. No quotation from, or citation entry for, that decision is included in this clause's citations array as a result, consistent with this tool's practice of not fabricating case-law quotations; the distinction is stated in the clause body as a widely-reported doctrinal description rather than as a verified holding. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific trade dress is inherently distinctive or has acquired secondary meaning, and completing this information sheet does not itself assert or waive any right. This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule.
