citations.quote: Except as expressly excluded in subsections (a), (b), (c), (d), (e)(3), and (e)(5) of this section, nothing in this chapter shall prevent the registration of a mark used by the applicant which has become distinctive of the applicant’s goods in commerce. The Director may accept as prima facie evidence that the mark has become distinctive, as used on or in connection with the applicant’s goods in commerce, proof of substantially exclusive and continuous use thereof as a mark by the applicant in commerce for the five years before the date on which the claim of distinctiveness is made.

clauses.title: Federal Registration of Trade Dress Is Available but Not Required
clauses.body: Federal registration is available for trade dress, but it is not required in order to have protectable trade dress rights. Registration can be sought on the principal register — the primary federal trademark register, and the one associated with the additional statutory benefits (such as constructive nationwide notice and eligibility for incontestable status) described in this tool's Trademark Registration Information Sheet — if the trade dress is shown to be inherently distinctive or to have acquired secondary meaning. Separately, federal law also maintains a supplemental register for marks not yet eligible for the principal register. The statute governing that register expressly identifies "package" and "configuration of goods" among the categories of subject matter that may be registered there, alongside more familiar categories like trademarks, symbols, and words — confirming that packaging and product-configuration trade dress are subject matter Congress specifically contemplated for federal registration — but the same statutory sentence also requires that the matter sought to be registered, "as a whole," be "not functional" and be "capable of distinguishing the applicant's goods or services." Apart from any registration, common-law trade dress rights can also exist, based on actual use and distinctiveness in the marketplace, in the same way this tool's existing trademark documents describe common-law rights existing for word marks and logos independent of registration.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence that (a) trade dress subject matter — specifically "package" and "configuration of goods" — is expressly named as registrable on the supplemental register, and (b) that register's own statutory non-functionality and distinguishing-capability requirements — not a claim that any specific trade dress described on this sheet would qualify for registration on either register, which depends on facts and USPTO examination this clause does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (15 U.S.C. § 1091(c)); no additional independent statutory source was needed for it. This clause does not restate the principal register's own inherent-distinctiveness/secondary-meaning standard, which this document's own distinctiveness clause (tradedress_distinctiveness_requirement) already addresses with its own statutory citation, or the incontestability and constructive-notice benefits of principal-register registration, which this tool's existing Trademark Registration Information Sheet document already addresses with its own statutory citations, to avoid duplicating that coverage. It also does not restate the common-law-rights-independent-of-registration point in detail, which this tool's existing Trademark Infringement Cease and Desist Letter Information Sheet and Trademark Registration Information Sheet documents already address with their own statutory citations (15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(1)(A) and Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 14259); this clause states the general common-law point only to connect trade dress to that existing, non-duplicated coverage. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific trade dress is registered, registrable, or entitled to common-law protection, and completing this information sheet does not itself file any application or assert any right. This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule.

clauses.title: Remedies for Trade Dress Infringement: Cross-Reference to the General Lanham Act Remedial Framework
clauses.body: A trade dress infringement claim under 15 U.S.C. § 1125(a) draws on the same general federal remedial framework available for other claims under that statute. This tool's existing Trademark Infringement Cease and Desist Letter Information Sheet document separately addresses, with its own verified statutory citations, the monetary remedies available for a Lanham Act violation (the defendant's profits, the plaintiff's damages, costs, discretionary enhancement of damages, and attorney's fees limited to "exceptional cases," plus a separate mandatory treble-damages rule for certain counterfeiting) and the availability of injunctive relief. The statute governing injunctive relief expressly extends that remedy to actions to prevent "a violation under subsection (a) ... of section 1125" — the same subsection under which trade dress claims are brought — confirming that trade dress claims fall within, not outside, that existing remedial framework, rather than requiring this document to restate a separate, trade-dress-specific set of remedies.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence that the injunctive-relief statute's cross-reference to "a violation under subsection (a)... of section 1125" includes trade dress claims (which arise under that same subsection) within its scope — not a claim that any court would grant an injunction, or award any monetary remedy, with respect to any specific trade dress described on this sheet, which this clause does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (15 U.S.C. § 1116(a)); no additional independent statutory source was needed for it. This clause deliberately does not restate the monetary-remedies statute (15 U.S.C. § 1117) or requote the injunctive-relief provision's full text beyond the cross-reference language relevant here, both of which are already quoted and verified in this tool's existing Trademark Infringement Cease and Desist Letter Information Sheet document (clauses trademarkcd_remedies_monetary and trademarkcd_injunctive_relief); this clause instead connects trade dress claims to that existing, independently verified coverage rather than duplicating it. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific trade dress claim would succeed or that any specific remedy would be awarded, and completing this information sheet does not itself commence any legal proceeding. clauses.title: California Law: General Unfair Competition Statute, Not a Trade-Dress-Specific Doctrine
clauses.body: California does not have a standalone statute captioned "trade dress" or specifically addressed to product packaging or product design. California's general unfair competition statute defines "unfair competition" broadly, to mean and include "any unlawful, unfair or fraudulent business act or practice" as well as unfair, deceptive, untrue, or misleading advertising and violations of the state's separate false-advertising statute. This definition is not limited to any specific subject matter, and it does not mention trademarks, trade dress, packaging, or product design; by its own terms, it could potentially reach conduct involving a product's or service's appearance to the same broad extent it could reach any other unlawful, unfair, or fraudulent business conduct. Whether, and to what extent, this general statute has actually been applied by California courts to trade-dress-type claims specifically is a question this clause does not resolve; no case law confirming or describing such an application was verified this session (see this clause's gap note).
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence only of the broad, general text of California's unfair competition statute — not a claim that California courts have applied, or would apply, this statute to any trade-dress-type claim, or that a robust, trade-dress-specific body of California doctrine exists under it; no case law confirming that application was located or verified this session. This clause cites a single statutory section (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200); no additional independent statutory source was needed for it. A CourtListener search for California case law applying this statute to trade-dress-type claims was not attempted this session because CourtListener's 125/day rate limit was already confirmed exhausted at the time of drafting; consequently, this clause reports only the statute's general text and expressly declines to assert that California has a developed trade-dress-specific doctrine under it, rather than overstating what the bare statutory text supports. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific product's, package's, or service's appearance is protected by, or that any specific conduct violates, this or any other California statute, and completing this information sheet does not itself assert or waive any right. This clause addresses California law only; it does not address the law of any other state.

clauses.title: Definition of "Apprentice"
clauses.body: California Labor Code Chapter 4 defines an “apprentice,” for purposes of that chapter, as a person at least 16 years of age who has entered into a written apprentice agreement with an employer or a program sponsor. The statute names the employer or program sponsor — not a joint apprenticeship committee — as the counterparty to that written agreement; a joint apprenticeship committee's role, described elsewhere in this chapter, is to help establish, administer, and approve apprenticeship programs and agreements, not to be the party who signs the agreement with the apprentice.
clauses.gap: This is a single California statutory section (Cal. Labor Code § 3077); no additional independent source was found for the definition itself. The 16-year minimum age and the written-agreement requirement stated here define “apprentice” only for purposes of this specific chapter of California's Labor Code — a different statute, a different state's law, or a federal Registered Apprenticeship program could define the term differently, and this document does not identify which definition, if any, applies outside California's own statutory apprenticeship scheme. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific individual qualifies as an apprentice under this chapter, and does not determine that any specific written agreement is, or is not, a valid apprentice agreement.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 3077 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: The term “apprentice” as used in this chapter, means a person at least 16 years of age who has entered into a written agreement, in this chapter called an “apprentice agreement,” with an employer or program sponsor.

clauses.title: Required Content of an Apprentice Agreement
clauses.body: California Labor Code § 3078 requires that every apprentice agreement made under this chapter contain, directly or by reference: the names of the contracting parties; the apprentice's date of birth; a statement of the trade, craft, or business to be taught and when the apprenticeship begins and ends; a statement of the hours to be spent in work and the learning objectives for related and supplemental instruction (subject to a combined weekly-hours cap tied to the apprentice's age); a schedule of the trade processes to be taught and the approximate time for each; a statement of the graduated wage scale and whether required school time is compensated; a probationary-period provision; a provision routing unresolved disputes to the administrator; a provision allowing an employer who cannot continue to transfer the agreement to another employer with the administrator's approval and the apprentice's consent; any additional terms prescribed by the California Apprenticeship Council or the Chief of the Division of Apprenticeship Standards; and a clause addressing liability for an injury sustained during school work after employment has ended. This list is more extensive than a shorter list built only around parties, trade, term, wages, hours, and a probationary period — the statute requires several additional specific items, including the apprentice's date of birth and a process-by-process training schedule.
clauses.gap: Both citations below quote different subdivisions of the same statutory section, Cal. Labor Code § 3078, and are treated as one source, not independent. This document is informational only: it does not itself draft, complete, or file any apprentice agreement, and does not determine that any specific document satisfies § 3078's content requirements. This is California's own statutory list for its own apprenticeship framework; whether, and what, an equivalent list requires under any other state's apprenticeship law is not addressed here.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 3078 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Every apprentice agreement entered into under this chapter shall directly, or by reference, contain: (a) The names of the contracting parties. (b) The date of birth of the apprentice. (c) A statement of the trade, craft, or business which the apprentice is to be taught, and the time at which the apprenticeship will begin and end. (d) A statement showing the number of hours to be spent by the apprentice in work and the learning objectives to be accomplished through related and supplemental instruction, except as otherwise provided under Section 3074.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 3078 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: (e) A statement setting forth a schedule of the processes in the trade or industry divisions in which the apprentice is to be taught and the approximate time to be spent at each process. (f) A statement of the graduated scale of wages to be paid the apprentice and whether the required schooltime shall be compensated. (g) A statement providing for a period of probation during which time the apprentice agreement may be terminated by the program sponsor at the request in writing of either party, and providing that after the probationary period the apprentice agreement may be terminated by the administrator by mutual agreement of all parties thereto, or canceled by the administrator for good and sufficient reason.

clauses.title: Approval of an Apprentice Agreement
clauses.body: An apprentice agreement made under this chapter must be approved — by the local joint apprenticeship committee, or by the parties to a collective bargaining agreement, or, where neither exists, by the administrator — and a copy of the approved agreement must be filed with the Division of Apprenticeship Standards. Separately, the term of apprenticeship for each apprenticeable occupation is itself approved by the Chief of the Division of Apprenticeship Standards, applying the standards set out at Labor Code § 3078.5. Approval, in other words, is not a single event performed only by the Division or its Chief directly on every agreement: the immediate approving body is ordinarily the joint committee, the collective-bargaining parties, or the administrator, with the Division receiving a filed copy and the Chief separately approving the occupation's term.
clauses.gap: The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Labor Code §§ 3077 and 3079, not subsections of one section. Neither section quoted here states, in so many words, what legal consequence follows for an apprentice agreement that was never approved or never filed with the Division — this document does not assume, and the statutory text located does not itself say, that an unapproved agreement is void or unenforceable as a general matter; that specific consequence is not resolved by the statutory text found and is left as an open point. This document is informational only: it does not itself approve, execute, or file any apprentice agreement with any committee, administrator, or the Division of Apprenticeship Standards, and does not determine that any specific agreement has been, or will be, approved.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 3079 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Every apprentice agreement under this chapter shall be approved by the local joint apprenticeship committee or the parties to a collective bargaining agreement, or by the administrator where there is no collective bargaining agreement or joint committee, a copy of which shall be filed with the Division of Apprenticeship Standards.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 3077 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: The term of apprenticeship for each apprenticeable occupation shall be approved by the chief in accordance with the standards set forth in Section 3078.5.

clauses.title: Wage Schedule for Apprentices
clauses.body: Every apprentice agreement made under this chapter must contain a statement of the graduated scale of wages to be paid the apprentice and whether required school time is compensated — the statute requires the agreement to state a graduated wage scale, but its own text does not itself set out specific percentages of a journey-level wage or a specific schedule of increases. Those figures are instead set at the program-standards level: for programs in the building and construction trades and for firefighter occupations, the California Apprenticeship Council issues rules and regulations establishing minimum-wage, maximum-hours, and working-condition standards (no lower than this chapter's own floor); for other programs, an equivalent standard-setting role is assigned to the Chief of the Division of Apprenticeship Standards, and a joint apprenticeship committee with delegated written authority is assigned the function of establishing wage rates in accordance with whichever of those two standards applies to its program.
clauses.gap: The three citations below are drawn from three independently enacted sections of the same chapter — Cal. Labor Code §§ 3078(f), 3071, and 3076 — not subsections of one section. Section 3071's own quoted text expressly scopes the California Apprenticeship Council's wage-standards authority to programs in the building and construction trades and for firefighter occupations; § 3076 (quoted for the Chief's parallel role for "other programs") does not itself spell out that Chief-set wage-standard-setting process in the same regulatory detail as § 3071 does for the Council, and this document does not independently verify the content of any specific program's wage schedule or regulations issued under either section. This document is informational only: it does not itself state, calculate, or verify the graduated wage schedule, percentage, or rate that applies to any specific apprentice or program.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 3078 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: A statement of the graduated scale of wages to be paid the apprentice and whether the required schooltime shall be compensated.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 3071 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: The council shall issue rules and regulations which establish standards for minimum wages, maximum hours, and working conditions for apprentice agreements in the building and construction trades and for firefighter occupations, hereinafter in this chapter referred to as apprenticeship standards, which in no case shall be lower than those prescribed by this chapter

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 3076 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: The function of a joint apprenticeship committee, when specific written authority is delegated by the parent organizations represented, shall be to establish work processes, wage rates, working conditions for apprentices, the number of apprentices which shall be employed in the trade under apprentice agreements, and aid in the adjustment of apprenticeship disputes in accordance with standards for apprenticeship set up by the California Apprenticeship Council for programs in the building and construction trades and for firefighters or by the Chief of the Division of Apprenticeship Standards for other programs.

clauses.title: Related and Supplemental Instruction Requirement
clauses.body: An apprentice agreement must state the number of hours the apprentice will spend in work and the learning objectives to be met through related and supplemental instruction, and the combined weekly hours of work and required instruction may not exceed the maximum hours of work the law otherwise prescribes for a person of the apprentice's age. Where a program measures its apprenticeship term using the time-based approach — the approach that programs in the building and construction trades and for firefighter occupations must use — the statute itself specifies a minimum: at least 144 hours of related and supplemental instruction and 2,000 hours of on-the-job learning, as described in a work process schedule. A program outside those two categories is not required to use the time-based approach, however; it may instead measure the term using a competency-based or hybrid approach, each of which the statute defines by a minimum on-the-job-learning period of at least six months rather than by a fixed related-and-supplemental-instruction hour count.
clauses.gap: The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Labor Code §§ 3078(d) and 3078.5, not subsections of one section. The 144-hour and 2,000-hour figures quoted below apply specifically to programs using the time-based approach to measuring the apprenticeship term; this document does not determine which measurement approach — time-based, competency-based, or hybrid — any specific program outside the building and construction trades or firefighter occupations has adopted, and does not calculate the specific related-and-supplemental-instruction hours that would apply under a competency-based or hybrid program. This document is informational only: it does not itself schedule, track, or verify the instruction or on-the-job hours completed by any specific apprentice.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 3078 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: A statement showing the number of hours to be spent by the apprentice in work and the learning objectives to be accomplished through related and supplemental instruction, except as otherwise provided under Section 3074. In no case shall the combined weekly hours of work and required related and supplemental instruction of the apprentice exceed the maximum number of hours of work prescribed by law for a person of the age of the apprentice.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 3078.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: The time-based approach measures skill acquisition through the individual apprentice’s completion of at least 144 hours of related and supplemental instruction and 2,000 hours of on-the-job learning as described in a work process schedule.

clauses.title: Termination and Cancellation of an Apprentice Agreement
clauses.body: Every apprentice agreement must provide for a probationary period during which the program sponsor may terminate the agreement at the written request of either party; the statute caps that probationary period at whichever is shorter — 25 percent of the length of the program or one year — with full credit given toward completion of the apprenticeship for time already served during probation. After the probationary period, the statute allows the agreement to be terminated by the administrator by mutual agreement of all parties, or canceled by the administrator for good and sufficient reason. Separately, the administrator may investigate — on the complaint of any interested person, or on the administrator's own initiative — whether there has been a violation of an apprentice agreement's terms, and must give the parties a fair and impartial hearing after reasonable notice before making a determination; that determination can itself be appealed, and no lawsuit to enforce an apprentice agreement or recover damages for its breach may be filed until this chapter's administrative remedies have been exhausted.
clauses.gap: The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted provisions, Cal. Labor Code § 3078(g) and § 3081, not subsections of one section. The statutory text located requires the original apprentice agreement to be approved with a copy filed with the Division of Apprenticeship Standards at the outset (§ 3079, addressed in a separate clause in this document), but this document did not locate statutory text imposing a separate, independent notice-to-the-Division requirement specifically triggered by a later termination or cancellation, as distinct from the administrator's and Division's general administrative role in the agreement — that is disclosed here as a genuine gap in what was found in the statutory text, not as an affirmative statement that no such requirement exists anywhere in this chapter's implementing regulations. This document is informational only: it does not itself terminate, cancel, investigate, or adjudicate any specific apprentice agreement, and does not determine that any specific ground for termination or cancellation exists in any specific case.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 3078 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: A statement providing for a period of probation during which time the apprentice agreement may be terminated by the program sponsor at the request in writing of either party, and providing that after the probationary period the apprentice agreement may be terminated by the administrator by mutual agreement of all parties thereto, or canceled by the administrator for good and sufficient reason. The period of probation shall be reasonable in relation to the full apprenticeship term, with full credit given for such period toward completion of the apprenticeship, and in no event shall exceed the shorter of 25 percent of the length of the program or one year.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 3081 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Upon the complaint of any interested person or upon his or her own initiative, the administrator may investigate to determine if there has been a violation of the terms of an apprentice agreement, made under this chapter, and he or she may hold hearings, inquiries, and other proceedings necessary to such investigations and determinations.

clauses.title: The Statutory Waiver Thresholds
clauses.body: Cal. Labor Code § 512(a) permits a meal period to be waived in exactly two circumstances, both tied to shift length. First, if {{employeeName}}'s total work period for the day is no more than six hours, the otherwise-required first meal period may be waived by mutual consent of {{companyName}} and {{employeeName}}. Second, if {{employeeName}} works more than 10 hours but no more than 12 hours in a day, the second meal period (otherwise required for a shift over 10 hours) may be waived by mutual consent of {{companyName}} and {{employeeName}} — but only if the first meal period was not itself waived. There is no statutory waiver available for a shift longer than 12 hours, and the second-meal-period waiver is unavailable on any shift, however short, if the first meal period was waived.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Labor Code § 512(a)), offered as documented evidence of what that provision says — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. Federal law imposes no meal-period requirement at all, and most other states either have no meal-break statute or a far less detailed one. This clause quotes the same statutory subsection already quoted in full in this corpus's separate Meal and Rest Break Policy document (its meal_period_requirement clause); it is restated here, standing alone, because this information sheet is meant to be usable independently, not because it is offered as a second, independent source for the same text. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 512(a)); no additional independent source was found for this specific text.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 512(a)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 512, subd. (a)
citations.quote: An employer shall not employ an employee for a work period of more than five hours per day without providing the employee with a meal period of not less than 30 minutes, except that if the total work period per day of the employee is no more than six hours, the meal period may be waived by mutual consent of both the employer and employee. An employer shall not employ an employee for a work period of more than 10 hours per day without providing the employee with a second meal period of not less than 30 minutes, except that if the total hours worked is no more than 12 hours, the second meal period may be waived by mutual consent of the employer and the employee only if the first meal period was not waived.

clauses.title: "Mutual Consent" — Whether a Writing Is Required
clauses.body: The statutory text of Cal. Labor Code § 512(a) conditions both meal-period waivers described above on "mutual consent of both the employer and employee" — it does not, in these words, require that consent be documented in writing. By contrast, elsewhere in the same body of law, where a writing is required for a different kind of meal-period arrangement, the text says so explicitly: a wage-order provision governing health care industry employees who work shifts of more than eight hours conditions a related but separate meal-period waiver on the waiver being "documented in a written agreement that is voluntarily signed by both the employee and the employer." The bare § 512(a) waiver described above is not made subject to that same written-and-signed language.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute and one state's regulation (Cal. Labor Code § 512(a) and IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001 § 11(D)), offered as documented evidence of what those provisions say — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee, and not a claim that no court has ever read an unstated writing requirement into § 512(a)'s bare text. These two citations are genuinely independent instruments (a Labor Code statute and a separate Industrial Welfare Commission wage order provision), not subsections of the same source. Separately, and without a citable source for it, many employers document meal-period waivers in writing as a matter of practice or evidentiary caution — that is a risk-management choice, not itself a statutory command, and is not asserted here as one.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 512(a)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 512, subd. (a)
citations.quote: An employer shall not employ an employee for a work period of more than five hours per day without providing the employee with a meal period of not less than 30 minutes, except that if the total work period per day of the employee is no more than six hours, the meal period may be waived by mutual consent of both the employer and employee.

citations.case: IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 11(D)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 11(D)
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other provision of this order, employees in the health care industry who work shifts in excess of eight (8) total hours in a workday may voluntarily waive their right to one of their two meal periods. In order to be valid, any such waiver must be documented in a written agreement that is voluntarily signed by both the employee and the employer.

clauses.title: On-Duty Meal Periods Are a Different Arrangement Than a Waiver
clauses.body: An "on-duty" meal period is analytically distinct from waiving a meal period under Cal. Labor Code § 512(a). Waiving a meal period means the meal period does not happen at all and is not paid separately. An on-duty meal period, by contrast, means {{employeeName}} remains on duty during the 30 minutes and is paid for that time as hours worked; California law treats it as "on duty" precisely because {{employeeName}} was not relieved of all duty. IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001 permits an on-duty meal period only when the nature of {{employeeName}}'s work prevents {{employeeName}} from being relieved of all duty, and only by written agreement between {{companyName}} and {{employeeName}}. The DLSE has stated that whether the nature of the work prevents relief from duty is judged by an objective standard, not simply by the parties' say-so.
clauses.gap: This is one state's regulatory text (an IWC wage order provision) and a passage from a DLSE public guidance page describing that same regulatory structure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer. The wage-order citation here restates the same provision already quoted in full in this corpus's separate Meal and Rest Break Policy document (its on_duty_meal_period clause); it is restated here because this information sheet is meant to be usable independently, not as a second, independent source for that text. The DLSE FAQ citation is a genuinely separate source (agency guidance, not the regulation itself), though it is not binding law and reflects the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's own interpretation rather than a statute, regulation, or published court opinion.

citations.case: IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 11(A)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 11(A)
citations.quote: Unless the employee is relieved of all duty during a 30 minute meal period, the meal period shall be considered an “on duty” meal period and counted as time worked. An “on duty” meal period shall be permitted only when the nature of the work prevents an employee from being relieved of all duty and when by written agreement between the parties an on-the-job paid meal period is agreed to.

citations.case: DLSE, Meal Periods FAQ
citations.cite: Cal. Dep't of Indus. Relations, Div. of Labor Standards Enforcement, Meal Periods FAQ (rev. July 11, 2012)
citations.quote: The test of whether the nature of the work prevents an employee from being relieved of all duty is an objective one. An employer and employee may not agree to an on-duty meal period unless, based on objective criteria, any employee would be prevented from being relieved of all duty based on the necessary job duties.

clauses.title: Revoking a Written On-Duty or Health Care Industry Meal-Period Agreement
clauses.body: A written on-duty meal period agreement between {{companyName}} and {{employeeName}} must itself state that {{employeeName}} may revoke it in writing at any time. A related but distinct arrangement — the separate written waiver available under the wage order to health care industry employees working shifts of more than eight hours, covering one of their two meal periods — is revocable on different terms: {{employeeName}} may revoke that waiver at any time, but only by giving {{companyName}} at least one day's written notice. Revocation is therefore not a single, uniform rule across every meal-period arrangement described in this document; its terms depend on which specific arrangement is at issue.
clauses.gap: This is one state's regulatory text (an IWC wage order provision), offered as documented evidence of what it says — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer. Both citations here are subdivisions of the same wage order section (§ 11 of IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001); they are treated as one source, not independent. The on-duty-agreement citation restates the same provision already quoted in full in this corpus's separate Meal and Rest Break Policy document; it is restated here so this information sheet can be read on its own.

citations.case: IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 11(A)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 11(A)
citations.quote: The written agreement shall state that the employee may, in writing, revoke the agreement at any time.

citations.case: IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 11(D)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 11(D)
citations.quote: The employee may revoke the waiver at any time by providing the employer at least one (1) day’s written notice.

clauses.title: An Involuntary or Coerced "Waiver" Does Not Excuse the Meal Period Obligation
clauses.body: A meal-period waiver is valid only if it reflects {{employeeName}}'s genuine mutual consent. The California Supreme Court has stated, as quoted in the DLSE's own public guidance on meal periods, that "the wage orders and governing statute do not countenance an employer's exerting coercion against the taking of, creating incentives to forego, or otherwise encouraging the skipping of legally protected breaks." If a purported waiver is not the product of {{employeeName}}'s free choice — because it was coerced, pressured, or the product of an incentive to skip the meal period rather than a genuine mutual decision — it does not satisfy Cal. Labor Code § 512(a), and the meal period is treated as one {{companyName}} did not provide. California law then requires {{companyName}} to pay {{employeeName}} one additional hour of pay at {{employeeName}}'s regular rate of pay for that workday — the same premium that applies to any other missed, short, or late meal period.
clauses.gap: This is one state's case law and agency guidance describing one state's statutory scheme (California) — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employment relationship, and not a claim that federal law imposes any comparable rule (it does not; federal law has no meal-period requirement to excuse or enforce). Both citations here are drawn from the same DLSE public guidance page; they are treated as one source, not independent — the coercion language originates in the California Supreme Court's Brinker decision and is quoted by the DLSE, and the premium-pay language restates the same one-additional-hour remedy documented, with its own independently verified citation to Cal. Labor Code § 226.7(b)-(c), in this corpus's separate Meal and Rest Break Policy document; it is not re-derived independently here.

citations.case: DLSE, Meal Periods FAQ
citations.cite: Cal. Dep't of Indus. Relations, Div. of Labor Standards Enforcement, Meal Periods FAQ (rev. July 11, 2012)
citations.quote: The wage orders and governing statute do not countenance an employer's exerting coercion against the taking of, creating incentives to forego, or otherwise encouraging the skipping of legally protected breaks.

citations.case: DLSE, Meal Periods FAQ
citations.cite: Cal. Dep't of Indus. Relations, Div. of Labor Standards Enforcement, Meal Periods FAQ (rev. July 11, 2012)
citations.quote: If an employer fails to provide an employee a meal period in accordance with an applicable IWC Order, the employer must pay one additional hour of pay at the employee's regular rate of pay for each workday that the meal period is not provided.

clauses.title: Life Insurance as a Nonprobate Transfer by Written Instrument
clauses.body: California's Probate Code addresses this directly, not as an aside. Prob. Code § 5000(a) provides that a written instrument's provision for a nonprobate transfer at {{policyOwnerName}}'s death is not invalid merely because the instrument doesn't comply with the requirements for executing a will — and the statute names an insurance policy specifically as one kind of instrument this covers, alongside things like a trust, a deed of gift, and a revocable transfer on death deed. In other words, a beneficiary designation on a life insurance policy such as the one {{policyOwnerName}} holds with {{insurerName}} (policy number {{policyNumber}}) is one of the statute's own named examples of a California-recognized nonprobate transfer: on {{policyOwnerName}}'s death, the policy's proceeds are paid according to the beneficiary designation on file with {{insurerName}}, without going through probate and without that designation itself needing to satisfy will-execution formalities like witnesses. This Probate Code provision validates that kind of arrangement generally; it is a separate question — addressed elsewhere in this document — what specifically authorizes and governs the mechanics of naming, and later changing, a beneficiary under a particular life insurance policy.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's policy, and not advice about what any particular reader should name as a beneficiary or do with their own policy. Prob. Code § 5000 is Probate Code Division 5's general nonprobate-transfer provision; it sits alongside, and does not replace, the separate scheme in the Insurance Code that regulates the life-insurance beneficiary-designation mechanism itself (addressed in this document's next clause). This is a single statutory subdivision; no additional independent source was located or needed to confirm this specific enumeration.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5000(a)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, nonprobate transfer by written instrument, naming an insurance policy
citations.quote: A provision for a nonprobate transfer on death in an insurance policy, contract of employment, bond, mortgage, promissory note, certificated or uncertificated security, account agreement, custodial agreement, deposit agreement, compensation plan, pension plan, individual retirement plan, employee benefit plan, trust, conveyance, deed of gift, revocable transfer on death deed, marital property agreement, or other written instrument of a similar nature is not invalid because the instrument does not comply with the requirements for execution of a will, and this code does not invalidate the instrument.

clauses.title: Source of the Beneficiary-Designation Mechanism, and Its Revocability
clauses.body: The specific power that lets {{policyOwnerName}} name {{beneficiaryName}} as beneficiary under the policy {{policyOwnerName}} holds with {{insurerName}}, and later change that designation, comes from the policy itself — not from a Probate Code command dictating who must be named. Cal. Ins. Code § 10170(e) makes this explicit: the terms and restrictions governing revocation by the policyholder, and control by beneficiaries, are those "agreed to in writing by the insurer and the policyholder" (or, if the insurer and policyholder never agreed to terms during {{policyOwnerName}}'s lifetime, those later agreed to in writing by the insurer and the beneficiaries). The same subdivision then supplies the default rule for how those terms can be undone: an agreement — including its terms on revocation — may generally be rescinded or amended by the parties to it without {{beneficiaryName}}'s consent, unless {{beneficiaryName}}'s rights have been expressly declared irrevocable, in which case that consent is required to change the designation. So the beneficiary-designation mechanism itself is fundamentally a matter of the insurance contract; what the Insurance Code supplies is the background default rule about when a beneficiary's consent is, and is not, required to change it.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's policy, and not advice about whether any particular policy owner should designate a beneficiary as revocable or irrevocable. Cal. Ins. Code § 10170 has several lettered subdivisions describing the different ways life insurance may be made payable; only subdivision (e), which supplies the revocation and irrevocable-consent rule, is quoted here. This is a single statutory subdivision; no additional independent source was located for it. Separately, this section describes what California's default statutory framework permits the policy to say — it does not itself state what any specific insurer's policy form actually provides, which controls in practice and can vary by insurer and by policy.

citations.case: Cal. Ins. Code § 10170(e)
citations.cite: California Insurance Code, terms of revocation and control by beneficiaries; irrevocable-beneficiary consent rule
citations.quote: Upon those terms and conditions and subject to those restrictions as to revocation by the policyholder and control by beneficiaries as shall have been agreed to in writing by the insurer and the policyholder. If no terms and conditions have been agreed to by the insurer and the policyholder during the insured’s lifetime then upon those terms and conditions and subject to those restrictions as may be agreed to in writing by the insurer and the beneficiaries. Any agreement may be rescinded or amended by the parties to the agreement without the consent of any designated beneficiary unless the rights of any beneficiary have been expressly declared to be irrevocable.

clauses.title: Community Property Premiums and a Beneficiary Other Than the Owner's Spouse
clauses.body: If {{policyOwnerName}} is married, and premiums on the policy with {{insurerName}} were paid using community property funds, naming someone other than {{policyOwnerName}}'s spouse as {{beneficiaryName}} intersects with California's community property law in a way this document flags rather than resolves. Two separate statutes bear on it. First, Fam. Code § 1100(b) provides that a spouse "may not make a gift of community personal property, or dispose of community personal property for less than fair and reasonable value, without the written consent of the other spouse" — and naming a non-spouse as the beneficiary of a policy funded with community property premiums can be treated as this kind of disposition. Second, Prob. Code § 5011 provides that the rights of the parties in a nonprobate transfer of community property on death — a category that, per this document's first clause, expressly includes a life insurance policy — are subject to the terms of the instrument, any contrary statute specifically applicable to it, and a written expression of intent or consent by a party. Neither statute, on its own text, announces a single fixed outcome for every such policy; together they establish that a non-owner spouse's community property interest in a policy is a real, statutorily-recognized issue when the named beneficiary isn't that spouse, not something a beneficiary designation alone necessarily overrides. What community property and quasi-community property mean under California law generally is addressed elsewhere in this corpus's community property materials.
clauses.gap: This is California's law, used as evidence of what California statutes provide — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's marriage or policy, and not advice about whether any specific policy, premium history, or beneficiary designation does or does not require a spouse's consent. Fam. Code § 1100(b) and Prob. Code § 5011 are separate statutes in different codes, each independently retrieved and verified — not subsections of the same section. California case law bearing specifically on a non-owner spouse's interest in a life insurance policy naming a third party — the kind of authority one might expect alongside these statutes — could not be verified this session: the case-law research tool available for this task returned a rate-limit error (daily quota exhausted) before any case could be retrieved and confirmed, so no case citation is included here; that gap is disclosed rather than filled with an unverified case. This clause relies on, rather than re-derives, this corpus's own existing statutory definition of community and quasi-community property.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 1100(b)
citations.cite: California Family Code, spousal consent required for a gift of community personal property
citations.quote: A spouse may not make a gift of community personal property, or dispose of community personal property for less than fair and reasonable value, without the written consent of the other spouse.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5011
citations.cite: California Probate Code, rights of parties in a nonprobate transfer of community property on death
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other provision of this part, the rights of the parties in a nonprobate transfer of community property on death are subject to all of the following: (a) The terms of the instrument under which the nonprobate transfer is made. (b) A contrary state statute specifically applicable to the instrument under which the nonprobate transfer is made. (c) A written expression of intent of a party in the provision for transfer of the property or in a written consent to the provision.

clauses.title: Simultaneous Death of the Insured and a Beneficiary
clauses.body: California has a default rule specifically for a life insurance beneficiary who dies at the same time as the insured, or where it can't be established by clear and convincing evidence which of them survived the other — and it is not the 120-hour survival rule that governs wills and intestate succession. Under Prob. Code § 224, if it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that {{beneficiaryName}} survived {{policyOwnerName}} as the insured, the policy's proceeds are administered as if {{policyOwnerName}} survived {{beneficiaryName}} — meaning {{beneficiaryName}}'s designation is treated as though it lapsed — except that if the policy is community or quasi-community property of {{policyOwnerName}} and {{policyOwnerName}}'s spouse, and there is no other named beneficiary besides {{policyOwnerName}}'s own estate or personal representative, the proceeds are instead distributed as community property under a separate statute. This default rule has real limits on when it applies: under Prob. Code § 221, this chapter's simultaneous-death rules do not apply at all if the policy or a related agreement contains its own explicit provision addressing simultaneous deaths, a common-disaster clause, or a stated survival period different from what this default rule provides — so a policy or beneficiary form that speaks to the issue directly controls instead of this default.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides for a life insurance beneficiary specifically — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's policy, and not advice about how a specific policy's own survivorship language should be drafted or interpreted. Prob. Code § 224 and § 221 are separate, independently retrieved and verified statutory sections within the same chapter of the Probate Code (the Uniform Simultaneous Death Act as adopted in California) — they are treated as independent sources of what each provides, not as subsections of one section, though both come from the same statutory chapter. This clause does not address the separate 120-hour survival requirement that Prob. Code § 6403 applies to wills and intestate succession; § 221(a) itself provides that this chapter does not apply where § 6403 (among other sections) applies, so the two default rules are not interchangeable, and this document does not assume the 120-hour rule extends to a life insurance beneficiary designation.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 224
citations.cite: California Probate Code, simultaneous death of insured and beneficiary under a life or accident policy
citations.quote: If the insured and a beneficiary under a policy of life or accident insurance have died and it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that the beneficiary survived the insured, the proceeds of the policy shall be administered or distributed, or otherwise dealt with, as if the insured had survived the beneficiary, except if the policy is community or quasi-community property of the insured and the spouse of the insured and there is no alternative beneficiary except the estate or personal representative of the insured, the proceeds shall be distributed as community property under Section 103.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 221(b)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, chapter inapplicable where the policy addresses simultaneous death itself
citations.quote: This chapter does not apply in the case of a trust, deed, or contract of insurance, or any other situation, where (1) provision is made dealing explicitly with simultaneous deaths or deaths in a common disaster or otherwise providing for distribution of property different from the provisions of this chapter or (2) provision is made requiring one person to survive another for a stated period in order to take property or providing for a presumption as to survivorship that results in a distribution of property different from that provided by this chapter.

clauses.title: A Beneficiary Who Feloniously and Intentionally Kills the Insured
clauses.body: California's slayer statute reaches a life insurance beneficiary specifically, not only a probate or intestate heir. Prob. Code § 252 provides that a named beneficiary of a bond, life insurance policy, or other contractual arrangement who feloniously and intentionally kills the person on whose life the policy is issued is not entitled to any benefit under it, and the policy becomes payable as though the killer had predeceased the insured — so if {{beneficiaryName}} feloniously and intentionally killed {{policyOwnerName}} as the insured, {{beneficiaryName}} forfeits the designation under this statute regardless of what the policy's own paperwork says. This isn't limited to that dedicated life-insurance provision: the general slayer-disqualification statute, Prob. Code § 250(a)(4), separately disqualifies a feloniously-and-intentionally-killing beneficiary from "any property of the decedent under Division 5 (commencing with Section 5000)" — the same Probate Code division that, as described elsewhere in this document, expressly includes a life insurance policy's nonprobate transfer provision — confirming the slayer rule isn't confined to wills and intestate succession. How the killing itself gets established for these purposes is addressed by Prob. Code § 254: a final criminal conviction for the felonious and intentional killing is conclusive, and without one, a court may find it by a preponderance of the evidence, with the burden on whoever is asserting the disqualification.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's policy, and not advice about, or a finding regarding, whether any actual beneficiary of any actual policy has committed a disqualifying act; whether a specific killing was "felonious and intentional" within the meaning of this statute is a fact-specific determination for a court, as § 254 itself describes, not something this document resolves. Prob. Code §§ 252, 250(a)(4), and 254 are three separate, independently retrieved and verified statutory sections; § 250(a)(4) is quoted only for its cross-reference to Division 5, not for the full list of interests it disqualifies.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 252
citations.cite: California Probate Code, slayer disqualification for a named life insurance beneficiary
citations.quote: A named beneficiary of a bond, life insurance policy, or other contractual arrangement who feloniously and intentionally kills the principal obligee or the person upon whose life the policy is issued is not entitled to any benefit under the bond, policy, or other contractual arrangement, and it becomes payable as though the killer had predeceased the decedent.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 250(a)(4)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, general slayer statute's cross-reference to Division 5 nonprobate transfers
citations.quote: Any property of the decedent under Division 5 (commencing with Section 5000).

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 254(a)-(b)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, how a felonious and intentional killing is established
citations.quote: A final judgment of conviction of felonious and intentional killing is conclusive for purposes of this part. (b) In the absence of a final judgment of conviction of felonious and intentional killing, the court may determine by a preponderance of evidence whether the killing was felonious and intentional for purposes of this part. The burden of proof is on the party seeking to establish that the killing was felonious and intentional for the purposes of this part.

clauses.title: What a Benefit Corporation Is and the General Public Benefit Purpose Requirement
clauses.body: California's Corporations Code contains a distinct statutory part governing the for-profit "benefit corporation" — Part 13 of Division 3 of Title 1, Corp. Code §§ 14600-14631 — that is a different corporate form both from an ordinary for-profit corporation formed only under the General Corporation Law and from the differently-named nonprofit "public benefit corporation," which is formed under a separate part of the Nonprofit Corporation Law, has no shareholders, and may not distribute profits. By statutory definition, a "benefit corporation" is "a corporation organized under the General Corporation Law that has elected to become subject to this part and whose status as a benefit corporation has not been terminated as provided in this part" — meaning the entity starts as an ordinary for-profit corporation and becomes a benefit corporation only by an affirmative election, not automatically. Once elected, the statute requires the corporation to "have the purpose of creating general public benefit," a term the same statute defines as "a material positive impact on society and the environment, taken as a whole, as assessed against a third-party standard, from the business and operations of a benefit corporation." This general-public-benefit purpose is layered onto, not a substitute for, the corporation's ordinary for-profit purpose: the statute states that it is "in addition to, and may be a limitation on," the corporation's purpose under the General Corporation Law's own purpose provision, and a benefit corporation may, but need not, also adopt one or more narrower "specific public benefit" purposes alongside the required general one.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one state defines and structures this specific for-profit corporate form — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation's formation, and not a claim that every state with a benefit corporation statute defines or structures the form identically; benefit corporation statutes vary by state. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 14601 and Cal. Corp. Code § 14610, and are treated as two independent sources; within the first citation, the two quoted subsections, (a) and (c), are both drawn from the same section, § 14601, and are not independent of each other. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any corporation, does not itself elect benefit corporation status for any corporation, and does not determine federal tax treatment of any corporation, which is a separate question this document does not address.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 14601(a), (c)
citations.cite: California benefit corporation statute, definitions of "benefit corporation" and "general public benefit"
citations.quote: “Benefit corporation” means a corporation organized under the General Corporation Law that has elected to become subject to this part and whose status as a benefit corporation has not been terminated as provided in this part.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 14610(a)
citations.cite: California benefit corporation statute, the required general public benefit purpose
citations.quote: A benefit corporation shall have the purpose of creating general public benefit. This purpose is in addition to, and may be a limitation on, the corporation’s purpose under Section 206 and any specific purpose set forth in its articles in accordance with subdivision (b).

clauses.title: Required Content of Benefit Corporation Articles of Incorporation
clauses.body: A California benefit corporation's formation filing is not a separate document from an ordinary for-profit corporation's articles — it is formed "in accordance with Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 200) of Division 1," the same General Corporation Law formation chapter every for-profit corporation uses — but the benefit corporation statute adds specific required content on top of that ordinary chapter: "the articles shall also state that the corporation is a benefit corporation and shall identify any specific public benefit" the corporation has adopted. A separate section of the same statutory part supplies the exact required language: "the articles of incorporation of a benefit corporation shall contain the following statement: 'This corporation is a benefit corporation.'" That same section also permits, but does not require, the articles to identify one or more specific public benefits as the corporation's purpose, and states that doing so does not narrow the corporation's separate obligation to also pursue general public benefit. Both of these requirements are additional to, not substitutes for, the content requirements that already apply to every for-profit corporation's articles under the General Corporation Law.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what one state's required formation-document content for this specific type of for-profit corporation looks like — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation's formation, and required content for a benefit corporation's articles varies by state. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 14602 and Cal. Corp. Code § 14610(b), and are treated as two independent sources, not subsections of one section. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any corporation, does not itself file anything with the California Secretary of State, and does not itself elect benefit corporation status for any corporation.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 14602
citations.cite: California benefit corporation statute, formation under the General Corporation Law plus the added statement and specific-benefit identification requirement
citations.quote: A benefit corporation shall be formed in accordance with Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 200) of Division 1 except that the articles shall also state that the corporation is a benefit corporation and shall identify any specific public benefit adopted pursuant to Section 14610.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 14610(b)
citations.cite: California benefit corporation statute, the required articles statement electing benefit corporation status
citations.quote: In addition to the provisions required by Section 202, the articles of incorporation of a benefit corporation shall contain the following statement: “This corporation is a benefit corporation.”

clauses.title: Annual Benefit Report: Content, Delivery to Shareholders, and Public Posting
clauses.body: California's benefit corporation statute requires an annual benefit report, and states what it must contain, who must receive it, and when. On content, the statute states that "a benefit corporation shall deliver to each shareholder an annual benefit report" that must include, among other required elements, "an assessment of the overall social and environmental performance of the benefit corporation, prepared in accordance with a third-party standard applied consistently with any application of that standard in prior benefit reports or accompanied by an explanation of the reasons for any inconsistent application" — and the statute is explicit that "the assessment does not need to be audited or certified by a third party." A separate section of the same statutory part requires the report to include a further, specific statement: the board of directors must prepare, "for inclusion in the annual benefit report to shareholders required by Section 14630, a statement indicating whether, in the opinion of the board of directors, the benefit corporation failed to pursue its general, and any specific, public benefit purpose in all material respects during the period covered by the report." On timing and recipients, the report "shall be sent annually to each shareholder within 120 days following the end of the fiscal year of the benefit corporation or at the same time that the benefit corporation delivers any other annual report to its shareholders" — so delivery runs to shareholders, not to the general public, by default. Public availability is nonetheless required in a different way: "a benefit corporation shall post all of its benefit reports on the public portion of its Internet Web site, if any," though compensation and certain financial or proprietary information may be omitted from that publicly posted version.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one state's own annual-report content, delivery, and public-posting requirements for this specific type of for-profit corporation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and annual benefit reporting requirements, if any, vary by state. The first three citations below are all drawn from subsections of the same section, Cal. Corp. Code § 14630(a), (b), and (c), and are treated as one source, not three independent ones; the fourth citation, Cal. Corp. Code § 14621(a), is an independently enacted section and is treated as a second, independent source. This document is informational only: it does not itself prepare, deliver, or post any benefit report on behalf of any corporation.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 14630(a)
citations.cite: California benefit corporation statute, duty to deliver an annual benefit report to shareholders and the required third-party-standard assessment
citations.quote: An assessment of the overall social and environmental performance of the benefit corporation, prepared in accordance with a third-party standard applied consistently with any application of that standard in prior benefit reports or accompanied by an explanation of the reasons for any inconsistent application. The assessment does not need to be audited or certified by a third party.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 14630(b)
citations.cite: California benefit corporation statute, 120-day annual delivery deadline to shareholders
citations.quote: The benefit report shall be sent annually to each shareholder within 120 days following the end of the fiscal year of the benefit corporation or at the same time that the benefit corporation delivers any other annual report to its shareholders.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 14630(c)
citations.cite: California benefit corporation statute, requirement to post benefit reports on the corporation's public website
citations.quote: A benefit corporation shall post all of its benefit reports on the public portion of its Internet Web site, if any, except that the compensation paid to directors and any financial or proprietary information included in the benefit report may be omitted from the benefit report as posted on the Internet Web site.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 14621(a)
citations.cite: California benefit corporation statute, required board statement on whether the public benefit purpose was pursued
citations.quote: The board of directors of a benefit corporation shall prepare for inclusion in the annual benefit report to shareholders required by Section 14630, a statement indicating whether, in the opinion of the board of directors, the benefit corporation failed to pursue its general, and any specific, public benefit purpose in all material respects during the period covered by the report.

clauses.title: Director Duties: Required Consideration of Non-Shareholder Interests
clauses.body: California's benefit corporation statute states a director's duty of care in language close to the General Corporation Law's ordinary standard — acting "in good faith, in a manner the director believes to be in the best interests of the benefit corporation and with that care, including reasonable inquiry, as an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances" — but then adds a list of interests a director must consider that reaches well beyond shareholder profit. The statute requires that in discharging their duties and considering the corporation's best interests, "the board of directors, committees of the board, and individual directors of a benefit corporation shall consider the impacts of any action or proposed action upon all of the following": the shareholders; "the employees and workforce of the benefit corporation and its subsidiaries and suppliers"; customers, "as beneficiaries of the general or specific public benefit purposes of the benefit corporation"; "community and societal considerations, including those of any community in which offices or facilities of the benefit corporation or its subsidiaries or suppliers are located"; and "the local and global environment." This is a mandatory consideration requirement, not merely a permitted one — the statute elsewhere makes certain other factors optional for a director to consider, but places shareholders, employees, customers, community, and the environment in the mandatory list.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one state's benefit corporation law modifies the ordinary director duty of care for this specific corporate form — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation's directors, and how (or whether) a state modifies director duties for a benefit-type corporation varies by state. The single citation below combines two subsections of the same section, Cal. Corp. Code § 14620(a) and (b), and is treated as one source; the statute contains further subsections addressing director liability limits and reliance on others' reports that are not quoted here. This document is informational only: it does not itself impose or interpret any specific director's duties and does not evaluate whether any specific director's conduct complied with this statute.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 14620(a), (b)
citations.cite: California benefit corporation statute, director duty of care and required consideration of non-shareholder interests
citations.quote: A director shall perform the duties of a director including duties as a member of any committee of the board upon which the director may serve, in good faith, in a manner the director believes to be in the best interests of the benefit corporation and with that care, including reasonable inquiry, as an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances.

clauses.title: Benefit Enforcement Proceedings: Exclusive Remedy, Standing, and Available Relief
clauses.body: California's benefit corporation statute channels claims about a benefit corporation's public-benefit obligations into a single, narrowly defined procedural vehicle rather than leaving them to ordinary shareholder litigation. The statute defines a "benefit enforcement proceeding" as "a claim or action relating to any of the following: (1) Failure to pursue the general public benefit purpose of the benefit corporation or any specific public benefit purpose set forth in its articles. (2) Violation of a duty or standard of conduct imposed on a director pursuant to this part. (3) Failure of the benefit corporation to deliver or post an annual benefit report as required by Section 14630." A separate section makes that vehicle exclusive and limits who may use it: "no person may bring an action or assert a claim against a benefit corporation or its directors or officers under this chapter except in a benefit enforcement proceeding," and such a proceeding "may be commenced or maintained only" directly by the benefit corporation itself, or derivatively by a shareholder, a director, a person or group owning 5 percent or more of an entity of which the benefit corporation is a subsidiary, or other persons specified in the corporation's own articles or bylaws — a narrower list than the general universe of persons who might otherwise sue a corporation. On remedy, the same section provides that "if the court in a benefit enforcement proceeding finds that a failure to comply with this part was without justification, the court may award an amount sufficient to reimburse the plaintiff for the reasonable expenses incurred by the plaintiff, including attorney's fees and expenses, in connection with the benefit enforcement proceeding" — an expense-reimbursement remedy tied to the litigation itself, not a monetary damages award against the corporation for failing to create public benefit, which the same statutory part separately forecloses.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one state defines, channels, and remedies claims about a benefit corporation's public-benefit obligations — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation's litigation, and enforcement mechanisms for a benefit-type corporation, including who has standing and what remedy is available, vary by state. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 14601(b) and Cal. Corp. Code § 14623; within the second citation, the quoted subsections (a), (b), and (d) are all drawn from the same section, § 14623, and are not independent of each other. This document is informational only: it does not itself bring, defend, or evaluate the merits of any claim, and it does not determine whether any specific person has standing to bring a benefit enforcement proceeding.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 14601(b)
citations.cite: California benefit corporation statute, definition of "benefit enforcement proceeding"
citations.quote: “Benefit enforcement proceeding” means a claim or action relating to any of the following: (1) Failure to pursue the general public benefit purpose of the benefit corporation or any specific public benefit purpose set forth in its articles. (2) Violation of a duty or standard of conduct imposed on a director pursuant to this part. (3)  Failure of the benefit corporation to deliver or post an annual benefit report as required by Section 14630.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 14623(a), (b), (d)
citations.cite: California benefit corporation statute, exclusivity of the benefit enforcement proceeding, standing to bring one, and the expense-reimbursement remedy
citations.quote: No person may bring an action or assert a claim against a benefit corporation or its directors or officers under this chapter except in a benefit enforcement proceeding.

clauses.title: Terminating Benefit Corporation Status: Minimum Status Vote and Dissenting Shareholder Rights
clauses.body: California's benefit corporation statute sets a heightened, defined vote threshold for a corporation to drop out of benefit corporation status, rather than leaving that decision to whatever vote an ordinary articles amendment would otherwise require. The statute provides that "a benefit corporation may terminate its status as a benefit corporation and cease to be subject to this part by amending the corporation's articles to delete the provision required by Section 14602" — the statement electing benefit corporation status — but "the amendment shall not be effective unless the amendment is adopted by at least the minimum status vote," and further provides that a shareholder who dissents from that amendment may require the corporation to purchase the shareholder's shares at fair market value, following the same statutory dissenters'-rights procedure used for a reorganization. "Minimum status vote" is itself a defined statutory term, and for a corporation it requires more than an ordinary majority: "in addition to any other approval or vote required by Division 1 (commencing with Section 100) or the articles of incorporation," every class or series of shareholders is entitled to vote "regardless of any limitation stated in the articles or bylaws on the voting rights of any class or series," and "the corporate action shall be approved by the outstanding shares of each class or series by at least two-thirds of the votes, or greater vote if required in the articles of incorporation, that all shareholders of the class or series are entitled to cast on that action." The same defined "minimum status vote" threshold also governs a corporation electing into benefit corporation status in the first place, and certain reorganizations, conversions, and asset-sale transactions that would have the effect of terminating that status.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one state's own vote threshold and dissenters'-rights procedure for exiting this specific corporate status — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation's amendment process, and whether a state imposes a heightened vote threshold for terminating benefit corporation status, and what that threshold is, varies by state. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 14604(a) and Cal. Corp. Code § 14601(d)(1)(A)-(B), and are treated as two independent sources. This document is informational only: it does not itself amend any corporation's articles, does not itself terminate benefit corporation status for any corporation, and does not calculate the specific vote threshold or fair market value applicable to any specific corporation's shares.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 14604(a)
citations.cite: California benefit corporation statute, terminating benefit corporation status by articles amendment and resulting dissenters' rights
citations.quote: A benefit corporation may terminate its status as a benefit corporation and cease to be subject to this part by amending the corporation’s articles to delete the provision required by Section 14602. The amendment shall not be effective unless the amendment is adopted by at least the minimum status vote.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 14601(d)(1)(A)-(B)
citations.cite: California benefit corporation statute, definition of "minimum status vote" for a corporation
citations.quote: The shareholders of every class or series shall be entitled to vote on the corporate action regardless of any limitation stated in the articles or bylaws on the voting rights of any class or series. (B) The corporate action shall be approved by the outstanding shares of each class or series by at least two-thirds of the votes, or greater vote if required in the articles of incorporation, that all shareholders of the class or series are entitled to cast on that action.
