clauses.title: The ACPA's Core Cause of Action: Bad-Faith Intent to Profit From a Domain Name
clauses.body: A federal statute, commonly called the Anticybersquatting Consumer Protection Act (ACPA), creates civil liability for a person who has a bad faith intent to profit from a mark and who registers, traffics in, or uses a domain name that meets one of two distinct tests, depending on the mark. Where the mark is distinctive (but not necessarily famous) at the time the domain name is registered, the domain name must be identical or confusingly similar to that mark. Where the mark is famous at that time, the standard is broader: the domain name must be identical or confusingly similar to the mark, or dilutive of it — dilution alone is sufficient for a famous mark, but the statute does not extend the dilution-alone route to a mark that is merely distinctive without also being famous. Both bad-faith intent and one of these domain-name tests must be shown; neither alone is sufficient under this provision. The statute also limits who can be held liable for "using" a domain name under this cause of action: only the domain name registrant or that registrant's authorized licensee, not, for example, a web host or other third party merely providing services to the registrant.
clauses.gap: This is federal law (the Lanham Act, applicable nationwide), used as real evidence of the ACPA's core statutory elements — not a claim that any specific domain name registration or use described on this sheet involves bad-faith intent, or that any specific mark is distinctive or famous, all of which this clause does not resolve. This clause quotes three passages from the same statutory paragraph, 15 U.S.C. § 1125(d)(1)(A) (the bad-faith-intent language and the two domain-name tests), plus one passage from the same paragraph's subparagraph (D) (the who-can-be-liable limitation); all four quotes are from a single statutory paragraph, 15 U.S.C. § 1125(d)(1), and are not independent corroborating sources of each other. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific registration or use of a domain name violates any right, and completing this information sheet does not itself send any demand letter or file any lawsuit or administrative complaint.

clauses.title: The ACPA's Statutory Bad-Faith Factors and Its Fair-Use Safe Harbor
clauses.body: The ACPA does not leave "bad faith intent to profit" undefined for a court to construe from nothing: the statute lists nine specific factors a court may consider, expressly stating that this list is illustrative and not exhaustive ("factors such as, but not limited to"). Among the statutory factors are the domain name registrant's own trademark or other intellectual property rights, if any, in the domain name; the registrant's prior use, if any, of the domain name in connection with a bona fide offering of goods or services; the registrant's bona fide noncommercial or fair use of the mark in a site accessible under the domain name; the registrant's intent to divert consumers from the mark owner's online location to a site that could harm the goodwill represented by the mark, for commercial gain or with intent to tarnish or disparage the mark, by creating a likelihood of confusion as to source, sponsorship, affiliation, or endorsement; and the registrant's offer to transfer, sell, or otherwise assign the domain name to the mark owner or a third party for financial gain, without having used, or having an intent to use, the domain name in a bona fide offering of goods or services. The statute also states an express limit on all of this: bad faith intent shall not be found in any case in which the court determines that the registrant believed, and had reasonable grounds to believe, that use of the domain name was a fair use or otherwise lawful.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of specific statutory factors that exist and of the statute's own express fair-use safe harbor — not a claim that any specific registration or use described on this sheet satisfies, or fails to satisfy, any of these factors or the safe harbor, all of which this clause does not resolve. This clause and the companion "core cause of action" clause in this document both quote passages from the same overall statutory paragraph, 15 U.S.C. § 1125(d)(1), specifically subparagraph (B) here; they are not independent sources. The statute lists nine factors in total (labeled (I) through (IX)); this clause quotes five of them as illustrative examples rather than reproducing the full list, and the statute's own "but not limited to" language means even the full nine-factor list is not exhaustive of what a court may weigh. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific registration or use of a domain name reflects bad faith, or a fair use, and completing this information sheet does not itself send any demand letter or file any lawsuit or administrative complaint.

clauses.title: ACPA Remedies: Court-Ordered Transfer or Cancellation, and Statutory Damages Per Domain Name
clauses.body: Where a violation of the ACPA's cause of action is established in a civil action, the statute authorizes a court to order the forfeiture or cancellation of the domain name, or the transfer of the domain name to the owner of the mark — a remedy aimed at the domain name itself rather than solely at the registrant. Separately, the statute gives a mark owner the option to recover statutory damages instead of actual damages and profits, specifically for a violation of the ACPA's cyberpiracy provision: an award of not less than $1,000 and not more than $100,000 per domain name, in an amount the court considers just, elected by the plaintiff at any time before final judgment. This statutory-damages figure and election right apply specifically to ACPA violations; they are a distinct remedy from the general profits/damages/costs framework that applies to other Lanham Act violations such as ordinary infringement or dilution.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the remedies the ACPA itself authorizes — not a claim that a court would order any particular remedy, or award any particular dollar amount within the statutory range, for any specific domain name registration or use described on this sheet, all of which this clause does not resolve and which depends on facts and judicial discretion this clause does not evaluate. This clause cites two different statutory sections that together form the ACPA's coordinated remedial scheme rather than two independent corroborating sources: 15 U.S.C. § 1125(d)(1)(C) (the forfeiture/cancellation/transfer remedy, located within the cyberpiracy provision itself) and 15 U.S.C. § 1117(d) (the statutory-damages election, which by its own text applies specifically "[i]n a case involving a violation of section 1125(d)(1)"). This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific registration or use of a domain name violates the ACPA or any other right, and completing this information sheet does not itself send any demand letter or file any lawsuit.

citations.quote: In any civil action involving the registration, trafficking, or use of a domain name under this paragraph, a court may order the forfeiture or cancellation of the domain name or the transfer of the domain name to the owner of the mark.

clauses.title: The ACPA's In Rem Option When the Domain Name Registrant Cannot Be Sued Directly
clauses.body: The ACPA includes a second, distinct procedural route beyond an ordinary civil action against a person: a mark owner may file an in rem civil action against the domain name itself, in the judicial district where the domain name registrar, registry, or other domain name authority that registered or assigned the domain name is located, if the domain name violates a right of the owner of a mark registered with the Patent and Trademark Office, or a right protected under the statute's false-designation-of-origin or dilution provisions, and the court finds that the mark owner either cannot obtain personal jurisdiction over a person who would have been a defendant in an ordinary civil action, or, through due diligence, was unable to find such a person after sending notice to the registrant's postal and e-mail address on file and publishing notice of the action as the court directs. This route exists precisely for situations — common in domain disputes — where the registrant is anonymous, has supplied false contact information, or is outside the court's personal jurisdiction. The remedies available in an in rem action are narrower than in an ordinary civil action: the statute limits them to a court order for the forfeiture or cancellation of the domain name, or its transfer to the mark owner; no monetary damages are available in an in rem action, consistent with the fact that no person is a defendant in it.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence that this in rem procedural option and its jurisdictional prerequisites exist, and of the narrower remedies the statute allows in that posture — not a claim that in rem jurisdiction would be available for any specific domain name or registrant described on this sheet, which depends on facts (such as whether personal jurisdiction exists or due diligence was exercised) this clause does not evaluate. This clause quotes two passages from the same statutory paragraph, 15 U.S.C. § 1125(d)(2) (subparagraphs (A) and (D)(i)); they are not independent sources. This clause reports, without resolving, an open interpretive point: the in rem provision's own text cross-references a violation of rights protected under a registered mark or under subsection (a) (false designation of origin) or subsection (c) (dilution), rather than in terms repeating the "bad faith intent to profit" language used in the in personam cause of action at 15 U.S.C. § 1125(d)(1)(A); whether and how courts have required a showing equivalent to that bad-faith element in an in rem case is a case-law question this clause does not resolve, because a CourtListener case-law search on this point returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit error (daily quota exhausted) this session before any case could be retrieved. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that in rem jurisdiction would be available for any specific domain name, and completing this information sheet does not itself file any lawsuit.

clauses.title: Federal Court Review After a Domain Name Is Suspended, Disabled, or Transferred Under a Registrar's Anti-Cybersquatting Policy
clauses.body: Separately from the ACPA's own cause of action, federal trademark law addresses what happens when a domain name registrar, registry, or other domain name authority itself takes action against a domain name — refusing to register it, removing it, transferring it, temporarily disabling it, or permanently canceling it — under the registrar's own reasonable policy prohibiting registration of a domain name that is identical to, confusingly similar to, or dilutive of another's mark. Where a domain name registrant's domain name has been suspended, disabled, or transferred under such a policy, the statute gives that registrant a route back into federal court: upon notice to the mark owner, the registrant may file a civil action to establish that the registrant's registration or use of the domain name is not unlawful, and the court may grant injunctive relief, including reactivation of the domain name or its transfer back to the registrant. This means a private, registrar-level or administrative dispute outcome adverse to a domain name registrant is not necessarily the end of the matter: this statute gives the registrant an avenue to seek reversal in federal court.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence that this specific statutory route back into federal court exists for a registrant whose domain name was suspended, disabled, or transferred under a registrar's or registry's own anti-cybersquatting policy — not a claim that this route would succeed for any specific domain name or registrant described on this sheet. This clause quotes two passages from the same statutory paragraph, 15 U.S.C. § 1114(2)(D) (subparagraphs (ii)(II) and (v)); they are not independent sources. Important limitation of this clause, disclosed here rather than glossed over: this document's research task asked whether this provision specifically overrides or interacts with ICANN's Uniform Domain-Name Dispute-Resolution Policy (UDRP), and, if verifiable, to include UDRP's own three-element test as a separate clause. Neither could be verified this session. Direct fetch attempts to icann.org and to wipo.int both failed with a network-egress-policy block (the proxy returned "CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403" for both hosts, confirmed by direct testing, not merely assumed), and a Wayback Machine mirror attempt (web.archive.org) was blocked the same way. A CourtListener case-law search for a federal opinion quoting the UDRP or discussing its relationship to this statute was attempted and returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit error ("Rate limit exceeded: 125/day") before any case could be retrieved. Consequently: the quotations above are strictly to the statutory text itself, which describes a "reasonable policy... prohibiting the registration of a domain name that is identical to, confusingly similar to, or dilutive of another's mark" without naming the UDRP or any other specific policy; this clause does not assert that the UDRP is the policy the statute describes (although that identification is common outside this document, it was not verified from a primary or judicially-quoted source this session); and this document accordingly omits any separate clause purporting to state UDRP's own three-element test, rather than including one with an unverified or placeholder citation. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific domain name registrant is entitled to reactivation or transfer of any domain name, and completing this information sheet does not itself file any lawsuit.

The court may grant injunctive relief to the domain name registrant, including the reactivation of the domain name or transfer of the domain name to the domain name registrant.

clauses.title: Declaration and Scope of This Equity Vesting at Termination Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Deferred Compensation and Equity Vesting at Termination — Information Sheet is prepared with respect to {{employeeName}}'s employment with {{companyName}}, which ended on {{terminationDate}}. It addresses a different legal question from the one covered by this project's Vacation/PTO Payout at Termination document: not whether already-accrued vacation or paid time off must be paid out at termination, but how stock options, restricted stock units (RSUs), and other equity compensation granted by {{companyName}} are treated when employment ends — including whether unvested equity is itself a form of "wages" under California law, what governs whether unvested equity is forfeited when employment ends, and the separate federal tax mechanics that bear on how long a former employee has to exercise a vested-but-unexercised incentive stock option. The equity compensation addressed in this document is described as: {{equityType}}, granted under: {{equityPlanName}}.

clauses.title: Whether Unvested Equity Compensation Is "Wages": An Unresolved Statutory Text
clauses.body: California's core wage statute defines "wages" broadly, as "all amounts for labor performed by employees of every description," measured by the standard of time, task, piece, "commission basis," or "other method of calculation." This definition expressly names commission-based pay as one of its examples, and California's Division of Labor Standards Enforcement has separately published guidance treating a promised bonus tied to a specific result as falling within it as well. Stock options, restricted stock units, and other forms of equity compensation are not named anywhere in this statutory text, and no comparable published agency interpretation naming them was located this session. Whether, and under what circumstances, unvested equity compensation is or is not a "wage" within this definition is therefore a question this statute's own text does not resolve on its face.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence only of what Labor Code section 200(a)'s definition of "wages" does and does not name on its face — not a claim that unvested equity compensation is, or is not, a "wage" under California law, which this clause does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 200(a)); the same subsection is already independently verified elsewhere in this project's own corpus, applied to commissions and to bonus pay respectively (this project's Commission Payout Upon Termination and Bonus and Incentive Compensation at Termination documents), and this clause does not treat those prior verifications as an independent second source — it instead fetched the same statutory text fresh, directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, twice this session with two different User-Agent headers, and found it byte-identical both times. This clause separately confirmed, by fetching the California Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's own published glossary pages for the letters E, S, and V directly from dir.ca.gov (each fetched and byte-compared across two User-Agent headers), that the glossary contains no entry for "equity," "stock option," "RSU," "restricted stock," or "vesting," as it does for "bonus." A California Supreme Court decision is widely reported, in secondary legal sources, to have addressed a closely related question — whether unvested, contingent equity-type compensation that is forfeited under a deferred-compensation plan's own terms when an employee voluntarily resigns is "wages already earned" that other Labor Code wage-protection statutes would prohibit an employer from taking back — commonly cited as Schachter v. Citigroup, Inc., 47 Cal. 4th 610 (2009). That decision was not independently fetched or read this session: CourtListener case-law search returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, 125/day daily limit, confirmed exhausted this session with several hours remaining before reset) before it could be retrieved. No quotation from, or citation entry for, that decision is included in this clause's citations array as a result; it is described here only as a widely-reported case name and general subject matter, not as a verified holding, consistent with this tool's practice of not fabricating case-law quotations. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific stock option, RSU, or other equity award described in this document is or is not a "wage" under California law.

citations.quote: “Wages” includes all amounts for labor performed by employees of every description, whether the amount is fixed or ascertained by the standard of time, task, piece, commission basis, or other method of calculation.

clauses.title: Distinguishing Equity Compensation From Vacation Wages Under Section 227.3 and Suastez
clauses.body: California's vacation-vesting rule, addressed in full in this project's Vacation/PTO Payout at Termination document, is built on a specific statute and a specific line of case law, neither of which mentions stock options, restricted stock units, or other equity compensation. Labor Code section 227.3's no-forfeiture protection applies, by its own text, only "whenever a contract of employment or employer policy provides for paid vacations" — its operative language is limited to vacation, not to compensation generally. The California Supreme Court's reasoning in Suastez v. Plastic Dress-Up Co. for why vacation pay vests as it is earned rests on vacation's specific character as "deferred wages for services rendered" that vests "as the labor is rendered" — a day-by-day accrual tied to time already worked, rather than to a future date, cliff, or milestone that has not yet occurred. Because neither the statute's text nor this reasoning refers to equity compensation, this vacation-specific, no-forfeiture rule does not, by its own terms, extend to stock options, RSUs, or other equity awards, and no comparable California statute barring forfeiture of unvested equity compensation upon termination was located this session. Absent such a statute, whether and on what terms unvested equity is forfeited when employment with {{companyName}} ends is instead governed by the terms of the specific equity plan, option agreement, or grant agreement under which the equity described in this document was awarded.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute and case law, used as real evidence that section 227.3's anti-forfeiture protection and the Suastez vesting rationale are textually and doctrinally specific to vacation pay — not a claim that equity compensation could never be treated as earned or vested wages under some other legal theory, which this clause does not resolve. The statutory text of section 227.3 quoted below was fetched twice this session, directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, using two different User-Agent headers, found byte-identical both times, and matches the same section already independently verified elsewhere in this project's own corpus (Vacation/PTO Payout at Termination document, checked 2026-09-02). This session's CourtListener access was confirmed exhausted (HTTP 429, 125/day daily limit) before the Suastez opinion could be independently re-fetched and re-read this session; the quotation below is therefore reused verbatim from that already-verified corpus entry rather than re-fetched, disclosed here rather than presented as an independent re-verification. This clause's statement that no comparable California statute overriding an equity plan's own forfeiture-on-termination terms was located rests on the plain text of section 227.3 (which names only vacation) together with a review of the California Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's published glossary (letters E, S, and V, each fetched and byte-compared across two User-Agent headers this session), which contains no entry for equity compensation, stock options, RSUs, restricted stock, or vesting; that same review also did not surface any California statute requiring an employer to disclose equity status or exercise deadlines specifically at termination, a gap disclosed here rather than an invented requirement. Neither review is an exhaustive canvass of the entire Labor Code, and CourtListener's unavailability this session means no case law search for a judicially created exception was possible; this clause reports what was and was not found this session rather than asserting the absence is definitive. This is one state's law; it does not address whether any other state has enacted a broader statute reaching equity compensation specifically.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 227.3 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Unless otherwise provided by a collective-bargaining agreement, whenever a contract of employment or employer policy provides for paid vacations, and an employee is terminated without having taken off his vested vacation time, all vested vacation shall be paid to him as wages at his final rate in accordance with such contract of employment or employer policy respecting eligibility or time served; provided, however, that an employment contract or employer policy shall not provide for forfeiture of vested vacation time upon termination.

citations.case: Suastez v. Plastic Dress-Up Co.
citations.quote: The right to a paid vacation, when offered in an employer's policy or contract of employment, constitutes deferred wages for services rendered. Case law from this state and others, as well as principles of equity and justice, compel the conclusion that a proportionate right to a paid vacation "vests" as the labor is rendered.

clauses.title: Federal Tax Law's Post-Termination Exercise Window for Incentive Stock Options
clauses.body: Federal tax law's favorable treatment for an incentive stock option ("ISO") — deferring taxation until the underlying stock is later sold, rather than at exercise — is conditioned on the option holder having remained an employee of the granting corporation, or a qualifying parent, subsidiary, or successor corporation, continuously up until a point no earlier than three months before the option is exercised. Once employment ends, an ISO exercised more than three months later no longer meets this condition, and the exercise is treated under federal tax law as an exercise of a nonstatutory stock option rather than an ISO for tax purposes. This three-month figure is a federal tax-qualification condition on favorable ISO tax treatment, not itself a statutory deadline after which the option is forfeited; whether the option agreement or equity plan sets its own, separate post-termination exercise deadline — after which the option lapses entirely, regardless of its tax treatment — is a matter of that agreement's own terms, described in this document as: {{postTerminationExerciseWindow}}. A post-termination exercise window commonly used in practice and often described as roughly ninety days is, on this statute's own text, an approximation of the three-month period this federal tax rule specifies for retaining ISO tax treatment, not a period this or any statute itself requires an option to remain exercisable.
clauses.gap: This is federal tax law (26 U.S.C. § 422(a)(2)), not California state law, and it applies the same way regardless of which state's law otherwise governs the employment relationship. This clause cites a single statutory subsection; the surrounding provisions of the same section — defining what counts as an "incentive stock option" in the first place (§ 422(b)), and separately extending the three-month period to one year for a person disabled within the meaning of a cross-referenced statute (§ 422(c)(6)) — are not quoted or independently addressed here, since they define eligibility and a specific disability exception this clause does not resolve. The statutory text was fetched twice this session, directly from law.cornell.edu, using two different User-Agent headers, and found byte-identical both times. This clause does not address nonqualified stock options (which carry no comparable federal statutory holding-period or post-termination timing condition), restricted stock units (which are generally taxed on vesting rather than exercise and so raise no comparable exercise-window question), or the separate, contract-based question of what post-termination exercise deadline any specific option agreement or equity plan actually sets — that deadline is a matter of the specific agreement's own terms, not this statute. This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule.

citations.quote: at all times during the period beginning on the date of the granting of the option and ending on the day 3 months before the date of such exercise, such individual was an employee of either the corporation granting such option, a parent or subsidiary corporation of such corporation, or a corporation or a parent or subsidiary corporation of such corporation issuing or assuming a stock option in a transaction to which section 424(a) applies.

clauses.title: Two Statutory Pathways to Adverse Possession: Under Color of Title, and Under Claim of Right Alone
clauses.body: California's Code of Civil Procedure sets out two distinct statutory pathways by which land may be "deemed to have been held adversely," both located in the same chapter governing the time for commencing actions to recover real property. The first pathway applies where a claimant's possession is founded upon a written instrument (such as a deed purporting to convey the property), a judgment, or a decree — commonly called possession "under color of title." That statute requires that the occupant, or those under whom the occupant claims, entered into possession "under claim of title, exclusive of other right," founding that claim on the written instrument, judgment, or decree, and that there has been continued occupation and possession of the property described in it, under that claim, for five years; the property so included is then "deemed to have been held adversely." The second pathway applies where the claimant's possession is not founded on any written instrument, judgment, or decree — possession under a bare "claim of right." That statute uses closely parallel language: where there has been actual continued occupation of land "under a claim of title, exclusive of any other right," the land actually occupied (and no other) is "deemed to have been held adversely." The recurring statutory phrase "claim of title, exclusive of other right" is the textual source of what is commonly called the claim-of-right or hostility element of adverse possession, and the statutes' own "held adversely" language is the source of the term "adverse possession" itself, even though neither statute uses the word "hostile."
clauses.gap: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 322 and § 324 are genuinely separate statutory sections, treated here as two independent sources. This clause states only the statutory text of these two provisions; it does not address, and this research session could not independently verify through case law, the further question of whether, or how, possession that began with the true owner's permission can satisfy the "claim of title, exclusive of other right" language these two sections use — a question commonly discussed in adverse-possession case law and secondary commentary as the "permissive use" rule, but neither of which this clause found stated in the statutory text itself. A CourtListener case-law search attempted in this research session for California authority on that point returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit error (this account's 125-requests-per-day cap already exhausted, with the tool reporting the next availability roughly 8.3 hours out), so no case is cited or relied on in this clause for any rule about permissive use, and this document does not state one. This clause also does not address California's separate statutes on tacking successive possessors' periods together, or on the manner of possession (enclosure, cultivation, and similar tests) required to satisfy either pathway, which are addressed, to the extent this document addresses them, in a separate clause. This clause does not evaluate whether any specific claimant's possession in fact satisfies either statutory pathway on the facts of a specific dispute. This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of California's adverse possession law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of real property; other states' adverse possession doctrines, including on hostility and permissive use, may differ from California's statutory text described here.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 322
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, adverse possession under color of title (written instrument, judgment, or decree)
citations.quote: When it appears that the occupant, or those under whom he claims, entered into the possession of the property under claim of title, exclusive of other right, founding such claim upon a written instrument, as being a conveyance of the property in question, or upon the decree or judgment of a competent Court, and that there has been a continued occupation and possession of the property included in such instrument, decree, or judgment, or of some part of the property, under such claim, for five years, the property so included is deemed to have been held adversely

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 324
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, adverse possession under a bare claim of right, without a written instrument
citations.quote: Where it appears that there has been an actual continued occupation of land, under a claim of title, exclusive of any other right, but not founded upon a written instrument, judgment, or decree, the land so actually occupied, and no other, is deemed to have been held adversely.

clauses.title: The Manner of Possession Required: Enclosure, Cultivation, and Related Statutory Tests
clauses.body: California's Code of Civil Procedure states, separately for each of the two statutory pathways to adverse possession, what specifically counts as land having been "possessed and occupied." For a claim founded upon a written instrument, judgment, or decree (possession under color of title), land is deemed possessed and occupied where it has been usually cultivated or improved; where it has been protected by a substantial enclosure; where, although not enclosed, it has been used for the supply of fuel or fencing timber for husbandry, for pasturage, or for the occupant's ordinary use; or, for a known farm or single lot partly improved, where the unimproved or unenclosed portion is deemed occupied for the same length of time as the improved portion, following the usual course and custom of the surrounding area. For a claim not founded on any written instrument (a bare claim of right), the statute is narrower: land is deemed possessed and occupied only where it has been protected by a substantial enclosure, or where it has been usually cultivated or improved. Both statutes describe concrete, physical manifestations of possession — enclosure, cultivation, or specified uses of unenclosed land — rather than using the phrase "open and notorious," which does not appear in either provision's text.
clauses.gap: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 323 and § 325, subdivision (a), are genuinely separate statutory sections, treated here as two independent sources. Adverse possession is commonly described, including in case law and secondary commentary, as requiring "open and notorious" possession; this clause treats that phrase as conventional shorthand for how courts have construed these two statutes' own enclosure, cultivation, and specified-use language, but that construction is itself case law, and this research session's CourtListener attempts were rate-limited (see the companion clause on the two statutory pathways for the specific rate-limit details) before any case law construing § 323 or § 325(a) could be independently verified. This clause does not evaluate whether any specific fence, cultivation, or other use in fact satisfies either statute's manner-of-possession test on the facts of a specific parcel. This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of California's manner-of-possession requirements for adverse possession — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of real property; other states' tests for what possession must consist of, if any, may differ from California's.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 323
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, manner of possession required under color of title
citations.quote: For the purpose of constituting an adverse possession by any person claiming a title founded upon a written instrument, or a judgment or decree, land is deemed to have been possessed and occupied in the following cases: 1. Where it has been usually cultivated or improved; 2. Where it has been protected by a substantial inclosure; 3. Where, although not inclosed, it has been used for the supply of fuel, or of fencing timber for the purposes of husbandry, or for pasturage, or for the ordinary use of the occupant; 4. Where a known farm or single lot has been partly improved, the portion of such farm or lot that may have been left not cleared, or not inclosed according to the usual course and custom of the adjoining country, shall be deemed to have been occupied for the same length of time as the part improved and cultivated.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 325(a)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, manner of possession required under a bare claim of right
citations.quote: (a) For the purpose of constituting an adverse possession by a person claiming title, not founded upon a written instrument, judgment, or decree, land is deemed to have been possessed and occupied in the following cases only: (1) Where it has been protected by a substantial enclosure. (2) Where it has been usually cultivated or improved.

clauses.title: The Property-Tax-Payment Requirement, and Its Certified-Record Proof Mechanism
clauses.body: California's adverse possession statute states that in no case is adverse possession considered established, under any section of the Code of Civil Procedure, unless the land has been occupied and claimed continuously for five years, and the claimant, or the claimant's predecessors and grantors, timely paid all state, county, or municipal taxes levied and assessed on the land during that same five-year period. The same statute states how that tax payment is to be proved: payment of those taxes by the claimant, or the claimant's predecessors and grantors, must be established by certified records of the county tax collector. This tax-payment requirement is stated in a provision captioned as applying to a claim not founded on a written instrument, but its own text states that no adverse possession is established "under the provision of any section of this code" absent the five-year continuous occupation and tax payment described — language broad enough to extend the tax-payment requirement to a claim proceeding under the separate color-of-title pathway as well, not only to the bare-claim-of-right pathway in which this provision itself appears.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes and relies on a single statutory subdivision, Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 325(b), as one source. The final sentence of this clause's body — that § 325(b)'s "under the provision of any section of this code" language extends its tax-payment requirement to the separate color-of-title pathway addressed in § 322 and § 323 — is this clause's own reading of § 325(b)'s text in relation to those other sections, not an independently verified judicial holding construing the interaction between these provisions; this research session's CourtListener attempts were rate-limited before any case law confirming or rejecting that reading could be checked (see the companion clause on the two statutory pathways for the specific rate-limit details). This clause does not evaluate whether any specific tax payment history, or any specific set of county tax collector records, in fact satisfies this element on the facts of a particular parcel. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's tax-payment requirement for adverse possession — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of real property; other states' adverse possession doctrines may or may not include a comparable tax-payment element.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 325(b)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, five-year continuous occupation, tax-payment requirement, and its certified-record proof mechanism
citations.quote: (b) In no case shall adverse possession be considered established under the provision of any section of this code, unless it shall be shown that the land has been occupied and claimed for the period of five years continuously, and the party or persons, their predecessors and grantors, have timely paid all state, county, or municipal taxes that have been levied and assessed upon the land for the period of five years during which the land has been occupied and claimed. Payment of those taxes by the party or persons, their predecessors and grantors shall be established by certified records of the county tax collector.

clauses.title: The Five-Year Statutory Period for Adverse Possession
clauses.body: California's Code of Civil Procedure states the five-year period governing adverse possession from two directions within the same statutory chapter. One statute bars the true owner's own remedy: no action for the recovery of real property, or its possession, can be maintained unless the plaintiff, or the plaintiff's ancestor, predecessor, or grantor, was seized or possessed of the property within five years before the action is commenced. A second, related statute states a presumption and its rebuttal: in an action to recover real property, a person establishing legal title is presumed to have been possessed of the property within the time required by law, and another person's occupation is deemed subordinate to that legal title — unless the property has been held and possessed adversely to the legal title for five years before the action is commenced. Read together with the separate statutes on the manner of possession and, where applicable, tax payment (addressed in other clauses of this document), these two provisions confirm that five years, not some other figure, is the statutory period applicable to adverse possession in California.
clauses.gap: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 318 and § 321 are genuinely separate statutory sections within the same chapter, treated here as two independent sources. Neither section is captioned or organized as an "adverse possession" statute standing alone; § 318 bars the true owner's action without using the word "adverse," while § 321 uses the phrase "held and possessed adversely." This clause states the five-year period these two provisions establish; it does not restate the separate statutory elements (manner of possession, claim of title, tax payment) that must also be satisfied before adverse possession is established, which are addressed, to the extent this document addresses them, in other clauses. This clause does not evaluate whether any specific claimant's possession in fact spanned five continuous years on the facts of a particular parcel. This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of California's five-year adverse possession period — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of real property; other states' adverse possession statutes commonly use different periods, some considerably longer than California's.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 318
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, five-year bar on the true owner's action to recover real property
citations.quote: No action for the recovery of real property, or for the recovery of the possession thereof, can be maintained, unless it appear that the plaintiff, his ancestor, predecessor, or grantor, was seized or possessed of the property in question, within five years before the commencement of the action.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 321
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, presumption of the title holder's possession, rebutted by five years of adverse possession
citations.quote: In every action for the recovery of real property, or the possession thereof, the person establishing a legal title to the property is presumed to have been possessed thereof within the time required by law, and the occupation of the property by any other person is deemed to have been under and in subordination to the legal title, unless it appear that the property has been held and possessed adversely to such legal title, for five years before the commencement of the action.

clauses.title: Adverse Possession Is Unavailable Against Publicly Owned or Publicly Dedicated Land
clauses.body: California's Civil Code states the general rule that occupancy, for the period the Code of Civil Procedure prescribes as sufficient to bar an action for recovery of the property, confers a title by prescription that is sufficient against all persons — the general prescriptive-title consequence of the Code of Civil Procedure's adverse possession statutes described in other clauses of this document. The same statute then states an express, unqualified exception: no possession by any person, firm, or corporation, no matter how long continued, of any land, water, water right, easement, or other property dedicated to a public use by a public utility, or dedicated to or owned by the state or any public entity, shall ever ripen into any title, interest, or right against that owner. This exception is not limited by any time period of its own — the statute states that such possession "shall ever" fail to ripen into title, regardless of duration.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes and relies on a single statutory section, Cal. Civ. Code § 1007, as one source. This clause does not independently research, and does not address, how a court determines whether particular property is in fact "dedicated to a public use" or "owned by" a public entity within the meaning of this statute, and does not evaluate whether any specific parcel is publicly owned or dedicated on the facts of a particular case. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California law bars adverse possession against publicly owned or publicly dedicated property — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of real property; other states' rules on the availability of adverse possession against government-owned land, and the statutory basis for any such rule, may differ from California's.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1007
citations.cite: California Civil Code, prescriptive title generally, and its exception for land dedicated to public use or owned by the state or a public entity
citations.quote: Occupancy for the period prescribed by the Code of Civil Procedure as sufficient to bar any action for the recovery of the property confers a title thereto, denominated a title by prescription, which is sufficient against all, but no possession by any person, firm or corporation no matter how long continued of any land, water, water right, easement, or other property whatsoever dedicated to a public use by a public utility, or dedicated to or owned by the state or any public entity, shall ever ripen into any title, interest or right against the owner thereof.

clauses.body: I, {{transferorName}}, transfer the property described below to {{custodianName}}, as custodian for {{minorName}} under the California Uniform Transfers to Minors Act. The property transferred is described as follows: {{propertyDescription}}. This transfer is made pursuant to Probate Code Part 9 (commencing with Section 3900). Signing this declaration alone does not create custodial property; the applicable statutory method of transfer under § 3909 must actually be completed.

clauses.title: How a Custodial Transfer Is Created
clauses.body: California Probate Code § 3909(a) specifies that "[c]ustodial property is created and a transfer is made whenever any of the following occurs," and then lists distinct statutory methods keyed to the type of property involved. Securities are registered or delivered to the custodian; under § 3909(a)(2), "[m]oney is paid or delivered, or a security held in the name of a broker, financial institution, or its nominee is transferred, to a broker or financial institution for credit to an account in the name of the transferor, an adult other than the transferor, or a trust company, followed in substance by the words" of the statutory custodial designation. Life insurance and annuity interests, contract rights, and — under § 3909(a)(5) — real property ("[a]n interest in real property is recorded in the name of the transferor, an adult other than the transferor, or a trust company, followed in substance by the words" of that designation) each have their own listed method, and vehicle certificates of title have theirs. A residual category, § 3909(a)(7), covers "[a]n interest in any property not described in paragraphs (1) through (6)" and requires transfer "by a written instrument in substantially the form set forth in subdivision (b)." Across every one of these methods, the statutory designation itself takes the same recurring form: the recipient's name "followed in substance by the words" "as custodian for _____ (Name of Minor) _____ under the California Uniform Transfers to Minors Act."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Prob. Code § 3909), used as real evidence of California's specific statutory methods for creating custodial property under its version of the Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transfer, and other states' Uniform Transfers/Gifts to Minors Act statutes use similar but not identical mechanics. The clause draws on four subdivisions of a single code section — 3909(a) introductory language, (a)(2), (a)(5), and (a)(7) — as one source; no independent second source was located or is needed, since the statute itself is the primary and controlling authority for its own creation mechanics. This clause does not address which specific method applies to a given item of property, and does not itself create custodial property for anyone.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 3909 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Custodial property is created and a transfer is made whenever any of the following occurs:

clauses.title: Custodian's Powers and Standard of Care
clauses.body: California Probate Code § 3912(a) requires a custodian to "do all of the following: (1) Take control of custodial property. (2) Register or record title to custodial property if appropriate. (3) Collect, hold, manage, invest, and reinvest custodial property." In carrying out that management role, § 3912(b) sets the governing standard: "[i]n dealing with custodial property, a custodian shall observe the standard of care that would be observed by a prudent person dealing with property of another and is not limited by any other statute restricting investments by fiduciaries," subject to specified exceptions for an uncompensated custodian's liability for losses and for a custodian's discretion to retain property received from the transferor. Separately, Probate Code § 3913(a) grants broad authority over the property itself: "a custodian, acting in a custodial capacity, has all the rights, powers, and authority over custodial property that unmarried adult owners have over their own property, but a custodian may exercise those rights, powers, and authority in that capacity only."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the management duties and "prudent person" standard California's Act actually imposes — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular custodianship, and not investment or fiduciary advice about how any specific custodian should manage any specific property. § 3912 and § 3913 are two different code sections addressing related but distinct points (day-to-day management duties and standard of care, versus the scope of the custodian's authority over the property), so they are treated here as two sources within the same statutory part rather than one; no source independent of the California Probate Code itself was located or is needed, since the statute is the primary authority for its own standard of care. This clause does not evaluate whether any particular custodian's conduct has met or fallen short of the prudent-person standard.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 3912 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: In dealing with custodial property, a custodian shall observe the standard of care that would be observed by a prudent person dealing with property of another and is not limited by any other statute restricting investments by fiduciaries

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 3913(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 3913(a)
citations.quote: A custodian, acting in a custodial capacity, has all the rights, powers, and authority over custodial property that unmarried adult owners have over their own property, but a custodian may exercise those rights, powers, and authority in that capacity only.

clauses.title: Permitted Uses of Custodial Property for the Minor
clauses.body: California Probate Code § 3914(a) states that "[a] custodian may deliver or pay to the minor or expend for the minor's benefit as much of the custodial property as the custodian considers advisable for the use and benefit of the minor, without court order and without regard to (1) the duty or ability of the custodian personally, or of any other person, to support the minor or (2) any other income or property of the minor which may be applicable or available for that purpose." Section 3914(c) clarifies that such a delivery, payment, or expenditure "is in addition to, not in substitution for, and does not affect, any obligation of a person to support the minor." Section 3914(d) also allows a transferor who is also the custodian to instead irrevocably elect a more restrictive standard, under which the custodian may not expend custodial property for the minor's use before the statutory transfer age except by court order on a showing that the expenditure is necessary for the minor's support, maintenance, or education.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's default standard for a custodian's discretionary spending on a minor's behalf, and of the separate, more restrictive standard a transferor-custodian may elect instead — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular custodianship, and not a statement about what any particular custodian should or must do with any particular minor's property. The clause draws on three subdivisions of a single code section, § 3914(a), (c), and (d), as one source; no independent second source was located or is needed. This clause does not determine whether any specific expenditure is or is not advisable for a specific minor's use and benefit.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 3914(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 3914(a)
citations.quote: A custodian may deliver or pay to the minor or expend for the minor’s benefit as much of the custodial property as the custodian considers advisable for the use and benefit of the minor, without court order and without regard to (1) the duty or ability of the custodian personally, or of any other person, to support the minor or (2) any other income or property of the minor which may be applicable or available for that purpose.

clauses.title: Termination of the Custodianship and Transfer Age
clauses.body: Under California Probate Code § 3920, a custodian "shall transfer in an appropriate manner the custodial property to the minor or to the minor's estate" upon the earliest of the minor's death or, absent a delayed transfer age, "[t]he minor's attainment of 18 years of age unless the time of transfer of the custodial property to the minor is delayed under Section 3920.5 to a time after the time the minor attains the age of 18 years." California's default transfer age under the Act is therefore 18, not a later age. Section 3920.5, however, lets a transferor specify a later transfer age in the instrument creating the transfer, within limits that vary by how the transfer was made: for a transfer by irrevocable gift under Section 3904, § 3920.5(e) allows delay only if the custodianship is to continue "until the time the minor attains a specified age, which time may not be later than the time the minor attains 21 years of age," while for a transfer made under a nomination or under a governing will or trust (Sections 3903 or 3905), § 3920.5(c) allows delay only up to "the time the minor attains 25 years of age."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California's Act sets a default transfer age of 18 — not 21 — with a transferor-selected later age (up to 21 or 25, depending on how the transfer was made) available only if specified in the transfer instrument under § 3920.5; this corrects a common assumption, since some other states' versions of the Act default to a later age. This is not a claim about which state's law governs a particular custodianship, nor a statement of what transfer age is or should be selected for any specific minor. § 3920 and § 3920.5 are two different code sections working together (the general termination rule and the age-delay mechanism), so they are treated as two sources within the same statutory part; no source independent of the California Probate Code itself was located or is needed. This clause does not address the delayed ages available for transfers made under Section 3906 (trustee transfers to a custodian) or under an irrevocable exercise of a power of appointment under Section 3904, which the statute also treats somewhat differently.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 3920(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 3920(a)
citations.quote: The minor’s attainment of 18 years of age unless the time of transfer of the custodial property to the minor is delayed under Section 3920.5 to a time after the time the minor attains the age of 18 years.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 3920.5(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The time for transfer to the minor of custodial property transferred by irrevocable gift under Section 3904 may be delayed under this section only if the transfer pursuant to Section 3909 provides in substance that the custodianship is to continue until the time the minor attains a specified age, which time may not be later than the time the minor attains 21 years of age.

clauses.title: Irrevocability and Vested Title in the Minor
clauses.body: California Probate Code § 3911(b) provides that "[a] transfer made pursuant to Section 3909 is irrevocable, and the custodial property is indefeasibly vested in the minor, but the custodian has all the rights, powers, duties, and authority provided in this part, and neither the minor nor the minor's legal representative has any right, power, duty, or authority with respect to the custodial property except as provided in this part." Legal title thus vests in the minor immediately and irrevocably once a transfer is made in the statutory manner, while control and management of the property remain with the custodian under the Act's own rules rather than with the minor.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a properly completed transfer under California's Act is irrevocable and vests indefeasible legal title in the minor, subject to the custodian's statutory management powers — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular transfer, and not a statement about whether any specific transfer was, in fact, completed in the manner Section 3909 requires. Only Section 3911(b) is cited for this specific proposition; no independent second source was located or is needed, since the statute is the primary and controlling authority for the legal effect of its own transfers. This clause does not itself make, complete, or validate any transfer.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 3911(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 3911(b)
citations.quote: A transfer made pursuant to Section 3909 is irrevocable, and the custodial property is indefeasibly vested in the minor, but the custodian has all the rights, powers, duties, and authority provided in this part, and neither the minor nor the minor’s legal representative has any right, power, duty, or authority with respect to the custodial property except as provided in this part.

clauses.title: Custodian's Liability and Successor Custodians
clauses.body: California Probate Code § 3917(b) limits a custodian's personal liability, providing that "[a] custodian is not personally liable for either of the following: (1) On a contract properly entered into in the custodial capacity unless the custodian fails to reveal that capacity and to identify the custodianship in the contract. (2) For an obligation arising from control of custodial property or for a tort committed during the custodianship unless the custodian is personally at fault." Section 3918 separately addresses how a successor custodian can be put in place. Under § 3918(b), "[a] custodian at any time may designate a trust company or an adult other than a transferor under Section 3904 as successor custodian by executing and dating an instrument of designation before a subscribing witness other than the successor." If no successor was effectively designated and the custodian becomes ineligible, dies, or becomes incapacitated, § 3918(d) allows a minor who has attained 14 years of age to designate a successor, and otherwise provides that the minor's conservator becomes successor custodian, or that interested persons may petition the court to designate one. Section 3918(f) also lets specified persons, including the minor if 14 or older, "petition the court to remove the custodian for cause and to designate a successor custodian other than a transferor under Section 3904 or to require the custodian to give appropriate bond."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's specific rules limiting custodian liability absent personal fault and governing successor-custodian designation and court appointment — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular custodianship, and not an assessment of any specific custodian's liability or fitness to continue serving. § 3917 and § 3918 are two different code sections addressing distinct topics (liability, and succession), so they are treated as two sources within the same statutory part; the clause also draws on three subdivisions of § 3918 — (b), (d), and (f) — as parts of that single second source. No source independent of the California Probate Code itself was located or is needed. This clause does not address a custodian's compensation or bond requirements under Section 3915, which the statute treats separately.

citations.quote: A custodian is not personally liable for either of the following: (1) On a contract properly entered into in the custodial capacity unless the custodian fails to reveal that capacity and to identify the custodianship in the contract. (2) For an obligation arising from control of custodial property or for a tort committed during the custodianship unless the custodian is personally at fault.
