clauses.title: Notice of an Overpayment Determination and the Overpayment-Specific Right to Appeal
clauses.body: An overpayment determination is not self-executing; a specific statute requires the director to determine the amount of the overpayment and any fraud-penalty assessment, and to notify the liable person of the basis for that determination. That same statute also times-bar the EDD's own notice in the ordinary case: in the absence of fraud, misrepresentation, or willful nondisclosure, notice of the overpayment determination must be served within the latest of one year after the close of the benefit year in which the overpayment was made, or six months after the date of a backpay award — a deadline that, by its own terms, does not constrain the EDD's timing where fraud, misrepresentation, or willful nondisclosure is involved. Once notice is served, a separate statute gives the person affected — not only the EDD or an employer — the right to appeal to an administrative law judge within 30 days from the date the notice of overpayment was mailed or served, with the director treated as an interested party to that appeal and the administrative law judge empowered to affirm, reverse, modify, or set aside the findings in the notice. This overpayment appeal right is its own, separately numbered statutory provision, not a bare cross-reference to the general benefits-eligibility appeal statute this corpus's existing Unemployment Insurance Appeal — Information Sheet document addresses — though it is structurally parallel to that general appeal right, running the same 30 days and leading to the same further-appeal path to the CUIAB.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutes (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1376, for the notice requirement and its timing, and § 1377(a), for the overpayment-specific appeal right and deadline), used as real evidence that California gives overpayment determinations their own dedicated notice-and-appeal statutes, distinct from (though procedurally similar to) the general benefits-determination appeal statute (§ 1328(a)) this corpus's existing Unemployment Insurance Appeal — Information Sheet document already covers — not a claim about which state's law governs a given determination, and not a statement that any appeal from any specific claimant's overpayment determination has been, or should be, filed. These are two independent statutory sections, not subsections of a single section, and neither has been previously cited anywhere else in this corpus. Section 1377(a) itself provides, in language this clause does not separately quote to avoid an overlong citation, that a further appeal from the administrative law judge's decision may be taken to the appeals board under Section 1336 within 30 days, and that both 30-day periods may be extended for good cause defined the same way as in the general appeal statute; this document does not restate that further-appeal mechanic in full here because this corpus's existing appeal document already verifies the materially identical CUIAB further-appeal and judicial-review process, and that overlap is disclosed rather than treated as unaddressed. This document does not itself serve any notice or file any appeal, and does not calculate the actual notice or appeal deadlines applicable to any specific claimant's determination.

clauses.title: How California May Recover an Overpayment
clauses.body: Once an overpayment is established, a specific statute lists what the director may do to recover it, and recovery is not limited to a single mechanism. One option is a civil action against the liable person, which the director may file within one year of the overpayment becoming final in the ordinary case, or within three years where the overpayment involved fraud, misrepresentation, or nondisclosure. A second, separate option lets the director offset the overpaid amount against any future benefits to which the liable person may become entitled, within six years of the date notice of the overpayment determination was served — meaning a claimant who later files a new, otherwise-valid claim can have that new claim's benefits reduced to satisfy an old overpayment, rather than receiving the full new benefit amount in hand. The same statute also authorizes a summary judgment procedure and the ability to reduce or vacate a summary judgment already obtained. Beyond the director's own tools, a further statute directs the state Controller to collect certain overpayment amounts under a general Government Code interagency-intercept collection provision, with amounts collected deposited back into the fund from which the overpayment was made.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutes (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1379, for the director's own civil-action, summary-judgment, and offset-against-future-benefits tools, and § 1384, for the Controller's separate intercept-based collection role under Government Code § 12419.2), used as real evidence of the actual, sourced recovery mechanisms California's overpayment statute provides — not a claim about which state's law governs a given overpayment, and not a statement that any specific recovery method has been, or will be, used against any specific claimant. The two § 1379 passages quoted here, subdivisions (a) and (d), come from the same statutory section and are being treated as one source, not independent corroborating sources, though each states a substantively distinct recovery tool (civil action and offset, respectively); § 1384 is an independent, separately numbered section citing a different code (Government Code § 12419.2) for the Controller's own collection role, and is genuinely independent of § 1379. This document's drafter was specifically asked to verify, rather than assume, whether wage garnishment and tax-refund interception are among California's statutory recovery mechanisms for this specific type of overpayment. Having checked § 1379 and § 1384 directly, the honest answer is narrower than that framing suggested: § 1379 does not itself name wage garnishment as a distinct recovery tool (though a civil judgment obtained under its summary-judgment procedure could, once entered, be enforced by the general civil-judgment-enforcement remedies available to any money judgment, a point this document does not independently verify here), and this document did not independently fetch or verify the text of Government Code § 12419.2 itself — it relies only on Unemployment Insurance Code § 1384's own description of that cross-referenced provision as an interagency intercept-style collection mechanism administered by the Controller, without separately confirming § 12419.2's own statutory text against its primary source in this session. This document does not itself take any recovery action, and does not determine which, if any, of these methods applies to any specific claimant's overpayment.

clauses.title: Opposition to Registration: Who May Oppose, and the Statutory Deadline
clauses.body: Federal trademark law allows any person who believes that he would be damaged by the registration of a mark on the principal register — including damage from a likelihood of dilution by blurring or tarnishment — to file an opposition in the Patent and Trademark Office, upon payment of the prescribed fee and stating the grounds for the opposition. The statute sets a firm deadline for doing so: an opposition must be filed within thirty days after the mark sought to be registered is published for opposition. That thirty-day period is not absolute, however. Upon written request made before the initial thirty-day period expires, the statute extends the time for filing an additional thirty days, and it allows the Director to grant further extensions for good cause when requested before an already-granted extension expires. An opposition proceeding exists only against a mark that has been published but not yet registered; once the opposition period passes without a successful opposition, the statute directs that the mark proceed either to registration or, for an intent-to-use application, to a notice of allowance.
clauses.gap: This is federal law (the Lanham Act, which applies nationwide), used as real evidence of the statutory opposition deadline and who may invoke it — not a claim that any opposition to the mark described on this sheet has been or should be filed, which this clause does not resolve. This clause quotes a single statutory subsection (15 U.S.C. § 1063(a)); its two citations are both drawn from that one subsection and are not independent sources of each other. The statute's text itself does not enumerate which substantive grounds an opposition may assert — it requires only that the opposition state its grounds; see the companion clause on grounds common to both opposition and cancellation proceedings. This research pass found uspto.gov unreachable from this session (a direct request returned a blocked connection), so this clause is built on the statutory text itself rather than on the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board's own procedural rules (for example, the specific mechanics of requesting or opposing an extension), which this clause does not describe. This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule.

clauses.title: Cancellation of a Registered Mark: Who May Petition, and How the Available Grounds Narrow Over Time
clauses.body: Federal trademark law allows a petition to cancel a registration, stating the grounds relied upon, to be filed upon payment of the prescribed fee by any person who believes that he is or will be damaged by the registration of a mark on the principal register — including damage from a likelihood of dilution. The statute then sets the timing for that petition in two structurally different ways. First, a petition may be filed within five years from the date of registration, without that time-limited provision itself restricting, in its own text, which grounds may be raised during that window. Second, and separately, the statute lists specific grounds that may instead be asserted at any time — meaning without regard to whether the five-year period above has already run — including that the registered mark has become the generic name for the goods or services (or a portion of them) for which it is registered, that it has become functional, that it has been abandoned, or that its registration was obtained fraudulently or contrary to certain other statutory provisions. Because those specific grounds are the ones the statute frees from the five-year time limit, a registration that has stood for more than five years can still be challenged, but the challenge must fit within one of those enumerated "at any time" grounds rather than being filed as an otherwise-unrestricted five-year-window petition.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the cancellation standing requirement and the statute's two-track timing structure — not a claim that any registration described on this sheet is or is not subject to cancellation on any particular ground or within any particular window, which this clause does not resolve. This clause's three citations are all drawn from the same statutory section (15 U.S.C. § 1064, its introductory clause and paragraphs (1) and (3)); they are not independent of each other. The statute also lists additional "at any time" grounds this clause does not quote in full — including issues specific to a mark registered under superseded 1881 or 1905 Acts, grounds specific to certification marks, and a mark that has never been used in commerce within three years after registration — and a separate, narrower ground already addressed elsewhere in this corpus (abandonment through inadequate licensing control, see the trademark-license document's cancellation-ground clause) is one instance of the "abandoned" ground quoted here, not a duplicate treatment of it. This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule.

clauses.title: Statutory Grounds That May Support an Opposition or a Cancellation
clauses.body: Two different statutory provisions supply the substantive grounds that can support either type of Trademark Trial and Appeal Board proceeding. The cancellation statute itself names several grounds that are available against a registration at any time: that the registered mark has become the generic name for the goods or services for which it is registered, that it has become functional, that it has been abandoned, or that its registration was obtained fraudulently or contrary to section 1054 or subsection (a), (b), or (c) of section 1052 of the same title (which bar registration of immoral, deceptive, or scandalous matter; certain flags and insignia; and certain names, portraits, or signatures of living individuals, respectively). Separately, the statute governing which marks are registrable in the first place bars registration of a mark that so resembles a mark already registered, or a mark or trade name already used in the United States and not abandoned, that it is likely to cause confusion, mistake, or deception, and separately bars registration of a mark that is merely descriptive or deceptively misdescriptive of the goods on which it is used (subject to the same statute's separate allowance for a mark that has become distinctive through substantially exclusive and continuous use). Confusing similarity and mere descriptiveness are not among the grounds the cancellation statute frees from its five-year time limit; an opposition, by contrast, is filed before registration ever issues and is not subject to that five-year framework at all.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of two textually distinct statutory sources of substantive grounds (15 U.S.C. §§ 1064(3) and 1052(d), (e)(1), (f)) — not a claim that any particular ground applies to the mark described on this sheet, which this clause does not evaluate. These are two genuinely independent statutory sections, not subsections of one provision. Note on inference, stated honestly: the opposition statute (15 U.S.C. § 1063(a)) requires only that an opposition "state the grounds therefor" without itself naming which grounds qualify; this clause's statement that confusing similarity and descriptiveness are available in an opposition rests on the registrability statute (§ 1052) defining what disqualifies a mark from registration in the first place, not on § 1063's text naming those grounds explicitly — that connection is well-established Board practice, but this research pass did not verify it against a case or a Board rule (uspto.gov was unreachable this session), so it is disclosed here rather than presented as an explicit statutory statement. This clause does not restate the cancellation statute's other "at any time" grounds not concerning confusion or descriptiveness (certification-mark misuse, nonuse, and marks under superseded acts) — see the companion clause on cancellation timing. This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule.

clauses.title: The Trademark Trial and Appeal Board's Authority Is Limited to the Right to Register
clauses.body: Federal trademark law establishes the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board as the body directed to determine and decide the respective rights of registration in every case of opposition, cancellation, interference, or an application to register as a lawful concurrent user; the Director gives notice to the parties and directs the Board to hear the case. The statute then enumerates what the Board (acting through the Director) may do in deciding such a proceeding: refuse to register the opposed mark, cancel a registration in whole or in part, modify an application or registration by limiting the goods or services it covers, otherwise restrict or rectify the register, refuse to register interfering marks, or register the mark for the party entitled to it. That enumerated list of available actions is limited to the register itself; it does not include an award of money damages or an injunction against anyone's use of a mark. Those latter remedies are instead granted, under separate statutory provisions, to "the several courts vested with jurisdiction of civil actions" arising under the same title — a power given to courts hearing civil actions, not to the Board.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of a structural distinction the statute itself draws between the Board's registration-focused authority and a court's authority in a civil action — not a claim about how any particular dispute involving the mark described on this sheet would or should be brought, which this clause does not address. This clause draws on three independent statutory sections: 15 U.S.C. § 1067(a) (establishing the Board and its charge), § 1068 (the enumerated list of actions available in a Board proceeding), and § 1116(a) (injunctive relief, granted to courts). This clause infers the damages/injunction distinction from what § 1068's enumerated list does and does not include, rather than from a single sentence stating the limitation directly; the same inference is reinforced by 15 U.S.C. § 1117(a), which likewise conditions a damages recovery on a violation "established in any civil action," though that fourth citation is not separately quoted here to avoid restating the same point three times. This research pass found uspto.gov unreachable from this session, so this clause is built on the Lanham Act's own text rather than on the Board's procedural rules (37 C.F.R. Part 2, Subpart D) or on case law describing this distinction, neither of which is cited here. This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule.

clauses.title: Abandonment as a Ground in a Board Proceeding: The Statutory Definition and the Nonuse Presumption
clauses.body: Abandonment is one of the grounds the cancellation statute makes available against a registration at any time, without regard to the general five-year filing window. The statute separately defines what "abandoned" means. One of the two statutory ways a mark is deemed abandoned is when its use has been discontinued with intent not to resume that use; the statute allows that intent to be inferred from the surrounding circumstances, and it sets a specific evidentiary rule: nonuse of a mark for three consecutive years is prima facie evidence of abandonment. The statute also defines "use" for this purpose as bona fide use made in the ordinary course of trade, not use made merely to reserve a right in a mark. Prima facie evidence under this provision shifts the practical burden to the registrant to come forward with evidence of an intent to resume use or otherwise rebut the presumption; it is a presumption arising from a fixed period of nonuse, not itself a finding that abandonment has occurred.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the statutory abandonment definition and its three-year nonuse presumption — not a claim that any mark described on this sheet has or has not been abandoned, which depends on facts about actual use this clause does not evaluate. This clause treats a different statutory basis than the two abandonment-related clauses already in this corpus: the trademark-license document's cancellation-ground clause cites this same cancellation provision (15 U.S.C. § 1064(3)) for the general point that abandonment is a no-time-limit cancellation ground, and its naked-licensing clause cites the definition's second prong (15 U.S.C. § 1127(2), loss of significance through the owner's course of conduct); this clause instead verifies, independently and for the first time in this corpus, the definition's first prong (15 U.S.C. § 1127(1)) — the nonuse-with-intent-not-to-resume definition and its three-year prima facie presumption — as the ground most likely to be at issue specifically in a Board opposition or cancellation proceeding built around nonuse. This clause's two citations are to two independent statutory sections (§ 1064(3) and § 1127(1)), not subsections of the same provision. This research pass found uspto.gov unreachable from this session, so no Board decision applying this presumption is cited here. This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule.

citations.quote: At any time if the registered mark becomes the generic name for the goods or services, or a portion thereof, for which it is registered, or is functional, or has been abandoned, or its registration was obtained fraudulently

citations.quote: When its use has been discontinued with intent not to resume such use . Intent not to resume may be inferred from circumstances. Nonuse for 3 consecutive years shall be prima facie evidence of abandonment.

clauses.title: The Statutory Definition of a Close Corporation
clauses.body: California's General Corporation Law treats "close corporation" status as an election available within the ordinary corporate form, not a separate type of entity. A corporation qualifies as a close corporation only if its articles of incorporation contain two things beyond the content every corporation's articles must already include under Section 202: a provision capping the number of persons who may hold record ownership of all of the corporation's issued shares of all classes at a specific number the corporation chooses, which cannot exceed 35, and the literal statement "This corporation is a close corporation." Separately, a corporation's name must contain the word "corporation," "incorporated," or "limited" (or an abbreviation of one of those words) in order for the corporation to be subject to the General Corporation Law's close-corporation provisions at all — a naming requirement that does not apply to corporations generally.
clauses.gap: This is one state's election mechanism within one state's general corporation statute, used as real evidence of what qualifies a specific corporation for status as a "close corporation" under California law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, or that other states offer an equivalent election at all; some states have no statutory close-corporation supplement to their general corporation law, and among those that do, the qualifying shareholder cap and required election language vary. The two citations below come from two independently enacted sections of the General Corporation Law: Cal. Corp. Code § 158(a) is the source of the definition itself, and Cal. Corp. Code § 202(a) is an independently verified second source for the corporate-name designator requirement that the close-corporation election specifically triggers.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 158(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the definition of a close corporation
citations.quote: “Close corporation” means a corporation, including a close social purpose corporation, whose articles contain, in addition to the provisions required by Section 202, a provision that all of the corporation’s issued shares of all classes shall be held of record by not more than a specified number of persons, not exceeding 35, and a statement, “This corporation is a close corporation.”

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 202(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the close-corporation name designator requirement
citations.quote: The name of the corporation; provided, however, that in order for the corporation to be subject to the provisions of this division applicable to a close corporation (Section 158), the name of the corporation must contain the word “corporation,” “incorporated,” or “limited” or an abbreviation of one of such words.

clauses.title: Adding or Removing the Close Corporation Election After Incorporation
clauses.body: The close-corporation provision described above does not have to be included in a corporation's original articles of incorporation; California's statute lets a corporation add it later by amending its articles. But the vote required to make that change depends on timing. If the amendment adding the close-corporation provision is adopted after the corporation has already issued shares, it takes the affirmative vote of all of the corporation's issued and outstanding shares of every class — unanimous shareholder approval, not merely a majority. Removing the provision, or changing the specific shareholder-number cap once it is in the articles, works differently: if that amendment is likewise adopted after shares have been issued, the default rule requires the affirmative vote of at least two-thirds of the outstanding shares of each class, though the articles themselves may set a lower threshold (down to, but not below, a majority of the outstanding shares) or may deny a vote entirely to any particular class.
clauses.gap: This is one state's amendment-voting mechanics for a specific statutory election, used as real evidence of a genuine formal requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a given corporation, and not a claim that every state offering an equivalent election requires the same voting thresholds. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 158(b) and § 158(c), so they are treated as one source, not two independent ones; no additional independent source was located for these amendment-vote thresholds specifically.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 158(b)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, adding the close-corporation election by amendment
citations.quote: The special provisions referred to in subdivision (a) may be included in the articles by amendment, but if such amendment is adopted after the issuance of shares only by the affirmative vote of all of the issued and outstanding shares of all classes.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 158(c)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, removing or changing the election by amendment
citations.quote: The special provisions referred to in subdivision (a) may be deleted from the articles by amendment, or the number of shareholders specified may be changed by amendment, but if such amendment is adopted after the issuance of shares, only by the affirmative vote of at least two-thirds of each class of the outstanding shares; provided, however, that the articles may provide for a lesser vote, but not less than a majority of the outstanding shares, or may deny a vote to any class, or both.

clauses.title: The Required Share Certificate Legend and the Consequence of Exceeding the Cap
clauses.body: Close corporation status carries its own certificate-disclosure requirement, separate from and stricter than the general share-transfer-restriction disclosure that applies to any California corporation's shares. Every certificate representing shares of a close corporation must carry a specific, conspicuous legend on its face stating that the corporation is a close corporation, naming the maximum number of holders of record its shares of all classes may have (a number not exceeding 35), and warning that any attempted voluntary inter vivos transfer that would violate that cap is void. That warning is not merely disclosure: if the certificate carries the required legend, an attempted voluntary transfer that would push the number of record holders of the corporation's shares past the maximum stated in the articles is void by statute, not just unenforceable against an unknowing transferee. Separately, the statute treats a shareholder's acceptance of a certificate bearing that legend as the shareholder's own consent to the restriction — including a waiver of any right the shareholder might otherwise have to sell to a broader pool of purchasers or to demand registration of the shares under federal securities law, for as long as the corporation remains a close corporation.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine formal requirement specific to a corporate subtype that has elected close-corporation status — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and it applies only if that election was actually made, which most small corporations have not done. This project's Buy-Sell Agreement document separately covers Cal. Corp. Code § 418(c) and (d) for a different purpose — what a departing close-corporation shareholder's transfer restriction means for a buy-sell counterparty; this clause covers the same statutory legend requirement from the formation side, as something the articles and share certificates must build in from the outset. The § 418 citations below are both subsections of the same statutory section and are treated as one source; Cal. Corp. Code § 421 is an independently enacted second source confirming the consent-and-waiver consequence that attaches to accepting a legended certificate.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 418(c)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the required close-corporation certificate legend
citations.quote: All certificates representing shares of a close corporation shall contain in addition to any other statements required by this section, the following conspicuous legend on the face thereof: “This corporation is a close corporation. The number of holders of record of its shares of all classes cannot exceed ____ [a number not in excess of 35]. Any attempted voluntary inter vivos transfer which would violate this requirement is void. Refer to the articles, bylaws and any agreements on file with the secretary of the corporation for further restrictions.”

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 418(d)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, a transfer past the cap is void
citations.quote: Any attempted voluntary inter vivos transfer of the shares of a close corporation which would result in the number of holders of record of its shares exceeding the maximum number specified in its articles is void if the certificate contains the legend required by subdivision (c).

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 421
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, a shareholder's consent to the legend by accepting the certificate
citations.quote: Each holder of shares of a close corporation, whether original or subsequent, by accepting the certificates for the shares which contain the legend required by subdivision (c) of Section 418 agrees and consents that such holder cannot make any transfer of shares which would violate the provisions of subdivision (d) of Section 418 and waives any right which such holder might otherwise have under any other law to sell such shares to a greater number of purchasers or to demand any registration thereof under the Securities Act of 1933

clauses.title: Shareholder Management Agreements in Place of a Board
clauses.body: The central practical feature of close corporation status is a statutory exception to the rule that a corporation's business and affairs must be managed by or under the direction of a board of directors. California's statute allows the shareholders of a close corporation to enter into a written shareholders' agreement — by definition, one signed by all of the corporation's shareholders — that governs any phase of the corporation's affairs, including management of its business, division of profits, or distribution of assets on liquidation. Such an agreement is not invalid merely because it interferes with the board's ordinary discretion or because it treats the corporation as if it were a partnership; the statute expressly protects an agreement of this kind from that objection. There are limits: the agreement cannot alter or waive certain other listed provisions of the General Corporation Law, and to the extent the agreement transfers the board's managerial discretion to particular shareholders, those shareholders take on the liability a director would otherwise bear for the same managerial acts, while the directors are relieved of that liability to the same extent. The statute also specifically provides that failing to observe ordinary corporate formalities around director or shareholder meetings, when that failure results from following such an agreement, is not by itself a factor supporting personal liability for the corporation's obligations.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutory basis for shareholders replacing board governance with a private agreement, used as real evidence that such a mechanism exists in at least one state's close-corporation law — not a claim about which state's law governs a given corporation, and the scope of any equivalent mechanism (and whether one exists at all) varies by state. Cal. Corp. Code § 300(b), (d), and (e) are subsections of one statutory section and are treated as one source; Cal. Corp. Code § 186, which supplies the statutory definition of a "shareholders' agreement" and cross-references § 300(b) directly, is an independently enacted second source. This clause does not itemize the specific other General Corporation Law provisions such an agreement cannot alter or waive; Section 300(c) lists them and was reviewed as part of this verification, but its list was not reproduced quote-by-quote here.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 300(b)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, a close corporation shareholders' agreement is not invalid for displacing board discretion
citations.quote: no shareholders’ agreement, which relates to any phase of the affairs of a close corporation, including but not limited to management of its business, division of its profits or distribution of its assets on liquidation, shall be invalid as between the parties thereto on the ground that it so relates to the conduct of the affairs of the corporation as to interfere with the discretion of the board or that it is an attempt to treat the corporation as if it were a partnership or to arrange their relationships in a manner that would be appropriate only between partners.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 300(d)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, managing shareholders take on director-level liability
citations.quote: An agreement of the type referred to in subdivision (b) shall, to the extent and so long as the discretion or powers of the board in its management of corporate affairs is controlled by such agreement, impose upon each shareholder who is a party thereto liability for managerial acts performed or omitted by such person pursuant thereto that is otherwise imposed by this division upon directors, and the directors shall be relieved to that extent from such liability.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 300(e)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, relaxed corporate formalities under such an agreement are not evidence of personal liability
citations.quote: The failure of a close corporation to observe corporate formalities relating to meetings of directors or shareholders in connection with the management of its affairs, pursuant to an agreement authorized by subdivision (b), shall not be considered a factor tending to establish that the shareholders have personal liability for corporate obligations.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 186
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the definition of a close corporation shareholders' agreement
citations.quote: “Shareholders’ agreement” means a written agreement among all of the shareholders of a close corporation, or if a close corporation has only one shareholder between such shareholder and the corporation, as authorized by subdivision (b) of Section 300.

clauses.title: Expanded Standing for Close-Corporation Shareholders in Deadlock and Dissolution
clauses.body: California's involuntary-dissolution statute ordinarily limits who may file a court action to dissolve a corporation to specific, defined groups — among them, half or more of the sitting directors, or shareholders who together hold at least one-third of the corporation's outstanding shares. Close corporation status changes that threshold: the same statute separately grants standing to file for involuntary dissolution to any shareholder or shareholders of a close corporation, without regard to what percentage of the shares that shareholder holds. A parallel expansion applies to a related but distinct proceeding — asking a court to take jurisdiction over a corporation's voluntary winding up — where the statute again grants standing to any close-corporation shareholder, alongside the corporation itself, holders of five percent or more of a class of shares, and creditors. Separately, and not limited to formally-elected close corporations specifically, the same involuntary-dissolution statute lists a further ground available to any corporation with 35 or fewer shareholders: dissolution on the basis that liquidation is reasonably necessary to protect the complaining shareholder's rights or interests, without requiring the fraud, mismanagement, or board deadlock that the statute's other grounds demand. By contrast, California's court-appointed "provisional director" remedy for a deadlocked board or a deadlocked shareholder vote is a general corporate remedy available to any California corporation meeting its own conditions — it is not one of the sections the close-corporation definition itself identifies as containing close-corporation-specific provisions.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that at least one state's close-corporation law expands standing to sue for involuntary dissolution or court supervision of winding up, and as evidence that a separate, nearby remedy (the provisional-director statute) is not itself limited to close corporations — not a claim about which state's law governs a given corporation, and not a claim that dissolution, winding-up supervision, or a provisional-director petition is warranted for any specific corporation. This clause corrects an assumption worth stating plainly: Cal. Corp. Code § 158(g), the close-corporation definition section, lists the specific sections it identifies as containing close-corporation-specific provisions (Sections 186, 202, 204, 300, 418, 421, 1111, 1201, 1800, and 1904), and Section 308, the provisional-director statute, is not among them — that remedy exists for any corporation with an even-numbered deadlocked board or a deadlocked shareholder vote, not as a feature exclusive to close corporations. Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(a)(2) and § 1800(b)(5) are subsections of one statutory section and are treated as one source; Cal. Corp. Code § 1904 is an independently enacted second source; Cal. Corp. Code § 308 is cited here specifically to support the corrective point that it is a general remedy, not a close-corporation-specific one.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(a)(2)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, standing to petition for involuntary dissolution
citations.quote: A shareholder or shareholders who hold shares representing not less than 33 1 / 3 percent of (i) the total number of outstanding shares (assuming conversion of any preferred shares convertible into common shares) or (ii) the outstanding common shares or (iii) the equity of the corporation, exclusive in each case of shares owned by persons who have personally participated in any of the transactions enumerated in paragraph (4) of subdivision (b), or any shareholder or shareholders of a close corporation.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(b)(5)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the 35-or-fewer-shareholder involuntary dissolution ground
citations.quote: In the case of any corporation with 35 or fewer shareholders (determined as provided in Section 605), liquidation is reasonably necessary for the protection of the rights or interests of the complaining shareholder or shareholders.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1904
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, standing to petition for court supervision of a voluntary winding up
citations.quote: upon the petition of (a) the corporation, or (b) a shareholder or shareholders who hold shares representing 5 percent or more of the total number of any class of outstanding shares, or (c) any shareholder or shareholders of a close corporation, or (d) three or more creditors

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 308(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the provisional-director remedy is a general corporate remedy, not close-corporation-specific
citations.quote: If a corporation has an even number of directors who are equally divided and cannot agree as to the management of its affairs, so that its business can no longer be conducted to advantage or so that there is danger that its property and business will be impaired or lost, the superior court of the proper county may, notwithstanding any provisions of the articles or bylaws and whether or not an action is pending for an involuntary winding up or dissolution of the corporation, appoint a provisional director pursuant to this section.

Purpose of This Mobilehome Park Tenancy Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Information Sheet describes California's Mobilehome Residency Law (Civil Code sections 798-799.13) as it may relate to the tenancy of a mobilehome space at {{parkName}}, located at {{parkAddress}}, space number {{spaceNumber}}, occupied by {{homeownerName}} as homeowner, with {{parkOwnerName}} as management. Under this statutory scheme, the mobilehome itself -- described as {{mobilehomeDescription}} -- is typically owned by the resident, while the space or lot it sits on is rented from the park; this is a materially different tenancy structure from an ordinary residential lease, in which the landlord typically owns both the dwelling unit and the land. The current space rent is {{monthlyRent}} per month. This Information Sheet describes the statutory definitions that give this tenancy its structure, the statute's requirements for the park's rental agreement and rules, the statute's own closed list of grounds on which a tenancy may be terminated, the statutory notice periods for a rent increase and for termination, and the statute's protection of a homeowner's right to sell the mobilehome in place. It is a general informational reference, not a rental agreement, a notice of rent increase, a notice of termination, or a determination that any specific ground for termination, notice, or rule applies to this tenancy.

clauses.title: The Statutory Structure: A Resident-Owned Home on Park-Owned, Rented Land
clauses.body: The Mobilehome Residency Law defines a mobilehome park tenancy around a split between ownership of the home and ownership of the land. Civil Code section 798.9 defines a "homeowner" as "a person who has a tenancy in a mobilehome park under a rental agreement," and section 798.12 defines that "tenancy" itself as "the right of a homeowner to the use of a site within a mobilehome park on which to locate, maintain, and occupy a mobilehome, site improvements, and accessory structures for human habitation, including the use of the services and facilities of the park." What the homeowner rents, in other words, is the site -- not the mobilehome. Section 798.3(a) separately defines "mobilehome" as "a structure designed for human habitation and for being moved on a street or highway under permit," a structure the statute treats as distinct from the land under it, and section 798.4 defines the "mobilehome park" itself as "an area of land where two or more mobilehome sites are rented, or held out for rent, to accommodate mobilehomes used for human habitation." The park side of the relationship is handled by "management," which section 798.2 defines as "the owner of a mobilehome park or an agent or representative authorized to act on his behalf in connection with matters relating to a tenancy in the park." Together, these definitions describe a tenancy structurally different from an ordinary residential lease: the homeowner typically owns the physical mobilehome and rents only the space beneath it from management, rather than renting a dwelling unit that belongs to the landlord.
clauses.gap: Section 798.3(a) is quoted only through its core structural definition; the statute goes on, in the remainder of subdivision (a) and in subdivision (b), to include manufactured homes and (for this chapter, with one exception) certain long-term-sited recreational vehicles within "mobilehome," and to exclude motor homes, truck campers, and camping trailers -- distinctions this clause does not reproduce. The statute also defines "resident" (Civil Code section 798.11) as a broader category than "homeowner" -- a homeowner or any other person who lawfully occupies a mobilehome -- which this clause does not address. This clause cites five different, independently numbered code sections (798.2, 798.3, 798.4, 798.9, and 798.12); each is treated as an independent source, though all five sit within the same "General" article of the same statutory chapter. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Mobilehome Residency Law -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific mobilehome tenancy; the treatment of a resident-owned home on rented land varies by state, and some states have no comparable statute at all. This document addresses California's statewide Mobilehome Residency Law (Civil Code sections 798-799.13) only; it does not catalog any local mobilehome park rent-stabilization ordinances that a number of California cities and counties have adopted, which may impose additional or different requirements on top of this statewide law. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether any specific space, rental agreement, notice, or sale complies with the Mobilehome Residency Law, and it is not itself a rental agreement, a notice, or a substitute for either.

clauses.title: Required Contents of the Park Rental Agreement
clauses.body: Civil Code section 798.15 requires that the park rental agreement be in writing and requires it to contain a specific list of provisions: "The rental agreement shall be in writing and shall contain, in addition to the provisions otherwise required by law to be included, all of the following." That list begins with "the term of the tenancy and the rent therefor" and "the rules and regulations of the park," and it also requires that "a copy of the text of this chapter shall be provided as an exhibit and shall be incorporated into the rental agreement by reference" -- meaning the Mobilehome Residency Law itself is deemed part of every park rental agreement. The statute separately requires prompt return of a signed agreement: Civil Code section 798.16(b) provides that "management shall return an executed copy of the rental agreement to the homeowner within 15 business days after management has received the rental agreement signed by the homeowner."
clauses.gap: Section 798.15 lists nine lettered requirements, (a) through (i), including provisions on maintenance of common-facility improvements, a description of physical improvements to be provided, a listing of services and fees, a maintenance-fee mechanism with its own 14-day cure notice, and an annually-updated statutory notice to homeowners; this clause quotes only the introductory sentence and paragraphs (a), (b), and part of (c), and does not reproduce the remaining lettered requirements. This clause cites two independent code sections (798.15 and 798.16); the several quotations drawn from section 798.15 are treated as one source, not independently corroborating sources. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Mobilehome Residency Law -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific mobilehome tenancy; the treatment of a resident-owned home on rented land varies by state, and some states have no comparable statute at all. This document addresses California's statewide Mobilehome Residency Law (Civil Code sections 798-799.13) only; it does not catalog any local mobilehome park rent-stabilization ordinances that a number of California cities and counties have adopted, which may impose additional or different requirements on top of this statewide law. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether any specific space, rental agreement, notice, or sale complies with the Mobilehome Residency Law, and it is not itself a rental agreement, a notice, or a substitute for either.

citations.quote: (a) The term of the tenancy and the rent therefor.

clauses.title: Rules Must Be in the Rental Agreement, and Statutory Rights Cannot Be Waived
clauses.body: The Mobilehome Residency Law places two specific limits on a park's rules and on the rental agreement that contains them. First, Civil Code section 798.19 makes the statute's protections non-waivable: "No rental agreement for a mobilehome shall contain a provision by which the homeowner waives his or her rights under the provisions of Articles 1 to 8, inclusive, of this chapter. Any such waiver shall be deemed contrary to public policy and void." Second, a park rule is only enforceable as grounds for termination if it is both reasonable and actually part of the rental agreement: Civil Code section 798.56(a)(4) makes it a termination ground only when there is "failure of the homeowner or resident to comply with a reasonable rule or regulation of the park that is part of the rental agreement or any amendment thereto."
clauses.gap: Neither section 798.19 nor section 798.56(a)(4) defines what makes a rule "reasonable"; that determination is fact-specific and this clause does not resolve it. Section 798.56(a)(4) also imposes its own notice-and-cure procedure before a rule violation can support termination (written notice of the alleged violation and seven days to comply, with an exception after three violations of the same rule within 12 months); this clause quotes only the underlying substantive standard, not that full procedural mechanism. This clause cites two independent code sections (798.19 and 798.56); section 798.56 is also cited, for a different point (the full list of termination grounds), in a separate clause of this document. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Mobilehome Residency Law -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific mobilehome tenancy; the treatment of a resident-owned home on rented land varies by state, and some states have no comparable statute at all. clauses.title: The Statute's Own Closed List of Grounds for Terminating a Mobilehome Space Tenancy
clauses.body: The Mobilehome Residency Law gives management a narrower, more specific set of termination grounds than ordinary residential tenancy law, and states expressly that the list is exclusive. Civil Code section 798.56(a) provides: "A tenancy shall be terminated by the management only for one or more of the following reasons." The seven enumerated grounds are: (1) "Failure of the homeowner or resident to comply with a local ordinance or state law or regulation relating to mobilehomes within a reasonable time after the homeowner receives a notice of noncompliance from the appropriate governmental agency"; (2) "Conduct by the homeowner or resident, upon the park premises, that constitutes a substantial annoyance to other homeowners or residents"; (3) conviction of the homeowner or resident of certain enumerated crimes committed on the park premises; (4) "Failure of the homeowner or resident to comply with a reasonable rule or regulation of the park that is part of the rental agreement or any amendment thereto"; (5) "Nonpayment of rent, utility charges, or reasonable incidental service charges; provided that the amount due has been unpaid for a period of at least five days from its due date, and provided that the homeowner shall be given a three-day written notice subsequent to that five-day period to pay the amount due or to vacate the tenancy"; (6) "Condemnation of the park"; and (7) "Change of use of the park or any portion thereof, provided" specific advance-notice conditions are met. The Legislature's own stated reason for this narrower list, set out in Civil Code section 798.55(a), is that "because of the high cost of moving mobilehomes, the potential for damage resulting therefrom, the requirements relating to the installation of mobilehomes, and the cost of landscaping or lot preparation, it is necessary that the owners of mobilehomes occupied within mobilehome parks be provided with the unique protection from actual or constructive eviction afforded by the provisions of this chapter."
clauses.gap: Ground (3) (criminal conviction) is summarized rather than quoted verbatim, because its text is a long cross-reference to specific Penal Code sections; this clause does not reproduce that cross-reference. Each ground carries its own additional procedural detail not reproduced here in full -- for example, ground (5)'s cure mechanics and repeat-notice rule, and ground (7)'s tiered advance-notice periods (addressed in part in a separate clause of this document on notice periods). This clause cites two independent code sections (798.55 and 798.56); the seven numbered grounds quoted from section 798.56(a) are treated as one source for those grounds, with section 798.55(a) cited independently for the Legislature's stated rationale for the narrower list. clauses.title: Statutory Notice Periods for a Rent Increase and for Termination of Tenancy
clauses.body: The Mobilehome Residency Law sets its own specific advance-notice periods, distinct from the notice periods that apply to an ordinary residential tenancy. For a rent increase, Civil Code section 798.30 requires that "the management shall give a homeowner written notice of any increase in his or her rent at least 90 days before the date of the increase." For termination of the tenancy generally, Civil Code section 798.55(b)(1) requires written notice, in the manner prescribed for an unlawful detainer notice under Code of Civil Procedure section 1162, giving the homeowner the choice to sell or remove the mobilehome "within a period of not less than 60 days, which period shall be specified in the notice." A termination based on a park's change of use carries longer, tiered notice periods instead of the general 60 days: Civil Code section 798.56(a)(7)(B) requires that, once required permits for the change of use have been approved, "the management shall give the homeowners six months' or more written notice of termination of tenancy" -- or twelve months or more if the change of use requires no local governmental permit.
clauses.gap: This clause does not address every notice period the statute sets for every termination ground -- for example, the distinct five-day/three-day sequence that applies specifically to a nonpayment-of-rent termination under section 798.56(a)(5), which is shorter than the general 60-day notice and is addressed only in the separate clause of this document on termination grounds. It also does not address any local rent-stabilization ordinance that might impose a different, and possibly longer, rent-increase notice period on top of this statewide 90-day minimum. This clause cites three independent code sections (798.30, 798.55, and 798.56); section 798.56 is also cited, for a different point (the full list of termination grounds), in a separate clause of this document. clauses.title: The Right to Sell the Mobilehome in Place, and the Park's Limited Approval Discretion
clauses.body: The Mobilehome Residency Law protects a homeowner's ability to sell the mobilehome without removing it from the park, subject to a narrow set of exceptions and a regulated approval process for the buyer. Civil Code section 798.73 provides that "the management shall not require the removal of a mobilehome from the park in the event of the sale of the mobilehome to a third party during the term of the homeowner's rental agreement or in the 60 days following the initial notice required by paragraph (1) of subdivision (b) of Section 798.55," subject to limited exceptions tied to the home's age, size, condition, and compliance with construction and safety standards; even then, section 798.73(e) requires that "the management shall not require a mobilehome to be removed from the park, pursuant to this section, unless the management has provided to the homeowner notice particularly specifying the condition that permits the removal of the mobilehome." As to the buyer, Civil Code section 798.74(a) allows the park to "require the right of prior approval of a prospective purchaser of a mobilehome that will remain in the park," but section 798.74(c) sharply limits that discretion: "Management shall not withhold approval from a prospective purchase of a mobilehome unless any of the following apply" -- (1) management reasonably determines, based on the purchaser's prior tenancies, that the purchaser will not comply with the park's rules and regulations; (2) "the purchaser does not have the financial ability to pay the rent, estimated utilities, and other charges of the park"; or (3) "the purchaser has committed fraud, deceit, or concealment of material facts during the application process." The statute also builds in a default in the homeowner's favor: under section 798.74(e)(3), "if the management fails or refuses to notify the seller and the prospective purchaser, in writing, of either acceptance or rejection of the application" within the statutory 15-business-day period, "the management shall be deemed to have approved the application of the prospective purchaser."
clauses.gap: Section 798.73's exceptions permitting park-required removal -- for a home that does not meet the statutory definition of "mobilehome," or that is beyond a specified age and fails specified health and safety standards, or that is in significantly rundown condition or disrepair -- are summarized rather than quoted in full here. Section 798.74 also contains additional procedural detail this clause does not reproduce, including the specific disclosures management must give the seller and buyer, limits on what financial documentation management may demand, and a requirement to credit or refund any application fee. This clause cites two independent code sections (798.73 and 798.74); the several quotations drawn from section 798.74 are treated as one source, not independently corroborating sources. clauses.title: The Break Time Duty and Its Relationship to Paid Rest Breaks
clauses.body: California law requires {{companyName}}, as an employer, to provide {{employeeName}} a reasonable amount of break time to express breast milk for {{employeeName}}'s infant child each time {{employeeName}} has need to do so. This break time must, if possible, run concurrently with any break time already provided to {{employeeName}}, such as an existing paid rest period. Break time that does not run concurrently with the rest time otherwise authorized for {{employeeName}} under the applicable Industrial Welfare Commission wage order is unpaid.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute (Cal. Lab. Code § 1030), offered as documented evidence of what that provision says — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. Federal law provides a separate, less detailed break-time requirement for nursing employees (29 U.S.C. § 218d, the PUMP Act), and most other states have no comparable statute. This is a single, self-contained statutory section; no additional independent source was located for this specific text.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1030
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1030
citations.quote: Every employer, including the state and any political subdivision, shall provide a reasonable amount of break time to accommodate an employee desiring to express breast milk for the employee’s infant child each time the employee has need to express milk. The break time shall, if possible, run concurrently with any break time already provided to the employee. Break time for an employee that does not run concurrently with the rest time authorized for the employee by the applicable wage order of the Industrial Welfare Commission shall be unpaid.

clauses.title: The Core Lactation Location Requirement
clauses.body: California law requires {{companyName}}, as an employer, to provide {{employeeName}} the use of a room or other location to express milk in private; this may include the place where {{employeeName}} normally works if that place otherwise meets the statutory requirements. The location must not be a bathroom, and it must be in close proximity to {{employeeName}}'s work area, shielded from view, and free from intrusion while {{employeeName}} is expressing milk.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute (Cal. Lab. Code § 1031, subds. (a)-(b)), offered as documented evidence of what that provision says — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. Federal law's parallel provision (29 U.S.C. § 218d) similarly requires a private, non-bathroom space, but California's statute is more detailed. This clause and the following one (on the location's specific features) are drawn from subdivisions of the same statutory section, not independent sources of each other; the exemption clause covering fewer-than-50-employee employers (§ 1031(i)) is likewise part of this same section.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1031(a)-(b)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1031, subds. (a)-(b)
citations.quote: An employer shall provide an employee with the use of a room or other location for the employee to express milk in private. The room or location may include the place where the employee normally works if it otherwise meets the requirements of this section. (b) A lactation room or location shall not be a bathroom and shall be in close proximity to the employee’s work area, shielded from view, and free from intrusion while the employee is expressing milk.

clauses.title: Required Features of the Lactation Location
clauses.body: California law requires that the lactation location {{companyName}} provides to {{employeeName}} be safe, clean, and free of hazardous materials; contain a surface to place a breast pump and personal items; contain a place to sit; and have access to electricity or an alternative such as an extension cord or charging station needed to operate a breast pump. California law separately requires {{companyName}} to provide access to a sink with running water and a refrigerator suitable for storing milk in close proximity to {{employeeName}}'s workspace, or, if a refrigerator cannot be provided, another suitable cooling device such as an employer-provided cooler.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute (Cal. Lab. Code § 1031, subds. (c)-(d)), offered as documented evidence of what that provision says — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. This level of itemized detail (surface, seating, electricity, sink, refrigeration) goes beyond the federal PUMP Act's more general private-space requirement. This clause is drawn from the same statutory section as the two other § 1031 clauses in this document (location duty; small-employer exemption), not an independent source of either.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1031(c)-(d)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1031, subds. (c)-(d)
citations.quote: A lactation room or location shall comply with all of the following requirements: (1) Be safe, clean, and free of hazardous materials, as defined in Section 6382. (2) Contain a surface to place a breast pump and personal items. (3) Contain a place to sit. (4) Have access to electricity or alternative devices, including, but not limited to, extension cords or charging stations, needed to operate an electric or battery-powered breast pump. (d) The employer shall provide access to a sink with running water and a refrigerator suitable for storing milk in close proximity to the employee’s workspace. If a refrigerator cannot be provided, an employer may provide another cooling device suitable for storing milk, such as an employer-provided cooler.

clauses.title: The "Seriously Disrupt Operations" Exemption From the Break Time Duty
clauses.body: California law provides that an employer is not required to provide break time under this chapter if doing so would seriously disrupt the employer's operations. This exemption applies to the break-time duty and is not, by its terms, limited to employers below a particular size.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute (Cal. Lab. Code § 1032), offered as documented evidence of what that provision says — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer, nor an assessment of whether any particular employer's operations would in fact be seriously disrupted. This provision is easily confused with the separate, differently-worded exemption in § 1031(i) (covered in a companion clause in this document), which applies only to the location requirements and only for employers with fewer than 50 employees; § 1032's "seriously disrupt operations" standard, by contrast, applies to the break-time duty of § 1030 and contains no employee-count threshold. This is a single, self-contained statutory section unchanged since its original 2001 enactment; no additional independent source was located for this specific text.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1032
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1032
citations.quote: An employer is not required to provide break time under this chapter if to do so would seriously disrupt the operations of the employer.

clauses.title: The Fewer-Than-50-Employees Undue Hardship Exemption From Location Requirements
clauses.body: California law provides that an employer with fewer than 50 employees may be exempt from a requirement of the lactation-location statute if it can demonstrate that the requirement would impose an undue hardship, by causing the employer significant difficulty or expense, when considered in relation to the size, financial resources, nature, or structure of the employer's business. Where an employer with fewer than 50 employees demonstrates that providing a room or other location other than a bathroom would impose such undue hardship, that employer is still required to make reasonable efforts to provide the use of a room or other location, other than a toilet stall, in close proximity to the employee's work area, for the employee to express milk in private.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute (Cal. Lab. Code § 1031(i)), offered as documented evidence of what that provision says — not an assessment of whether any particular employer qualifies for the exemption or has fewer than 50 employees. This exemption applies specifically to the location requirements of § 1031; it is a distinct provision from the separately worded, employer-size-neutral "seriously disrupt operations" exemption from the break-time duty in § 1032 (covered in a companion clause in this document) and should not be conflated with it. This clause is drawn from the same statutory section (§ 1031) as the two other location-requirement clauses in this document, not an independent source of either.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1031(i)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1031, subd. (i)
citations.quote: An employer that employs fewer than 50 employees may be exempt from a requirement of this section if it can demonstrate that a requirement would impose an undue hardship by causing the employer significant difficulty or expense when considered in relation to the size, financial resources, nature, or structure of the employer’s business. If that employer can demonstrate that the requirement to provide an employee with the use of a room or other location, other than a bathroom, would impose such undue hardship, the employer shall make reasonable efforts to provide the employee with the use of a room or other location, other than a toilet stall, in close proximity to the employee’s work area, for the employee to express milk in private.

clauses.title: The Written Lactation Accommodation Policy Requirement
clauses.body: California law requires an employer to develop and implement a policy regarding lactation accommodation that includes a statement about an employee's right to request lactation accommodation, the process by which an employee makes that request, the employer's obligation to respond to the request, and a statement about the employee's right to file a complaint with the Labor Commissioner for a violation of this chapter. The employer must include this policy in an employee handbook or set of policies made available to employees, and must distribute the policy to new employees upon hiring and to any employee who inquires about or requests parental leave. If an employer cannot provide break time or a location that complies with the policy, the employer must provide a written response to the employee.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute (Cal. Lab. Code § 1034), offered as documented evidence of what that provision says. This requirement was added effective January 1, 2020 by SB 142 (Stats. 2019, Ch. 720); it did not exist in the statute's original 2001 form. This is a single, self-contained statutory section; no additional independent source was located for this specific text.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1034
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1034
citations.quote: An employer shall develop and implement a policy regarding lactation accommodation that includes the following: (1) A statement about an employee’s right to request lactation accommodation. (2) The process by which the employee makes the request described in paragraph (1). (3) An employer’s obligation to respond to the request described in paragraph (1) as outlined in subdivision (d). (4) A statement about an employee’s right to file a complaint with the Labor Commissioner for any violation of a right under this chapter. (b) The employer shall include the policy described in subdivision (a) in an employee handbook or set of policies that the employer makes available to employees. (c) The employer shall distribute the policy described in subdivision (a) to new employees upon hiring and when an employee makes an inquiry about or requests parental leave. (d) If an employer cannot provide break time or a location that complies with the policy described in subdivision (a), the employer shall provide a written response to the employee.

clauses.title: Enforcement, Anti-Retaliation Protection, and Civil Penalties
clauses.body: California law treats the denial of reasonable break time or adequate space to express milk as a failure to comply with Labor Code Section 226.7, and an aggrieved employee may file a complaint with the Labor Commissioner under Section 98. Separately, an employer may not discharge, discriminate, or retaliate against an employee for exercising or attempting to exercise a right protected under this chapter, and an aggrieved employee may file a retaliation complaint with the Labor Commissioner under Section 98.7. An employee may also report a violation to the Labor Commissioner's field enforcement unit; if the Labor Commissioner finds a violation after inspection or investigation, the Labor Commissioner may issue a citation and impose a civil penalty of $100 for each day an employee is denied reasonable break time or adequate space, using the same procedures that apply to citations under Section 1197.1. Violations of this chapter are not misdemeanors under the Labor Code.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute (Cal. Lab. Code § 1033), offered as documented evidence of what that provision says — not an assessment of whether any particular denial or dispute amounts to a violation. Because § 1033(a) deems a denial of break time or space a failure to comply with the separate meal-and-rest-period statute (§ 226.7), the practical remedies available for a lactation-accommodation violation may overlap with meal/rest-break remedies described elsewhere in this document; that cross-reference is stated by the statute itself, not inferred here. This is a single, self-contained statutory section; no additional independent source was located for this specific text.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1033
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1033
citations.quote: The denial of reasonable break time or adequate space to express milk in accordance with this chapter shall be deemed a failure to comply for purposes of Section 226.7. An aggrieved employee may file a complaint under this subdivision with the Labor Commissioner pursuant to Section 98. (b) An employer shall not discharge, or in any other manner discriminate or retaliate against, an employee for exercising or attempting to exercise any right protected under this chapter. This subdivision is not intended to limit or expand an employee’s rights pursuant to Section 98.6. An aggrieved employee may file a complaint under this subdivision with the Labor Commissioner pursuant to Section 98.7. (c) An employee may report a violation of this chapter to the Labor Commissioner’s field enforcement unit. If, upon inspection or investigation, the Labor Commissioner determines that a violation of this chapter has occurred, the Labor Commissioner may issue a citation and may impose a civil penalty in the amount of one hundred dollars ($100) for each day that an employee is denied reasonable break time or adequate space to express milk in violation of this chapter. The procedures for issuing, contesting, and enforcing judgments for citations or civil penalties issued by the Labor Commissioner for violations of this chapter shall be the same as those set forth in Section 1197.1. (d) Notwithstanding any other provision of this code, violations of this chapter shall not be misdemeanors under this code.
