An actual charge must be submitted in writing, under oath or affirmation, to the Special Counsel.]

clauses.title: The Three Categories of Prohibited Conduct Under § 1324b(a)(1)
clauses.body: 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(a)(1) makes it an unfair immigration-related employment practice for a person or other entity to discriminate against an individual with respect to three specific employment actions: hiring, recruitment or referral for a fee, and discharging the individual from employment. The statute draws a distinction in whose protection applies to which basis: discrimination because of national origin is prohibited as to any individual other than an unauthorized alien, while discrimination because of citizenship status is prohibited only as to a narrower, separately defined category called a "protected individual." National origin and citizenship status are treated as two distinct prohibited bases, each covering a different, specifically defined set of individuals.
clauses.gap: This is federal statutory text, used as evidence of what § 1324b(a)(1) itself prohibits — not a claim about which basis or which employment action applies to any specific individual's actual situation, and not a claim that discrimination did or did not occur in fact. The quoted language is § 1324b(a)(1) alone; the statute's exceptions to this general rule (a small-employer exception, a Title VII-overlap exception for national-origin discrimination, and a law/contract-required exception for citizenship-status discrimination) and the definition of "protected individual" are addressed in the separate clauses of this document. "Unauthorized alien" is defined by cross-reference to 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(h)(3), a section this document does not independently verify or quote.

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(a)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, general prohibition on national-origin and citizenship-status discrimination
citations.quote: It is an unfair immigration-related employment practice for a person or other entity to discriminate against any individual (other than an unauthorized alien, as defined in section 1324a(h)(3) of this title) with respect to the hiring, or recruitment or referral for a fee, of the individual for employment or the discharging of the individual from employment— (A) because of such individual’s national origin, or (B) in the case of a protected individual (as defined in paragraph (3)), because of such individual’s citizenship status.

clauses.title: Who Qualifies as a "Protected Individual"
clauses.body: 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(a)(3) defines "protected individual" — the narrower category to whom the statute's citizenship-status protection applies — as an individual who is a citizen or national of the United States, or who is an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence, granted status as a lawfully admitted temporary resident under specific legalization provisions, admitted as a refugee, or granted asylum. That definition carries two statutory exclusions: an alien who fails to apply for naturalization within six months of first becoming eligible to do so is excluded, and an alien who applies on a timely basis but is not naturalized within two years of the application is also excluded — unless that alien can establish active pursuit of naturalization, in which case time the government itself spends processing the application does not count against the two years.
clauses.gap: This is federal statutory text, used as evidence of the definition itself — not a determination of any specific individual's actual citizenship, national origin, or immigration status, and not an exhaustive restatement of every underlying category (for example, the specific temporary-residence legalization provisions cross-referenced, 8 U.S.C. §§ 1160(a) and 1255a(a)(1), are not independently verified or quoted here). Both citations below are to the same statutory paragraph, § 1324b(a)(3) — its main clause and exclusion (i), and its exclusion (ii) — not independent sources. This definition marks the outer limit of who § 1324b protects against citizenship-status discrimination specifically; the statute's broader national-origin protection covers a wider set of individuals (any individual other than an unauthorized alien), described in a separate clause of this document.

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(a)(3) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, "protected individual" defined — categories and exclusion (i)
citations.quote: the term “protected individual” means an individual who— (A) is a citizen or national of the United States, or (B) is an alien who is lawfully admitted for permanent residence, is granted the status of an alien lawfully admitted for temporary residence under section 1160(a) or 1255a(a)(1) of this title, is admitted as a refugee under section 1157 of this title, or is granted asylum under section 1158 of this title; but does not include (i) an alien who fails to apply for naturalization within six months of the date the alien first becomes eligible (by virtue of period of lawful permanent residence) to apply for naturalization

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(a)(3) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, "protected individual" defined — exclusion (ii)
citations.quote: (ii) an alien who has applied on a timely basis, but has not been naturalized as a citizen within 2 years after the date of the application, unless the alien can establish that the alien is actively pursuing naturalization

clauses.title: "Document Abuse" as a Distinct Prohibited Practice
clauses.body: Separately from the hiring/discharge discrimination described above, § 1324b(a)(6) makes it an unfair immigration-related employment practice for an employer, when carrying out Form I-9 verification, to request more or different documents than the verification statute requires, or to refuse to honor documents that reasonably appear genuine on their face — but only when that request or refusal is made for the purpose or with the intent of discriminating against an individual in violation of the core prohibition described above. This is commonly referred to as "document abuse." The statute treats it as a separately defined violation category: the civil-penalty range an administrative law judge may order specifically for a document-abuse violation is set at a different, generally lower dollar amount than the range for other § 1324b violations.
clauses.gap: This is federal statutory text, used as evidence that document abuse is a defined, purpose-requiring violation category distinct from the general hiring/discharge prohibition — not a claim that any specific request for documents was, or was not, made with discriminatory intent. Both citations are to different provisions of the same statutory section, § 1324b — paragraph (a)(6) (the violation) and paragraph (g)(2)(B)(iv)(IV) (its penalty range) — not independent sources.

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(a)(6) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, document-abuse practices
citations.quote: A person’s or other entity’s request, for purposes of satisfying the requirements of section 1324a(b) of this title, for more or different documents than are required under such section or refusing to honor documents tendered that on their face reasonably appear to be genuine shall be treated as an unfair immigration-related employment practice if made for the purpose or with the intent of discriminating against an individual in violation of paragraph (1).

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(g)(2)(B)(iv)(IV) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, separate civil-penalty range for document-abuse violations
citations.quote: in the case of an unfair immigration-related employment practice described in subsection (a)(6), to pay a civil penalty of not less than $100 and not more than $1,000 for each individual discriminated against

clauses.title: Filing a Charge With the Special Counsel, and the 180-Day Deadline
clauses.body: A charge alleging an unfair immigration-related employment practice under § 1324b is filed with the Special Counsel for Immigration-Related Unfair Employment Practices — an office within the U.S. Department of Justice, headed by a presidential appointee confirmed by the Senate to a four-year term. The charge may be filed by the person directly and adversely affected, by someone filing on that person's behalf, or by an officer of the relevant federal agency, and it must be in writing, under oath or affirmation. The statute sets a firm outer limit on timing: no complaint may later be filed regarding a practice that occurred more than 180 days before the charge was filed with the Special Counsel.
clauses.gap: This is federal statutory text, used as evidence of the filing mechanism and the 180-day limitation period themselves — not legal advice about whether any specific charge is or is not timely, and not a claim about how the 180-day count applies to a continuing practice or a later-discovered practice. The three citations below are to three different subsections of the same statutory section, § 1324b — (b)(1) (who may file, and with whom), (c)(1) (the Special Counsel's appointment and department), and (d)(3) (the 180-day limit) — not independent sources. Section 1324b(b)(2) also bars filing the same set of facts as both a § 1324b charge and an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission charge under Title VII, addressed further in the employer-size clause of this document; this document does not verify the separate EEOC charge-filing deadline under Title VII itself. The statutory text refers to "the Service" (the former Immigration and Naturalization Service) for certain investigative-officer references; this document does not independently verify the successor agency structure under the current Department of Homeland Security.

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(b)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, who may file a charge and with whom
citations.quote: any person alleging that the person is adversely affected directly by an unfair immigration-related employment practice (or a person on that person’s behalf) or an officer of the Service alleging that an unfair immigration-related employment practice has occurred or is occurring may file a charge respecting such practice or violation with the Special Counsel (appointed under subsection (c)).

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(c)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Special Counsel's appointment and department
citations.quote: The President shall appoint, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, a Special Counsel for Immigration-Related Unfair Employment Practices (hereinafter in this section referred to as the “Special Counsel”) within the Department of Justice to serve for a term of four years.

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(d)(3) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, 180-day time limitation on complaints
citations.quote: No complaint may be filed respecting any unfair immigration-related employment practice occurring more than 180 days prior to the date of the filing of the charge with the Special Counsel.

clauses.title: Remedies an Administrative Law Judge May Order
clauses.body: If, after a hearing, an administrative law judge determines by a preponderance of the evidence that a person or entity has engaged in an unfair immigration-related employment practice, the judge must issue an order requiring that person or entity to cease and desist from the practice. The judge may also order additional remedies, including hiring the individuals directly and adversely affected, with or without back pay, and a civil penalty for each individual discriminated against — set, for a first-time violation other than document abuse, at not less than $250 and not more than $2,000 per individual, with higher statutory ranges for repeat violators and a separate, lower range specifically for document-abuse violations. Back pay is limited: it cannot accrue from a date more than two years before the charge was filed with the Special Counsel, and interim earnings reduce whatever back pay would otherwise be owed.
clauses.gap: This is federal statutory text, used as evidence of the available remedies and the dollar figures and time limits the statute itself attaches to them — not a claim about what remedy, if any, a judge would order in a specific case, and not the complete remedy list: the statute also authorizes notice-posting, personnel-training, personnel-file-correction, and record-retention orders, not quoted here. All four citations below are to different provisions within the same statutory subsection, § 1324b(g) — (g)(2)(A) (the cease-and-desist requirement), (g)(2)(B)(iii) (hiring with back pay), (g)(2)(B)(iv)(I) (the first-tier civil-penalty range), and (g)(2)(C) (the back-pay limitation) — not independent sources. The civil-penalty dollar figures quoted are the amounts set out in the statutory text itself; this document does not independently verify whether a later inflation-adjustment regulation — which federal civil-penalty statutes are periodically required to receive — has since revised these figures upward, so an actually-assessed penalty today may differ from the statutory figures quoted here.

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(g)(2)(A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, mandatory cease-and-desist order
citations.quote: the judge shall state his findings of fact and shall issue and cause to be served on such person or entity an order which requires such person or entity to cease and desist from such unfair immigration-related employment practice.

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(g)(2)(B)(iii) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, hiring with or without back pay
citations.quote: to hire individuals directly and adversely affected, with or without back pay

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(g)(2)(B)(iv)(I) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, first-tier civil-penalty range
citations.quote: to pay a civil penalty of not less than $250 and not more than $2,000 for each individual discriminated against

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(g)(2)(C) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, back-pay accrual limit
citations.quote: back pay liability shall not accrue from a date more than two years prior to the date of the filing of a charge with the Special Counsel

clauses.title: Employer-Size Threshold, and How It Relates to Title VII
clauses.body: Section 1324b(a)(1)'s general prohibition does not apply to a person or entity that employs three or fewer employees — so, on its face, the statute's protection reaches only employers with four or more employees. The statute also withdraws its own national-origin-discrimination coverage where the same person or entity and the same individual are already covered, for that same discrimination, under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Title VII's own coverage is not universal: a separate federal statute, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(b), defines a covered Title VII "employer" as one with fifteen or more employees for each working day in each of twenty or more calendar weeks in the current or preceding calendar year. Read together, these two statutes leave a specific band of employers — more than three but fewer than fifteen employees — where § 1324b's national-origin protection applies but Title VII's does not.
clauses.gap: The first two citations below are to two different paragraphs of the same statutory subsection, § 1324b(a)(2) — the three-or-fewer-employee exception and the Title VII-overlap exception — not independent sources; the third citation, to 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(b), is a genuinely independent statute (a different U.S. Code title, from a different Act, Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964) confirming the fifteen-employee figure used above. This clause states what the two statutes' employee-count thresholds are and how they interact on their face; it is not a claim that Title VII does or does not apply to any specific employer, which also depends on facts such as whether the employer is "engaged in an industry affecting commerce" and the applicable calendar-week count, not verified here. Citizenship-status discrimination has no comparable Title VII-overlap exception: § 1324b(a)(2)(B)'s overlap exception is expressly limited to discrimination "because of an individual's national origin," so on this statute's text the three-or-fewer-employee threshold is the only employer-size boundary that applies to § 1324b's citizenship-status protection.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, three-or-fewer-employee exception
citations.quote: Paragraph (1) shall not apply to— (A) a person or other entity that employs three or fewer employees

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(a)(2)(B) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Title VII-overlap exception for national-origin discrimination
citations.quote: a person’s or entity’s discrimination because of an individual’s national origin if the discrimination with respect to that person or entity and that individual is covered under section 703 of the Civil Rights Act of 1964

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(b) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Title VII "employer" defined — fifteen-employee threshold
citations.quote: The term “employer” means a person engaged in an industry affecting commerce who has fifteen or more employees for each working day in each of twenty or more calendar weeks in the current or preceding calendar year

clauses.title: No-Contest Clause
clauses.body: If any beneficiary under this instrument, directly or indirectly, brings a contest of a type that California Probate Code Part 3 (commencing with Section 21310) permits {{testatorName}} to enforce against it, then that beneficiary shall take nothing under this instrument, and any share or interest that beneficiary would otherwise have received shall pass as though that beneficiary had predeceased {{testatorName}} without surviving issue. This clause is intended to apply only to the extent, and only against the specific categories of contest, that California law permits it to be enforced, and no further; it is not intended to and does not penalize a beneficiary for a contest brought with probable cause.

clauses.title: Certification of Understanding
clauses.body: I, {{testatorName}}, certify that I have read this information sheet on the enforceability limits that apply to a no-contest clause under California law, that any no-contest clause in my will or trust will be enforced only to the narrow extent this sheet describes and not beyond it, and that this sheet states facts about the law generally rather than advising me on whether to include a no-contest clause or on what to do about my own situation.

clauses.title: The Default Rule: Only Three Narrow Categories of Contest Are Enforceable
clauses.body: Under California law, a no-contest clause has no legal effect against nearly every possible challenge — it can be enforced only against three specific categories of contest, and nothing else. The first is a direct contest (a challenge to the validity of the instrument itself) brought without probable cause. The second is a pleading that challenges a property transfer on the ground the property wasn't the transferor's to give in the first place — but a no-contest clause reaches this only if it expressly says so. The third is filing a creditor's claim, or prosecuting an action based on one — again, only if the no-contest clause expressly says so. On top of that narrow list, a court deciding what a no-contest clause covers must construe it strictly against the person who wrote it, rather than read it broadly to maximize forfeiture.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how narrow no-contest enforcement actually is under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will or trust, and not advice about whether to include a no-contest clause. The three-category list and the express-provision requirements for categories two and three come from § 21311(a); the strict-construction rule comes from a separate section, § 21312 — these are two independently-numbered sections, not subsections of one. This sheet's separate clauses on the probable-cause standard and on the definition of a direct contest draw on § 21311(b) and § 21310(b) respectively; § 21311(b) is a subsection of the same § 21311 used here, disclosed rather than presented as an independent source of the same fact.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21311(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the three categories a no-contest clause can reach
citations.quote: A no contest clause shall only be enforced against the following types of contests: (1) A direct contest that is brought without probable cause. (2) A pleading to challenge a transfer of property on the grounds that it was not the transferor’s property at the time of the transfer. A no contest clause shall only be enforced under this paragraph if the no contest clause expressly provides for that application. (3) The filing of a creditor’s claim or prosecution of an action based on it. A no contest clause shall only be enforced under this paragraph if the no contest clause expressly provides for that application.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21312 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the strict-construction rule for no-contest clauses
citations.quote: In determining the intent of the transferor, a no contest clause shall be strictly construed.

clauses.title: What Counts as Probable Cause
clauses.body: The probable-cause safe harbor turns entirely on what the contestant knew at the time they filed, not on whether the contest ultimately succeeds. Under California law, probable cause exists for these purposes if the facts known to the contestant, at the time of filing, would lead a reasonable person to believe there's a reasonable likelihood the requested relief will be granted after a further opportunity to investigate or take discovery. A contest that turns out to lose doesn't retroactively lose its probable cause; the standard is assessed as of the filing, on what a reasonable person would have believed was worth pursuing given a chance to dig further — not on hindsight, and not on the eventual outcome.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual, filing-time-focused definition of probable cause for no-contest purposes — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will or trust. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 21311(b)); this sheet's other clause on the narrow default rule and the three enforceable categories draws on subsection (a) of that same section, disclosed as the same source rather than an independent one.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21311(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the definition of probable cause
citations.quote: For the purposes of this section, probable cause exists if, at the time of filing a contest, the facts known to the contestant would cause a reasonable person to believe that there is a reasonable likelihood that the requested relief will be granted after an opportunity for further investigation or discovery.

clauses.title: What Makes a Challenge a "Direct Contest"
clauses.body: Not every challenge to a will or trust is a "direct contest" for no-contest purposes — the term covers only a challenge to the validity of the instrument (or one of its terms) on one of six specific grounds: forgery; lack of due execution; lack of capacity; menace, duress, fraud, or undue influence; revocation — of a will under the state's will-revocation statute, of a trust under the state's trust-revocation statute, or of another kind of instrument under whatever revocation procedure the statute or the instrument itself provides; or disqualification of a beneficiary under one of three specific disqualification statutes. A challenge resting on some other ground isn't a "direct contest" under this definition, whatever else it might be.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual, enumerated definition of a direct contest — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will or trust. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 21310(b)); no additional independent source was found for this. The statute cross-references three further statutes for the disqualification ground and two further statutes for the revocation ground; this sheet doesn't independently verify or restate the content of those cross-referenced statutes, only that § 21310(b) cites them by number.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21310(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the definition of a direct contest
citations.quote: “Direct contest” means a contest that alleges the invalidity of a protected instrument or one or more of its terms, based on one or more of the following grounds: (1) Forgery. (2) Lack of due execution. (3) Lack of capacity. (4) Menace, duress, fraud, or undue influence. (5) Revocation of a will pursuant to Section 6120, revocation of a trust pursuant to Section 15401, or revocation of an instrument other than a will or trust pursuant to the procedure for revocation that is provided by statute or by the instrument. (6) Disqualification of a beneficiary under Section 6112, 21350, or 21380.

clauses.title: This Scheme Applies Alike to Wills and Trusts
clauses.body: California's no-contest statute isn't will-specific — it's written in terms of an "instrument," and a trust counts just as much as a will. The statute defines what it protects (a "protected instrument") as the instrument that contains the no-contest clause itself, plus any other instrument in existence when that one was executed that the no-contest clause expressly identifies as covered — language that applies equally whether the underlying document is a will, a trust, or another kind of instrument. Consistent with that, the direct-contest definition elsewhere in this statute separately addresses revocation of a will and revocation of a trust as two of the specific grounds a direct contest can rest on. And this entire part of the statute applies to any instrument, however and whenever executed, that became irrevocable on or after January 1, 2001 — again, instrument-neutral language, not limited to wills.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that its no-contest scheme is written to reach both wills and trusts (and other instruments) rather than wills alone — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will or trust. The "protected instrument" definition comes from § 21310(e); the scope-of-application rule comes from a separate section, § 21315(a)-(b) — these are two independently-numbered sections, not subsections of one. The observation about the direct-contest definition's separate will/trust revocation grounds draws on the same § 21310(b) quoted in this sheet's clause on the definition of a direct contest, disclosed as the same source rather than an independent one; § 21315(b) also states, conversely, that this part does not apply to an instrument that became irrevocable before January 1, 2001.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21310(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the definition of a protected instrument
citations.quote: “Protected instrument” means all of the following instruments: (1) The instrument that contains the no contest clause. (2) An instrument that is in existence on the date that the instrument containing the no contest clause is executed and is expressly identified in the no contest clause, either individually or as part of an identifiable class of instruments, as being governed by the no contest clause.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21315(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the instrument-neutral scope of this part
citations.quote: This part applies to any instrument, whenever executed, that became irrevocable on or after January 1, 2001.

clauses.title: A Floor, Not a Complete Code — and Not Something the Instrument Can Override
clauses.body: Two further structural facts shape how this statute operates. First, it isn't meant to be the complete law of no-contest enforcement: to the extent this statutory part doesn't address a particular question, the state's older common-law rules governing no-contest clauses continue to govern. Second, this part applies regardless of anything the instrument itself says to the contrary — a drafter cannot write around these limits by including instrument language purporting to expand enforcement beyond what this statute allows.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that its no-contest limits are both a gap-filled-by-common-law floor and a mandatory rule an instrument can't override by its own terms — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will or trust, and not advice about drafting around it. The gap-filling rule comes from § 21313; the mandatory-application rule comes from a separate section, § 21314 — these are two independently-numbered sections, not subsections of one, and neither is used elsewhere in this sheet.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21313 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, common law fills any gap this part leaves
citations.quote: This part is not intended as a complete codification of the law governing enforcement of a no contest clause. The common law governs enforcement of a no contest clause to the extent this part does not apply.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21314 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, this part applies regardless of contrary instrument language
citations.quote: This part applies notwithstanding a contrary provision in the instrument.

clauses.title: Nonparent Custody/Visitation Request — Information and Declaration
clauses.body: I, {{petitionerName}}, am not a legal parent of {{childName}}, a minor born {{childDOB}}. My relationship to {{childName}} is: {{relationshipToChild}}. This declaration provides background information for use with an actual request for custody or visitation of {{childName}}, to be raised within an existing California proceeding of the kind described in Family Code § 3021 (for example, a dissolution, legal separation, nullity, Domestic Violence Prevention Act, or Uniform Parentage Act proceeding), under the standards described in Family Code §§ 3040, 3041, and 3100. This declaration is not itself a court filing, and signing it does not grant {{petitionerName}} custody or visitation of {{childName}}. {{childName}}'s parent(s) of record, so far as known, are {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}}, where applicable. Only a court order issued after the applicable proceeding, notice, and hearing process — including, where a parent objects to custody, the finding of detriment to the child that Family Code § 3041 requires — can grant custody, and only a court's own determination that visitation is in {{childName}}'s best interest under the applicable statute can grant visitation.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment Block — Nonparent Custody/Visitation Information Sheet
clauses.body:
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{petitionerName}}: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet is prepared for use alongside an actual request for custody or visitation raised within a pending California proceeding of the kind described in Family Code § 3021, in the {{countyOfFiling}} Superior Court or other court of competent jurisdiction. It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete that request, and it does not grant custody or visitation rights; only a court order does that.]

clauses.title: The General Custody Preference Order, Including a Nonparent — Family Code § 3040(a)
clauses.body: California Family Code § 3040(a) states the order of preference a court applies when awarding custody of {{childName}}, according to {{childName}}'s best interest: first, "[t]o both parents jointly ... or to either parent"; second, "[i]f to neither parent, to the person or persons in whose home the child has been living in a wholesome and stable environment"; and third, "[t]o any other person or persons deemed by the court to be suitable and able to provide adequate and proper care and guidance for the child." This third-tier language is the statutory hook that allows a nonparent — such as {{petitionerName}}, if {{petitionerName}} is not {{childName}}'s legal parent — to be awarded custody at all, but only where the first two, parent-preferring tiers do not apply.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's general custody preference order — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case, and not a claim that a nonparent's suitability alone entitles that nonparent to custody. This clause cites a single statutory subsection, § 3040(a); no additional independent source was found for it. Section 3040(a) does not itself define "wholesome and stable environment" or "suitable and able to provide adequate and proper care," and this clause does not resolve what either phrase means on any specific family's facts. Separately, and importantly, § 3040(a) states this preference order but does not itself state the heightened finding a court must make before awarding custody to a nonparent over a parent's objection — that heightened finding is addressed in this document's companion clause on Family Code § 3041 — nor does § 3040(a) itself give a nonparent standing to bring a custody request; standing is addressed in this document's companion clause on Family Code § 3021.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3040(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Custody should be granted in the following order of preference according to the best interest of the child as provided in Sections 3011 and 3020: (1) To both parents jointly pursuant to Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 3080) or to either parent. In making an order granting custody to either parent, the court shall consider, among other factors, which parent is more likely to allow the child frequent and continuing contact with the noncustodial parent, consistent with Sections 3011 and 3020. The court, in its discretion, may require the parents to submit to the court a plan for the implementation of the custody order. (2) If to neither parent, to the person or persons in whose home the child has been living in a wholesome and stable environment. (3) To any other person or persons deemed by the court to be suitable and able to provide adequate and proper care and guidance for the child.

clauses.title: The Heightened Detriment Finding Required to Award a Nonparent Custody Over a Parent's Objection, and the Statute's Own Definition of "Detriment" — Family Code § 3041(a)-(c)
clauses.body: Family Code § 3041(a) states that "[b]efore making an order granting custody to a person other than a parent, over the objection of a parent, the court shall make a finding that granting custody to a parent would be detrimental to the child and that granting custody to the nonparent is required to serve the best interest of the child." The same subdivision states that "[a]llegations that parental custody would be detrimental to the child, other than a statement of that ultimate fact, shall not appear in the pleadings." Under § 3041(b), "a finding that parental custody would be detrimental to the child shall be supported by clear and convincing evidence" — a heightened evidentiary standard, subject to a different, lower standard the same section separately provides for in subdivision (d). Section 3041(c) itself defines the key term: "'detriment to the child' includes the harm of removal from a stable placement of a child with a person who has assumed, on a day-to-day basis, the role of the child's parent, fulfilling both the child's physical needs and the child's psychological needs for care and affection, and who has assumed that role for a substantial period of time," and the same subdivision states that "[a] finding of detriment does not require a finding of unfitness of the parents."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the heightened detriment finding governing nonparent custody over a parent's objection, and of that statute's own definition of "detriment to the child" — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case, and not a claim that meeting this standard alone guarantees any particular custody outcome. This clause cites three subsections of the same statutory section, § 3041(a), (b), and (c); no additional independent source beyond § 3041 itself was found for this. This corrects an assumption in the research request that prompted this clause: "detriment to the child" is not left entirely to case law to define — § 3041(c)'s own text gives it express statutory content, centered on removal from a person who has assumed a day-to-day parental role for a substantial period of time — although the statute's use of the word "includes" signals that this definition is illustrative rather than necessarily exhaustive, and how it applies to any specific family's facts is not resolved by the statute's text alone. This clause does not address § 3041(d), which creates a separate, lower preponderance-of-the-evidence presumption for a person who meets the § 3041(c) description, or § 3041(e), which applies distinct evidentiary standards under the Indian Child Welfare Act; neither subdivision (d) nor (e) was independently verified for inclusion as a quoted citation in this document.

Allegations that parental custody would be detrimental to the child, other than a statement of that ultimate fact, shall not appear in the pleadings.

A finding of detriment does not require a finding of unfitness of the parents.

clauses.title: The General, Discretionary Nonparent Visitation Provision — Family Code § 3100(a)
clauses.body: Family Code § 3100(a) is the statutory chapeau of California's Chapter 5 visitation-rights framework. After stating the standard for visitation between {{childName}} and a parent, the same subdivision provides, in a single additional sentence: "In the discretion of the court, reasonable visitation rights may be granted to any other person having an interest in the welfare of the child." This is the general, catch-all statutory basis for a nonparent — someone other than {{childName}}'s legal parent, and other than a grandparent (whose visitation rights arise under the separate statutes addressed in this corpus's Grandparent Visitation document) — to be granted visitation with {{childName}}.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the general, discretionary nonparent visitation provision within California's visitation-rights chapter — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case, and not a claim that having "an interest in the welfare of the child" by itself entitles any particular person to visitation. This clause cites a single statutory subsection, § 3100(a); no additional independent source was found for it. This corrects a framing assumption in the research request that prompted this clause: Family Code § 3101 is not the general nonparent visitation provision — its own text, addressed in this document's companion clause, is limited specifically to stepparents. The broader, catch-all "any other person having an interest in the welfare of the child" language instead appears in § 3100(a) itself. Section 3100(a)'s grant of discretion is also textually tied to "making an order pursuant to Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 3080)" — meaning it operates within an existing custody-related order-making process, not as its own freestanding petition mechanism; this document's companion clause on Family Code § 3021 addresses that procedural threshold separately. This clause does not restate § 3100(b) through (f), which address visitation limits and safeguards in cases involving a protective order, domestic violence, or a confidential shelter address, and which were not independently verified for inclusion as quoted citations in this document.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3100(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: In the discretion of the court, reasonable visitation rights may be granted to any other person having an interest in the welfare of the child.

clauses.title: Stepparent Visitation Is a Separate, Narrower Statutory Pathway — Family Code § 3101(a), (c)
clauses.body: Alongside the general, discretionary nonparent visitation provision in Family Code § 3100(a), California provides a separate, more specific pathway for a stepparent. Family Code § 3101(a) provides: "Notwithstanding any other provision of law, the court may grant reasonable visitation to a stepparent, if visitation by the stepparent is determined to be in the best interest of the minor child." That grant has an express limit: § 3101(c) states that "[v]isitation rights may not be ordered under this section that would conflict with a right of custody or visitation of a birth parent who is not a party to the proceeding." Section 3101(d)(2) defines "stepparent," for purposes of this section, as "a person who is a party to the marriage that is the subject of the proceeding, with respect to a minor child of the other party to the marriage" — a narrower category than "any other person having an interest in the welfare of the child" under § 3100(a).
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a distinct, stepparent-specific visitation pathway — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case, and not a claim that this document exhaustively covers stepparent visitation or stepparent adoption (a separate document elsewhere in this corpus addresses stepparent adoption specifically, which is a different legal mechanism entirely). This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, § 3101(a) and (c); the definitional subdivision § 3101(d)(2) is paraphrased rather than separately quoted as its own citation. Because § 3101's own definition of "stepparent" is tied to being "a party to the marriage that is the subject of the proceeding," it does not, by its terms, extend to a former stepparent whose marriage to the child's parent has ended, to an unmarried partner of a parent, or to a former domestic partner who is not a stepparent as the statute defines that term — such a person's visitation request, if any, would fall instead under the general § 3100(a) provision addressed in this document's companion clause, not under this section. This clause does not resolve whether any specific person qualifies as a "stepparent" under § 3101(d)(2) on particular facts.

citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other provision of law, the court may grant reasonable visitation to a stepparent, if visitation by the stepparent is determined to be in the best interest of the minor child.

clauses.title: Nonparent Custody and Visitation Determinations Arise Within an Already-Pending Proceeding, Not a Freestanding Petition — Family Code § 3021
clauses.body: Family Code § 3021 defines the scope of Part 2 of Division 8 of the Family Code — the part of the Family Code that contains both the general custody-preference and detriment provisions (§§ 3040, 3041) and the general nonparent visitation provision (§ 3100(a)) addressed in this document's other clauses. Section 3021 provides: "This part applies in any of the following: (a) A proceeding for dissolution of marriage. (b) A proceeding for nullity of marriage. (c) A proceeding for legal separation of the parties. (d) An action for exclusive custody pursuant to Section 3120. (e) A proceeding to determine physical or legal custody or for visitation in a proceeding pursuant to the Domestic Violence Prevention Act (Division 10 (commencing with Section 6200)). ... (f) A proceeding to determine physical or legal custody or visitation in an action pursuant to the Uniform Parentage Act (Part 3 (commencing with Section 7600) of Division 12). (g) A proceeding to determine physical or legal custody or visitation in an action brought by the district attorney pursuant to Section 17404." Unlike the grandparent-specific statute addressed in this corpus's separate Grandparent Visitation document, which lets a grandparent file a freestanding petition under Family Code § 3104 without any other proceeding pending, Part 2's general custody and visitation provisions apply only inside one of the proceeding types § 3021 lists.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California's general nonparent custody and visitation provisions operate within an already-pending or properly commenced proceeding rather than through their own freestanding petition mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. This clause cites a single statutory section, § 3021, and quotes it with one internal sentence (a caveat within subdivision (e) about Domestic Violence Prevention Act proceedings and established parent-child relationships) omitted for length, marked by ellipsis; no additional independent source was found for this. This clause corrects an assumption in the research request that prompted it: the general nonparent custody and visitation provisions in Family Code §§ 3040, 3041, and 3100(a) do not themselves state what gives a nonparent standing to start a case — the statute's own text does not describe a nonparent-initiated freestanding petition comparable to grandparent visitation's § 3104 mechanism. Instead, a nonparent's practical route into one of the § 3021 proceeding types (for example, becoming a party to a pending dissolution, legal separation, Domestic Violence Prevention Act, or Uniform Parentage Act proceeding, or bringing a Uniform Parentage Act action) is a fact- and procedure-specific question this clause does not resolve, and this document does not verify or address the entirely separate Probate Code guardianship process, which is a distinct, non-Family-Code mechanism by which a nonparent can obtain custody-like authority over a child and which was not researched for this document. This clause also notes, without independently quoting it as a separate citation, that § 3021(d)'s cross-referenced exclusive-custody action under Family Code § 3120 is by that section's own text available only to "a spouse" — not to a nonparent — so § 3120 does not itself supply nonparent standing either.

clauses.title: Cross-Reference: The Constitutional Backdrop for Nonparent Custody and Visitation Orders
clauses.body: The heightened detriment finding Family Code § 3041 requires before a court awards a nonparent custody over a parent's objection, and the discretionary nature of Family Code § 3100(a)'s nonparent visitation provision, operate against a constitutional backdrop the U.S. Supreme Court articulated in Troxel v. Granville (2000) 530 U.S. 57: "In light of this extensive precedent, it cannot now be doubted that the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment protects the fundamental right of parents to make decisions concerning the care, custody, and control of their children."
clauses.gap: This citation and its exact quoted text are reused from this corpus's existing, already-verified Grandparent Visitation document (clause grandvis_3104b_filing_restriction) rather than independently re-fetched from CourtListener during this session; that reuse is disclosed here rather than presented as a fresh verification. Troxel addressed a Washington visitation statute, Wash. Rev. Code § 26.10.160(3), not any California statute, and its plurality opinion did not construe Family Code § 3040, § 3041, or § 3100 specifically. This session did not locate or verify any California case law applying Troxel's holding directly to §§ 3040, 3041, or 3100(a) the way California's courts have applied it to the grandparent-specific § 3104(e) and (f) presumptions (addressed in this corpus's existing grandvis_3104ef_presumptions clause, citing In re Marriage of Harris (2004) 34 Cal.4th 210) — that case-law connection was not researched for this document and is not claimed here. This clause states Troxel's general constitutional principle as background context for why California's nonparent custody and visitation statutes require the specific findings and presumptions described in this document's other clauses, not as a holding that Troxel itself resolved any question under §§ 3040, 3041, or 3100.

clauses.title: The Definition of Direct Patent Infringement
clauses.body: Federal patent law defines direct infringement in a single sentence: whoever, without authority, makes, uses, offers to sell, or sells any patented invention within the United States, or imports a patented invention into the United States, during the term of the patent, infringes the patent. Several features of this definition are easy to miss. First, it names five distinct infringing acts — making, using, offering to sell, selling, and importing — any one of which is independently sufficient; a person who only imports a patented device, for example, without ever making or selling it, is still described by the statute. Second, the statute's text does not require that the person accused of infringing knew about the patent, intended to infringe it, or copied the invention; as written, it describes the making, using, offering to sell, selling, or importing itself, without reference to the actor's state of mind, which is why direct infringement is often described as not requiring intent (this differs from indirect infringement, addressed separately, where knowledge does play a role). Third, infringement under this provision is limited to the patent's territorial and temporal scope: the conduct must occur within the United States (or as an importation into the United States) and during the patent's term — a patent that has expired, or conduct that occurs entirely outside the United States, falls outside what this particular provision describes. Where {{patentDescription}} is the patent or patented invention in question, and {{allegedInfringerName}} is the party whose making, using, offering to sell, selling, or importing of it is at issue, this is the statutory definition against which that conduct would be measured.
clauses.gap: This is federal law — patent infringement is governed exclusively by the Patent Act and by decisions of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, which has exclusive nationwide appellate jurisdiction over patent cases, so there is no state-by-state variation to resolve. The statutory text was checked directly against the U.S. Code at Cornell's Legal Information Institute, fetched twice with different request headers to confirm the returned text was byte-identical both times. This clause states the bare definitional rule only. It does not resolve whether any specific product or activity actually falls within a particular patent's claims — that determination (called claim construction and infringement analysis) requires comparing the accused product or activity to the specific claims of the specific patent at issue, which this sheet does not do and which is a fact- and document-intensive inquiry beyond what a general information sheet can perform. It also does not address the statute's separate provisions on process-patent infringement, infringement by supplying components for combination outside the United States, or the pharmaceutical-specific infringement provisions found elsewhere in the same section — none of which are summarized here.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 271(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, infringement of patent — direct infringement
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided in this title, whoever without authority makes, uses, offers to sell, or sells any patented invention, within the United States or imports into the United States any patented invention during the term of the patent therefor, infringes the patent.

clauses.title: Indirect Infringement: Inducement and Contributory Infringement
clauses.body: Beyond direct infringement, federal patent law separately describes two ways a person can be liable for someone else's infringing conduct. The first, active inducement, makes liable whoever actively induces infringement of a patent — a short statutory phrase that courts have read to require that the inducing party knew of the patent and knew (or was willfully blind to the fact) that the induced acts would constitute infringement; inducement liability depends on an underlying act of direct infringement by someone else that the defendant encouraged, instructed, or otherwise brought about. The second, contributory infringement, is narrower and more specific: it applies to whoever offers to sell or sells within the United States, or imports into the United States, a component of a patented machine, manufacture, combination, or composition — or a material or apparatus for use in practicing a patented process — that constitutes a material part of the invention, knowing it to be especially made or especially adapted for use in an infringement of the patent, and that is not a staple article or commodity of commerce suitable for substantial noninfringing use. In plain terms, contributory infringement targets suppliers of a specialized component that has essentially no legitimate use other than completing someone else's infringement, while inducement reaches anyone who knowingly encourages another party's infringing conduct regardless of whether they supply any component at all. Where {{allegedInfringerName}}'s conduct relative to {{patentDescription}} does not consist of directly making, using, selling, or importing the patented invention, these are the two statutory provisions under which conduct that facilitates someone else's infringement can independently give rise to liability.
clauses.gap: Both provisions summarized here — 35 U.S.C. § 271(b) and § 271(c) — are subsections of the same statutory section as the direct-infringement provision addressed in a separate clause, so this clause and that one draw on the same source rather than two independent ones; the statutory text was checked directly against the U.S. Code at Cornell's Legal Information Institute, fetched twice with different request headers to confirm byte-identical results. This is federal law, uniform nationwide. This clause states the statutory text of both provisions; it does not restate the substantial body of Federal Circuit and Supreme Court case law interpreting what "knowledge" of the patent and of infringement means for inducement purposes (including how that knowledge requirement applies where a defendant was willfully blind, or genuinely believed in good faith that the patent was invalid) — that case law was not independently verified for this clause and is not summarized here. It also does not resolve whether any specific conduct actually satisfies either provision's requirements for any particular set of facts.

clauses.title: Injunctions Are a Discretionary Equitable Remedy, Not an Automatic One
clauses.body: The federal statute governing injunctions in patent cases states that courts having jurisdiction of patent cases may grant injunctions in accordance with the principles of equity to prevent the violation of any right secured by a patent, on such terms as the court deems reasonable. Two things about that wording matter. First, the word is "may," not "shall" — the statute makes an injunction available, but it does not make one automatic upon a finding of infringement. Second, the statute ties the remedy to "the principles of equity," which is a body of traditional, judge-made standards governing when a court will order or forbid specific conduct, as opposed to simply awarding money. Historically, some courts applied a presumption that a patent owner who proved infringement was entitled to an injunction as a matter of course. The U.S. Supreme Court's 2006 decision in eBay Inc. v. MercExchange, L.L.C. is widely cited for rejecting that presumption and holding that the traditional four-factor equitable test — requiring a patent owner seeking a permanent injunction to demonstrate irreparable injury, that remedies available at law (such as money damages) are inadequate to compensate for that injury, that the balance of hardships between the parties favors an injunction, and that the public interest would not be disserved by a permanent injunction — applies in patent cases just as in other areas of law, with no automatic entitlement to injunctive relief simply because infringement is shown. Whether an injunction would actually issue against {{allegedInfringerName}}'s conduct involving {{patentDescription}} is not something this sheet determines; it depends on how a court applying these equitable factors would weigh the specific facts of a specific case.

The description of eBay Inc. v. MercExchange and its four-factor test in the body above is stated as a widely-known principle of patent law, not as a verified quotation from the opinion — CourtListener, the case-law database used to verify authority clauses in this project, returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429) when queried for that decision during this research session, and no other primary source was substituted for it. Accordingly, the eBay decision is not listed as a citation here, and its four-factor test should be understood as unverified background rather than a confirmed quotation from the case. This is federal law — patent remedies are governed by the Patent Act and by Federal Circuit and Supreme Court precedent applying it nationwide, without state-by-state variation.

clauses.title: Damages: A Reasonable-Royalty Floor, and Discretionary Trebling
clauses.body: Federal patent law sets a floor, not a fixed amount, for money damages in an infringement case. Upon finding for the patent owner, the statute directs the court to award damages adequate to compensate for the infringement, but in no event less than a reasonable royalty for the use the infringer made of the invention, together with interest and costs as fixed by the court. "Adequate to compensate" and "reasonable royalty" are not the same figure in every case — actual damages (such as the patent owner's own lost profits) can exceed a royalty figure, but a reasonable royalty operates as the statutory minimum even where the patent owner cannot prove a higher actual-damages amount. Separately, the statute gives the court discretion — not an obligation — to increase the damages found or assessed, up to three times that amount; this is the source of what is commonly called treble damages, and courts have limited its use to cases involving egregious or willful infringement rather than applying it routinely to every infringement finding. The statute also allows the court to receive expert testimony to help determine damages or what royalty would be reasonable under the circumstances. Whether {{allegedInfringerName}}'s use of {{patentDescription}} would support a particular damages figure, or whether any enhancement would be available, is not something this sheet calculates.

Pulse Electronics, Inc. narrowing the standard for when enhanced damages are available, since that decision was not independently verified against a primary source in this research session and is not cited here. It also does not address the separate statutory carve-out, found in the same section of Title 35 as the marking statute, exempting increased damages from applying to certain provisional-rights infringement under 35 U.S.C. § 154(d).

clauses.title: The Marking Statute: Unmarked Products Can Cut Off Damages
clauses.body: A separate statute affects how far back in time a patent owner can recover damages, based on whether patented products were marked. The statute permits — but does not require — a patentee, or a person making, offering for sale, or selling a patented article under the patentee, to give public notice that an article is patented, by marking the article itself (or, if that isn't practical, its packaging) with the word "patent" or the abbreviation "pat." together with the patent number, or with an internet address that associates the article with the patent number. The consequence for not marking is direct: in the event of a failure to mark, no damages may be recovered by the patentee in an infringement action, except on proof that the infringer was actually notified of the infringement and continued to infringe afterward — and even then, damages may be recovered only for infringement occurring after that notice. The statute also states that filing an infringement lawsuit itself counts as this kind of notice. In practical terms, a patent owner who never marked a patented product and never separately notified an accused infringer of the alleged infringement is limited, under this statute, to damages for infringement occurring on or after the date the lawsuit was filed — not for years of earlier unmarked, un-notified infringement, even if that infringement can otherwise be proven. Whether {{patentHolderName}} marked products embodying {{patentDescription}}, or gave {{allegedInfringerName}} actual notice of the alleged infringement, and when, are factual questions this sheet does not answer, but they are the specific facts this statute makes relevant to how far back damages can reach.

This is federal law, uniform nationwide. This clause addresses subsection (a) only; it does not address the separate, more specialized damages limitations for process-patent infringement under 35 U.S.C. § 271(g) found later in the same section, nor an additional marking-related notice-of-suit provision found elsewhere in the same subsection concerning actions the patentee failed to bring within a set period — neither was independently verified for inclusion here. It also does not resolve whether marking obligations under this statute actually applied to any specific product, or whether any specific communication would count as "actual notice" of infringement sufficient to satisfy the statute's proof requirement — both are fact-specific determinations beyond what a general information sheet addresses.

clauses.title: The Six-Year Damages Limitations Period
clauses.body: Federal patent law places a firm time limit on how far back damages can be recovered, stated in its own terms rather than as an ordinary filing deadline: except as otherwise provided by law, no recovery may be had for any infringement committed more than six years before the filing of the complaint (or a counterclaim for infringement) in the action. Note precisely what this provision limits — it caps how far back in time damages can be recovered once a suit is filed, measured backward six years from the filing date, rather than setting a deadline by which a lawsuit itself must be filed after infringement is discovered or occurs. Ongoing infringement that continues within the six years before filing remains fully within reach even if the same infringing conduct began earlier; what falls outside the statute is recovery for the portion of infringement that occurred more than six years before the complaint or counterclaim was filed. Where the conduct at issue involving {{patentDescription}} occurred, and how it relates to any complaint's filing date, are the facts this six-year measurement would be applied to; this sheet does not calculate that period for any specific timeline.

clauses.title: What a Cooperative Corporation Is and the Patronage-Based Purpose Requirement
clauses.body: California's Corporations Code contains a distinct statutory part governing the "cooperative corporation" — Part 2 of Division 3 of Title 1, Corp. Code §§ 12200-12704, titled the "Cooperative Corporation Law" — that is a different corporate form from an ordinary for-profit corporation formed only under the General Corporation Law, from the nonprofit public benefit, mutual benefit, and religious corporation laws, and from the for-profit benefit corporation statute, all covered elsewhere in this corpus. By its own terms, this part "is intended primarily to apply to the organization and operation of cooperatives, including, but not limited to, consumer cooperatives, worker cooperatives, and cooperatives formed for the purpose of recycling or treating hazardous waste that elect to incorporate under its provisions." The statute defining a cooperative corporation's core purpose states that a corporation formed under this part "shall be organized and shall conduct its business primarily for the mutual benefit of its members as patrons of the corporation" — that is, based on their use of the cooperative's goods, services, or marketing activities, rather than to maximize a financial return on invested capital. The same section elsewhere states that these corporations "are democratically controlled and are not organized to make a profit for themselves, as such, or for their members, as such, but primarily for their members as patrons."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one state defines and structures this specific corporate form — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific cooperative's formation, and not a claim that every state with a cooperative corporation statute defines or structures the form identically; cooperative statutes vary by state, and some states place agricultural, consumer, worker, or housing cooperatives under separate statutes rather than one unified law. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 12200 and Cal. Corp. Code § 12201, and are treated as two independent sources. Note that this California statute's own listed scope — consumer cooperatives, worker cooperatives, and hazardous-waste or recycling cooperatives — does not on its face include agricultural cooperatives; a separate citation below (in the required-articles-content clause) reflects the statute's own cross-reference showing agricultural cooperative associations are instead organized under a distinct body of law, the Food and Agricultural Code. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any corporation and does not determine which statute governs the formation of any specific cooperative enterprise.

This part is intended primarily to apply to the organization and operation of cooperatives, including, but not limited to, consumer cooperatives, worker cooperatives, and cooperatives formed for the purpose of recycling or treating hazardous waste that elect to incorporate under its provisions.

clauses.title: One Member, One Vote: The Default Rule and Its Narrow Exception
clauses.body: California's Cooperative Corporation Law states a one-member-one-vote rule as the governing default for member voting, in contrast to an ordinary corporation's voting power, which is generally based on the number of shares owned. The statute provides that, subject to two identified exceptions, "each member entitled to vote shall be entitled to one vote on each matter submitted to a vote of the members." This is a default that applies broadly, but it is not absolute: one of the two statutory exceptions applies specifically to a "central organization" — a cooperative whose own membership is composed, in whole or in part, of other cooperative corporations — whose articles of incorporation "may provide for unequal voting power of its members based upon the number of its members' members, the patronage of its members, or both." Even within that narrow exception, the statute preserves a voting-power floor rather than permitting it to be varied without limit: "in no event shall any member have less than one vote."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one state structures member voting for this specific corporate form — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific cooperative's voting rules, and whether a state defaults to one-member-one-vote, and how freely that default can be varied, varies by state. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 12480 and Cal. Corp. Code § 12314, and are treated as two independent sources; the statute's other referenced exception, Cal. Corp. Code § 12484 (governing cumulative voting, chiefly for central organizations), was located but is not independently quoted here. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine the voting rules that apply to any specific cooperative corporation's members, and does not determine whether any specific cooperative qualifies as a "central organization" under this statute.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 12480
citations.cite: California Cooperative Corporation Law, default one-member-one-vote rule
citations.quote: Except as provided in Sections 12314 and 12484, each member entitled to vote shall be entitled to one vote on each matter submitted to a vote of the members.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 12314
citations.cite: California Cooperative Corporation Law, unequal voting power exception for central organizations, with a one-vote floor
citations.quote: The articles of incorporation of a central organization, as defined in Section 12256, organized under or subject to this part may provide for unequal voting power of its members based upon the number of its members’ members, the patronage of its members, or both. In no event shall any member have less than one vote.

clauses.title: Patronage Dividends: The Statutory Basis and Definition of "Patronage"
clauses.body: California's Cooperative Corporation Law ties the distribution of a cooperative's net earnings to members' patronage — their business done with the cooperative — rather than to their capital investment. The statute defining a cooperative corporation's core purpose states that "the earnings, savings, or benefits of the corporation shall be used for the general welfare of the members or shall be proportionately and equitably distributed to some or all of its members or its patrons, based upon their patronage of the corporation, in the form of cash, property, evidences of indebtedness, capital credits, memberships, or services." A separate section of the same part supplies the statutory measure of "patronage" itself: for a cooperative organized to provide goods or services, "'[p]atronage' of a patron is measured by the volume or value, or both, of a patron's purchases of products from, and use of services furnished by, the corporation, and by products and services provided by the patron to the corporation for marketing" — with a separate, work-based measure supplied elsewhere in the same section for worker cooperatives.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one state's own statutory basis for patronage-based distribution and its own definition of "patronage" for this specific corporate form — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific cooperative's distributions, and how a state defines and measures patronage, if at all, varies by state. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 12201 and Cal. Corp. Code § 12243(a)(2); the quoted sentence from § 12201 is a different sentence of that same section than the one quoted in this document's definition-and-purpose clause, and § 12243 contains a further subsection, (b), addressing the separate patronage measure for worker cooperatives, which is not independently quoted here. This document is informational only: it does not itself calculate, declare, or distribute any patronage dividend or refund for any specific cooperative, and does not address the separate question of the federal income tax treatment of patronage dividends.

citations.quote: The earnings, savings, or benefits of the corporation shall be used for the general welfare of the members or shall be proportionately and equitably distributed to some or all of its members or its patrons, based upon their patronage (Section 12243) of the corporation, in the form of cash, property, evidences of indebtedness, capital credits, memberships, or services.

clauses.title: Limits on Distributions: The Statutory Cap on Return Payable for Capital Contributions
clauses.body: California's Cooperative Corporation Law caps the annual return a cooperative may pay on members' capital contributions, a limit that has no counterpart for an ordinary for-profit corporation's payments to its shareholders. The statute provides that "distributions in any fiscal year shall not exceed 15 percent, multiplied by contributions (whether by membership fees, capital credits, or otherwise) to capital." This cap applies to a specifically defined term, and that definition is itself narrower than it might first appear: a separate section defines "distribution," for purposes of this cap, to mean "the distribution of any gains, profits or dividends to any member as such, but does not include patronage distributions." Read together, the 15-percent cap constrains what a cooperative pays as a return on capital contributed by its members, while leaving patronage-based distributions — the earnings distributed based on members' business done with the cooperative, discussed elsewhere in this document — outside that specific statutory ceiling.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one state's own numeric cap on capital-return distributions for this specific corporate form — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific cooperative's distributions, and whether a state caps the return payable on capital contributions, and at what rate, varies by state. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 12451 and Cal. Corp. Code § 12235, and are treated as two independent sources. A related, separately enacted section, Cal. Corp. Code § 12453, also restricts a cooperative's ability to make patronage distributions out of earnings attributable to business with nonmembers, and to redeem memberships, when the cooperative is or would become unable to meet its liabilities as they mature — that solvency-linked restriction was located but is not independently quoted or relied upon in this clause. This document could not verify, and accordingly does not state, any separate statutory cap on the volume or proportion of business a California cooperative corporation may transact with nonmembers as such; no such numeric limit was found in the sections of this statute reviewed, and that sub-topic is omitted here rather than guessed at. This document is informational only: it does not itself calculate or authorize any specific distribution for any specific cooperative.

citations.quote: Distributions (Section 12235) in any fiscal year shall not exceed 15 percent, multiplied by contributions (whether by membership fees, capital credits, or otherwise) to capital.

clauses.title: Required Content of Cooperative Corporation Articles of Incorporation
clauses.body: California's Cooperative Corporation Law adds required content to a cooperative's articles of incorporation on top of what an ordinary corporation's articles must contain, including a mandatory statement identifying the entity as a cooperative and disclosing how member voting power and proprietary interests are structured. The statute lists what the articles "shall set forth," including the corporation's name and required agent and address information, and further requires "the following statement: 'This corporation is a cooperative corporation organized under the Cooperative Corporation Law. The purpose of this corporation is to engage in any lawful act or activity for which a corporation may be organized under the law.'" The same list requires the articles to disclose "[w]hether the voting power or the proprietary interests of the members are equal or unequal," and, if unequal, to state the general rule for determining them or that the rule will be set in the bylaws. Separately, the statute governs use of the word "cooperative" itself in a corporate name: "the names of all corporations formed under this part shall include 'cooperative,'" and no corporation may adopt that word as part of its name unless incorporated under this part or under one of several other specifically listed cooperative-type statutes.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one state's own required formation-document content for this specific corporate form — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific cooperative's formation, and required articles content for a cooperative corporation varies by state. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 12310 and Cal. Corp. Code § 12311(a), and are treated as two independent sources; § 12310 contains further subsections, including an optional worker-cooperative election under subdivision (g), that are not independently quoted here. Notably, the naming statute's own text (§ 12311(b)) cross-references a separate body of law for a different, related cooperative form: it excepts from its restriction a corporation "incorporated as a nonprofit cooperative association under Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 54001) of Division 20 of the Food and Agricultural Code" — confirming that California's agricultural cooperatives are organized under the Food and Agricultural Code rather than under the Corporations Code Cooperative Corporation Law covered in this document; this document does not address that separate agricultural-cooperative statute. This document is informational only: it does not itself draft, file, or submit articles of incorporation for any specific cooperative, and does not itself elect any optional statutory provision, such as worker-cooperative status, on behalf of any corporation.

(b) The following statement: “This corporation is a cooperative corporation organized under the Cooperative Corporation Law. The purpose of this corporation is to engage in any lawful act or activity for which a corporation may be organized under the law.”
