clauses.title: Cooperative Corporation Incorporator Signature
Common Interest Development Formation — Introduction and Scope
clauses.body: This information sheet describes, in general terms, how a common interest development is created under California's Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act, Civil Code § 4000 et seq. It concerns a proposed or existing common interest development to be known as {{projectName}}, located at or encompassing {{propertyAddress}} in {{county}} County, California, to be created (or previously created) by {{declarantName}} as declarant. This document addresses formation — the statutory definition of a common interest development, the recorded declaration that creates it, the recording steps that bring it into existence, the requirement that an association be formed to manage it, and the association's statutory authority to levy assessments once formed. It is distinct from, and does not address, a seller's document-disclosure obligations to a buyer of an existing separate interest (Civil Code § 4525 et seq.) or an association's lien and foreclosure remedies for delinquent assessments (Civil Code §§ 5650–5740), both addressed in other documents in this library. This sheet is informational only. It does not itself create a common interest development, does not record any document, does not form or incorporate any association, and does not determine whether any specific declaration, condominium plan, map, articles, bylaws, or assessment described in connection with {{projectName}} complies with the statutory requirements it describes.

clauses.title: The Statutory Definition of a Common Interest Development
clauses.body: California law defines "common interest development" as a specific, closed list of four project types — not a general catch-all for any residential development with shared ownership or a homeowners association. Civil Code § 4100 provides: "'Common interest development' means any of the following: (a) A community apartment project. (b) A condominium project. (c) A planned development. (d) A stock cooperative." Each of these four terms is itself separately defined elsewhere in the Act. Whether the project contemplated in connection with {{projectName}} falls within one of these four statutory categories, and which one, is a factual and legal question this document does not resolve.
clauses.gap: Both quoted sentences come from the same statutory section, Civil Code § 4100; they are not independent sections corroborating each other, though the closing sentence enumerating subdivisions (a) through (d) is itself the complete operative definition, not an excerpt combined from elsewhere. This document does not separately quote the individual definitions of "community apartment project," "condominium project," "planned development," or "stock cooperative" (found at Civil Code §§ 4105, 4125, 4175, and 4190, respectively) beyond what this clause's companion clauses touch on for condominium projects; a reader needing the precise statutory definition of one of the other three categories should consult that section directly. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act's threshold definition — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific project; other states define comparable development types differently or not at all.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4100 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: “Common interest development” means any of the following:

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4100(a)-(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) A community apartment project. (b) A condominium project. (c) A planned development. (d) A stock cooperative.

clauses.title: The Declaration — Definition and Required Statutory Content
clauses.body: The declaration is the foundational recorded document that establishes a common interest development's covenants, conditions, and restrictions. Civil Code § 4135 defines it: "'Declaration' means the document, however denominated, that contains the information required by Sections 4250 and 4255." Civil Code § 4250(a) states what a declaration recorded on or after January 1, 1986 must contain: "A declaration, recorded on or after January 1, 1986, shall contain a legal description of the common interest development, and a statement that the common interest development is a community apartment project, condominium project, planned development, stock cooperative, or combination thereof. The declaration shall additionally set forth the name of the association and the restrictions on the use or enjoyment of any portion of the common interest development that are intended to be enforceable equitable servitudes." Beyond that required minimum, § 4250(b) permits the declaration to address other matters: "The declaration may contain any other matters the declarant or the members consider appropriate." If a declaration for {{projectName}} has been recorded, its recording information is stated as: {{declarationRecordingInfo}}.
clauses.gap: The definition in Civil Code § 4135 cross-references two sections — § 4250 and § 4255 — as together supplying a declaration's required content; this clause quotes § 4250(a)'s general content requirements (legal description, project-type statement, association name, and enforceable-restriction language) but does not quote § 4255, which requires additional, narrower notice language only when the project is located within a statutorily defined airport influence area or within the San Francisco Bay Conservation and Development Commission's jurisdiction — conditions that will not apply to every project. The citations to § 4135 and § 4250(a)-(b) are to two separate statutory sections; § 4250(a) and (b) are subsections of the same section, quoted together because (b) clarifies that (a)'s list is a floor, not a ceiling, on permissible content. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act's declaration requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific project, and not a determination that any specific declaration recorded or proposed for the development named in this document in fact contains the statutorily required content.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4250(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: A declaration, recorded on or after January 1, 1986, shall contain a legal description of the common interest development, and a statement that the common interest development is a community apartment project, condominium project, planned development, stock cooperative, or combination thereof. The declaration shall additionally set forth the name of the association and the restrictions on the use or enjoyment of any portion of the common interest development that are intended to be enforceable equitable servitudes.

clauses.title: Formation Mechanics — What Must Be Recorded to Create the CID
clauses.body: A common interest development is not created merely by a declarant's intent, a marketing plan, or an unrecorded set of restrictions; the Act ties formation to specific recorded documents. Civil Code § 4200 provides: "This act applies and a common interest development is created whenever a separate interest coupled with an interest in the common area or membership in the association is, or has been, conveyed, provided all of the following are recorded: (a) A declaration. (b) A condominium plan, if any exists. (c) A final map or parcel map, if Division 2 (commencing with Section 66410) of Title 7 of the Government Code requires the recording of either a final map or parcel map for the common interest development." Where the project is a condominium project, the recorded condominium plan referenced in § 4200(b) has its own required content: Civil Code § 4285 provides that "[a] condominium plan shall contain all of the following: (a) A description or survey map of a condominium project, which shall refer to or show monumentation on the ground." If a condominium plan and/or final or parcel map affecting {{projectName}} has been recorded, its recording information is stated as: {{conditionsRecordingInfo}}.
clauses.gap: Civil Code § 4200 is the operative formation trigger — it does not, by itself, describe everything a condominium plan must contain; that additional content requirement (a description or survey map, a three-dimensional description sufficient to identify the common area and each separate interest, and a signed consent certificate) comes from a separate section, Civil Code § 4285, of which this clause quotes only subdivision (a) as illustrative; subdivisions (b) and (c) of § 4285 (the three-dimensional description and consent-certificate requirements) and § 4290 (who must sign that certificate) are not quoted here. The citations to § 4200 and § 4285 are to two separate statutory sections. This clause does not address whether a final map or parcel map is required for the development named in this document under the Subdivision Map Act (Government Code § 66410 et seq.), which § 4200(c) itself cross-references and which this document does not independently research. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act's formation-by-recording requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific project, and not a determination that any specific recording for that development has occurred or was effective to create a common interest development.

citations.quote: This act applies and a common interest development is created whenever a separate interest coupled with an interest in the common area or membership in the association is, or has been, conveyed, provided all of the following are recorded: (a) A declaration. (b) A condominium plan, if any exists. (c) A final map or parcel map, if Division 2 (commencing with Section 66410) of Title 7 of the Government Code requires the recording of either a final map or parcel map for the common interest development.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4285(a) (California Legislative Information text)

clauses.title: The Association's Mandatory Formation and What Governs It
clauses.body: California law does not leave it optional whether a common interest development has a managing association — it requires one. Civil Code § 4800 provides: "A common interest development shall be managed by an association that may be incorporated or unincorporated. The association may be referred to as an owners' association or a community association." The association's own governance is not left to informal practice; it is defined by a specific set of "governing documents." Civil Code § 4150 provides: "'Governing documents' means the declaration and any other documents, such as bylaws, operating rules, articles of incorporation, or articles of association, which govern the operation of the common interest development or association." If {{projectName}}'s association is to be, or has been, formed as {{associationName}}, and if it is or is intended to be incorporated, that status is stated as: {{associationIncorporationStatus}}.
clauses.gap: Civil Code § 4800 establishes only that an association — incorporated or unincorporated — must exist to manage the development; it does not itself prescribe the content of that association's bylaws or articles. This clause instead relies on Civil Code § 4150's definition of "governing documents," which identifies bylaws, operating rules, and articles of incorporation or association as the categories of documents that govern the association's operation, without reproducing any one of those documents' own required content in full; a reader needing the specific statutory content required of an incorporated association's articles of incorporation should consult Civil Code § 4280 separately, which this clause does not quote. The citations to § 4800 and § 4150 are to two separate statutory sections. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act's mandatory-association requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific project, and not a determination that any specific association formed or proposed in connection with the development named in this document has been validly incorporated or organized.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4150 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: “Governing documents” means the declaration and any other documents, such as bylaws, operating rules, articles of incorporation, or articles of association, which govern the operation of the common interest development or association.

clauses.title: Assessments — The Formation-Stage Statutory Basis for the Power to Levy
clauses.body: Once a common interest development and its association exist, California law imposes an affirmative statutory duty on the association to levy assessments, and separately caps what it may charge. Civil Code § 5600(a) provides: "Except as provided in Section 5605, the association shall levy regular and special assessments sufficient to perform its obligations under the governing documents and this act." Section 5600(b) adds a limiting principle: "An association shall not impose or collect an assessment or fee that exceeds the amount necessary to defray the costs for which it is levied." This clause addresses only the association's underlying statutory authority and duty to levy assessments once the common interest development and association are formed; it does not address how an unpaid assessment becomes a recorded, enforceable lien against a specific owner's separate interest, the pre-lien notice an association must give, lien priority, or the foreclosure process — all addressed in this library's separate HOA Assessment Lien and Foreclosure information sheet, which governs collection and enforcement rather than formation-stage authority.
clauses.gap: Both quoted provisions are subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code § 5600(a) and (b); they are not independent sections corroborating each other, and are disclosed together here because they state, respectively, the duty to levy and the limit on how much may be levied. Section 5600(a) itself cross-references Civil Code § 5605, which sets a percentage cap on year-over-year increases in regular assessments and on aggregate special assessments absent membership approval; this clause does not quote § 5605, since the annual-increase cap is a procedural constraint on an already-operating association's later assessment decisions, not part of the formation-stage authority to levy in the first instance that this clause addresses. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act's assessment-levy authority — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific project, and not a determination of whether any specific assessment levied or proposed by the association named in this document in fact complies with these or other statutory requirements.

clauses.body: This Formation Statement is prepared by {{declarantName}}, as declarant, in connection with the proposed or existing common interest development known as {{projectName}}, located at or encompassing {{propertyAddress}} in {{county}} County, California. The development is stated to be a: {{cidCategory}}. The association to be formed or already formed to manage the development is stated to be: {{associationName}}. This statement records, for reference, background information about the intended or completed formation of {{projectName}} as a common interest development under California's Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act. clauses.title: Bereavement Leave Entitlement
clauses.body: Under California law, it is an unlawful employment practice for a covered employer to refuse a covered employee's request to take up to five days of bereavement leave upon the death of a family member. The five days need not be taken consecutively. For this purpose, "family member" means a spouse, child, parent, sibling, grandparent, grandchild, domestic partner, or parent-in-law.
clauses.gap: Five days is a ceiling this statute sets, not a floor every workplace defaults to in the same way — how those days interact with an employer's own bereavement policy is a separate question addressed elsewhere in this document. The statute's family-member list is mostly self-defining, but "parent-in-law" is defined by cross-reference to the California Family Rights Act (Gov. Code § 12945.2); that cross-referenced CFRA definition was not independently fetched or verified for this document, so it isn't restated here. This document also doesn't cover a separate carve-out in the statute for employees covered by certain collective bargaining agreements that already provide equivalent bereavement leave.

citations.quote: It shall be an unlawful employment practice for an employer to refuse to grant a request by any employee to take up to five days of bereavement leave upon the death of a family member.

clauses.title: Employer Coverage
clauses.body: This bereavement leave requirement applies to an "employer," defined as a person who employs five or more persons to perform services for a wage or salary, as well as to the state and any of its political or civil subdivisions, including cities and counties.
clauses.gap: The five-employee threshold tracks the general coverage threshold used elsewhere in California's Fair Employment and Housing Act, of which this section is part, but this document doesn't verify that every other FEHA provision uses an identical threshold — only that this specific bereavement leave provision does.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7(a)(2), definition of “employer”
citations.quote: “Employer” means either of the following: (A) A person who employs five or more persons to perform services for a wage or salary. (B) The state and any political or civil subdivision of the state, including, but not limited to, cities and counties.

clauses.title: Employee Eligibility
clauses.body: For purposes of this leave, an "employee" is a person who has been employed by the employer for at least 30 days before the leave begins. The statute separately excludes from this definition a person covered by Government Code section 19859.3.
clauses.gap: This document verified and quotes the 30-day threshold and the fact of the section 19859.3 exclusion directly from the statute, but did not separately fetch or verify the text of section 19859.3 itself, so it doesn't describe what that excluded category covers.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7(a)(1)(A), definition of “employee”
citations.quote: “Employee” means a person employed by the employer for at least 30 days prior to the commencement of the leave.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7(a)(1)(B), exclusion from “employee” definition
citations.quote: “Employee” does not include a person who is covered by Section 19859.3.

clauses.title: Timing and Paid/Unpaid Status
clauses.body: The bereavement leave must be completed within three months of the family member's date of death. The leave is taken under the employer's own existing bereavement leave policy, if it has one. If the employer has no existing bereavement leave policy, the leave may be unpaid, except that the employee may use vacation, personal leave, accrued and available sick leave, or compensatory time off that is otherwise available.
clauses.gap: This is a floor, not a formula for every scenario: the statute separately addresses what happens when an employer's existing policy provides fewer than five days of paid leave, or fewer than five days of unpaid leave, topping each up to a five-day minimum in different ways — those blending rules aren't restated in this clause. The statute doesn't create a freestanding state-paid bereavement benefit; payment, where it exists, comes from the employer's own policy or the employee's own accrued paid leave.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7(d), timing of leave
citations.quote: The bereavement leave shall be completed within three months of the date of death of the family member.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7(e)(1)-(2), paid/unpaid status
citations.quote: The bereavement leave shall be taken pursuant to any existing bereavement leave policy of the employer.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7(e)(2), default unpaid status absent an employer policy
citations.quote: If there is no existing bereavement leave policy, the bereavement leave may be unpaid, except that an employee may use vacation, personal leave, accrued and available sick leave, or compensatory time off that is otherwise available to the employee.

clauses.title: Documentation of Death
clauses.body: If the employer requests it within 30 days of the first day of leave, the employee must provide documentation of the family member's death. "Documentation" includes, but isn't limited to, a death certificate, a published obituary, or written verification of death, burial, or memorial services from a mortuary, funeral home, burial society, crematorium, religious institution, or governmental agency. The employer must maintain the confidentiality of any employee requesting this leave, and any documentation the employee provides must be kept confidential and disclosed only to internal personnel or counsel as necessary, or as otherwise required by law.
clauses.gap: The statute gives examples of acceptable documentation rather than a fixed, exclusive list ("includes, but is not limited to"), so what satisfies a given employer's request beyond those examples is not fixed by this text alone.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7(f), documentation the employer may require
citations.quote: The employee, if requested by the employer, within 30 days of the first day of the leave, shall provide documentation of the death of the family member. As used in this subdivision, “documentation” includes, but is not limited to, a death certificate, a published obituary, or written verification of death, burial, or memorial services from a mortuary, funeral home, burial society, crematorium, religious institution, or governmental agency.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7(i), confidentiality of leave request and documentation
citations.quote: The employer shall maintain the confidentiality of any employee requesting leave under this section. Any documentation provided to the employer pursuant to subdivision (f) or subdivision (g) shall be maintained as confidential and shall not be disclosed except to internal personnel or counsel, as necessary, or as required by law.

clauses.title: No Retaliation or Discrimination
clauses.body: This same statute makes it a separate unlawful employment practice for an employer to refuse to hire, or to discharge, demote, fine, suspend, expel, or discriminate against, an individual because that individual exercised the right to bereavement leave, or gave information or testimony about their own or someone else's bereavement leave in a related inquiry or proceeding. It is likewise unlawful for an employer to interfere with, restrain, or deny the exercise of, or the attempt to exercise, any right this section provides.
clauses.gap: This anti-retaliation protection is written directly into this bereavement leave statute itself (Gov. Code § 12945.7(g)-(h)) — it is not solely a byproduct of FEHA's general anti-retaliation provisions elsewhere in the code, though it operates as an unlawful employment practice within that same statutory scheme.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7(g), retaliation for exercising or discussing bereavement leave rights
citations.quote: It shall be an unlawful employment practice for an employer to refuse to hire, or to discharge, demote, fine, suspend, expel, or discriminate against, an individual because of either of the following: (1) An individual’s exercise of the right to bereavement leave provided by subdivision (b). (2) An individual’s giving information or testimony as to their own bereavement leave, or another person’s bereavement leave, in an inquiry or proceeding related to rights guaranteed under this section.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7(h), interference with the right to bereavement leave
citations.quote: It shall be an unlawful employment practice for an employer to interfere with, restrain, or deny the exercise of, or the attempt to exercise, any right provided under this section.

clauses.title: Bereavement Leave Request
clauses.body:
{{employeeName}} requests bereavement leave from {{companyName}} as described below.

Family member (relationship): _______________________________________________
Date of death: _______________
Dates of leave requested (need not be consecutive): _______________________________________________
Total days requested (up to 5): _______________
Documentation of death, if requested by {{companyName}} within 30 days of the first day of leave, will be provided separately.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Military Service / Leave Declaration
Right to Reemployment After Service
clauses.body: Under the federal Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act (USERRA), {{employeeName}} is entitled to reemployment with {{companyName}} after a period of service in the uniformed services if: advance written or verbal notice of the service was given to {{companyName}} (unless notice was precluded by military necessity or was otherwise impossible or unreasonable); the cumulative length of this and all previous service-related absences from employment with {{companyName}} does not exceed five years (subject to statutory exceptions to that cap); and {{employeeName}} reports back to work or applies for reemployment within the time limits the statute sets, which vary by the length of the service period. This reemployment right also depends on the character of {{employeeName}}'s discharge from the uniformed service not being dishonorable, bad-conduct, or under other-than-honorable conditions.
clauses.gap: This clause states the conditions for entitlement to reemployment; it doesn't determine whether a particular employee's notice, service length, or application timing actually satisfies them. The five-year cumulative service cap has several statutory exceptions not restated here (for example, service required beyond five years to complete an initial period of obligated service, or an inability to obtain release orders through no fault of the service member). Separately, an employer isn't required to reemploy someone under this law if the employer's circumstances have so changed that reemployment is impossible or unreasonable, if reemployment would impose an undue hardship in certain accommodation situations, or if the pre-service job was for a brief, nonrecurrent period with no reasonable expectation of continuing — and the employer bears the burden of proving any of those exceptions applies. This document doesn't resolve whether any of those exceptions apply to a given situation.

citations.case: 38 U.S.C. § 4312(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, USERRA reemployment rights
citations.quote: any person whose absence from a position of employment is necessitated by reason of service in the uniformed services shall be entitled to the reemployment rights and benefits and other employment benefits of this chapter if— (1) the person (or an appropriate officer of the uniformed service in which such service is performed) has given advance written or verbal notice of such service to such person’s employer; (2) the cumulative length of the absence and of all previous absences from a position of employment with that employer by reason of service in the uniformed services does not exceed five years; and (3) except as provided in subsection (f), the person reports to, or submits an application for reemployment to, such employer in accordance with the provisions of subsection (e).

citations.case: 38 U.S.C. § 4304 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, USERRA character-of-service disqualification
citations.quote: A person’s entitlement to the benefits of this chapter by reason of the service of such person in one of the uniformed services terminates upon the occurrence of any of the following events: (1) A separation of such person from such uniformed service with a dishonorable or bad conduct discharge. (2) A separation of such person from such uniformed service under other than honorable conditions, as characterized pursuant to regulations

clauses.title: The Reemployment Position — the "Escalator Principle"
clauses.body: USERRA doesn't simply return a reemployed person to the job they had before their service began. Under 38 U.S.C. § 4313, a person whose service lasted less than 91 days is generally reemployed in the position they would have been employed in had their employment not been interrupted by that service (the position they are qualified to perform); if their service lasted more than 90 days, that same rule applies, or a position of like seniority, status, and pay. Courts and the Department of Labor refer to this as the "escalator principle": {{employeeName}}'s reemployment position accounts for the seniority, status, and pay {{employeeName}} would reasonably have attained by continuing to work through the period of service, not merely a return to the pre-service job.
clauses.gap: The specific position-determination rule this clause describes covers the two most common service-length tiers. The statute sets out additional, more specific rules for a person who becomes disabled during service and cannot perform the escalator position even with reasonable accommodation, and separate rules apply to reemployment by the federal government. This document doesn't determine which tier or exception applies to a specific period of service.

citations.case: 38 U.S.C. § 4313(a)(1)-(2) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, USERRA reemployment positions
citations.quote: (1) Except as provided in paragraphs (3) and (4), in the case of a person whose period of service in the uniformed services was for less than 91 days— (A) in the position of employment in which the person would have been employed if the continuous employment of such person with the employer had not been interrupted by such service, the duties of which the person is qualified to perform; or (B) in the position of employment in which the person was employed on the date of the commencement of the service in the uniformed services , only if the person is not qualified to perform the duties of the position referred to in subparagraph (A) after reasonable efforts by the employer to qualify the person. (2) Except as provided in paragraphs (3) and (4), in the case of a person whose period of service in the uniformed services was for more than 90 days— (A) in the position of employment in which the person would have been employed if the continuous employment of such person with the employer had not been interrupted by such service, or a position of like seniority , status and pay, the duties of which the person is qualified to perform

clauses.title: Protection Against Discharge After Reemployment
clauses.body: Once {{employeeName}} is reemployed by {{companyName}} under USERRA, {{employeeName}} may not be discharged from that job except for cause for a period set by the length of the service that preceded reemployment: one year after the date of reemployment if that period of service was more than 180 days, or 180 days after the date of reemployment if that period of service was more than 30 days but less than 181 days.
clauses.gap: The statute ties this heightened for-cause protection to two specific service-length tiers — more than 180 days, and more than 30 but fewer than 181 days — and doesn't itself set a separate heightened protection period for service of 30 days or less. "For cause" is not defined by this clause; USERRA and its implementing regulations address what counts as cause elsewhere. This document doesn't determine which tier applies to a specific reemployment or whether a specific discharge decision was actually for cause.

citations.case: 38 U.S.C. § 4316(c) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, USERRA discharge protection after reemployment
citations.quote: A person who is reemployed by an employer under this chapter shall not be discharged from such employment, except for cause— (1) within one year after the date of such reemployment, if the person’s period of service before the reemployment was more than 180 days; or (2) within 180 days after the date of such reemployment, if the person’s period of service before the reemployment was more than 30 days but less than 181 days.

clauses.title: Non-Discrimination and Anti-Retaliation
clauses.body: USERRA prohibits {{companyName}} from denying {{employeeName}} initial employment, reemployment, retention in employment, promotion, or any benefit of employment because of {{employeeName}}'s membership, application for membership, performance of service, application to perform service, or obligation to perform service in a uniformed service. Separately, an employer may not discriminate or retaliate against a person because that person has taken action to enforce a USERRA protection, testified or made a statement in a USERRA proceeding, assisted or participated in a USERRA investigation, or exercised a right under USERRA — and this anti-retaliation protection applies whether or not the person has ever served in the uniformed services.
clauses.gap: Under the statute, a violation of the membership/service-basis rule is established if that status was a "motivating factor" in the employer's action, unless the employer proves it would have taken the same action anyway — this document doesn't apply that burden-shifting standard to any specific decision or determine whether service was in fact a motivating factor here.

citations.case: 38 U.S.C. § 4311(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, USERRA discrimination prohibition
citations.quote: A person who is a member of, applies to be a member of, performs, has performed, applies to perform, or has an obligation to perform service in a uniformed service shall not be denied initial employment, reemployment, retention in employment, promotion, or any benefit of employment by an employer on the basis of that membership, application for membership, performance of service, application for service, or obligation.

citations.case: 38 U.S.C. § 4311(b) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, USERRA anti-retaliation protection
citations.quote: An employer may not discriminate in employment against or take any adverse employment action or other retaliatory action against any person because such person (1) has taken an action to enforce a protection afforded any person under this chapter, (2) has testified or otherwise made a statement in or in connection with any proceeding under this chapter, (3) has assisted or otherwise participated in an investigation under this chapter, or (4) has exercised a right provided for in this chapter. The prohibition in this subsection shall apply with respect to a person regardless of whether that person has performed service in the uniformed services .

clauses.title: Continuation of Health Plan Coverage During Service
clauses.body: If {{employeeName}} (or {{employeeName}}'s dependents) has coverage under {{companyName}}'s health plan in connection with {{employeeName}}'s job, USERRA lets {{employeeName}} elect to continue that coverage during the period of absence for uniformed service. The maximum period of continued coverage under that election is the lesser of the 24-month period beginning when the absence begins, or the day after {{employeeName}} fails to apply for or return to a position of employment within USERRA's applicable time limits. A person who elects continued coverage may be required to pay up to 102% of the full premium, except that a person who serves less than 31 days may not be charged more than the employee's normal share, if any.
clauses.gap: This describes the maximum continuation period and premium cap set by the statute itself; it doesn't state every rule governing multiemployer health plans or how liability for continued coverage is allocated between employers and plans in that setting, which the statute addresses separately.

citations.case: 38 U.S.C. § 4317(a)(1)-(2) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, USERRA health plan continuation
citations.quote: The maximum period of coverage of a person and the person’s dependents under such an election shall be the lesser of— (A) the 24-month period beginning on the date on which the person’s absence begins; or (B) the day after the date on which the person fails to apply for or return to a position of employment, as determined under section 4312(e). (2) A person who elects to continue health-plan coverage under this paragraph may be required to pay not more than 102 percent of the full premium under the plan (determined in the same manner as the applicable premium under section 4980B(f)(4) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 ) associated with such coverage for the employer’s other employees, except that in the case of a person who performs service in the uniformed services for less than 31 days, such person may not be required to pay more than the employee share, if any, for such coverage.

clauses.title: How USERRA Is Enforced
clauses.body: A person who believes their USERRA rights have been violated may file a written complaint with the Secretary of Labor, who investigates it through the Department of Labor's Veterans' Employment and Training Service (VETS). If that effort to resolve the complaint against a state or private employer is unsuccessful, the person may ask the Secretary to refer the complaint to the U.S. Attorney General, who may choose to represent the person and sue on their behalf. Separately, a person may bring their own private lawsuit for USERRA relief against a state or private employer — without going through the Secretary or Attorney General at all, or after declining referral to the Attorney General, or after being refused representation by the Attorney General.
clauses.gap: This describes the enforcement path for complaints against a state (as employer) or a private employer. USERRA sets out a separate enforcement mechanism, not described here, for complaints against the federal government as employer or against the Office of Personnel Management. This document doesn't evaluate the merits of any particular complaint.

citations.case: 38 U.S.C. § 4321 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, USERRA reemployment assistance through VETS
citations.quote: The Secretary (through the Veterans’ Employment and Training Service) shall provide assistance to any person with respect to the employment and reemployment rights and benefits to which such person is entitled under this chapter.

citations.case: 38 U.S.C. § 4323(a)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, USERRA referral to the Attorney General and private right of action
citations.quote: A person who receives from the Secretary a notification pursuant to section 4322(e) of this title of an unsuccessful effort to resolve a complaint relating to a State (as an employer) or a private employer may request that the Secretary refer the complaint to the Attorney General. Not later than 60 days after the Secretary receives such a request with respect to a complaint, the Secretary shall refer the complaint to the Attorney General. If the Attorney General is reasonably satisfied that the person on whose behalf the complaint is referred is entitled to the rights or benefits sought, the Attorney General may appear on behalf of, and act as attorney for, the person on whose behalf the complaint is submitted and commence an action for relief under this chapter for such person.

citations.case: 38 U.S.C. § 4323(a)(3) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, USERRA private right of action
citations.quote: A person may commence an action for relief with respect to a complaint against a State (as an employer) or a private employer if the person— (A) has chosen not to apply to the Secretary for assistance under section 4322(a) of this title ; (B) has chosen not to request that the Secretary refer the complaint to the Attorney General under paragraph (1); or (C) has been refused representation by the Attorney General with respect to the complaint under such paragraph.

clauses.title: USERRA Information Acknowledgment and Signature
Proposed Petitioner — Information and Declaration in Support of Ancillary Petition
clauses.body: I, {{petitionerName}}, am {{relationshipToDecedent}} of {{decedentName}}, who died on {{dateOfDeath}} while domiciled in {{domiciliaryState}}. {{decedentName}}'s estate is the subject of a primary probate or estate administration proceeding outside California: {{domiciliaryCourtInfo}}. {{decedentName}} also owned real property located in California, described as: {{californiaPropertyDescription}}. This declaration provides background information for use with an actual petition for ancillary administration, to be filed in the California superior court for {{countyOfFiling}} under Probate Code Part 13 (commencing with Section 12500), for probate of {{decedentName}}'s will and/or appointment of a California personal representative with respect to the California property described above. The character and estimated value of that California property is: {{estimatedEstateValue}}. This declaration is not itself a court filing, and signing it does not open an ancillary administration proceeding, admit any will to probate in California, appoint {{petitionerName}} — or anyone else — as a California personal representative, or transfer or distribute any interest in the California property described above. Only a California court order issued after the statutory ancillary petition, notice, and hearing process described in this document can do that, and only the subsequent issuance of California letters gives a California personal representative actual authority to act with respect to the California property.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment Block — Ancillary Probate Information Sheet
clauses.body:
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{petitionerName}}: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet is prepared for use alongside an actual petition for ancillary administration filed with the California superior court under Probate Code Part 13 (commencing with Section 12500). It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete that petition, and it does not open an ancillary administration proceeding, admit a will to probate in California, appoint a California personal representative, or transfer or distribute any interest in California property; only a California court order, followed by the issuance of California letters, does that.]

clauses.title: Why a Separate California Proceeding Is Needed — Property Location, Not a Free-Standing 'Situs' Statute
clauses.body: Real property is generally administered, for probate purposes, under the law of the state where it is physically located, regardless of the decedent's domicile — a principle usually described as the property's "situs." California's Probate Code does not contain a single section that states this situs principle as a free-standing rule; instead, California implements it through its jurisdiction and venue provisions. Probate Code § 7051 provides that if {{decedentName}} was domiciled in California at the time of death, the proper county for estate-administration proceedings is the county of {{decedentName}}'s domicile, regardless of where {{decedentName}} died. Probate Code § 7052 supplies the converse rule for a nondomiciliary decedent: if {{decedentName}} was not domiciled in California at the time of death, the proper county for proceedings under the Probate Code is instead tied to where {{decedentName}} died (if property is located in that county) or, otherwise, to any county in which {{decedentName}}'s property is located — venue that turns on property location rather than domicile. Probate Code § 12505 in turn defines a "nondomiciliary decedent," for purposes of the ancillary administration provisions discussed elsewhere in this document, as "a person who dies domiciled in a sister state or foreign nation."
clauses.gap: This corrects an assumption in the original research brief: California's Probate Code does not state the situs principle as an explicit, free-standing declarative rule (e.g., a section reading "real property is governed by the law of the state where located"); the principle is instead implemented structurally, through the jurisdiction and venue provisions cited here (§§ 7051-7052) and the ancillary-administration framework described in this document's other clauses. This document does not independently verify a California case establishing the situs principle as a matter of common law or conflict-of-laws doctrine; it relies solely on how these statutory venue provisions are written. This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of California's own venue rules for estate administration — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's property, and not a claim that California's ancillary administration provisions apply to a California domiciliary's property located in a different state (that question is governed by the other state's law, not California's Probate Code, and is outside the scope of this document, which addresses only California as the ancillary jurisdiction). This clause cites three different statutory sections (§ 7051, § 7052, and § 12505); no single section is cited more than once in this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 7051 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 7051
citations.quote: If the decedent was domiciled in this state at the time of death, the proper county for proceedings concerning administration of the decedent’s estate is the county in which the decedent was domiciled, regardless of where the decedent died.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 7052 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 7052
citations.quote: If the decedent was not domiciled in this state at the time of death, the proper county for proceedings under this code concerning the administration of the decedent’s estate is one of the following: (a) If property of the nondomiciliary decedent is located in the county in which the nondomiciliary decedent died, the county in which the nondomiciliary decedent died. (b) If no property of the nondomiciliary decedent is located in the county in which the nondomiciliary decedent died or if the nondomiciliary decedent did not die in this state, any county in which property of the nondomiciliary decedent is located, regardless of where the nondomiciliary decedent died.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 12505 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: “Nondomiciliary decedent” means a person who dies domiciled in a sister state or foreign nation.

clauses.title: California's Ancillary Administration Procedure — Who May Petition, and What Must (and Need Not) Be Shown
clauses.body: Probate Code § 12501 defines "ancillary administration" as "proceedings in this state for administration of the estate of a nondomiciliary decedent." Probate Code § 12510 provides that any interested person, or a sister state or foreign nation personal representative, may commence an ancillary administration proceeding in California by a petition to the court for either or both of: probate of {{decedentName}}'s will, and appointment of a local (California) personal representative. Where {{decedentName}}'s will has already been admitted to probate in the sister state or foreign nation of domicile, Probate Code § 12520(a) allows that will to be probated in the California ancillary proceeding under a separate, comity-based procedure described elsewhere in Part 13 of the Probate Code; where the will has not been admitted to probate elsewhere, or does not satisfy that procedure's requirements, § 12520(b) provides that the will may instead be probated in the ancillary proceeding under the same general procedure — Part 2 of Division 7, commencing with Section 8000 — that governs an ordinary California probate petition.
clauses.gap: This corrects an assumption in the original research brief: § 12510's own text does not require the petitioner to show, as a precondition to commencing a California ancillary administration proceeding, that a domiciliary or primary probate proceeding has already been opened (or completed) in the decedent's state or country of domicile. A domiciliary proceeding's existence and outcome matter for two narrower, related purposes addressed elsewhere in this document: whether the streamlined comity procedure of § 12520(a) is available for probating a will already admitted elsewhere, and who has statutory priority to be appointed as the California ancillary personal representative. The ancillary petition under § 12510 itself, however, may be commenced by any interested person, or by a sister state or foreign nation personal representative, without a threshold showing that a domiciliary proceeding exists. This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of California's own ancillary-administration procedure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate, and not a claim that any specific estate qualifies for or requires this procedure. This clause cites three different statutory sections (§ 12501, § 12510, and § 12520); no single section is cited more than once in this clause. This document is informational: it does not itself open an ancillary administration proceeding, admit any will to probate in California, or appoint any personal representative — only a California court order issued after the statutory petition, notice, and hearing process can do that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 12501 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: “Ancillary administration” means proceedings in this state for administration of the estate of a nondomiciliary decedent.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 12510 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Any interested person, or a sister state or foreign nation personal representative, may commence an ancillary administration proceeding by a petition to the court for either or both of the following: (a) Probate of the nondomiciliary decedent’s will. (b) Appointment of a local personal representative.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 12520 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) If a nondomiciliary decedent’s will has been admitted to probate in a sister state or foreign nation and satisfies the requirements of this article, probate of the will in an ancillary administration proceeding is governed by this article. (b) If a nondomiciliary decedent’s will has been admitted to probate in a sister state or foreign nation, but does not satisfy the requirements of this article, the will may be probated in an ancillary administration proceeding pursuant to Part 2 (commencing with Section 8000).

clauses.title: The California Ancillary Personal Representative's Authority, and Priority for Appointment
clauses.body: Probate Code § 12530 provides that, except to the extent Part 13 of the Probate Code otherwise provides, ancillary administration of {{decedentName}}'s estate "is subject to all other provisions of this code concerning the administration of the decedent's estate, including, but not limited to, opening estate administration, inventory and appraisal, creditor claims, estate management, independent administration, compensation, accounts, payment of debts, distribution, and closing estate administration." Probate Code § 12512 similarly provides that notice of an ancillary administration proceeding is given, and the same proceedings are had, as in an ordinary California probate of a will or appointment of a personal representative for a person who died domiciled in California — except as Article 2 (the will-probate procedure discussed elsewhere in this document, commencing with § 12520) otherwise provides. On the question of who is appointed, § 12513 gives a specific priority: if {{decedentName}} died while domiciled in a sister state, a personal representative already appointed by a court of {{decedentName}}'s domicile has priority over all other persons for appointment as the California ancillary personal representative — except where {{decedentName}}'s will nominates a different person for that California role — and that domiciliary personal representative may instead nominate another person to serve, with that nominee taking the same priority.
clauses.gap: This clause addresses the ancillary personal representative's authority and duties relative to the domiciliary representative's role: California's default rule is that the California ancillary personal representative exercises the same general powers, and is subject to the same general duties, as any other California personal representative under the Probate Code (§ 12530), rather than a categorically narrower or different set of powers — subject only to the specific modifications Part 13 makes elsewhere, including the priority rule described here and the distribution rule addressed in a separate clause of this document. This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of California's own ancillary-administration procedure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate. This clause cites three different statutory sections (§ 12530, § 12512, and § 12513); no single section is cited more than once in this clause. This document is informational: it does not itself appoint any personal representative or determine priority for any specific estate — only a California court order does that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 12530 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Except to the extent otherwise provided in this chapter, ancillary administration of a decedent’s estate is subject to all other provisions of this code concerning the administration of the decedent’s estate, including, but not limited to, opening estate administration, inventory and appraisal, creditor claims, estate management, independent administration, compensation, accounts, payment of debts, distribution, and closing estate administration.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 12512 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Notice of an ancillary administration proceeding shall be given and, except as provided in Article 2 (commencing with Section 12520), the same proceedings had as in the case of a petition for probate of a will or appointment of a personal representative of a person who dies domiciled in this state.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 12513 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: If the decedent dies while domiciled in a sister state, a personal representative appointed by a court of the decedent’s domicile has priority over all other persons except where the decedent’s will nominates a different person to be the personal representative in this state. The sister state personal representative may nominate another person as personal representative and the nominee has the same priority as the sister state personal representative.

clauses.title: Distribution of California Assets After Ancillary Administration — Two Statutory Paths, Not One
clauses.body: California's Probate Code provides for two distinct paths by which {{decedentName}}'s California assets can be distributed following ancillary administration. By default, under Probate Code § 12530, distribution of {{decedentName}}'s California property proceeds under the general Probate Code distribution provisions applicable to any California estate — that is, under {{decedentName}}'s will or, if {{decedentName}} died intestate, under California's intestate succession rules — the same as in an ordinary, non-ancillary probate. Separately, Probate Code § 12540(a) gives the court discretion, in an ancillary administration proceeding, to instead order preliminary or final distribution of all or part of {{decedentName}}'s personal property located in California to the sister state personal representative, "if distribution is in the best interest of the estate or interested persons." Where distribution to the sister state personal representative is necessary, § 12541 allows real property in {{decedentName}}'s estate to be sold, with the court ordering the sale proceeds — rather than the real property itself — distributed to the sister state personal representative, using the same procedures that apply to other sales of a decedent's real property. Finally, § 12542 provides that if the estate in {{decedentName}}'s sister state of domicile is insolvent, distribution of the property described in this article may be made only to the sister state personal representative, and not directly to beneficiaries.
clauses.gap: This corrects an assumption embedded in the original research brief's framing (direct distribution under the will or intestate succession, versus transmission to the domiciliary representative, as though only one applies): both paths exist under California law, and which one a court uses is discretionary rather than automatic. The default, absent a court order under Article 4, is direct California distribution under § 12530's general rule; transmission of personal property (or real property sale proceeds) to the sister state personal representative under §§ 12540-12542 requires an affirmative court finding that it serves the best interest of the estate or interested persons, and — for real property specifically — the statute's text authorizes selling the property and distributing the proceeds, not distributing the real property itself in kind, to the sister state personal representative. This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of California's own ancillary-administration distribution rules — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate, and not a claim that a court will order any particular distribution in any specific case. This clause cites four different statutory sections (§ 12530, § 12540, § 12541, and § 12542); no single section is cited more than once in this clause. This document is informational: it does not itself order any distribution — only a California court order does that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 12530 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Except to the extent otherwise provided in this chapter, ancillary administration of a decedent’s estate is subject to all other provisions of this code concerning the administration of the decedent’s estate, including, but not limited to, opening estate administration, inventory and appraisal, creditor claims, estate management, independent administration, compensation, accounts, payment of debts, distribution, and closing estate administration.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 12540(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: If a person dies while domiciled in a sister state, the court in an ancillary administration proceeding may make an order for preliminary or final distribution of all or part of the decedent’s personal property in this state to the sister state personal representative if distribution is in the best interest of the estate or interested persons.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 12541 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: If necessary to make distribution pursuant to this article, real property in the nondomiciliary decedent’s estate may be sold and the court may order the proceeds to be distributed to the sister state personal representative. The sale shall be made in the same manner as other sales of real property of a decedent.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 12542 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: If the nondomiciliary decedent’s estate in the sister state where the decedent was domiciled is insolvent, distribution may be made only to the sister state personal representative and not to the beneficiaries.

clauses.title: A Simplified Alternative to Ancillary Probate for a Nonresident Decedent's Smaller California Property
clauses.body: Ancillary probate is not required for every nonresident decedent's California property, regardless of value. For California real property specifically, Probate Code § 13200(a) allows a successor of {{decedentName}} to file a small-value real property affidavit — no sooner than six months after {{decedentName}}'s death — in the superior court for the county in which the real property is located, when {{decedentName}} was not domiciled in California at the time of death. That subdivision requires the affidavit to state, among other things, that "[n]o proceeding is now being or has been conducted in California for administration of the decedent's estate," or, alternatively, that "the decedent's personal representative has consented in writing to use of the procedure provided by this chapter." Separately, for California personal property, Probate Code § 12570 allows a sister state personal representative to use the ordinary personal-property small-estate affidavit procedure of Probate Code § 13100 — without petitioning for ancillary administration at all — whenever {{decedentName}}'s California property "satisfies the requirements of Section 13100," which itself applies (subject to its own dollar threshold and 40-day waiting period) when "the gross value of the decedent's real and personal property in this state does not exceed one hundred sixty-six thousand two hundred fifty dollars ($166,250), as adjusted periodically."
clauses.gap: This confirms, with an important nuance, the framing in the original research brief: California does offer a simplified, non-ancillary alternative for a nonresident decedent's California property, but the statute provides it through two different mechanisms depending on the type of property, not one unified small-estate procedure. The real-property affidavit of § 13200 is available for a nonresident decedent's California real property on its own terms — it expressly addresses a decedent "not domiciled in this state" — independent of the cross-reference in Probate Code Part 13's ancillary-administration chapter, which instead reaches only the personal-property affidavit of § 13100 through § 12570, and is limited there to use by a sister state personal representative rather than any successor. Both mechanisms remain unavailable, per their own text, once a California administration proceeding is pending or has been conducted, unless the decedent's personal representative has consented in writing — so if ancillary probate has already been opened for the decedent's California property, these simplified alternatives are foreclosed absent that consent. This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of California's own small-estate and ancillary-administration procedures — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate, and not a claim that any specific estate qualifies for these procedures, which also depend on statutory dollar thresholds and waiting periods this clause does not fully restate. This clause cites three different statutory sections (§ 13200(a), § 12570, and § 13100); no single section is cited more than once in this clause. This document is informational: it does not itself transfer any property or determine whether a specific estate qualifies for these procedures.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13200(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: No sooner than six months from the death of a decedent, a person or persons claiming as successor of the decedent to a particular item of property that is real property may file in the superior court in the county in which the decedent was domiciled at the time of death, or if the decedent was not domiciled in this state at the time of death, then in any county in which real property of the decedent is located, an affidavit in the form prescribed by the Judicial Council pursuant to Section 1001 stating all of the following

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 12570 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: If a nondomiciliary decedent’s property in this state satisfies the requirements of Section 13100, a sister state personal representative may, without petitioning for ancillary administration, use the affidavit procedure provided by Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 13100) of Part 1 of Division 8 to collect personal property of the decedent.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13100 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Excluding the property described in Section 13050 and any property included in a petition filed under Section 13151, if the gross value of the decedent’s real and personal property in this state does not exceed one hundred sixty-six thousand two hundred fifty dollars ($166,250), as adjusted periodically in accordance with Section 890, and if 40 days have elapsed since the death of the decedent, the successor of the decedent may, without procuring letters of administration or awaiting probate of the will, do any of the following with respect to one or more particular items of property

clauses.title: The Family Code's Relocation Right and the Court's Power to Restrain It
clauses.body: California's move-away framework starts from a general statute, not a custody-specific one: a parent entitled to custody of a child has a right to change the child's residence, subject to the power of the court to restrain a removal that would prejudice the child's rights or welfare. That statute does more than state a bare right. In the same section, the Legislature separately declared its intent to affirm a specific California Supreme Court decision, In re Marriage of Burgess (1996) 13 Cal.4th 25, and to make that decision's rule the declared public policy and law of the state. The statute's structure -- a right to relocate, an express carve-out for a court's power to restrain a prejudicial move, and a legislative endorsement of a named judicial decision -- is what makes the case law discussed elsewhere in this document (rather than freestanding policy argument) the operative gloss on how the restraint power is actually exercised for {{childName}}, whose parents are {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}}.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific presumptive relocation right for a parent entitled to custody, expressly subject to a court's power to restrain a prejudicial move -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific relocation dispute, and not a claim that this right is unconditional or self-executing. This provision sits in Division 12 (Parent and Child Relationship) of the Family Code, a different division than the custody definitions, best-interest standard, and joint-custody provisions cited elsewhere in this document's companion clauses, which sit in Division 8 (Custody of Children). This is a single statutory section (Section 7501, both subdivisions); no additional independent statutory source was found for the relocation right itself. This corpus's Parenting Plan document independently cites the same section (clause parenting_relocation) for its own, briefer purpose; it is cited again here, independently re-verified against the statute's live text on the date above, for this document's deeper treatment of the same right and the case law it points to.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 7501(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the presumptive relocation right and the court's power to restrain it
citations.quote: (a) A parent entitled to the custody of a child has a right to change the residence of the child, subject to the power of the court to restrain a removal that would prejudice the rights or welfare of the child.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 7501(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the Legislature's stated intent to affirm Burgess as state policy and law
citations.quote: It is the intent of the Legislature to affirm the decision in In re Marriage of Burgess (1996) 13 Cal.4th 25, and to declare that ruling to be the public policy and law of this state.

clauses.title: The Notice Requirement Depends on the Custody Order, Not on a Statewide Default
clauses.body: California does not impose a single, automatic statewide notice period before every relocation. Instead, one Family Code section authorizes a California court, when making a custody order, to include a notice term in that order: the court may specify that a parent shall notify the other parent if the parent plans to change the residence of the child for more than 30 days, unless the parents have a prior written agreement to the removal. Where such a term exists in an order, the statute describes how and when notice is to be given: before the contemplated move, by mail, return receipt requested, postage prepaid, to the other parent's last known address, with a copy to that parent's counsel of record, and -- to the extent feasible -- provided at least 45 days before the proposed change of residence so as to allow time for mediation of a new custody agreement. Whether a notice term of this kind applies to {{childName}}'s parents, {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}}, therefore depends on whether their own custody order in {{countyOfFiling}} (or elsewhere) actually contains one -- not on this statute alone.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific, court-order-contingent notice mechanism -- not a claim that California law requires advance notice of every relocation in every case, and not a claim about which state's law governs a specific custody matter. The statute is framed as a grant of authority to the court ("the court may specify"), not as a self-executing duty on every parent; a parent's actual notice obligation, if any, comes from the specific custody order a court has entered, or from the parents' own prior written agreement, not from this section standing alone. This is a single statutory section (Section 3024); no additional independent source was found for it, and no California Rule of Court imposing a separate, freestanding move-away notice requirement was independently verified for this document. This section also does not apply to custody orders made before January 1, 1989, a limitation this clause does not further explore because it is unlikely to affect a current relocation dispute.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 3024 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the court-authorized notice term and its content, timing, and method
citations.quote: In making an order for custody, if the court does not consider it inappropriate, the court may specify that a parent shall notify the other parent if the parent plans to change the residence of the child for more than 30 days, unless there is prior written agreement to the removal.

clauses.title: A Court-Ordered Custody Evaluation's Report Is Confidential
clauses.body: A contested move-away dispute is, procedurally, a child custody proceeding, and California law contains a general rule that applies to any such proceeding, not only to relocation disputes: if a report containing psychological evaluations of a child, or recommendations regarding the child's custody or visitation, is submitted to the court -- including, but not limited to, a report prepared under the Family Code chapter governing court-appointed child custody evaluations -- that report must be placed in the confidential portion of the court file and may not be disclosed except to a limited list of persons: a party and the party's attorney, specified law enforcement, licensing, judicial, court, or family court facilitator personnel acting within the scope of their duties, counsel appointed for the child, or any other person on a court order for good cause. Where a court orders a custody evaluation in connection with {{childName}}'s parents' move-away dispute, this confidentiality rule -- not a general assumption that court records are public -- governs who may see the resulting report.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific confidentiality rule for evaluation and recommendation reports submitted in a child custody or visitation proceeding -- not a claim that every move-away dispute involves a custody evaluation, and not a claim about which state's law governs a specific proceeding. This clause quotes only subdivision (a) of Section 3025.5; subdivision (b), which separately addresses confidentiality of information disclosed to a custody evaluator's licensing entity for professional-conduct investigations, is not restated here. This document does not independently verify the custody-evaluation procedure itself (Family Code Section 3111 and the surrounding chapter, referenced in this section but not separately fetched or quoted here) -- only the confidentiality rule that applies once such a report exists. This is a single statutory section; no additional independent source was found for it.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 3025.5(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the confidentiality of custody-evaluation and recommendation reports, and the limited list of persons who may see them
citations.quote: In a proceeding involving child custody or visitation rights, if a report containing psychological evaluations of a child or recommendations regarding custody of, or visitation with, a child is submitted to the court, including, but not limited to, a report created pursuant to Chapter 6 (commencing with Section 3110) of this part and a recommendation made to the court pursuant to Section 3183, that information shall be contained in a document that shall be placed in the confidential portion of the court file of the proceeding, and may not be disclosed, except to the following persons: (1) A party to the proceeding and the party’s attorney. (2) A federal or state law enforcement officer, the licensing entity of a child custody evaluator, a judicial officer, court employee, or family court facilitator of the superior court of the county in which the action was filed, or an employee or agent of that facilitator, acting within the scope of the facilitator’s duties. (3) Counsel appointed for the child pursuant to Section 3150. (4) Any other person upon order of the court for good cause.

clauses.title: Relocation Notice and Basic Information
clauses.body: This Move-Away Custody Information Sheet concerns {{childName}}, whose parents are {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}}, subject to an existing or contemplated custody arrangement associated with {{countyOfFiling}}. The proposed new residence address identified for {{childName}} is: {{proposedNewAddress}}. The proposed date of the move identified is: {{proposedMoveDate}}. The reason identified for the proposed move is: {{reasonForProposedMove}}. This notice is dated {{noticeDate}}. It is not itself a court order, a court filing, or a determination of any party's rights, and completing it does not itself authorize, restrain, or resolve the proposed relocation. Whether a court-ordered notice term already applies to {{childName}}'s parents, what notice period or procedure it requires, and what county-specific local forms or rules apply, depend on the terms of any existing custody order and are not supplied by this document.
