clauses.title: Kin Care Enforcement and Remedies for a Violation
clauses.body: Labor Code § 233(d) states that an employee aggrieved by a violation of the kin care statute is entitled to reinstatement and actual damages or one day's pay, whichever is greater, plus appropriate equitable relief. Section 233(e) gives the employee two enforcement paths rather than one: upon the filing of a complaint by an employee, the Labor Commissioner is directed to enforce the section under the same enforcement chapter of the Labor Code that governs Labor Commissioner enforcement generally (Chapter 4 of Division 1, including Sections 92, 96.7, 98, and 98.1 to 98.8), or, alternatively, the employee may bring a civil action for the remedies the section provides in a court of competent jurisdiction, with the court authorized to award reasonable attorney's fees to a prevailing employee.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own kin care enforcement mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific act by any specific employer was or was not a violation of Labor Code § 233. Both citations below are to subdivisions (d) and (e) of the single statutory section addressed throughout this document, § 233; they are treated here as one source describing that section's own remedies and enforcement mechanism, not as independent corroborating sources, and not as independent of this document's other § 233 citations. This clause does not independently verify the substance of the cross-referenced general Labor Commissioner enforcement provisions themselves (Sections 92, 96.7, 98, and 98.1 through 98.8), beyond the fact that § 233(e) names them as the enforcement chapter that applies; their own text was not fetched or verified as part of this research. The statutory text quoted below was fetched twice this session, directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, using two different User-Agent headers, and found byte-identical both times. This clause, and this document as a whole, is informational only: it does not itself determine that any particular employer's conduct toward any particular employee was or was not a violation of Labor Code § 233, and does not itself award, calculate, or deny any specific remedy.

If the employee prevails, the court may award reasonable attorney’s fees.

clauses.title: No Separate Mental Health Advance Directive Statute
clauses.body: California does not maintain a separate statute for a "mental health advance directive." A statement of {{patientName}}'s wishes for future mental health treatment is created and governed the same way as any other advance health care directive, under the single Health Care Decisions Law (Cal. Prob. Code § 4600 et seq.), because that law's own definition of "health care" already covers a patient's mental health condition, not just physical health.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California addresses mental health treatment wishes within its one general Health Care Decisions Law rather than through a separate, dedicated "mental health advance directive" statute — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive. Both citations below sit in the same division and part of the Probate Code (Division 4.7, Part 1, Chapter 1) rather than in unrelated bodies of law, so they are read together as evidence of that single division's own structure and scope, not as two independent confirmations from separate legal sources.

citations.cite: the short title of the single, general statute
citations.quote: This division may be cited as the Health Care Decisions Law.

citations.quote: “Health care” means any care, treatment, service, or procedure to maintain, diagnose, or otherwise affect a patient’s physical or mental health condition.

clauses.title: What This Directive May Address
clauses.body: Within the same Health Care Decisions Law that governs any advance health care directive, a statement of {{patientName}}'s wishes for future mental health treatment may address the selection or discharge of specific mental health care providers and treatment facilities, and the approval or disapproval of specific mental health medications or programs of medication. California's own optional statutory advance directive form reflects this same scope, describing an agent's authority in matching terms.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual categories of mental-health-specific content the law recognizes — not a generic, assumed list, and not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive. The second citation is drawn from the explanatory and operative text of California's own statutory advance directive form (§ 4701), which corroborates § 4617's definition in plain language but is still part of the same Health Care Decisions Law rather than an independent body of law.

(2) Approval or disapproval of diagnostic tests, surgical procedures, and programs of medication, including mental health conditions.

clauses.title: What This Directive Cannot Authorize: Commitment and ECT
clauses.body: Regardless of what {{patientName}} writes in a mental health treatment directive, and regardless of what authority is given to {{agentName}}, the Health Care Decisions Law itself does not authorize anyone to consent, on {{patientName}}'s behalf, to commitment to or placement in a mental health treatment facility, or to convulsive treatment — a defined term that includes electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). California's own optional statutory advance directive form states the same limitation directly to the person filling it out.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a real, categorical statutory carve-out from what any advance health care directive can authorize under this division — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive. The second citation corroborates the first in plain language but is drawn from the same Health Care Decisions Law (the statutory form itself, § 4701) rather than an independent body of law.

clauses.title: Electroconvulsive Therapy Has Its Own Separate Consent Procedure
clauses.body: Consent to convulsive treatment, including electroconvulsive therapy, is governed by a separate statutory scheme in the Welfare and Institutions Code (part of the Lanterman-Petris-Short Act), not by the Health Care Decisions Law that governs the rest of this directive. That scheme gives a person a statutory right to refuse convulsive treatment, and — where written informed consent to it is given at all — requires that consent to be time-limited (to no more than 30 days of treatment) and freely revocable at any time.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence that California regulates convulsive treatment consent through a distinct statutory scheme with its own time-limited, revocable consent requirement — not a full account of every procedural safeguard in that scheme (which also includes, for patients who cannot give that contemporaneous consent, review by a two-physician committee and, if capacity is disputed, a superior court hearing), and not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive. This is a genuinely complex, only partially verified area: this session did not verify whether, or how, a written mental-health treatment directive's ECT-related wishes are actually taken into account within that separate Welfare and Institutions Code procedure — the two statutory schemes were confirmed to be independent, but their practical interaction was not verified and is not asserted here. The two citations below are from two different, independently numbered sections of the Welfare and Institutions Code, not subsections of one section.

Such consent shall be for a specified maximum number of treatments over a specified maximum period of time not to exceed 30 days, and shall be revocable at any time before or between treatments.

clauses.title: Capacity Determination Uses the Same Rule as the General Directive
clauses.body: The Health Care Decisions Law does not set a different or additional capacity-determination rule for the mental-health-treatment portion of an advance directive. The same default rule that applies to the rest of an advance health care directive applies here: unless this directive specifies otherwise, a determination that {{patientName}} lacks or has recovered the capacity needed for these mental health treatment instructions (or for {{agentName}}'s authority regarding them) to take or lose effect is made by {{patientName}}'s primary physician.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that no separate mental-health-specific capacity rule exists — the same general rule already used in this site's Advance Health Care Directive document applies, and is cited again here only so this document is independently complete on its own. This is a single statutory section (§ 4658); no additional independent source was found for this, and none was needed since the point is that no distinct rule exists.

clauses.title: The FLSA's Broad "Employ" Definition and the Judicially Recognized Volunteer Exception
clauses.body: The Fair Labor Standards Act defines "employ" very broadly. The statute itself states only that '"Employ" includes to suffer or permit to work.' That text, standing alone, says nothing about volunteers and states no exception for unpaid civic, charitable, or humanitarian service. The exception for genuine volunteers comes not from this statutory language but from judicial interpretation. In a 1947 decision addressing unpaid railroad trainees, the Supreme Court held that this "suffer or permit to work" language "was obviously not intended to stamp all persons as employees who, without any express or implied compensation agreement, might work for their own advantage on the premises of another," and that the Act's broad definitions do not sweep in "each person who, without promise or expectation of compensation, but solely for his personal purpose or pleasure, worked in activities carried on by other persons either for their pleasure or profit." The Department of Labor has applied this same reasoning specifically to unpaid volunteers, including in the private nonprofit and charitable sector. Separately, federal regulations at 29 C.F.R. Part 553 define "volunteer" and address volunteer compensation in detail, but by that Part's own terms those regulations govern only public agencies — state and local government employers — not private employers, whether nonprofit or for-profit. This document did not locate a Department of Labor regulation of comparable specificity governing private-sector or nonprofit-sector volunteers; their status instead continues to be assessed under the judicially developed doctrine described here together with related sub-regulatory DOL guidance discussed elsewhere in this document.
clauses.gap: This clause describes a general judicial doctrine; it does not itself determine that any particular unpaid arrangement is, or is not, genuine volunteering. The 1947 case quoted here concerned unpaid trainees, not volunteers at a nonprofit or charitable organization as such, and predates the modern nonprofit-sector case law discussed in a separate clause in this document; this document does not claim that case addressed nonprofit volunteering directly, only that later authorities have relied on its reasoning in that context.

clauses.title: Considerations Distinguishing a Volunteer from an Employee
clauses.body: Beyond the basic requirement that a genuine volunteer not expect or receive compensation, DOL guidance and case law examine further considerations. One is whether the service was offered freely, without pressure or coercion — federal regulations describe this as central to Congress's intent "to prevent any manipulation or abuse of minimum wage or overtime requirements through coercion or undue pressure upon individuals to 'volunteer' their services," and state that "[i]ndividuals shall be considered volunteers only where their services are offered freely and without pressure or coercion, direct or implied, from an employer." A second is whether the work is the same type of work the individual is otherwise employed, for pay, to perform for the same organization; the same regulations state that "[a]n individual shall not be considered a volunteer if the individual is otherwise employed by the same public agency to perform the same type of services as those for which the individual proposes to volunteer." The Department of Labor's Wage and Hour Division Field Operations Handbook applies a similar concept outside the public-agency context, stating, in discussing volunteers at religious, charitable, and nonprofit organizations, that "this does not mean that a regular office employee of a charitable organization can volunteer services on an uncompensated basis to handle correspondence in connection with a special fund drive or to handle other work arising from exigencies of the operations conducted by the employer" — meaning an employee's after-hours help in a different capacity may be genuine volunteering, while donating unpaid time to do more of the person's own paid job typically is not.
clauses.gap: The "offered freely and without coercion" and "not the same type of services" language quoted here from 29 C.F.R. § 553.101 comes from a regulation that, by its own terms, governs volunteers at public agencies, not private or nonprofit employers; this document could not verify that an identically worded regulation applies by its own terms outside that context, and presents these considerations as ones DOL sub-regulatory guidance (the Field Operations Handbook) and the same underlying policy concern apply by analogy in the private and nonprofit context, not as a codified private-sector test carrying the same regulatory force. This document does not itself weigh these considerations for any specific arrangement.

citations.quote: Congress did not intend to discourage or impede volunteer activities undertaken for civic, charitable, or humanitarian purposes, but expressed its wish to prevent any manipulation or abuse of minimum wage or overtime requirements through coercion or undue pressure upon individuals to “volunteer” their services.

citations.quote: Individuals shall be considered volunteers only where their services are offered freely and without pressure or coercion, direct or implied, from an employer.

clauses.title: For-Profit Employers and Volunteer Status
clauses.body: Department of Labor guidance draws a sharper line between nonprofit and for-profit employers than is sometimes assumed. The Department's own published FLSA Advisor states plainly: "Under the FLSA, employees may not volunteer services to for-profit private sector employers," while noting that, by contrast, "in the vast majority of circumstances, individuals can volunteer services to public sector employers." The same DOL guidance describes the volunteer doctrine discussed elsewhere in this document as applying to individuals who donate their services "usually on a part-time basis, for public service, religious or humanitarian objectives, not as employees and without contemplation of pay," and states that such individuals "are not considered employees of the religious, charitable or similar non-profit organizations that receive their service" — language limited to nonprofit organizations receiving the service, not ordinary for-profit businesses.
clauses.gap: This is sub-regulatory DOL informal guidance (an elaws Advisor page), not a statute or regulation, and this document did not locate a court decision squarely addressing whether an individual could ever be found a bona fide unpaid volunteer at a for-profit employer under some other doctrine. An unpaid worker at a for-profit company is more likely to be analyzed under this corpus's separate discussion of unpaid interns and trainees than treated as a "volunteer" in the sense this document otherwise addresses; this document does not itself determine whether any specific for-profit arrangement is lawful.

clauses.title: A Charitable Purpose Alone Does Not Create Volunteer Status
clauses.body: A nonprofit organization is not categorically exempt from the FLSA merely because of its charitable purpose — a point this corpus also makes in its separate discussion of unpaid internships — and the same is true specifically for people an organization calls "volunteers." In a 2023 decision, the Fifth Circuit affirmed a district court's application of the Supreme Court's "economic reality" test to unpaid participants in a nonprofit drug-and-alcohol rehabilitation program's work program, holding that the district court's "threshold determination that the rehabilitation patients constitute 'employees' under the Act because they worked in expectation of compensation was not an abuse of discretion." The court also rejected the argument that the organization's own paperwork could settle the question: although participants had signed forms stating they were "beneficiaries," not employees, the court held that "any forms patients sign indicating that they are beneficiaries and not employees do not control this analysis," because rights under the FLSA cannot be waived by agreement. In other words, what an organization calls an unpaid worker, or what that worker agrees to be called, does not itself determine status under the Act.
clauses.gap: This Fifth Circuit decision resolved an interlocutory appeal about whether a collective action could be certified and whether the district court used the correct legal framework — it did not itself finally decide, on the merits, that the rehabilitation program's participants were employees; that question was left for further proceedings. This document does not restate the separate primary-beneficiary internship test or the Tony and Susan Alamo Foundation Supreme Court decision discussed in this corpus's Unpaid Internship Compliance Information Sheet, which it treats as a related but distinct topic rather than duplicating here. This document does not itself determine that any specific nonprofit's unpaid workers are, or are not, employees under the Act.

clauses.title: California Substantially Follows the Federal Volunteer Framework
clauses.body: California's Labor Code and the Industrial Welfare Commission's Wage Orders do not set out a separate statutory or regulatory definition of "volunteer" distinct from the federal approach described elsewhere in this document. California's Division of Labor Standards Enforcement (DLSE), in its own currently published Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual, addresses unpaid workers at nonprofit organizations by stating that a person who donates services to a religious, charitable, or similar nonprofit corporation, acting "without contemplation of pay and for public service, religious, or humanitarian objectives, are not employees" — a standard the manual attributes to a 1988 DLSE opinion letter, not to any specific Labor Code section or Wage Order provision addressing volunteers. As with the federal DOL guidance discussed elsewhere in this document, this DLSE position is limited to religious, charitable, or similar nonprofit corporations; it does not, by its own terms, extend to for-profit businesses.
clauses.gap: This document located no separate California statute or regulation defining "volunteer" for wage-and-hour purposes distinct from this DLSE guidance. The DLSE manual attributes this specific position to a 1988 opinion letter without a more recent restatement on this point, so this document cannot rule out that DLSE's position has evolved since 1988 in ways this publicly posted manual excerpt does not reflect; this document fetched the manual live from California's Department of Industrial Relations website on the date shown above and quotes it as currently published there. This document is informational only; it does not itself determine that any specific California unpaid arrangement is, or is not, a lawful volunteer relationship.

citations.quote: without contemplation of pay and for public service, religious, or humanitarian objectives, are not employees.

clauses.title: Nominal Fees, Benefits, and Expense Reimbursement for Volunteers
clauses.body: Federal regulations addressing volunteers who serve public agencies provide that "[v]olunteers may be paid expenses, reasonable benefits, a nominal fee, or any combination thereof, for their service without losing their status as volunteers," and separately specify that "[a] nominal fee is not a substitute for compensation and must not be tied to productivity." These regulations decline to set a fixed dollar figure for what counts as "nominal." Instead, they state that "[w]hether the furnishing of expenses, benefits, or fees would result in individuals' losing their status as volunteers under the FLSA can only be determined by examining the total amount of payments made (expenses, benefits, fees) in the context of the economic realities of the particular situation" — a fact-specific inquiry that also considers factors such as the distance traveled, the time and effort expended, and whether the individual is available around-the-clock or only periodically.
clauses.gap: These regulations, by their own terms (29 C.F.R. Part 553), govern volunteers at public agencies — state and local governments — not private employers, whether nonprofit or for-profit. This document did not locate a Department of Labor regulation of equivalent specificity addressing what expense reimbursement, benefits, or nominal fees a private-sector or nonprofit volunteer may receive without losing volunteer status, and did not verify whether, or to what extent, courts or DOL guidance apply this public-agency "nominal fee" framework by analogy outside the public-agency context. This is accordingly presented as an unsettled, fact-specific area for private-sector and nonprofit volunteers rather than one governed by a confirmed bright-line rule; this document does not itself determine whether any particular payment or benefit is "nominal."

clauses.title: Declaration of Parties, Marriage Date, and Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Petition for Legal Separation — Information Sheet concerns the marriage of {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}, who were married on {{marriageDate}} and identify {{separationDate}} as their date of separation. It is prepared for use alongside an actual petition for legal separation of the parties that would be filed in the California superior court for {{countyOfFiling}}. As California's Family Code recognizes, a petition seeking to end or alter a marriage's legal status may instead seek dissolution of the marriage or a judgment of nullity — two other, distinct proceedings addressed in this corpus's separate Petition for Dissolution of Marriage (Divorce) — Information Sheet and Nullity of Marriage (Annulment) — Petition Information Sheet documents, not restated here. This information sheet describes what is distinctive about legal separation as its own statutory proceeding — that it has no residency requirement to file, that a resulting judgment does not end the parties' marital status, and how it relates procedurally to dissolution — as background for that filing. It is not itself a court filing, and completing it does not legally separate, dissolve, or otherwise change the marital status of {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}. Only a court judgment can do that.

clauses.title: No Residency or Durational Requirement to File for Legal Separation — Unlike Dissolution
clauses.body: California's Family Code imposes a residency requirement on dissolution that it does not impose in the same terms on legal separation. A judgment of dissolution of marriage may not be entered unless one of the parties has been a resident of California for six months and a resident of the county where the proceeding is filed for three months, both periods measured immediately before the petition is filed. The statute governing amendment of a legal separation proceeding confirms, by its own terms, that this residency requirement does not likewise gate a legal separation filing: it expressly contemplates "a proceeding for legal separation of the parties in which neither party, at the time the proceeding was commenced, has complied with the residence requirements of Section 2320," and provides that once a party later does comply with those requirements, that party may amend the petition or responsive pleading to instead request a judgment of dissolution — with the amendment's filing date deemed the commencement date of the dissolution proceeding for residency purposes only. California's official courts self-help website describes the same distinction in plain language: to file for a legal separation, only one spouse must live in California, and "There's no time requirement," while a divorce filing requires one spouse to have lived in California for the past six months and in the filing county for at least three months.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute and its own self-help publication, used as real evidence of California's legal-separation process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage. This document is informational: it does not itself determine whether either party satisfies any residency requirement, or whether amending a specific petition from legal separation to dissolution would be proper; only a court can make that determination. The two Family Code citations are to two different sections (§ 2320 and § 2321), and are independent of each other; the California Courts self-help page is a separate, non-statutory source independent of both, though its own two quoted sentences come from the same single web page and are not independent of one another. This clause's first sentence characterizes § 2320 as not imposing a residency requirement on legal separation "in the same terms"; that characterization rests on § 2320(a)'s own text, which speaks only of "a judgment of dissolution of marriage," and on § 2321(a)'s express contemplation of a legal-separation proceeding filed without compliance with § 2320 — not on any statute that affirmatively states legal separation has no residency requirement in so many words. Section 2320(b), a same-sex-marriage residency exception, does expressly extend to legal separation and is addressed in this corpus's companion dissolution document rather than restated here. Section 2321(b), governing notice of such an amendment, was read but is not quoted here.

citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivision (b), a judgment of dissolution of marriage may not be entered unless one of the parties to the marriage has been a resident of this state for six months and of the county in which the proceeding is filed for three months next preceding the filing of the petition.

clauses.title: A Judgment of Legal Separation Does Not End Marital Status
clauses.body: California's Family Code gives dissolution, but not legal separation, a dedicated statutory statement of what its judgment does to the parties' marital status: the Family Code's chapter titled "Effect of Dissolution" — consisting of a single section — states that "the effect of a judgment of dissolution of marriage when it becomes final is to restore the parties to the state of unmarried persons." No parallel Family Code chapter gives a judgment of legal separation that same status-restoring effect. Consistent with that statutory structure, California's official courts self-help website states the practical consequence in plain terms: in a legal separation, "you stay married," and "When it's final, you are still legally married" — with the further, related consequence that a party who has legally separated "can't marry or enter into a domestic partnership with someone else." A legal separation proceeding can still result in the same kinds of financial and parenting orders as a dissolution — division of property and debts, spousal or domestic partner support, and child custody, visitation, and support — addressed in a separate clause of this document; what it does not do is change either party's marital status.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute and its own self-help publication, used as real evidence of California's legal-separation process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage. This document is informational: it does not itself enter a judgment of legal separation or determine any party's marital status; only a court judgment does that. The Family Code citation (§ 2300) and the California Courts self-help page are independent, non-overlapping sources; the self-help page's own three quoted phrases come from the same single web page and are not independent of one another. This clause's statement that no parallel Family Code chapter restores unmarried status upon legal separation is an inference from the structure of Division 6, Part 3 of the Family Code — specifically, that Chapter 1, captioned "Effect of Dissolution" and spanning only Section 2300, addresses solely dissolution's effect — rather than a claim independently verified against every other chapter of that Part; this document's research did not exhaustively review every section of Division 6 to confirm no other provision addresses legal separation's status effect.

citations.quote: The effect of a judgment of dissolution of marriage when it becomes final is to restore the parties to the state of unmarried persons.

clauses.title: The Same No-Fault Grounds and Community-Property Default Apply to Legal Separation as to Dissolution
clauses.body: Rather than maintaining a separate substantive framework, California's Family Code repeatedly folds legal separation into the same statutory rules it applies to dissolution, stating each rule for both proceedings in a single sentence. The two available grounds are shared and stated together: "Dissolution of the marriage or legal separation of the parties may be based on either of the following grounds, which shall be pleaded generally" — irreconcilable differences causing the irremediable breakdown of the marriage, or permanent legal incapacity to make decisions — the same two no-fault grounds, defined the same way, addressed more fully in this corpus's companion dissolution document rather than restated here. Property division follows the same pattern: absent the parties' written agreement, their oral stipulation in open court, or another statutory exception, the court "shall, either in its judgment of dissolution of the marriage, in its judgment of legal separation of the parties, or at a later time if it expressly reserves jurisdiction to make such a property division, divide the community estate of the parties equally" — one statute, naming both judgment types side by side, governing the community-property default for either proceeding alike.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's legal-separation process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage. This document is informational: it does not itself determine grounds, divide property, or order support or custody in any specific case; only a court can do that. The two citations are to two different Family Code sections (§ 2310 and § 2550), and are independent of each other. This clause addresses only the grounds and the community-property default; it does not restate this corpus's companion dissolution document's fuller treatment of those same two statutes (including § 2311's definition of irreconcilable differences and § 2312's proof standard for legal incapacity), and it does not independently verify the spousal-support or child-custody statutes, which this document's research did not separately confirm apply to legal separation by their own text in the way § 2310 and § 2550 do — a reader should not assume every dissolution-related statute extends to legal separation without checking that statute's own language.

(b) Permanent legal incapacity to make decisions.

clauses.title: No Six-Month Waiting Period, and Commonly Cited Reasons for Choosing Legal Separation
clauses.body: Just as the residency requirement is stated only for dissolution, so is the Family Code's mandatory waiting period: subject to a small set of statutory exceptions, "no judgment of dissolution is final for the purpose of terminating the marriage relationship of the parties until six months have expired" from service of the petition or the respondent's appearance, whichever occurs first — a rule addressed more fully in this corpus's companion dissolution document. California's official courts self-help website confirms that legal separation has no counterpart to that wait: describing the six-month period as running to when a couple can divorce, it states, "There isn't one for a legal separation." The same source identifies reasons some spouses choose legal separation over dissolution: "Some couples don't want to get divorced for religious reasons, personal beliefs, or financial reasons. For example, they stay married to keep a spouse or domestic partner on an insurance or benefit plan." It also notes that a spouse who wants a divorce but has not yet met dissolution's residency requirement may file for legal separation first and later amend to seek dissolution, and states, "You can usually change a legal separation to a divorce" if the case is not yet final — consistent with the amendment mechanism in Family Code § 2321 addressed in a separate clause of this document.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute and its own self-help publication, used as real evidence of California's legal-separation process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage. This document is informational: it does not itself waive any waiting period or determine why any specific party is choosing legal separation; only a court proceeding resolves a specific case, and the reasons stated here are commonly cited background drawn from California's own self-help publication, not a statement of any specific party's motivation or of settled case law. The Family Code citation (§ 2339) and the California Courts self-help page are independent, non-overlapping sources; the self-help page's several quoted phrases come from the same single web page and are not independent of one another. Section 2339(a) itself cross-references further exceptions (Sections 2340 to 2344) that this document's research did not independently fetch or verify, consistent with this corpus's companion dissolution document's treatment of the same statute.

clauses.title: Statutory Definitions of "Elder" and "Dependent Adult"
clauses.body: A petition for protective orders under the Elder Abuse and Dependent Adult Civil Protection Act, Welfare and Institutions Code section 15657.03, is available only on behalf of a person who meets one of two statutory categories. Section 15610.27 defines "elder" as any person residing in California who is 65 years of age or older — an age-and-residency test with no separate requirement of incapacity or vulnerability. Section 15610.23 defines "dependent adult" in two independent ways: first, as a California resident between 18 and 64 years old who has physical or mental limitations restricting the ability to carry out normal activities or protect one's rights, expressly including people with physical or developmental disabilities and people whose abilities have diminished because of age; second, regardless of any disability finding, as any person between 18 and 64 admitted as an inpatient to a 24-hour health facility as defined in specified Health and Safety Code sections. These are the same statutory definitions of "elder" and "dependent adult" used throughout the Act, including for a financial-abuse civil claim; here they set the threshold question of who the restraining-order remedy in section 15657.03 is available to protect.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California defines "elder" and "dependent adult" for purposes of the Elder Abuse and Dependent Adult Civil Protection Act's restraining-order remedy specifically — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person or situation. These two statutory definitions (Welf. & Inst. Code §§ 15610.27 and 15610.23) are the same definitions this corpus's separate Elder and Dependent Adult Financial Abuse Information Sheet document cites for the Act's financial-abuse remedy; the underlying statute is identical because both remedies are drawn from the same Act, so the definitions are restated here — independently re-fetched and re-verified for this document, not copied from that document — rather than cross-referenced, consistent with this corpus's practice of each document standing on its own. This clause cites two code sections (§ 15610.27, a single subsection, and § 15610.23(a)-(b), two subsections of the same section); the two subsections of § 15610.23 are treated as one source, not independent corroborating sources, and § 15610.27 is treated as a second, independent source from a different code section. This clause states only the statutory definitions; it does not itself determine that any specific person is an "elder" or "dependent adult," or that any specific person is entitled to protective orders under section 15657.03.

clauses.title: Statutory Definition of "Abuse of an Elder or a Dependent Adult"
clauses.body: Welfare and Institutions Code section 15610.07(a) defines "abuse of an elder or a dependent adult," for purposes of the entire Elder Abuse and Dependent Adult Civil Protection Act — including the restraining-order remedy in section 15657.03 — as any of three categories: (1) physical abuse, neglect, abandonment, isolation, abduction, or other treatment with resulting physical harm or pain or mental suffering; (2) the deprivation by a care custodian of goods or services that are necessary to avoid physical harm or mental suffering; or (3) financial abuse, as separately defined in section 15610.30. These three categories are independent alternatives, and the second is narrower than the first in one respect: it applies specifically to a "care custodian's" deprivation of necessary goods or services, not to a deprivation by any person. Section 15657.03(a)(1) conditions eligibility to petition for protective orders on the elder or dependent adult having "suffered abuse, as defined in Section 15610.07" — so this definition, rather than a separate restraining-order-specific abuse definition, is the operative standard for what conduct may support a petition under section 15657.03.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California defines "abuse of an elder or a dependent adult" for purposes of the Act, including the restraining-order remedy — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific set of facts. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 15610.07(a)); no additional independent source was found for this. Subsection (b), stating only an operative date (July 1, 2016) for the current version of this definition, is not quoted or described here because it carries no substantive content. This clause states only the statutory definition; it does not itself determine that any specific conduct constitutes abuse of an elder or dependent adult, or that any specific person committed or suffered such abuse.

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15610.07(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) “Abuse of an elder or a dependent adult” means any of the following: (1) Physical abuse, neglect, abandonment, isolation, abduction, or other treatment with resulting physical harm or pain or mental suffering. (2) The deprivation by a care custodian of goods or services that are necessary to avoid physical harm or mental suffering. (3) Financial abuse, as defined in Section 15610.30.

clauses.title: Eligibility to Petition: The Elder or Dependent Adult, or Specified Others on Their Behalf
clauses.body: Welfare and Institutions Code section 15657.03(a) identifies who may bring a petition for protective orders under the Elder Abuse and Dependent Adult Civil Protection Act. Under section 15657.03(a)(1), the elder or dependent adult who has suffered abuse, as defined in section 15610.07, may petition on their own behalf. Under section 15657.03(a)(2)(A), a petition may also be brought on that person's behalf by one of four specified categories: a conservator or trustee of the elder or dependent adult, an attorney-in-fact acting within the authority of a power of attorney, a person appointed as a guardian ad litem, or "other person legally authorized to seek the relief." Section 15657.03(a)(2)(B) narrows that last, catch-all category for one specific type of petition: where the petition alleges abuse in the form of isolation, "other person legally authorized to seek the relief" also includes an "interested party" — defined in section 15657.03(b)(3) as an individual with a personal, preexisting relationship with the elder or dependent adult — but only for the purpose of seeking the isolation-specific order described in section 15657.03(b)(5)(E). Separately, section 15657.03(a)(3)(A) allows a petition to be brought on an elder or dependent adult's behalf by a county adult protective services agency, but only where the elder or dependent adult has suffered abuse and has an impaired ability to appreciate and understand the circumstances placing them at risk, or where the elder or dependent adult has given written authorization for the agency to act on their behalf. Two further defined terms from section 15657.03(b) describe the parties once a petition is filed: "Petitioner" means the elder or dependent adult to be protected — not necessarily the person who signed and filed the petition — and, if the petition is granted, the protected person; "Respondent" means the person against whom the protective orders are sought.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of who may petition for protective orders under Welfare and Institutions Code section 15657.03 — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petition. Correction to a naive assumption: section 15657.03's eligibility structure does not include a general "certain relatives" category comparable to the family/household-member categories that appear in California's civil harassment (Code Civ. Proc. § 527.6) or domestic violence (Fam. Code § 6211) statutes; the actual text authorizes only the elder or dependent adult, a conservator, a trustee, an attorney-in-fact under a power of attorney, a guardian ad litem, or an "other person legally authorized to seek the relief" (a catch-all, not an enumerated list of relatives), plus — narrowly, and only for an isolation-based petition — an "interested party" defined by a personal, preexisting relationship rather than family status, plus a county adult protective services agency under the two specific circumstances stated in section 15657.03(a)(3)(A). This clause also flags a defined-term subtlety: the statute's own definition of "Petitioner" in section 15657.03(b)(4) is the protected elder or dependent adult, not necessarily the person who signs and files the petition when someone else petitions on that person's behalf — a distinction this document's drafting clauses account for by separating the filer (the petitionerName field) from the protected person (the elderOrDependentAdultName field) as separate fields. This clause cites five subsections of the same statutory section (§ 15657.03(a)(1), (a)(2)(A), (a)(2)(B), (a)(3)(A), and (b)(2)-(4)); they are treated as one source, not independent corroborating sources. Subsections (a)(3)(B)-(C), addressing a required referral to the public guardian and confidentiality restrictions specific to a county adult protective services agency's petition, are not quoted or described in this clause. This clause states only the statutory eligibility categories; it does not itself determine that any specific person is eligible to petition, or that a specific filer falls within any of these categories.

citations.quote: (B) (i) Subject to clause (ii), if the petition alleges abuse of an elder or dependent adult in the form of isolation, the term “other person legally authorized to seek the relief” as used in subparagraph (A) includes an interested party as defined in paragraph (3) of subdivision (b). (ii) Clause (i) shall apply only for the purpose of seeking an order enjoining isolation under subparagraph (E) of paragraph (5) of subdivision (b).

citations.quote: (3) (A) A petition under this section may be brought on behalf of an elder or dependent adult by a county adult protective services agency in either of the following circumstances: (i) If the elder or dependent adult has suffered abuse as defined in subdivision (b) and has an impaired ability to appreciate and understand the circumstances that place the elder or dependent at risk of harm. (ii) If the elder or dependent adult has provided written authorization to a county adult protective services agency to act on that person’s behalf.

(3) “Interested party” means an individual with a personal, preexisting relationship with the elder or dependent adult. A preexisting relationship may be shown by a description of past involvement with the elder or dependent adult, time spent together, and any other proof that the individual spent time with the elder or dependent adult. (4) “Petitioner” means the elder or dependent adult to be protected by the protective orders and, if the court grants the petition, the protected person.

clauses.title: Relief a Protective Order May Include — Personal Conduct Orders, Residence Exclusion, and Its Limits
clauses.body: Welfare and Institutions Code section 15657.03(b)(5) defines "protective order," for purposes of section 15657.03, to include several categories of restraining order, issuable ex parte, after notice and hearing, or in a judgment. Section 15657.03(b)(5)(A) authorizes a personal-conduct order enjoining a party from abusing, intimidating, molesting, attacking, striking, stalking, threatening, sexually assaulting, battering, harassing, telephoning (including annoying calls under Penal Code section 653m), destroying personal property, contacting (directly or indirectly), or coming within a specified distance of, or disturbing the peace of, the petitioner, and, on a showing of good cause, of other named family or household members or a conservator of the petitioner; the same subparagraph separately authorizes the court, on a showing of good cause, to grant the petitioner exclusive care, possession, or control of an animal, or to order the respondent to stay away from it. Section 15657.03(b)(5)(B) authorizes an order excluding a party from the petitioner's residence or dwelling — but this residence-exclusion order carries an express statutory limit: it may not be issued if legal or equitable title to, or a lease of, the residence is in the sole name of the party to be excluded, or in that party's name together with any other party besides the petitioner. Section 15657.03(b)(5)(C) authorizes an order enjoining other specified behavior the court determines necessary to effectuate either of the first two categories.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the categories of relief California authorizes under Welfare and Institutions Code section 15657.03 — not a claim about which state's law, or which categories of relief, govern a specific petition. This clause cites three subparagraphs of a single statutory paragraph (§ 15657.03(b)(5)(A)-(C)); they are treated as one source, not independent corroborating sources. Section 15657.03(b)(5) also authorizes two further, narrower categories of order not described in this clause: subparagraph (D), available after notice and a hearing only, permits a finding that specific debts were incurred as a result of financial abuse; and subparagraph (E), also available after notice and a hearing only, permits an order enjoining a respondent from isolating the elder or dependent adult, but only on a three-part evidentiary showing and only in favor of an "interested party" as described in this document's eligibility clause, and never where the elder or dependent adult resides in a long-term care facility or is a patient of specified health facilities. This clause states only the categories of relief the statute authorizes; it does not itself determine which category of relief is appropriate for any specific petition, or that any specific order will issue.

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15657.03(b)(5)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (A) An order enjoining a party from abusing, intimidating, molesting, attacking, striking, stalking, threatening, sexually assaulting, battering, harassing, telephoning, including, but not limited to, making annoying telephone calls as described in Section 653m of the Penal Code, destroying personal property, contacting, either directly or indirectly, by mail or otherwise, or coming within a specified distance of, or disturbing the peace of, the petitioner, and, in the discretion of the court, on a showing of good cause, of other named family or household members or a conservator, if any, of the petitioner.

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15657.03(b)(5)(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (B) An order excluding a party from the petitioner’s residence or dwelling, except that this order shall not be issued if legal or equitable title to, or lease of, the residence or dwelling is in the sole name of the party to be excluded, or is in the name of the party to be excluded and any other party besides the petitioner.

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15657.03(b)(5)(C) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (C) An order enjoining a party from specified behavior that the court determines is necessary to effectuate orders described in subparagraph (A) or (B).

clauses.title: Standard for an Order, Duration and Renewal, and the Consequence of Violating One
clauses.body: Welfare and Institutions Code section 15657.03(c) states the standard for a protective order under this section: with or without notice, an order may issue to restrain any person for the purpose of preventing a recurrence of abuse if a declaration shows, to the satisfaction of the court, reasonable proof of a past act or acts of abuse of the petitioning elder or dependent adult. This standard does not include a separate showing that "great or irreparable harm would result" absent an order — a phrase that appears in California's civil harassment TRO statute, Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(d), but that is not part of section 15657.03(c)'s text. Once an order issues after notice and a hearing, section 15657.03(i)(1) allows a duration of not more than five years, and allows renewal, on a party's request, for either five additional years or permanently, without a showing of any further abuse since the original order issued; a renewal request may be made at any time within the three months before the order's expiration. Section 15657.03(i)(2) provides that an order silent on its expiration date defaults to a three-year duration from issuance. Separately, section 15657.03(x) states that willful disobedience of a temporary restraining order or restraining order after hearing granted under this section is punishable under Penal Code section 273.6.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the standard, duration, renewal rule, and violation consequence that apply to a protective order under Welfare and Institutions Code section 15657.03 — not a claim about which state's law, or which standard or duration, governs a specific order. Point worth flagging rather than assuming: section 15657.03(i)(1)'s renewal language — "either for five years or permanently" — is broader than the renewal language in California's civil harassment statute, Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(j)(1), which (as already verified elsewhere in this corpus's Civil Harassment Restraining Order document) caps a renewal at five additional years and does not offer a permanent-renewal option; that comparison statute's text was not independently re-fetched or re-verified in this research session, and this gap discloses that rather than presenting it as freshly verified, while the section 15657.03 text quoted in this clause was independently fetched and verified twice for this document. This clause cites three subsections of the same statutory section (§ 15657.03(c), (i)(1)-(2), and (x)); they are treated as one source, not independent corroborating sources. Section 15657.03(i)(3), governing notice requirements when someone other than the protected party moves to terminate or modify an order before its stated expiration date, is not quoted or described in this clause. This clause states only the statutory standard, duration, renewal rule, and violation consequence; it does not itself determine that any specific declaration meets the reasonable-proof standard, that any specific order will be renewed, or that any specific person has violated an order.

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15657.03(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Welf. & Inst. C. § 15657.03(c)
citations.quote: (c) Except as provided in subdivision (b), an order may be issued under this section, with or without notice, to restrain any person for the purpose of preventing a recurrence of abuse, if a declaration shows, to the satisfaction of the court, reasonable proof of a past act or acts of abuse of the petitioning elder or dependent adult.

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15657.03(i)(1)-(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (i) (1) In the discretion of the court, an order issued after notice and a hearing under this section may have a duration of not more than five years, subject to termination or modification by further order of the court either on written stipulation filed with the court or on the motion of a party. These orders may be renewed upon the request of a party, either for five years or permanently, without a showing of any further abuse since the issuance of the original order, subject to termination or modification by further order of the court either on written stipulation filed with the court or on the motion of a party. The request for renewal may be brought at any time within the three months before the expiration of the order. (2) The failure to state the expiration date on the face of the form creates an order with a duration of three years from the date of issuance.

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15657.03(x) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Welf. & Inst. C. § 15657.03(x)
citations.quote: (x) Willful disobedience of a temporary restraining order or restraining order after hearing granted under this section is punishable pursuant to Section 273.6 of the Penal Code.

clauses.title: How This Differs From a Civil Harassment or Domestic Violence Restraining Order
clauses.body: Welfare and Institutions Code section 15657.03(y) states that section 15657.03 does not apply to any action or proceeding governed by Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 525) of Title 7 of Part 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure — the chapter that includes California's civil harassment restraining order statute, Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6 — or by Division 10 (commencing with Section 6200) of the Family Code, California's Domestic Violence Prevention Act. Section 15657.03's own eligibility structure, in turn, does not rest on the kind of relationship-based test that governs those two other statutes: it turns instead on whether the person to be protected is an "elder" (65 or older) or a "dependent adult," as defined in sections 15610.27 and 15610.23, and on whether that person has suffered "abuse," as defined in section 15610.07 — with no requirement, as there is for a domestic violence restraining order, that the parties be spouses, cohabitants, dating partners, co-parents, or relatives within a specified degree, and no requirement, as there is for a civil harassment restraining order, that the parties fall outside such a relationship. An elder or dependent adult abused by a spouse, an adult child, a caregiver, or a stranger can each potentially fall within section 15657.03's coverage, provided the abuse and elder/dependent-adult definitions are met; which statute in fact governs a given set of facts depends on the parties' actual relationship and the nature of the alleged conduct.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California's Elder Abuse and Dependent Adult Civil Protection Act restraining-order remedy (§ 15657.03) is, by its own terms, mutually exclusive with the state's civil harassment and domestic violence restraining-order statutes, and that its eligibility test turns on elder/dependent-adult status and abuse rather than on relationship category — not a claim about which state's law, or which category of order, governs a specific set of facts. The quoted § 15657.03(y) text was independently fetched and verified twice for this document. This clause's characterization of Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(w) and Family Code section 6211 relies on this corpus's own already-verified citations for those two statutes, found in this corpus's Civil Harassment Restraining Order document; those two statutes were not independently re-fetched or re-verified in this research session, and this gap discloses that rather than presenting them as freshly verified in this session. This clause states only the statutory scope and eligibility structure; it does not itself determine which restraining-order statute governs any specific petitioner, respondent, or set of facts.

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15657.03(y) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Welf. & Inst. C. § 15657.03(y)
citations.quote: (y) This section does not apply to any action or proceeding governed by Title 1.6C (commencing with Section 1788) of Part 4 of Division 3 of the Civil Code, Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 525) of Title 7 of Part 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, or Division 10 (commencing with Section 6200) of the Family Code. This section does not preclude a petitioner’s right to use other existing civil remedies.

clauses.title: Employer Identification Number Information Sheet — Purpose and Scope
clauses.body: This information sheet relates to {{companyName}}, a {{entityType}}, regarding a federal Employer Identification Number (EIN) — the taxpayer identifying number the Internal Revenue Service assigns under 26 U.S.C. § 6109 and its implementing Treasury regulations. It describes what an EIN is, the federal rules that determine which entities and individuals are required or permitted to use one, situations in which an existing Social Security number or an already-issued EIN may continue to be used instead of a new one, how an EIN application is made, and a point of confusion the IRS's own published guidance directly addresses: when reorganizing or restructuring an existing entity does, and does not, require a new EIN. {{responsiblePartyName}} is named below only as the individual this information sheet's declarations concern; naming that person here does not itself complete, sign, or submit IRS Form SS-4, Application for Employer Identification Number, or any other IRS filing, and this information sheet does not itself apply for, obtain, or record {{responsiblePartyName}}'s taxpayer identifying number ({{ssnOrItin}}) with the IRS. This document is not this project's LLC Articles of Organization, Articles of Incorporation, Statement of Information, Seller's Permit (CDTFA) Information Sheet, or Local Business License Information Sheet. Those documents concern separate filings and separate agencies; forming {{companyName}} as a legal entity with the California Secretary of State, if {{companyName}} is a corporation or LLC, is a distinct step that IRS guidance describes as ordinarily coming before an EIN application, not a step this information sheet performs. This information sheet also does not itself obtain an EIN for {{companyName}}, does not determine whether {{companyName}}'s specific circumstances require an EIN, and does not constitute legal or tax advice.

clauses.title: The EIN's Statutory and Regulatory Basis
clauses.body: Federal law requires that a person who must make a return, statement, or other document under the Internal Revenue Code include on it an identifying number the Secretary of the Treasury prescribes for that purpose. Treasury's implementing regulation identifies the Employer Identification Number (EIN) as one of several types of federal "taxpayer identifying numbers" — alongside the Social Security number, the IRS individual taxpayer identification number, and the IRS adoption taxpayer identification number — and gives it its own distinct numeric format, different from the Social Security-number format used for the other types. The same regulation states that these other identifying numbers are used to identify individual persons, while the EIN is used to identify employers and other nonindividual persons. This regulatory numbering scheme is the source of the EIN itself: an EIN is not a state-issued business registration number, a business license number, or a trade name registration; it is a number the IRS assigns under this specific federal statutory and regulatory authority.
clauses.gap: This clause cites a statute and its implementing Treasury regulation, not two independent sources on the same question — the regulation exists to carry out the statute's own mandate, so the two citations corroborate one underlying authority rather than confirming it from separate directions. Both are hosted on law.cornell.edu's Legal Information Institute (LII), an unofficial but widely used repository of the U.S. Code and Code of Federal Regulations, drawn from (but not itself) the U.S. Government Publishing Office's official text; this clause was not separately checked against govinfo.gov's official text. This clause states only the identifying-number scheme's basic structure; it does not address every identifying-number type the same regulation covers, and it is informational only — it does not itself assign, apply for, or verify an EIN for any person.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 6109(a)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Statutory requirement to include a prescribed identifying number on a return, statement, or other document
citations.quote: Any person required under the authority of this title to make a return, statement, or other document shall include in such return, statement, or other document such identifying number as may be prescribed for securing proper identification of such person.

citations.case: 26 C.F.R. § 301.6109-1(a)(1)(i) (Cornell LII e-CFR text)
citations.cite: Treasury regulation defining the EIN's numeric form as one of several taxpayer identifying number types
citations.quote: Employer identification numbers take the form 00-0000000.

clauses.title: Which Entities and Individuals the IRS Says Need an EIN
clauses.body: Treasury's identifying-number regulation draws a basic line by entity type: any person other than an individual — its own examples include corporations, partnerships, nonprofit associations, trusts, and estates — that is required to furnish a taxpayer identifying number must use an EIN, while an individual who is an employer or who conducts a trade or business as a sole proprietor is separately instructed to use an EIN as well. The IRS's own published guidance states the same basic rule in operational terms: an EIN is described as required for a business, organization, or certain retirement trust that has employees, that will need to pay employment, excise, or alcohol/tobacco/firearms taxes, or that withholds tax on certain income paid to a non-resident alien, and for an entity operating as a partnership, limited liability company, corporation, tax-exempt organization, estate, or trust (with an exception the same guidance states for certain grantor-owned revocable trusts), as well as a retirement plan or IRA, a real estate mortgage investment conduit, or a farmers' cooperative. That same IRS guidance adds that an entity that does not need an EIN for federal tax purposes may still request one for banking or state tax purposes.
clauses.gap: The regulation and the IRS's own guidance page are treated as two distinct sources here — the first is a legally binding Treasury regulation, the second is the IRS's own explanatory, non-binding guidance page — but both describe the same underlying rule, so this is corroboration of one settled point rather than two independently reached legal conclusions. The quoted IRS entity list is exactly the text of that page's bulleted list after removing its bullet formatting, not additional or paraphrased content. This clause does not repeat every item on the IRS's list in the citations below (retirement plans, IRAs, real estate mortgage investment conduits, and farmers' cooperatives are described in the body text above but not separately quoted), and it does not evaluate whether any specific person's or entity's activities actually trigger this requirement.

citations.case: 26 C.F.R. § 301.6109-1(a)(1)(ii)(C) (Cornell LII e-CFR text)
citations.cite: Treasury regulation requiring a nonindividual person required to furnish a taxpayer identifying number to use an EIN
citations.quote: Any person other than an individual (such as corporations, partnerships, nonprofit associations, trusts, estates, and similar nonindividual persons) that is required to furnish a taxpayer identifying number must use an employer identification number.

citations.case: IRS.gov, "Employer identification number" (Internal Revenue Service)
citations.cite: IRS's own published list of entities that need an EIN to operate
citations.quote: You also need an EIN to operate any of these entities: Partnership Limited liability company (LLC) Corporation Tax-exempt organization Estate Trust

clauses.title: A Single-Member LLC or Sole Proprietor May Sometimes Use an Existing Number Instead of a New EIN
clauses.body: Not every business needs its own separate EIN. Treasury's regulations state that, except as otherwise provided elsewhere in the same regulations, a business entity with a single owner that is "disregarded" as separate from that owner under the federal check-the-box entity-classification rules — the classification a single-member LLC receives by default unless it elects to be taxed as a corporation — must use its owner's own taxpayer identifying number for federal tax purposes, rather than obtaining a separate number for the LLC itself; for an individual owner, that identifying number is typically the owner's own Social Security number. The IRS's own published guidance on when a new EIN is required states a matching conclusion in practical terms for this situation: an existing sole proprietor's EIN may continue to be used for that person's single-member LLC, without obtaining a new EIN for the LLC, when the LLC has not elected to be taxed as a corporation or S corporation and does not have employees or an excise tax obligation. The same IRS guidance also marks the boundary of that rule: a single-member LLC does need its own, separate EIN once it must file excise or employment tax returns.
clauses.gap: Both citations make the same underlying point from different sources — a binding Treasury regulation and the IRS's own non-binding guidance page — so they corroborate rather than independently establish it. This clause describes only the "disregarded entity" default classification that applies unless the LLC has affirmatively elected corporate tax treatment; it does not describe the check-the-box election mechanics themselves (26 C.F.R. § 301.7701-3), which are outside this clause's scope. This is informational only: it does not determine whether any specific single-member LLC has, or should have, its own EIN, and it does not address non-tax reasons — for example, a particular bank's own account-opening requirements — that may lead an LLC to obtain a separate EIN even when federal tax law alone would not require one.

citations.case: 26 C.F.R. § 301.6109-1(h)(2)(i) (Cornell LII e-CFR text)
citations.cite: Treasury regulation requiring a disregarded single-owner entity to use its owner's taxpayer identifying number
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided in regulations or other guidance, a single owner entity that is disregarded as an entity separate from its owner under § 301.7701-3, must use its owner's taxpayer identifying number (TIN) for federal tax purposes.

citations.case: IRS.gov, "When to get a new EIN" (Internal Revenue Service)
citations.cite: IRS's own guidance permitting a single-member LLC to continue using the sole proprietor's existing EIN in certain circumstances
citations.quote: Use your sole proprietor EIN for your single-member LLC and don’t choose to be taxed as a corporation or an S corporation and don’t have employees or owe excise tax.

clauses.title: Common Point of Confusion: Assuming Every Business Reorganization Requires a New EIN
clauses.body: A frequent point of confusion is whether reorganizing, converting, or otherwise changing the structure of an existing business automatically requires applying for a new EIN. Treasury's regulations state a general retention rule for one specific category of change: an entity that already has an EIN keeps that same EIN even when its federal tax classification changes under the check-the-box entity-classification regulations. The IRS's own published list of when a new EIN is, and is not, required goes further and gives specific examples for corporations on both sides of the line. That list identifies several situations as NOT requiring a new EIN — including changing a corporation's name or location, reorganizing to change only the corporation's identity or location, remaining the surviving corporation after a merger, converting at the state level without changing the underlying business structure, and electing to be taxed as an S corporation. By contrast, the same IRS list identifies other events — obtaining a new charter for the corporation from the secretary of state, becoming a subsidiary of another corporation, changing to a partnership or sole proprietorship, or merging in a way that creates a new corporation — as situations that do require a new EIN. Because the dividing line depends on which of these specific, IRS-enumerated events has occurred, an entity's own EIN is not something that resets automatically every time the entity's structure, ownership, or paperwork changes.
clauses.gap: The Treasury regulation cited below supports the narrower proposition that an EIN survives a change in federal tax classification specifically; the broader corporate examples in the IRS's own "When to get a new EIN" list — for example, remaining the surviving corporation after a merger, or converting at the state level — rest on that IRS guidance page itself rather than being separately traceable, word for word, to the cited regulatory text. The two citations are therefore best read as a binding regulation establishing the general retention principle for tax-classification changes, corroborated (not independently proven) by the IRS's own more detailed, non-binding illustration of that principle across a wider range of corporate events. This clause addresses only the corporation-specific portion of the IRS's list; the same IRS page states separate, differently worded rules for sole proprietorships, partnerships, LLCs, trusts, and estates that are not repeated here. This is informational only: it does not determine whether any specific entity's own reorganization or restructuring does or does not require a new EIN.

citations.case: 26 C.F.R. § 301.6109-1(h)(1) (Cornell LII e-CFR text)
citations.cite: Treasury regulation providing that an entity retains its EIN when its federal tax classification changes
citations.quote: Any entity that has an employer identification number (EIN) will retain that EIN if its federal tax classification changes under § 301.7701-3.

citations.case: IRS.gov, "When to get a new EIN" (Internal Revenue Service)
citations.cite: IRS's own list identifying a corporate reorganization limited to identity or location as not requiring a new EIN
citations.quote: Reorganize to change only your identity or location.

clauses.title: How an EIN Application Is Made, and the IRS's Own No-Fee Warning
clauses.body: An EIN is obtained by application, not automatically or by mere formation of a business. Treasury's regulations state that a person required to furnish an EIN must apply for one using Form SS-4, Application for Employer Identification Number, which is obtainable from any office of the Internal Revenue Service, a U.S. consular office abroad, or an IRS-authorized acceptance agent, and must be filed far enough in advance of the number's first required use to permit issuance in time for that use. The IRS's own current guidance describes its own online EIN tool as the way to get an EIN directly from the IRS, at no cost, within minutes of a successful application, available to a domestic organization whose principal place of business is in the United States or a U.S. territory and whose application is made by the entity's own responsible party or an authorized representative holding that party's Social Security number or individual taxpayer identification number; an applicant whose principal place of business is outside the United States must instead apply by phone, fax, or mail. That same IRS guidance states directly that applicants should be alert to non-IRS websites that charge a fee for an EIN, because obtaining an EIN from the IRS itself never carries a fee. Separately, the IRS's own guidance states that a person forming a corporation or LLC should register that entity with the state before applying for an EIN, and that EIN issuance is limited to one EIN per responsible party per day, regardless of whether the application is made online, by phone, by fax, or by mail.
clauses.gap: The Treasury regulation and the IRS guidance page corroborate the same general point — that an EIN is obtained by application, historically on Form SS-4 — but the specific online-tool mechanics, its free-of-charge nature, the fee-scam warning, the form-your-entity-first sequencing, and the one-per-responsible-party-per-day limit described in this clause come only from the IRS's own guidance page, not from the cited regulatory text itself, which predates the online tool and speaks only in terms of the paper Form SS-4 process. This clause does not restate the regulation's separate provisions on international applicants, acceptance agents, or updating application information after an EIN is issued. The online tool's stated availability windows and other operational details reflect the IRS's guidance page as fetched on the date shown above and may change without updating this clause. This is informational only: it does not itself submit an EIN application for any person, and it does not determine whether a particular applicant qualifies to use the IRS's online tool.

citations.case: 26 C.F.R. § 301.6109-1(d)(2)(i) (Cornell LII e-CFR text)
citations.cite: Treasury regulation requiring an EIN application on Form SS-4
citations.quote: Any person required to furnish an employer identification number must apply for one, if not done so previously, on Form SS-4. A Form SS-4 may be obtained from any office of the Internal Revenue Service, U.S. consular office abroad, or from an acceptance agent described in paragraph (d)(3)(iv) of this section.

citations.case: IRS.gov, "Get an employer identification number" (Internal Revenue Service)
citations.cite: IRS's own description of its free online EIN tool and its warning against fee-charging websites
citations.quote: Use this tool to get an EIN directly from the IRS in minutes for free. Answer questions and submit the application. If it’s approved, we’ll issue your EIN immediately online. Beware of websites that charge for an EIN. You never have to pay a fee for an EIN.

clauses.title: California's EDD Payroll Tax Account Number Is a Separate State Number, Not the Federal EIN
clauses.body: A federal EIN is not the same number as the account number the California Employment Development Department (EDD) issues to a registered California employer. California's EDD states that once an employer registers with EDD, the department issues its own eight-digit "employer payroll tax account number" — also called a State Employer Identification Number (SEIN) or State ID number — which is required for the employer's dealings with EDD, including filing state payroll tax returns and wage reports. EDD's own registration guidance separately instructs an employer registering for that state account number to include its federal EIN on the registration, explaining that doing so helps ensure the employer's state unemployment insurance tax payments are properly credited when the employer later files its federal unemployment tax return (IRS Form 940) with the IRS. An employer that registers with EDD therefore ordinarily holds two distinct numbers for two distinct purposes: a federal EIN issued by the IRS, and a separate state payroll tax account number issued by EDD; providing the EIN on an EDD registration does not substitute for, or duplicate, that separate state registration.
clauses.gap: Both citations below come from the same California EDD web page, not from two independent sources — this clause has only one primary source for the state-number side of this disambiguation. That page was fetched twice, using different request headers, to confirm its content was stable and not tailored to a particular requester, but that is a stability check, not independent corroboration from a second source. This clause does not address household-employer or other specialized EDD registration variants, does not state EDD's current registration fee, deadline, or online portal procedure (it is limited to the numbering distinction), and does not address any other state's analogous employer identification number, which may work differently. This is informational only: it does not register any employer with EDD and does not obtain a SEIN or EIN for any person.

citations.quote: After you register with EDD, you will receive an eight-digit employer payroll tax account number (example: 000-0000-0). This is also called a State Employer Identification Number (SEIN) or State ID number.

citations.cite: EDD's own instruction to include the federal EIN on state payroll tax account registration
