clauses.title: Who Is Eligible to Serve as an Agent for Service of Process
clauses.body: California recognizes two categories of eligible agent for service of process: an individual who resides in California, or a corporation that has separately registered with the Secretary of State as a corporate agent under Corporations Code section 1505 (commonly called a "1505 agent"). A business entity cannot designate itself as its own agent for service of process. Where a corporation is named as the agent, that corporation must currently be authorized to engage in business in California and in good standing on the Secretary of State's records before it may file the certificate that qualifies it to act as a registered corporate agent in the first place. The Secretary of State's own published guidance adds a practical detail not found in the statute's text: advance approval is ordinarily obtained from a registered corporate agent before that corporation is named as an entity's agent for service of process.
clauses.gap: This is one state's eligibility rule, not a claim about what any other state requires. The individual-resident-or-qualifying-corporation dichotomy stated here is the same underlying eligibility rule already verified elsewhere in this project's corpus for LLC and corporation formation documents (at Cal. Corp. Code section 17701.13(c) and section 1502(b) respectively); this clause does not re-quote those provisions, and instead supplies the deeper, previously unresearched layer -- what actually qualifies a corporation to be the "corporation that has complied with Section 1505" those other provisions refer to. Two of the three citations below (the definition and the advance-approval note) come from the same Secretary of State FAQ page and are treated as one source, not independent of each other; the good-standing requirement is independently verified against the statutory text of Cal. Corp. Code section 1505(c) itself, a separate primary source.

citations.case: Cal. Sec'y of State, Business Entities FAQ — Agent for Service of Process
citations.cite: California Secretary of State, published guidance defining who may serve as an agent for service of process
citations.quote: An agent for service of process is an individual who resides in California, or a registered 1505 corporate agent, designated to accept service of process (court papers) if the business entity is sued.

citations.case: Cal. Sec'y of State, Business Entities FAQ — Agent for Service of Process
citations.cite: California Secretary of State, published guidance on obtaining a registered corporate agent's approval before designation
citations.quote: Note: Advanced approval must be obtained from a Registered Corporate Agent prior to designating that corporation as your agent for service of process.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1505(c)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, prerequisite to filing a corporate-agent certificate
citations.quote: No domestic or foreign corporation may file a certificate pursuant to this section unless it is currently authorized to engage in business in this state and is in good standing on the records of the Secretary of State.

clauses.title: The Certificate a Corporation Must File to Become a Registered Corporate Agent
clauses.body: Becoming eligible to act as a corporate agent for service of process requires an affirmative filing, not merely satisfying the good-standing requirement described elsewhere. Before any corporation may be designated as an agent for service of process, it must file a certificate, executed by one of its officers, stating the complete street address in California of the office or offices where it may be served, the name of each person it authorizes to accept delivery of process at each such office, and its consent that delivery to any such person constitutes delivery to the corporation as agent. A corporation that has filed this certificate may later file any number of supplemental certificates restating this information, and each supplemental filing supersedes the statements in the original certificate or any earlier supplemental certificate. The Secretary of State's own form for this filing confirms that any active corporation registered with the Secretary of State may file it to become authorized to act as a corporate agent for other registered business entities.
clauses.gap: This is one state's certificate-filing requirement, not a claim about what any other state requires. The two statutory quotes below are subsections of the same section, Cal. Corp. Code section 1505 -- subdivision (a) for the certificate's required content and subdivision (b) for supplemental certificates -- and are treated as one source, not independent ones. The Secretary of State's Form 1505 instructions are an independently fetched, separate primary source (the agency's own published form and instructions, not the statutory text itself) that corroborates, in the agency's own words, who may file this certificate.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1505(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, required content of a corporate agent's certificate
citations.quote: Any domestic or foreign corporation, before it may be designated as the agent for the purpose of service of process of any entity pursuant to any law which refers to this section, shall file a certificate executed in the name of the corporation by an officer thereof stating all of the following: (1) The complete street address of its office or offices in this state, wherein any entity designating it as such agent may be served with process. (2) The name of each person employed by it at each such office to whom it authorizes the delivery of a copy of any such process. (3) Its consent that delivery thereof to any such person at the office where the person is employed shall constitute delivery of any such copy to it, as such agent.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1505(b)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, supplemental certificates
citations.quote: Any corporation which has filed the certificate provided for in subdivision (a) may file any number of supplemental certificates containing all the statements provided for in subdivision (a), which, upon the filing thereof, shall supersede the statements contained in the original or in any supplemental certificate previously filed.

citations.case: Cal. Sec'y of State, Form 1505 Instructions (Registered Corporate Agent for Service of Process Certificate)
citations.cite: California Secretary of State, official form instructions describing who may file Form 1505
citations.quote: Who Can File? Any active corporation that is registered with the California Secretary of State can file this Form 1505 to become authorized to be a corporate agent for service of process for other business entities that are registered with the Secretary of State.

clauses.title: How an Entity Changes Its Agent After Formation: A Current Statement of Information, Not a Separate Filing
clauses.body: California does not provide a distinct "change of agent" filing separate from the Statement of Information system. For a corporation, the statute is explicit: in order to change its agent for service of process, or the address of its existing agent, the corporation must file a current statement containing all of the information the Statement of Information statute otherwise requires -- the same filing used for periodic reporting, not a different form. The California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act imposes the identical mechanism on an LLC, in mandatory terms: when changing its agent for service of process, or when the agent's address changes, the LLC must file a current statement containing all of the information its own Statement of Information statute requires. Unlike the ordinary periodic filing, which follows the entity's assigned filing period, an agent change is not deferred to that period -- the current statement reflecting the new agent may be, and for the entity's own updated public record must eventually be, filed once the change occurs. The Secretary of State's own published guidance directs entities to the same mechanism: a California stock corporation files its Statement of Information, and a California LLC files its own Statement of Information, to reflect a changed agent for service of process.
clauses.gap: This is one state's mechanism, not a claim about what any other state requires. The corporation-specific and LLC-specific statutory quotes below come from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code section 1502(e) and Cal. Corp. Code section 17702.09(d), and are treated as two independent statutory sources, not subsections of one section. The Secretary of State FAQ quote is a third, independent-of-statute source (agency guidance rather than statutory text), though it is drawn from the same FAQ page already cited elsewhere in this document for a different question, and is not independent of those other FAQ citations. This finding corrects a plausible but incorrect assumption: an entity does not change its agent by amending its original articles of incorporation or articles of organization. This project's Certificate of Amendment document already establishes, at Cal. Corp. Code section 900(b), that a corporation's articles generally cannot be amended to alter the agent information stated in the original articles, except to correct an error or to delete that information once a Statement of Information has since been filed; that existing clause is not re-quoted here.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1502(e)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, filing a current statement to change the agent for service of process
citations.quote: Whenever any of the information required by subdivision (a) is changed, the corporation may file a current statement containing all the information required by subdivisions (a) and (b). In order to change its agent for service of process or the address of the agent, the corporation must file a current statement containing all the information required by subdivisions (a) and (b). Whenever any statement is filed pursuant to this section, it supersedes any previously filed statement and the statement in the articles as to the agent for service of process and the address of the agent.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17702.09(d)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, filing a current statement to change the agent for service of process
citations.quote: Whenever any of the information required by subdivision (a) changes, other than the name and address of the agent for service of process, the limited liability company or foreign limited liability company may file a current statement containing all the information required by subdivision (a). When changing its agent for service of process or when the address of the agent changes, the limited liability company or foreign limited liability company shall file a current statement containing all the information required by subdivision (a).

citations.case: Cal. Sec'y of State, Business Entities FAQ — Agent for Service of Process
citations.cite: California Secretary of State, published guidance on changing an entity's agent for service of process
citations.quote: A business registered with the California Secretary of State may change its address(es) by submitting the appropriate document: California Stock Corporation and Out-of-State Corporation: File online at bizfileOnline.sos.ca.gov the Statement of Information – CA and Out-of-State Corporation.

clauses.title: The Agent's Own Resignation — a Filing the Agent, Not the Entity, Makes
clauses.body: Separate from an entity's own act of changing its designated agent by filing a current Statement of Information, California law gives the agent itself an independent, agent-initiated way to end its own service in that role. An agent designated for a corporation's service of process may deliver to the Secretary of State a signed and acknowledged statement of resignation, on a form the Secretary of State prescribes, stating the corporation's name and Secretary of State file number, the resigning agent's name, and that the agent is resigning; once filed, the agent's authority to act in that capacity ceases, and the Secretary of State provides written notice of the resignation to the corporation at its principal office. California's LLC statute gives an LLC's agent the same independent power, through nearly identical language: the agent delivers its own signed and acknowledged statement of resignation to the Secretary of State, the agent's authority ceases upon that filing, and the Secretary of State notifies the LLC's principal office. In both cases, this resignation filing ends the resigning party's own status as agent; it does not itself name a replacement agent for the entity.
clauses.gap: This is one state's mechanism, not a claim about what any other state requires. The corporation-specific and LLC-specific statutory quotes below come from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code section 1503(a) and Cal. Corp. Code section 17701.15(a), and are treated as two independent statutory sources, not subsections of one section, though the Legislature drafted their operative language in closely parallel terms. This is the one genuinely separate statutory filing this document identifies: unlike the entity's own change-of-agent filing (a current Statement of Information, described in a separate clause of this document), a resignation under these sections is filed by the agent itself, on its own initiative, using a distinct Secretary of State form for that purpose.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1503(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, an agent's own resignation as agent for service of process
citations.quote: An agent designated for service of process pursuant to Section 202, 1502, 2105, or 2117 may deliver to the Secretary of State, on a form prescribed by the Secretary of State for filing, a signed and acknowledged written statement of resignation as an agent for service of process. The form shall contain the name of the corporation, the Secretary of State’s file number of the corporation, the name of the resigning agent for service of process, and a statement that the agent is resigning. Thereupon the authority of the agent to act in such capacity shall cease and the Secretary of State forthwith shall mail or otherwise provide written notice of the filing of the statement of resignation to the corporation at its principal office.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.15(a)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, an agent's own resignation as agent for service of process
citations.quote: To resign as an agent for service of process of a limited liability company or foreign limited liability company, the agent shall deliver to the Secretary of State for filing, on a form prescribed by the Secretary of State for filing, a signed and acknowledged statement of resignation as an agent for service of process containing the name of the limited liability company or foreign limited liability company, the Secretary of State’s file number for the limited liability company or foreign limited liability company, the name of the resigning agent for service of process, and a statement that the agent is resigning.

clauses.title: Consequences When No Valid Agent Can Be Found
clauses.body: California's LLC statute lists the specific events that trigger a duty to promptly update an LLC's agent designation: if an individual designated as agent dies, resigns, or no longer resides in the state, or if a corporate agent resigns, dissolves, withdraws from the state, forfeits its right to transact intrastate business, has its corporate rights, powers, or privileges suspended, or ceases to exist, the LLC must promptly file an initial or amended Statement of Information reflecting the change. Beyond that filing duty, both a corporation and an LLC face a separate, litigation-facing consequence when service cannot actually be accomplished on a designated agent: if the agent has resigned and not been replaced, or cannot with reasonable diligence be found at its listed address, a court may order that service instead be made by delivering process to the Secretary of State, with service deemed complete on the tenth day after that delivery. For a corporation specifically, this same substituted-service mechanism is also available if no agent has been designated for it at all.
clauses.gap: This is one state's rule, not a claim about what any other state requires. The two statutory quotes below come from two independently enacted sections, one for each entity type: Cal. Corp. Code section 17701.15(e) and Cal. Corp. Code section 1702(a); they are treated as independent sources, not subsections of one section. This project's existing LLC Articles of Organization document already quotes the LLC's own parallel substituted-service provision, Cal. Corp. Code section 17701.16(c), and that quote is not repeated here to avoid duplicating an already-verified citation. This clause instead supplies two pieces of previously unresearched material: the LLC statute's specific list of triggering events at section 17701.15(e) (a different subsection of a different section than 17701.16, addressing when the duty to update arises rather than how substituted service works), and the corporation's own substituted-service statute, section 1702(a), which had not previously been cited anywhere in this project's corpus.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.15(e)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, duty to update the Statement of Information when an agent can no longer serve
citations.quote: If an individual who has been designated agent for service of process dies or resigns or no longer resides in the state, or if the corporate agent for that purpose resigns, dissolves, withdraws from the state, forfeits its right to transact intrastate business in this state, has its corporate rights, powers, and privileges suspended, or ceases to exist, the limited liability company or foreign limited liability company shall promptly file an initial or amended statement of information as set forth in Section 17702.09.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1702(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, service on the Secretary of State when a corporation's agent cannot be found or none has been designated
citations.quote: If an agent for the purpose of service of process has resigned and has not been replaced or if the agent designated cannot with reasonable diligence be found at the address designated for personally delivering the process, or if no agent has been designated, and it is shown by affidavit to the satisfaction of the court that process against a domestic corporation cannot be served with reasonable diligence upon the designated agent by hand in the manner provided in Section 415.10, subdivision (a) of Section 415.20 or subdivision (a) of Section 415.30 of the Code of Civil Procedure or upon the corporation in the manner provided in subdivision (a), (b), or (c) of Section 416.10 or subdivision (a) of Section 416.20 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court may make an order that the service be made upon the corporation by delivering by hand to the Secretary of State, or to any person employed in the Secretary of State’s office in the capacity of assistant or deputy, one copy of the process for each defendant to be served, together with a copy of the order authorizing such service. Service in this manner is deemed complete on the 10th day after delivery of the process to the Secretary of State.

clauses.title: Change of Agent for Service of Process — Declaration
clauses.body: {{companyName}}, a California {{entityType}}, is changing its agent for service of process on file with the California Secretary of State. {{companyName}}'s prior agent for service of process was {{priorAgentName}}. {{companyName}}'s new agent for service of process is {{newAgentName}}. {{newAgentName}}'s California street address is {{newAgentAddress}} (omitted if {{newAgentName}} is a registered corporate agent). This declaration organizes the information needed to complete {{companyName}}'s current Statement of Information reflecting this change. It is not itself the Secretary of State's official statement form, which must be completed and filed in the format the Secretary of State prescribes, and it does not itself effect the change until that filing is accepted.

clauses.title: Closing and Signature Block — Agent for Service of Process Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This information sheet regarding {{companyName}}'s agent for service of process was prepared by {{authorizedSignerName}}.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{authorizedSignerName}}: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet describes California's statutory rules governing who is eligible to serve as an agent for service of process, the certificate that qualifies a corporation to serve as a registered corporate agent, and the separate statutory mechanisms for an agent's own resignation and for an entity's own change of its designated agent after formation. It is not the Secretary of State's official Statement of Information form or Form 1505 certificate, does not itself change {{companyName}}'s agent for service of process on file with the Secretary of State, and does not constitute legal advice. The current official forms and instructions are published by the California Secretary of State.]

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes federal and California law governing when {{companyName}} may require {{employeeName}}, as a job applicant, to undergo a medical examination or answer disability-related medical questions during the hiring process. It states facts about what the Americans with Disabilities Act, its implementing federal regulation, and California's Fair Employment and Housing Act permit, require, and restrict in this area. It is not itself a medical examination, a consent form, or an authorization for any specific examination, and it does not tell {{companyName}} or {{employeeName}} what to do about any particular hiring decision.

clauses.title: Before a Job Offer: No Medical Exams or Disability Inquiries
clauses.body: Before {{companyName}} extends a conditional job offer, federal law prohibits it from conducting a medical examination of {{employeeName}} or asking whether {{employeeName}} has a disability or about the nature or severity of a disability. California law separately prohibits requiring a medical or psychological examination, making a medical or psychological inquiry, or asking whether an applicant has a mental disability, physical disability, or medical condition, at the pre-offer stage. Both laws permit one specific kind of pre-offer question during this stage: {{companyName}} may ask about {{employeeName}}'s ability to perform job-related functions, and may ask {{employeeName}} to describe or demonstrate how those functions would be performed, with or without reasonable accommodation.
clauses.gap: Federal and California law are independent sources here, and each is treated as a source in its own right below. The federal EEOC regulation's description of the acceptable pre-offer inquiry (asking an applicant to describe or demonstrate how job functions would be performed, with or without reasonable accommodation) is more specific than the bare statutory text, which speaks only of inquiries into the ability to perform job-related functions; both are quoted below. This document is informational only: it does not itself authorize, conduct, or determine the lawfulness of any specific examination or inquiry, and it does not determine whether a conditional offer has been extended in any given case.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 12112(d)(2)(A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Americans with Disabilities Act, pre-offer prohibition
citations.quote: a covered entity shall not conduct a medical examination or make inquiries of a job applicant as to whether such applicant is an individual with a disability or as to the nature or severity of such disability

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 12112(d)(2)(B) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Americans with Disabilities Act, acceptable pre-offer inquiry
citations.quote: A covered entity may make preemployment inquiries into the ability of an applicant to perform job-related functions.

citations.case: 29 C.F.R. § 1630.14(a) (Cornell LII / e-CFR text)
citations.cite: EEOC ADA regulation, acceptable pre-employment inquiry
citations.quote: A covered entity may make pre-employment inquiries into the ability of an applicant to perform job-related functions, and/or may ask an applicant to describe or to demonstrate how, with or without reasonable accommodation, the applicant will be able to perform job-related functions.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(e)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California FEHA, pre-offer prohibition on medical or psychological examination and inquiry
citations.quote: for any employer or employment agency to require any medical or psychological examination of an applicant, to make any medical or psychological inquiry of an applicant, to make any inquiry whether an applicant has a mental disability or physical disability or medical condition, or to make any inquiry regarding the nature or severity of a physical disability, mental disability, or medical condition.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(e)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California FEHA, acceptable pre-offer inquiry and accommodation response
citations.quote: an employer or employment agency may inquire into the ability of an applicant to perform job-related functions and may respond to an applicant’s request for reasonable accommodation.

clauses.title: After a Conditional Offer: A Medical Exam May Be Required
clauses.body: After {{companyName}} has extended a conditional offer of employment to {{employeeName}}, and before {{employeeName}} begins job duties, federal law permits {{companyName}} to require a medical examination and to condition the offer on its results — but only if all entering employees in the same job category are required to undergo the same examination, regardless of disability. California law permits the same thing under a parallel, but not identical, standard: it additionally requires that the examination or inquiry itself be job-related and consistent with business necessity, on top of requiring that all entering employees in the same job classification be subject to the same examination or inquiry.
clauses.gap: This is a genuine difference between the two laws, not a restatement of one by the other: the federal statute's own text conditions the post-offer exam only on its being required of all entering employees regardless of disability, without an express job-related/business-necessity requirement for the exam itself (the federal EEOC regulation confirms this — it states that exams conducted under this provision "do not have to be job-related and consistent with business necessity," though any criteria later used to screen someone out because of the results must independently meet that standard); California's statute, by contrast, writes a job-related/business-necessity requirement directly into the authorization for the exam itself. An employer relying on this document should not assume the federal and state standards are interchangeable. Both the federal regulation and the state statute independently use the phrase "same job category" / "same job classification" — a detail the bare federal statutory text doesn't include but the regulation adds. This document is informational only: it does not itself authorize, conduct, or determine the lawfulness of any specific examination, and it does not determine whether any particular offer is "conditional" for these purposes.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 12112(d)(3)(A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Americans with Disabilities Act, permitted post-offer employment entrance examination
citations.quote: A covered entity may require a medical examination after an offer of employment has been made to a job applicant and prior to the commencement of the employment duties of such applicant, and may condition an offer of employment on the results of such examination, if— (A) all entering employees are subjected to such an examination regardless of disability;

citations.case: 29 C.F.R. § 1630.14(b) (Cornell LII / e-CFR text)
citations.cite: EEOC ADA regulation, employment entrance examination and same-job-category requirement
citations.quote: A covered entity may require a medical examination (and/or inquiry) after making an offer of employment to a job applicant and before the applicant begins his or her employment duties, and may condition an offer of employment on the results of such examination (and/or inquiry), if all entering employees in the same job category are subjected to such an examination (and/or inquiry) regardless of disability.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(e)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California FEHA, permitted post-offer examination with added job-related/business-necessity requirement
citations.quote: an employer or employment agency may require a medical or psychological examination or make a medical or psychological inquiry of a job applicant after an employment offer has been made but prior to the commencement of employment duties, provided that the examination or inquiry is job related and consistent with business necessity and that all entering employees in the same job classification are subject to the same examination or inquiry.

clauses.title: Confidentiality of Medical Examination Results
clauses.body: Under federal law, information {{companyName}} obtains about {{employeeName}}'s medical condition or history through a permitted post-offer examination must be collected and kept on separate forms, kept in separate medical files apart from {{employeeName}}'s regular personnel file, and treated as a confidential medical record. This confidentiality requirement has three specific, limited exceptions: supervisors and managers may be informed of necessary work restrictions and accommodations, first aid and safety personnel may be informed if the condition might require emergency treatment, and government officials investigating compliance may be given relevant information on request.
clauses.gap: The federal statute and its implementing regulation are being treated together here as one connected source on this point, not as independent corroborating sources — the regulation restates the same rule the statute establishes. This document's research did not find a confidentiality provision written into California Government Code § 12940 itself paralleling this federal one; § 12940, as fetched for this document, describes when a pre- or post-offer examination or inquiry is permitted but does not itself impose separate-file or separate-form confidentiality requirements on the results. That does not mean California applicants and employees have no other confidentiality protection for medical information under state law generally — only that this particular statute, the one this document otherwise relies on for the pre-offer/post-offer distinction, does not contain one, and no other California confidentiality statute was researched or verified for purposes of this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself authorize, conduct, or determine the lawfulness of any specific examination, and it does not itself establish or enforce any recordkeeping practice.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 12112(d)(3)(B) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Americans with Disabilities Act, confidentiality requirements and exceptions for post-offer exam results
citations.quote: information obtained regarding the medical condition or history of the applicant is collected and maintained on separate forms and in separate medical files and is treated as a confidential medical record, except that— (i) supervisors and managers may be informed regarding necessary restrictions on the work or duties of the employee and necessary accommodations; (ii) first aid and safety personnel may be informed, when appropriate, if the disability might require emergency treatment; and (iii) government officials investigating compliance with this chapter shall be provided relevant information on request

citations.case: 29 C.F.R. § 1630.14(b)(1) (Cornell LII / e-CFR text)
citations.cite: EEOC ADA regulation, confidentiality requirement for post-offer exam results
citations.quote: Information obtained under paragraph (b) of this section regarding the medical condition or history of the applicant shall be collected and maintained on separate forms and in separate medical files and be treated as a confidential medical record, except that: (i) Supervisors and managers may be informed regarding necessary restrictions on the work or duties of the employee and necessary accommodations; (ii) First aid and safety personnel may be informed, when appropriate, if the disability might require emergency treatment; and (iii) Government officials investigating compliance with this part shall be provided relevant information on request.

clauses.title: If the Exam Reveals a Disability
clauses.body: A permitted post-offer medical examination does not itself have to be job-related and consistent with business necessity to be lawful under the federal regulation — but if {{companyName}} uses the results to screen {{employeeName}} out because of a disability, the specific exclusionary criteria used must be job-related and consistent with business necessity, and the exclusion must hold up even considering whether the essential job functions could be performed with reasonable accommodation. California law reaches a similar substantive result through its disability-discrimination provisions generally: it does not prohibit an employer from refusing to hire, or from discharging, a person with a physical or mental disability or a medical condition if that person, because of the disability or condition, cannot perform the job's essential duties even with reasonable accommodations, or cannot perform them without endangering their own health or safety or the health or safety of others, even with reasonable accommodations.
clauses.gap: The federal point is drawn from the EEOC's own regulation interpreting the ADA's post-offer-examination provision specifically; the California point is drawn from a general disability-discrimination provision of FEHA rather than a subsection addressed specifically to post-offer examinations, since this document's research did not find a FEHA provision addressing withdrawal of an offer after a post-offer exam as specifically as the federal regulation does. The two are stated as separate, independent sources reaching a similar substantive outcome, not as one confirming the other. Neither source is quoted here as resolving whether accommodating any particular condition is possible, what counts as an undue hardship, or what a specific employer's job-related, business-necessity showing must contain in a specific case — both bodies of law require that showing to be made on the specific facts, which this document does not do. This document is informational only: it does not itself authorize, conduct, or determine the lawfulness of any specific decision to withdraw an offer.

citations.case: 29 C.F.R. § 1630.14(b)(3) (Cornell LII / e-CFR text)

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Employee Invention Assignment — Statutory Limits and Shop Right Information Sheet is prepared with reference to {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}}. It describes two things California law does with an invention-assignment provision like the one in an Invention Assignment & Confidentiality Agreement between {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}}: first, a statutory limit on which inventions such a provision can validly reach at all (California Labor Code §§ 2870–2872), and second, a separate common-law doctrine — the "shop right" — under which {{companyName}} can hold an implied, nonexistent-in-writing, nonexclusive license to use an invention {{employeeName}} made using {{companyName}}'s time or materials, independent of whether any assignment provision applies to that invention at all. This sheet is an informational record only. It does not itself determine whether any specific invention created by {{employeeName}} falls inside or outside the statutory carve-out described below, does not determine whether a shop right exists as to any specific invention, and does not modify, waive, or supersede the terms of any assignment agreement actually signed by {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}}.

clauses.title: The Statutory Limit on What Inventions Can Be Required to Be Assigned
clauses.body: California Labor Code § 2870 places a limit on what an invention-assignment provision — the kind of clause that appears in an Invention Assignment & Confidentiality Agreement between {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}} — can validly require. By its terms, such a provision does not apply to an invention {{employeeName}} developed entirely on {{employeeName}}'s own time, without using {{companyName}}'s equipment, supplies, facilities, or trade secret information, unless the invention either (1) relates, at the time of conception or reduction to practice, to {{companyName}}'s business, or to {{companyName}}'s actual or demonstrably anticipated research or development, or (2) results from work {{employeeName}} performed for {{companyName}}. Subdivision (b) then states the consequence: to the extent an assignment provision purports to reach an invention that subdivision (a) excludes, that provision is against the public policy of California and is unenforceable to that extent — the rest of the agreement is not necessarily affected.
clauses.gap: The exclusion in subdivision (a) is cumulative, not alternative: an invention loses the exclusion (and can validly be required to be assigned) if it was developed using any of the employer's equipment, supplies, facilities, or trade secret information, even if it has nothing to do with the employer's business — and separately, even an invention developed with none of those resources loses the exclusion if it relates to the employer's business or actual or demonstrably anticipated research or development, or results from work performed for the employer. Whether a specific invention meets these fact-dependent conditions — what counts as the employee's "own time," what "relates to" the business means, what research is "demonstrably anticipated" — is not resolved by the statutory text itself and is not addressed by this document for any invention actually created by the employee named in this document. This section does not itself invalidate an entire assignment agreement; by its own terms it makes an offending provision unenforceable only to the extent it reaches an excluded invention, and it says nothing about whether an employer can require an employee to disclose an invention to test whether it qualifies for the exclusion (California courts have addressed disclosure obligations in this context, but that question was not independently verified in this research session and is not covered here).

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 2870(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the statutory carve-out for inventions developed on the employee's own time
citations.quote: (a) Any provision in an employment agreement which provides that an employee shall assign, or offer to assign, any of his or her rights in an invention to his or her employer shall not apply to an invention that the employee developed entirely on his or her own time without using the employer’s equipment, supplies, facilities, or trade secret information except for those inventions that either: (1) Relate at the time of conception or reduction to practice of the invention to the employer’s business, or actual or demonstrably anticipated research or development of the employer; or (2) Result from any work performed by the employee for the employer.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 2870(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: unenforceability of a provision that reaches an excluded invention
citations.quote: (b) To the extent a provision in an employment agreement purports to require an employee to assign an invention otherwise excluded from being required to be assigned under subdivision (a), the provision is against the public policy of this state and is unenforceable.

clauses.title: The Employer's Notice Requirement — and the Statute's Silence on What Happens Without It
clauses.body: California Labor Code § 2872 addresses employment agreements entered into after January 1, 1980 that contain an invention-assignment provision. Where such a provision is present — as in an agreement between {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}} — the statute requires {{companyName}}, at the time the agreement is made, to also provide {{employeeName}} written notification that the agreement does not apply to an invention that qualifies fully under Labor Code § 2870. The same section places the burden of proof in any resulting suit or action on the employee claiming the benefit of that exclusion — meaning {{employeeName}}, not {{companyName}}, would bear the burden of showing that a given invention qualifies for the § 2870 carve-out.
clauses.gap: Section 2872's text does not state what happens if an employer fails to give the required written notification — no invalidation of the assignment provision, no separate penalty, and no other stated consequence for noncompliance appears anywhere in the section as fetched and verified for this document. This document did not locate, and does not assert, any consequence for a missing § 2872 notice beyond what the statute's own text says (nothing) — that silence should not be read as either "the notice requirement is toothless" or "noncompliance has no legal significance"; the statute simply does not address it, and this document takes no position on how a court might treat noncompliance. Separately, § 2872 does not specify a required form for the written notification (e.g., a standalone notice versus language embedded in the assignment agreement itself), and that question is not addressed here.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 2872 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the required written notification and burden of proof
citations.quote: If an employment agreement entered into after January 1, 1980, contains a provision requiring the employee to assign or offer to assign any of his or her rights in any invention to his or her employer, the employer must also, at the time the agreement is made, provide a written notification to the employee that the agreement does not apply to an invention which qualifies fully under the provisions of Section 2870. In any suit or action arising thereunder, the burden of proof shall be on the employee claiming the benefits of its provisions.

clauses.title: The Shop Right Doctrine — An Employer's Implied Nonexclusive License
clauses.body: Separate from any written assignment provision, and separate from Labor Code § 2870's limits on what such a provision can require, courts recognize a common-law doctrine sometimes called the "shop right." The U.S. Supreme Court described it in United States v. Dubilier Condenser Corp.: where an employee, during working hours and using the employer's materials and appliances, conceives and perfects an invention for which the employee (not the employer) obtains a patent, the employee must accord the employer a nonexclusive right to practice — that is, to use — that invention. This is an implied right that can arise from the circumstances of how the invention was made, without depending on any signed assignment agreement between {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}}.
clauses.gap: Dubilier is a 1933 U.S. Supreme Court decision applying general federal common-law principles to a dispute over patents obtained by federal government radio-laboratory employees; it is not a California case, and this research session did not independently verify a California appellate decision applying the shop-right doctrine on facts involving a private employer. The quoted passage is the Court's own general description of the shop-right doctrine as then already "settled as respects private employment" (citing 19th-century precedent), not language specific to any particular company's or employee's circumstances, and it does not itself decide whether a shop right exists for any invention the employee named in this document may have made. This corpus separately cites Dubilier's distinct holding about an employee "hired to invent" being bound to assign the resulting patent (clause patentassign_hired_to_invent in another document); that holding and this shop-right passage address different fact patterns within the same opinion and should not be conflated — the shop-right passage applies to an employee whose employment does not itself contemplate inventing, while the "hired to invent" holding applies where it does.

citations.case: United States v. Dubilier Condenser Corp.
citations.quote: Recognition of the nature of the act of invention also defines the limits of the so-called shop right, which, shortly stated, is that, where a servant, during his hours of employment, working with his master's materials and appliances, conceives and perfects an invention for which he obtains a patent, he must accord his master a nonexclusive right to practice the invention.

clauses.title: Shop Right Is a License to Use, Not Ownership of the Invention
clauses.body: The same Dubilier opinion draws a sharp line between the shop right and ownership of the invention itself. Because a shop right rests on equitable principles — the employer having supplied the time, facilities, and materials used to reach the result — the employer is entitled to use what was built with its own resources. But that entitlement does not extend to the invention's ownership: the opinion states that the employer "has no equity to demand a conveyance of the invention," which remains the property of the employee who conceived it, together with the patent right to exclude others (other than the employer) from it. A shop right is therefore narrower than an assignment: it gives {{companyName}}, where it applies, a nonexclusive right to use an invention {{employeeName}} made with {{companyName}}'s time or materials, without giving {{companyName}} title to the invention or the right to stop {{employeeName}} from licensing or using it elsewhere (subject to any separate confidentiality or trade secret obligations, which this clause does not address).
clauses.gap: This is the same 1933 U.S. Supreme Court opinion cited in the companion clause inventionlimits_shop_right_definition in this document — both citations come from a single source, independently re-verified for this specific point (the ownership/license distinction) rather than reused from the earlier quote, but they are not two separate sources. This passage describes the shop right's effect where it applies; it does not itself establish that a shop right exists for any invention the employee named in this document may have made, and it does not address how a shop right interacts with a written assignment provision that Labor Code § 2870 excludes from applying to a given invention — that interaction (whether an employer can hold a shop right to use an invention that § 2870 says it cannot require to be assigned) was not addressed in the text of § 2870 itself and was not independently verified against case law in this research session.

citations.case: United States v. Dubilier Condenser Corp.
citations.quote: Since the servant uses his master's time, facilities, and materials to attain a concrete result, the latter is in equity entitled to use that which embodies his own property and to duplicate it as often as he may find occasion to employ similar appliances in his business. But the employer in such a case has no equity to demand a conveyance of the invention, which is the original conception of the employee alone, in which the employer had no part. This remains the property of him who conceived it, together with the right conferred by the patent, to exclude all others than the employer from the accruing benefits. These principles are settled as respects private employment.

clauses.title: Signature and Record
Information and Background — Alleged Workers' Compensation Retaliation
clauses.body:
I, {{employeeName}}, am completing this information sheet in connection with my employment with {{companyName}}. The workers' compensation-related activity I believe may be connected to an adverse action against me is described here as: {{allegedProtectedActivity}}. The adverse action I believe may be connected to that activity is described here as: {{allegedAdverseAction}}, which I understand to have occurred on {{adverseActionDate}}.

This information sheet describes California Labor Code section 132a — a statute that separately prohibits certain kinds of employer and insurer conduct connected to a workers' compensation claim, and that is enforced through its own petition procedure before the Workers' Compensation Appeals Board rather than through a lawsuit filed in superior court. It is not a Labor Code section 132a petition, is not filed with the Workers' Compensation Appeals Board, any court, or any agency by completing it, and does not initiate any proceeding. Completing it does not establish that {{employeeName}} was in fact discharged, threatened, or discriminated against by {{companyName}} in violation of Labor Code section 132a, or that any specific fact stated here is true. Only the Workers' Compensation Appeals Board, or a court on judicial review of the appeals board's decision, can determine whether a violation of Labor Code section 132a occurred.

clauses.title: Declared Policy and the Core Prohibition — Discharge, Threat, or Discrimination for a Workers' Compensation Claim
clauses.body: California law declares it the policy of this state that there should not be discrimination against workers who are injured in the course and scope of their employment. Consistent with that declared policy, the same statute makes it a misdemeanor for an employer to discharge, threaten to discharge, or in any manner discriminate against an employee because the employee has filed or made known an intention to file a workers' compensation claim with the employer, or an application for adjudication, or because the employee has received a workers' compensation rating, award, or settlement.
clauses.gap: The two sentences quoted in this clause are the opening declaration and paragraph (1) of the same statutory section — Labor Code § 132a — not independent sources from each other; that is disclosed here rather than presented as two separate authorities. This is California's own statute, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings (a standard browser string and a distinct research-tool string); each quote in this clause was confirmed programmatically as an exact (whitespace-normalized) substring of that fetched text. Labor Code § 132a is enforced through a separate, Workers' Compensation Appeals Board-specific petition procedure addressed in a separate clause of this document — a genuinely distinct statutory scheme from Labor Code §§ 1102.5 and 98.6, the whistleblower and wage-claim retaliation statutes addressed in this corpus's separate Wrongful Termination in Violation of Public Policy information sheet, which are instead enforced through a civil action filed in superior court. No claim is made here about which of these statutes, if any, actually applies to a specific set of facts, or about which state's law governs a specific employment relationship. This document is informational: it does not itself determine that any specific discharge, threat, or discrimination occurred, that a specific employee's described adverse action was connected to the described activity, or that a violation of Labor Code § 132a occurred in this or any specific case.

citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: It is the declared policy of this state that there should not be discrimination against workers who are injured in the course and scope of their employment.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 132a, paragraph (1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Any employer who discharges, or threatens to discharge, or in any manner discriminates against any employee because he or she has filed or made known his or her intention to file a claim for compensation with his or her employer or an application for adjudication, or because the employee has received a rating, award, or settlement, is guilty of a misdemeanor

clauses.title: A Parallel Prohibition on Insurers That Pressure an Employer to Discharge
clauses.body: The same statute separately prohibits an insurer from advising, directing, or threatening an insured employer — under penalty of cancellation, a raise in premium, or for any other reason — to discharge an employee because the employee has filed or made known an intention to file a workers' compensation claim, or because the employee has received a rating, award, or settlement. An insurer that does so is guilty of a misdemeanor and is made subject to the same increased-compensation and cost remedy that applies to the employer's own violation of this statute.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes paragraph (2) of the same statutory section addressed in a separate clause of this document — Labor Code § 132a — and is not an independent source from it. Paragraph (2) expressly cross-references paragraph (1)'s remedy language ('subject to the increased compensation and costs provided in paragraph (1)'); the specific dollar and percentage figures that remedy carries are quoted in a separate clause of this document rather than repeated here. This is California's own statute, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings; the quote in this clause was confirmed as an exact (whitespace-normalized) substring of that fetched text. This document is informational: it does not itself determine that any specific insurer engaged in this conduct, or that a violation occurred in this or any specific case.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 132a, paragraph (2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Any insurer that advises, directs, or threatens an insured under penalty of cancellation or a raise in premium or for any other reason, to discharge an employee because he or she has filed or made known his or her intention to file a claim for compensation with his or her employer or an application for adjudication, or because the employee has received a rating, award, or settlement, is guilty of a misdemeanor and subject to the increased compensation and costs provided in paragraph (1).

clauses.title: A Separate Protection — Testifying, or Intending to Testify, in Another Employee's Case
clauses.body: The same statute also separately makes it a misdemeanor for an employer to discharge, threaten to discharge, or in any manner discriminate against an employee because the employee testified, or made known an intention to testify, in another employee's case before the appeals board — a distinct category of prohibited conduct from the claim-filing protection addressed elsewhere in this document, and one that does not depend on the testifying employee having filed, or intending to file, any workers' compensation claim of their own. A parallel prohibition applies to an insurer that pressures an insured employer, under penalty of cancellation, a raise in premium, or for any other reason, to discharge or discriminate against an employee for that same reason.
clauses.gap: This clause verifies, directly against the statute's own current text, that Labor Code § 132a's protection reaches beyond an employee's own claim: paragraph (3) protects an employee who testified or made known an intention to testify in another employee's case before the appeals board, regardless of whether the testifying employee has any pending claim of their own — this was confirmed rather than assumed, and is a genuinely distinct prohibited-conduct category from paragraph (1)'s claim-filing protection addressed in a separate clause of this document. A further, easily-missed distinction: paragraph (3)'s own remedy language — entitling the employee only to 'reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the acts of the employer' — does not include paragraph (1)'s increased-compensation-by-one-half-up-to-$10,000 remedy. That broader remedy appears only in paragraph (1), and is cross-referenced into paragraph (2)'s insurer-inducement provision, but paragraphs (3) and (4) do not cross-reference it and do not themselves state it. This document does not assume the remedy structures for these two categories of prohibited conduct are identical; it states each precisely as the statute's own text provides. All four numbered paragraphs quoted across this clause and two other clauses in this document are subsections of the same statutory section (Labor Code § 132a), not independent sources from each other. This is California's own statute, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings; each quote was confirmed as an exact (whitespace-normalized) substring of that fetched text. This document is informational: it does not itself determine that any specific employee's testimony or intended testimony was the actual reason for any adverse action, or that a violation occurred in this or any specific case.

citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Any employer who discharges, or threatens to discharge, or in any manner discriminates against any employee because the employee testified or made known his or her intentions to testify in another employee’s case before the appeals board, is guilty of a misdemeanor, and the employee shall be entitled to reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the acts of the employer.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 132a, paragraph (4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Any insurer that advises, directs, or threatens an insured employer under penalty of cancellation or a raise in premium or for any other reason, to discharge or in any manner discriminate against an employee because the employee testified or made known his or her intention to testify in another employee’s case before the appeals board, is guilty of a misdemeanor.

clauses.title: The Remedy This Statute Itself Authorizes — Current Dollar and Percentage Figures
clauses.body: For a violation of the claim-filing or rating/award/settlement-based prohibition, the statute itself increases the employee's workers' compensation by one-half, subject to a cap of ten thousand dollars, together with costs and expenses not exceeding two hundred fifty dollars; the same employee is also entitled to reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the employer's acts. This dollar and percentage structure was confirmed directly against the statute's own current, published text rather than assumed from an earlier or unverified figure.
clauses.gap: This document independently fetched Labor Code § 132a's current text rather than assuming an earlier-known figure was still accurate, and confirms the increased-compensation figure remains one-half of compensation capped at $10,000, with a separate $250 cost-and-expenses cap. The statute's own amendment history, as displayed on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov directly beneath the section text, reads '(Amended by Stats. 1990, Ch. 1550, Sec. 13.)' with no later amendment shown — meaning these specific dollar and percentage figures have not been statutorily updated since 1990. That is reported here as a fact about the current, operative statutory text as fetched on 2026-09-02, confirmed identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings, not carried over from an earlier or unverified source. This clause quotes paragraph (1) of the same statutory section addressed in two other clauses of this document (the core-prohibition and insurer-inducement clauses) and is not an independent source from those. As addressed in a separate clause of this document, paragraph (3)'s testimony-based protection carries only the reinstatement-and-reimbursement remedy, not this increased-compensation figure — the two remedy structures are not identical, and this document does not treat them as interchangeable. This document is informational: it does not itself calculate, determine, or award any specific dollar amount in this or any specific case.

citations.quote: the employee’s compensation shall be increased by one-half, but in no event more than ten thousand dollars ($10,000), together with costs and expenses not in excess of two hundred fifty dollars ($250).

citations.quote: Any such employee shall also be entitled to reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the acts of the employer.

clauses.title: Filed With the Workers' Compensation Appeals Board — Petition Procedure and One-Year Time Limit
clauses.body: The statute itself states that proceedings for the increased-compensation remedy, or for reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits, are instituted by filing a petition with the Workers' Compensation Appeals Board — not by filing a civil action in superior court — and that these proceedings may not be commenced more than one year from the discriminatory act or the date the employee's employment was terminated. The appeals board is vested with full power, authority, and jurisdiction to try and finally determine matters under this statute, subject only to judicial review, except that the appeals board has no jurisdiction to try or determine a misdemeanor charge; suspected misdemeanor violations may instead be referred to the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement or directly to a public prosecutor. The Workers' Compensation Appeals Board's own regulation implementing this statute requires that a petition set forth specifically and in detail the nature of each violation alleged, the facts relied upon, and the relief sought, with each alleged violation separately pleaded.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on two independent types of primary authority, fetched from two different sources, and discloses that distinction rather than presenting them as one: (1) the unnumbered closing paragraph of Labor Code § 132a itself, fetched from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings; and (2) California Code of Regulations, Title 8, section 10528 — the Workers' Compensation Appeals Board's own procedural regulation implementing this statute — fetched from dir.ca.gov and likewise confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings. Both quotes were confirmed as exact (whitespace-normalized) substrings of their respective fetched texts. A third, non-binding source was consulted only for corroboration and is not separately quoted or relied on for any statutory fact stated in this clause's body: the Department of Industrial Relations' own Division of Workers' Compensation "Information & Assistance Unit Guide 7 — How to file a petition for discrimination (Labor Code section 132a)" (fetched from dir.ca.gov, confirmed byte-identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings) states, consistent with the statute, that 'this petition must be filed within one year of the discriminatory act or date you were fired,' and additionally states — a procedural detail not found in the statute's or the regulation's own text, and not independently verified against a regulation in this research session — that 'A 132a petition can only be filed if you have a pending Workers' Compensation Appeals Board (WCAB) case,' opened by filing a separate application for adjudication of claim; that additional detail is disclosed here as agency guidance rather than quoted statutory or regulatory text, and this document does not treat it as verified to the same standard as the statute and regulation it is consulted alongside. This is the jurisdictional and procedural distinction that separates Labor Code § 132a from Labor Code §§ 1102.5 and 98.6, the whistleblower and wage-claim retaliation statutes addressed in this corpus's separate Wrongful Termination in Violation of Public Policy information sheet: those statutes are enforced through a civil action filed in superior court, while Labor Code § 132a is enforced through a petition filed with, and adjudicated by, the Workers' Compensation Appeals Board. This document is informational: it does not itself file any petition, does not determine that any specific petition would be timely, properly pleaded, or successful, and does not determine that any violation of Labor Code § 132a occurred in this or any specific case.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Where This Protection Is Codified Today
clauses.body: California's job protections for employees who take time off for jury duty or to appear in court as a witness were relocated out of the Labor Code and into the Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA), effective January 1, 2025. They are now codified at Government Code § 12945.8, most recently amended by AB 406 (Stats. 2025, Ch. 148), effective October 1, 2025, and are enforced by California's Civil Rights Department. Labor Code § 230 — which for many years contained these same jury-duty and witness-leave protections, and is still sometimes cited under that older number — remains on the books only in a transitional form: by its own terms it applies solely to alleged actions or inactions occurring on or before December 31, 2024, and it is scheduled to be repealed on January 1, 2035.
clauses.gap: This document treats Government Code § 12945.8, not Labor Code § 230, as the operative source of law for present-day jury-duty and witness-leave situations, because directly verifying the current statutory text — rather than assuming an older, frequently-cited Labor Code section still controls — showed the Legislature moved this protection. The Labor Code § 230(k) and § 230(l) citations below are two subsections of that same single Labor Code source, not independent sources of one another; the real independence in this clause is between the Government Code source and the Labor Code source, each fetched and confirmed identical twice, using two distinct User-Agent strings, directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov. This document does not independently verify secondary commentary (bill-tracking pages or law-firm summaries) about the legislative history of AB 2499 or AB 406; only the current statutory text itself, and Labor Code § 230's own applicability clause, were verified as primary sources.

clauses.title: Jury Duty Leave Protection
clauses.body: Under Government Code § 12945.8, an employer may not discharge an employee, or discriminate against an employee in any manner, for taking time off to serve as required by law on an inquest jury or trial jury. As a condition of taking that time off, the employee must give the employer reasonable advance notice of the employee's intention to take the time off, unless advance notice is not feasible.
clauses.gap: The jury-duty protection (subdivision (a)(1)) and its notice condition (subdivision (c)(1)) are two subsections of the same Government Code section, not independent sources of each other — both were confirmed against one fetched-and-verified copy of § 12945.8, checked twice with distinct User-Agent strings. This clause does not define how much notice counts as 'reasonable,' which the statute does not itself specify, and it does not restate the separate certification provisions in subdivision (c)(2)-(3) that can apply after an unscheduled absence, since this document did not resolve how those provisions interact with a jury summons an employee typically cannot schedule around.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(a)(1), jury duty leave protection
citations.quote: (1) Discharge or in any manner discriminate against an employee for taking time off to serve as required by law on an inquest jury or trial jury.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(c)(1), advance notice condition
citations.quote: (c) (1) As a condition of taking time off for a purpose set forth in paragraph (1), (3), or (4) of subdivision (a), or subdivision (b), the employee shall give the employer reasonable advance notice of the employee’s intention to take time off, unless the advance notice is not feasible.

clauses.title: Witness Leave Protection (Subpoena or Court Order)
clauses.body: Under Government Code § 12945.8, an employer may not discharge an employee, or discriminate or retaliate against an employee in any manner, for taking time off to appear in court to comply with a subpoena or other court order as a witness in any judicial proceeding. This protection is expressly extended to, but is not limited to, an employee who is a victim — it is not a victim-only protection.
clauses.gap: This protection covers an employee compelled to appear as a witness by a subpoena or other court order; the verified text does not extend it to a voluntary or informal court appearance that isn't compelled that way. Unlike jury duty leave under paragraph (a)(1), the advance-notice condition in subdivision (c)(1) lists only paragraphs (1), (3), and (4) of subdivision (a), and subdivision (b), as subject to it — paragraph (a)(2), the witness-leave paragraph quoted here, is not among them. This document flags that omission as a deliberate reading of the statute's own enumeration, rather than assuming a notice requirement applies to witness leave by analogy to jury duty leave. Both citations below come from the same fetched-and-verified copy of § 12945.8, not from two independent sources.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(a)(2), witness leave protection
citations.quote: (2) Discharge or in any manner discriminate or retaliate against an employee, including, but not limited to, an employee who is a victim, for taking time off to appear in court to comply with a subpoena or other court order as a witness in any judicial proceeding.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(c)(1), advance notice condition (paragraphs it covers)
citations.quote: (c) (1) As a condition of taking time off for a purpose set forth in paragraph (1), (3), or (4) of subdivision (a), or subdivision (b), the employee shall give the employer reasonable advance notice of the employee’s intention to take time off, unless the advance notice is not feasible.

clauses.title: Pay Status and Use of Accrued Leave
clauses.body: Government Code § 12945.8 does not itself require an employer to pay an employee's wages during jury duty or witness leave. Instead, the statute allows an employee to use vacation, personal leave, paid sick leave, or compensatory time off that is otherwise available to the employee under the employee's applicable terms of employment — unless a collective bargaining agreement provides otherwise — for time taken off for jury duty, witness leave, or the crime-victim leave purposes this same section separately addresses. The statute also states that it does not create a right to unpaid leave beyond, or in addition to, the 12 weeks of unpaid leave available under the federal Family and Medical Leave Act.
clauses.gap: This section does not create its own paid-leave benefit; whether time off is actually paid depends on whether the employee has, and chooses to use, other accrued paid leave, or on a separate employer policy or agreement this document doesn't address. This document does not independently verify other California statutes that address jury fees or per diem payments made to jurors by the court itself (as distinct from wages paid by the employer), which is a distinct topic from what this clause covers. Both citations below are subsections of the same fetched-and-verified copy of § 12945.8.

citations.cite: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(g), use of accrued vacation, personal leave, paid sick leave, or compensatory time
citations.quote: (g) An employee may use vacation, personal leave, paid sick leave, or compensatory time off that is otherwise available to the employee under the applicable terms of employment, unless otherwise provided by a collective bargaining agreement, for time taken off for a purpose specified in subdivision (a) or (b). The entitlement of any employee under this section shall not be diminished by any collective bargaining agreement term or condition.

Sec. 2601 et seq.).

clauses.title: No Interference With Leave Rights
clauses.body: It is an unlawful employment practice under Government Code § 12945.8 for an employer to interfere with, restrain, or deny the exercise of, or the attempt to exercise, any right this section provides — including the jury duty and witness leave rights described above.
clauses.gap: This section is part of the Fair Employment and Housing Act; this document does not detail FEHA's general administrative complaint and civil remedy process (filing with the Civil Rights Department, right-to-sue notices, and civil litigation under the surrounding FEHA statutes), because those general FEHA enforcement mechanics were not independently fetched and verified for this document. This is a deliberate correction against a natural assumption: the former Labor Code § 230 contained its own self-contained reinstatement-and-reimbursement remedy clause and its own misdemeanor penalty provision for willful refusal to rehire after a grievance determination, but the verified text of Government Code § 12945.8 fetched for this document contains neither a comparable self-contained remedy clause nor a misdemeanor provision — so this document does not assert that either exists in current law, only that interference with the section's rights is an unlawful employment practice, which the verified text does say.

citations.cite: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(f), prohibition on interference with section rights
citations.quote: (f) It shall be an unlawful employment practice for an employer to interfere with, restrain, or deny the exercise of, or the attempt to exercise, any right provided under this section.

clauses.title: Related But Distinct: Crime-Victim and Domestic-Violence Leave
clauses.body: The same Government Code § 12945.8 that protects jury duty and witness leave also contains separate protections for an employee who is a victim of a qualifying act of violence, or who has a family member who is — covering time off to obtain a restraining order or other relief, time off to attend certain judicial proceedings related to the crime (a protection that, by the statute's own terms, commences January 1, 2026), and, for employers with 25 or more employees, a broader set of purposes such as relocating, seeking medical or psychological care, or arranging childcare because of the qualifying act of violence. This information sheet addresses only the jury-duty and witness-leave portions of this section.
clauses.gap: These crime-victim and domestic-violence leave protections are a substantial, separately defined topic — with their own definitions of 'victim,' 'qualifying act of violence,' 'family member,' and 'designated person,' their own notice and certification rules, a reasonable-accommodation requirement, and employer-size-dependent leave caps — that this document does not attempt to cover; it is flagged here only so a reader who came looking for the older, separately-known 'domestic violence leave' or Labor Code § 230.1 topic knows where that subject now lives. This document did not independently fetch or verify the current status of former Labor Code § 230.1, so it makes no claim about that section specifically.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: {{preparerName}} is reviewing this information sheet in connection with the estate of {{decedentName}}. This sheet explains, on a general informational basis only, California's "slayer statute" doctrine under Probate Code Part 7 (commencing with Section 250) — the rule that disqualifies a person who feloniously and intentionally kills a decedent from inheriting or otherwise benefiting from that decedent's estate — as it applies broadly to a will, a trust, intestate succession, a joint tenancy interest, and other property or benefits passing by reason of a decedent's death. It does not separately restate the corpus's existing, life-insurance-specific treatment of Prob. Code § 252 found in the Life Insurance Beneficiary Designation Information Sheet; a reader concerned with a named life insurance beneficiary should consult that document instead. This sheet states general facts about how California's slayer statute works. It is not, and does not attempt to be, a finding, determination, accusation, or admission that {{decedentName}} died as a result of a felonious and intentional killing, or that any particular person committed one; it does not identify, name, or make any claim about any individual, and it does not advise {{preparerName}} or anyone else on what to do about any actual situation.

clauses.body:

Code § 254 describes — and is not something this information sheet determines, and not something it advises {{preparerName}} on.
