clauses.title: What the Slayer Statute Disqualifies a Killer From
clauses.body: Prob. Code § 250(a) states the core rule broadly: a person who feloniously and intentionally kills the decedent — that is, kills {{decedentName}} — is not entitled to five categories of property, interest, or benefit. The first is any property, interest, or benefit under a will of the decedent or a trust created by or for the decedent's benefit or in which the decedent has an interest, which reaches not only outright gifts but also a general or special power of appointment the will or trust confers on the killer and any nomination of the killer as executor, trustee, guardian, conservator, or custodian. The second is any property passing by intestate succession. The third is the decedent's quasi-community property the killer would otherwise acquire under Prob. Code § 101 or § 102 on the decedent's death. The fourth is any property under Division 5 (commencing with Section 5000) — California's nonprobate-transfers division, which includes the payable-on-death and beneficiary-designation mechanisms addressed elsewhere in this corpus (including a life insurance policy's nonprobate transfer provision, separately covered by the Life Insurance Beneficiary Designation Information Sheet's own § 252 and § 250(a)(4) clause). The fifth is any property under Division 6, Part 3 (commencing with Section 6500) — the family-protection provisions governing a surviving spouse's or minor children's temporary possession of the family dwelling and certain exempt property.
clauses.gap: This quotes subdivision (a) of a single statutory section, Prob. Code § 250; it was fetched twice independently (two distinct browser User-Agent strings against leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) and the retrieved text was identical both times. Paragraph (a)(4)'s cross-reference to Division 5 is the same statutory text already quoted in this corpus's separate lifeinsbene_slayer_statute clause for the life-insurance-specific context — it is not an independent source, and this clause does not re-describe what Division 5 or §§ 101–102 (quasi-community property) themselves provide beyond what § 250(a) states about them. This clause does not determine, and is not evidence of, whether any actual killing occurred or was felonious and intentional; that question, and how it is established, is addressed separately (see § 254, below).

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 250(a)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, general slayer statute — categories of disqualified property, interests, and benefits
citations.quote: (a) A person who feloniously and intentionally kills the decedent is not entitled to any of the following: (1) Any property, interest, or benefit under a will of the decedent, or a trust created by or for the benefit of the decedent or in which the decedent has an interest, including any general or special power of appointment conferred by the will or trust on the killer and any nomination of the killer as executor, trustee, guardian, or conservator or custodian made by the will or trust. (2) Any property of the decedent by intestate succession. (3) Any of the decedent’s quasi-community property the killer would otherwise acquire under Section 101 or 102 upon the death of the decedent. (4) Any property of the decedent under Division 5 (commencing with Section 5000). (5) Any property of the decedent under Part 3 (commencing with Section 6500) of Division 6.

clauses.title: The Statutory Mechanism: Treated as Having Predeceased the Decedent
clauses.body: Prob. Code § 250(b) specifies how disqualified property is redirected, rather than simply leaving it undistributed. For the will-or-trust interests described in § 250(a)(1), the property or benefit passes as if the killer had predeceased the decedent, and the statute expressly states that Prob. Code § 21110 (the anti-lapse statute governing what happens when a beneficiary predeceases a testator) does not apply to that substitution. The same predecease treatment applies to a property interest or benefit that passes to the killer under a power of appointment by reason of the decedent's death, with § 250(b)(2) similarly stating that Prob. Code § 673 does not apply. And any nomination of the killer as executor, trustee, guardian, conservator, or custodian that would otherwise become effective on the decedent's death is likewise interpreted as if the killer had predeceased the decedent — meaning an alternate or successor named in the governing instrument, rather than the disqualified killer, takes the nominated role.
clauses.gap: This quotes subdivision (b) of the same statutory section already quoted for subdivision (a) in the slayerstatute_core_disqualification clause above — not an independently distinct source, though it was itself fetched and confirmed identical across two independent requests. This clause states only what § 250(b) itself says about Prob. Code §§ 21110 and 673 (that they do not apply in this context); it does not independently research, quote, or describe what those two cross-referenced sections otherwise provide, and a reader wanting to understand California's general anti-lapse rule or power-of-appointment revocation rule should consult those sections directly rather than this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 250(b)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, general slayer statute — predecease mechanism for redirecting disqualified property
citations.quote: (b) In the cases covered by subdivision (a): (1) The property interest or benefit referred to in paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) passes as if the killer had predeceased the decedent and Section 21110 does not apply. (2) Any property interest or benefit referred to in paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) which passes under a power of appointment and by reason of the death of the decedent passes as if the killer had predeceased the decedent, and Section 673 does not apply. (3) Any nomination in a will or trust of the killer as executor, trustee, guardian, conservator, or custodian which becomes effective as a result of the death of the decedent shall be interpreted as if the killer had predeceased the decedent.

clauses.title: Joint Tenancy: Severance Rather Than Automatic Survivorship
clauses.body: Joint tenancy property is addressed by its own statute, separate from § 250. Prob. Code § 251 provides that a joint tenant who feloniously and intentionally kills another joint tenant — rather than being outright disqualified from the whole property — effects a severance of the deceased joint tenant's interest, so that the deceased joint tenant's share passes as that decedent's own property (through their will, trust, or intestate succession, subject to the ordinary rules, including § 250 itself if the killer would otherwise take a share of it), and the killer acquires no right to the property by survivorship. The statute is not limited to real property joint tenancies: it expressly applies to joint tenancies in real and personal property, joint and multiple-party financial institution accounts, and any other form of coownership carrying survivorship incidents.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory section, Prob. Code § 251, fetched twice independently (two distinct User-Agent strings) with identical results both times, and is a source independent of §§ 250, 253, and 254 quoted in the other clauses of this document. The statute's text does not itself spell out every downstream consequence of the severance — for example, exactly how the severed share is then divided among surviving co-tenants or distributed through the decedent's estate — and this clause does not go beyond what § 251 states to resolve that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 251
citations.cite: California Probate Code, slayer statute's joint tenancy severance rule
citations.quote: A joint tenant who feloniously and intentionally kills another joint tenant thereby effects a severance of the interest of the decedent so that the share of the decedent passes as the decedent’s property and the killer has no rights by survivorship. This section applies to joint tenancies in real and personal property, joint and multiple-party accounts in financial institutions, and any other form of coownership with survivorship incidents.

clauses.title: How a "Felonious and Intentional Killing" Is Established
clauses.body: California's slayer statute does not require a criminal conviction before its disqualification rules can operate. Prob. Code § 254(a) makes a final judgment of conviction of felonious and intentional killing conclusive for purposes of Part 7 (the slayer-statute part). But § 254(b) goes further: in the absence of a final conviction — for example, where no criminal charges were ever filed, charges were dismissed, or the person was acquitted — a court (typically the probate court handling the estate, trust, or property dispute) may still determine by a preponderance of the evidence, the ordinary civil standard, whether the killing was felonious and intentional for purposes of the statute. That is a lower standard than the "beyond a reasonable doubt" standard used in a criminal trial. The statute places the burden of proof on whoever is asserting that the killing was felonious and intentional — that is, on the party seeking to disqualify the alleged killer, not on the alleged killer to disprove it.
clauses.gap: Prob. Code § 254 is the identical statutory section already quoted elsewhere in this corpus, in the lifeinsbene_slayer_statute clause of the Life Insurance Beneficiary Designation Information Sheet, for the narrower life-insurance context; it is not an independent statutory source from that clause, though this document re-verifies it separately here (fetched twice independently, both times against leginfo.legislature.ca.gov with different User-Agent strings, with identical results) because the § 254 conviction-or-preponderance standard applies identically across every category the slayer statute reaches — wills, trusts, intestate succession, joint tenancy, and the other categories described in this document's other clauses — not only life insurance. This clause does not determine, and is not evidence toward, whether any actual killing occurred or was felonious and intentional in any particular case.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 254(a)-(b)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, how a felonious and intentional killing is established for slayer-statute purposes
citations.quote: A final judgment of conviction of felonious and intentional killing is conclusive for purposes of this part. (b) In the absence of a final judgment of conviction of felonious and intentional killing, the court may determine by a preponderance of evidence whether the killing was felonious and intentional for purposes of this part. The burden of proof is on the party seeking to establish that the killing was felonious and intentional for the purposes of this part.

clauses.title: The Residual Rule for Other Property a Killer Might Acquire
clauses.body: The categories in § 250 (wills, trusts, intestate succession, quasi-community property, Division 5 nonprobate transfers, and Division 6 Part 3 family-protection property), § 251 (joint tenancy), and § 252 (a named beneficiary of a bond, life insurance policy, or other contractual arrangement — already addressed elsewhere in this corpus) do not exhaust every way a killer might acquire property, an interest, or a benefit as a result of a killing. Prob. Code § 253 supplies a residual rule for whatever is left over: in any case not described in § 250, § 251, or § 252 in which one person feloniously and intentionally kills another, any acquisition of property, interest, or benefit by the killer as a result of the killing is to be treated in accordance with the principles of Part 7 — that is, the same disqualification-and-predecease principles reflected in §§ 250–252, extended by analogy to the acquisition at hand.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory section, Prob. Code § 253, fetched and independently confirmed twice (two distinct User-Agent strings, identical results). Section 253's own text names § 252 as one of the three specifically-addressed categories it does not duplicate; § 252 is the life-insurance-beneficiary provision already covered by this corpus's separate lifeinsbene_slayer_statute clause, which is why this document does not separately quote or restate § 252 here. Because § 253 is a deliberately open-ended catch-all, the statute's text does not itself specify how its "principles of this part" apply to any particular kind of property or benefit not otherwise enumerated; that application is necessarily case-specific and left to the courts, and this clause does not resolve it for any actual situation.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 253
citations.cite: California Probate Code, slayer statute's residual rule for property not otherwise addressed
citations.quote: In any case not described in Section 250, 251, or 252 in which one person feloniously and intentionally kills another, any acquisition of property, interest, or benefit by the killer as a result of the killing of the decedent shall be treated in accordance with the principles of this part.

clauses.title: Tenant's Notice and Declaration — Habitability Defect, Repair-and-Deduct, and Retaliation Information
clauses.body:
I, {{tenantName}}, am the tenant renting {{propertyAddress}} from {{landlordName}} ("Landlord"). On {{noticeDate}}, I gave Landlord notice of the following condition at the property that I believe needs repair: {{habitabilityDefectDescription}}.

This information sheet describes two separate provisions of California law: Civil Code section 1942, which addresses a tenant's ability, in specified circumstances, to repair a dilapidated condition and deduct the cost from rent, or to vacate the premises; and Civil Code section 1942.5, which addresses certain landlord conduct following specified tenant activity, including a notice of the kind described above. Filling in this information sheet is not itself the notice required by Civil Code section 1942, does not by itself exercise any right to repair and deduct or to vacate, does not file anything with any court or agency, and does not determine that the condition described above in fact renders {{propertyAddress}} untenantable, that Landlord in fact neglected to repair it within a reasonable time, or that any specific conduct by Landlord was in fact retaliatory.

clauses.title: The Repair-and-Deduct (or Vacate) Remedy
clauses.body: If, within a reasonable time after written or oral notice to the landlord (or the landlord's agent) of a dilapidated condition making the premises untenantable that the landlord ought to repair, the landlord neglects to do so, the tenant may repair the condition and deduct the cost from the rent when due — so long as the cost of the repair does not require spending more than one month's rent on the premises — or the tenant may instead vacate the premises, in which case the tenant is discharged from paying further rent or performing other lease conditions as of the date of vacating. This remedy is not available to a tenant more than twice in any 12-month period.
clauses.gap: The dollar limit on this remedy is not a fixed figure — it is one month's rent, which scales with whatever the rent for the specific unit happens to be, rather than a flat statutory cap; a fixed-dollar-cap assumption for this statute would be inaccurate as applied to current text. The statute's trigger — a dilapidation "rendering the premises untenantable" — uses the same "untenantable" concept this corpus's Residential Lease Agreement document already addresses in its own habitability clauses (drawing on Civil Code §§ 1941 and 1941.1); this clause does not restate that definition and should be read together with those clauses rather than as an independent definition of untenantability. The twice-in-any-12-month-period limit stated here is specific to this repair-and-deduct/vacate remedy; a separate, differently-worded 12-month limit exists elsewhere in this document for the retaliation-protection remedy addressed in Civil Code § 1942.5, and the two should not be conflated. This is California's own statute, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings (a standard browser string and a distinct research-tool string); each quote in this clause was confirmed programmatically as an exact substring of that fetched text. This is one state's statute; repair-and-deduct rights, where they exist, vary by state in their dollar limits, frequency limits, and notice requirements. This document is informational only: it does not determine that any specific condition renders a specific unit untenantable, that a specific landlord failed to repair within a reasonable time, or that a specific tenant properly exercised this remedy.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1942(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the repair-and-deduct or vacate remedy and its cost/frequency limits
citations.quote: If within a reasonable time after written or oral notice to the landlord or his agent, as defined in subdivision (a) of Section 1962, of dilapidations rendering the premises untenantable which the landlord ought to repair, the landlord neglects to do so, the tenant may repair the same himself where the cost of such repairs does not require an expenditure more than one month’s rent of the premises and deduct the expenses of such repairs from the rent when due, or the tenant may vacate the premises, in which case the tenant shall be discharged from further payment of rent, or performance of other conditions as of the date of vacating the premises. This remedy shall not be available to the tenant more than twice in any 12-month period.

clauses.title: Notice-Timing Presumption, Tenant-Caused Conditions, and Cumulative Remedies
clauses.body: If a tenant acts to repair and deduct after the 30th day following notice to the landlord, the tenant is presumed to have acted after a reasonable time — a rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of producing evidence, and one that does not prevent a tenant from repairing and deducting after a shorter notice if the circumstances require it. The repair-and-deduct remedy described elsewhere in this document is not available if the condition was caused by the tenant's own violation of a separate statute (Civil Code §§ 1929 and 1941.2). That remedy is in addition to any other remedy available under this chapter, the rental agreement, or other applicable statutory or common law.
clauses.gap: This 30-day "reasonable time" presumption is a distinct legal concept from the rebuttable-presumption-style protection this document's retaliation clauses describe under Civil Code § 1942.5 — this one is about whether a tenant waited long enough after giving notice before repairing and deducting, not about whether a landlord's later conduct toward the tenant was retaliatory; the two shouldn't be read as the same presumption. The excluding condition referenced here — a condition caused by violation of Civil Code § 1929 or § 1941.2 — is quoted from § 1942 by cross-reference only; this document does not independently fetch, verify, or describe the text of § 1929 or § 1941.2 themselves, and no claim is made here about what conduct those sections actually require of a tenant. All three citations below are subsections ((b), (c), and (d)) of the same statutory section as the remedy described in this document's companion clause, not independently authored sources; this is disclosed here rather than presented as multiple separate authorities. This is California's own statute, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings (a standard browser string and a distinct research-tool string); each quote in this clause was confirmed programmatically as an exact substring of that fetched text. This document is informational only: it does not determine that any specific tenant's repair-and-deduct timing was reasonable, or that any specific condition falls within this exclusion.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1942(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the 30-day reasonable-time presumption
citations.quote: For the purposes of this section, if a tenant acts to repair and deduct after the 30th day following notice, he is presumed to have acted after a reasonable time. The presumption established by this subdivision is a rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of producing evidence and shall not be construed to prevent a tenant from repairing and deducting after a shorter notice if all the circumstances require shorter notice.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1942(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, exclusion for tenant-caused conditions
citations.quote: The tenant’s remedy under subdivision (a) shall not be available if the condition was caused by the violation of Section 1929 or 1941.2.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1942(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, this remedy is cumulative with other remedies
citations.quote: The remedy provided by this section is in addition to any other remedy provided by this chapter, the rental agreement, or other applicable statutory or common law.

clauses.title: Retaliation Protection: The 180-Day Rule and the Protected Tenant Conduct It Covers
clauses.body: If a landlord retaliates against a tenant because the tenant exercised rights under this chapter of the Civil Code — which includes the habitability and repair-and-deduct rights addressed elsewhere in this document — or because the tenant complained to an appropriate agency about the tenantability of a dwelling, and the tenant is not in default on rent, the landlord may not recover possession of the dwelling, cause the tenant to quit involuntarily, increase the rent, or decrease any services within 180 days after any of the following: the tenant's good-faith notice given under Civil Code section 1942, notice of a suspected bed bug infestation, or oral complaint to the landlord about tenantability; the tenant's good-faith written complaint (or oral complaint that is registered or otherwise recorded in writing) to an appropriate agency, of which the landlord has notice, made for the purpose of getting a tenantability condition corrected; an inspection or citation resulting from that agency complaint, where the landlord did not have notice of the complaint itself; the filing of a judicial or arbitration proceeding involving a tenantability issue; or a judgment or arbitration award on a tenantability issue decided against the landlord. The 180-day period runs from the latest of these dates.
clauses.gap: The statute's own text does not use the word "presumption" anywhere in this subsection — it is written as a direct prohibition on specified landlord conduct within the 180-day window, not as an evidentiary presumption the tenant must invoke; describing it as creating a "presumption of retaliation" is a common shorthand, but not the statute's own terminology, and this document uses the statute's own "may not" framing instead. One of the listed triggering events — the tenant's good-faith notice "pursuant to Section 1942" — is the direct textual link between this retaliation protection and the repair-and-deduct notice described in this document's other clauses; the broader "exercise ... of rights under this chapter" language in the opening sentence extends further, to the habitability rights this corpus's existing Residential Lease Agreement document separately addresses, but this document does not independently trace every right "under this chapter" beyond what the quoted text itself lists. This section separately contains a broader anti-retaliation prohibition, in subdivisions (d) and (e), covering a landlord's retaliation against a tenant for organizing or participating in a tenants' association or lawfully exercising rights generally (with the tenant bearing the burden of producing evidence of retaliation, rather than the 180-day timing rule described here) — that broader prohibition is not covered by this document's clauses. Both citations below are from the same statutory subsection, (a), not independently authored sources. This is California's own statute, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings (a standard browser string and a distinct research-tool string); each quote in this clause was confirmed programmatically as an exact substring of that fetched text. This is one state's statute; retaliation protections for tenants, where they exist, vary by state in their triggers, timing windows, and remedies. This document is informational only: it does not determine that any specific landlord conduct was in fact retaliatory, or that any specific tenant conduct falls within the protected categories described here.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1942.5(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the core 180-day retaliation prohibition
citations.quote: If the lessor retaliates against the lessee because of the exercise by the lessee of the lessee’s rights under this chapter or because of the lessee’s complaint to an appropriate agency as to tenantability of a dwelling, and if the lessee of a dwelling is not in default as to the payment of rent, the lessor may not recover possession of a dwelling in any action or proceeding, cause the lessee to quit involuntarily, increase the rent, or decrease any services within 180 days of any of the following:

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1942.5(a)(1)-(5) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the specific list of triggering tenant conduct and dates
citations.quote: (1) After the date upon which the lessee, in good faith, has given notice pursuant to Section 1942, has provided notice of a suspected bed bug infestation, or has made an oral complaint to the lessor regarding tenantability.(2) After the date upon which the lessee, in good faith, has filed a written complaint, or an oral complaint which is registered or otherwise recorded in writing, with an appropriate agency, of which the lessor has notice, for the purpose of obtaining correction of a condition relating to tenantability.(3) After the date of an inspection or issuance of a citation, resulting from a complaint described in paragraph (2) of which the lessor did not have notice.(4) After the filing of appropriate documents commencing a judicial or arbitration proceeding involving the issue of tenantability.(5) After entry of judgment or the signing of an arbitration award, if any, when in the judicial proceeding or arbitration the issue of tenantability is determined adversely to the lessor.In each instance, the 180-day period shall run from the latest applicable date referred to in paragraphs (1) to (5), inclusive.

clauses.title: Frequency Limit, Immigration-Status Reporting, and the Landlord's Opportunity to Show a Lawful Reason
clauses.body: A tenant may not invoke the 180-day retaliation rule described elsewhere in this document more than once in any 12-month period. Reporting, or threatening to report, the tenant or individuals known to the landlord to be associated with the tenant to immigration authorities is itself a form of retaliatory conduct the statute prohibits, and that specific prohibition does not limit the broader definition of retaliatory conduct the statute otherwise covers. The statute does not limit a landlord's lawful exercise of rights under a lease, agreement, or other law, or a landlord's right to take the described actions for any lawful cause, and any waiver by a tenant of rights under this statute is void as against public policy. Despite the 180-day rule, a landlord may still recover possession, increase rent, decrease services, or take the other described actions within that period if the notice of termination, rent increase, or other act — or a pleading or statement of issues in an arbitration — states the ground on which the landlord, in good faith, is acting; if the tenant disputes that stated ground, the landlord must establish its truth at the trial or other hearing.
clauses.gap: This 12-month, once-per-period limit on invoking the retaliation rule is a different limit from the twice-in-any-12-month-period limit this document describes for actually exercising the repair-and-deduct remedy itself under Civil Code § 1942(a) — the two limits apply to different rights and should not be treated as the same rule. The stated-ground mechanism described in this clause is, on this statute's own text, the actual rebuttal-like structure built into this protection: rather than a labeled presumption the tenant must overcome, the statute lets a landlord act within the 180-day window if the landlord states a good-faith, non-retaliatory ground in the notice or pleading itself, with the landlord bearing the burden of proving that stated ground true if the tenant disputes it. All four citations below are subsections — (b), (c), (f), and (g) — of the same statutory section as the core prohibition described in this document's companion clause, not independently authored sources. This is California's own statute, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings (a standard browser string and a distinct research-tool string); each quote in this clause was confirmed programmatically as an exact substring of that fetched text. This document is informational only: it does not determine that any specific landlord's stated ground was in fact lawful and non-retaliatory, or that any specific landlord conduct involving immigration status was in fact retaliatory.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the once-per-12-months limit on invoking this protection
citations.quote: A lessee may not invoke subdivision (a) more than once in any 12-month period.

citations.quote: To report, or to threaten to report, the lessee or individuals known to the landlord to be associated with the lessee to immigration authorities is a form of retaliatory conduct prohibited under subdivision (a). This subdivision shall in no way limit the definition of retaliatory conduct prohibited under this section.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1942.5(f) (California Legislative Information text)

citations.quote: This section does not limit in any way the exercise by the lessor of the lessor’s rights under any lease or agreement or any law pertaining to the hiring of property or the lessor’s right to do any of the acts described in subdivision (a) or (d) for any lawful cause. Any waiver by a lessee of the lessee’s rights under this section is void as contrary to public policy.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1942.5(g) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the landlord's stated-ground safe harbor and burden at hearing
citations.quote: Notwithstanding subdivisions (a) to (f), inclusive, a lessor may recover possession of a dwelling and do any of the other acts described in subdivision (a) within the period or periods prescribed therein, or within subdivision (d), if the notice of termination, rent increase, or other act, and any pleading or statement of issues in an arbitration, if any, states the ground upon which the lessor, in good faith, seeks to recover possession, increase rent, or do any of the other acts described in subdivision (a) or (d). If the statement is controverted, the lessor shall establish its truth at the trial or other hearing.

clauses.title: Remedies and Penalties Under Civil Code Section 1942.5
clauses.body: A landlord or a landlord's agent who violates this statute is liable to the tenant in a civil action for the tenant's actual damages, plus punitive damages of not less than $100 nor more than $2,000 for each retaliatory act, where the landlord or agent has been guilty of fraud, oppression, or malice with respect to that act. In an action brought for damages for retaliatory eviction, the court awards reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing party if either party requests attorney's fees at the initiation of the action. These remedies are in addition to any other remedies provided by statutory or decisional law.
clauses.gap: The punitive-damages range stated here — not less than $100 nor more than $2,000 per retaliatory act — is the statute's own current figure, verified against the actual fetched text rather than assumed; it applies only where the landlord or agent has been guilty of fraud, oppression, or malice with respect to that specific act, not to every violation of the statute. The attorney's-fee provision is not one-directional on its face: it states that the court awards fees "to the prevailing party," not only to a prevailing tenant, if either party requests fees when the action is initiated. This clause describes only the remedies the statute itself authorizes; the statute's text does not specify, and this document does not independently address, the procedural vehicle for bringing such an action (for example, as an affirmative civil suit versus as a defense or cross-complaint in an unlawful detainer proceeding), which is a different question from what remedies the statute makes available. All four citations below are subsections — (h) (in two parts) and (i) and (j) — of the same statutory section as this document's other Civil Code § 1942.5 clauses, not independently authored sources. This is California's own statute, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings (a standard browser string and a distinct research-tool string); each quote in this clause was confirmed programmatically as an exact substring of that fetched text. This is one state's statute; remedies for landlord retaliation, where recognized, vary by state. This document is informational only: it does not determine that any specific landlord violated this statute, that any specific conduct involved fraud, oppression, or malice, or that any specific tenant or landlord is entitled to any specific award.

clauses.body:

clauses.title: Who May Make an Anatomical Gift of Their Own Body
clauses.body: California Health & Safety Code § 7150.15 lets an anatomical gift of a donor's own body or part be made, during the donor's life, for the purpose of transplantation, therapy, research, or education, by: the donor, if the donor is an adult; the donor, if the donor is a minor, but only if the minor is an emancipated minor, or is between 15 and 18 years of age and has the written consent of a parent or guardian; or an agent of the donor, provided the power of attorney for health care or other record expressly permits the agent to make an anatomical gift. Health & Safety Code § 7150.10(a) defines an “adult” as an individual at least 18 years of age, and a “minor” as an individual under 18. The statute conditions eligibility to act on one's own behalf on age, emancipation status, and (for a minor between 15 and 18) parental or guardian consent — its text does not separately state a “sound mind” or other mental-capacity standard for an adult donor acting for themselves.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence of one state's rule for who may make an anatomical gift of their own body — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person, or that other states use the same age thresholds or consent mechanics for minors; some states set different ages or procedures. § 7150.15 (who may act) and § 7150.10 (the chapter's definitions of “adult” and “minor”) are treated here as effectively one source rather than independent ones: § 7150.10 supplies only the defined terms that § 7150.15 uses, not a separate substantive eligibility rule.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7150.15
citations.cite: who may make an anatomical gift of one's own body during life
citations.quote: Subject to Section 7150.35, an anatomical gift of a donor’s body or part may be made during the life of the donor for the purpose of transplantation, therapy, research, or education in the manner provided in Section 7150.20 by any of the following individuals:(a) The donor, if the donor is an adult or if the donor is a minor and is either of the following:(1) An emancipated minor.(2) Between 15 and 18 years of age, only upon the written consent of a parent or guardian.(b) An agent of the donor, provided that the power of attorney for health care or other record expressly permits the agent to make an anatomical gift.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7150.10(a)(1)
citations.cite: definition of “adult”
citations.quote: (1) “Adult” means an individual who is at least 18 years of age.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7150.10(a)(15)
citations.cite: definition of “minor”
citations.quote: (15) “Minor” means an individual who is under 18 years of age.

clauses.title: How an Anatomical Gift of One's Own Body Can Be Made
clauses.body: California Health & Safety Code § 7150.20(a) lists the ways a donor may make an anatomical gift: by authorizing a statement or symbol indicating the gift to be imprinted on the donor's driver's license or identification card and included on a donor database registry; directly through the Donate Life California Organ and Tissue Donor Registry internet website; in a will; during a terminal illness or injury, by any form of communication that clearly expresses the donor's wish, addressed to at least two adults, at least one of whom is a disinterested witness, memorialized in a signed and dated writing by the witnesses; or by a donor card or other signed record under subdivision (b). Under subdivision (b), if the donor is physically unable to sign that record personally, another individual may sign it at the donor's direction, but the signing must then be witnessed by at least two adults, at least one of whom is a disinterested witness, and the record must state that it was signed and witnessed in that manner. Revocation, suspension, expiration, or cancellation of a driver's license or identification card on which a gift is indicated does not by itself invalidate the gift, and a gift made by will takes effect at death regardless of whether the will is ever probated or is later invalidated.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence of one state's specific list of methods for making an anatomical gift of one's own body — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person, or that other states recognize the same methods; some states, for example, do not treat a driver's license notation alone as sufficient without separate registry enrollment. § 7150.20(a) and § 7150.20(b)-(d) are subsections of the same statutory section, not independent sources, so they are disclosed here as a single source.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7150.20(a)
citations.cite: the five listed methods of making a gift
citations.quote: (a) A donor may make an anatomical gift through any of the following:(1) By authorizing a statement or symbol indicating that the donor has made an anatomical gift to be imprinted on the donor’s driver’s license or identification card and included on a donor database registry.(2) Directly through the Donate Life California Organ and Tissue Donor Registry Internet Web site.(3) In a will.(4) During a terminal illness or injury of the donor, by any form of communication that clearly expresses the donor’s wish, addressed to at least two adults, at least one of whom is a disinterested witness. The witnesses shall memorialize this communication in a writing and sign and date the writing.(5) As provided in subdivision (b).

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7150.20(b)
citations.cite: donor card/signed record, and witnessing when signed by another at the donor's direction
citations.quote: (b) A donor or other person authorized to make an anatomical gift under Section 7150.15 may make a gift by a donor card or other record signed by the donor or other person making the gift or by authorizing that a statement or symbol, indicating that the donor has made an anatomical gift, be included on a donor registry. If the donor or other person is physically unable to sign a record, the record may be signed by another individual at the direction of the donor or other person and shall comply with all of the following:(1) Be witnessed by at least two adults, at least one of whom is a disinterested witness, who have signed at the request of the donor or the other person.(2) State that it has been signed and witnessed as provided in paragraph (1).

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7150.20(c)-(d)
citations.cite: license/ID changes don't invalidate the gift; a will-based gift takes effect regardless of probate
citations.quote: (c) Revocation, suspension, expiration, or cancellation of a driver’s license or identification card upon which an anatomical gift is indicated does not invalidate the gift.(d) An anatomical gift made by will takes effect upon the donor’s death whether or not the will is probated. Invalidation of the will after the donor’s death does not invalidate the gift.

clauses.title: How an Anatomical Gift Can Be Amended or Revoked by the Donor
clauses.body: California Health & Safety Code § 7150.25 lets a donor (or other person authorized under § 7150.15) amend or revoke an anatomical gift by: a record signed by the donor, the other authorized person, or — subject to a witnessing requirement — someone signing at that person's direction because they are physically unable to sign, recorded in a donor registry database; or a later-executed document of gift that amends or revokes the earlier gift, either expressly or by inconsistency. A donor may also revoke a gift by destroying the document of gift, or by canceling it on a donor database registry, with the intent to revoke it. A donor may amend or revoke a gift that was not made in a will by any form of communication during a terminal illness or injury addressed to at least two adults, at least one of whom is a disinterested witness, memorialized in a signed and dated writing. A donor who made the gift in a will may amend or revoke it in the manner used for amending or revoking wills generally, or by the methods described above. Separately, Health & Safety Code § 7150.35(b) clarifies that a donor's own revocation of their gift is not treated as a refusal, and does not by itself bar another authorized person from later making an anatomical gift of the same body or part.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence of one state's revocation mechanics for an anatomical gift made by the donor — not a claim about which state's law governs, or that other states offer the same range of revocation methods. The first citation below draws on subdivisions (a) through (e) of a single statutory section (§ 7150.25); the second citation is subdivision (b) of a genuinely different section (§ 7150.35), so the two citations are one source (§ 7150.25) plus one independent source (§ 7150.35(b)), not two fully independent sources.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7150.25
citations.cite: the donor's own methods of amending or revoking a gift
citations.quote: (a) Subject to Section 7150.35, a donor or other person authorized to make an anatomical gift under Section 7150.15 may amend or revoke an anatomical gift by either of the following:(1) A record signed by any of the following and recorded in a donor registry database:(A) The donor.(B) The other person.(C) Subject to subdivision (b), another individual acting at the direction of the donor or of the other person, if the donor or other person is physically unable to sign.(2) A later-executed document of gift that amends or revokes a previous anatomical gift or portion of an anatomical gift, either expressly or by inconsistency.(b) A record signed pursuant to subparagraph (C) of paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) shall comply with all of the following:(1) It shall be witnessed by at least two adults, at least one of whom is a disinterested witness, who have signed at the request of the donor or the other person.(2) It shall state that it has been signed and witnessed as provided in paragraph (1).(c) Subject to Section 7150.35, a donor or other person authorized to make an anatomical gift under Section 7150.15 may revoke an anatomical gift by the destruction of the document of gift or cancellation of the document of gift on a donor database registry, or the portion of the document of gift used to make the gift, with the intent to revoke the gift.(d) A donor may amend or revoke an anatomical gift that was not made in a will by any form of communication during a terminal illness or injury addressed to at least two adults, at least one of whom is a disinterested witness. The witnesses shall memorialize this communication in a writing and sign and date the writing.(e) A donor who makes an anatomical gift in a will may amend or revoke the gift in the manner provided for amendment or revocation of wills or as provided in subdivision (a).

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7150.35(b)
citations.cite: a donor's revocation is not a refusal and does not by itself bar others
citations.quote: (b) A donor’s revocation of an anatomical gift of the donor’s body or part under Section 7150.25 is not a refusal and does not bar another person specified in Section 7150.15 or 7150.40 from making an anatomical gift of the donor’s body or part under Section 7150.20 or 7150.45.

clauses.title: Priority Order to Make a Gift on Behalf of Someone Who Did Not Make One
clauses.body: Unless barred by a refusal under § 7150.30 or by the preclusive-effect rules of § 7150.35, California Health & Safety Code § 7150.40(a) lets an anatomical gift of a decedent's body or part be made, for transplantation, therapy, research, or education, by any reasonably available member of the following classes, in this order of priority: (1) an agent of the decedent who could have made the gift under § 7150.15(b) immediately before death; (2) the decedent's spouse or domestic partner; (3) the decedent's adult children; (4) the decedent's parents; (5) the decedent's adult siblings; (6) the decedent's adult grandchildren; (7) the decedent's grandparents; (8) an adult who exhibited special care and concern for the decedent during the decedent's lifetime; (9) the persons acting as guardian or conservator of the decedent's person at the time of death; and (10) any other person with authority to dispose of the decedent's body — including a coroner, medical examiner, or hospital administrator — but only after a reasonable effort (deemed satisfied by at least a 12-hour search, with a narrow exception) has been made to locate and inform the higher-priority persons listed. If more than one member of most of these classes is reasonably available, any one of them may make the gift unless that member (or the person the gift would pass to) knows of an objection from another member of the same class, in which case a majority of the reasonably available members must agree. A person may not make the gift if a person in a higher-priority class is reasonably available to make it or to object to it.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence of one state's default priority scheme for who may make an anatomical gift on behalf of someone who did not make one themselves — not a claim about which state's law governs, or that other states order priority the same way. This list is governed by a different statute than, and is not identical to, the priority list this corpus's Disposition of Remains Instructions document cites under Health & Safety Code § 7100(a) for who controls burial/cremation decisions; the two statutes were checked independently here rather than assumed to match. Concrete differences found: this anatomical-gift list expressly names ‘the spouse or domestic partner’ at position (2), while the remains-disposition list's statutory text names only a ‘competent surviving spouse’ with no mention of a domestic partner; this list also includes two classes with no counterpart in the remains list — adult grandchildren (6) and grandparents (7) — and ‘an adult who exhibited special care and concern for the decedent’ (8), which the remains list does not have at all; and where the remains list separately names a conservator of the person and a conservator of the estate as two distinct classes, this list combines only ‘guardians or conservators of the person’ into a single class (9), has no counterpart for a conservator of the estate, and instead ends in a residual class (10) for any other person with authority over the body (coroner, medical examiner, hospital administrator) after a documented search. All quoted text in this clause is drawn from subdivisions (a) through (c) of a single statutory section (§ 7150.40); no additional independent source was found for this specific list.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7150.40(a)
citations.cite: the ten-class statutory priority list
citations.quote: (a) Subject to subdivisions (b) and (c), and unless barred by Section 7150.30 or 7150.35, an anatomical gift of a decedent’s body or part for the purpose of transplantation, therapy, research, or education may be made by any member of the following classes of persons who is reasonably available, in the following order of priority:(1) An agent of the decedent at the time of death who could have made an anatomical gift under subdivision (b) of Section 7150.15 immediately before the decedent’s death.(2) The spouse or domestic partner of the decedent.(3) Adult children of the decedent.(4) Parents of the decedent.(5) Adult siblings of the decedent.(6) Adult grandchildren of the decedent.(7) Grandparents of the decedent.(8) An adult who exhibited special care and concern for the decedent during the decedent’s lifetime.(9) The persons who were acting as the guardians or conservators of the person of the decedent at the time of death.(10) (A) Any other person having the authority to dispose of the decedent’s body, including, but not limited to, a coroner, medical examiner, or hospital administrator, provided that reasonable effort has been made to locate and inform persons listed in paragraphs (1) to (9), inclusive, of their option to make, or object to making, an anatomical gift.(B) Except in the case where the useful life of the part does not permit, a reasonable effort shall be deemed to have been made when a search for the persons has been underway for at least 12 hours. The search shall include a check of local police missing persons records, examination of personal effects, and the questioning of any persons visiting the decedent before his or her death or in the hospital, accompanying the decedent’s body, or reporting the death, in order to obtain information that might lead to the location of any persons listed.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7150.40(b)-(c)
citations.cite: majority rule within a class, and the higher-priority-bars-lower rule
citations.quote: (b) If there is more than one member of a class listed in paragraph (1), (3), (4), (5), (6), (7), or (9) of subdivision (a) entitled to make an anatomical gift, an anatomical gift may be made by a member of the class unless that member or a person to which the gift may pass under Section 7150.50 knows of an objection by another member of the class. If an objection is known, the gift may be made only by a majority of the members of the class who are reasonably available.(c) A person shall not make an anatomical gift if, at the time of the decedent’s death, a person in a prior class under subdivision (a) is reasonably available to make, or to object to the making of, an anatomical gift.

clauses.title: How an Anatomical Gift Interacts With an Advance Health Care Directive
clauses.body: An anatomical gift can be made through an Advance Health Care Directive itself, not only through a separate donor-registry enrollment, license designation, or will: California's optional statutory Advance Health Care Directive form, set out in Probate Code § 4701, states that the form “lets you do either or both of these things. It also lets you express your wishes regarding donation of organs and the designation of your primary physician,” and includes an optional Part 3 letting the person completing it state, “Upon my death, I give my organs, tissues, and parts,” for one or more of transplant, therapy, research, or education purposes. The same statutory form's Part 1 separately gives the named health care agent postdeath authority: “My agent is authorized to donate my organs, tissues, and parts, authorize an autopsy, and direct disposition of my remains, except as I state here or in Part 3 of this form” — meaning an agent's default authority under an Advance Health Care Directive already reaches organ and tissue donation unless the directive limits it. Separately, Health & Safety Code § 7151.10 addresses a possible conflict between an Advance Health Care Directive (or an end-of-life declaration) and a potential anatomical gift over the medical measures needed to keep a part suitable for transplantation or therapy: if the directive's terms conflict with what the gift requires, the prospective donor's attending physician and the prospective donor confer to resolve it; if the prospective donor is incapable of resolving it, the directive's agent (or, absent one or if the agent is not reasonably available, another person otherwise authorized by law to make health care decisions for the prospective donor) acts to resolve it, as expeditiously as possible, and the measures are not withheld or withdrawn before resolution unless doing so is not contraindicated by appropriate end-of-life care.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on two genuinely independent statutory sources from two different California codes: Probate Code § 4701 (the AHCD statutory form, confirming a gift can be made within an Advance Health Care Directive and describing the agent's default postdeath donation authority) and Health & Safety Code § 7151.10 (the anatomical-gift chapter's own conflict-resolution rule for when a directive's terms and a potential gift's needs collide). The three quotes drawn from § 4701 are the same statutory section, not independent of one another, but they are independent of the Health & Safety Code § 7151.10 citation. This is not a claim that using the statutory form is required — Probate Code § 4700, already cited elsewhere in this corpus's Advance Health Care Directive document, states that using it is optional — only that the form the statute itself sets out treats organ donation as something an Advance Health Care Directive can cover. § 7151.10's conflict-resolution rule is narrower than it may first appear: by its own terms it applies specifically to a conflict over ‘measures necessary to ensure the medical suitability of a part for transplantation or therapy’ — not to every possible interaction between a directive and a gift.

citations.quote: (1.5) AGENT’S POSTDEATH AUTHORITY: My agent is authorized to donate my organs, tissues, and parts, authorize an autopsy, and direct disposition of my remains, except as I state here or in Part 3 of this form:

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7151.10(b)
citations.cite: resolving a conflict between a directive/declaration and a potential gift
citations.quote: (b) If a prospective donor has a declaration or advance health care directive and the terms of the declaration or directive and the express or implied terms of a potential anatomical gift are in conflict with regard to the administration of measures necessary to ensure the medical suitability of a part for transplantation or therapy, the prospective donor’s attending physician and prospective donor shall confer to resolve the conflict. If the prospective donor is incapable of resolving the conflict, an agent acting under the prospective donor’s declaration or directive, or, if none, or the agent is not reasonably available, another person authorized by law other than this chapter to make health care decisions on behalf of the prospective donor, shall act for the donor to resolve the conflict. The conflict shall be resolved as expeditiously as possible. Information relevant to the resolution of the conflict may be obtained from the appropriate procurement organization and any other person authorized to make an anatomical gift for the prospective donor under Section 7150.40. Before resolution of the conflict, measures necessary to ensure the medical suitability of the part shall not be withheld or withdrawn from the prospective donor if withholding or withdrawing the measures is not contraindicated by appropriate end-of-life care.

clauses.title: Documenting a Refusal to Make an Anatomical Gift, and Its Binding Effect
clauses.body: Separately from making a gift, California Health & Safety Code § 7150.30(a) lets a person refuse to make an anatomical gift of their own body or part by: a record signed by the person (or, subject to a witnessing requirement, signed by someone else at the person's direction if the person is physically unable to sign); the person's will, whether or not it is ever admitted to probate or is later invalidated; or, during the person's terminal illness or injury, any form of communication that clearly expresses the refusal, addressed to at least two adults, at least one of whom is a disinterested witness, memorialized in a signed and dated writing. A refusal, once made, can itself be amended or revoked: in the same manner used to make a refusal, by later making an anatomical gift under § 7150.20 that is inconsistent with the refusal, or by destroying or canceling the record of refusal with the intent to revoke it. On binding effect, § 7150.30(d) states that, absent an express, contrary statement by the person within the refusal itself, an unrevoked refusal “bars all other persons from making an anatomical gift of the individual's body or part” after that person's death — meaning none of the priority-order decision-makers described elsewhere in this chapter can override it.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence that a refusal is a real, separately documented act under this chapter, with real binding force on others after death — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person, or that every state gives a refusal the same binding effect. The first two citations below are subdivisions (a) and (c) of a single statutory section (§ 7150.30); no additional independent source was found for those specific points. A verified, notable finding on the third citation: § 7150.30(d)'s binding-effect rule states it applies “Except as otherwise provided in subdivision (h) of Section 7150.35” — but the current text of § 7150.35, fetched and independently re-verified in full (the fourth citation below), contains only subdivisions (a) through (g); no subdivision (h) exists in it as currently published. This cross-reference in the current statutory text could not be resolved from the statute's own language, and is reported here honestly rather than silently corrected or omitted.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7150.30(a)
citations.cite: how a refusal to make a gift can be made
citations.quote: (a) An individual may refuse to make an anatomical gift of the individual’s body or part by any of the following:(1) A record signed by either of the following:(A) The individual.(B) Subject to subdivision (b), another individual acting at the direction of the individual if the individual is physically unable to sign.(2) The individual’s will, whether or not the will is admitted to probate or invalidated after the individual’s death.(3) Any form of communication made by the individual during the individual’s terminal illness or injury addressed to at least two adults, at least one of whom is a disinterested witness. The witnesses shall memorialize this communication in a writing and sign and date the writing.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7150.30(c)
citations.cite: how a refusal can itself be amended or revoked
citations.quote: (c) An individual who has made a refusal may amend or revoke the refusal by any of the following:(1) In the manner provided in subdivision (a) for making a refusal.(2) By subsequently making an anatomical gift pursuant to Section 7150.20 that is inconsistent with the refusal.(3) By destroying or canceling the record evidencing the refusal, or the portion of the record used to make the refusal, with the intent to revoke the refusal.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7150.30(d)
citations.cite: an unrevoked refusal bars all other persons from making a gift
citations.quote: (d) Except as otherwise provided in subdivision (h) of Section 7150.35, in the absence of an express, contrary indication by the individual set forth in the refusal, an individual’s unrevoked refusal to make an anatomical gift of the individual’s body or part bars all other persons from making an anatomical gift of the individual’s body or part.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 7150.35 (full text, subdivisions (a)-(g))
citations.cite: the cross-referenced section, as currently published, contains no subdivision (h)
citations.quote: (a) Except as otherwise provided in subdivision (g) and subject to subdivision (f), in the absence of an express, contrary indication by the donor, a person other than the donor is barred from making, amending, or revoking an anatomical gift of a donor’s body or part if the donor made an anatomical gift of the donor’s body or part under Section 7150.20 or an amendment to an anatomical gift of the donor’s body or part under Section 7150.25.(b) A donor’s revocation of an anatomical gift of the donor’s body or part under Section 7150.25 is not a refusal and does not bar another person specified in Section 7150.15 or 7150.40 from making an anatomical gift of the donor’s body or part under Section 7150.20 or 7150.45.(c) If a person other than the donor makes an unrevoked anatomical gift of the donor’s body or part under Section 7150.20 or an amendment to an anatomical gift of the donor’s body or part under Section 7150.25, another person may not make, amend, or revoke the gift of the donor’s body or part under Section 7150.45.(d) A revocation of an anatomical gift of a donor’s body or part under Section 7150.25 by a person other than the donor does not bar another person from making an anatomical gift of the body or part under Section 7150.20 or 7150.45.(e) In the absence of an express, contrary indication by the donor or other person authorized to make an anatomical gift under Section 7150.15, an anatomical gift of a part is neither a refusal to give another part nor a limitation on the making of an anatomical gift of another part at a later time by the donor or another person.(f) In the absence of an express, contrary indication by the donor or other person authorized to make an anatomical gift under Section 7150.15, an anatomical gift of a part for one or more of the purposes set forth in Section 7150.15 is not a limitation on the making of an anatomical gift of the part for any of the other purposes by the donor or any other person under Section 7150.20 or 7150.45.(g) Notwithstanding subdivision (a), an individual who is between 15 and 18 years of age may make an anatomical gift for any purpose authorized in this chapter, may limit an anatomical gift to one or more of those purposes, may refuse to make an anatomical gift, or may amend or revoke an anatomical gift, only upon the written consent of the parent or guardian. If a donor who is an unemancipated minor dies, a parent of the donor who is reasonably available may revoke or amend an anatomical gift of the donor’s body or part.

clauses.title: Who May Terminate a Lease Under the SCRA
clauses.body: A federal statute, the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act (SCRA), gives the tenant on a covered lease the option to terminate the lease at any time after one of two events. First: the lease was executed by, or on behalf of, a person who thereafter and during the term of the lease enters military service. Second: the tenant was already in military service when the lease was signed, and afterward receives military orders for a permanent change of station, or to deploy with a military unit (or as an individual in support of a military operation), for a period of not less than 90 days.
clauses.gap: This covers the two most common triggers, but the statute lists two further, narrower ones this clause doesn't detail: a tenant who executed a lease upon already having PCS or deployment orders and then separately receives a stop-movement order (a different timing rule applies to that trigger, described below in this document's effective-date clause); and a one-year window for a lessee's spouse or dependent to terminate if the lessee dies while in military service, or if the lessee incurs a catastrophic injury or illness (as separately defined by statute) during military service — neither of which this clause's citations cover. A lessee's termination under this section also ends any dependent's own obligations under the same lease, per a separate subsection not quoted here. The 90-day threshold above is specific to a premises lease; the same statutory section sets a 180-day threshold instead for the motor-vehicle-lease branch of this law, which this document doesn't otherwise cover. All citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (50 U.S.C. § 3955) rather than independently authored sources. The text was fetched twice independently from law.cornell.edu (byte-identical both times) and cross-checked against a separate two-fetch retrieval of the official U.S. House Office of the Law Revision Counsel text at uscode.house.gov (also identical on both fetches, and matching Cornell's text word for word) — both mirror the same enacted U.S. Code text rather than being independently authored sources of their own.

clauses.title: Which Leases This Covers
clauses.body: This SCRA provision applies to a lease of premises occupied, or intended to be occupied, by a servicemember or the servicemember's dependents, for a residential, professional, business, agricultural, or similar purpose. The same statutory section separately covers a lease of a motor vehicle used, or intended to be used, by a servicemember or dependents for personal or business transportation, on different terms this document doesn't address.
clauses.gap: This is broader than just a dwelling lease: the statute's own words cover a premises lease used for a "residential, professional, business, agricultural, or similar purpose," not "residential" alone — this document's focus on the residential/dwelling situation is a narrowing choice, not the full reach of the statute. The motor-vehicle-lease branch of the same section uses a materially different threshold than the premises-lease branch covered above: a 180-day PCS or deployment order requirement (versus 90 days for a premises lease), plus its own geographic conditions for a change-of-station trigger and its own vehicle-return mechanics — a reader shouldn't assume the 90-day premises-lease threshold carries over to a motor-vehicle lease under this same law. All citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (50 U.S.C. § 3955) rather than independently authored sources. The text was fetched twice independently from law.cornell.edu (byte-identical both times) and cross-checked against a separate two-fetch retrieval of uscode.house.gov (also identical on both fetches, and matching Cornell's text word for word) — both mirror the same enacted U.S. Code text rather than being independently authored sources of their own.

citations.quote: A lease of premises occupied, or intended to be occupied, by a servicemember or a servicemember’s dependents for a residential, professional, business, agricultural, or similar purpose if—
