clauses.title: How Termination Notice Must Be Given
clauses.body: Terminating a covered premises lease under this provision requires the tenant to deliver written notice of the termination, together with a copy of the servicemember's military orders, to the landlord (or the landlord's grantee), or to the landlord's agent (or the agent's grantee). The statute defines "military orders" broadly: the term means official military orders (including orders for separation or retirement), or any notification, certification, or verification from the servicemember's commanding officer regarding the servicemember's current or future military duty status.
clauses.gap: A common assumption is that the statute offers two separate, alternative documents a tenant can attach to the notice — either military orders or a commanding officer's letter. That's not quite how the text is built: the definition of "military orders" itself already includes a notification, certification, or verification from the commanding officer as one qualifying form of "military orders," so there is one document requirement (a copy of "military orders," broadly defined), not two independent alternatives. Separately, the statute lists four specific permitted methods for delivering the notice itself — hand delivery, private business carrier, U.S. mail with return receipt requested, or specified electronic means — in a subsection this clause doesn't quote directly; this document's signature/delivery block reflects those methods as checkboxes. All citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (50 U.S.C. § 3955) rather than independently authored sources. The text was fetched twice independently from law.cornell.edu (byte-identical both times) and cross-checked against a separate two-fetch retrieval of uscode.house.gov (also identical on both fetches, and matching Cornell's text word for word) — both mirror the same enacted U.S. Code text rather than being independently authored sources of their own.

citations.case: 50 U.S.C. § 3955(c)(1)(A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, written notice plus a copy of military orders
citations.quote: by delivery by the lessee of written notice of such termination, and a copy of the servicemember’s military orders, to the lessor (or the lessor’s grantee), or to the lessor’s agent (or the agent’s grantee); and

citations.case: 50 U.S.C. § 3955(i)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, definition of “military orders”
citations.quote: The term “military orders”, with respect to a servicemember, means official military orders (including orders for separation or retirement), or any notification, certification, or verification from the servicemember’s commanding officer, with respect to the servicemember’s current or future military duty status.

clauses.title: When Termination Takes Effect
clauses.body: For a covered premises lease that provides for monthly rent, once notice of termination is delivered, the lease terminates 30 days after the first date on which the next rent payment is due and payable following that delivery. For a covered premises lease that isn't a monthly-rent lease, termination is effective on the last day of the month following the month in which notice was delivered.
clauses.gap: The 30-day period does not run from the date notice is delivered — it runs from the next rent due date after delivery. Depending on where in the rent cycle the notice lands, the lease can therefore stay in effect well beyond 30 days from the date of the notice itself (for example, notice delivered the day after rent was due can push the effective termination date close to two months out, once the following month's due date plus 30 days is reached). This timing rule applies specifically to a lease covered by the two triggers in this document's eligibility clause (entering military service, or receiving PCS/deployment orders); the same statutory section sets a different rule for the narrower stop-movement-order trigger not covered by that clause — termination there is effective on the date the notice-and-orders requirement is met, with no 30-day or month-end wait. This is a single statutory subsection; no additional independent source was found for this. The text was fetched twice independently from law.cornell.edu (byte-identical both times) and cross-checked against a separate two-fetch retrieval of uscode.house.gov (also identical on both fetches, and matching Cornell's text word for word) — both mirror the same enacted U.S. Code text rather than being independently authored sources of their own.

citations.case: 50 U.S.C. § 3955(d)(1)(A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, effective date for a monthly-rent premises lease
citations.quote: In the case of a lease described in subparagraph (A) or (B) of subsection (b)(1) that provides for monthly payment of rent, termination of the lease under subsection (a) is effective 30 days after the first date on which the next rental payment is due and payable after the date on which the notice under subsection (c) is delivered. In the case of any other lease described in subparagraphs (A) and (B) of subsection (b)(1) termination of the lease under subsection (a) is effective on the last day of the month following the month in which the notice is delivered.

clauses.title: No Early-Termination Charge; What Remains Owed
clauses.body: A landlord may not impose an early termination charge because a lease is terminated under this provision. Rent that was unpaid for the period before the termination's effective date must still be paid, on a prorated basis, and any other obligation under the lease's terms — such as taxes, summonses, or reasonable charges for excess wear — that is due and unpaid at the time of termination remains the tenant's responsibility. Rent paid in advance for any period after the termination's effective date must be refunded to the tenant within 30 days of that effective date.
clauses.gap: "No early termination charge" is not the same as "nothing owed": arrearages, excess-wear charges, and taxes or summonses tied to the lease survive termination and remain collectible from the tenant. Separately, the statute makes it a misdemeanor, punishable under Title 18 or by up to a year's imprisonment (or both), for anyone to knowingly seize, hold, or detain a servicemember's personal effects, security deposit, or other property — or to knowingly interfere with removing that property — for the purpose of subjecting it to a claim for rent accruing after the termination date; that penalty provision exists in the same statutory section but isn't independently quoted in this clause's citations. All citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (50 U.S.C. § 3955) rather than independently authored sources. The text was fetched twice independently from law.cornell.edu (byte-identical both times) and cross-checked against a separate two-fetch retrieval of uscode.house.gov (also identical on both fetches, and matching Cornell's text word for word) — both mirror the same enacted U.S. Code text rather than being independently authored sources of their own.

citations.case: 50 U.S.C. § 3955(e)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, prorated arrearages and no early-termination charge
citations.quote: Rent amounts for a lease described in subsection (b)(1) that are unpaid for the period preceding the effective date of the lease termination shall be paid on a prorated basis. The lessor may not impose an early termination charge, but any taxes, summonses, or other obligations and liabilities of the lessee in accordance with the terms of the lease, including reasonable charges to the lessee for excess wear, that are due and unpaid at the time of termination of the lease shall be paid by the lessee.

citations.case: 50 U.S.C. § 3955(f) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, refund of rent paid in advance
citations.quote: Rents or lease amounts paid in advance for a period after the effective date of the termination of the lease shall be refunded to the lessee by the lessor (or the lessor’s assignee or the assignee’s agent) within 30 days of the effective date of the termination of the lease.

clauses.title: Declaration Regarding Child Abduction Prevention Information
clauses.body: This information sheet concerns a child custody or visitation proceeding involving {{childName}}, filed or to be filed in {{countyOfFiling}} County, California, between {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}. It is prepared to explain California Family Code section 3048 -- the statute that governs (1) certain contents every custody or visitation order must contain, and (2) the specific findings a court must consider, and the specific preventive measures a court may order, when the court becomes aware of facts that may indicate a risk that a party will abduct {{childName}}. This information sheet does not itself assert that any risk of abduction exists in this matter, does not request or oppose any specific preventive measure, and does not make or substitute for any finding a court is required to make under Family Code section 3048 -- only the court, applying section 3048 to the evidence and facts of the case before it, can make that determination.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment -- Not a Court Finding
clauses.body:
I, {{party1Name}}, acknowledge that I have reviewed this information sheet regarding California Family Code section 3048 in connection with the custody or visitation proceeding concerning {{childName}}.

Executed on {{dateSigned}}, at {{cityState}}.

☐ _________________________ {{party1Name}}, signature

[This information sheet is prepared for use alongside an actual filing in the appropriate California superior court. It does not itself determine whether a risk of abduction exists, does not order any preventive measure, and does not modify any existing custody or visitation order concerning {{childName}}. Only a court, applying Family Code section 3048 to the specific facts and evidence presented to it, can make the findings and orders that section describes.]

clauses.title: Family Code Section 3048(a): Contents Required in Every Custody or Visitation Order
clauses.body: Family Code section 3048(a) is not limited to cases involving a risk of abduction: it states that, notwithstanding any other law, in a proceeding to determine child custody or visitation, every custody or visitation order shall contain (1) the basis for the court's exercise of jurisdiction, (2) the manner in which notice and opportunity to be heard were given, (3) a clear description of the custody and visitation rights of each party, (4) a provision stating that a violation of the order may subject the violating party to civil or criminal penalties, or both, and (5) identification of the country of habitual residence of the child or children. As fetched and verified, subdivision (a)'s five requirements apply generally to every custody or visitation order issued in a California proceeding to determine custody or visitation -- the statutory text does not condition subdivision (a) on any prior finding, or even any suspicion, that a risk of abduction exists. The abduction-risk-specific provisions of the statute -- the court's duty to consider risk factors and preventive measures -- are addressed separately in subdivision (b), covered in other clauses of this document.
clauses.gap: Fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (California Family Code section 3048) and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings (a browser-style User-Agent and a plain curl User-Agent). Subdivision (a) is one subdivision of a single statutory section, so it is one source, not independent of the other subdivisions of section 3048 cited elsewhere in this document. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what California's own Family Code requires a California custody or visitation order to contain -- not a claim about what any other state requires, and not a claim about what any specific court has ordered or will order in any individual case. Correction of a naive assumption: subdivision (a)'s five required order contents are NOT limited to abduction-risk cases -- they apply to every custody or visitation order in a California proceeding to determine custody or visitation, regardless of whether abduction risk is ever raised. No case law is cited in this clause; this topic is governed by clear, mandatory statutory text ("every custody or visitation order shall contain all of the following") rather than by contested judicial interpretation, and CourtListener was not queried for it this session.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3048(a)
citations.cite: required contents of every custody or visitation order
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other law, in a proceeding to determine child custody or visitation with a child, every custody or visitation order shall contain all of the following: (1) The basis for the court’s exercise of jurisdiction. (2) The manner in which notice and opportunity to be heard were given. (3) A clear description of the custody and visitation rights of each party. (4) A provision stating that a violation of the order may subject the party in violation to civil or criminal penalties, or both. (5) Identification of the country of habitual residence of the child or children.

clauses.title: Family Code Section 3048(b)(1): The Court's Duty to Consider Abduction Risk Factors
clauses.body: Family Code section 3048(b)(1) states that in cases in which the court becomes aware of facts that may indicate a risk of abduction of a child, the court shall, either on its own motion or at the request of a party, determine whether measures are needed to prevent the abduction of the child by one parent. In making that determination, the court is directed to consider the risk of abduction of the child, obstacles to the child's location, recovery, and return if the child is abducted, and potential harm to the child if the child is abducted. Section 3048(b)(1) then enumerates eight specific factors the court shall consider to determine whether a risk of abduction exists: (A) whether a party has previously taken, enticed away, kept, withheld, or concealed a child in violation of another person's right of custody or visitation; (B) whether a party has previously threatened to do any of those things; (C) whether a party lacks strong ties to California; (D) whether a party has strong familial, emotional, or cultural ties to another state or country, including foreign citizenship -- a factor the statute says shall be considered only if evidence exists in support of another listed factor; (E) whether a party has no financial reason to stay in California; (F) whether a party has engaged in planning activities that would facilitate removing the child from the state, with consideration given to whether the party is instead carrying out a safety plan to flee from domestic violence; (G) whether a party has a history of a lack of parental cooperation or child abuse, or there is substantiated evidence a party has perpetrated domestic violence; and (H) whether a party has a criminal record. As fetched and verified, these eight factors are stated directly in section 3048(b)(1) itself -- the statute does not cross-reference the Uniform Child Abduction Prevention Act (UCAPA) or any other named uniform act for this risk-factor list.
clauses.gap: Fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (California Family Code section 3048) and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings (a browser-style User-Agent and a plain curl User-Agent). Subdivision (b)(1) is one paragraph of a single statutory section and is treated as one source, not independent of the other subdivisions of section 3048 cited elsewhere in this document. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own risk-factor framework -- not a claim that any other state uses the same factors, and not a claim about whether these factors are, or are not, present in any specific case. Correction of a naive research assumption: the eight risk factors are NOT drawn by cross-reference from the Uniform Child Abduction Prevention Act (a model act that a number of other states have enacted) -- as verified, the phrase "Uniform Child Abduction Prevention Act" does not appear anywhere in section 3048's text, and California has codified its own, separately worded list of risk factors directly within section 3048(b)(1) rather than adopting UCAPA. Section 3048(b)(1) does cross-reference a different uniform act -- the Uniform Child Custody Jurisdiction and Enforcement Act -- but only later, within subdivision (b)(2)(J)'s list of preventive measures, covered in a separate clause of this document; that cross-reference does not supply the risk-factor list itself. No case law is cited in this clause; the risk factors are stated in enumerated statutory text rather than developed through contested judicial interpretation, and CourtListener was not queried for it this session.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3048(b)(1)
citations.cite: duty to determine whether abduction-prevention measures are needed, and the factors considered
citations.quote: In cases in which the court becomes aware of facts that may indicate that there is a risk of abduction of a child, the court shall, either on its own motion or at the request of a party, determine whether measures are needed to prevent the abduction of the child by one parent. To make that determination, the court shall consider the risk of abduction of the child, obstacles to location, recovery, and return if the child is abducted, and potential harm to the child if the child is abducted. To determine whether there is a risk of abduction, the court shall consider the following factors:

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3048(b)(1)(F)
citations.cite: planning-activities risk factor, and its domestic-violence safety-plan qualifier
citations.quote: Whether a party has engaged in planning activities that would facilitate the removal of a child from the state, including quitting a job, selling the primary residence, terminating a lease, closing a bank account, liquidating other assets, hiding or destroying documents, applying for a passport, applying to obtain a birth certificate or school or medical records, or purchasing airplane or other travel tickets, with consideration given to whether a party is carrying out a safety plan to flee from domestic violence.

clauses.title: Family Code Section 3048(b)(2): Preventive Measures the Court May Order
clauses.body: Family Code section 3048(b)(2) states that if the court makes a finding that there is a need for preventative measures after considering the risk factors in section 3048(b)(1), the court shall consider taking one or more of eleven listed categories of measures to prevent the abduction of the child: (A) ordering supervised visitation; (B) requiring a parent to post a bond sufficient to serve as a financial deterrent to abduction, whose proceeds may offset the cost of recovering the child if an abduction occurs; (C) restricting the custodial or noncustodial parent's right to remove the child from the county, the state, or the country; (D) restricting the custodial parent's right to relocate with the child unless advance notice and the noncustodial parent's written agreement, or the court's approval, are obtained first; (E) requiring the surrender of passports and other travel documents; (F) prohibiting a parent from applying for a new or replacement passport for the child; (G) requiring a parent to notify a relevant foreign consulate or embassy of passport restrictions and to provide the court with proof of that notification; (H) requiring registration of a California order in another state, or an order from another country with identical terms, as a prerequisite to the child traveling there for visits; (I) obtaining assurances a traveling parent will return from foreign visits, such as a travel itinerary, copies of round-trip airline tickets, a list of addresses and telephone numbers where the child can be reached, or an open airline ticket for the left-behind parent; (J) including provisions to facilitate use of the Uniform Child Custody Jurisdiction and Enforcement Act and the Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction, such as identifying California as the child's home state or the United States as the child's country of habitual residence; and (K) authorizing the assistance of law enforcement. Section 3048(b)(3) further states that if the court imposes any of these conditions, they shall be specifically noted on the minute order of the court proceedings.
clauses.gap: Fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (California Family Code section 3048) and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings (a browser-style User-Agent and a plain curl User-Agent). Subdivisions (b)(2) and (b)(3), both cited above, are paragraphs of a single statutory section and are treated as one source, not independent of the other subdivisions of section 3048 cited elsewhere in this document. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the specific preventive measures California's own Family Code authorizes a court to consider -- not a claim that a court will order any particular measure in any specific case, and not a claim that every state authorizes the same list of measures. Correction of a naive assumption: the statute's list of eleven measure-categories is considerably longer and more specific than a generic "supervised visitation, bond, or passport surrender" summary might suggest -- it separately addresses new/replacement passport applications, foreign consulate notification, registration of the order in another state or country, travel-assurance documentation, UCCJEA/Hague-facilitating provisions, and law enforcement assistance, each as its own lettered measure. No case law is cited in this clause; the preventive measures are stated in enumerated statutory text rather than developed through contested judicial interpretation, and CourtListener was not queried for it this session.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3048(b)(2)
citations.cite: the court's duty to consider preventive measures after a finding of need
citations.quote: If the court makes a finding that there is a need for preventative measures after considering the factors listed in paragraph (1), the court shall consider taking one or more of the following measures to prevent the abduction of the child:

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3048(b)(2)(E)
citations.cite: surrender of passports and other travel documents
citations.quote: Requiring the surrender of passports and other travel documents.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3048(b)(3)
citations.cite: requirement that imposed conditions be noted on the minute order
citations.quote: If the court imposes any or all of the conditions listed in paragraph (2), those conditions shall be specifically noted on the minute order of the court proceedings.

clauses.title: Family Code Section 3048(b)(4): Required Notice of the District Attorney's Child Abduction Unit
clauses.body: Family Code section 3048(b)(4) states that if the court determines there is a risk of abduction sufficient to warrant applying one or more of the prevention measures the statute authorizes, the court shall inform the parties of the telephone number and address of the Child Abduction Unit in the office of the district attorney in the county where the custody or visitation order is being entered. Section 3048(c) separately directs the Judicial Council to make the changes to its child custody order forms necessary to implement subdivision (b). Section 3048(d) states that section 3048 does not affect the applicability of Penal Code section 278.7 -- meaning, as fetched and verified, that section 3048's civil custody-order provisions and Penal Code section 278.7 (a distinct statute addressing custodial interference in violation of a court order) each continue to apply on their own terms; section 3048 does not state that it modifies, limits, or replaces Penal Code section 278.7.
clauses.gap: Fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (California Family Code section 3048) and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings (a browser-style User-Agent and a plain curl User-Agent). Subdivisions (b)(4), (c), and (d), all cited above, are provisions of a single statutory section and are treated as one source, not independent of the other subdivisions of section 3048 cited elsewhere in this document. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what California's own Family Code requires and cross-references -- not a claim about the current substantive content of Penal Code section 278.7, which was not independently fetched or verified this session; this clause reports only that section 3048(d) states it does not affect that section's applicability, without describing what Penal Code section 278.7 itself provides. No case law is cited in this clause; this topic is governed by direct statutory text rather than by contested judicial interpretation, and CourtListener was not queried for it this session.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3048(b)(4)
citations.cite: required notice of the district attorney's Child Abduction Unit
citations.quote: If the court determines there is a risk of abduction that is sufficient to warrant the application of one or more of the prevention measures authorized by this section, the court shall inform the parties of the telephone number and address of the Child Abduction Unit in the office of the district attorney in the county where the custody or visitation order is being entered.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3048(d)
citations.cite: relationship to Penal Code section 278.7
citations.quote: This section does not affect the applicability of Section 278.7 of the Penal Code.

clauses.title: Family Code Section 3048(b)(2)(J): Relationship to the UCCJEA and the Hague Convention
clauses.body: Among the preventive measures listed in Family Code section 3048(b)(2), subdivision (J) authorizes the court to consider including provisions in the custody order to facilitate use of the Uniform Child Custody Jurisdiction and Enforcement Act (Part 3, commencing with section 3400) and the Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction (implemented pursuant to 42 U.S.C. section 11601 et seq.). As fetched and verified, examples the statute itself gives include identifying California as the child's home state or otherwise defining the basis for the California court's exercise of jurisdiction under the UCCJEA, identifying the United States as the child's country of habitual residence under the Hague Convention, defining custody rights under the Hague Convention, and obtaining the parents' express agreement that the United States is the child's country of habitual residence or that California or the United States is the most appropriate forum for custody and visitation orders. This measure connects section 3048's abduction-prevention framework to the UCCJEA's separate jurisdictional framework (Family Code sections 3400-3465, addressed in this corpus's separate Child Custody Jurisdiction (UCCJEA) Information Sheet) and to the Hague Convention's separate international framework -- section 3048 does not itself restate the UCCJEA's jurisdictional rules or the Hague Convention's return procedures; it authorizes a California custody order to include provisions that make later use of those other frameworks more effective.
clauses.gap: Fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (California Family Code section 3048) and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings (a browser-style User-Agent and a plain curl User-Agent). Subdivision (b)(2)(J), cited above, is one lettered measure within a single statutory section's paragraph (b)(2) and is treated as one source, not independent of the other subdivisions of section 3048 cited elsewhere in this document. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what California's own Family Code authorizes a court to include in a custody order -- not a claim about the current substantive content of the UCCJEA's jurisdictional rules or the Hague Convention's return procedures, neither of which was independently re-verified in this clause (the UCCJEA's home-state and jurisdictional provisions are separately verified in this corpus's Child Custody Jurisdiction (UCCJEA) Information Sheet). This clause exists to make an accurate distinction, not to duplicate that other document: section 3048(b)(2)(J) is a preventive measure a court may include in a custody order in an abduction-risk case, while the UCCJEA document addresses which state's courts have jurisdiction to hear a custody case in the first place -- related but legally distinct questions. No case law is cited in this clause; this topic is governed by direct statutory cross-reference rather than by contested judicial interpretation, and CourtListener was not queried for it this session.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3048(b)(2)(J)
citations.cite: measure facilitating use of the UCCJEA and the Hague Convention
citations.quote: Including provisions in the custody order to facilitate use of the Uniform Child Custody Jurisdiction and Enforcement Act (Part 3 (commencing with Section 3400)) and the Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction (implemented pursuant to 42 U.S.C. Sec. 11601 et seq.)

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope — Inspection Rights Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This information sheet relates to {{companyName}}, a {{entityType}} organized under the laws of California, and to {{shareholderOrMemberName}}'s status as a shareholder or member of {{companyName}}. It describes the statutory rights a California corporation's shareholder or a California LLC's member has to inspect and copy the entity's books, records, and minutes, along with the written-demand process those statutes describe and the remedy available if a demand is refused. Stated purpose for a records request under this information sheet, if one is being made: {{inspectionPurpose}}.

This information sheet is educational only. It does not itself constitute a written demand on {{companyName}}, does not determine whether {{shareholderOrMemberName}}'s stated purpose is one a court would find "reasonably related" to their interest as a shareholder or member within the meaning of the statutes described below, and does not determine whether any ownership threshold that applies to a particular right described below is met. This document is not this project's Corporate Bylaws or Multi-Member LLC Operating Agreement document, which govern {{companyName}}'s internal affairs generally; this document instead focuses specifically on the inspection-and-copying statutes.

clauses.title: Closing and Signature Block — Inspection Rights Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This information sheet regarding {{companyName}} was prepared by {{shareholderOrMemberName}}.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{shareholderOrMemberName}}: ☐ _________________________
Approximate ownership or membership interest in {{companyName}}, if known: {{ownershipPercentage}}

[This information sheet describes the California statutes giving a shareholder or LLC member the right to inspect and copy an entity's books, records, and minutes, the written-demand process those statutes describe, and the court remedy available if a demand is refused. It is not a completed written demand, does not itself compel {{companyName}} to permit any inspection, and does not constitute legal advice. The current statutory text is published by the California Legislative Information website (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov).]

clauses.title: Shareholder's Right to Inspect Accounting Books, Records, and Minutes
clauses.body: A California corporation's accounting books, records, and minutes of proceedings of the shareholders, the board, and board committees must be open to inspection at the corporation's principal office in California (or, if it has none, at its registered agent's location), on the written demand of any shareholder or voting trust certificate holder, at any reasonable time during usual business hours, for a purpose reasonably related to that person's interest as a shareholder or voting trust certificate holder. This right carries no minimum-ownership threshold — it belongs to any shareholder, whether they hold one share or many. As an alternative to inspecting in person, the shareholder or certificate holder can instead ask the corporation to produce the books, records, and minutes by mail or electronically, if they pay the reasonable cost of copying or converting the documents. The right extends to the records of each of the corporation's subsidiaries, and it may be exercised in person or through an agent or attorney, including the right to copy and make extracts.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine, unconditional shareholder right — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. Unlike the shareholder-list right described elsewhere in this document (Corp. Code § 1600(a)), this records-and-minutes right under § 1601 carries no ownership-percentage or dollar-value threshold at all; a single share is enough, as long as the shareholder's purpose is reasonably related to their interest as a shareholder. This document doesn't resolve what counts as a "purpose reasonably related" to that interest in any specific case — that determination is fact-specific and, if contested, is for a court. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1601) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1601(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, shareholder right to inspect books, records, and minutes
citations.quote: The accounting books, records, and minutes of proceedings of the shareholders and the board and committees of the board of any domestic corporation, and of any foreign corporation keeping any records in this state or having its principal office in California, or a true and accurate copy thereof if the original has been lost, destroyed, or is not normally physically located within this state shall be open to inspection at the corporation’s principal office in California, or if none, at the physical location for the corporation’s registered agent for service of process in this state, upon the written demand on the corporation of any shareholder or holder of a voting trust certificate at any reasonable time during usual business hours, for a purpose reasonably related to the holder’s interests as a shareholder or as the holder of a voting trust certificate.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1601(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, method of inspection and non-waivability
citations.quote: The inspection by a shareholder or holder of a voting trust certificate may be made in person or by agent or attorney, and the right of inspection includes the right to copy and make extracts. The right of the shareholders to inspect the corporate records may not be limited by the articles or bylaws.

clauses.title: Shareholder's Right to Inspect and Copy the Shareholder List
clauses.body: California corporate law gives two distinct rights covering the list of a corporation's shareholders, and they are not the same right. First, a shareholder or shareholders holding at least 5% in the aggregate of the corporation's outstanding voting shares — or holding at least 1% of those voting shares and having filed a Schedule 14A with the SEC — has an absolute right to inspect and copy the shareholder record (names, addresses, and shareholdings) during business hours, on five business days' prior written demand, or to obtain a compiled list of voting shareholders from the corporation's transfer agent on written demand and payment of the agent's usual charges. Separately, and without any ownership threshold at all, the shareholder record is also open to inspection and copying by any shareholder or voting trust certificate holder, at any time during usual business hours, on written demand, for a purpose reasonably related to that person's interest as a shareholder or certificate holder.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine ownership-linked right — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. It's worth stating precisely because it corrects a natural assumption: the 5%-or-1%-with-Schedule-14A threshold in subdivision (a) applies specifically to the streamlined, no-purpose-required procedure for getting a compiled shareholder list on five business days' notice (including from the transfer agent) — it is not the threshold for inspecting the shareholder record at all. Subdivision (c) gives every shareholder and voting trust certificate holder, regardless of how small their holding is, a separate right to inspect and copy that same shareholder record at any time during business hours, without the five-business-day mechanism, as long as their purpose is reasonably related to their interest as a shareholder. This document doesn't restate subdivision (b)'s separate remedy (a court order postponing a shareholders' meeting) for a corporation's delay in complying with a subdivision (a) demand. Citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1600) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1600(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, ownership threshold for the streamlined shareholder-list right
citations.quote: A shareholder or shareholders holding at least 5 percent in the aggregate of the outstanding voting shares of a corporation or who hold at least 1 percent of those voting shares and have filed a Schedule 14A with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission shall have an absolute right to do either or both of the following: (1) inspect and copy the record of shareholders’ names and addresses and shareholdings during usual business hours upon five business days’ prior written demand upon the corporation, or (2) obtain from the transfer agent for the corporation, upon written demand and upon the tender of its usual charges for such a list

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1600(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, general shareholder-list inspection right with no ownership threshold
citations.quote: The record of shareholders shall also be open to inspection and copying by any shareholder or holder of a voting trust certificate at any time during usual business hours upon written demand on the corporation, for a purpose reasonably related to such holder’s interests as a shareholder or holder of a voting trust certificate.

clauses.title: Remedy for a Corporation's Refusal to Permit Inspection
clauses.body: If a corporation refuses a lawful demand for inspection, the superior court of the proper county may enforce the right of inspection on just and proper conditions, or, for good cause shown, appoint one or more competent inspectors or accountants to audit the corporation's books and records and investigate its property, funds, and affairs (including those of its subsidiaries), and report to the court. Officers and agents of the corporation must produce all books and documents in their custody to inspectors or accountants appointed this way, on penalty of contempt of court. The expenses of that investigation or audit are paid by the person who applied for it, unless the court orders the corporation to pay or share them.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual court remedy for a refused demand — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. It's worth stating precisely because it corrects a natural assumption: this statute does not create a fixed per-day or per-violation monetary penalty for refusing inspection (unlike some other California recordkeeping statutes, such as the wage-statement inspection right elsewhere in this project's corpus, which does carry a specific dollar penalty). The remedy here is a court order compelling inspection or an audit, with the cost of that audit defaulting to the person who sought it unless the court shifts it to the corporation — the statute does not by its own terms award the shareholder attorney's fees or other damages for the refusal itself. This document doesn't address whether a shareholder could pursue a different remedy (such as a general civil action) outside this specific statute. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1603) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1603(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, court enforcement of a refused inspection demand
citations.quote: Upon refusal of a lawful demand for inspection, the superior court of the proper county, may enforce the right of inspection with just and proper conditions or may, for good cause shown, appoint one or more competent inspectors or accountants to audit the books and records kept in this state and investigate the property, funds and affairs of any domestic corporation or any foreign corporation keeping records in this state and of any subsidiary corporation thereof, domestic or foreign, keeping records in this state and to report thereon in such manner as the court may direct.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1603(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, duty to produce records to a court-appointed inspector
citations.quote: All officers and agents of the corporation shall produce to the inspectors or accountants so appointed all books and documents in their custody or power, under penalty of punishment for contempt of court.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1603(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, who pays for the court-ordered audit
citations.quote: All expenses of the investigation or audit shall be defrayed by the applicant unless the court orders them to be paid or shared by the corporation.

clauses.title: LLC Member's and Transferee's Right to Inspect Company Records
clauses.body: Under the California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, each member, manager, and transferee of a California LLC has the right, on reasonable request and for purposes reasonably related to that person's interest as a member, manager, or transferee, to inspect and copy — during normal business hours — any of the records the LLC is statutorily required to maintain, and to obtain a written copy of the LLC's federal, state, and local income tax returns for each year, promptly after they become available. The records the LLC must maintain and make available for this purpose include a current alphabetical list of each member's and transferee's name, address, contribution, and share of profits and losses; the articles of organization and any amendments; the written operating agreement, if any, and its amendments; copies of the LLC's tax returns and financial statements for the six most recent fiscal years; and the LLC's internal-affairs books and records for at least the current and past four fiscal years.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine default access right — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC. This is the correct current citation for the LLC member/transferee inspection right itself (Corp. Code § 17704.10(b)); § 17701.13 is a distinct section that separately defines which records an LLC must maintain in the first place — § 17704.10(b) cross-references it rather than duplicating it, so both sections matter to understanding the full scope of what can be inspected. Like the corporate right described elsewhere in this document, this right is phrased around a "purpose reasonably related to the interest" of the person requesting it, and it belongs to a transferee (someone who has received an economic interest, such as an heir, without becoming a full member) as well as to members and managers — not only to those with voting or management rights. Unlike the corporate shareholder-list right described elsewhere in this document, this LLC right carries no minimum-ownership-percentage threshold. This document doesn't restate the additional annual and interim financial-reporting duties this same statute imposes once an LLC has more than 35 members. Citations below are from two separate statutory sections within the same LLC Act (§ 17704.10 and § 17701.13) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.10(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, member and transferee inspection and tax-return rights
citations.quote: Each member, manager, and transferee has the right, upon reasonable request, for purposes reasonably related to the interest of that person as a member, manager, or transferee, to each of the following: (1) To inspect and copy during normal business hours any of the records required to be maintained pursuant to Section 17701.13. (2) To obtain in writing from the limited liability company, promptly after becoming available, a copy of the limited liability company’s federal, state, and local income tax returns for each year.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.13(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, the records an LLC must maintain and make available
citations.quote: Each limited liability company shall maintain in writing or in any other form capable of being converted into clearly legible tangible form at the office referred to in subdivision (a) all of the following: (1) A current list of the full name and last known business or residence address of each member and of each transferee set forth in alphabetical order, together with the contribution and the share in profits and losses of each member and transferee.

clauses.title: These Rights Can't Be Limited by the Entity's Own Governing Documents
clauses.body: Neither entity type lets its own governing documents cut back these inspection rights. For a California corporation, the statutes creating both the shareholder-list right and the books-records-and-minutes right each say directly that the right "may not be limited by the articles or bylaws." For a California LLC, the member/transferee inspection statute states even more broadly that "any waiver of the rights provided in this section shall be unenforceable" — not limited to a waiver in the articles of organization or operating agreement specifically. The LLC statute also gives a court a broader toolkit than the corporate remedy described elsewhere in this document: beyond enforcing the right itself, a court may award the person who brought the action their reasonable expenses, including attorney's fees, if it finds the LLC's noncompliance was without justification.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of a genuine non-waivability rule for both entity types — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation or LLC. The corporate non-waivability language (Corp. Code §§ 1600(d), 1601(b)) is textually narrower than the LLC's (§ 17704.10(h)): the corporate statutes bar limiting the right only through "the articles or bylaws," while the LLC statute bars "any waiver of the rights" without naming a specific document — this document doesn't resolve whether that difference in wording would actually produce a different outcome for, say, a side agreement that isn't part of the articles or bylaws. This document also doesn't address whether a corporation's shareholders agreement (a separate contract from the articles or bylaws) could have a different effect than the bylaws themselves on the corporate right, since the quoted statutes name only the articles and bylaws. The three citations below are drawn from two separate statutory sections of the corporate inspection chapter (§§ 1600, 1601) and one section of a separate LLC statute (§ 17704.10) — related but independently enacted provisions, not a single independently authored source, and not identical in scope to each other.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1600(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, shareholder-list right can't be limited by articles or bylaws
citations.quote: Any inspection and copying under this section may be made in person or by agent or attorney. The rights provided in this section may not be limited by the articles or bylaws.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1601(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, books-and-records right can't be limited by articles or bylaws
citations.quote: The inspection by a shareholder or holder of a voting trust certificate may be made in person or by agent or attorney, and the right of inspection includes the right to copy and make extracts. The right of the shareholders to inspect the corporate records may not be limited by the articles or bylaws.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.10(h) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, waiver of the inspection right is unenforceable
citations.quote: Any waiver of the rights provided in this section shall be unenforceable.

clauses.title: Sperm/Egg/Embryo Donor Parentage — Facts Declaration
clauses.body:
This information sheet concerns assisted reproduction described in Cal. Fam. Code § 7613, involving {{intendedParent1Name}}{{intendedParent2Name}} (the intended parent or parents) and {{donorName}} (the donor). The parties state, for purposes of the statutory framework described in this document, the following facts about the donation: {{donationType}}.

This information sheet records these facts as stated by the parties; it does not itself determine whether {{donorName}} is, or is not, treated in law as a parent of any child conceived, and it does not itself determine whether {{intendedParent2Name}} — if applicable — is treated in law as a parent. Those outcomes depend on which provision of Cal. Fam. Code § 7613 applies to the facts as they actually occurred, including whether the donated material was provided to a licensed physician and surgeon or a licensed sperm bank, and whether, and when, any written or oral agreement about parentage was made.

This information sheet is not itself a written agreement under Cal. Fam. Code § 7613(a), (b), (c), or (d), and does not itself satisfy any writing requirement described in this document unless it independently meets the content and signature elements those provisions require.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment Block — Donor Parentage Information Sheet
clauses.body:
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of Intended Parent, {{intendedParent1Name}}: ☐ _________________________

Signature of Intended Parent, {{intendedParent2Name}}: ☐ _________________________ (if applicable)

Signature of Donor, {{donorName}}: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet is prepared for use alongside, and not as a substitute for, an actual written agreement described in Cal. Fam. Code § 7613, or one of the optional California Statutory Forms for Assisted Reproduction described in Cal. Fam. Code § 7613.5. It does not itself establish, or fail to establish, any party's parentage of a child conceived through assisted reproduction; that outcome is determined by which provision of § 7613 applies to the facts as they occurred. Unlike this corpus's separate Gestational Carrier (Surrogacy) Agreement Information Sheet, nothing in the text of Cal. Fam. Code § 7613 requires that signatures on a donor written agreement be notarized or witnessed, though the optional statutory forms under § 7613.5 each include their own notary acknowledgment block for parties who choose to use one of them.]

clauses.title: The Sperm Donor's Own Parentage — Two Different Default Rules Depending on How the Semen Was Provided
clauses.body: Family Code § 7613(b) does not impose one single rule for a semen donor; it sets up two different default outcomes depending on how the semen reached the woman who conceives, and each default can be overcome in a different way. Under § 7613(b)(1), if the semen was "provided to a licensed physician and surgeon or to a licensed sperm bank" for use in assisted reproduction by a woman other than the donor's spouse, the donor is treated by default as if the donor is not the natural parent of any child conceived — and that default only flips if the donor and the woman signed a written agreement, before conception, that the donor would be a parent. Under § 7613(b)(2), if the semen was not provided through a licensed physician or sperm bank in that way — the more informal, "known donor" fact pattern — the default runs the other direction by negative implication of the statute's own conditional structure: the donor is treated as not the natural parent only "if either of the following are met": (A) the donor and the woman signed a written agreement, before conception, that the donor would not be a parent, or (B) a court finds by clear and convincing evidence that, before conception, the woman and the donor had an oral agreement that the donor would not be a parent. Neither pathway in current law makes physician involvement a universal precondition to a donor's non-parent status — a donation made outside a licensed physician's or sperm bank's involvement can still result in the donor not being treated as a parent, but only through one of the two mechanisms listed in § 7613(b)(2), and with the practical default running toward the donor being a parent absent one of those mechanisms, rather than away from it as under § 7613(b)(1).
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own current text — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific donation, nor that every state draws this same physician/non-physician distinction or assigns these same defaults. This clause cites two paragraphs of a single statutory subdivision, Family Code § 7613(b)(1) and § 7613(b)(2), both part of the same statutory section verified from a single fetch of that section's full text — they are treated as one source, not independent. No case law was researched for this clause; the two-default structure is stated directly from the current statutory text, which is the version amended by Stats. 2023, Ch. 851, Sec. 5 (AB 1650), effective January 1, 2024, as shown at the end of the fetched section text — this clause does not rely on, and readers should not assume it reflects, any older (e.g., 1990s-era) version of § 7613 that may have imposed a categorical licensed-physician requirement without the alternative pathway described here. Separately, this clause corrects a framing this research started with: the statutory text found here never uses the words "anonymous" or "known" to describe a donor, and draws no distinction under those labels; the physician/sperm-bank-versus-not distinction in § 7613(b)(1)-(2) is a functional analog to what is sometimes informally called an anonymous-donor versus known-donor arrangement, but that is this document's own description of the practical effect, not language the statute itself uses.

clauses.title: The Ova Provider's and Embryo Provider's Own Parentage — A Different Rule Than the Semen-Donor Rule
clauses.body: Family Code § 7613 treats a provider of ova, and a provider of a pre-existing embryo, differently from how it treats a semen donor under § 7613(b) — both in what triggers the default non-parent outcome and in the standard used to overcome it. Under § 7613(c), "a person providing ova for use in assisted reproduction by a person other than the provider's spouse or nonmarital partner is treated in law as if the provider is not the natural parent of a child thereby conceived unless the court finds satisfactory evidence that the provider of the ova, and each recipient, intended for that provider to have parental rights." Under § 7613(d)(1), the same non-parent default applies to "a provider of an embryo for use in assisted reproduction to an intended parent who is not the provider's spouse or nonmarital partner," rebuttable only if the court finds satisfactory evidence that the provider and the intended parent intended for the provider to be a parent. Neither § 7613(c) nor § 7613(d)(1) conditions the ova or embryo provider's non-parent default on the material having passed through a licensed physician, surgeon, or bank — that physician/bank distinction appears only in § 7613(b)'s semen-donor rule, not here. The two provisions also use a different evidentiary phrase — "satisfactory evidence" of shared intent that the provider have parental rights — than the "clear and convincing evidence" of a prior oral non-parent agreement used as the fallback path in § 7613(b)(2)(B) and in § 7613(a)(2)'s intended-parent-consent rule.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own current text — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific donation, nor that every state treats an ova or embryo provider the same way it treats a semen donor. This clause cites Family Code § 7613(c) and § 7613(d)(1), two subdivisions of the same statutory section fetched together as one document — treated as one source, not independent. This clause corrects a framing this research started with: an assumption that egg/ova donation is governed by the same licensed-physician-or-bank distinction that applies to semen donation under § 7613(b) is not supported by the text found here — § 7613(c) and § 7613(d)(1) contain no such distinction.

clauses.title: The Other (Non-Birth-Giving) Intended Parent's Own Parentage — Established by Consent, Not Genetics
clauses.body: Family Code § 7613 also addresses, within its own text, the parentage of the intended parent who is not the donor and not the person who conceives and gives birth. Under § 7613(a)(1), if a woman conceives through assisted reproduction using semen or ova, or both, donated by a donor who is not the woman's spouse, and does so "with the consent of another intended parent," that other intended parent "is treated in law as if that intended parent is the natural parent of a child thereby conceived." That consent "shall be in writing and signed by the other intended parent and the woman conceiving through assisted reproduction." Under § 7613(a)(2), the absence of a signed writing does not automatically defeat that intended parent's status: a court may still find the intended parent consented if it finds, by clear and convincing evidence, that before conception the woman and the intended parent had an oral agreement that both would be parents of the child. Nothing in the text of § 7613(a) conditions this outcome on the parties' marital status, on the intended parent's or woman's sex or gender, or on the involvement of a licensed physician.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own current text — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific arrangement, nor that every state extends parentage to a non-genetic, non-birth-giving intended parent on these same consent-based terms. This clause cites Family Code § 7613(a)(1) and § 7613(a)(2), two paragraphs of the same statutory subdivision fetched together as one document — treated as one source, not independent. No case law was researched for this clause; the rule is stated directly from statutory text. This directly answers the research question of whether a person who is not the donor, but who intends to be a parent via assisted reproduction, has their own parentage addressed by § 7613 itself: it does, within § 7613(a), rather than requiring resort to a separate companion section. A separate section, § 7613.5, does exist and is addressed in a companion clause of this document, but § 7613.5 provides optional forms to help satisfy § 7613(a)'s own writing requirement — it does not itself impose a different or additional substantive rule about this intended parent's parentage.

The other intended parent’s consent shall be in writing and signed by the other intended parent and the woman conceiving through assisted reproduction.

clauses.title: Optional Statutory Forms Under § 7613.5, and How This Framework Relates to the Gestational Carrier Statute
clauses.body: Family Code § 7613.5 is a separate, companion statutory section that supplies optional fill-in forms for use alongside § 7613, not a different substantive parentage rule. Section 7613.5(a) states that "an intended parent may, but is not required to, use the forms set forth in this section to demonstrate the intent to be a legal parent of a child conceived through assisted reproduction," and that "these forms shall satisfy the writing requirement specified in Section 7613," while also making clear that the forms "do not affect any presumptions of parentage based on Section 7611, and do not preclude a court from considering any other claims to parentage under California statute or case law." Section 7613.5(d) confirms use of these particular forms is optional: "this section does not require the use of one of these forms to satisfy the writing requirement of Section 7613" — a different written agreement can also satisfy § 7613's own writing elements. Critically for how this framework relates to this corpus's separate Gestational Carrier (Surrogacy) Agreement Information Sheet, § 7613.5(c) states directly that "these forms do not apply to assisted reproduction agreements for gestational carriers or surrogacy agreements." Sections 7613 and 7613.5 (governing a donor or genetic-material provider's own parentage, and an intended parent's consent-based parentage, outside a gestational-carrier arrangement) and Family Code §§ 7960-7962 (governing an assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers specifically) are two distinct, parallel statutory frameworks within the same Uniform Parentage Act part of the Family Code, addressing different fact patterns: this framework does not itself impose, and its text does not cross-reference, the independent-counsel, notarization-or-witnessing, or pre-embryo-transfer-execution requirements that § 7962 imposes specifically on gestational carrier agreements, and conversely the optional § 7613.5 forms are, by their own terms, unusable for a gestational carrier or surrogacy agreement.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own current text and of how its own two frameworks relate to each other as the statute itself states that relationship — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific arrangement, nor that every state maintains separate donor-parentage and gestational-carrier statutes, or relates them the same way. This clause cites Family Code § 7613.5(a), § 7613.5(c), and § 7613.5(d), three subdivisions of the same statutory section fetched together as one document — treated as one source, not independent; the separately verified § 7613 text and this corpus's already-verified §§ 7960-7962 gestational-carrier clauses are used here only to state the textual relationship between the frameworks (each framework's own text disclaims coverage of the other), not as newly re-verified citations in this clause. No case law was researched for this clause; the relationship between the two frameworks is stated directly from each statute's own text.

clauses.title: When Genetic Material Passed Through Multiple Hands, and Embryo-Disposition Renunciation Agreements Between Co-Owners
clauses.body: Family Code § 7613 addresses two further, more specific situations beyond the core donor and provider rules described elsewhere in this document. First, § 7613(d)(2) addresses a chain-of-custody problem: "if the provider of ova, semen, or embryos is not the original source of the ova or sperm, each original provider's written consent to the donation is required unless that person has executed a writing to consent to the donation, or to waive or relinquish their right to the genetic material, or as otherwise ordered by a court of law." Second, § 7613(e) addresses a written renunciation agreement between two people who jointly control the disposition of stored embryos. Under § 7613(e)(1), if those two people "are not married to one another," they may enter a written agreement in which one of them "renounces all legal interest in the embryos, with the specific intent that the person renouncing all legal interest shall not be a legal parent of any child conceived with use of the embryos," and once that renunciation is signed by everyone with a legal interest in or control over the embryos, "the renouncing person shall be treated in law as a donor, and not a legal parent"; either party may then file the agreement with the court for "an order establishing the nonparentage of the donor." Under § 7613(e)(2), if the two people sharing control of the embryos are instead married to one another at the time they sign such an agreement, it does not become legally binding until "the court's entry of a final decree of dissolution that incorporates the agreement," after which specified marital-presumption provisions (Family Code § 7540, and § 7611(a)-(c)) no longer apply.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own current text — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific arrangement, nor that every state has a comparable rule for multi-hand genetic material or embryo-disposition renunciation agreements. This clause cites Family Code § 7613(d)(2) and § 7613(e)(1)-(2), all part of the same statutory section fetched together as one document — treated as one source, not independent. No case law was researched for this clause; both rules are stated directly from statutory text. This clause deliberately covers a narrower topic than a general framework for resolving a contested embryo-disposition dispute: § 7613(e) addresses only a written renunciation agreement voluntarily entered between people who already share legal control over stored embryos, not a court's resolution of a dispute over embryo disposition where no such agreement exists; that broader topic was not researched for this clause and is outside what this clause covers.

clauses.title: Alter Ego / Piercing the Corporate Veil Information Sheet — Purpose and Scope
clauses.body: This information sheet relates to {{companyName}}, a {{entityType}} formed under the law of {{stateOfFormation}}. It describes California's common-law "alter ego" doctrine — the equitable doctrine under which a court, in a lawsuit against a corporation or limited liability company, may disregard the separate legal existence of that entity ("pierce the corporate veil") and hold a shareholder, member, or other owner personally liable for the entity's debts, obligations, or other liabilities. Alter ego is not a separate statute or a fixed checklist; it is a judge-made doctrine developed and applied case by case by California courts, and the same doctrine and the same case law govern whether an individual owner, or a parent corporation, can be held liable as the alter ego of a corporation or an LLC it owns or controls. This information sheet does not itself pierce or preserve {{companyName}}'s liability shield, does not determine whether {{companyName}}'s specific facts would or would not support alter ego liability, and does not evaluate any specific owner's specific liability exposure. Whether the doctrine applies to any particular entity and any particular owner in any particular dispute is a fact-intensive determination made by a court considering the totality of the circumstances presented in that case.

clauses.title: The Two-Part Test for Alter Ego Liability
clauses.body: California courts have long applied a two-part test to decide whether to disregard the corporate (or LLC) entity and hold an owner personally liable under the alter ego doctrine: first, that there be such a unity of interest and ownership between the entity and its equitable owner that the separate personalities of the entity and the owner no longer exist in reality; and second, that treating the entity's acts as its own alone — that is, honoring the separate entity — would bring about an inequitable result. Both parts of the test must be satisfied; unity of interest and ownership alone, without an inequitable result, is not enough to pierce the veil, and California's own courts have said there is no fixed, mechanical test ("litmus test") for when the veil will be pierced — the outcome depends on the circumstances of each particular case. The same two-part test applies, with only a difference in wording, when the owner sought to be held liable is another corporation (for example, a parent corporation held liable for a subsidiary's conduct) rather than an individual shareholder.
clauses.gap: The two-part test is stated in these terms in Automotriz del Golfo de California, S.A. de C.V. v. Resnick (1957) 47 Cal.2d 792, 796, and is restated verbatim, quoting Automotriz directly, in Mesler v. Bragg Management Co. (1985) 39 Cal.3d 290, 300 ("There is no litmus test to determine when the corporate veil will be pierced; rather the result will depend on the circumstances of each particular case. There are, nevertheless, two general requirements..."). Because Mesler is quoting the identical Automotriz passage rather than independently restating it, these two cases are not independent sources for the wording of the test itself — they are treated here as one source (Automotriz) plus one later California Supreme Court decision confirming that the same wording remains the operative test and extending it, in identical substance, to entity-versus-entity alter ego claims. Sonora Diamond Corp. v. Superior Court (2000) 83 Cal.App.4th 523, 538 independently paraphrases (not quotes) the same two-part test in its own words while citing back to Automotriz, which corroborates that the test has not changed but is likewise not an independently worded source. This is case law, not a statute; no California statute states this general common-law test for corporations. This document does not evaluate whether either part of the test would be met for any specific entity or any specific owner.

citations.case: Automotriz del Golfo de California, S.A. de C.V. v. Resnick
citations.quote: It has been stated that the two requirements for application of this doctrine are (1) that there be such unity of interest and ownership that the separate personalities of the corporation and the individual no longer exist and (2) that, if the acts are treated as those of the corporation alone, an inequitable result will follow.

citations.case: Mesler v. Bragg Management Co.
citations.quote: There is no litmus test to determine when the corporate veil will be pierced; rather the result will depend on the circumstances of each particular case. There are, nevertheless, two general requirements: “(1) that there be such unity of interest and ownership that the separate personalities of the corporation and the individual no longer exist and (2) that, if the acts are treated as those of the corporation alone, an inequitable result will follow.” (Automotriz etc. de California v. Resnick (1957) 47 Cal.2d 792, 796 [306 P.2d 1, 63 A.L.R.2d 1042].) And “only a difference in wording is used in stating the same concept where the entity sought to be held liable is another corporation instead of an individual.” (McLoughlin v. L. Bloom Sons Co., Inc. (1962) 206 Cal.App.2d 848, 851 [24 Cal.Rptr. 311].)

clauses.title: Factors Courts Consider — No Fixed Checklist
clauses.body: California courts have identified a range of factors relevant to whether an entity's separate existence should be disregarded, including: commingling of funds and other assets of the entity and its owner; one party holding out that it is liable for the other's debts; identical equitable ownership between the entity and the person or entity claimed to control it; use of the same offices and employees; treating one as a mere shell or conduit for the affairs of the other; inadequate capitalization; disregard of corporate or entity formalities; failure to segregate records; and identical directors and officers. No single factor is decisive, and no fixed number of factors is required — California courts weigh the totality of the circumstances of each case to decide whether disregarding the entity is warranted. Because alter ego is treated as an extreme remedy, applied sparingly, satisfying some of these factors does not by itself establish alter ego liability; a court must also find that treating the entity's acts as its own alone would produce an inequitable result, and mere difficulty collecting a debt or enforcing a judgment against an entity does not, by itself, meet that standard.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on Sonora Diamond Corp. v. Superior Court (2000) 83 Cal.App.4th 523, 538-540, a published California Court of Appeal decision, which in turn cites and synthesizes factors identified in earlier California cases (principally Roman Catholic Archbishop v. Superior Court (1971) 15 Cal.App.3d 405 and Associated Vendors, Inc. v. Oakland Meat Co. (1962) 210 Cal.App.2d 825, among others cited within Sonora Diamond itself). This document quotes Sonora Diamond's own restatement of those factors rather than independently re-verifying each underlying case Sonora Diamond cites, so this is effectively one appellate source's synthesis of the factor list, not several independently verified sources. Sonora Diamond itself involved a personal-jurisdiction dispute over a parent/subsidiary relationship, not a judgment-collection case, and the court there found the doctrine did not apply on the facts before it because no inequitable result was shown — illustrating that meeting some of these factors does not guarantee a finding of alter ego liability. This document does not assess whether any specific factor is present for any specific entity or owner.

citations.case: Sonora Diamond Corp. v. Superior Court
citations.quote: Among the factors to be considered in applying the doctrine are commingling of funds and other assets of the two entities, the holding out by one entity that it is liable for the debts of the other, identical equitable ownership in the two entities, use of the same offices and employees, and use of one as a mere shell or conduit for the affairs of the other. (Roman Catholic Archbishop v. Superior Court, supra, 15 Cal.App.3d at pp. 406, 411; Associated Vendors, Inc. v. Oakland Meat Co., supra, 210 Cal.App.2d at pp. 838-839.) Other factors which have been described in the case law include inadequate capitalization, disregard of corporate formalities, lack of segregation of corporate records, and identical directors and officers. (See Tomaselli v. Transamerica Ins. Co. (1994) 25 Cal.App.4th 1269, 1285 [31 Cal.Rptr.2d 433]; Associated Vendors, Inc. v. Oakland Meat Co., supra, 210 Cal.App.2d at pp. 838-839; Alberto v. Diversified Group, Inc., supra, 55 F.3d at p. 205.) No one characteristic governs, but the courts must look at all the circumstances to determine whether the doctrine should be applied. (Talbot v. Fresno-Pacific Corp. (1960) 181 Cal.App.2d 425, 432 [5 Cal.Rptr. 361].) Alter ego is an extreme remedy, sparingly used.

citations.case: Sonora Diamond Corp. v. Superior Court
citations.quote: Misconduct or injustice was not proved by Sonora Mining’s apparent inability to meet the balance of its endowment obligation to the District. The alter ego doctrine does not guard every unsatisfied creditor of a corporation but instead affords protectioh where some conduct amounting to bad faith makes it inequitable for the corporate owner to hide behind the corporate form. Difficulty in enforcing a judgment or collecting a debt does not satisfy this standard.

clauses.title: LLCs Are Treated the Same as Corporations
clauses.body: California has codified that the alter ego doctrine applies to limited liability companies to the same extent it applies to corporations: a member of an LLC is subject to liability under the common law governing alter ego liability, and is personally liable for the LLC's debts, obligations, or other liabilities under the same or similar circumstances and to the same extent as a shareholder of a corporation may be personally liable for the corporation's debts, obligations, or liabilities. The statute also creates one specific, narrow carve-out: the failure to hold member or manager meetings, or the failure to observe formalities for calling or conducting such meetings, is not by itself a factor tending to establish alter ego or personal liability for an LLC's member — but only where the articles of organization or operating agreement does not itself expressly require holding such meetings. Apart from that one carve-out, the statute does not otherwise limit or list the factors relevant to alter ego liability for an LLC member; it incorporates the same common-law doctrine, and the same case law, that governs corporate shareholders.
clauses.gap: This is a single California statute (Cal. Corp. Code § 17703.04(a)-(b)), part of the California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, used here as direct statutory evidence that California law extends the common-law alter ego doctrine to LLC members on the same terms as corporate shareholders — not a claim about any other state's law, and not a claim about the alter ego doctrine as applied to any specific California LLC or member. This clause's two citations are subdivisions of the same statutory section (17703.04(a) and (b)), not independently sourced provisions; they are reproduced together because subdivision (a) establishes the baseline liability shield that subdivision (b) then subjects to the common-law alter ego exception. This corpus's Single-Member LLC Operating Agreement document already cites subdivision (a) and (b) together for the liability-shield side of this same statute; this clause cites the identical statutory text for the alter ego side specifically. This document does not determine whether any specific LLC has held member or manager meetings, or whether its governing documents require them.
