citations.quote: All of the following apply to debts, obligations, or other liabilities of a limited liability company, whether arising in contract, tort, or otherwise: (1) They are solely the debts, obligations, or other liabilities of the limited liability company to which the debts, obligations, or other liabilities relate. (2) They do not become the debts, obligations, or other liabilities of a member or manager solely by reason of the member acting as a member or manager acting as a manager for the limited liability company.

clauses.title: An Equitable Doctrine, Not a Dissolution of the Entity
clauses.body: The alter ego doctrine is an equitable doctrine for imposing liability, not a mechanism that dissolves or merges the entity itself. When a court disregards an entity's separate existence for alter ego purposes, it does not hold that the entity and its owner were "really" only ever one and the same for all purposes; rather, the entity continues to exist, and the court instead permits the owner to be held liable, alongside the entity, for a particular debt or judgment because equity requires that result under the circumstances of that case. The doctrine arises when a party claims that another party is using the entity form unjustly and to that party's detriment, and the corporate form will be disregarded only in narrowly defined circumstances, and only when the ends of justice require it — not automatically whenever an entity's owner exercises control over it, and not merely because a creditor has difficulty collecting from the entity itself.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on the California Supreme Court's discussion in Mesler v. Bragg Management Co. (1985) 39 Cal.3d 290, 300-301, describing the alter ego doctrine's equitable character and its effect (a parent corporation held liable as alter ego of a subsidiary remains, and is sued as, a separate entity — "the wall remains" even though "a hole will be drilled" in it for that purpose), and on Sonora Diamond Corp. v. Superior Court (2000) 83 Cal.App.4th 523, 538, which independently states that the corporate form is disregarded only "where an abuse of the corporate privilege justifies" it. These are two different, independently worded California appellate sources describing the same general equitable character of the doctrine, though both ultimately trace the same body of common law. Neither case holds, in so many words, that "alter ego" is not itself an independent cause of action separate from the underlying claim against the entity; this document does not make that specific characterization because it was not independently verified against primary case text within the scope of this research, and it is omitted rather than asserted on the strength of secondary sources alone.

citations.case: Mesler v. Bragg Management Co.
citations.quote: It is not that a corporation will be held liable for the acts of another corporation because there is really only one corporation. Rather, it is that under certain circumstances a hole will be drilled in the wall of limited liability erected by the corporate form; for all purposes other than that for which the hole was drilled, the wall still stands. When it is claimed that a parent corporation should be liable because it is the alter ego of its subsidiary, equity commands that the corporate wall be breached. Yet the wall remains: the parent is liable through the acts of the subsidiary, but as a separate entity.

citations.case: Sonora Diamond Corp. v. Superior Court
citations.cite: 83 Cal.App.4th 523, 538 (Cal. Ct. App. 2000)
citations.quote: A corporate identity may be disregarded—the “corporate veil” pierced—where an abuse of the corporate privilege justifies holding the equitable ownership of a corporation liable for the actions of the corporation. (Roman Catholic Archbishop v. Superior Court (1971) 15 Cal.App.3d 405, 411 [93 Cal.Rptr. 338].) Under the alter ego doctrine, then, when the corporate form is used to perpetrate a fraud, circumvent a statute, or accomplish some other wrongful or inequitable purpose, the courts will ignore the corporate entity and deem the corporation’s acts to be those of the persons or organizations actually controlling the corporation, in most instances the equitable owners.

clauses.title: Declaration and Purpose
clauses.body:
This information sheet concerns a work described as {{workDescription}}, titled {{workTitle}}, created by {{artistName}} (the "work"). {{ownerName}} is identified here as the work's current owner or possessor, for reference only. This sheet summarizes provisions of California Civil Code § 987, the California Art Preservation Act, which addresses the intentional physical defacement, mutilation, alteration, or destruction of certain works of fine art by someone other than the artist who created them, and the artist's related right to claim or disclaim authorship of such a work.

This sheet is an informational record only. It states general provisions of California Civil Code § 987 as written; it does not determine whether {{workDescription}} meets that section's own definition of "fine art," does not determine whether any act taken with respect to {{workDescription}} would or would not violate the section, and does not itself assert, waive, reserve, or enforce any right under § 987 or any other law. It is not legal advice and is not a substitute for reading the statute directly.

clauses.title: Record and Signature
The Core Prohibition and the Statutory Definition of “Fine Art”
clauses.body:
California Civil Code § 987, known as the California Art Preservation Act, restricts who may intentionally alter or destroy certain works of visual art once they exist outside the artist's own hands. Subdivision (c)(1) states: "No person, except an artist who owns and possesses a work of fine art which the artist has created, shall intentionally commit, or authorize the intentional commission of, any physical defacement, mutilation, alteration, or destruction of a work of fine art." A related but separate rule addresses professionals who work on the piece: under subdivision (c)(2), "In addition to the prohibitions contained in paragraph (1), no person who frames, conserves, or restores a work of fine art shall commit, or authorize the commission of, any physical defacement, mutilation, alteration, or destruction of a work of fine art by any act constituting gross negligence. For purposes of this section, the term “gross negligence” shall mean the exercise of so slight a degree of care as to justify the belief that there was an indifference to the particular work of fine art."

Both rules apply only to a work meeting the statute's own, narrow definition of the protected category. Subdivision (b)(2) defines it as follows: "“Fine art” means an original painting, sculpture, or drawing, or an original work of art in glass, of recognized quality, but shall not include work prepared under contract for commercial use by its purchaser." Whether {{workDescription}} falls within that definition — including whether it is of "recognized quality" and was not created under a commercial-use, work-for-hire arrangement — is a determination the statute leaves to be made under its own terms; this sheet does not make that determination.

This is one primary source checked twice for consistency, not two independent sources, and every citation in this document is disclosed on that basis. Section 987 does not, anywhere in its text, mention the federal Visual Artists Rights Act (17 U.S.C. § 106A) or otherwise address how its own protections relate to, overlap with, or are preempted by federal law; this document does not characterize that relationship because the statute itself is silent on it. This clause quotes subdivisions (c)(1), (c)(2), and (b)(2) of the same section; they are treated here as one integrated statutory scheme, not as independently corroborating sources. The statute's definition of "fine art" is narrow: an original painting, sculpture, drawing, or an original work of art in glass, of recognized quality, that was not prepared under contract for commercial use by its purchaser. It does not, on its face, extend to photographs, prints, works in other media, or editioned or reproduced pieces the way some other art-related statutes (including the federal Visual Artists Rights Act's definition of a "work of visual art") separately do; subdivision (f), addressed in this document only in passing, leaves the fact-specific question of "recognized quality" to be decided from the opinions of artists, art dealers, collectors, and museum curators, not by this sheet.

clauses.title: The Artist's Right to Claim or Disclaim Authorship
clauses.body: Separately from its protection against physical alteration or destruction, California Civil Code § 987 also gives the artist a form of attribution right over a work of fine art. Subdivision (d) states: "The artist shall retain at all times the right to claim authorship, or, for a just and valid reason, to disclaim authorship of his or her work of fine art." This right sits within the same statutory section as the alteration and destruction protection described elsewhere in this document, rather than in a separate statute, and it applies to the same category of "fine art" that the section defines.

clauses.title: Remedies the Statute Authorizes, and the Time Limit to Sue
clauses.body:
California Civil Code § 987 identifies specific remedies available to enforce the rights it creates. Subdivision (e) states: "To effectuate the rights created by this section, the artist may commence an action to recover or obtain any of the following:" followed by five enumerated items — "Injunctive relief."; "Actual damages."; "Punitive damages. In the event that punitive damages are awarded, the court shall, in its discretion, select an organization or organizations engaged in charitable or educational activities involving the fine arts in California to receive any punitive damages."; "Reasonable attorneys’ and expert witness fees."; and "Any other relief which the court deems proper."

The statute also sets a deadline for bringing such an action. Subdivision (i) states: "No action may be maintained to enforce any liability under this section unless brought within three years of the act complained of or one year after discovery of the act, whichever is longer."

clauses.title: Fine Art That Is Part of a Building
clauses.body:
California Civil Code § 987 addresses separately the situation where a work of fine art has become part of a building. Where the work cannot be removed without substantial harm to it, subdivision (h)(1) states: "If a work of fine art cannot be removed from a building without substantial physical defacement, mutilation, alteration, or destruction of the work, the rights and duties created under this section, unless expressly reserved by an instrument in writing signed by the owner of the building, containing a legal description of the property and properly recorded, shall be deemed waived. The instrument, if properly recorded, shall be binding on subsequent owners of the building."

Where the work can instead be removed without substantial harm, subdivision (h)(2) ties the section's continued protection to a notice procedure: if a building owner intends to remove such a work and, in the course of or after removal, cause or allow it to suffer physical defacement, mutilation, alteration, or destruction, the section's rights and duties apply "unless the owner has diligently attempted without success to notify the artist, or, if the artist is deceased, his or her heir, beneficiary, devisee, or personal representative, in writing of his or her intended action affecting the work of fine art, or unless he or she did provide notice and that person failed within 90 days either to remove the work or to pay for its removal. If the work is removed at the expense of the artist, his or her heir, beneficiary, devisee, or personal representative, title to the fine art shall pass to that person."

clauses.body: California Civil Code § 987 also fixes how long its protections last and the general rule for giving them up. Subdivision (g)(1) states that the rights and duties the section creates "Shall, with respect to the artist, or if any artist is deceased, his or her heir, beneficiary, devisee, or personal representative, exist until the 50th anniversary of the death of the artist." The referenced exception — subdivision (h)(1) — applies specifically to a work of fine art that has become part of a building and cannot be removed without substantial harm, and is addressed separately in this document.

clauses.title: Information and Background — Willful Misclassification Penalties (Labor Code § 226.8)
clauses.body:
This information sheet describes California's civil penalty scheme for "willful misclassification" of an employee as an independent contractor under Labor Code § 226.8. It is prepared in connection with a working relationship between {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}}.

Labor Code § 226.8 is a separate, narrower statute from the general test for whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor in the first place (addressed in this corpus's own Independent Contractor Agreement document). Section 226.8 does not decide whether {{employeeName}} is or was an employee or an independent contractor of {{companyName}}. It instead describes what additional civil penalties, notice-posting duties, and other consequences California law attaches when a person or employer is separately found — by the Labor and Workforce Development Agency or a court — to have engaged in a specific, elevated form of misclassification that the statute calls "willful."

This information sheet does not itself determine that {{companyName}} did or did not willfully misclassify {{employeeName}}, does not investigate or make any finding about any specific working relationship, does not file anything with any agency or court, and does not initiate or constitute any legal proceeding.

clauses.title: Closing and Signature Block — Willful Misclassification Penalties Information Sheet
clauses.body:
I declare that I have reviewed the information above.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

[This information sheet describes California's statutory civil penalty scheme for willful misclassification of an employee as an independent contractor under Labor Code § 226.8, and the related advisor-liability statute, Labor Code § 2753. It is not a Labor Commissioner complaint form or citation, is not filed with any agency by completing it, does not itself determine that {{companyName}} willfully misclassified {{employeeName}} or that any penalty applies, is not a substitute for the actual statutes, regulations, and Labor Commissioner procedures governing this process, does not constitute legal advice, and is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney.]

clauses.title: The Statute's Definition of "Willful Misclassification" and the Conduct It Prohibits
clauses.body:
California law makes it unlawful for any person or employer to willfully misclassify an individual as an independent contractor. It separately makes it unlawful to charge a fee, or make any deduction from compensation, against an individual who has been willfully misclassified — for example for goods, materials, space rental, services, government licenses, repairs, equipment maintenance, or fines arising from that individual's employment — where the charge or deduction would have violated the law had the individual not been misclassified.

The statute defines "willful misclassification" itself in specific, elevated terms: it means avoiding employee status for an individual by voluntarily and knowingly misclassifying that individual as an independent contractor. By this statutory definition, the penalties described elsewhere in this information sheet attach to a voluntary and knowing act of misclassification, as the statute itself defines that term — not, by this definition alone, to every instance of misclassification.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what conduct it prohibits and how it defines "willful misclassification" — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific working relationship, and not a claim that any specific person or employer did or did not willfully misclassify any specific individual within the meaning of this statute. Both citations below are to the same statutory section, Labor Code § 226.8, subdivisions (a) and (i)(4); that is disclosed here rather than presented as independent corroborating sources. This document does not independently verify, through reported case law, how courts have applied the "voluntarily and knowingly" standard to specific facts, or how it differs in practice from an employer's good-faith but mistaken classification decision; that question was not researched for this document. This document is informational only: it does not determine that any specific individual was willfully misclassified and does not determine the outcome of any specific matter.

citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: (a) It is unlawful for any person or employer to engage in any of the following activities:(1) Willful misclassification of an individual as an independent contractor.(2) Charging an individual who has been willfully misclassified as an independent contractor a fee, or making any deductions from compensation, for any purpose, including for goods, materials, space rental, services, government licenses, repairs, equipment maintenance, or fines arising from the individual’s employment where any of the acts described in this paragraph would have violated the law if the individual had not been misclassified.

clauses.title: Civil Penalty Ranges: Per-Violation and Enhanced Pattern-or-Practice Penalties
clauses.body:
If the Labor and Workforce Development Agency or a court issues a determination that a person or employer has engaged in willful misclassification or the related fee-charging conduct described elsewhere in this statute, California law sets a civil penalty of not less than $5,000 and not more than $15,000 for each violation, in addition to any other penalties or fines otherwise permitted by law.

The statute sets a separate, higher penalty range where the same kind of determination also finds that the person or employer has engaged in, or is engaging in, a pattern or practice of these violations: in that circumstance, the civil penalty is not less than $10,000 and not more than $25,000 for each violation, again in addition to any other penalties or fines otherwise permitted by law.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the two civil penalty ranges it authorizes — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific working relationship, and not a claim about what penalty amount, if any, would apply to any specific violation. Both citations below are to the same statutory section, Labor Code § 226.8, subdivisions (b) and (c); that is disclosed here rather than presented as independent corroborating sources. This document does not address how many separate "violations" a given course of conduct is treated as constituting for penalty-stacking purposes, or what showing establishes a "pattern or practice" as opposed to a single violation; those questions were not researched for this document. This document is informational only: it does not determine that any penalty applies to any specific person or employer and does not calculate any specific penalty amount.

citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: (b) If the Labor and Workforce Development Agency or a court issues a determination that a person or employer has engaged in any of the enumerated violations of subdivision (a), the person or employer shall be subject to a civil penalty of not less than five thousand dollars ($5,000) and not more than fifteen thousand dollars ($15,000) for each violation, in addition to any other penalties or fines permitted by law.

citations.quote: (c) If the Labor and Workforce Development Agency or a court issues a determination that a person or employer has engaged in any of the enumerated violations of subdivision (a) and the person or employer has engaged in or is engaging in a pattern or practice of these violations, the person or employer shall be subject to a civil penalty of not less than ten thousand dollars ($10,000) and not more than twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000) for each violation, in addition to any other penalties or fines permitted by law.

clauses.title: Referral to the Contractors State License Board for a Licensed Contractor
clauses.body:
California law imposes an additional consequence where the person or employer found to have violated this statute is itself a licensed contractor under the Contractors State License Law. In that circumstance, the Labor and Workforce Development Agency or court, in addition to any other remedy already ordered, must transmit a certified copy of the order to the Contractors State License Board.

Once the registrar of the Contractors State License Board receives a certified copy of an agency or court order that resulted in disbarment under this referral requirement, California law requires the registrar to initiate disciplinary action against the licensee within 30 days of receiving it.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the referral and disciplinary-action requirements it imposes when a violator is a licensed contractor — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific working relationship, and not a claim that any specific person or employer is a licensed contractor or that any referral has occurred. Both citations below are to the same statutory section, Labor Code § 226.8, subdivisions (d)(1) and (d)(2); that is disclosed here rather than presented as independent corroborating sources. The statute's own text uses the word "disbarment" to describe the underlying order that triggers the registrar's 30-day disciplinary-action duty, without itself defining that term or cross-referencing the specific Contractors State License Law provision that authorizes disbarment as a licensing sanction; this document quotes that statutory language rather than independently verifying, through the separate Contractors State License Law provisions, the exact licensing consequence "disbarment" refers to there. This document is informational only: it does not determine that any specific contractor's license would be referred or disciplined and does not determine the outcome of any specific matter.

citations.quote: (d) (1) If the Labor and Workforce Development Agency or a court issues a determination that a person or employer that is a licensed contractor pursuant to the Contractors State License Law has violated subdivision (a), the agency, in addition to any other remedy that has been ordered, shall transmit a certified copy of the order to the Contractors State License Board.

clauses.title: The Public Notice-Posting Requirement Upon a Finding of Violation
clauses.body:
When the Labor and Workforce Development Agency or a court issues a determination that a person or employer has violated this statute, California law requires — in addition to any other remedy already ordered — that the person or employer display a notice prominently on its internet website, in an area accessible to all employees and the general public; or, if it has no internet website, display the notice prominently in an area accessible to all employees and the general public at each location where a violation occurred.

The statute specifies what the notice must say: that the Labor and Workforce Development Agency or a court, as applicable, found that the person or employer committed a serious violation of the law by engaging in the willful misclassification of employees; that the person or employer has changed its business practices to avoid further violations; that any employee who believes they are being misclassified as an independent contractor may contact the Labor and Workforce Development Agency, with the agency's mailing address, email address, and telephone number included; and that the notice is being posted pursuant to a state order.

California law adds two further requirements for preparing the notice: an officer must sign it, and it must be posted for one year commencing with the date of the final decision and order.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the notice-posting requirement and its required content — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific working relationship, and not a claim that any specific notice has been or must be posted by any specific person or employer. All three citations below are to the same statutory section, Labor Code § 226.8, subdivisions (e), (e)(1)-(4), and (f); that is disclosed here rather than presented as independent corroborating sources. This document does not address enforcement of the posting requirement itself — for example, what consequence follows if a person or employer fails to post or maintain the required notice for the full one-year period — because the statutory text reviewed for this document does not itself specify a separate penalty for noncompliance with the posting requirement apart from the underlying violation. This document is informational only: it does not determine that any specific notice obligation currently applies to any specific person or employer and does not determine the outcome of any specific matter.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 226.8(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: shall order the person or employer to display prominently on its internet website, in an area which is accessible to all employees and the general public, or, if the person or employer does not have an internet website, to display prominently in an area that is accessible to all employees and the general public at each location where a violation of subdivision (a) occurred, a notice that sets forth all of the following:

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 226.8(e)(1)-(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: (1) That the Labor and Workforce Development Agency or a court, as applicable, has found that the person or employer has committed a serious violation of the law by engaging in the willful misclassification of employees.(2) That the person or employer has changed its business practices in order to avoid committing further violations of this section.(3) That any employee who believes that they are being misclassified as an independent contractor may contact the Labor and Workforce Development Agency. The notice shall include the mailing address, email address, and telephone number of the agency.(4) That the notice is being posted pursuant to a state order.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 226.8(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: (f) In addition to including the information specified in subdivision (e), a person or employer also shall satisfy the following requirements in preparing the notice:(1) An officer shall sign the notice.(2) It shall post the notice for one year commencing with the date of the final decision and order.

clauses.title: Liability for a Paid Advisor Who Knowingly Advises Misclassification — and Its Exemptions (Labor Code § 2753)
clauses.body:
California's willful-misclassification penalty scheme is not the only statute addressing who can be held responsible when a worker is wrongly classified as an independent contractor. A separate statute, Labor Code § 2753, addresses a paid advisor: it provides that a person who, for money or other valuable consideration, knowingly advises an employer to treat an individual as an independent contractor to avoid employee status for that individual is jointly and severally liable with the employer if the individual is later found not to be an independent contractor.

That advisor-liability statute states two exemptions from its own reach. It does not apply to a person who provides advice to their own employer. And it does not apply to an attorney authorized to practice law in California or another United States jurisdiction who provides legal advice in the course of the practice of law.
clauses.gap: Labor Code § 2753 is a distinct statutory section from Labor Code § 226.8, which is the primary basis for the rest of this information sheet; it was fetched and verified separately, and this document draws it in because it is a closely related, distinctively named form of misclassification-related liability, not because it is part of § 226.8 itself. A researcher approaching this topic without checking the statutory text directly might reasonably assume that any "advising liability" provision would appear within § 226.8 — it does not; § 226.8's own text, as fetched and quoted elsewhere in this document, contains no reference to advisors, consultants, or anyone other than "any person or employer" who commits the underlying violation. Both § 2753 citations below are to the same statutory section, subdivisions (a) and (b); that is disclosed here rather than presented as independent corroborating sources. This document does not address case law interpreting "knowingly advises," what counts as "money or other valuable consideration," or how courts have applied the two exemptions to specific facts; that research was not conducted for this document. This document is informational only: it does not determine that any specific person or firm advised any specific employer regarding the classification of any specific individual, and does not determine the outcome of any specific matter.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2753(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: (a) A person who, for money or other valuable consideration, knowingly advises an employer to treat an individual as an independent contractor to avoid employee status for that individual shall be jointly and severally liable with the employer if the individual is found not to be an independent contractor.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2753(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: (b) This section does not apply to the following persons:(1) A person who provides advice to his or her employer.(2) An attorney authorized to practice law in California or another United States jurisdiction who provides legal advice in the course of the practice of law.

clauses.title: Who Enforces This Statute, How a Proceeding Is Initiated, and the Election-of-Remedies Rule
clauses.body:
California law authorizes the Labor Commissioner to enforce this statute and to issue a determination that a person or employer has violated it, following the same procedures set out in Labor Code Sections 98, 98.1, 98.2, 98.3, 98.7, 98.74, or 1197.1 — the general wage-claim and citation procedures administered by the Labor Commissioner's office. Enforcement under this statute may include investigating an alleged violation, ordering appropriate temporary relief to mitigate the violation or maintain the status quo while an investigation or hearing is pending, issuing a citation against a violating employer, and filing a civil action; where a citation issues, the procedures for issuing, contesting, and enforcing it follow the same rules that apply to citations issued under Section 98.74 or 1197.1. A public prosecutor, as the statute defines that term by reference to Labor Code § 181(a), may also separately enforce this statute by seeking the damages described below.

The statute also gives an enforcing party — the Labor Commissioner or a public prosecutor — the alternative of recovering, for each employee, the civil penalties described elsewhere in this statute as damages payable directly to the employee rather than as a civil penalty. But an employee is entitled to either recover those damages under this statute or to enforce a civil penalty under the separate Private Attorneys General Act provision, Labor Code § 2699(a), for the same violation — not both.

A "determination" under this statute, for all of the purposes described above, means an order, decision, award, or citation issued by an agency or a court of competent jurisdiction for which the time to appeal has expired and for which no appeal is pending.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of who may enforce it and how a proceeding under it may be initiated — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific working relationship, and not a claim that any specific enforcement proceeding has been or will be initiated regarding any specific person or employer. All three citations below are to the same statutory section, Labor Code § 226.8, subdivisions (g)(1), (g)(2), and (i)(1); that is disclosed here rather than presented as independent corroborating sources. This document does not independently verify, by fetching Labor Code §§ 98, 98.1, 98.2, 98.3, 98.7, 98.74, 1197.1, 181, or 2699 directly, the full content of those cross-referenced procedures and definitions; it reports only what § 226.8's own text says about them, which is the verified source for this clause. This document is informational only: it does not initiate any enforcement proceeding, does not determine that any specific person or employer has violated this statute, and does not determine the outcome of any specific matter.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 226.8(g)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: (g) (1) In accordance with the procedures set forth in Sections 98, 98.1, 98.2, 98.3, 98.7, 98.74, or 1197.1, the Labor Commissioner may enforce this section and issue a determination that a person or employer has violated subdivision (a). This enforcement of this section may include investigating an alleged violation of subdivision (a), ordering appropriate temporary relief to mitigate the violation or to maintain the status quo pending the completion of an investigation or hearing, issuance of a citation against an employer who violates subdivision (a), and filing a civil action. If a citation is issued, the procedures for issuing, contesting, and enforcing judgments for citations and civil penalties issued by the Labor Commissioner shall be the same as those set out in Section 98.74 or 1197.1, as appropriate. A public prosecutor, as defined in subdivision (a) of Section 181, may also enforce this section by seeking the damages described in paragraph (2).

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 226.8(g)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: (2) In any enforcement pursuant to this subdivision, for each employee subject to Sections 98 to 98.2, inclusive, the Labor Commissioner under Section 98.3, 98.7, 98.74, or 1197.1, or a public prosecutor, as defined in subdivision (a) of Section 181, may alternatively recover the penalties set forth in subdivisions (b) and (c) as damages payable to the employee. An employee is entitled to either recover the damages as provided for in this section or to enforce a civil penalty, as set forth in subdivision (a) of Section 2699, but not both, for the same violation.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 226.8(i)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: “Determination” means an order, decision, award, or citation issued by an agency or a court of competent jurisdiction for which the time to appeal has expired and for which no appeal is pending.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act (ICRAA), California Civil Code §§ 1786 et seq. — a separate California statute from the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) and from California's parallel Consumer Credit Reporting Agencies Act (CCRAA), both addressed elsewhere in this corpus's background-check documents. ICRAA applies specifically to an "investigative consumer report": a report on a person's character, general reputation, personal characteristics, or mode of living, typically compiled through personal interviews, rather than an ordinary credit-based consumer report. This document states facts about what ICRAA requires of {{companyName}} before procuring an investigative consumer report on {{employeeName}}, what ICRAA requires {{companyName}} to certify to the investigative consumer reporting agency, what happens if such a report leads to an adverse decision, and what remedies ICRAA authorizes for a violation. It is not itself the disclosure ICRAA requires, an authorization, a certification to an investigative consumer reporting agency, or an adverse-action notice, and it does not tell {{companyName}} or {{employeeName}} what to do about any particular investigative consumer report.

clauses.title: What ICRAA Covers: The Definition of an Investigative Consumer Report
clauses.body: California's Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act (ICRAA) defines an "investigative consumer report" as a consumer report in which information on a person's character, general reputation, personal characteristics, or mode of living is obtained through any means — a category the statute expressly separates from an ordinary credit-based report limited to specific factual information about a person's credit record or manner of obtaining credit. California's separate Consumer Credit Reporting Agencies Act (CCRAA), which governs that ordinary credit-based "consumer credit report," contains the mirror-image exclusion: a report containing information solely on a person's character, general reputation, personal characteristics, or mode of living, obtained through personal interviews with neighbors, friends, or associates, is expressly carved out of CCRAA's own definition of "consumer credit report." The two statutes are written to be mutually exclusive by category, not by degree — the same background check does not become an ICRAA report just because it happens to be unfavorable, and it does not become a CCRAA report just because it discusses credit.
clauses.gap: This corpus's existing Background Check Disclosure & Authorization and Background Check Adverse Action Notice — Information Sheet documents describe the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act's disclosure, authorization, and adverse-action process (and, for the adverse-action document, California's Fair Chance Act) — neither document addresses ICRAA, or this credit-report/investigative-report distinction, which is a matter of California statute rather than federal law. The two citations below come from two separate Civil Code titles (Title 1.6, the CCRAA, at Civil Code § 1785.3, and Title 1.6A, the ICRAA, at Civil Code § 1786.2) and were each independently fetched, so they corroborate each other as an intentional statutory boundary rather than restating the same source twice. This clause does not address the separate definition ICRAA borrows for insurance-sector investigative consumer reports, which the statute cross-references to Insurance Code § 791.02 rather than defining independently — that cross-reference was not independently verified here.

citations.case: Cal. Civil Code § 1786.2(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act, definition of "investigative consumer report"
citations.quote: The term “investigative consumer report” means a consumer report in which information on a consumer’s character, general reputation, personal characteristics, or mode of living is obtained through any means. The term does not include a consumer report or other compilation of information that is limited to specific factual information relating to a consumer’s credit record or manner of obtaining credit obtained directly from a creditor of the consumer or from a consumer reporting agency when that information was obtained directly from a potential or existing creditor of the consumer or from the consumer.

citations.case: Cal. Civil Code § 1785.3(c)(5) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, Consumer Credit Reporting Agencies Act, exclusion from "consumer credit report"
citations.quote: any report containing information solely on a consumer’s character, general reputation, personal characteristics, or mode of living which is obtained through personal interviews with neighbors, friends, or associates of the consumer reported on, or others with whom the consumer is acquainted or who may have knowledge concerning those items of information

clauses.title: The Employment Disclosure ICRAA Requires Before Procuring the Report
clauses.body: Before {{companyName}} may procure, or cause to be prepared, an investigative consumer report on {{employeeName}} for employment purposes, ICRAA requires a clear and conspicuous disclosure in writing, provided at any time before the report is procured, in a document that consists solely of the disclosure. That disclosure must state that an investigative consumer report may be obtained, identify the permissible purpose for the report, state that the report may include information on {{employeeName}}'s character, general reputation, personal characteristics, and mode of living, and identify the name, address, and telephone number of the investigative consumer reporting agency conducting the investigation, along with the nature and scope of the investigation requested. {{employeeName}} must also authorize the procurement of the report in writing.
clauses.gap: This stand-alone-document requirement reads similarly to the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act's own stand-alone-disclosure rule that this corpus's existing Background Check Disclosure & Authorization document already describes — but it is a separate California statute with its own, longer required content: ICRAA's list adds the permissible-purpose statement, the agency's name, address, and telephone number, and the nature-and-scope-of-investigation notice, none of which the FCRA's own stand-alone-disclosure provision requires by its own text. This particular set of requirements — Civil Code § 1786.16(a)(2) — applies only to an investigative consumer report sought for employment purposes other than suspicion of wrongdoing or misconduct by the applicant or employee; a separate paragraph of the same section, not quoted here, sets different disclosure timing for reports sought in connection with insurance underwriting or the hiring of a dwelling unit, and subdivision (c) of the same section states that subdivisions (a) and (b) of § 1786.16 — including this disclosure requirement — do not apply at all where the employer procures the report because of suspicion of wrongdoing or misconduct by the applicant or employee. This document also did not independently verify a separate clause of § 1786.16(a)(2)(B), operative since January 1, 2012, that adds a website/privacy-practices notice requirement to this same disclosure — that additional element is quoted and covered in this document's certification clause context rather than restated here. Both citations below come from the same Civil Code section, § 1786.16, so they are one statutory source, not two independent ones — disclosed here rather than presented as separate corroboration.

citations.case: Cal. Civil Code § 1786.16(a)(2)(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act, employment disclosure content
citations.quote: (B) The person procuring or causing the report to be made provides a clear and conspicuous disclosure in writing to the consumer at any time before the report is procured or caused to be made in a document that consists solely of the disclosure, that: (i) An investigative consumer report may be obtained. (ii) The permissible purpose of the report is identified. (iii) The disclosure may include information on the consumer’s character, general reputation, personal characteristics, and mode of living. (iv) Identifies the name, address, and telephone number of the investigative consumer reporting agency conducting the investigation. (v) Notifies the consumer in writing of the nature and scope of the investigation requested, including a summary of the provisions of Section 1786.22.

citations.case: Cal. Civil Code § 1786.16(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act, suspicion-of-wrongdoing carve-out
citations.quote: Subdivisions (a) and (b) do not apply to an investigative consumer report procured or caused to be prepared by an employer, if the report is sought for employment purposes due to suspicion held by an employer of wrongdoing or misconduct by the subject of the investigation.

clauses.title: The Certification ICRAA Requires to the Investigative Consumer Reporting Agency
clauses.body: Separately from the disclosure it must give {{employeeName}}, ICRAA requires {{companyName}} to certify to the investigative consumer reporting agency that it has made the disclosures the statute requires and that it will comply with the statute's copy-of-report and adverse-action provisions described below. An investigative consumer reporting agency may not prepare or furnish an investigative consumer report to {{companyName}} at all unless it has first received that certification.
clauses.gap: This certification runs from the employer to the investigative consumer reporting agency — a separate document, addressed to a different recipient, from the disclosure the employer gives the applicant or employee described in the clause above. ICRAA's statutory text does not specify a particular form the certification must take (written, electronic, or otherwise), only what it must state. This document did not independently verify the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act's own, separate certification requirement running from an employer to a consumer reporting agency (15 U.S.C. § 1681b(b)(1)) — that federal provision is not currently covered anywhere in this corpus and is not restated or assumed here.

citations.case: Cal. Civil Code § 1786.16(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act, employer certification requirement
citations.quote: The person procuring or causing the request to be made shall certify to the investigative consumer reporting agency that the person has made the applicable disclosures to the consumer required by this subdivision and that the person will comply with subdivision (b).

citations.case: Cal. Civil Code § 1786.12(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act, certification as precondition to furnishing a report
citations.quote: An investigative consumer reporting agency shall not prepare or furnish an investigative consumer report to a person described in subdivision (d) unless the agency has received the certification under paragraph (4) of subdivision (a) of Section 1786.16 from the person requesting the report.

clauses.title: The Right to a Copy of the Report, and ICRAA's Own Adverse-Action Notice
clauses.body: ICRAA requires {{companyName}} to give {{employeeName}} a way to check a box on a written form indicating that {{employeeName}} wants a copy of the investigative consumer report once it is prepared; if {{employeeName}} checks that box, a copy must be sent within three business days of the date the report is provided. Separately, if an investigative consumer report obtained from an investigative consumer reporting agency leads {{companyName}} to deny employment or take another adverse action, ICRAA requires {{companyName}} to advise {{employeeName}} of that fact and supply the name and address of the investigative consumer reporting agency that made the report.
clauses.gap: This is a California-statute notice obligation distinct from the two-step federal Fair Credit Reporting Act pre-adverse-action and final adverse-action process this corpus's existing Background Check Adverse Action Notice — Information Sheet document already describes; both can apply to the same background check, the way this document's own definitional clause above describes the overlapping character of ICRAA and the corpus's federal-law documents. This ICRAA adverse-action provision, Civil Code § 1786.40(a), requires less content than the FCRA's own final adverse-action notice — by its own text it does not require providing a copy of the report or a description of consumer rights; that separate content comes from the box-to-check copy right described above, and from the federal notice already covered elsewhere in this corpus, not from this specific California provision. This document did not verify Civil Code § 1786.40(b), which addresses insurance-related adverse action based on information obtained from a source other than an investigative consumer reporting agency, since that provision does not apply to an employment background check. Both citations below trace back to Civil Code § 1786.16 and § 1786.40 respectively — two separate sections of the same title, independently fetched.

citations.case: Cal. Civil Code § 1786.16(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act, right to a copy of the report
citations.quote: Provide the consumer a means by which the consumer may indicate on a written form, by means of a box to check, that the consumer wishes to receive a copy of any report that is prepared. If the consumer wishes to receive a copy of the report, the recipient of the report shall send a copy of the report to the consumer within three business days of the date that the report is provided to the recipient, who may contract with any other entity to send a copy to the consumer.

citations.case: Cal. Civil Code § 1786.40(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act, adverse-action notice
citations.quote: Whenever insurance for personal, family, or household purposes, employment, or the hiring of a dwelling unit involving a consumer is denied, or the charge for that insurance or the hiring of a dwelling unit is increased, under circumstances in which a report regarding the consumer was obtained from an investigative consumer reporting agency, the user of the investigative consumer report shall so advise the consumer against whom the adverse action has been taken and supply the name and address of the investigative consumer reporting agency making the report.

clauses.title: Remedies ICRAA Authorizes for a Violation
clauses.body: ICRAA makes an investigative consumer reporting agency or a user of an investigative consumer report — such as an employer — liable to the consumer who is the report's subject for any actual damages the consumer sustained, or, except in a class action, ten thousand dollars, whichever amount is greater, plus the costs and reasonable attorney's fees of a successful action to enforce that liability. If a court finds the violation grossly negligent or willful, the court may also award punitive damages. ICRAA also states that this liability does not attach where the noncompliance actually resulted in a more favorable investigative consumer report than the consumer would otherwise have received. A separate provision sets a two-year period from the date of discovery to bring an action to enforce liability under the statute, and bars pursuing the same act or omission under both this California statute and the parallel federal Fair Credit Reporting Act liability provisions once a final judgment has been entered in the other.
clauses.gap: ICRAA's statutory-damages figure — a flat ten thousand dollars where actual damages are lower or hard to prove, outside the class-action context — is not a figure this document assumed by analogy to the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act's own damages provisions; it was verified against the current statutory text quoted below, and a reader should not assume California's figure matches, or was modeled on, any particular federal dollar amount without checking each statute independently. The statutory text as fetched contains no inflation-adjustment or CPI-indexing mechanism for the ten-thousand-dollar figure — it is stated as a fixed dollar amount as of the section's last amendment (Stats. 2003, Ch. 146). This clause states the remedy structure ICRAA itself provides; it does not calculate, estimate, or apply that structure to any actual dispute. The two citations below are two separate Civil Code sections, § 1786.50 and § 1786.52, both within Article 4 ("Remedies") of the same title — independently fetched, but disclosed here as sections of one statutory article rather than as fully unrelated sources.

citations.case: Cal. Civil Code § 1786.50(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act, civil liability for noncompliance
citations.quote: An investigative consumer reporting agency or user of information that fails to comply with any requirement under this title with respect to an investigative consumer report is liable to the consumer who is the subject of the report in an amount equal to the sum of all the following: (1) Any actual damages sustained by the consumer as a result of the failure or, except in the case of class actions, ten thousand dollars ($10,000), whichever sum is greater. (2) In the case of any successful action to enforce any liability under this chapter, the costs of the action together with reasonable attorney’s fees as determined by the court.

citations.case: Cal. Civil Code § 1786.50(b)-(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act, punitive damages and safe harbor
citations.quote: (b) If the court determines that the violation was grossly negligent or willful, the court may, in addition, assess, and the consumer may recover, punitive damages. (c) Notwithstanding subdivision (a), an investigative consumer reporting agency or user of information that fails to comply with any requirement under this title with respect to an investigative consumer report shall not be liable to a consumer who is the subject of the report where the failure to comply results in a more favorable investigative consumer report than if there had not been a failure to comply.

citations.case: Cal. Civil Code § 1786.52 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act, limitations period and bar on double recovery with the FCRA
citations.quote: An action to enforce any liability created under this title may be brought in any appropriate court of competent jurisdiction within two years from the date of discovery. (a) Any investigative consumer reporting agency or user of information against whom an action brought pursuant to Section 1681n or 1681o of Title 15 of the United States Code is pending shall not be subject to suit for the same act or omission under Section 1786.50. (b) The entry of a final judgment against the investigative consumer reporting agency or user of information in an action brought pursuant to the provisions of Section 1681n or 1681o of Title 15 of the United States Code shall be a bar to the maintenance of any action based on the same act or omission which might be brought under this title.

clauses.title: About This IIPP Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This Injury and Illness Prevention Program (IIPP) — Information Sheet describes California's statutory requirement that every employer establish, implement, and maintain a written injury prevention program, set out in Labor Code § 6401.7, and the implementing Cal/OSHA regulation that specifies the program's required written elements, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203, as those requirements relate to the working relationship between {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}}.

It summarizes selected requirements of that statute and regulation: the statute's own list of required program elements, who must be identified as having authority and responsibility for the program, what triggers a hazard evaluation and how identified hazards must be corrected, when employee training is required, what records must be kept and how an employee may access the written program, and how the program is enforced, including the statute's own safe harbor for an employer that adopts Cal/OSHA's model program.

{{companyName}} has identified {{programAdministratorName}} as the person with authority and responsibility for implementing its Program.

This information sheet is not itself {{companyName}}'s written Injury and Illness Prevention Program, does not itself satisfy Labor Code § 6401.7's or 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203's written-program requirement, and does not determine that any particular practice of {{companyName}}'s is or is not compliant with California law.

clauses.title: The Statutory Duty to Establish a Written Program
clauses.body: California Labor Code § 6401.7(a) itself states that every employer shall establish, implement, and maintain an effective injury prevention program, that the program shall be written (except for a narrower class of employers addressed in subdivision (e)), and that the written program shall include, but is not limited to, a list of elements the statute itself enumerates: identification of the person or persons responsible for implementing the program; a system for identifying and evaluating workplace hazards, including scheduled periodic inspections; methods and procedures for correcting unsafe or unhealthy conditions in a timely manner; an occupational health and safety training program; a system for communicating with employees on safety matters without fear of reprisal; a system for ensuring employee compliance with safe work practices; and, as of a 2024 amendment, a workplace violence prevention plan conforming to the separate requirements of Labor Code § 6401.9. Subdivision (e)(1) then directs the Occupational Safety and Health Standards Board to adopt a regulation setting forth the employer's duties under the section, consistent with the requirements the statute specifies in subdivisions (a) through (d). That regulation is 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203, addressed in the companion clauses of this information sheet.
clauses.gap: The statute itself is not a bare delegation to Cal/OSHA — it enumerates the program's required elements in subdivision (a) and separately directs the standards board to adopt an implementing regulation 'consistent with' subdivisions (a) through (d), rather than leaving the entire content of the program to the regulation to invent. Both quotations in this clause are drawn from the same enacted statute, Labor Code § 6401.7 — different subdivisions of one section, not independent sources from one another. This clause does not independently verify Labor Code § 6401.9 (the workplace violence prevention plan requirement subdivision (a)(7) now cross-references) or the small-employer and low-hazard-industry modifications in subdivision (e); those are named here only as topics the statute itself flags, not as verified content, and are omitted from the citations below rather than summarized as fact. This is a description of what one state's statute requires, not a claim about what any particular employer has or has not done.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 6401.7 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 6401.7, subd. (a)
citations.quote: Every employer shall establish, implement, and maintain an effective injury prevention program. The program shall be written, except as provided in subdivision (e), and shall include, but not be limited to, the following elements:

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 6401.7 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 6401.7, subd. (e)(1)
citations.quote: The standards board shall adopt a standard setting forth the employer’s duties under this section, on or before January 1, 1991, consistent with the requirements specified in subdivisions (a), (b), (c), and (d).

clauses.title: Identifying Who Has Authority and Responsibility for the Program
clauses.body: Both the statute and its implementing regulation require a written Injury and Illness Prevention Program to identify who is responsible for it, though they phrase the requirement slightly differently. Labor Code § 6401.7(a)(1) requires 'identification of the person or persons responsible for implementing the program.' The implementing regulation, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203(a)(1), requires the written program to 'identify the person or persons with authority and responsibility for implementing the Program' — adding 'authority' to the statute's 'responsibility.' Neither source requires that this person hold any particular job title, such as 'safety officer' or 'safety coordinator'; both allow more than one person to be identified. {{companyName}} has identified {{programAdministratorName}} as the person with authority and responsibility for implementing its Program.
clauses.gap: The regulation's phrase — 'authority and responsibility' — is not a verbatim restatement of the statute's phrase — 'responsible for implementing.' This clause draws on two formally distinct primary sources: Labor Code § 6401.7, enacted by the Legislature, and 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203, adopted by the Occupational Safety and Health Standards Board under authority the statute itself confers in subdivision (e)(1); they are independent legal instruments even though the regulation implements the statute. Neither source was found to require a specific job title, credential, or minimum authority level for the person identified, beyond the words quoted here.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 6401.7 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 6401.7, subd. (a)(1)
citations.quote: Identification of the person or persons responsible for implementing the program.

citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3203, subd. (a)(1)

clauses.title: When Hazard Evaluation Is Required and How Hazards Must Be Corrected
clauses.body: The implementing regulation requires the written program to include procedures for identifying and evaluating workplace hazards, including scheduled periodic inspections to identify unsafe conditions and work practices, and it specifies three triggering events for such an inspection or evaluation: when the program is first established; whenever new substances, processes, procedures, or equipment are introduced to the workplace that represent a new occupational safety and health hazard; and whenever the employer is made aware of a new or previously unrecognized hazard. The regulation's own text requires that these be 'scheduled periodic inspections,' without stating a specific numeric interval (such as monthly, quarterly, or annually) at which they must recur. Once a hazard is identified, the regulation separately requires methods or procedures for correcting unsafe or unhealthy conditions, work practices, and work procedures in a timely manner based on the severity of the hazard, and, for an imminent hazard that cannot be immediately abated without endangering employees or property, it requires removing all exposed personnel from the area except those necessary to correct the condition, who must be provided the necessary safeguards. The statute itself states the same timely-correction duty at the statutory level, separately from the regulation's more detailed treatment.
clauses.gap: This corrects an assumption that the regulation fixes a specific inspection frequency, such as an annual or quarterly schedule — the regulatory text located and quoted here does not state one; it requires only that inspections be 'scheduled periodic inspections' tied to the three triggering events quoted above, leaving the specific interval for the employer's own program to set. The three subsections of this clause drawn from the hazard-identification and hazard-correction requirements — subdivisions (a)(4) and (a)(6) — are both part of the same regulation, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203, and are not independent of each other; the statutory quotation is drawn from a separate, independent source, Labor Code § 6401.7, though it states only the general correction duty and not the regulation's inspection triggers or its imminent-hazard removal procedure. This is a statement of what the regulation and statute require in general, not a claim about whether any specific inspection or correction has occurred.

clauses.title: When Employee Training Is Required
clauses.body: Labor Code § 6401.7(c) itself requires the employer to train all employees when the training program is first established, all new employees, and all employees given a new job assignment, and to train employees whenever new substances, processes, procedures, or equipment are introduced to the workplace and represent a new hazard, or whenever the employer receives notification of a new or previously unrecognized hazard. The implementing regulation, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203(a)(7), requires the written program to 'provide training and instruction' and lists the same triggering events in more granular form — first establishment of the program, new employees, employees given a new job assignment for which training has not previously been received, new substances/processes/procedures/equipment representing a new hazard, and a newly recognized hazard — and it adds one requirement the statutory text quoted here does not separately spell out: training for supervisors specifically, so that supervisors familiarize themselves with the safety and health hazards to which the employees under their immediate direction and control may be exposed.
clauses.gap: The regulation's supervisor-specific training item, subdivision (a)(7)(F), is not a restatement of anything found in the statutory text of § 6401.7(c) quoted here — the statute's own text speaks only of training 'employees' and does not use the word 'supervisor.' This clause draws on two independent primary sources — the enacted statute and the standards board's implementing regulation — rather than restating one source's language as though it appeared in both.

clauses.title: Recordkeeping and Employee Access to the Program
clauses.body: Labor Code § 6401.7(d) itself requires the employer to keep appropriate records of the steps taken to implement and maintain the program. The implementing regulation, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203(b), specifies two categories those records must include: records of the scheduled and periodic inspections required by subdivision (a)(4), including who conducted the inspection, the unsafe conditions and work practices identified, and the action taken to correct them, which must be maintained for at least one year; and documentation of the safety and health training required by subdivision (a)(7) for each employee, including the employee's name or other identifier, training dates, the type of training, and the training providers, also maintained for at least one year. Separately, subdivision (a)(8) of the regulation requires the employer to allow an employee access to the Program, and subdivision (a)(8)(B)(1) requires that access be provided in a reasonable time, place, and manner, but in no event later than five business days after the employer receives a request for access from an employee or a designated representative.
clauses.gap: The one-year retention period and the five-business-day access deadline are both regulatory requirements found in 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203, not language found in the statutory text of Labor Code § 6401.7(d) quoted here, which states only a general duty to keep 'appropriate records' without specifying a retention period. The three regulatory subsections cited in this clause — (b)(1), (b)(2), and (a)(8)(B)(1) — are all part of the same regulation, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203, and are not independent of one another or of the other clauses of this information sheet that also cite that regulation; the statutory quotation is drawn from the separate, independent source, Labor Code § 6401.7. This document did not independently verify the regulation's further exceptions for employers with fewer than 10 or fewer than 20 employees, which shorten or modify some of these recordkeeping obligations; those exceptions are not summarized here and no citation is offered for their specific terms.

clauses.title: Enforcement and the Model Program Safe Harbor
clauses.body: Neither the text of Labor Code § 6401.7 nor the text of 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203 quoted in this information sheet states a specific civil penalty amount for a violation. Section 6401.7(j)(1) does, however, confirm that a violation of the section is enforced through a 'citation' process and can carry a 'civil penalty': it directs the Division of Occupational Safety and Health to prepare a Model Injury and Illness Prevention Program for Non-High-Hazard Employment and make it available to employers on request, and it provides that an employer who adopts and implements that model program in good faith shall not be assessed a civil penalty for the first citation for a violation of the section issued after the employer's adoption and implementation of the model program.
clauses.gap: This clause corrects an assumption that § 6401.7 itself states a penalty schedule or dollar figure for a violation — the statutory text located and quoted here does not; it establishes only a first-citation safe harbor tied to good-faith adoption of the Division's model program, and its wording ('citation,' 'civil penalty') presupposes that the general Cal/OSHA citation and civil-penalty framework — found elsewhere in the Labor Code and in Cal/OSHA's own citation regulations, not in § 6401.7 or § 3203 themselves — is what actually sets citation classifications and penalty amounts for a violation of this section. This document did not independently fetch or verify that separate citation-and-penalty framework, so no citation or quotation is offered for it here, and it should not be inferred from anything quoted in this information sheet. This clause's quotation is drawn from the same statute, Labor Code § 6401.7, cited in the other clauses of this information sheet, not from an independent second source.

An employer who adopts and implements the model program prepared by the division pursuant to this paragraph in good faith shall not be assessed a civil penalty for the first citation for a violation of this section issued after the employer’s adoption and implementation of the model program.

clauses.title: HOA Board Election Procedures — Introduction and Scope
clauses.body: This information sheet describes, in general terms, the secret-ballot election procedures that apply to a California common interest development association under the Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act, Civil Code §§ 5100–5145, in connection with {{hoaName}}. It covers when those procedures apply, the requirement that the association adopt its own election operating rules, the requirement that an independent third party conduct the election, and the statutory notice-timing and double-envelope ballot mechanics. This topic is distinct from a seller's document-disclosure obligations to a buyer under the Davis-Stirling Act's disclosure article (addressed in this corpus's HOA/CC&R Disclosure document), from an association's lien and foreclosure remedy for unpaid assessments (addressed in this corpus's HOA Assessment Lien and Foreclosure — Information Sheet), and from the recording mechanics that create a common interest development in the first place (addressed in this corpus's Common Interest Development Formation — Information Sheet). This sheet is informational only. It does not itself call, notice, conduct, or certify any election; it does not select, appoint, or evaluate any inspector of elections; it does not adopt, amend, or interpret any specific association's election operating rules or governing documents; and it does not determine whether any actual election, notice, ballot procedure, or vote count relating to {{hoaName}} has complied — or failed to comply — with the statutory requirements it describes.

clauses.title: When the Secret-Ballot Election Procedures Apply
clauses.body: California law does not require every association vote to be conducted by secret ballot — it specifies particular categories of votes to which the secret-ballot procedures apply. Civil Code § 5100(a)(1) provides: "Notwithstanding any other law or provision of the governing documents, elections regarding assessments legally requiring a vote, election and removal of directors, amendments to the governing documents, or the grant of exclusive use of common area pursuant to Section 4600 shall be held by secret ballot in accordance with the procedures set forth in this article." Section 5100(a)(2) adds a timing requirement specific to director elections: "An association shall hold an election for a seat on the board of directors in accordance with the procedures set forth in this article at the expiration of the corresponding director's term and at least once every four years." Section 5100(b) extends the article to "any topic that is expressly identified in the operating rules as being governed by this article," and Section 5100(c) makes the article apply "to both incorporated and unincorporated associations, notwithstanding any contrary provision of the governing documents." Section 5100(d) limits the article to "votes cast directly by the membership," not votes cast by delegates or other elected representatives, and Section 5100(e) provides that this article prevails over any conflicting election provision of the Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law. Section 5100(f) provides an exception where a director seat is not filled by election: directors "shall not be required to be elected pursuant to this article if the governing documents provide that one member from each separate interest is a director." This scope provision concerns {{hoaName}} in general terms; it does not determine whether any specific vote by {{hoaName}}'s membership falls within one of these categories.
clauses.gap: All quoted material in this clause comes from subsections (a) through (f) of a single statutory section, Civil Code § 5100; it is one source, not independent corroborating sources, even though it is presented as several numbered points. As verified against the current statutory text, § 5100(a)(1) itself requires secret-ballot procedures for "election and removal of directors" without qualifying that requirement by whether the election is contested or by how many candidates are nominated — a narrower assumption (that the secret-ballot requirement is limited to contested director elections, or triggers only once nominations exceed open seats) is not supported by the text of § 5100 as fetched. California law does contain a related but separate and narrower mechanism, at Civil Code § 5103, allowing (not requiring) an association to seat qualified candidates "by acclamation" without a secret ballot when nominations do not exceed the number of open seats and several additional conditions are met; that section was fetched only once during this research (not independently double-verified under this document's verification protocol) and its contents are accordingly not described or quoted here, so as not to state anything about it that has not been confirmed. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's HOA board-election framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific association; other states impose different or no comparable secret-ballot requirements.
