clauses.title: About This Workplace Violence Prevention Plan Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This Workplace Violence Prevention Plan — Information Sheet describes California's requirement that most employers establish, implement, and maintain a written workplace violence prevention plan, set out in Labor Code § 6401.9 (added by SB 553 and operative, for most of its requirements, on and after July 1, 2024), as that requirement relates to the working relationship between {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}}.

It summarizes selected requirements of that statute: which employers, employees, and places of employment the requirement covers and one example of a statutory exemption; the duty to have a written plan and how the plan may be maintained; selected elements the plan itself must contain, including identifying who is responsible for it, procedures for accepting and responding to reports of workplace violence without retaliation, and procedures for identifying, evaluating, and correcting workplace violence hazards; the training the statute requires; the violent incident log requirement; and recordkeeping, including employee access to certain records.

This corpus's separate Injury and Illness Prevention Program (IIPP) — Information Sheet describes a related but distinct statute, Labor Code § 6401.7, and its implementing regulation, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203; that document's own "gap" disclosures note that it named § 6401.9 only as a topic § 6401.7 cross-references, without independently fetching or verifying § 6401.9's own text. This information sheet is the independent verification of § 6401.9 itself that the IIPP document deliberately deferred; it does not restate the IIPP document's content, and it does not independently verify 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203 beyond quoting the handful of places where § 6401.9's own text cross-references that regulation by section and subdivision number.

{{companyName}} has identified {{programAdministratorName}} as a person responsible for implementing its plan.

This information sheet is not itself {{companyName}}'s written workplace violence prevention plan, does not itself satisfy Labor Code § 6401.9's written-plan requirement, and does not determine that any particular practice of {{companyName}}'s is or is not compliant with California law.

clauses.title: Which Employers and Workplaces the Requirement Covers
clauses.body: Labor Code § 6401.9(b)(1) itself states the requirement's general reach: 'Except as provided in paragraph (2), this section applies to all employers, employees, places of employment, and employer-provided housing.' Paragraph (2) of subdivision (b) then lists categories of employers, employees, and places of employment that are exempt from the section, subject to the division's authority in paragraph (3) to order an otherwise-exempt employer to comply anyway. One example of a listed exemption, subdivision (b)(2)(E), exempts 'Employees teleworking from a location of the employee's choice, which is not under the control of the employer.' The statute lists five other exempt categories in subdivision (b)(2) — health care facilities and employers already covered by a separate Title 8 regulation on workplace violence in health care (Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3342), certain Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation facilities, certain law-enforcement agencies meeting POST compliance requirements, and small worksites with fewer than 10 employees that are not accessible to the public and that comply with 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203 — none of which are quoted or summarized further in this clause.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the general applicability rule in subdivision (b)(1) and one of the six exemption categories listed in subdivision (b)(2), the teleworking exemption in subparagraph (E); it does not quote or fully summarize the other five exemption categories (health care facilities and employers subject to 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3342, Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation facilities, qualifying law enforcement agencies, and small non-public worksites under 10 employees), each of which carries its own conditions in the statutory text. Both quotations in this clause are drawn from the same enacted statute, Labor Code § 6401.9 — subdivisions (b)(1) and (b)(2)(E) of one section — not independent sources from one another; this document's only independent source is § 6401.9 itself, fetched twice from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov using two distinct request methods and confirmed byte-identical (after whitespace normalization) before any of its text was treated as verified. This clause does not independently verify the separate regulation it names in passing, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3342 (the health-care-specific workplace violence prevention standard) or § 3203, beyond quoting § 6401.9's own cross-reference to their section numbers; no claim is made here about either regulation's content. This is a description of what one state's statute requires in general, not a determination that any particular employer, employee, or place of employment does or does not fall within an exemption.

clauses.title: The Duty to Have a Written Plan and How It May Be Maintained
clauses.body: Labor Code § 6401.9(c)(1)(A) states the core duty in a single sentence: 'An employer shall establish, implement, and maintain an effective workplace violence prevention plan.' Subdivision (c)(1)(B) then adds three requirements about the plan's form and availability: it 'shall be in writing and shall be available and easily accessible to employees, authorized employee representatives, and representatives of the division at all times'; it 'shall be in effect at all times and in all work areas and be specific to the hazards and corrective measures for each work area and operation'; and — addressing how it relates to the separate Injury and Illness Prevention Program (IIPP) requirement of Labor Code § 6401.7 and 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203 — 'The written plan may be incorporated as a stand-alone section in the written injury and illness prevention program required by Section 3203 of Title 8 of the California Code of Regulations or maintained as a separate document.'
clauses.gap: This clause corrects an assumption that a workplace violence prevention plan must always be a document separate from an employer's IIPP — the statutory text quoted here expressly allows the plan to be incorporated as a stand-alone section of the written IIPP instead. Both quotations are drawn from the same enacted statute, Labor Code § 6401.9 — subparagraphs (A) and (B) of a single paragraph, (c)(1) — not independent sources from one another; this document's only independent source is § 6401.9 itself, fetched twice from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov using two distinct request methods and confirmed byte-identical (after whitespace normalization) before any of its text was treated as verified. This clause does not independently verify the separate IIPP statute or regulation it names, Labor Code § 6401.7 or 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203; those are addressed, on their own terms, in this corpus's separate Injury and Illness Prevention Program (IIPP) — Information Sheet, and no claim about their content beyond the bare cross-reference is made here.

clauses.title: Selected Elements the Plan Itself Must Contain
clauses.body: Labor Code § 6401.9(c)(2) states that '[t]he plan shall include all of the following:' and then enumerates thirteen lettered elements, subparagraphs (A) through (M). This clause quotes a selection of those elements rather than all thirteen. Subparagraph (A) requires 'Names or job titles of the persons responsible for implementing the plan. If there are multiple persons responsible for the plan, their roles shall be clearly described.' Subparagraph (D) requires 'Effective procedures for the employer to accept and respond to reports of workplace violence, and to prohibit retaliation against an employee who makes such a report.' Subparagraph (I) requires 'Procedures to identify and evaluate workplace violence hazards, including, but not limited to, scheduled periodic inspections to identify unsafe conditions and work practices and employee reports and concerns. Inspections shall be conducted when the plan is first established, after each workplace violence incident, and whenever the employer is made aware of a new or previously unrecognized hazard.' Subparagraph (J) requires 'Procedures to correct workplace violence hazards identified and evaluated in subparagraph (I) in a timely manner consistent with paragraph (6) of subdivision (a) of Section 3203 of Title 8 of the California Code of Regulations.'
clauses.gap: This clause quotes 4 of the 13 lettered elements the statute requires the plan to contain — subparagraphs (A), (D), (I), and (J). It does not quote or summarize the other 9 (employee-involvement procedures, multi-employer coordination, supervisory-compliance procedures, communication procedures, emergency-response procedures, training-development procedures, postincident-response and investigation procedures, plan-review procedures, and a catch-all for standards the division and standards board may later require); those are named in this document's introductory clause only as topics the statute covers, not summarized or quoted here, so as not to state anything about their specific content that has not been verified. All four quotations are drawn from the same enacted statute, Labor Code § 6401.9 — subparagraphs of a single paragraph, (c)(2) — not independent sources from one another; this document's only independent source is § 6401.9 itself, fetched twice from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov using two distinct request methods and confirmed byte-identical (after whitespace normalization) before any of its text was treated as verified. Subparagraph (J)'s cross-reference to 'paragraph (6) of subdivision (a) of Section 3203 of Title 8 of the California Code of Regulations' is quoted here only as § 6401.9's own text; this document does not independently verify what that regulatory paragraph itself says, and no claim is made about its content. This is a description of what the statute requires a plan to contain in general, not a claim about the content of any particular employer's actual plan.

clauses.title: When Employee Training Is Required
clauses.body: Labor Code § 6401.9(e)(1) states the general training duty: 'The employer shall provide effective training to employees, as specified in paragraphs (2) and (3).' Subdivision (e)(2) then fixes the timing of the main round of training: 'The employer shall provide employees with initial training when the plan is first established, and annually thereafter, on all of the following:' — followed by six lettered topics the statute requires that training to cover, including the employer's plan itself, the definitions and requirements of the section, how to report incidents without fear of reprisal, and the job-specific hazards and corrective measures relevant to the employees being trained. Subdivision (e)(3) then adds a second, event-triggered training duty distinct from the annual cycle: 'Additional training shall be provided when a new or previously unrecognized workplace violence hazard has been identified and when changes are made to the plan. The additional training may be limited to addressing the new workplace violence hazard or changes to the plan.'
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the introductory sentence of subdivision (e)(2) but does not quote or fully summarize all six lettered topics that paragraph requires the annual training to cover; only a general description of some of those topics is given in the body text above, not a verified quotation of each one. All three quotations in this clause are drawn from the same enacted statute, Labor Code § 6401.9 — paragraphs (1), (2), and (3) of a single subdivision, (e) — not independent sources from one another; this document's only independent source is § 6401.9 itself, fetched twice from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov using two distinct request methods and confirmed byte-identical (after whitespace normalization) before any of its text was treated as verified. This is a description of what the statute requires in general, not a claim about the content or timing of any training a particular employer has or has not provided to a particular employee.

clauses.title: The Violent Incident Log Requirement
clauses.body: Labor Code § 6401.9(d)(1)(A) states a duty distinct from the plan itself: 'The employer shall record information in a violent incident log for every workplace violence incident.' The statute separately protects the privacy of the people involved: subdivision (d)(1)(B) requires that 'The employer shall omit any element of personal identifying information sufficient to allow identification of any person involved in a violent incident, such as the person's name, address, electronic mail address, telephone number, social security number, or other information that, alone or in combination with other publicly available information, reveals the person's identity.' Subdivision (d)(2) then lists categories of information the log must include for each incident — such as the date, time, and location of the incident, the type of workplace violence involved, a description of the incident, and a classification of who committed it and the circumstances — which are not separately quoted in this clause.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the log's basic recording duty and its anonymization requirement, subparagraphs (A) and (B) of paragraph (1) of subdivision (d), but does not quote or fully summarize the itemized list of information categories in paragraph (2) of subdivision (d), nor the multiemployer-worksite provision in subparagraph (C) of paragraph (1). Both quotations are drawn from the same enacted statute, Labor Code § 6401.9 — subparagraphs of a single paragraph, (d)(1) — not independent sources from one another; this document's only independent source is § 6401.9 itself, fetched twice from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov using two distinct request methods and confirmed byte-identical (after whitespace normalization) before any of its text was treated as verified. This is a description of what the statute requires the log to contain and how identifying details must be handled in general, not a record of any actual incident involving any particular employer or employee.

clauses.title: Record Retention Periods and Employee Access
clauses.body: Labor Code § 6401.9(f) sets specific minimum retention periods for several categories of records, longer than the one-year periods this corpus's IIPP information sheet describes for the general IIPP's inspection and training records under 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203(b). Subdivision (f)(1) provides that 'Records of workplace violence hazard identification, evaluation, and correction shall be created and maintained for a minimum of five years.' Subdivision (f)(3) separately provides that 'Violent incident logs required by subdivision (d) shall be maintained for a minimum of five years.' Subdivision (f)(6) then gives employees and their representatives a right to see certain of these records: 'All records required by paragraphs (1) to (3), inclusive, shall be made available to employees and their representatives, upon request and without cost, for examination and copying within 15 calendar days of a request.'
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only three of the six paragraphs of subdivision (f) — the hazard-record and log retention periods in (f)(1) and (f)(3), and the employee-access right in (f)(6) — and does not quote or fully summarize (f)(2) (one-year training-record retention), (f)(4) (five-year retention for incident investigation records, with a restriction on retaining 'medical information'), or (f)(5) (division access to records on request). All three quotations are drawn from the same enacted statute, Labor Code § 6401.9 — paragraphs of a single subdivision, (f) — not independent sources from one another; this document's only independent source is § 6401.9 itself, fetched twice from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov using two distinct request methods and confirmed byte-identical (after whitespace normalization) before any of its text was treated as verified. The 15-calendar-day access deadline stated here for records under paragraphs (1) through (3) of subdivision (f) is a different number and a different unit (calendar days, not business days) from the five-business-day access deadline this corpus's IIPP information sheet describes for the separate written IIPP itself under 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203(a)(8)(B)(1); the two access rights are not the same requirement and should not be conflated. This is a description of what the statute requires in general, not a record of any request made by or to any particular employer or employee.

clauses.title: Enforcement and the July 1, 2024 Effective Date
clauses.body: Labor Code § 6401.9(g) states how the section is enforced: 'The division shall enforce this section by the issuance of a citation alleging a violation of this section and a notice of civil penalty in a manner consistent with Section 6317.' The statute does not itself state a specific penalty amount in the text quoted here; it ties enforcement to the citation-and-penalty framework of a separate statute, Labor Code § 6317, which this clause does not independently verify or quote. On timing, subdivision (i) fixes when most of the section's substantive requirements took effect: 'Subdivisions (b) to (g), inclusive, shall be operative on and after July 1, 2024.' The statute was added by Stats. 2023, Ch. 289, § 4 (Senate Bill 553), with an original effective date of January 1, 2024, but subdivision (i) delays the operative date of subdivisions (b) through (g) — including the applicability rule, the plan requirement, the log requirement, training, and recordkeeping addressed in this information sheet's other clauses — to July 1, 2024.

Both quotations are drawn from the same enacted statute, Labor Code § 6401.9 — subdivisions (g) and (i) of one section — not independent sources from one another; this document's only independent source is § 6401.9 itself, fetched twice from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov using two distinct request methods and confirmed byte-identical (after whitespace normalization) before any of its text was treated as verified. clauses.title: Certification
Duty to Conspicuously Post a Privacy Policy, and the 30-Day Cure Period
clauses.body: California law requires an operator of a commercial Web site or online service that collects personally identifiable information through the Internet about individual consumers residing in California who use or visit that Web site or online service to conspicuously post its privacy policy on the Web site, or, in the case of an operator of an online service, to make that policy available by one of the alternative means the statute recognizes for online services. An operator is in violation of this posting duty only if it fails to post its policy within 30 days after being notified of noncompliance — the statute builds in a cure period rather than imposing liability for a first, uncured lapse.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes a single subdivision, Business and Professions Code § 22575(a). That subdivision's own text cross-references "paragraph (5) of subdivision (b) of Section 22577" for the alternative means by which an operator of an online service (as opposed to a Web site) may make its policy available; this document verifies and quotes that cross-referenced provision independently in a separate clause below (§ 22577(b)), so the two clauses together, though drawn from different sections of the same chapter, cover the full posting-method rule. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's CalOPPA website-privacy-policy-posting requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific operator; CalOPPA is narrower than, and predates, the California Consumer Privacy Act, and this document does not address CCPA's substantive consumer rights, which are covered in this site's separate CCPA consumer-facing disclosure document. This clause does not determine whether a specific website or service is "commercial," whether a specific visitor "resides in California," or whether a specific operator has in fact been "notified of noncompliance" so as to start the 30-day cure period running — those are fact-specific determinations this document does not make. No case law was checked on this provision; the statute's own text is unambiguous, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

An operator shall be in violation of this subdivision only if the operator fails to post its policy within 30 days after being notified of noncompliance.

clauses.title: Required Content of the Privacy Policy: Categories of PII and Third Parties, Review Process, Change Notification, and Effective Date
clauses.body: California law requires that the privacy policy an operator posts under CalOPPA identify the categories of personally identifiable information the operator collects through its Web site or online service about individual consumers who use or visit it, and the categories of third-party persons or entities with whom the operator may share that personally identifiable information. If — but only if — the operator maintains a process for an individual consumer to review and request changes to his or her personally identifiable information collected through the Web site or online service, the policy must describe that process; the statute does not itself require an operator to establish such a review-and-change process, only to describe one if it has one. The policy must also describe the process by which the operator notifies consumers of material changes to its privacy policy, and must identify the policy's effective date.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Business and Professions Code § 22575(b), paragraphs (1) through (4), as a single integrated statutory list; all four paragraphs come from the same subdivision of the same section as the posting duty quoted in this document's prior clause (§ 22575(a)), so both clauses draw on the same statutory section rather than fully independent sources — they are quoted separately here because they impose distinct obligations (the duty to post, versus the content the posted policy must contain). This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's CalOPPA requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific operator. This clause does not address paragraphs (5) through (7) of the same subdivision, which concern "do not track" disclosure and are covered in a separate clause below, nor does it determine what categories of personally identifiable information or third parties a specific operator must list — that depends on what the specific operator actually collects and shares, which this document does not know. No case law was checked on this provision; the statute's own text is unambiguous, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22575(b)(1)-(4) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Online Privacy Protection Act, required privacy policy content: categories of PII and third parties, review process, change notification, effective date
citations.quote: (b) The privacy policy required by subdivision (a) shall do all of the following: (1) Identify the categories of personally identifiable information that the operator collects through the Web site or online service about individual consumers who use or visit its commercial Web site or online service and the categories of third-party persons or entities with whom the operator may share that personally identifiable information. (2) If the operator maintains a process for an individual consumer who uses or visits its commercial Web site or online service to review and request changes to any of his or her personally identifiable information that is collected through the Web site or online service, provide a description of that process. (3) Describe the process by which the operator notifies consumers who use or visit its commercial Web site or online service of material changes to the operator’s privacy policy for that Web site or online service. (4) Identify its effective date.

clauses.title: Disclosure of "Do Not Track" Response and Cross-Site Tracking by Other Parties
clauses.body: California law requires that the privacy policy also disclose how the operator responds to Web browser "do not track" signals or other mechanisms that give consumers the ability to exercise choice regarding the collection of personally identifiable information about an individual consumer's online activities over time and across third-party Web sites or online services — but only if the operator engages in that kind of collection. Separately, the policy must disclose whether other parties may collect personally identifiable information about a consumer's online activities over time and across different Web sites when the consumer uses the operator's Web site or service. The statute allows an operator to satisfy the "do not track" response disclosure by providing a clear and conspicuous hyperlink in its privacy policy to an online location containing a description, including the effects, of any program or protocol the operator follows that offers the consumer that choice.
clauses.gap: Correction to the research brief that prompted this clause: the brief described the "do not track" signal disclosure duty as located at § 22575(b)(7). The verified statutory text shows the disclosure duty itself is in paragraph (5) of subdivision (b); paragraph (7) is instead a safe harbor letting the operator satisfy paragraph (5) through a hyperlink to an external description, rather than the disclosure duty itself. This clause quotes all three paragraphs — (5), (6), and (7) — together because the hyperlink safe harbor in (7) cannot be described accurately without the paragraph (5) duty it modifies, and because (6) is a related but textually separate disclosure duty (about tracking by other parties, not the operator's own "do not track" response) appearing between them. All three paragraphs come from the same subdivision (b) of the same section, § 22575, as the categories/process/effective-date content quoted in this document's prior clause — this document's coverage of § 22575's required-content list rests on that one section, not on independent statutes. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's CalOPPA requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific operator. This clause does not identify any specific technology (such as the Global Privacy Control) as a qualifying "do not track" signal; the statute's text does not name one, and this document does not represent that any particular signal satisfies paragraph (5) for a specific operator. No case law was checked on this provision; the statute's own text is unambiguous, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22575(b)(5)-(7) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Online Privacy Protection Act, "do not track" response disclosure, cross-site tracking by other parties, and hyperlink safe harbor
citations.quote: (5) Disclose how the operator responds to Web browser “do not track” signals or other mechanisms that provide consumers the ability to exercise choice regarding the collection of personally identifiable information about an individual consumer’s online activities over time and across third-party Web sites or online services, if the operator engages in that collection. (6) Disclose whether other parties may collect personally identifiable information about an individual consumer’s online activities over time and across different Web sites when a consumer uses the operator’s Web site or service. (7) An operator may satisfy the requirement of paragraph (5) by providing a clear and conspicuous hyperlink in the operator’s privacy policy to an online location containing a description, including the effects, of any program or protocol the operator follows that offers the consumer that choice.

clauses.title: Statutory Definitions: "Personally Identifiable Information" and "Operator"
clauses.body: California law defines "personally identifiable information," for purposes of this chapter, as individually identifiable information about an individual consumer that is collected online by the operator from that individual and maintained by the operator in an accessible form, including a first and last name; a home or other physical address, including street name and city or town; an email address; a telephone number; a Social Security number; any other identifier that permits the physical or online contacting of a specific individual; and information concerning a user that the Web site or online service collects online from the user and maintains in personally identifiable form in combination with any of the identifiers just listed. Separately, California law defines "operator," for purposes of this chapter, as any person or entity that owns a Web site located on the Internet or an online service that collects and maintains personally identifiable information from a California-resident consumer who uses or visits it, where the Web site or online service is operated for commercial purposes; the definition expressly excludes a third party that operates, hosts, or manages — but does not own — a Web site or online service on the owner's behalf, or that processes information on the owner's behalf.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes two subdivisions of the same statutory section, Business and Professions Code § 22577 — subdivision (a) (the definition of "personally identifiable information") and subdivision (c) (the definition of "operator") — because both are definitions the chapter applies throughout, and are grouped here rather than attached separately to each clause that uses the defined terms. This document's overall verified coverage of CalOPPA rests on two sections of the same chapter, § 22575 and § 22577, rather than on fully independent statutes; that is expected for a definitions section that exists to support the operative section, and is disclosed here for transparency. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's CalOPPA requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific operator. This clause does not quote or verify subdivision (d)'s definition of "consumer," which was not independently checked for this clause; nor does it determine, for a specific business, whether a specific third-party vendor that hosts or manages a Web site on that business's behalf falls within the "operator" definition's exclusion or is itself an owner-operator — that is a fact-specific determination this document does not make. No case law was checked on this provision; the statute's own text is unambiguous, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22577(a) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Online Privacy Protection Act, definition of "personally identifiable information"
citations.quote: (a) The term “personally identifiable information” means individually identifiable information about an individual consumer collected online by the operator from that individual and maintained by the operator in an accessible form, including any of the following: (1) A first and last name. (2) A home or other physical address, including street name and name of a city or town. (3) An e-mail address. (4) A telephone number. (5) A social security number. (6) Any other identifier that permits the physical or online contacting of a specific individual. (7) Information concerning a user that the Web site or online service collects online from the user and maintains in personally identifiable form in combination with an identifier described in this subdivision.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22577(c) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Online Privacy Protection Act, definition of "operator"
citations.quote: (c) The term “operator” means any person or entity that owns a Web site located on the Internet or an online service that collects and maintains personally identifiable information from a consumer residing in California who uses or visits the Web site or online service if the Web site or online service is operated for commercial purposes. It does not include any third party that operates, hosts, or manages, but does not own, a Web site or online service on the owner’s behalf or by processing information on behalf of the owner.

clauses.title: What Counts as "Conspicuously Post" Under the Statute
clauses.body: California law defines "conspicuously post," with respect to a privacy policy, to include posting it by any of several methods: a Web page on which the actual privacy policy is posted, if that page is the homepage or the first significant page after entering the Web site; an icon that hyperlinks to a Web page where the actual policy is posted, if the icon is on the homepage or first significant page, contains the word "privacy," and uses a color that contrasts with the page's background or is otherwise distinguishable; a text link that hyperlinks to a Web page where the actual policy is posted, if the link is on the homepage or first significant page and either includes the word "privacy," is written in capital letters at least as large as the surrounding text, or is written in larger, contrasting, or otherwise set-off type that calls attention to it; any other functional hyperlink displayed so that a reasonable person would notice it; or, in the case of an online service, any other reasonably accessible means of making the privacy policy available to the online service's consumers.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes a single subdivision, Business and Professions Code § 22577(b), in full, including its numbered paragraphs (1) through (5) and lettered subparagraphs (A) through (C). Paragraph (5) of this subdivision is the same alternative-means provision that § 22575(a), quoted in an earlier clause of this document, cross-references for an operator of an online service (as opposed to a Web site); the two clauses are therefore linked, though each independently quotes only its own subdivision. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's CalOPPA requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific operator. This clause states the statutory test for what posting methods qualify as "conspicuous"; it does not determine whether a specific operator's actual Web page, icon, or link design in fact satisfies that test — that is a fact-specific, visual-design determination this document does not make. No case law was checked on this provision; the statute's own text is unambiguous, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22577(b) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Online Privacy Protection Act, definition of "conspicuously post"
citations.quote: (b) The term “conspicuously post” with respect to a privacy policy shall include posting the privacy policy through any of the following: (1) A Web page on which the actual privacy policy is posted if the Web page is the homepage or first significant page after entering the Web site. (2) An icon that hyperlinks to a Web page on which the actual privacy policy is posted, if the icon is located on the homepage or the first significant page after entering the Web site, and if the icon contains the word “privacy.” The icon shall also use a color that contrasts with the background color of the Web page or is otherwise distinguishable. (3) A text link that hyperlinks to a Web page on which the actual privacy policy is posted, if the text link is located on the homepage or first significant page after entering the Web site, and if the text link does one of the following: (A) Includes the word “privacy.” (B) Is written in capital letters equal to or greater in size than the surrounding text. (C) Is written in larger type than the surrounding text, or in contrasting type, font, or color to the surrounding text of the same size, or set off from the surrounding text of the same size by symbols or other marks that call attention to the language. (4) Any other functional hyperlink that is so displayed that a reasonable person would notice it. (5) In the case of an online service, any other reasonably accessible means of making the privacy policy available for consumers of the online service.

clauses.title: Violation Standard, Chapter Operative Date, and Preemption of Local Privacy-Posting Laws
clauses.body: California law provides that an operator of a commercial Web site or online service that collects personally identifiable information from individual California-resident consumers who use or visit it is in violation of this chapter if it fails to comply with the posting requirement described elsewhere in this Notice, or with the provisions of its own posted privacy policy, and does so either knowingly and willfully, or negligently and materially — a mental-state and materiality threshold, rather than strict liability for any noncompliance. This chapter became operative on July 1, 2004. Separately, the Legislature declared that this chapter addresses a matter of statewide concern, and that it supersedes and preempts all rules, regulations, codes, ordinances, and other laws adopted by a city, county, city and county, municipality, or local agency regarding the posting of a privacy policy on an Internet Web site.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on three separate statutory sections of the same chapter — Business and Professions Code §§ 22576 (the violation standard), 22578 (the preemption declaration), and 22579 (the chapter's operative date) — each independently verified and quoted from its own section rather than from subdivisions of one section, so each citation here is a genuinely separate authority within the chapter. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's CalOPPA requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific operator. This clause does not address whether CalOPPA itself creates a private right of action for a consumer, or whether a violation might instead (or additionally) be pursued under some other statute, such as the Unfair Competition Law; that question was not researched for this clause and this document takes no position on it. The July 1, 2004 operative date and the chapter's 2003 enactment history are stated here for completeness of the compliance timeline; they are historical facts about when the chapter took effect, not a live deadline for an operator setting up a privacy policy today. No case law was checked on any of these three provisions; each statute's own text is unambiguous, so the statutes stand as the source here without a corroborating case.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22576 (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Online Privacy Protection Act, violation standard: knowing and willful, or negligent and material, noncompliance
citations.quote: An operator of a commercial Web site or online service that collects personally identifiable information through the Web site or online service from individual consumers who use or visit the commercial Web site or online service and who reside in California shall be in violation of this section if the operator fails to comply with the provisions of Section 22575 or with the provisions of its posted privacy policy in either of the following ways: (a) Knowingly and willfully. (b) Negligently and materially.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22578 (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Online Privacy Protection Act, statewide concern and preemption of local privacy-posting laws
citations.quote: It is the intent of the Legislature that this chapter is a matter of statewide concern. This chapter supersedes and preempts all rules, regulations, codes, ordinances, and other laws adopted by a city, county, city and county, municipality, or local agency regarding the posting of a privacy policy on an Internet Web site.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22579 (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Online Privacy Protection Act, chapter operative date
citations.quote: This chapter shall become operative on July 1, 2004.

clauses.title: Whether This Notice Is Required
clauses.body: California has its own layoff-notice law — the California Worker Adjustment and Retraining Act, commonly called "Cal/WARN" — separate from the federal WARN Act. It applies to {{companyName}} only if {{companyName}} operates a "covered establishment": a facility that employs, or has employed at any point in the preceding 12 months, 75 or more people. That threshold is lower than federal WARN's 100-employee threshold, and the California statute's definition doesn't exclude part-time workers the way the federal one does. An "employer" under this law is whoever directly or indirectly owns and operates that covered establishment — including a parent corporation, as to a covered establishment owned and operated by its subsidiary. And a covered "employee" — the person to whom the liability described elsewhere in this document can run — is someone who has worked for the employer at least 6 of the 12 months before the date notice would be due.
clauses.gap: The three quotes below are all subdivisions of a single statutory section (Labor Code § 1400.5) rather than independently authored sources, so they aren't cross-corroborated against each other. Separately: Labor Code § 1400.5(b) defines "employer" by cross-referencing the general "person" definition in Labor Code § 18; that cross-referenced section wasn't independently fetched and verified for this document, so this clause states the covered-establishment/employer/employee definitions only as directly written in § 1400.5 itself.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1400.5(a) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, "covered establishment" definition
citations.quote: “Covered establishment” means any industrial or commercial facility or part thereof that employs, or has employed within the preceding 12 months, 75 or more persons.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1400.5(b) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, "employer" definition
citations.quote: “Employer” means any person, as defined by Section 18, who directly or indirectly owns and operates a covered establishment. A parent corporation is an employer as to any covered establishment directly owned and operated by its corporate subsidiary.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1400.5(h) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, "employee" definition
citations.quote: “Employee” means a person employed by an employer for at least 6 months of the 12 months preceding the date on which notice is required.

clauses.title: What Counts as a Mass Layoff, Relocation, or Termination
clauses.body: Cal/WARN's notice duty is triggered by three distinct events at a covered establishment: a "mass layoff" — a layoff of 50 or more employees during any 30-day period — a "relocation" — moving all or substantially all of the covered establishment's operations 100 or more miles away — or a "termination" — ceasing or substantially ceasing operations there. Unlike the federal mass-layoff definition, California's has no separate test tied to what percentage of the workforce is affected; a flat count of 50 or more employees within 30 days is enough regardless of how large the covered establishment's total workforce is. The chapter also carves out two situations entirely: layoffs from the completion of a project-based job in the broadcasting, motion picture, or certain on-site construction/drilling/logging/mining industries where the employee understood the job was tied to that project, and layoffs of employees hired with the understanding that the work was seasonal and temporary.
clauses.gap: All quotes below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (Labor Code § 1400.5) rather than independently authored sources. This clause also doesn't address Cal/WARN's separate call-center-relocation article (Labor Code §§ 1409-1413), which applies its own relocation definition to call centers specifically and was outside the scope of this document's research.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1400.5(d) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, "mass layoff" definition
citations.quote: “Mass layoff” means a layoff during any 30-day period of 50 or more employees at a covered establishment.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1400.5(e)-(f) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, "relocation" and "termination" definitions
citations.quote: “Relocation” means the removal of all or substantially all of the industrial or commercial operations in a covered establishment to a different location 100 miles or more away.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1400.5(f) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, "termination" definition
citations.quote: “Termination” means the cessation or substantial cessation of industrial or commercial operations in a covered establishment.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1400.5(g) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, project-based and seasonal-employment carve-outs
citations.quote: (g) (1) This chapter does not apply where the closing or layoff is the result of the completion of a particular project or undertaking of an employer subject to Wage Order 11, regulating the Broadcasting Industry, Wage Order 12, regulating the Motion Picture Industry, or Wage Order 16, regulating Certain On-Site Occupations in the Construction, Drilling, Logging and Mining Industries, of the Industrial Welfare Commission, and the employees were hired with the understanding that their employment was limited to the duration of that project or undertaking. (2) This chapter does not apply to employees who are employed in seasonal employment where the employees were hired with the understanding that their employment was seasonal and temporary.

clauses.title: The 60-Day Notice Requirement and What It Must Contain
clauses.body: If the thresholds above are met, California law requires {{companyName}} to give written notice at least 60 days before {{terminationDate}}, the date the mass layoff, relocation, or termination is expected to take effect. Notice goes not only to {{employeeName}} and the other affected employees, but also to the Employment Development Department, the local workforce development board, and the chief elected official of each city and county government where the event will occur. The notice itself has to include everything the federal WARN Act requires, plus several California-specific items: a functioning email and phone number for the local workforce development board along with a required description of that board's rapid-response services (this applies regardless of whether {{companyName}} plans to coordinate with the board or with someone else), a description of the CalFresh food-assistance program with its benefits helpline and a link to the CalFresh website, and a functioning email and phone number for {{companyName}} itself.
clauses.gap: The four citations below are all subdivisions of a single statutory section (Labor Code § 1401) rather than independently authored sources. Section 1401(c)(2) separately requires that if the employer does choose to coordinate rapid-response services through the workforce board or another entity, those services be arranged within 30 days of the notice — a scheduling duty this clause doesn't restate in full. This document doesn't separately verify or reproduce the exact wording the federal WARN Act itself requires notices to contain; see this project's federal WARN Act document for that.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1401(a) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, 60-day notice requirement and recipients
citations.quote: An employer may not order a mass layoff, relocation, or termination at a covered establishment unless, 60 days before the order takes effect, the employer gives written notice of the order to the following: (1) The employees of the covered establishment affected by the order. (2) The Employment Development Department, the local workforce development board, and the chief elected official of each city and county government within which the termination, relocation, or mass layoff occurs.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1401(b) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, incorporation of federal notice elements
citations.quote: An employer required to give notice of any mass layoff, relocation, or termination under this chapter shall include in its notice the elements required by the federal Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act (29 U.S.C. Sec. 2101 et seq.).

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1401(c)(1) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, required rapid-response-service disclosure
citations.quote: Regardless of whether the employer chooses to coordinate services with the local workforce development board or another entity, the employer shall include in the notice a functioning email and telephone number of the board and the following description of the rapid response activities offered by the local workforce development board

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1401(d)-(e) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, required CalFresh and employer-contact disclosures
citations.quote: An employer required to give notice of any mass layoff, relocation, or termination under this chapter shall include in the notice a description of the statewide food assistance program known as CalFresh (Chapter 10 (commencing with Section 18900) of Part 6 of Division 9 of the Welfare and Institutions Code), the CalFresh benefits helpline, and a link to the CalFresh internet website.

clauses.title: When Notice Isn't Required
clauses.body: California law recognizes two situations where the 60-day notice described above isn't required. First, no notice at all is required if the mass layoff, relocation, or termination is necessitated by a physical calamity or act of war. Second, an employer need not comply with the notice requirement for a relocation or termination — not a mass layoff — if the state Employment Development Department determines that the employer was actively and in good faith seeking capital or business that, if obtained, would have let it avoid or postpone the relocation or termination, and that the employer reasonably believed giving notice would have prevented it from getting that capital or business. That second exception isn't self-executing the way its closest federal counterpart is: before it applies, the employer has to give the department a written record of the documents relevant to that determination, along with an affidavit — signed under penalty of perjury — verifying the record's contents. Cal/WARN does not have a standalone exception for generic "unforeseeable business circumstances" the way federal WARN does.
clauses.gap: Labor Code § 1402.5(d) — the provision stating the active-seeking-capital exception doesn't apply to mass layoffs — refers to a mass-layoff definition at "subdivision (d) of Section 1400." As currently published, however, Section 1400 contains only the Act's short title and has no lettered subdivisions; the mass-layoff definition this document found is instead at subdivision (d) of Section 1400.5. This appears to be an uncorrected cross-reference left over from a 2022 amendment that renumbered the definitions out of Section 1400 and into a new Section 1400.5 without updating this particular internal citation. This clause treats § 1402.5(d)'s carve-out as referring to the current mass-layoff definition despite that stale section number, but does not independently resolve the discrepancy. Separately, the two citations below come from two different statutory sections (§ 1401(f) and § 1402.5), so they are independent of each other within the same chapter.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1401(f) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, physical-calamity/act-of-war exception
citations.quote: Notwithstanding the requirements of subdivision (a), an employer is not required to provide notice if a mass layoff, relocation, or termination is necessitated by a physical calamity or act of war.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1402.5(a)-(d) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, active-seeking-capital-or-business exception and its procedural conditions
citations.quote: An employer is not required to comply with the notice requirement contained in subdivision (a) of Section 1401 if the department determines that all of the following conditions exist: (1) As of the time that notice would have been required, the employer was actively seeking capital or business. (2) The capital or business sought, if obtained, would have enabled the employer to avoid or postpone the relocation or termination. (3) The employer reasonably and in good faith believed that giving the notice required by subdivision (a) of Section 1401 would have precluded the employer from obtaining the needed capital or business.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1402.5(b)-(c) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, written-record and sworn-affidavit conditions
citations.quote: The department may not determine that the employer was actively seeking capital or business under subdivision (a) unless the employer provides the department with both of the following: (1) A written record consisting of all documents relevant to the determination of whether the employer was actively seeking capital or business, as specified by the department. (2) An affidavit verifying the contents of the documents contained in the record.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1402.5(d) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, exclusion of mass layoffs from the active-seeking-capital exception
citations.quote: This section does not apply to notice of a mass layoff as defined by subdivision (d) of Section 1400.

clauses.title: What Happens If Notice Isn't Given — Employee Liability
clauses.body: An employer that orders a mass layoff, relocation, or termination without giving employees the notice described above is liable to each employee who lost their job and was entitled to notice for back pay — at the higher of the employee's average regular rate over their last three years of employment or their final rate of compensation — plus the value of any benefits, including medical expenses, the employee would have received had the employment loss not happened. This liability runs for the period of the violation, up to a maximum of 60 days, or half the number of days the employee actually worked for the employer, whichever is smaller. It's reduced by wages the employer actually paid during the violation period (except accrued vacation pay), any voluntary payment not otherwise legally required, and certain third-party benefit payments made on the employee's behalf.
clauses.gap: The three citations below are all subdivisions of a single statutory section (Labor Code § 1402) rather than independently authored sources. This liability formula tracks the structure of the parallel federal WARN Act damages provision closely, but this clause states only the California statute's own text; it doesn't address how an employee's rights under the two statutes for the same layoff relate to each other, which the sections fetched for this document do not say.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1402(a) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, back pay and benefits liability
citations.quote: An employer who fails to give notice as required by paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 1401 before ordering a mass layoff, relocation, or termination is liable to each employee entitled to notice who lost his or her employment for: (1) Back pay at the average regular rate of compensation received by the employee during the last three years of his or her employment, or the employee’s final rate of compensation, whichever is higher. (2) The value of the cost of any benefits to which the employee would have been entitled had his or her employment not been lost, including the cost of any medical expenses incurred by the employee that would have been covered under an employee benefit plan.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1402(b) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, liability cap
citations.quote: Liability under this section is calculated for the period of the employer’s violation, up to a maximum of 60 days, or one-half the number of days that the employee was employed by the employer, whichever period is smaller.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1402(c) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Cal/WARN Act, offsets against liability
citations.quote: The amount of an employer’s liability under subdivision (a) is reduced by the following: (1) Any wages, except vacation moneys accrued prior to the period of the employer’s violation, paid by the employer to the employee during the period of the employer’s violation. (2) Any voluntary and unconditional payments made by the employer to the employee that were not required to satisfy any legal obligation. (3) Any payments by the employer to a third party or trustee, such as premiums for health benefits or payments to a defined contribution pension plan, on behalf of and attributable to the employee for the period of the violation.

clauses.title: Government Penalty, Private Lawsuits, and State Enforcement
clauses.body: Beyond the per-employee liability described above, an employer that fails to notify the Employment Development Department, local workforce board, and local officials is subject to a civil penalty of up to $500 for each day of the violation — waived if the employer pays everything owed to affected employees within three weeks of ordering the layoff, relocation, or termination. Any person seeking to establish liability against an employer under this chapter, including a local government or an employee representative, may bring a civil action, including on behalf of others similarly situated, and a court may award reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing plaintiff. A court may also reduce a penalty if the employer shows it conducted a reasonable, good-faith investigation and had reasonable grounds to believe its conduct wasn't a violation. Separately from any private lawsuit, California's Labor Commissioner has independent authority to examine an employer's books and records and to enforce the notice requirement directly — including by investigating a violation, ordering temporary relief, and issuing a citation against the employer.
clauses.gap: The four citations below come from four different statutory sections (§§ 1403, 1404, 1405, and 1406), so they are independently drawn from separate parts of the chapter rather than repeated subdivisions of one section. The $500-per-day civil penalty described first is tied specifically to a failure to notify the government recipients under Labor Code § 1401(a)(2) — the Employment Development Department, workforce board, and local officials — not to a failure to notify employees themselves, which is a narrower trigger than it may first appear.

The employer is not subject to a civil penalty under this section, however, if the employer pays to all applicable employees the amounts for which the employer is liable under Section 1402 within three weeks from the date the employer orders the mass layoff, relocation, or termination.

The court may award reasonable attorney’s fees as part of costs to any plaintiff who prevails in a civil action brought under this chapter.

clauses.title: Notice of Layoff, Relocation, or Termination
clauses.body:
This notice is provided to {{employeeName}} by {{companyName}} pursuant to the California Worker Adjustment and Retraining Act (Cal/WARN Act), Labor Code § 1400 et seq.

{{companyName}} anticipates a mass layoff, relocation, or termination affecting {{employeeName}}'s position, expected to take effect on or about {{terminationDate}}.

A copy of this notice, or one materially like it, is also being sent to the California Employment Development Department, the applicable local workforce development board, and the chief elected official of each city and county government where this event will occur, as required by California law.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
About This Information Sheet and Covered-Employer Self-Assessment
clauses.body:
This information sheet describes selected requirements of California's annual pay data reporting law, Government Code section 12999, as it may apply to a private employer such as {{companyName}}. Section 12999 requires certain private employers to submit an annual pay data report to California's Civil Rights Department, covering workforce composition by pay band, job category, race, ethnicity, and sex, and, separately, to submit a related report covering employees supplied through labor contractors. This document is distinct from this project's separate Pay Scale Disclosure and Salary History Ban Information Sheet, which addresses a different obligation — disclosing a position's pay scale to applicants, employees, and in job postings under Labor Code section 432.3 — not the annual workforce data-reporting obligation addressed here.

This section is a self-assessment worksheet, not a determination that {{companyName}} is or is not required to file a pay data report. {{companyName}}'s approximate total employee count is stated as {{employeeCount}}; the Reporting Year addressed is {{reportingYear}}; and {{companyName}}'s use, if any, of labor contractors is described as: {{laborContractorUseDescription}}. This information sheet does not itself calculate whether {{companyName}} met the 100-employee threshold described below, does not itself prepare or submit any report on {{companyName}}'s behalf, and does not itself satisfy any filing, recordkeeping, or disclosure duty Section 12999 may impose.

clauses.title: Which Employers Must File a Pay Data Report, and the Filing Deadline
clauses.body: California law requires a private employer that has 100 or more employees to submit a pay data report to the department on or before the second Wednesday of May 2023, and on or before the second Wednesday of May of each year thereafter. The report covers the prior calendar year, which the statute designates the “Reporting Year.” The statute's recurring filing duty runs to “the department,” meaning California's Civil Rights Department, and its own text does not state that an employer with fewer than 100 employees is subject to this particular filing duty.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Government Code section 12999(a)(1)), used as real evidence of California's pay-data-report filing threshold and deadline — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. The citation below is a single paragraph of a single statutory subdivision, not a composite of independent sources. Government Code section 12999 currently exists in two chaptered, time-phased versions from the same 2025 enacting bill: the version quoted here (added by Stats. 2025, Ch. 760, Sec. 1) is effective January 1, 2026 and, by its own terms, remains in effect only until January 1, 2027, when it is automatically repealed and superseded by a differently worded version (added by Sec. 2 of the same bill) that becomes operative that date; a separate clause in this information sheet addresses the one respect in which that later version differs from the text quoted here. This clause was checked against the text confirmed operative as of the checked date above; it does not itself count any employer's employees, does not itself determine that any particular employer met or did not meet the 100-employee threshold for any particular Reporting Year, and is informational only.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12999(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text, version effective Jan. 1, 2026 through Jan. 1, 2027, added by Stats. 2025, Ch. 760, Sec. 1)
citations.cite: California Government Code, pay data report filing threshold and annual deadline
citations.quote: On or before the second Wednesday of May 2023, and on or before the second Wednesday of May of each year thereafter, a private employer that has 100 or more employees shall submit a pay data report to the department covering the prior calendar year, which, for purposes of this section, shall be referred to as the “Reporting Year.”

clauses.title: Separate Report for Employees Hired Through Labor Contractors
clauses.body: Separately from the general pay data report, California law requires a private employer that has 100 or more employees hired through labor contractors within the prior calendar year to submit a separate pay data report to the department, covering those labor-contractor-supplied employees for that prior calendar year. The employer must also disclose on that report the ownership names of all labor contractors used to supply employees, and the statute places a corresponding duty on the labor contractor itself to supply all necessary pay data to the employer. Any demographic information gathered by an employer or a labor contractor under this section must be collected and stored separately from employees' personnel records.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Government Code section 12999(a)(2) and (a)(3)), used as real evidence of the labor-contractor pay data reporting duty — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. Both citations below are paragraphs of a single statutory subdivision, (a), of one section; they are treated here as one source describing one connected labor-contractor reporting duty, not as independent corroborating sources. This duty was added to Section 12999 by Senate Bill 1162 of the 2021–22 Regular Session and persists, with the wording quoted here, in the version of the section confirmed operative as of the checked date above. This clause does not itself determine that any particular employer used, or did not use, a labor contractor within the meaning of this section, and does not itself determine that any particular employer's labor-contractor pay data report was or was not filed, complete, or accurate.

citations.quote: a private employer that has 100 or more employees hired through labor contractors within the prior calendar year shall submit a separate pay data report to the department covering the employees hired through labor contractors in the prior calendar year. The private employer shall also disclose on the pay data report the ownership names of all labor contractors used to supply employees. A labor contractor shall supply all necessary pay data to the private employer.

citations.quote: Any demographic information gathered by an employer or labor contractor pursuant to this section shall be collected and stored separately from employees’ personnel records.

clauses.title: Required Contents of the Pay Data Report: Job Categories, Pay Bands, and Calculation Method
clauses.body: California law specifies what the pay data report must contain. It must report the number of employees by race, ethnicity, and sex within each of ten listed job categories (currently: executive or senior level officials and managers; first or mid-level officials and managers; professionals; technicians; sales workers; administrative support workers; craft workers; operatives; laborers and helpers; and service workers). It must also report the number of employees by race, ethnicity, and sex whose annual earnings fall within each of the pay bands used by the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics in its Occupational Employment Statistics survey, and, within each job category, the median and mean hourly rate for each combination of race, ethnicity, and sex. To generate these numbers, the employer must create a “snapshot” counting individuals in each job category, by race, ethnicity, and sex, employed during a single pay period of the employer's choice between October 1 and December 31 of the Reporting Year, and must calculate each snapshot employee's total earnings as shown on that employee's Form W-2 for the entire Reporting Year, tabulating how many employees' W-2 earnings fell within each pay band. The report must further include the total hours worked by each employee counted in each pay band during the Reporting Year, and the employer's North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) code.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Government Code section 12999(b)(1) through (b)(7)), used as real evidence of the pay data report's required contents — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. All citations below are paragraphs of a single statutory subdivision, (b), of one section; they are treated here as one source describing one connected set of reporting-content requirements, not as independent corroborating sources. The ten-job-category list quoted and paraphrased here is the list in the version of Section 12999 confirmed operative as of the checked date above; a separate clause in this information sheet discloses that an already-enacted, differently worded job-category list replaces this one starting January 1, 2027. This clause does not itself calculate any employer's pay bands, snapshot counts, median or mean hourly rates, or NAICS code, and does not itself determine that any particular employer's report was, or was not, complete or accurate.

clauses.title: Already-Enacted Change Taking Effect January 1, 2027: New Job Category List
clauses.body: California has already enacted a further change to Government Code section 12999 that is not yet in effect. The version of the section described elsewhere in this information sheet remains in effect only until January 1, 2027, when it is automatically repealed by its own terms. On that same date, a second, already-chaptered version of the section becomes operative and replaces the current ten-item job-category list with a different, longer list of job categories for purposes of the race/ethnicity/sex headcount required by subdivision (b)(1) — for example, “chief executives” and “management occupations, except chief executives” as separate categories, along with categories such as computer and mathematical occupations, legal occupations, and health care support occupations, among others. The remainder of the reporting scheme described in this information sheet — the 100-employee threshold, the filing deadline, the labor-contractor report, the pay-band and snapshot methodology, and the penalty structure — is not altered by this already-enacted change.

The quotes below come from the version added by Sec. 2 of that bill (operative January 1, 2027) and, for the current sunset date, from the version added by Sec. 1 (effective through January 1, 2027); both were fetched and independently confirmed in the same manner as the currently operative text quoted elsewhere in this information sheet. clauses.title: Penalties for Failing to File, and How They Are Assessed
clauses.body: If the department does not receive a required pay data report from an employer, California law authorizes the department to seek a court order requiring the employer to comply, together with the department's costs of seeking that order. Upon the department's request, a court shall impose a civil penalty of up to $100 per employee on an employer that fails to file the required report, and up to $200 per employee for a subsequent failure to file. Any such penalty is payable to the Civil Rights Enforcement and Litigation Fund. If an employer is unable to submit a complete and accurate report because a labor contractor did not provide required pay data, the court may apportion an appropriate share of penalties to that labor contractor instead.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Government Code section 12999(f)), used as real evidence of California's civil-penalty and enforcement structure for a failure to file a pay data report — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. The citation below is a single paragraph of a single statutory subdivision, not a composite of independent sources. This clause does not identify any reported court decision applying this penalty range, an honest gap disclosed rather than resolved by assumption. This clause does not itself determine that any particular employer has or has not filed a required report, does not calculate any penalty amount, and is informational only.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12999(f) (California Legislative Information text, version effective Jan. 1, 2026 through Jan. 1, 2027, added by Stats. 2025, Ch. 760, Sec. 1)
citations.cite: California Government Code, civil penalty for failure to file a pay data report
citations.quote: Upon request by the department, a court shall impose a civil penalty not to exceed one hundred dollars ($100) per employee upon any employer who fails to file the required report and not to exceed two hundred dollars ($200) per employee upon any employer for a subsequent failure to file the required report. Any penalty under this subdivision shall be payable to the Civil Rights Enforcement and Litigation Fund established under Section 12907. If the employer is unable to submit a complete and accurate report because a labor contractor has not provided the pay data as required under paragraph (2) of subdivision (a), the court may apportion an appropriate amount of penalties to any labor contractor that has failed to provide the pay data to the employer.

clauses.title: Confidentiality of Filed Data, Recordkeeping, and Key Statutory Definitions
clauses.body: California law restricts what the department and the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement may do with individually identifiable information submitted in a pay data report: it is unlawful for an officer or employee of either agency to make that information public before an investigation or enforcement proceeding involving it has begun, and even then only to the extent necessary for that proceeding. Individually identifiable information submitted under this section is treated as confidential and is not subject to disclosure under the California Public Records Act. The department must maintain pay data reports for not less than 10 years. The statute also defines three key terms for purposes of this section: an “employee” is an individual on an employer's payroll, including a part-time individual, for whom the employer must withhold federal social security taxes; a “labor contractor” is an individual or entity that supplies, with or without a contract, a client employer with workers to perform labor within the client employer's usual course of business; and an “establishment” is an economic unit producing goods or services.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Government Code section 12999(g), (h), (j), and (k)(1) through (k)(3)), used as real evidence of California's confidentiality protections, recordkeeping duration, and statutory definitions — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. All citations below are paragraphs of two subdivisions, (g)/(h)/(j) and (k), of one section; they are treated here as one source describing related confidentiality, retention, and definitional provisions, not as independent corroborating sources. This clause does not restate subdivision (i), which separately allows the department to publish aggregate, de-identified reports; that provision is not quoted here. This clause does not itself determine whether any particular piece of information submitted by any particular employer is or is not “individually identifiable information” within this definition, and is informational only.
