clauses.title: Self-Assessment Summary and Signature
Charging Order Information Sheet — Purpose and Scope
clauses.body: This information sheet relates to {{companyName}}, a limited liability company formed under the law of {{stateOfFormation}}, and to {{memberName}}, a member (or transferee of a member's interest) of {{companyName}}. It describes California Corporations Code § 17705.03, part of the California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, which governs the remedy available to a judgment creditor of an LLC member or transferee against that person's transferable interest in the LLC — as distinct from any remedy against the LLC's own assets, and as distinct from this corpus's LLC Operating Agreement and LLC Dissolution and Cancellation documents, which address the LLC's own internal governance and winding up rather than a third party's remedy against an individual member's interest. This information sheet does not determine whether any judgment has been or will be entered against {{memberName}}, does not determine whether any specific creditor is entitled to a charging order or any further relief under § 17705.03, and does not evaluate any specific creditor's, member's, or transferee's rights or exposure under any specific set of facts. Whether a charging order should issue, and what further relief a court should order, are determinations made by a court applying § 17705.03 to the facts and evidence presented in that proceeding.

clauses.title: What a Charging Order Is and Does
clauses.body: Under California law, a judgment creditor of an LLC member or of a transferee of a member's interest may apply to a court for a charging order against that person's transferable interest in the LLC, for the unsatisfied amount of the judgment. A charging order operates in two ways at once: it constitutes a lien on the judgment debtor's transferable interest in the LLC, and it requires the LLC itself to pay over to the person the charging order was issued to any distribution that would otherwise be paid to the judgment debtor. The charging order therefore reaches only the judgment debtor's right to receive distributions and other economic rights that make up the transferable interest — the statute does not, by its own terms, transfer membership status, voting rights, or management rights to the judgment creditor.
clauses.gap: This clause is drawn entirely from California Corporations Code § 17705.03(a). It states only what a charging order is and what it directly requires (a lien plus a pay-over obligation on the LLC); it does not address separately, from any other statute, what rights a transferee (as opposed to the original member) otherwise holds, since that is addressed by a different section (§ 17705.02) that this document does not independently verify or cover here.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17705.03(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, charging order against a member's or transferee's interest
citations.quote: On application by a judgment creditor of a member or transferee, a court may enter a charging order against the transferable interest of the judgment debtor for the unsatisfied amount of the judgment. A charging order constitutes a lien on a judgment debtor’s transferable interest and requires the limited liability company to pay over to the person to which the charging order was issued any distribution that would otherwise be paid to the judgment debtor.

clauses.title: The Charging Order Is the Exclusive Remedy Against a Member's Interest
clauses.body: California's LLC statute states directly that the charging order procedure is the exclusive remedy by which a person seeking to enforce a judgment against a member or transferee may, acting as judgment creditor, satisfy the judgment out of the judgment debtor's transferable interest in the LLC. This exclusivity language governs remedies against the member's or transferee's transferable interest specifically — it does not, by its own terms, address or limit a creditor's remedies against assets that belong to the LLC itself rather than to the individual member, which is a different question from the one § 17705.03 answers.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes California Corporations Code § 17705.03(f) directly and states only what that subdivision itself says. This document does not address, and takes no position on, whether or how a creditor might separately reach LLC-owned assets directly (for example, through a judgment against the LLC itself), since that is outside the scope of what § 17705.03 governs and was not independently researched here.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17705.03(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, exclusive remedy against a transferable interest
citations.quote: This section provides the exclusive remedy by which a person seeking to enforce a judgment against a member or transferee may, in the capacity of judgment creditor, satisfy the judgment from the judgment debtor’s transferable interest.

clauses.title: What a Court May Additionally Order, Including Foreclosure
clauses.body: Beyond entering the charging order itself, the statute lists specific further steps a court may take, to the extent necessary to effectuate collection of distributions under a charging order already in effect: the court may appoint a receiver of the distributions subject to the charging order, with the power to make all inquiries the judgment debtor might have made, and the court may make all other orders necessary to give effect to the charging order. The statute also authorizes foreclosure specifically, but only upon a particular showing: if it is shown that distributions under the charging order will not pay the judgment debt within a reasonable time, the court may foreclose the lien and order the sale of the transferable interest. Even then, a purchaser at that foreclosure sale acquires only the transferable interest itself — the purchaser does not thereby become a member of the LLC, and the purchaser's rights are governed by the separate statute addressing transferees' rights generally.
clauses.gap: This clause is drawn entirely from California Corporations Code § 17705.03(b), a single subdivision with three numbered paragraphs (receiver appointment, other necessary orders, and conditioned foreclosure), reproduced together here because all three describe the same category of relief (further court orders to effectuate an existing charging order) and the third expressly conditions foreclosure on a showing not required for the first two. This document does not evaluate, for any specific case, whether distributions would or would not pay a judgment debt within a reasonable time, or whether a court would exercise its discretion to appoint a receiver or order foreclosure on any particular facts. Paragraph (b)(3)'s cross-reference to Section 17705.02 (governing a transferee's rights generally) was not independently verified against that section's own text and is stated here only as the cross-reference § 17705.03 itself makes, not as an independent characterization of what Section 17705.02 provides.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17705.03(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, further court orders and conditioned foreclosure
citations.quote: To the extent necessary to effectuate the collection of distributions pursuant to a charging order in effect under subdivision (a), the court may do any of the following: (1) Appoint a receiver of the distributions subject to the charging order, with the power to make all inquiries the judgment debtor might have made. (2) Make all other orders necessary to give effect to the charging order. (3) Upon a showing that distributions under a charging order will not pay the judgment debt within a reasonable time, foreclose the lien and order the sale of the transferable interest. The purchaser at the foreclosure sale obtains only the transferable interest, does not thereby become a member, and is subject to Section 17705.02.

clauses.title: Extinguishing the Charging Order and the LLC's or Other Members' Redemption Right
clauses.body: The statute gives two distinct paths to end a charging order before any foreclosure sale takes place. First, at any time before foreclosure, the member or transferee whose transferable interest is subject to the charging order may extinguish it by satisfying the judgment and filing a certified copy of the satisfaction with the court that issued the charging order. Second, and separately, at any time before foreclosure, the LLC itself, or one or more members whose transferable interests are not subject to the charging order, may pay the judgment creditor the full amount due under the judgment; doing so lets the LLC or those members succeed to the rights of the judgment creditor, including the charging order itself. The statute does not require the LLC or any other member to make this payment — it authorizes them to do so, at their option, as a way of controlling who holds the charging order against the debtor-member's interest.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on two adjacent subdivisions of the same statutory section, California Corporations Code § 17705.03(c) (the debtor-member's own extinguishment right) and § 17705.03(d) (the LLC's or other members' optional redemption right) — not independently sourced provisions, but two related mechanisms within the same section reproduced together because both operate on the same "before foreclosure" timing and both terminate the charging order in the debtor-member's favor. This document does not evaluate whether the LLC named in this information sheet or any specific member would choose to exercise the redemption right described here, and does not state that any such payment is required.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17705.03(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, extinguishing a charging order by satisfying the judgment
citations.quote: At any time before foreclosure under paragraph (3) of subdivision (b), the member or transferee whose transferable interest is subject to a charging order under subdivision (a) may extinguish the charging order by satisfying the judgment and filing a certified copy of the satisfaction with the court that issued the charging order.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17705.03(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, LLC or other members' right to pay the judgment and succeed to the creditor's rights
citations.quote: At any time before foreclosure under paragraph (3) of subdivision (b), a limited liability company or one or more members whose transferable interests are not subject to the charging order may pay to the judgment creditor the full amount due under the judgment and thereby succeed to the rights of the judgment creditor, including the charging order.

clauses.title: Exemption Laws Are Preserved — The Statute Does Not Itself Compel a Distribution
clauses.body: The statute expressly preserves any exemption laws that would otherwise apply to a member's or transferee's transferable interest: the LLC statute governing charging orders does not deprive any member or transferee of the benefit of any exemption laws applicable to that person's transferable interest. Separately, the mechanics described elsewhere in this statute show that a charging order operates by redirecting distributions the LLC decides to make, and by lien and (where the statutory showing is met) foreclosure of the interest itself — the statute's own text does not say that a charging order, by itself, forces the LLC or its other members to declare or make a distribution that the LLC would not otherwise have made.
clauses.gap: The exemption-law preservation is drawn directly from California Corporations Code § 17705.03(e). The second sentence of this clause is not a separate statutory quotation; it is this document's own observation, based on the absence of any compel-a-distribution language anywhere in the verified text of § 17705.03(a) through (f), that the section's mechanism (lien plus pay-over-if-distributed, or foreclosure on the stated showing) is what the statute provides, rather than a power to force a distribution — this document does not cite a separate statute or case establishing that no other law could compel a distribution, and takes no position on whether some other statute, the LLC's operating agreement, or common-law fiduciary duties might independently bear on if or when distributions must be made.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17705.03(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, preservation of exemption laws
citations.quote: This title does not deprive any member or transferee of the benefit of any exemption laws applicable to the member’s or transferee’s transferable interest.

clauses.title: Preparation and Signature Block — Charging Order Information Sheet
clauses.body:

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{authorizedSignerName}}: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet describes California Corporations Code § 17705.03 — the charging order remedy available to a judgment creditor of an LLC member or transferee, the exclusivity of that remedy against the member's or transferee's transferable interest, the further orders (including conditioned foreclosure) a court may make, the ways a charging order may be extinguished or redeemed before foreclosure, and the statute's preservation of exemption laws. It is educational only. It does not determine whether any judgment exists or will be entered against {{memberName}}, does not determine whether any specific creditor is entitled to a charging order or further relief, and does not constitute legal advice. Whether a charging order should issue, and what further relief is appropriate, are determinations made by a court applying this statute to the specific facts and evidence in that proceeding.]

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope — Shareholder Derivative Lawsuit Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This information sheet relates to {{companyName}}, a {{entityType}} organized under the laws of California, and to {{shareholderName}}'s status as a shareholder of {{companyName}}. It describes California Corporations Code § 800 — the statute setting the procedural conditions a shareholder must satisfy to bring or maintain a lawsuit "in right of" a corporation, meaning a derivative suit brought on the corporation's behalf to redress a wrong to the corporation itself, rather than an ordinary lawsuit brought in the shareholder's own name for a wrong done directly to that shareholder. Transaction or conduct this information sheet may relate to, if applicable: {{transactionDescription}}.

This information sheet is educational only. It does not itself constitute a complaint, a demand on the board, or any other filing; does not determine whether {{shareholderName}} meets § 800's ownership, demand, or any other requirement in any specific case; and does not determine whether a court would excuse {{shareholderName}} from a requirement described below or require a bond under the statute. This document is not this project's Shareholder and Member Inspection Rights document, which covers a separate, non-litigation right to inspect and copy corporate and LLC records — this document instead focuses on the distinct procedural prerequisites for a shareholder lawsuit brought on the corporation's behalf.

clauses.title: What Counts as a "Corporation," "Board," and "Shareholder" Under This Statute
clauses.body: California Corporations Code § 800 governs any action "instituted or maintained in right of" a domestic or foreign corporation by a holder of shares or voting trust certificates — that is, a derivative suit brought to enforce a claim belonging to the corporation itself. For purposes of this statute, the terms it uses are defined more broadly than they might first appear: "corporation" includes an unincorporated association, "board" includes the managing body of an unincorporated association, "shareholder" includes a member of an unincorporated association, and "shares" includes memberships in an unincorporated association. The statute states plainly that such an action may not be instituted or maintained at all unless both of two separate conditions — described in the clauses below — are satisfied.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual statutory prerequisites for a derivative suit — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, nor a claim that these are the only requirements a derivative suit is subject to (for example, this document does not address the separate demand-futility case law and pleading standards that inform how courts apply the demand requirement described elsewhere in this document, or federal or other states' analogous derivative-suit statutes). Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 800) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 800(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, definitions applicable to the shareholder derivative action statute
citations.quote: As used in this section, “corporation” includes an unincorporated association; “board” includes the managing body of an unincorporated association; “shareholder” includes a member of an unincorporated association; and “shares” includes memberships in an unincorporated association.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 800(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, both statutory conditions required before a derivative action may proceed
citations.quote: No action may be instituted or maintained in right of any domestic or foreign corporation by any holder of shares or of voting trust certificates of the corporation unless both of the following conditions exist:

clauses.title: First Condition — Plaintiff Must Have Held Shares at the Time of the Transaction Complained Of
clauses.body: The first of the two statutory conditions is a contemporaneous-ownership requirement. The plaintiff must allege in the complaint that they were a shareholder — of record or beneficially — or a holder of voting trust certificates, at the time of the transaction (or any part of it) that they complain of, or that their shares or voting trust certificates later devolved on them by operation of law from someone who did hold them at that time (for example, through inheritance). A shareholder who cannot make that allegation is not automatically barred: the statute lets a court, in its discretion, allow the action to proceed anyway on a preliminary motion and hearing, if the shareholder shows, among other things, that there is a strong prima facie case for the underlying claim, that no other similar action has been or is likely to be brought, that the shares were acquired before the wrongdoing was disclosed to the plaintiff or the public, that the defendant would otherwise be able to keep a gain from a willful breach of fiduciary duty, and that granting relief will not unjustly enrich the corporation or another shareholder.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine, real requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and not a claim about whether any particular shareholder's facts would satisfy either the contemporaneous-ownership rule or the discretionary exception to it. The statute lists five specific factors a court "shall consider" in deciding whether to allow the discretionary exception; this document paraphrases all five but does not resolve how a court would weigh them in any particular case. Both citations below are the same subsection of the same statutory section (§ 800(b)(1)) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 800(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, contemporaneous-ownership requirement for a derivative plaintiff
citations.quote: The plaintiff alleges in the complaint that plaintiff was a shareholder, of record or beneficially, or the holder of voting trust certificates at the time of the transaction or any part thereof of which plaintiff complains or that plaintiff’s shares or voting trust certificates thereafter devolved upon plaintiff by operation of law from a holder who was a holder at the time of the transaction or any part thereof complained of

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 800(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, discretionary court exception to the contemporaneous-ownership requirement
citations.quote: provided, that any shareholder who does not meet these requirements may nevertheless be allowed in the discretion of the court to maintain the action on a preliminary showing to and determination by the court, by motion and after a hearing, at which the court shall consider such evidence, by affidavit or testimony, as it deems material, that (i) there is a strong prima facie case in favor of the claim asserted on behalf of the corporation, (ii) no other similar action has been or is likely to be instituted, (iii) the plaintiff acquired the shares before there was disclosure to the public or to the plaintiff of the wrongdoing of which plaintiff complains, (iv) unless the action can be maintained the defendant may retain a gain derived from defendant’s willful breach of a fiduciary duty, and (v) the requested relief will not result in unjust enrichment of the corporation or any shareholder of the corporation

clauses.title: Second Condition — Pleading Efforts to Secure Board Action, or the Reasons for Not Making Them
clauses.body: The second statutory condition is a pleading requirement tied to the corporation's board. The plaintiff must allege in the complaint, with particularity, either their efforts to get the board to take the action the plaintiff wants, or the reasons for not making that effort. The plaintiff must also allege that they informed the corporation or the board, in writing, of the ultimate facts of each claim against each defendant, or instead delivered to the corporation or the board a true copy of the complaint the plaintiff proposes to file. The statute itself gives the plaintiff two paths to satisfy this second condition — pursue a pre-suit demand and plead those efforts, or plead particularized reasons for not making a demand — without specifying in its own text what reasons a court will accept as sufficient to excuse a demand.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine pleading requirement tied to board demand or its excuse — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and not a claim about what showing would satisfy a "reasons for not making such effort" allegation in any specific case (that determination is fact-specific and, if contested, is for a court applying this statute and the case law interpreting it, which this document does not catalog). This document also does not address the separate, board-controlled procedure by which a corporation can seek dismissal of a derivative suit through an independent committee's determination that the suit is not in the corporation's best interest — that is governed by different authority than the pleading condition described here. The citation below is a single subsection of a single statutory section (§ 800(b)(2)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 800(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, demand-on-the-board pleading requirement or excuse
citations.quote: The plaintiff alleges in the complaint with particularity plaintiff’s efforts to secure from the board such action as plaintiff desires, or the reasons for not making such effort, and alleges further that plaintiff has either informed the corporation or the board in writing of the ultimate facts of each cause of action against each defendant or delivered to the corporation or the board a true copy of the complaint which plaintiff proposes to file.

clauses.title: A Motion Requiring the Plaintiff to Furnish a Security Bond
clauses.body: Separately from the two pleading conditions above, § 800 lets the corporation or an individual defendant who is (or was, at the relevant time) an officer or director move the court, within 30 days after being served, for an order requiring the plaintiff to furnish a bond to secure the potential expenses of defending the suit. The court may extend that 30-day window, for good cause, by up to an additional 60 days. The motion must rest on one or both of two specific grounds stated in the statute: that there is no reasonable possibility the claim will benefit the corporation or its shareholders, or that the moving party (if not the corporation itself) did not participate in the transaction being complained of in any capacity. At the hearing on the motion, the court considers evidence relevant to those grounds and to the probable reasonable expenses — including attorneys' fees — the corporation and the moving party are likely to incur defending the action; if the moving party establishes a probability supporting one of the grounds, the court fixes the bond amount, capped at $50,000, covering expenses that may include amounts the corporation could become liable for under a separate indemnification statute (Corp. Code § 317). A ruling granting the motion does not decide the merits of the underlying claim.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine bond-motion mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. It's worth flagging a common imprecise shorthand for this statute: the bond requirement is sometimes summarized as applying to a shareholder who owns only a "small percentage" of the corporation's shares, but the statutory text quoted here does not condition the motion, or exempt any shareholder from it, based on the size of the plaintiff's ownership stake at all — the two grounds for the motion turn on the claim's likely benefit to the corporation and on the moving defendant's non-participation in the underlying transaction, not on how many shares the plaintiff holds. As a practical matter a shareholder with a small stake is more likely to be the one facing such a motion (a large, institutional shareholder's derivative suit is less likely to be characterized as lacking any reasonable possibility of benefiting the corporation), but that is a practical tendency, not a textual ownership threshold in this statute. This document does not address how a court would evaluate "no reasonable possibility" of benefit in any specific case, or the separate indemnification statute (§ 317) the bond-expense provision cross-references. Citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 800(c), (d)) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 800(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, motion for an order requiring a security bond and its grounds
citations.quote: the corporation or the defendant may move the court for an order, upon notice and hearing, requiring the plaintiff to furnish a bond as hereinafter provided. The motion shall be based upon one or both of the following grounds: (1) That there is no reasonable possibility that the prosecution of the cause of action alleged in the complaint against the moving party will benefit the corporation or its shareholders. (2) That the moving party, if other than the corporation, did not participate in the transaction complained of in any capacity.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 800(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, $50,000 statutory cap on the bond amount
citations.quote: the court shall fix the amount of the bond, not to exceed fifty thousand dollars ($50,000), to be furnished by the plaintiff for reasonable expenses, including attorneys’ fees, which may be incurred by the moving party and the corporation in connection with the action, including expenses for which the corporation may become liable pursuant to Section 317.

clauses.title: What Happens If the Bond Is, or Is Not, Furnished
clauses.body: The statute sets out concrete consequences tied to the bond. If the court determines a bond must be furnished as to one or more defendants, the action is dismissed as to that defendant or those defendants unless the required bond is furnished within whatever reasonable time the court sets. Conversely, if the plaintiff furnishes a bond in the full $50,000 aggregate amount — whether before or after a motion is made, or before or after any order on that motion — the plaintiff has satisfied the statute's bond requirement and any order for a bond already made, any pending motion on the subject is dismissed, and no further or additional bond may be required. Finally, once a bond motion is filed, no defendant needs to file any pleadings, and the prosecution of the action is stayed, until 10 days after the motion has been resolved.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual procedural consequences tied to the bond requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. This document does not address what "such reasonable time as may be fixed by the court" means in any specific case, nor whether or how a dismissal under this provision could be appealed or otherwise challenged. Citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 800(d), (e), (f)) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 800(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, dismissal for failure to furnish a court-ordered bond
citations.quote: If the court, upon the motion, makes a determination that a bond shall be furnished by the plaintiff as to any one or more defendants, the action shall be dismissed as to the defendant or defendants, unless the bond required by the court has been furnished within such reasonable time as may be fixed by the court.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 800(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, effect of voluntarily furnishing the full $50,000 bond
citations.quote: If the plaintiff shall, either before or after a motion is made pursuant to subdivision (c), or any order or determination pursuant to the motion, furnish a bond in the aggregate amount of fifty thousand dollars ($50,000) to secure the reasonable expenses of the parties entitled to make the motion, the plaintiff has complied with the requirements of this section and with any order for a bond theretofore made, and any such motion then pending shall be dismissed and no further or additional bond shall be required.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 800(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, stay of the action while a bond motion is pending
citations.quote: If a motion is filed pursuant to subdivision (c), no pleadings need be filed by the corporation or any other defendant and the prosecution of the action shall be stayed until 10 days after the motion has been disposed of.

It is not a completed complaint, demand letter, or bond, does not determine whether any requirement described in it is satisfied in a specific case, and does not constitute legal advice. clauses.title: Declaration of Parties and Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Automatic Temporary Restraining Orders (ATROS) Information Sheet concerns a proceeding for {{proceedingType}} between {{petitionerName}}, as petitioner, and {{respondentName}}, as respondent, filed or to be filed in the California superior court for {{countyOfFiling}}. It describes the temporary restraining orders that California Family Code section 2040 requires be included in the summons for such a proceeding — restraining orders that attach automatically upon the filing of the petition and the issuance of the summons, without either party separately requesting them and without a judge separately signing a further order. It is not itself a summons, petition, or restraining order, and completing it does not create, modify, or terminate any restraining order affecting {{petitionerName}} or {{respondentName}}. Only the summons issued in an actual proceeding, applying the statute described here, does that.

clauses.title: ATROS Attach Automatically to the Summons in a Dissolution, Nullity, or Legal Separation Proceeding
clauses.body: California Family Code section 2040(a) states that, in addition to the contents required by Code of Civil Procedure section 412.20, the summons in a covered proceeding "shall contain a temporary restraining order" — the orders are a required part of the summons itself, not a separate order a party must ask a judge to sign. Family Code section 231 states that this restraining-order framework applies to a summons issued under Family Code section 2040, which governs a proceeding for dissolution of marriage, for nullity of marriage, or for legal separation of the parties, and separately to a summons issued under Family Code section 7700, which governs a proceeding under the Uniform Parentage Act. Because the restraining orders described in this document are a mandatory component of the summons in these proceedings, they bind both the party who filed the petition and the other party without either party filing a separate request or declaration of abuse — unlike a domestic violence restraining order, which a party must actively request based on alleged abuse.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on two different, separately codified Family Code sections — section 2040(a) (the operative-text requirement that the summons contain the restraining order) and section 231 (the scope provision listing which types of summons the restraining-order framework applies to) — rather than multiple subsections of a single section, so no single-section disclosure applies here. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California structures its automatic restraining-order process for dissolution, nullity, and legal-separation proceedings — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petitioner's or respondent's proceeding, or that an equivalent automatic mechanism exists in any other state. This document addresses only the restraining orders under Family Code section 2040 (the dissolution/nullity/legal-separation branch of section 231); it does not address the separate restraining orders under Family Code section 7700 for Uniform Parentage Act proceedings, which this document's research did not independently verify.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2040(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the summons must contain the temporary restraining order
citations.quote: In addition to the contents required by Section 412.20 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the summons shall contain a temporary restraining order:

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 231 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: scope: applies to summonses under section 2040
citations.quote: This part applies to a temporary restraining order in a summons issued under any of the following provisions: (a) Section 2040 (proceeding for dissolution of marriage, for nullity of marriage, or for legal separation of the parties).

clauses.title: When ATROS Take Effect for the Petitioner and the Respondent, How Long They Last, and How They Are Enforced
clauses.body: California Family Code section 233(a) states that the temporary restraining order in the summons takes effect against a party at a different moment depending on which party that is: it is in effect against the petitioner upon the filing of the petition and issuance of the summons, and it is in effect against the respondent upon personal service of the petition and summons on the respondent, or upon the respondent's waiver and acceptance of service. Once in effect against a given party, the order remains in effect against that party until final judgment is entered, the petition is dismissed, or the court orders otherwise. Section 233(b) states that the order is enforceable anywhere in the state, but that a local law enforcement agency need not enforce it unless that agency has received mailed notice of the order, has otherwise received a copy of it, or has been shown a copy by the officer enforcing it. Section 233(c) states that a willful and knowing violation of the child-removal order is punishable under Penal Code section 278.5, and that a willful and knowing violation of any of the other orders in the summons is punishable under Penal Code section 273.6.
clauses.gap: This clause is drawn from the three subdivisions — (a), (b), and (c) — of a single Family Code section, section 233, so this is a single-section citation rather than independent corroboration from separate sections; the subdivisions are quoted together because they form one continuous statutory paragraph on timing, duration, and enforcement. Section 233 sits in Family Code Division 2 (General Provisions), not in Division 6 alongside section 2040 itself; this document treats it as governing the section 2040 restraining orders addressed here because Family Code section 231 (quoted in a separate clause of this document) expressly states that section 233's framework applies to a summons issued under section 2040. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's own timing and enforcement rules for this restraining order — not a claim about any other state's procedure, and not a determination that a specific violation in a specific case meets the statutory standard for a willful and knowing violation; that determination belongs to a court applying the statute and the Penal Code sections it references to particular facts.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 233(a)–(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: effective dates by party, duration, enforceability, and violation consequences
citations.quote: (a) Upon filing the petition and issuance of the summons and upon personal service of the petition and summons on the respondent or upon waiver and acceptance of service by the respondent, the temporary restraining order under this part shall be in effect against the parties until the final judgment is entered or the petition is dismissed, or until further order of the court. (b) The temporary restraining order is enforceable in any place in this state, but is not enforceable by a law enforcement agency of a political subdivision unless that law enforcement agency has received mailed notice of the order or has otherwise received a copy of the order or the officer enforcing the order has been shown a copy of the order. (c) A willful and knowing violation of the order included in the summons by removing a child from the state without the written consent of the other party or an order of the court is punishable as provided in Section 278.5 of the Penal Code. A willful and knowing violation of any of the other orders included in the summons is punishable as provided in Section 273.6 of the Penal Code.

clauses.title: Restraint on Transferring or Encumbering Property, and Its Stated Exceptions
clauses.body: California Family Code section 2040(a)(2)(A) restrains both parties from transferring, encumbering, hypothecating, concealing, or otherwise disposing of any real or personal property — whether community, quasi-community, or separate — without the other party's written consent or a court order. The statute states its own exceptions on the face of that same restraint: a transfer in the usual course of business, and a transfer for the necessities of life. The same provision also requires each party to notify the other of a proposed extraordinary expenditure at least five business days before incurring it, and to account to the court for extraordinary expenditures made after service of the summons. Section 2040(a)(2)(B) states a further, separate exception: the restraining order does not preclude a party from using community property, quasi-community property, or the party's own separate property to pay reasonable attorney's fees and costs to retain counsel in the proceeding, though a party who uses community or quasi-community property for that purpose must account to the community for its use, and a party who uses property later determined to be the other party's separate property must account to that other party for its use.
clauses.gap: This clause is drawn from subparagraphs (A) and (B) of a single paragraph — Family Code section 2040(a)(2) — of a single section, so this is a single-section citation, not independent corroboration from separate statutes. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's own property-transfer restraint and its stated exceptions — not a claim about any other state's equivalent restraining-order process. Whether a specific transaction falls within "the usual course of business," qualifies as a necessity of life, or was made with adequate written consent is a factual and legal determination this clause does not make for any individual case.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2040(a)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: property-transfer restraint and its exceptions
citations.quote: Restraining both parties from transferring, encumbering, hypothecating, concealing, or in any way disposing of, any property, real or personal, whether community, quasi-community, or separate, without the written consent of the other party or an order of the court, except in the usual course of business or for the necessities of life, and requiring each party to notify the other party of proposed extraordinary expenditures at least five business days before incurring those expenditures and to account to the court for all extraordinary expenditures made after service of the summons on that party.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2040(a)(2)(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: exception for paying attorney's fees and costs
citations.quote: the restraining order shall not preclude a party from using community property, quasi-community property, or the party’s own separate property to pay reasonable attorney’s fees and costs in order to retain legal counsel in the proceeding.

clauses.title: Restraint on Removing a Minor Child From the State or Applying for a Passport
clauses.body: California Family Code section 2040(a)(1) restrains both parties from removing a minor child of the parties from the state, and from applying for a new or replacement passport for that child, without either the other party's prior written consent or a court order. As with the property restraint described elsewhere in this document, the statute states the exceptions — prior written consent or a court order — on the face of the restraint itself, rather than leaving them to be inferred.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's own restriction on removing a child from the state or seeking a passport during a covered proceeding — not a claim about any other state's law, and not a determination of whether a specific planned trip or passport application in a specific case would violate this restraint or fall within its consent or court-order exception. Whether a particular consent was sufficiently "written" and given by the party with authority to give it is a factual question this clause does not resolve.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2040(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: restraint on removing a minor child from the state or applying for a passport
citations.quote: Restraining both parties from removing the minor child or children of the parties, if any, from the state, or from applying for a new or replacement passport for the minor child or children, without the prior written consent of the other party or an order of the court.

clauses.title: Restraint on Canceling Insurance Coverage or Changing Beneficiaries
clauses.body: California Family Code section 2040(a)(3), in the version of the statute operative from January 1, 2026 through January 1, 2027, restrains both parties from cashing, borrowing against, canceling, transferring, disposing of, or changing the beneficiaries of any insurance or other coverage — including life, health, automobile, and disability coverage — held for the benefit of the parties or their child or children for whom support may be ordered.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's own restraint on insurance and coverage changes during a covered proceeding — not a claim about any other state's law. Family Code section 2040 was amended by the same 2025 enactment (Stats. 2025, Ch. 48) in two operative-date phases: the text quoted above is Sec. 1 of that chapter, operative January 1, 2026 through January 1, 2027 (the version in effect as of this clause's checked date), and Sec. 2 of the same chapter adds further language to this identical paragraph — "allowing to lapse for nonpayment of premiums, failing to renew" — becoming operative January 1, 2027. Both citations below are two operative-date versions of the same enacted chapter and the same statutory paragraph, not independent corroboration from separate sources; the second is included only to disclose the change already fixed to take effect, not as evidence beyond what the first citation already establishes.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2040(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text; operative Jan. 1, 2026 – Jan. 1, 2027)
citations.cite: restraint on insurance/coverage changes and beneficiary designations
citations.quote: Restraining both parties from cashing, borrowing against, canceling, transferring, disposing of, or changing the beneficiaries of insurance or other coverage, including life, health, automobile, and disability, held for the benefit of the parties and their child or children for whom support may be ordered.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2040(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text; operative Jan. 1, 2027)

clauses.title: Restraint on Nonprobate Transfers, and What ATROS Do Not Restrain
clauses.body: California Family Code section 2040(a)(4) restrains both parties from creating or modifying a nonprobate transfer — an instrument other than a will that transfers property on death, such as a revocable trust, a pay-on-death account, or a transfer-on-death deed — in a manner that affects the disposition of the property it covers, without the other party's written consent or a court order. Section 2040(b) then states five things the statute does not restrain: creating, modifying, or revoking a will; revoking a nonprobate transfer such as a revocable trust according to its own terms, provided notice of the change is filed and served on the other party before the change takes effect; eliminating a right of survivorship to property, on the same filed-and-served-notice condition; creating an unfunded revocable or irrevocable trust; and filing a disclaimer under Probate Code Part 8 (commencing with section 260).
clauses.gap: This clause is drawn from subdivisions (a)(4) and (b) of a single Family Code section, section 2040, so this is a single-section citation, not independent corroboration from separate statutes. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's own nonprobate-transfer restraint and its stated exceptions — not a claim about any other state's law. This clause does not restate section 2040(d)'s statutory definition of "nonprobate transfer" in full, or the related carve-out in section 2040(d)(2) for a beneficiary designation in an insurance policy (which this document's insurance-restraint clause addresses separately); whether a specific instrument qualifies as a nonprobate transfer, or whether a specific notice was timely "filed and served" before a change took effect, is a factual and legal determination this clause does not make for any individual case.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2040(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: restraint on creating or modifying a nonprobate transfer
citations.quote: Restraining both parties from creating a nonprobate transfer or modifying a nonprobate transfer in a manner that affects the disposition of property subject to the transfer, without the written consent of the other party or an order of the court.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2040(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: five things ATROS do not restrain
citations.quote: This section does not restrain any of the following: (1) Creation, modification, or revocation of a will. (2) Revocation of a nonprobate transfer, including a revocable trust, pursuant to the instrument, provided that notice of the change is filed and served on the other party before the change takes effect. (3) Elimination of a right of survivorship to property, provided that notice of the change is filed and served on the other party before the change takes effect. (4) Creation of an unfunded revocable or irrevocable trust. (5) Execution and filing of a disclaimer pursuant to Part 8 (commencing with Section 260) of Division 2 of the Probate Code.

clauses.title: Declaration of Parties and Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Watts Charges and Epstein Credits Information Sheet concerns {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}, who separated on {{separationDate}} and whose marital dissolution or legal separation proceeding is pending, or may be filed, in the California superior court for {{countyOfFiling}}. It describes two related California case-law doctrines that can arise when such a proceeding remains pending after the date of separation but before trial or settlement: a "Watts charge," under which a spouse who has exclusive use of a community property asset after separation may be required to reimburse the community for the reasonable value of that use, and an "Epstein credit," under which a spouse who uses separate property funds to pay a preexisting community debt after separation may be entitled to reimbursement from the community for those payments. This information sheet states what California case law and the Family Code say about these two doctrines in general terms. It does not determine, calculate, or assert that either doctrine applies to {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}'s specific property, debts, or circumstances; whether a Watts charge or Epstein credit applies in a particular case, and in what amount, is a matter for the court to decide based on the specific facts, or for {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} to resolve by their own written agreement.

clauses.title: Watts Charges — Reimbursement for a Spouse's Exclusive Post-Separation Use of a Community Asset
clauses.body: California case law recognizes that where one spouse has had the exclusive use of a community property asset — such as the family residence — after the date of separation and before trial, a court has the authority to require that spouse to reimburse the community for the reasonable value of that exclusive use. This reimbursement is commonly called a "Watts charge," after the Court of Appeal decision recognizing it. A Watts charge is not automatic: whether to order one, and in what amount, is a determination the trial court makes after considering all the circumstances under which exclusive use or possession came about.
clauses.gap: This is real California case law, used as evidence of what a published Court of Appeal decision actually held about a court's authority to charge a spouse for exclusive post-separation use of a community asset — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case, and not a claim that a Watts charge will be ordered, or in what amount, in any specific case. All three citations below are drawn from the same case, In re Marriage of Watts (1985) 171 Cal.App.3d 366 — different passages of the same opinion, not independent corroborating sources. Watts itself distinguishes this exclusive-use-reimbursement doctrine from the separate doctrine, addressed in this document's companion clauses, concerning a spouse's use of separate funds to pay community debts after separation (an Epstein credit) — the third quotation below is Watts's own statement of that distinction. This document does not address how a court values the "reasonable value of use" in a particular case (for example, by fair rental value), which Watts itself left to the trial court's factual determination on remand.

citations.case: In re Marriage of Watts, 171 Cal.App.3d 366, 374 (1985) (California Court of Appeal, Fifth Appellate District; opinion text via CourtListener)
citations.cite: a spouse may be required to reimburse the community for the value of exclusive post-separation use of a community asset
citations.quote: We hold that the trial court erred in concluding that it had no authority to reimburse the community for the value of John’s exclusive use of the family residence and the medical practice between the date of separation and the date of trial.

citations.case: In re Marriage of Watts, 171 Cal.App.3d 366, 374 (1985) (California Court of Appeal, Fifth Appellate District; opinion text via CourtListener)
citations.cite: reimbursement is a discretionary, fact-specific determination on remand, not an automatic order
citations.quote: Upon remand, the trial court will determine whether John should be required to reimburse the community for the value of his use of community assets after the date of separation in accordance with its findings. That determination should be made after taking into account all the circumstances under which exclusive possession was ordered.

citations.case: In re Marriage of Watts, 171 Cal.App.3d 366, 373 (1985) (California Court of Appeal, Fifth Appellate District; opinion text via CourtListener)
citations.cite: Watts distinguishes exclusive-use reimbursement from reimbursement for separate funds used to pay community debts (the Epstein-credit doctrine)
citations.quote: The present case does not involve the use of separate property to pay community debts, and instead involves the reimbursement to the community for the exclusive use of a community property asset by one spouse.

clauses.title: Epstein Credits — Reimbursement for a Spouse's Use of Separate Funds to Pay a Community Debt After Separation
clauses.body: California case law recognizes that, although a spouse who uses separate property to pay a community obligation during marriage is generally not entitled to reimbursement absent an agreement, that no-reimbursement rule does not apply once the spouses have separated. The California Supreme Court has held that, as a general rule, a spouse who, after separation, uses earnings or other separate funds to pay a preexisting community obligation — such as a mortgage payment on the family residence — should be reimbursed for those payments from the community property upon dissolution. This reimbursement is commonly called an "Epstein credit," after the Supreme Court decision recognizing it. Reimbursement under this rule is not automatic; it is subject to exceptions addressed in this document's companion clause.
clauses.gap: This is real California Supreme Court case law, used as evidence of what the court actually held about reimbursement for separate funds used to pay community debts after separation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case, and not a claim that an Epstein credit will be awarded, or in what amount, in any specific case. Both citations below are drawn from the same case, In re Marriage of Epstein (1979) 24 Cal.3d 76 — different passages of the same opinion (the Supreme Court's own statement adopting the rule, and its statement of the rule itself), not independent corroborating sources. The Supreme Court adopted this rule from a Court of Appeal decision, In re Marriage of Smith (1978) 79 Cal.App.3d 725, quoting that decision's language directly rather than restating it; this document cites Epstein, where the language became binding California Supreme Court authority, rather than Smith itself.

citations.case: In re Marriage of Epstein, 24 Cal.3d 76, 84 (1979) (California Supreme Court; opinion text via CourtListener)
citations.cite: the Supreme Court expressly adopts the reimbursement rule from In re Marriage of Smith as its own holding
citations.quote: we agree with the conclusion of In re Marriage of Smith, and adopt as the view of this court the following portion of the Court of Appeal opinion of Justice Kaufman

citations.case: In re Marriage of Epstein, 24 Cal.3d 76, 84-85 (1979) (California Supreme Court; opinion text via CourtListener)
citations.cite: the general rule: separate funds used after separation to pay a preexisting community obligation should be reimbursed from the community upon dissolution
citations.quote: as a general rule, a spouse who, after separation of the parties, uses earnings or other separate funds to pay preexisting community obligations should be reimbursed therefor out of the community property upon dissolution. However, there are a number of situations in which reimbursement is inappropriate, so reimbursement should not be ordered automatically.

clauses.title: Limits on Epstein Credits — When Reimbursement Should Not Be Ordered
clauses.body: The reimbursement rule described in this document's companion clause is not automatic. California case law identifies several circumstances in which reimbursement for a spouse's post-separation payment of a community debt should not be ordered: where the parties agreed the payment would not be reimbursed, where the paying spouse truly intended the payment as a gift, where the payment was made on account of a debt for acquiring or preserving an asset the paying spouse was using and the amount paid was not substantially more than the value of that use, or where the payment in reality discharged the paying spouse's duty to support the other spouse or a dependent child.
clauses.gap: This is the same case cited in this document's companion clause on the Epstein-credit general rule — In re Marriage of Epstein (1979) 24 Cal.3d 76 — a different, adjoining passage of the same opinion (the exceptions the Supreme Court adopted alongside the general rule), not an independent corroborating source. The first two quotations below are split into separate citation entries only because a page break in the official reporter falls between them, not because they come from different sources. This document does not address the support-obligation exception's own sub-questions (for example, whether the spouses separated "by agreement" within the meaning of former Civil Code section 5131), which the Epstein opinion itself left for the trial court to determine on remand.

citations.case: In re Marriage of Epstein, 24 Cal.3d 76, 84 (1979) (California Supreme Court; opinion text via CourtListener)
citations.cite: reimbursement should not be ordered where there was an agreement not to reimburse, or the payment was intended as a gift
citations.quote: Reimbursement should not be ordered if payment was made under circumstances in which it would have been unreasonable to expect reimbursement, for example, where there was an agreement between the parties the payment would not be reimbursed or where the paying spouse truly intended the payment to constitute a gift

citations.case: In re Marriage of Epstein, 24 Cal.3d 76, 85 (1979) (California Supreme Court; opinion text via CourtListener)
citations.cite: reimbursement should not be ordered where the amount paid was not substantially in excess of the value of the paying spouse's use of the asset
citations.quote: payment was made on account of a debt for the acquisition or preservation of an asset the paying spouse was using and the amount paid was not substantially in excess of the value of the use.

citations.case: In re Marriage of Epstein, 24 Cal.3d 76, 85 (1979) (California Supreme Court; opinion text via CourtListener)
citations.cite: reimbursement should not be ordered where the payment in reality discharged the paying spouse's duty of spousal or child support
citations.quote: Likewise, reimbursement should not be ordered where the payment on account of a preexisting community obligation constituted in reality a discharge of the paying spouse’s duty to support the other spouse or a dependent child of the parties.

clauses.title: Statutory Codification — Family Code Section 2626
clauses.body: The California Legislature has given the family court express statutory jurisdiction to order the kind of post-separation reimbursement described in this document's companion clauses on Epstein credits: a court has jurisdiction to order reimbursement, in cases it deems appropriate, for debts paid after separation but before trial.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's codification of post-separation reimbursement jurisdiction — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. This is a single statutory section (Family Code § 2626); no additional independent statutory source was found for it. By its own text, § 2626 speaks to reimbursement for "debts paid after separation but before trial" — squarely the Epstein-credit side of this document. No comparable Family Code provision was located that specifically codifies reimbursement for a spouse's exclusive post-separation use of a community asset (the Watts-charge side of this document); that doctrine, as far as this research could confirm, remains case law rather than a codified statutory rule, and this document does not claim otherwise.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2626 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the court's statutory jurisdiction to order reimbursement for debts paid after separation but before trial
citations.quote: The court has jurisdiction to order reimbursement in cases it deems appropriate for debts paid after separation but before trial.

clauses.title: Covered Employers
clauses.body: The California Family Rights Act (CFRA) applies to any private employer that directly employs five or more persons to perform services for a wage or salary, and separately to the State of California and any political or civil subdivision of the state and cities, regardless of size.
clauses.gap: Five employees is a much lower bar than the federal FMLA, which this corpus's separate FMLA document ties to a 50-employees-within-75-miles worksite test. CFRA's statute doesn't carry forward any worksite-size or geographic-clustering requirement at all — the employer-coverage question under CFRA is simply how many people the employer directly employs, not how many work at the same location. This document doesn't address how 'directly employs' is counted for a business with multiple related entities, franchises, or a staffing-agency arrangement.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(b)(4)(A) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, private-employer definition
citations.quote: Any person who directly employs five or more persons to perform services for a wage or salary.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(b)(4)(B) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, public-employer definition
citations.quote: The state, and any political or civil subdivision of the state and cities.

clauses.title: Who Is Eligible
clauses.body: {{employeeName}} is eligible for CFRA leave if {{employeeName}} has more than 12 months of service with {{companyName}} and has at least 1,250 hours of service with {{companyName}} during the previous 12-month period. A separate hours test applies to flight deck and cabin crew employees of air carriers.
clauses.gap: CFRA's eligibility test uses the same two numeric thresholds as the federal FMLA — more than 12 months of service and at least 1,250 hours in the preceding 12-month period — but the statute does not include FMLA's separate worksite-size exclusion (FMLA excludes an employee whose worksite has fewer than 50 employees within 75 miles). CFRA eligibility turns only on the employee's own service with the employer, not on how many coworkers work at the same location. This document doesn't state the specific flight-crew alternative test in subdivision (r), which substitutes a monthly-guarantee percentage and a 504-hour floor for the standard 1,250-hour test.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(a) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, eligibility and leave grant
citations.quote: any employee with more than 12 months of service with the employer, and who has at least 1,250 hours of service with the employer during the previous 12-month period or who meets the requirements of subdivision (r), to take up to a total of 12 workweeks in any 12-month period for family care and medical leave.

clauses.title: Qualifying Reasons for Leave
clauses.body: CFRA leave may be taken for the birth of a child or the placement of a child for adoption or foster care; to care for a child, parent, grandparent, grandchild, sibling, spouse, domestic partner, or designated person who has a serious health condition; because of the employee's own serious health condition that makes the employee unable to perform the job, other than a disability on account of pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions; or because of a qualifying exigency related to a spouse's, domestic partner's, child's, or parent's covered active duty in the Armed Forces of the United States.
clauses.gap: The pregnancy/childbirth exclusion in the third reason is deliberate: California handles pregnancy disability through a separate statute, Government Code Section 12945, not through CFRA — this document doesn't cover that separate law. All four citations for this clause are subdivisions of the same statute, Government Code Section 12945.2(b)(5) — they are the different parts of one definition, not independent sources confirming each other.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(b)(5)(A) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, birth/placement leave
citations.quote: Leave for reason of the birth of a child of the employee or the placement of a child with an employee in connection with the adoption or foster care of the child by the employee.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(b)(5)(B) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, family-care leave
citations.quote: Leave to care for a child, parent, grandparent, grandchild, sibling, spouse, domestic partner, or designated person who has a serious health condition.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(b)(5)(C) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, employee's own serious health condition
citations.quote: Leave because of an employee’s own serious health condition that makes the employee unable to perform the functions of the position of that employee, except for leave taken for disability on account of pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(b)(5)(D) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, qualifying exigency leave
citations.quote: Leave because of a qualifying exigency related to the covered active duty or call to covered active duty of an employee’s spouse, domestic partner, child, or parent in the Armed Forces of the United States, as specified in Section 3302.2 of the Unemployment Insurance Code.

clauses.title: Family Members Covered
clauses.body: CFRA defines 'child' to include a biological, adopted, or foster child, a stepchild, a legal ward, a child of a domestic partner, or a person to whom the employee stands in loco parentis. It separately defines 'grandparent' as a parent of the employee's parent, 'grandchild' as a child of the employee's child, and 'sibling' as a person related to another by blood, adoption, or affinity through a common legal or biological parent. An employee may also identify one 'designated person' per 12-month period — any individual related by blood or whose association with the employee is the equivalent of a family relationship.
clauses.gap: This is materially broader than the FMLA's family-member coverage in this corpus's separate FMLA document, which reaches only a spouse, child, or parent with a serious health condition. CFRA additionally reaches domestic partners, grandparents, grandchildren, siblings, and one self-identified 'designated person' per 12-month period — categories FMLA's statute does not include at all. All citations for this clause are subdivisions of the same statute, Government Code Section 12945.2(b) — different parts of one set of definitions, not independent sources.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(b)(1) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, 'child' definition
citations.quote: “Child” means a biological, adopted, or foster child, a stepchild, a legal ward, a child of a domestic partner, or a person to whom the employee stands in loco parentis.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(b)(2) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, 'designated person' definition
citations.quote: “Designated person” means any individual related by blood or whose association with the employee is the equivalent of a family relationship. The designated person may be identified by the employee at the time the employee requests the leave. An employer may limit an employee to one designated person per 12-month period for family care and medical leave.

citations.quote: “Grandchild” means a child of the employee’s child.

citations.quote: “Grandparent” means a parent of the employee’s parent.

clauses.title: Returning From Leave
clauses.body: CFRA leave is not deemed granted unless {{companyName}} provides {{employeeName}}, upon granting the leave request, a guarantee of employment in the same or a comparable position at the end of the leave. During the leave, {{employeeName}} retains employee status with {{companyName}}, and the leave does not count as a break in service for purposes of longevity, seniority under any collective bargaining agreement, or any employee benefit plan. {{employeeName}} returns from leave with no less seniority than {{employeeName}} had when the leave began, for purposes of layoff, recall, promotion, job assignment, and seniority-related benefits such as vacation.
clauses.gap: 'Comparable position' is itself statutorily defined — one with the same or similar duties and pay that can be performed at the same or similar geographic location as the position held before the leave. It doesn't have to be the identical job, and this document doesn't resolve what counts as 'similar' in a specific case. Unlike this corpus's FMLA document, which quotes a highly-compensated-employee exception letting an employer deny restoration to certain top earners, CFRA's restoration guarantee in subdivision (a) doesn't carry that same statutory exception — this document doesn't independently verify whether any comparable carve-out exists elsewhere in CFRA's implementing regulations, so none is stated here.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(a) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, restoration guarantee
citations.quote: Family care and medical leave requested pursuant to this subdivision shall not be deemed to have been granted unless the employer provides the employee, upon granting the leave request, a guarantee of employment in the same or a comparable position upon the termination of the leave.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(f) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, employee status and seniority during leave
citations.quote: During a family care and medical leave period, the employee shall retain employee status with the employer, and the leave shall not constitute a break in service, for purposes of longevity, seniority under any collective bargaining agreement, or any employee benefit plan. An employee returning from leave shall return with no less seniority than the employee had when the leave commenced, for purposes of layoff, recall, promotion, job assignment, and seniority-related benefits such as vacation.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(b)(6) (leginfo text)
