citations.quote: “Employment in the same or a comparable position” means employment in a position that has the same or similar duties and pay that can be performed at the same or similar geographic location as the position held prior to the leave.

clauses.title: No Interference or Retaliation
clauses.body: {{companyName}} will not interfere with, restrain, or deny {{employeeName}}'s exercise of, or attempt to exercise, any right provided under CFRA. {{companyName}} will not refuse to hire, discharge, fine, suspend, expel, or discriminate against {{employeeName}} because {{employeeName}} exercised the right to CFRA leave, or because {{employeeName}} gave information or testimony about a CFRA leave request in an inquiry or proceeding related to rights guaranteed under this law.
clauses.gap: All citations for this clause are subdivisions of the same statute, Government Code Section 12945.2 — different parts of the same section, not independent sources confirming each other.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(k) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, prohibited discrimination
citations.quote: It shall be an unlawful employment practice for an employer to refuse to hire, or to discharge, fine, suspend, expel, or discriminate against, any individual because of any of the following: (1) An individual’s exercise of the right to family care and medical leave provided by subdivision (a). (2) An individual’s giving information or testimony as to the individual’s own family care and medical leave, or another person’s family care and medical leave, in any inquiry or proceeding related to rights guaranteed under this section.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(q) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, prohibited interference
citations.quote: It shall be an unlawful employment practice for an employer to interfere with, restrain, or deny the exercise of, or the attempt to exercise, any right provided under this section.

clauses.title: How CFRA Relates to FMLA
clauses.body: When {{employeeName}}'s leave qualifies under both CFRA and the federal FMLA, the two run concurrently: the 12-month period under CFRA runs together with the 12-month period under the FMLA, starting on the date FMLA leave begins, and the combined leave taken under CFRA and FMLA together is capped at 12 workweeks in that 12-month period. Leave taken under the FMLA for a disability on account of pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions does not count against that combined 12-week cap.
clauses.gap: That pregnancy exclusion lines up with the qualifying-reasons clause above: CFRA's own definition of family care and medical leave excludes pregnancy disability, so FMLA leave taken for that reason runs on its own track rather than sharing CFRA's 12 weeks. The statute cross-references a separate law, Government Code Section 12945 (California's pregnancy disability leave law), under which additional leave beyond the 12 weeks described here may be available on top of CFRA and FMLA leave — this document doesn't cover that separate law. All citations for this clause are subdivisions of the same statute, Government Code Section 12945.2 — different parts of the same section, not independent sources confirming each other.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(o) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, concurrent 12-month period
citations.quote: The 12-month period during which 12 workweeks of leave may be taken under this section shall run concurrently with the 12-month period under the FMLA, and shall commence the date leave taken under the FMLA commences.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(p) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, concurrent leave and pregnancy-disability carve-out
citations.quote: Leave taken by an employee pursuant to this section shall run concurrently with leave taken pursuant to the FMLA, except for any leave taken under the FMLA for disability on account of pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions. The aggregate amount of leave taken under this section or the FMLA, or both, except for leave taken for disability on account of pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions, shall not exceed 12 workweeks in a 12-month period. An employee is entitled to take, in addition to the leave provided for under this section and the FMLA, the leave provided for in Section 12945, if the employee is otherwise qualified for that leave.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet, prepared by {{preparerName}}, summarizes California Labor Code sections 1050 through 1054 — the statutory scheme, sometimes called the "blacklisting" statute, that makes it a crime for a former employer to prevent or attempt to prevent a former employee from obtaining new employment by misrepresentation, and that gives the affected employee a separate civil remedy. Where a specific employer and former employee are named below, those names are {{companyName}} and {{employeeName}}; this sheet can also be used and read on its own, without any specific employer or employee named, as a general reference to what this statute says. This sheet states the law; it does not evaluate whether any particular communication, policy, or practice complies with it, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice.

clauses.title: Core Prohibition — Preventing Re-Employment by Misrepresentation
clauses.body: California Labor Code section 1050 makes it a crime for any person, or an agent or officer of that person, to prevent or attempt to prevent a former employee from obtaining employment elsewhere by misrepresentation, once that employee has been discharged or has voluntarily left the job. The prohibited conduct is the misrepresentation itself, made with the purpose or effect of blocking the former employee's re-employment — the statute does not require that the attempt actually succeed; an unsuccessful attempt to prevent re-employment by misrepresentation is covered on the same terms as a successful one.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a prohibition of this kind exists in at least one jurisdiction — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular employer-employee relationship. The statute's coverage turns on the word "misrepresentation": it reaches false or misleading communications made to prevent re-employment, not merely negative-but-truthful ones, a line the companion safe-harbor provision (Labor Code section 1053, covered separately in this sheet) draws directly. Whether any given communication is a "misrepresentation" within the meaning of this statute is a fact-specific question this document does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1050); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1050 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Any person, or agent or officer thereof, who, after having discharged an employee from the service of such person or after an employee has voluntarily left such service, by any misrepresentation prevents or attempts to prevent the former employee from obtaining employment, is guilty of a misdemeanor.

clauses.title: Related Prohibition — Conditioning Employment on Photographs or Fingerprints Shared With Other Employers
clauses.body: In the same chapter as the core prohibition, Labor Code section 1051 separately makes it a crime to require, as a condition of getting or keeping a job, that an employee or applicant be photographed or fingerprinted by someone who wants that photograph, fingerprint, or related information in order to furnish it to another employer or third person — where the photograph or fingerprint could be used to the employee's or applicant's detriment. Unlike section 1050, this provision does not turn on whether a misrepresentation was made; it prohibits the underlying practice of conditioning employment on this kind of information-sharing arrangement, subject to an exception stated in a separate section of the same chapter (Labor Code section 1057) that this sheet does not independently address.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that this kind of related anti-blacklisting mechanism exists in at least one jurisdiction. The statute's own text carves out "[e]xcept as provided in Section 1057" — this sheet has not independently verified the content of section 1057 and does not describe what that exception covers; a reader relying on this section should look at section 1057 separately rather than assume no exception applies. Whether any particular photograph or fingerprint arrangement falls within this prohibition, or within the unverified section 1057 exception, is a fact-specific question this document does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1051); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1051 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Except as provided in Section 1057, any person or agent or officer thereof, who requires, as a condition precedent to securing or retaining employment, that an employee or applicant for employment be photographed or fingerprinted by any person who desires his or her photograph or fingerprints for the purpose of furnishing the same or information concerning the same or concerning the employee or applicant for employment to any other employer or third person, and these photographs and fingerprints could be used to the detriment of the employee or applicant for employment is guilty of a misdemeanor.

clauses.title: Liability for Knowingly Permitting a Violation
clauses.body: Labor Code section 1052 extends criminal exposure beyond the person who directly commits a violation. It is also a misdemeanor for a person to knowingly cause, suffer, or permit an agent, superintendent, manager, or employee working for that person to commit a violation of sections 1050 or 1051, or to fail to take all reasonable steps within that person's power to prevent such a violation.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of this kind of extended liability, not a claim about which state's law governs a particular workplace. By its own terms, section 1052 reaches violations of sections 1050 and 1051 only — it does not extend to section 1053, which (as the companion clause in this sheet explains) is a safe-harbor provision rather than a prohibition, so there is no "violation" of section 1053 for section 1052 to reach. What counts as "reasonable steps" to prevent a violation is a fact-specific question this document does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1052); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1052 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Any person who knowingly causes, suffers, or permits an agent, superintendent, manager, or employee in his employ to commit a violation of sections 1050 and 1051, or who fails to take all reasonable steps within his power to prevent such violation is guilty of a misdemeanor.

clauses.title: Truthful Statement Safe Harbor and Its Evidentiary Trap
clauses.body: Labor Code section 1053 affirmatively permits an employer, or an agent, employee, superintendent, or manager of the employer, to furnish a truthful statement about why an employee was discharged or why an employee voluntarily left, when that statement is given upon a special request for it. The same section then creates a specific evidentiary trap: if the statement conveys information through a mark, sign, or other means different from what its words say, that fact — or the fact that information of that kind was given without having been specially requested — is prima facie evidence of a violation of sections 1050 through 1053.
clauses.gap: This clause corrects a common mislabeling: section 1053 is not itself the criminal-penalty provision for blacklisting — the misdemeanor penalty is written into section 1050. Section 1053 instead operates as a safe harbor for a specific kind of truthful, specially-requested communication, while simultaneously creating an evidentiary presumption against coded or unsolicited signals. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a safe harbor and evidentiary rule of this kind exists — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reference request. Whether a specific communication was "specially requested," or used a "mark, sign, or other means" conveying information different from its words, are fact-specific questions this document does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1053); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1053 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Nothing in this chapter shall prevent an employer or an agent, employee, superintendent or manager thereof from furnishing, upon special request therefor, a truthful statement concerning the reason for the discharge of an employee or why an employee voluntarily left the service of the employer. If such statement furnishes any mark, sign, or other means conveying information different from that expressed by words therein, such fact, or the fact that such statement or other means of furnishing information was given without a special request therefor is prima facie evidence of a violation of sections 1050 to 1053.

clauses.title: Separate Civil Remedy — Treble Damages
clauses.body: Beyond misdemeanor criminal exposure, Labor Code section 1054 gives the person prevented from obtaining employment a separate civil remedy: any person, or agent or officer of that person, who violates sections 1050 through 1052 is liable to the aggrieved party, in a civil action, for treble damages — three times the actual damages sustained. That civil action may be brought by the aggrieved person or that person's assigns or successors in interest, and it may be brought without first establishing any criminal liability under this chapter.
clauses.gap: Source-independence disclosure: this civil remedy is codified in a section of the Labor Code (§ 1054) that sits immediately after, but is textually distinct from, the misdemeanor prohibition (§ 1050) and the safe harbor (§ 1053) covered elsewhere in this sheet — it is drawn from a different statutory section, not a subdivision of one already cited. Separately, by its own text the treble-damages remedy applies to violations of sections 1050 through 1052 only — it does not reach section 1053, which (as the companion clause in this sheet explains) is a safe-harbor provision rather than a prohibition, so there is no "violation" of section 1053 to trigger this remedy. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a private treble-damages remedy of this kind exists in at least one jurisdiction — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular dispute, and not a calculation of what damages, if any, would be available in a specific case. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1054); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1054 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: In addition to and apart from the criminal penalty provided any person or agent or officer thereof, who violates any provision of sections 1050 to 1052, inclusive, is liable to the party aggrieved, in a civil action, for treble damages. Such civil action may be brought by such aggrieved person or his assigns, or successors in interest, without first establishing any criminal liability under this article.

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Information Sheet describes California's "Shine the Light" law, Civil Code § 1798.83, prepared with reference to {{businessName}}, which may direct questions about this sheet to {{contactMethod}}. Section 1798.83 gives a California customer the right to request information about what personal information a business has disclosed to third parties for the third parties' own direct marketing purposes, and requires a covered business to either respond to such requests or adopt a specified alternative opt-out (or opt-in) policy instead. This is a distinct, older statute from the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA/CPRA) and from the California Online Privacy Protection Act (CalOPPA), addressed in other documents; § 1798.83 became operative January 1, 2005 and was last amended effective January 1, 2006, well before the CCPA (2018/2020) or CalOPPA's current form, and it targets a narrower question — third-party direct-marketing disclosure specifically — rather than a business's general data-collection or data-sale practices. Complying with the CCPA or CalOPPA does not by itself satisfy, and is not required in order to trigger, this separate duty, which has its own conditions, its own required response, and its own alternative compliance path. This sheet is an informational record only. It does not itself determine that {{businessName}} is a business covered by Civil Code § 1798.83, does not determine that any specific disclosure by {{businessName}} was made to a third party for the third party's direct marketing purposes, does not determine which of the statute's two compliance paths applies to {{businessName}} or satisfies either path, and does not respond to, or draft a response to, any actual customer request.

clauses.title: Which Businesses Are Covered, and the Small-Business Exemption
clauses.body: The statute's duty to respond to a customer's request is not owed by every business that handles personal information — it is conditioned on a specific combination of facts about an established customer relationship and a prior disclosure. Under Civil Code § 1798.83(a), the duty attaches "if a business has an established business relationship with a customer and has within the immediately preceding calendar year disclosed personal information that corresponds to any of the categories of personal information set forth in paragraph (6) of subdivision (e) to third parties, and if the business knows or reasonably should know that the third parties used the personal information for the third parties' direct marketing purposes." All three elements — an established business relationship, an actual disclosure of a statutorily listed category of personal information within the preceding calendar year, and the business's actual or constructive knowledge that the recipient used it for the recipient's own direct marketing purposes — are conditions of the trigger language itself, not independent alternative triggers. Separately, the statute carves out businesses below a fixed size, regardless of whether the trigger conditions above are otherwise met: under § 1798.83(c)(1), "A business with fewer than 20 full-time or part-time employees is exempt from the requirements of this section."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute — California's — used as real evidence of which businesses Civil Code § 1798.83 places under this specific disclosure duty and of the statute's own size-based exemption, not a claim about which state's law would govern any particular business or dataset, and not a claim that every business that collects or shares personal information is necessarily subject to this specific statute. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, § 1798.83(a) and § 1798.83(c)(1), treated here as one statutory source describing one integrated scope-and-exemption scheme, not as independent corroborating sources for one another. Both quotations were fetched directly from the official California Legislative Information website (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) on 2026-09-02, re-fetched a second time using a distinct User-Agent header, and confirmed byte-identical both times (after normalizing only incidental whitespace introduced by the source page's own line-wrapping); the fetched page's own amendment note reads "(Amended by Stats. 2005, Ch. 22, Sec. 16. Effective January 1, 2006.)," meaning this is the version of the statute currently in force as of the date this clause was checked, and that it has not been amended since 2006. This clause does not address § 1798.83(d)'s separate list of disclosures that are not deemed disclosures for a third party's direct marketing purposes at all (for example, disclosures to a data processor that does not itself use or redisclose the information for direct marketing, or disclosures made to jointly offer a product under specified conditions), § 1798.83(f)'s narrower rule for disclosures between affiliated companies sharing the same brand name, or § 1798.83(h)'s exemption for a financial institution that complies with the California Financial Information Privacy Act — none of which were the focus of this clause's research, and any of which could mean a business that appears to meet the general trigger in subdivision (a) is nonetheless not required to respond to a given disclosure under one of these separate carve-outs. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that the business identified in this document has an established business relationship with any customer, that it disclosed any listed category of personal information to a third party within the preceding calendar year, that it knew or reasonably should have known of the third party's direct marketing use, or that it has fewer than 20 full-time or part-time employees.

clauses.title: How a Customer Makes a Request, and the Business's Duty to Designate a Channel
clauses.body: The statute specifies both how a customer may submit a request and a business's own corresponding duty to designate where such requests should be sent. As to the customer's request, § 1798.83(a) provides that a covered business's duty runs "after the receipt of a written or electronic mail request, or, if the business chooses to receive requests by toll-free telephone or facsimile numbers, a telephone or facsimile request from the customer" — meaning a customer may always request by mail or email, and may additionally request by toll-free phone or fax only if the business has elected to accept requests through those channels. As to the business's own duty, § 1798.83(b)(1) requires that "A business required to comply with this section shall designate a mailing address, electronic mail address, or, if the business chooses to receive requests by telephone or facsimile, a toll-free telephone or facsimile number, to which customers may deliver requests pursuant to subdivision (a)." The same paragraph goes on to require the business to take at least one of several further steps to make that designated channel known — including notifying customer-facing employees of it, or adding a "Your Privacy Rights" link to the business's website — which this clause does not quote in full.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own rules for how a Shine the Light request may be made and what a covered business must do to designate a channel for it — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific request, and not a claim about any other jurisdiction's similar disclosure statute. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, § 1798.83(a) and § 1798.83(b)(1), treated as one integrated procedural scheme, not as independent corroborating sources for one another. Both quotations were fetched directly from the official California Legislative Information website on 2026-09-02, re-fetched a second time with a distinct User-Agent header, and confirmed byte-identical both times. This clause does not quote or independently detail the three further alternative steps listed in § 1798.83(b)(1)(A)-(C) that a business must take to publicize its designated channel (notifying customer-contact employees, posting a "Your Privacy Rights" website link meeting specific formatting requirements, or making the designated channel available on request at every California place of business), nor does it address § 1798.83(b)(2)'s separate safe harbor allowing a business already subject to the federal Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act's financial-privacy disclosure (15 U.S.C. § 6803) to comply with this section by providing that federal disclosure instead, if it also satisfies this section — a reader concerned with the specific mechanics of publicizing a designated channel, or with the GLBA safe harbor, would need those provisions separately researched. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine what channel, if any, the business identified in this document has designated for Shine the Light requests, does not determine whether that business has elected to accept telephone or facsimile requests, and does not itself designate, publicize, or operate any request channel.

clauses.title: What the Response Must Contain, and the Required Response Time
clauses.body: The statute fixes both the substance of a required response and the time within which it must be given, and separately limits how often a business must respond and how detailed the response must be. As to substance, § 1798.83(a) requires the business to provide, free of charge, two categories of information: under paragraph (1), "In writing or by electronic mail, a list of the categories set forth in paragraph (6) of subdivision (e) that correspond to the personal information disclosed by the business to third parties for the third parties' direct marketing purposes during the immediately preceding calendar year," and under paragraph (2), "In writing or by electronic mail, the names and addresses of all of the third parties that received personal information from the business for the third parties' direct marketing purposes during the preceding calendar year and, if the nature of the third parties' business cannot reasonably be determined from the third parties' name, examples of the products or services marketed, if known to the business, sufficient to give the customer a reasonable indication of the nature of the third parties' business." As to timing, § 1798.83(b)(1) sets two different deadlines depending on where the request was received: "The response to a request pursuant to this section received at one of the designated addresses or numbers shall be provided within 30 days. Requests received by the business at other than one of the designated addresses or numbers shall be provided within a reasonable period, in light of the circumstances related to how the request was received, but not to exceed 150 days from the date received." Two further limits apply regardless of content or timing: under § 1798.83(c)(1), "A business that is required to comply with this section is not obligated to do so in response to a request from a customer more than once during the course of any calendar year," and under § 1798.83(b)(3), "A business that is required to comply with this section is not obligated to provide information associated with specific individuals and may provide the information required by this section in standardized format."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what California law requires a Shine the Light response to contain, when it must be given, and its built-in frequency and format limits — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific response, and not a claim about the required content or timing of a disclosure response under any other jurisdiction's similar statute. This clause cites four separate provisions of the same statutory section — § 1798.83(a)(1), (a)(2), (b)(1), and both (c)(1) and (b)(3) — treated here as one statutory source describing one integrated content-timing-and-limits scheme, not as independent corroborating sources for one another. All quotations were fetched directly from the official California Legislative Information website on 2026-09-02, re-fetched a second time with a distinct User-Agent header, and confirmed byte-identical both times. This clause does not independently detail the full alphabetical list of statutorily defined "categories of personal information" referenced in § 1798.83(a)(1) and set out at § 1798.83(e)(6); a reader needing the complete list of categories that could appear in a required response would need that subdivision separately reviewed. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine what personal information, if any, the business identified in this document has actually disclosed to any third party, does not draft or send any response to any customer, and does not determine when any specific response deadline began to run or would expire.

clauses.title: The Alternative: A Stated "Do Not Share" Opt-Out (or Opt-In) Policy
clauses.body: The statute does not require every covered business to respond to individual customer requests at all — it offers a second, alternative compliance path built around a public policy statement rather than a per-request response. Under Civil Code § 1798.83(c)(2), "If a business that is required to comply with this section adopts and discloses to the public, in its privacy policy, a policy of not disclosing personal information of customers to third parties for the third parties' direct marketing purposes unless the customer first affirmatively agrees to that disclosure, or of not disclosing the personal information of customers to third parties for the third parties' direct marketing purposes if the customer has exercised an option that prevents that information from being disclosed to third parties for those purposes, as long as the business maintains and discloses the policies, the business may comply with subdivision (a) by notifying the customer of his or her right to prevent disclosure of personal information, and providing the customer with a cost-free means to exercise that right." This describes two alternative policy forms the statute treats as sufficient — an opt-in policy (no third-party direct-marketing disclosure absent the customer's affirmative agreement) or an opt-out policy (no such disclosure once the customer has exercised an option to prevent it) — either of which, if adopted, disclosed in the business's privacy policy, and actually maintained, lets the business satisfy subdivision (a) by pointing the customer to that right and a cost-free way to exercise it, rather than by compiling and sending the category-and-recipient-list response described elsewhere in this statute.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own alternative compliance mechanism for the Shine the Light disclosure duty — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific business's privacy policy, and not a claim about any similarly named "opt out of sharing" mechanism under a different California statute (including the CCPA's separate right to opt out of the sale or sharing of personal information, which arises under different statutory text, different definitions of "sale" and "sharing," and is not researched or relied on in this clause). This clause quotes a single statutory paragraph, § 1798.83(c)(2), in full, as one integrated provision. clauses.title: Statutory Definitions: "Customer" and "Direct Marketing Purposes"
clauses.body: Two of the statute's own defined terms materially narrow who can make a request and what kind of third-party use the statute is even concerned with. Under Civil Code § 1798.83(e)(1), "'Customer' means an individual who is a resident of California who provides personal information to a business during the creation of, or throughout the duration of, an established business relationship if the business relationship is primarily for personal, family, or household purposes" — meaning the statute's request right belongs to California residents in a personal-, family-, or household-purpose relationship with the business, not to every person about whom the business holds data, and not to a business-to-business counterparty. Under § 1798.83(e)(2), "'Direct marketing purposes' means the use of personal information to solicit or induce a purchase, rental, lease, or exchange of products, goods, property, or services directly to individuals by means of the mail, telephone, or electronic mail for their personal, family, or household purposes" — a definition centered on solicitation of individual consumers by mail, telephone, or email, rather than every commercial use a third party might make of shared data.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California law itself defines "customer" and "direct marketing purposes" for this specific statute — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific relationship or use, and not a claim that these definitions match the definitions of similar-sounding terms in any other California statute (including the CCPA, which defines "consumer" and addresses "sharing" for advertising purposes using different statutory language and for different purposes) or any other jurisdiction's law. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, § 1798.83(e)(1) and § 1798.83(e)(2), treated as one integrated set of definitions, not as independent corroborating sources for one another; the § 1798.83(e)(2) quotation above is the first sentence of that paragraph only — the same paragraph goes on to state that "direct marketing purposes" also includes selling, renting, exchanging, or leasing personal information for consideration to businesses, and separately excludes certain uses (including bona fide tax-exempt charitable or religious solicitation and political fundraising or communication), none of which is quoted or further researched in this clause. Both quotations were fetched directly from the official California Legislative Information website on 2026-09-02, re-fetched a second time with a distinct User-Agent header, and confirmed byte-identical both times. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific individual is a "customer" of the business identified in this document within this statutory definition, and does not determine that any specific use by any third party of information received from that business is a "direct marketing purpose" within this statutory definition.

clauses.title: Remedies Available for a Violation of Section 1798.83
clauses.body: The Customer Records title of the Civil Code — the same title that contains § 1798.83 — sets out several remedies in Civil Code § 1798.84, and several of them are drafted specifically around a § 1798.83 violation rather than only generally. A customer has a general civil action: under § 1798.84(b), "Any customer injured by a violation of this title may institute a civil action to recover damages." On top of that general action, § 1798.84(c) fixes a civil penalty specifically for a § 1798.83 violation: "for a willful, intentional, or reckless violation of Section 1798.83, a customer may recover a civil penalty not to exceed three thousand dollars ($3,000) per violation; otherwise, the customer may recover a civil penalty of up to five hundred dollars ($500) per violation for a violation of Section 1798.83." A prevailing customer-plaintiff can also recover fees: under § 1798.84(g), "A prevailing plaintiff in any action commenced under Section 1798.83 shall also be entitled to recover his or her reasonable attorney's fees and costs." The statute separately gives a business, short of a willful, intentional, or reckless violation, a specific cure opportunity: under § 1798.84(d), a business alleged to have failed to provide required § 1798.83 information, provided inaccurate information, or missed the statutory response deadline "may assert as a complete defense in any action in law or equity that it thereafter provided" the complete or accurate or timely information "to all customers who were provided incomplete or inaccurate information, respectively, within 90 days of the date the business knew" of the failure. Finally, injunctive relief is available under § 1798.84(e): "Any business that violates, proposes to violate, or has violated this title may be enjoined."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the remedies California law attaches to a violation of § 1798.83 specifically — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific dispute, and not a claim about remedies under any other jurisdiction's similar disclosure statute. This clause cites four subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code § 1798.84 — subsections (b), (c), (d), and (g), plus (e) — treated here as one statutory source describing one integrated remedies scheme, not as independent corroborating sources for one another; subsection (b)'s general civil action applies to a violation of the whole Customer Records title (of which § 1798.83 is one part), while subsections (c), (d), and (g) are each drafted, by their own text, specifically around "Section 1798.83" or "this section" (referring to § 1798.83) rather than the title generally. All quotations were fetched directly from the official California Legislative Information website on 2026-09-02, re-fetched a second time with a distinct User-Agent header, and confirmed byte-identical both times; the fetched page's own amendment note reads "(Amended by Stats. 2009, Ch. 134, Sec. 3. (AB 1094) Effective January 1, 2010.)" This clause independently verifies § 1798.84 for this document rather than relying on any prior verification of the same section performed for a different document in this collection. This clause does not address § 1798.84(a)'s separate anti-waiver provision (voiding any waiver of a Title 1.81 protection) or § 1798.84(f)'s safe harbor for record disposal, neither of which bears on a § 1798.83 request or response and neither of which was the focus of this clause's research. No case law interpreting § 1798.83 or § 1798.84 was located or relied on for this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any violation of § 1798.83 has occurred with respect to the business identified in this document, does not determine whether any such violation, if one occurred, was willful, intentional, or reckless, and does not determine what remedy, defense, or liability, if any, applies to any specific request or response.

clauses.title: Compliance-Method Declaration and Signature
Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's Fair Chance Act (Government Code § 12952) — the state law restricting when and how {{companyName}} may inquire about or consider the conviction history of an applicant for the position of {{jobTitle}}, including {{employeeName}}, before and after making a conditional offer of employment. It states facts about what the statute itself requires and who it covers. This corpus separately includes a Background Check Adverse Action Notice — Information Sheet, which covers in more depth what happens once an employer has already made a conditional offer and is considering denying employment based on conviction history — the individualized assessment, the preliminary notice, the response window, and the final notice. This document focuses instead on the restriction that applies before that point: what an employer may and may not ask about, or consider, before a conditional offer is made, and which employers and positions the statute does or does not cover. It is not itself a job application, a conditional offer, an individualized assessment, or any notice, and it does not tell {{companyName}} or {{employeeName}} what to do about any particular application, inquiry, or background-check result.

clauses.title: The Core Prohibition: No Inquiry Before a Conditional Offer
clauses.body: For a covered employer, California's Fair Chance Act makes it an unlawful employment practice to include any question seeking disclosure of an applicant's conviction history on a job application before a conditional offer of employment has been made, or to inquire into or consider an applicant's conviction history — including through any question on an employment application — at any point before a conditional offer of employment has been made. The statute states this obligation as applying to "an employer with five or more employees," subject to the exemptions described below.
clauses.gap: The statute doesn't itself define "conditional offer of employment." It also doesn't specify a required form for the offer (written, oral, or otherwise) or address what happens if an employer learns of conviction history involuntarily (for example, through a source other than its own inquiry) before making a conditional offer — this document does not address that scenario, which the statute's text doesn't speak to directly.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12952(a)(1)-(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, Fair Chance Act, pre-conditional-offer inquiry prohibition
citations.quote: (a) Except as provided in subdivision (d), it is an unlawful employment practice for an employer with five or more employees to do any of the following: (1) To include on any application for employment, before the employer makes a conditional offer of employment to the applicant, any question that seeks the disclosure of an applicant’s conviction history. (2) To inquire into or consider the conviction history of the applicant, including any inquiry about conviction history on any employment application, until after the employer has made a conditional offer of employment to the applicant.

clauses.title: What a Conviction History Background Check May Not Consider
clauses.body: Separately from the timing restriction above, when a covered employer conducts a conviction history background check in connection with a job application, California law prohibits considering, distributing, or disseminating information about an arrest that was not followed by a conviction (with narrow statutory exceptions), a referral to or participation in a pretrial or posttrial diversion program, or a conviction that has been sealed, dismissed, expunged, or statutorily eradicated, or for which the person received a full pardon or a certificate of rehabilitation.
clauses.gap: The narrow exception referenced for non-conviction arrests cross-references Labor Code § 432.7, subdivisions (a)(1) and (f) — this document did not independently fetch and verify the text of Labor Code § 432.7 itself, so it states only that Government Code § 12952 makes this cross-reference, not what Section 432.7's exception itself covers in detail.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12952(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, Fair Chance Act, prohibited background-check content
citations.quote: (3) To consider, distribute, or disseminate information about any of the following while conducting a conviction history background check in connection with any application for employment: (A) Arrest not followed by conviction, except in the circumstances as permitted in paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) and subdivision (f) of Section 432.7 of the Labor Code. (B) Referral to or participation in a pretrial or posttrial diversion program. (C) Convictions that have been sealed, dismissed, expunged, or statutorily eradicated pursuant to law, or any conviction for which the convicted person has received a full pardon or has been issued a certificate of rehabilitation.

clauses.title: A Background Check Itself Is Not Prohibited
clauses.body: The Fair Chance Act does not itself prohibit a covered employer from conducting a conviction history background check on an applicant. What the statute restricts is the timing of any inquiry into conviction history (not before a conditional offer) and, separately, what the background check may consider, distribute, or disseminate, as described above.
clauses.gap: This clause states only what Government Code § 12952 itself says about background checks generally; it does not address the separate federal Fair Credit Reporting Act disclosure-and-authorization requirements that also apply to a background check performed through a third-party consumer reporting agency, which this corpus's Background Check Disclosure & Authorization document covers.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12952(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, Fair Chance Act, background checks not otherwise prohibited
citations.quote: (b) This section shall not be construed to prevent an employer from conducting a conviction history background check not in conflict with the provisions of subdivision (a).

clauses.title: Which Employers and Positions Are Covered or Exempted
clauses.body: California's Fair Chance Act, by its own terms, applies to "an employer with five or more employees." The statute lists four circumstances in which the section does not apply at all: a position for which a state or local agency is otherwise required by law to conduct a conviction history background check; a position with a criminal justice agency, as that term is defined in Penal Code § 13101; a position as a Farm Labor Contractor, as described in Labor Code § 1685; and a position where the employer or its agent is required by state, federal, or local law to conduct criminal background checks for employment purposes or to restrict employment based on criminal history — a category the statute says includes rules or regulations issued by a self-regulatory organization under the federal Securities Exchange Act of 1934.
clauses.gap: This clause catalogs the exemptions that the corpus's existing Background Check Adverse Action Notice — Information Sheet document flagged but did not itself list (that document's gap field noted the five-or-more-employee threshold is "subject to statutory exceptions... that this document doesn't catalog"). The statute doesn't define "employee" for purposes of counting toward the five-employee threshold (for example, whether part-time, out-of-state, or temporary staffing employees count), and this document doesn't resolve that question.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12952(d)(1)-(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, Fair Chance Act, statutory exemptions
citations.quote: (d) This section does not apply in any of the following circumstances: (1) To a position for which a state or local agency is otherwise required by law to conduct a conviction history background check. (2) To a position with a criminal justice agency, as defined in Section 13101 of the Penal Code. (3) To a position as a Farm Labor Contractor, as described in Section 1685 of the Labor Code. (4) To a position where an employer or agent thereof is required by any state, federal, or local law to conduct criminal background checks for employment purposes or to restrict employment based on criminal history.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12952(d)(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, Fair Chance Act, self-regulatory-organization clause within the fourth exemption
citations.quote: For purposes of this paragraph, federal law shall include rules or regulations promulgated by a self-regulatory organization as defined in Section 3(a)(26) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended by 124 Stat. 1652 (Public Law 111-203), pursuant to the authority in Section 19(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended by 124 Stat. 1652 (Public Law 111-203).

clauses.title: How the Statute Defines "Conviction" and "Conviction History"
clauses.body: For purposes of the Fair Chance Act, "conviction" carries the same meaning given to it in Labor Code § 432.7(a)(1) and (a)(3). The broader term "conviction history" is defined to also include an arrest not resulting in conviction, but only in the specific, limited circumstance described in Labor Code § 432.7(f), where an employer at a health facility (as defined in Health and Safety Code § 1250) may ask an applicant for certain positions about specified types of arrests, and an arrest for which a person is out on bail or on their own recognizance pending trial.
clauses.gap: This document verified only the definitional text of Government Code § 12952(f) itself, which cross-references Labor Code § 432.7 for both the core definition of "conviction" and the health-facility arrest exception; it did not independently fetch and verify the text of Labor Code § 432.7, so it does not state what that section's own definitions or the health-facility exception specifically cover beyond what § 12952(f) itself says about them.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12952(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, Fair Chance Act, definitions of "conviction" and "conviction history"
citations.quote: (f) For purposes of this section: (1) “Conviction” has the same meaning as defined in paragraphs (1) and (3) of subdivision (a) of Section 432.7 of the Labor Code. (2) Notwithstanding paragraph (1), the term “conviction history” includes: (A) An arrest not resulting in conviction only in the specific, limited circumstances described in subdivision (f) of Section 432.7 of the Labor Code, when an employer at a health facility, as defined in Section 1250 of the Health and Safety Code, may ask an applicant for certain positions about specified types of arrests. (B) An arrest for which an individual is out on bail or his or her own recognizance pending trial.

clauses.title: After a Conditional Offer: The Individualized-Assessment Process Applies
clauses.body: The pre-offer inquiry restriction described above is not the end of the Fair Chance Act's protection. The same statute goes on to require, once a covered employer has made a conditional offer and is considering denying employment based on conviction history, an individualized assessment, a written preliminary notice with a right to respond, and — if a final decision to deny is made — a written final notice. The statute also requires the employer to consider any information the applicant submits in response to the preliminary notice before making that final decision.
clauses.gap: This corpus's Background Check Adverse Action Notice — Information Sheet document independently verifies and quotes the individualized-assessment factors, the required content of the preliminary and final notices, and the business-day response window (Gov. Code § 12952(c)(1)-(3) and (c)(5)); this clause does not restate those quotes. It instead verifies and quotes only paragraph (c)(4) — the requirement that the employer consider the applicant's submitted response before finalizing a decision — which that other document does not separately quote, so that this document's own overview of the full pre-offer-to-final-decision timeline rests on independently verified text rather than an unverified summary of the other document's content.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12952(c)(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, Fair Chance Act, employer must consider applicant's response before a final decision
citations.quote: (4) The employer shall consider information submitted by the applicant pursuant to paragraph (3) before making a final decision.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California statutory law on natural hazard disclosure, Civil Code section 1103 et seq., as it may relate to the transfer of the real property at {{propertyAddress}}, where {{sellerName}} is named as seller and {{buyerName}} is named as buyer. It states what California law provides about which transfers are covered, which statutorily defined hazard zones must be addressed, the required disclosure form, the good-faith and third-party-report safe harbor, and the statute's stated exemptions. It is separate from, and in addition to, any Transfer Disclosure Statement, real estate agency disclosure, or lead-based paint disclosure provided in connection with this transaction, each of which concerns different subject matter. This information sheet is not itself the statutory Natural Hazard Disclosure Statement that Civil Code section 1103.2 requires, and it does not tell {{sellerName}}, {{buyerName}}, or any real estate agent involved whether this transaction is covered, which box to check, or how to proceed.

clauses.title: Which Transfers This Disclosure Law Covers
clauses.body: California's natural hazard disclosure article (Civil Code sections 1103 through 1103.15) applies, except as exempted, to a sale, exchange, real property sales contract (as defined in Civil Code section 2985), lease with an option to purchase, any other option to purchase, or ground lease coupled with improvements, of single-family residential real property. Even within that class of transfer, the article's disclosure duty is not free-standing: by its own terms, the article applies to a covered transaction only if the seller or the seller's agent is already required — by one of six separately enumerated statutory triggers, one for each hazard-zone category — to disclose the property's location within that hazard zone. Each of those six triggers is satisfied either by the seller's or agent's actual knowledge that the property is within the zone, or by a public list or map having been provided to, and posted at, the offices of the county recorder, county assessor, and county planning agency.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction defines the transfers subject to its natural-hazard disclosure law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transfer; disclosure coverage and the underlying hazard-zone maps are jurisdiction- and geography-specific. The two citations below, to subdivisions (b) and (c) of Civil Code section 1103, are subsections of the same statutory section and are treated here as one source, not as independently corroborating sources.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1103(b)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, scope of the natural hazard disclosure article
citations.quote: Except as provided in Section 1103.1, this article applies to a sale, exchange, real property sales contract, as defined in Section 2985, lease with an option to purchase, any other option to purchase, or ground lease coupled with improvements, of any single-family residential real property.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1103(c)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, disclosure duty applies only when triggered by an enumerated hazard-zone provision
citations.quote: This article shall apply to the transactions described in subdivision (b) only if the seller or his or her agent is required by one or more of the following to disclose the property’s location within a hazard zone:

clauses.title: Sales Exempt From the Disclosure Requirement
clauses.body: The natural hazard disclosure article states that it does not apply to a list of specifically enumerated sales, including: sales or transfers pursuant to court order (such as a probate-administration sale, a sale on a writ of execution, a foreclosure sale, a bankruptcy-trustee sale, an eminent domain taking, or a sale on a decree for specific performance); certain sales or transfers to a mortgagee, beneficiary, or foreclosure purchaser following a default; sales or transfers by a fiduciary administering a trust, guardianship, conservatorship, or decedent's estate (though this particular exemption does not apply where the trustee is a natural person serving as trustee of a revocable trust and the seller was a former owner of the property, or an occupant of it within the preceding year); transfers between co-owners; transfers to a spouse or to a person within the line of consanguinity of a seller; transfers between spouses arising from a dissolution or legal-separation judgment or an incidental property settlement; certain sales by the Controller administering unclaimed-property law and certain tax-sale transfers; sales, transfers, or exchanges to or from a governmental entity; and the creation or transfer of a lease of any duration, except a lease with an option to purchase or a ground lease coupled with improvements. The statute separately notes that a sale falling outside this article may still be subject to other, distinct disclosure statutes, and that in such sales an agent may make those other required disclosures in a separate writing.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction defines its exemptions from natural-hazard disclosure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transfer. All five citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code section 1103.1, and are treated here as one source, not as independently corroborating sources.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, exemptions from the natural hazard disclosure article
citations.quote: (a) This article does not apply to the following sales:

citations.cite: California Civil Code, court-ordered and similar sales exemption
citations.quote: (1) Sales or transfers pursuant to court order, including, but not limited to, sales ordered by a probate court in administration of an estate, sales pursuant to a writ of execution, sales by any foreclosure sale, sales by a trustee in bankruptcy, sales by eminent domain, and sales resulting from a decree for specific performance.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1103.1(a)(3)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, fiduciary-administration sales exemption and its carve-out
citations.quote: (3) Sales or transfers by a fiduciary in the course of the administration of a trust, guardianship, conservatorship, or decedent’s estate. This exemption shall not apply to a sale if the trustee is a natural person who is a trustee of a revocable trust and the seller is a former owner of the property or an occupant in possession of the property within the preceding year.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1103.1(a)(5)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, transfers to a spouse or within the line of consanguinity
citations.quote: (5) Sales or transfers made to a spouse, or to a person or persons in the line of consanguinity of one or more of the sellers.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1103.1(a)(10)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, lease-of-any-duration exemption and its own exception
citations.quote: (10) The sale, creation, or transfer of any lease of any duration except a lease with an option to purchase or a ground lease coupled with improvements.

clauses.title: The Six Statutory Hazard Zone Categories
clauses.body: The statutory Natural Hazard Disclosure Statement itself states that the property may lie within six specifically defined hazardous areas, each with its own citation and its own Yes/No/Do-Not-Know checkboxes on the form: (1) a special flood hazard area, any type FEMA Zone "A" or "V"; (2) an area of potential flooding shown on a dam-failure inundation map under Government Code section 8589.5; (3) a high or very high fire hazard severity zone (FHSZ) as identified under Government Code section 51178 or the corresponding Public Resources Code provisions, which the form states also subjects the owner to the vegetation-maintenance requirements of Government Code section 51182; (4) a wildland area that may contain substantial forest fire risks and hazards under Public Resources Code section 4125, which the form states also subjects the owner to the maintenance requirements of Public Resources Code section 4291, and separately notes that the state is not responsible for providing fire protection services to a structure within the wildlands unless the Department of Forestry and Fire Protection has entered into a cooperative agreement with a local agency under Public Resources Code section 4142; (5) an earthquake fault zone under Public Resources Code section 2622; and (6) a seismic hazard zone (landslide zone, liquefaction zone, or a zone not yet mapped) under Public Resources Code section 2696. The form's own text warns that these hazards may limit the ability to develop the property, to obtain insurance, or to receive disaster assistance, and that the underlying maps estimate, rather than definitively indicate, where a natural hazard exists.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction defines its natural-hazard disclosure categories — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transfer; hazard-disclosure categories and the underlying hazard-zone maps are jurisdiction- and geography-specific. All six citations below are the six hazard-category paragraphs of the same statutory form text within Civil Code section 1103.2(a), and are treated here as one source, not as independently corroborating sources. The wildland-area category text quoted below (including the sentence on the state's fire-protection responsibility, tied to Public Resources Code section 4142) reflects the section as most recently amended (Stats. 2024, Ch. 80, effective January 1, 2025) and is more current than, and not identical to, any earlier-verified quotation of this same category elsewhere in this corpus.

citations.quote: AN AREA OF POTENTIAL FLOODING shown on a dam failure inundation map pursuant to Section 8589.5 of the Government Code.

citations.quote: A HIGH or VERY HIGH FIRE HAZARD SEVERITY ZONE (FHSZ) as identified by the Director of Forestry and Fire Protection pursuant to Section 51178 of the Government Code or Article 9 (commencing with Section 4201) of Chapter 1 of Part 2 of Division 4 of the Public Resources Code. The owner of this property is subject to the maintenance requirements of Section 51182 of the Government Code.

citations.quote: A WILDLAND AREA THAT MAY CONTAIN SUBSTANTIAL FOREST FIRE RISKS AND HAZARDS pursuant to Section 4125 of the Public Resources Code. The owner of this property is subject to the maintenance requirements of Section 4291 of the Public Resources Code. Additionally, it is not the state’s responsibility to provide fire protection services to any building or structure located within the wildlands unless the Department of Forestry and Fire Protection has entered into a cooperative agreement with a local agency for those purposes pursuant to Section 4142 of the Public Resources Code.

citations.quote: AN EARTHQUAKE FAULT ZONE pursuant to Section 2622 of the Public Resources Code.

citations.quote: A SEISMIC HAZARD ZONE pursuant to Section 2696 of the Public Resources Code.

clauses.title: The Required Disclosure Form and Its Stated Limits
clauses.body: The statute requires that the natural-hazard disclosures it covers be made on a copy of a specifically set-out form, the Natural Hazard Disclosure Statement — or, alternatively, that they be provided within the Local Option Real Estate Transfer Disclosure Statement described in Civil Code section 1102.6a, provided that document includes substantially the same information and substantially the same warnings the natural-hazard form itself requires. The form's own text states that the disclosed information is not a warranty, though it also states that prospective buyers may rely on it in deciding whether and on what terms to purchase. The statute further restricts who may use the completed disclosure: it states that the disclosure is only a disclosure between the seller, the seller's agent, and the prospective buyer, and that it is not to be used by any other party — including, but not limited to, insurance companies, lenders, or governmental agencies — for any purpose.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction structures its required natural-hazard disclosure form — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transfer. All four citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code section 1103.2, and are treated here as one source, not as independently corroborating sources.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, requirement to use the statutory disclosure form
citations.quote: The disclosures required by this article are set forth in, and shall be made on a copy of, the following Natural Hazard Disclosure Statement:

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1103.2(a)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the form is not a warranty
citations.quote: The seller and the seller’s agent(s) or a third-party consultant disclose the following information with the knowledge that even though this is not a warranty, prospective buyers may rely on this information in deciding whether and on what terms to purchase the subject property.

citations.quote: The disclosure required pursuant to this article may be provided by the seller and the seller’s agent in the Local Option Real Estate Transfer Disclosure Statement described in Section 1102.6a, provided that the Local Option Real Estate Transfer Disclosure Statement includes substantially the same information and substantially the same warnings that are required by this section.
